readme:anthropics/skills.text:
> **Note:** This repository contains Anthropic's implementation of skills for Claude. For information about the Agent Skills standard, see [agentskills.io](http://agentskills.io).

[![skills.sh](https://skills.sh/b/anthropics/skills)](https://skills.sh/anthropics/skills)

# Skills
Skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Claude loads dynamically to improve performance on specialized tasks. Skills teach Claude how to complete specific tasks in a repeatable way, whether that's creating documents with your company's brand guidelines, analyzing data using your organization's specific workflows, or automating personal tasks.

For more information, check out:
- [What are skills?](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12512176-what-are-skills)
- [Using skills in Claude](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12512180-using-skills-in-claude)
- [How to create custom skills](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12512198-creating-custom-skills)
- [Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills](https://anthropic.com/engineering/equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agent-skills)

# About This Repository

This repository contains skills that demonstrate what's possible with Claude's skills system. These skills range from creative applications (art, music, design) to technical tasks (testing web apps, MCP server generation) to enterprise workflows (communications, branding, etc.).

Each skill is self-contained in its own folder with a `SKILL.md` file containing the instructions and metadata that Claude uses. Browse through these skills to get inspiration for your own skills or to understand different patterns and approaches.

Many skills in this repo are open source (Apache 2.0). We've also included the document creation & editing skills that power [Claude's document capabilities](https://www.anthropic.com/news/create-files) under the hood in the [`skills/docx`](./skills/docx), [`skills/pdf`](./skills/pdf), [`skills/pptx`](./skills/pptx), and [`skills/xlsx`](./skills/xlsx) subfolders. These are source-available, not open source, but we wanted to share these with developers as a reference for more complex skills that are actively used in a production AI application.

## Disclaimer

**These skills are provided for demonstration and educational purposes only.** While some of these capabilities may be available in Claude, the implementations and behaviors you receive from Claude may differ from what is shown in these skills. These skills are meant to illustrate patterns and possibilities. Always test skills thoroughly in your own environment before relying on them for critical tasks.

# Skill Sets
- [./skills](./skills): Skill examples for Creative & Design, Development & Technical, Enterprise & Communication, and Document Skills
- [./spec](./spec): The Agent Skills specification
- [./template](./template): Skill template

# Try in Claude Code, Claude.ai, and the API

## Claude Code
You can register this repository as a Claude Code Plugin marketplace by running the following command in Claude Code:
```
/plugin marketplace add anthropics/skills
```

Then, to install a specific set of skills:
1. Select `Browse and install plugins`
2. Select `anthropic-agent-skills`
3. Select `document-skills` or `example-skills`
4. Select `Install now`

Alternatively, directly install either Plugin via:
```
/plugin install document-skills@anthropic-agent-skills
/plugin install example-skills@anthropic-agent-skills
```

After installing the plugin, you can use the skill by just mentioning it. For instance, if you install the `document-skills` plugin from the marketplace, you can ask Claude Code to do something like: "Use the PDF skill to extract the form fields from `path/to/some-file.pdf`"

## Claude.ai

These example skills are all already available to paid plans in Claude.ai. 

To use any skill from this repository or upload custom skills, follow the instructions in [Using skills in Claude](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12512180-using-skills-in-claude#h_a4222fa77b).

## Claude API

You can use Anthropic's pre-built skills, and upload custom skills, via the Claude API. See the [Skills API Quickstart](https://docs.claude.com/en/api/skills-guide#creating-a-skill) for more.

# Creating a Basic Skill

Skills are simple to create - just a folder with a `SKILL.md` file containing YAML frontmatter and instructions. You can use the **template-skill** in this repository as a starting point:

```markdown
---
name: my-skill-name
description: A clear description of what this skill does and when to use it
---

# My Skill Name

[Add your instructions here that Claude will follow when this skill is active]

## Examples
- Example usage 1
- Example usage 2

## Guidelines
- Guideline 1
- Guideline 2
```

The frontmatter requires only two fields:
- `name` - A unique identifier for your skill (lowercase, hyphens for spaces)
- `description` - A complete description of what the skill does and when to use it

The markdown content below contains the instructions, examples, and guidelines that Claude will follow. For more details, see [How to create custom skills](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12512198-creating-custom-skills).

# Partner Skills

Skills are a great way to teach Claude how to get better at using specific pieces of software. As we see awesome example skills from partners, we may highlight some of them here:

- **Notion** - [Notion Skills for Claude](https://www.notion.so/notiondevs/Notion-Skills-for-Claude-28da4445d27180c7af1df7d8615723d0)

page:https://www.anthropic.com/research/.text: Discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities in critical, real-world software with Claude \ Anthropic                                   Skip to main content       News  Research     Policy     Commitments                          Company        Try Claude                                              Chapter   01 :  One-click remote code execution in Chrome             Discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities in critical, real-world software with Claude         01  One-click remote code execution in Chrome      02  A one-click exploit chain in Safari      03  Android lock screen bypass      04  Windows remote denial of service      05  Zero-click remote code execution in Linux      06  What we learned      07  What this means for defenders           Published   Oct 27, 2026     Team   Frontier Red Team         Over the past few months, we’ve used an unreleased, internal research model to  find critical vulnerabilities  in some of the world’s most widely used software, such as browsers and operating systems. In this post, we share details of five attack chains, which led to remote code execution and other critical impacts with little to no user interaction. These attack chains demonstrate the model’s ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software. Any vulnerabilities in these products could affect billions of users. They’re also among the most security-critical software in the world, making them a bellwether for testing models’ vulnerability research and cyber capabilities.  We reported each vulnerability to the affected vendor under our  coordinated vulnerability disclosure , which gives developers 90 days to patch and a further 45 days before we discuss details beyond what is already included in a public advisory.  1. One-click remote code execution in Chrome  After initial prompting, Claude wrote a full exploit chain enabling an attacker to execute arbitrary code as the user, outside the browser’s sandbox. Our proof of concept launches the Calculator app from a stock default-configuration Chrome browser on macOS within seconds of the page loading, without any further user interaction:   Claude discovered a vulnerability in Chrome’s JavaScript engine, V8, that allowed a malicious web page to corrupt V8’s heap memory.  Claude discovered a second vulnerability to break out of V8’s memory region sandbox and defeat ASLR. This step located Chrome’s code in memory and used a return-oriented programming (ROP) chain to take full control of the renderer process.  The compromised renderer was confined by Chrome’s process sandbox. Claude then discovered a race condition in CacheStorage. The compromised renderer used the race condition to read memory outside the sandbox and learn the memory layout of the privileged browser process.  Finally, Claude discovered a use-after-free in FedCM, Chrome’s federated sign-in feature, that allowed the exploit to execute arbitrary code outside the sandbox.   We have reported our findings to Google: 62 CVEs have been assigned and  patched as of Chrome 156 , with all of them rated critical or high severity. Among them are 13 sandbox escapes and 21 vulnerabilities that could have been used to compromise the renderer.  2. A one-click exploit chain in Safari  After initial prompting, Claude wrote an exploit chain that let any website’s JavaScript completely bypass the same-origin policy (SOP). The exploit could access a user’s Safari history, cookies, and other sensitive data, and could send authenticated HTTP requests to other domains and read the responses. For example, if the user is signed in to their email account, the attacker can now read their email; if they’re logged into their bank account, the attacker can view account balances or attempt transfers.  To do this, Claude defeated several layers of protection built into Safari:   Claude discovered a use-after-free (UAF) vulnerability in JavaScriptCore, Safari’s JavaScript engine, which is written in C++. Certain TypedArray operations wrote through stale pointers to freed memory, overwriting TypedArray metadata.  WebKit’s Gigacage mitigates this type of attack by isolating TypedArray data in a separate region of memory. Claude discovered that certain variables in this region were used to index into other regions, which gave it an arbitrary read/write primitive outside the Gigacage.  All website JavaScript runs in the WebContent sandbox, which keeps bugs like the UAF from reaching sensitive browser data on disk. Claude discovered a vulnerability in the sandbox's IPC mechanism that let the exploit read Safari’s stored history, cookies, and session databases from disk.  Finally, Claude used the UAF to overwrite a variable in memory and disable the SOP, allowing the attacker’s page to read data from any other origin.   The chain is interesting because it is a data-only attack that never relies on arbitrary code execution. Instead, it uses full read/write access to the browser process’s memory to modify a security flag, an object size, and a URL. Several of the weaknesses are not vulnerabilities on their own but intended behaviors that become exploitable when combined.  Apple acknowledged our report the same day we submitted it and implemented a fix promptly.  That fix  is available to users.  3. Android lock screen bypass  After initial prompting, Claude wrote an exploit that let an attacker extract photos and other personal information from a stolen Android phone without unlocking it. The work combined three methods: source code analysis of the open-source parts of Android, reverse engineering and deobfuscation of the Google Play services binaries, and live testing on a physical Google Pixel 9. This turned up a wide range of vulnerabilities in both the open-source and proprietary components. Claude then chained three of them into the final exploit.  Android has several layers of protection against this attack. Claude found a way around each one:   A locked Android phone is designed not to transfer data over USB. Claude found that a USB host with a specific setting bypassed this.  The device-to-device transfer protocol refuses data commands from unauthorized peers. Claude found a way to skip the authorization check and start the pairing process.  Pairing is protected by an authenticated key agreement that asks the user to verify a six-digit code. Claude found a flaw that skipped this verification and behaved as if the user had tapped “Allow.”  USB transfers are not supposed to carry file contents, as enforced by a hardcoded check. Claude found a fallback mechanism that sent raw bytes over USB and was not covered by the check. The exploit requested file contents through it.   This issue has been addressed by Google.  4. Windows remote denial of service  After initial prompting, Claude wrote an exploit that would have allowed an attacker to remotely crash any Windows machine that responds to HTTP/3 requests using the native Windows implementation. The difficulty in this case was in identifying the vulnerability in the first place. Following that initial prompting, we reported this vulnerability directly to Microsoft, which resolved the vulnerability and assigned it  CVE-2026-33096 .  The vulnerability that Claude identified was a memory safety out-of-bounds read in the Windows kernel’s implementation of QUIC. An attacker could reach the vulnerable codepath remotely over the network and send a few packets of data to a listening server to crash and restart the machine. By repeatedly sending these requests, it is possible to continuously crash the server, which causes loss of access to the server for all of the users. We estimate that there are likely several million such servers listening on the internet.  Claude discovered this vulnerability through binary analysis. We provided the model with a copy of the Windows executable and asked Claude to reverse-engineer how the software works using the existing reverse-engineering tools (such as Ghidra), write a fully annotated C program that reproduces the relevant features, compare the behavior reproduced program to binary to ensure correctness, and then study the code for vulnerabilities. When we asked Claude to identify potentially higher-risk issues, it surfaced this remotely exploitable vulnerability.  5. Zero-click remote code execution in Linux  While this post focuses on third-party products, our work on open source has continued. With Claude, we discovered local privilege escalation vulnerabilities on OpenBSD, FreeBSD, and Linux; a number of sandbox escapes in popular sandboxing infrastructure; and numerous vulnerabilities in important web applications. We have also found remotely triggerable (zero-click) arbitrary code execution vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel’s networking stack, which have since been patched upstream and publicly disclosed. We detail one such example below.  After initial prompting, Claude wrote an exploit that allows a remote attacker to send packets to Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener to run arbitrary commands as root, without any credentials or user interaction. The underlying vulnerability is a race condition-induced UAF bug in the kernel networking stack. The full exploitation has two key stages:   In the first stage, the attacker defeats KASLR remotely. It exploits the race to make the kernel read an attacker-controlled length field to copy extra bytes and send them back to the attacker, and as long as one such overread contains a kernel pointer in the reply, the attacker learns the kernel address space layout.  In the second stage, the attacker hijacks the control flow. It exploits the same UAF bug to overflow a buffer and overwrite a callback pointer with the address of a payload the attacker has already staged in kernel memory via an ordinary protocol feature. When the kernel invokes the callback, the payload chains a series of calls to existing kernel functions. ending with an attacker-chosen shell command running as root.   An enabling property of this race condition is that a lost race only fails the handshake without crashing the whole system, so a determined attacker can retry indefinitely until they succeed. In our proof of concept, it takes 48 minutes to leak a kernel pointer and another five minutes to reach the shell command execution. This vulnerability ( CVE-2026-98432 ) was patched upstream and backported to all maintained stable kernel branches.  What we learned  Throughout our process of using Claude for this security work, we identified a number of insights that shaped our approach. We think two are particularly important.   Test-time compute scaling and scanner diversity substantially increase how many vulnerabilities you find.  We built a platform that runs large numbers of scanning agents in parallel, measures each scanner by how many additional vulnerabilities it contributes to the mix, and tracks coverage dynamically so the scanners process the entire codebase.  The strategies range from pure coverage (is there a vulnerability in this function?) to goal-based (does this app expose anything that could compromise customer data?) to threat model-based (does anything in this app bypass its documented threat model?). We also used Claude to run automated variant analysis on every confirmed finding. All findings pass through a standardized verification and risk rating pipeline, so we can experiment freely with new scanners without lowering the quality bar.   Fixing the existing backlog only solves half the problem; the other half is cutting the rate at which new vulnerabilities enter the codebase.  For that, we recommend scanning at PR time. We built security guidance directly into our development process through a Claude Code plugin, which we’ve  released publicly .  What this means for defenders  Frontier models have the ability to discover and combine multiple vulnerabilities into a working exploit. These skills have historically been the domain of few specialist teams with expertise in these targets. Now, it’s something models can do with little human involvement, and then prove by producing a working exploit that anyone can run and verify.  Enabling defenders with powerful models is critical to giving them a headstart on patching systems before attackers do. Recently, we released an expanded version of our  Cyber Verification Program , which makes advanced cyber capabilities and reduced blocking classifiers available to qualifying security professionals. It includes access to our most capable models, including Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Mythos 5.1, and other new models moving forward. Our advice to defenders remains the same: scanning your own code is more important than ever. Subject: 	[security] Protecting against CVE-2026-98432
Date: 	Thu, 29 Oct 2026 16:34:28 -0700 (PDT)
From: 	Neal Patel <neal@...ang.org>
To: 	golang-announce <golang-announce@...glegroups.com>

Hi Gophers,

The recent disclosure of CVE-2026-98432 
< https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-98432 > describes a use-after-free 
issue which impacts IPv4 TCP connection handling in the Linux kernel. In an 
exploit described by Anthropic 
< https://www.anthropic.com/research/discovering-vulnerabilities-with-claude >, a 
server using Multipath TCP < https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multipath_TCP > (MPTCP) 
listeners is shown to be vulnerable to Remote Code Execution (RCE).

*The best fix for this vulnerability is to upgrade to a patched kernel version.*

While the demonstrated exploit requires the target system to expose an MPTCP 
listener, the underlying bug is not specific to MPTCP. It is possible that 
systems with no MPTCP listeners are vulnerable to similar attacks.

As of Go 1.24 < https://go.dev/doc/godebug#go-124 >, Go programs enable MPTCP by 
default for listen sockets on Linux. This default may be changed by setting the 
"multipathtcp" GODEBUG:

   * Setting "GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0" in a program's environment will disable
     MPTCP by default at runtime.
   * Placing "godebug multipathtcp=0" in the main module's go.mod file will
     disable MPTCP by default at build time.


Programs may also explicitly enable or disable MPTCP on a per-socket basis, 
using net.Dialer.SetMultipathTCP < https://pkg.go.dev/net#Dialer.SetMultipathTCP > 
and net.ListenConfig.SetMultipathTCP 
< https://pkg.go.dev/net#ListenConfig.SetMultipathTCP >. These functions override 
the GODEBUG setting.

Note that disabling MPTCP on a program-by-program basis is a fragile mitigation. 
Accidentally leaving a single MPTCP listener exposed will still leave a system 
vulnerable. Further, it assumes that all viable exploits for this bug depend on 
MPTCP. Again, we strongly recommend upgrading to a patched kernel version.

At this time, we believe it is premature to consider making any changes to Go 
(such as changing the default MPTCP behavior) in reaction to this issue. Further 
discussion of the issue and how we might respond to it will happen on 
 https://go.dev/issue/82717  < https://go.dev/issue/82717 >.

- Go Security Team

                 Critical vulnerability found 
 A critical vulnerability affecting LXD and MicroCloud has been identified and addressed. This vulnerability was referred to us from the Incus project, and was confirmed to affect LXD as well. 
 The vulnerability allows an attacker that is able to reach the LXD HTTPS API to authenticate as any trusted TLS client, for which the attacker has the public certificate. 
 In MicroCloud, it is possible for an attacker to intercept the public TLS certificate of a joining cluster member, and subsequently authenticate as that joined member. 
 All LXD and MicroCloud users are urged to update to the latest versions immediately to mitigate this risk. 
   Summary 
 Remote API authentication logic for mutual TLS compared all peer certificates sent by the client to known trust store entries. However, only the leaf certificate proves ownership of the signing key. This allows an attacker to authenticate to the LXD or MicroCloud API as another identity by placing their trusted public TLS certificate as an intermediary certificate in the chain. 
 For more details, please see: 
 
   CVE-2026-112816    Authentication bypass through unverified client certificate chains  
 
   Impact 
 An attacker may gain trust with the LXD or MicroCloud daemon by impersonating another user with only their public client certificate. Depending on the privilege of the victim user, the attacker may gain root access to the host machine.

      Title: Broken on Arrival: Non-Functional Quantized LLM Artifacts in Public Model Registries and How to Catch Them 
      Authors:  Aditi Patodiya               View a PDF of the paper titled Broken on Arrival: Non-Functional Quantized LLM Artifacts in Public Model Registries and How to Catch Them, by Aditi Patodiya 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Developers download quantized large language models (LLMs) from public registries to run them locally. None of the registries we examined documented functional testing of their files. We tested all 305 eligible code-capable GGUF tags (the  this http URL  format) across 15 model lines in the official Ollama library, plus 22 popular Hugging Face community files. A 15-task code screen identified suspects, which we retested on all 164 HumanEval+ tasks. Seven official tags (2.3%) solved at most six of them. All were low-bit quantizations of models with at most four billion parameters. We rebuilt five suspect files from the original weights. All five registry files matched our uncalibrated rebuilds tensor for tensor, so none was corrupted. Exact reproducibility did not imply function. With the weights, toolchain and tensor mix held fixed, adding an importance matrix raised Qwen2.5-Coder-3B scores at three quantization levels from zero to 76-113 of 164 tasks. The same uncalibrated recipe left the smaller Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B functional, showing that the recipe alone does not predict failure. None of 66 sampled tags that passed the screen was non-functional. We release the audit data and the quantcheck tool and recommend screening low-bit tags before publication, then calibrating or withholding failures.
     

     
     
                
           Comments: 
           v3 revises the diagnosis of one community file pair (Sec. V, RQ2): a template test on the same hardware shows the two deepseek-coder-6.7B community files fail for lack of a chat template, not by backend; release v3.4 adds the test. All other results unchanged. Code and data:  this https URL  (release v3.4)

 Wang","user":"wanglucs","type":"user","name":"wanglucs"},"summary":"Recent advances in multimodal large language models have increased interest in interaction paradigms for video understanding. The evolution from offline to streaming and proactive interaction has gradually shifted models from passive responders toward more proactive agents that can decide when to answer. However, existing proactive paradigms typically assume that the information required to answer a query is complete, leaving models to only wait or answer. In the real world, however, information is often incomplete due to uncertainty from either the video or the user. In proactive paradigms, such uncertainty can cause the model to wait forever or generate highly hallucinatory responses. We therefore argue that proactive interaction should be redefined with a third action: ask, allowing models to actively ask for missing information. Dynamic block-sparse attention reduces this cost by computing exact attention only on key/value blocks selected from current activations. However, its fidelity degrades under aggressive sparsity: blocks are scored from coarse summaries or formed by costly global clustering, pruned blocks vanish from the softmax, and whole tiles are kept or dropped even when only a few of their keys matter. To address these limitations, we propose Accurate Block Attention (AB-Attention), a training-free method that accurately approximates dense attention at high sparsity. Its Intra-Block Clustering Selector (IBCS) estimates block importance faithfully yet cheaply by clustering queries only within each query block, without permuting tokens. Sampling with Inclusion-Probability Weighting (SIP) then samples blocks in proportion to these estimates and reweights them by inverse inclusion probability, so that one pass estimates dense attention rather than truncating it. Pramanik","user":"rishavpramanik","type":"user","name":"rishavpramanik"},"summary":"Autoregressive (AR) image generators are powerful in principle but inflexible in practice: training with a fixed raster-scan order hardcodes a single factorization of the image distribution into the model, leaving it unable to inpaint, outpaint, or edit at inference time. Existing solutions, including the modern discrete-diffusion family, train from scratch on a mixture of token orderings, paying roughly 3x the compute of standard raster-scan training; discrete diffusion further sacrifices compatibility with the AR inference ecosystem (KV caching, vLLM) by construction. We argue that this cost is unnecessary. A pretrained raster-scan AR model has already learned the joint distribution over image tokens; what it lacks is not knowledge but the ability to express that knowledge through non-sequential conditional pathways. We propose a recipe for adapting pretrained raster-scan models into any-order generators using two components: future-aware positional embeddings that resolve a target-position identifiability problem at negligible overhead, and an ordering curriculum that traces a stable optimization path from the pretrained solution to a good any-order basin. Zou","user":"ZouBo","type":"user","name":"ZouBo"},"summary":"In September 2026, a new large language model was released. Soon after, a new way of making explainer videos became very popular: people asked the model to write a program, and the program produced the video. \"One-click video\" content then appeared in large amounts on many platforms. On the surface, this is a rise in creative power at the level of the individual. We argue that, at a deeper level, it changes the structure of the content industry. This judgment rests on two observations. First, this wave of content is service-type content. People watch it to meet a need, not to enjoy the content itself. The other kind is work-type content. AI makes both kinds faster to produce. But anyone can come in and make service-type content, while work-type content is limited by the number of people who have something to say. So the ratio between the two slowly becomes unbalanced. Second, free platforms choose content through layers of trial viewing, and this uses up user attention. The total amount of attention is fixed. The unbalanced ratio also dilutes good content. # pgAdmin 4

pgAdmin 4 is a rewrite of the popular pgAdmin3 management tool for the
PostgreSQL (http://www.postgresql.org) database.

In the following documentation and examples, *$PGADMIN4_SRC/* is used to denote
the top-level directory of a copy of the pgAdmin source tree, either from a
tarball or a git checkout.

## Architecture

pgAdmin 4 is written as a web application with Python (Flask) on the server side
and ReactJS, HTML5 with CSS for the client side processing and UI.

Although developed using web technologies, pgAdmin 4 can be deployed either on
a web server using a browser, or standalone on a workstation. The runtime/
subdirectory contains an Electron-based runtime application intended to allow this,
which will fork a Python server process and display the UI.

## Prerequisites
1. Install Node.js 20 and above (https://nodejs.org/en/download)
2. yarn (https://yarnpkg.com/getting-started/install)
3. Python 3.9 and above (https://www.python.org/downloads/)
4. PostgreSQL server (https://www.postgresql.org/download)

Start by enabling Corepack, if it isn't already;
this will add the yarn binary to your PATH:
```bash
corepack enable
```

# Building the Web Assets

pgAdmin is dependent on a number of third-party JavaScript libraries. These,
along with its own JavaScript code, CSS code and images must be
compiled into a "bundle" which is transferred to the browser for execution
and rendering. This is far more efficient than simply requesting each
asset as it is needed by the client.

To create the bundle, you will need the 'yarn' package management tool to be
installed. Then, you can run the following commands on a *nix system to
download the required packages and build the bundle:

```bash
$ cd $PGADMIN4_SRC
$ make install-node
$ make bundle
```

On Windows systems (where "make" is not available), the following commands
can be used:

```
C:\> cd $PGADMIN4_SRC\web
C:\$PGADMIN4_SRC\web> yarn install
C:\$PGADMIN4_SRC\web> yarn run bundle
```

# Configuring the Python Environment

In order to run the Python code, a suitable runtime environment is required.
Python version 3.9 and later are currently supported. It is recommended that a
Python virtual environment is set up for this purpose, rather than using the
system Python environment. On Linux and Mac systems, the process is fairly
simple - adapt as required for your distribution:

1. Create a virtual environment in an appropriate directory. The last argument is
   the name of the environment; that can be changed as desired:

   ```bash
   $ python3 -m venv venv
   ```

2. Now activate the virtual environment:

   ```bash
   $ source venv/bin/activate
   ```

3. Some of the components used by pgAdmin require a very recent version of *pip*,
   so update that to the latest:

   ```bash
   (venv) $ pip install --upgrade pip
   ```

4. Ensure that a PostgreSQL installation's bin/ directory is in the path (so
   pg_config can be found for building psycopg3), and install the required
   packages:

   ```bash
   (venv) $ PATH=$PATH:/usr/local/pgsql/bin pip install -r $PGADMIN4_SRC/requirements.txt
   ```

   If you are planning to run the regression tests, you also need to install
   additional requirements from web/regression/requirements.txt:

   ```bash
   (venv) $ pip install -r $PGADMIN4_SRC/web/regression/requirements.txt
   ```

5. Create a local configuration file for pgAdmin. Edit
   $PGADMIN4_SRC/web/config_local.py and add any desired configuration options
   (use the config.py file as a reference - any settings duplicated in
   config_local.py will override those in config.py). A typical development
   configuration may look like:

    ```python
   import os
   import logging

   # Change pgAdmin data directory
   DATA_DIR = '/Users/myuser/.pgadmin_dev'

   # Change pgAdmin server and port
   DEFAULT_SERVER = '127.0.0.1'
   DEFAULT_SERVER_PORT = 5051

   # Switch between server and desktop mode
   SERVER_MODE = True

   # Change pgAdmin config DB path in case an external DB is used.
   CONFIG_DATABASE_URI="postgresql://postgres:postgres@localhost:5436/pgadmin"

   # Set up SMTP
   MAIL_SERVER = 'smtp.gmail.com'
   MAIL_PORT = 465
   MAIL_USE_SSL = True
   MAIL_USERNAME = 'user@gmail.com'
   MAIL_PASSWORD = 'xxxxxxxxxx'

   # Change log level
   CONSOLE_LOG_LEVEL = logging.INFO
   FILE_LOG_LEVEL = logging.INFO

   # Use a different config DB for each server mode.
   if SERVER_MODE == False:
     SQLITE_PATH = os.path.join(
         DATA_DIR,
         'pgadmin4-desktop.db'
     )
   else:
     SQLITE_PATH = os.path.join(
         DATA_DIR,
         'pgadmin4-server.db'
     )
   ```

   This configuration allows easy switching between server and desktop modes
   for testing.

6. The initial setup of the configuration database is interactive in server
   mode, and non-interactive in desktop mode. You can run it either by
   running:

   ```bash
   (venv) $ python3 $PGADMIN4_SRC/web/setup.py
   ```

   or by starting pgAdmin 4:

   ```bash
   (venv) $ python3 $PGADMIN4_SRC/web/pgAdmin4.py
   ```

Whilst it is possible to automatically run setup in desktop mode by running
the runtime, that will not work in server mode as the runtime doesn't allow
command line interaction with the setup program.

At this point you will be able to run pgAdmin 4 from the command line in either
server or desktop mode, and access it from a web browser using the URL shown in
the terminal once pgAdmin has started up.

Setup of an environment on Windows is somewhat more complicated unfortunately,
please see *pkg/win32/README.md* for complete details.

# Building the documentation

In order to build the docs, an additional Python package is required in the
virtual environment. This can be installed with the pip package manager:

```bash
$ source venv/bin/activate
(venv) $ pip install Sphinx
(venv) $ pip install sphinxcontrib-youtube
```

The docs can then be built using the Makefile in *$PGADMIN4_SRC*, e.g.

```bash
(venv) $ make docs
```

The output can be found in *$PGADMIN4_SRC/docs/en_US/_build/html/index.html*

## Building the Runtime
Change into the runtime directory, and run *yarn install*. This will install the
dependencies required.

In order to use the runtime in a development environment, you'll need to copy
*dev_config.json.in* file to *dev_config.json*, and edit the paths to the Python
executable and *pgAdmin.py* file, otherwise the runtime will use the default
paths it would expect to find in the standard package for your platform.

You can then execute the runtime by running something like:

```bash
yarn run start
```

# Building packages

Most packages can be built using the Makefile in $PGADMIN4_SRC, provided all
the setup and configuration above has been completed.

To build a source tarball:

```bash
(venv) $ make src
```

To build a PIP Wheel, activate either a Python 3 virtual environment, configured
with all the required packages, and then run:

```bash
(venv) $ make pip
```

To build the macOS AppBundle, please see *pkg/mac/README.md*.

To build the Windows installer, please see *pkg/win32/README.md*.
# Create Database Migrations

In order to make changes to the SQLite DB, navigate to the 'web' directory:

```bash
(venv) $ cd $PGADMIN4_SRC/web
```

Create a migration file with the following command:

```bash
(venv) $ FLASK_APP=pgAdmin4.py flask db revision
```

This will create a file in: $PGADMIN4_SRC/web/migrations/versions/ .
Add any changes to the 'upgrade' function.
Increment the SCHEMA_VERSION in $PGADMIN4_SRC/web/pgadmin/model/__init__.py file.

There is no need to increment the SETTINGS_SCHEMA_VERSION.

# Support

See https://www.pgadmin.org/support/ for support options.

# Security Issues

If you would like to report a security issue with pgAdmin, please email
**security (at) pgadmin (dot) org**.

Note that this address should only be used for reporting security issues
that you believe you've found in the design or code of pgAdmin, pgAgent,
and the pgAdmin website. It should not be used to ask security questions.

# Project info

A GitHub project for pgAdmin 4 can be found at the address below:

https://github.com/pgadmin-org/pgadmin4

Please submit any changes as Pull Requests against the *master* branch of the
*pgadmin-org/pgadmin4* repository.

If you wish to discuss pgAdmin 4, or contribute to the project, please use the
pgAdmin Hackers mailing list:

pgadmin-hackers@postgresql.org

   _is_query_parens_balanced() rejected a backslash inside a single-quoted
string but not inside a double-quoted identifier, where it treated the
next quote as closing the token. psql does not: strtokx in
parse_slash_copy takes its escape character from the connection's
standard_conforming_strings setting and applies it to whichever quote
opened the token, so with standard_conforming_strings off the \" in
"a\"b" is an escaped quote and the identifier runs on to the next quote.

That desynchronises our quote state from psql's in the opposite
direction to the case fixed in   1496fab  , and a query export such as
SELECT "a\"b"c) TO PROGRAM 'cmd' x" therefore passed the balance check
whilst the ) it hid closed the wrapping \copy (...) context, exposing a
live TO PROGRAM clause. psql calls popen() for a client-side
\copy ... TO PROGRAM before the backend sees the statement at all, so
the command runs on the pgAdmin host even though the query is then
rejected as a syntax error. An ordinary PostgreSQL role can set
standard_conforming_strings on itself, and a non-administrator pgAdmin
account holds tools_import_export_data by default, so no privileged
access of either kind is needed.

Apply the same treatment as the single-quoted branch and reject any
backslash encountered whilst scanning a double-quoted identifier, since
the correct interpretation still depends on a server setting we cannot
reliably know at validation time.

        Contributing         License         Security           More  items                    pgAdmin 4     
 pgAdmin 4 is a rewrite of the popular pgAdmin3 management tool for the
PostgreSQL ( http://www.postgresql.org ) database. 
 In the following documentation and examples,  $PGADMIN4_SRC/  is used to denote
the top-level directory of a copy of the pgAdmin source tree, either from a
tarball or a git checkout. 
  Architecture     
 pgAdmin 4 is written as a web application with Python (Flask) on the server side
and ReactJS, HTML5 with CSS for the client side processing and UI. 
 Although developed using web technologies, pgAdmin 4 can be deployed either on
a web server using a browser, or standalone on a workstation. The runtime/
subdirectory contains an Electron-based runtime application intended to allow this,
which will fork a Python server process and display the UI. 
  Prerequisites     
 
 Install Node.js 20 and above ( https://nodejs.org/en/download ) 
 yarn ( https://yarnpkg.com/getting-started/install ) 
 Python 3.9 and above ( https://www.python.org/downloads/ ) 
 PostgreSQL server ( https://www.postgresql.org/download ) 
 
 Start by enabling Corepack, if it isn't already;
this will add the yarn binary to your PATH: 
  corepack  enable   
  Building the Web Assets     
 pgAdmin is dependent on a number of third-party JavaScript libraries. These,
along with its own JavaScript code, CSS code and images must be
compiled into a "bundle" which is transferred to the browser for execution
and rendering. This is far more efficient than simply requesting each
asset as it is needed by the client. 
 To create the bundle, you will need the 'yarn' package management tool to be
installed. Then, you can run the following commands on a *nix system to
download the required packages and build the bundle: 
  $  cd   $PGADMIN4_SRC 
$ make install-node
$ make bundle  
 On Windows systems (where "make" is not available), the following commands
can be used: 
   C:\> cd $PGADMIN4_SRC\web
C:\$PGADMIN4_SRC\web> yarn install
C:\$PGADMIN4_SRC\web> yarn run bundle
   
  Configuring the Python Environment     
 In order to run the Python code, a suitable runtime environment is required.
Python version 3.9 and later are currently supported. It is recommended that a
Python virtual environment is set up for this purpose, rather than using the
system Python environment. On Linux and Mac systems, the process is fairly
simple - adapt as required for your distribution: 
 
 
 Create a virtual environment in an appropriate directory. The last argument is
the name of the environment; that can be changed as desired: 
  $ python3 -m venv venv  
 
 
 Now activate the virtual environment: 
  $  source  venv/bin/activate  
 
 
 Some of the components used by pgAdmin require a very recent version of  pip ,
so update that to the latest: 
  (venv) $ pip install --upgrade pip  
 
 
 Ensure that a PostgreSQL installation's bin/ directory is in the path (so
pg_config can be found for building psycopg3), and install the required
packages: 
  (venv) $ PATH= $PATH :/usr/local/pgsql/bin pip install -r  $PGADMIN4_SRC /requirements.txt  
 If you are planning to run the regression tests, you also need to install
additional requirements from web/regression/requirements.txt: 
  (venv) $ pip install -r  $PGADMIN4_SRC /web/regression/requirements.txt  
 
 
 Create a local configuration file for pgAdmin. Edit
$PGADMIN4_SRC/web/config_local.py and add any desired configuration options
(use the config.py file as a reference - any settings duplicated in
config_local.py will override those in config.py). A typical development
configuration may look like: 
   import   os 
 import   logging 

 # Change pgAdmin data directory 
 DATA_DIR   =   '/Users/myuser/.pgadmin_dev' 

 # Change pgAdmin server and port 
 DEFAULT_SERVER   =   '127.0.0.1' 
 DEFAULT_SERVER_PORT   =   5051 

 # Switch between server and desktop mode 
 SERVER_MODE   =   True 

 # Change pgAdmin config DB path in case an external DB is used. 
 CONFIG_DATABASE_URI  =  "postgresql://postgres:postgres@localhost:5436/pgadmin" 

 # Set up SMTP 
 MAIL_SERVER   =   'smtp.gmail.com' 
 MAIL_PORT   =   465 
 MAIL_USE_SSL   =   True 
 MAIL_USERNAME   =   'user@gmail.com' 
 MAIL_PASSWORD   =   'xxxxxxxxxx' 

 # Change log level 
 CONSOLE_LOG_LEVEL   =   logging . INFO 
 FILE_LOG_LEVEL   =   logging . INFO 

 # Use a different config DB for each server mode. 
 if   SERVER_MODE   ==   False :
  SQLITE_PATH   =   os . path . join (
      DATA_DIR ,
      'pgadmin4-desktop.db' 
 )
 else :
  SQLITE_PATH   =   os . path . join (
      DATA_DIR ,
      'pgadmin4-server.db' 
 )  
 This configuration allows easy switching between server and desktop modes
for testing. 
 
 
 The initial setup of the configuration database is interactive in server
mode, and non-interactive in desktop mode. You can run it either by
running: 
  (venv) $ python3  $PGADMIN4_SRC /web/setup.py  
 or by starting pgAdmin 4: 
  (venv) $ python3  $PGADMIN4_SRC /web/pgAdmin4.py  
 
 
 Whilst it is possible to automatically run setup in desktop mode by running
the runtime, that will not work in server mode as the runtime doesn't allow
command line interaction with the setup program. 
 At this point you will be able to run pgAdmin 4 from the command line in either
server or desktop mode, and access it from a web browser using the URL shown in
the terminal once pgAdmin has started up. 
 Setup of an environment on Windows is somewhat more complicated unfortunately,
please see  pkg/win32/README.md  for complete details. 
  Building the documentation     
 In order to build the docs, an additional Python package is required in the
virtual environment. This can be installed with the pip package manager: 
  $  source  venv/bin/activate
(venv) $ pip install Sphinx
(venv) $ pip install sphinxcontrib-youtube  
 The docs can then be built using the Makefile in  $PGADMIN4_SRC , e.g. 
  (venv) $ make docs  
 The output can be found in  $PGADMIN4_SRC/docs/en_US/_build/html/index.html  
  Building the Runtime     
 Change into the runtime directory, and run  yarn install . This will install the
dependencies required. 
 In order to use the runtime in a development environment, you'll need to copy
 dev_config.json.in  file to  dev_config.json , and edit the paths to the Python
executable and  pgAdmin.py  file, otherwise the runtime will use the default
paths it would expect to find in the standard package for your platform. 
 You can then execute the runtime by running something like: 
  yarn run start  
  Building packages     
 Most packages can be built using the Makefile in $PGADMIN4_SRC, provided all
the setup and configuration above has been completed. 
 To build a source tarball: 
  (venv) $ make src  
 To build a PIP Wheel, activate either a Python 3 virtual environment, configured
with all the required packages, and then run: 
  (venv) $ make pip  
 To build the macOS AppBundle, please see  pkg/mac/README.md . 
 To build the Windows installer, please see  pkg/win32/README.md . 
  Create Database Migrations     
 In order to make changes to the SQLite DB, navigate to the 'web' directory: 
  (venv) $  cd   $PGADMIN4_SRC /web  
 Create a migration file with the following command: 
  (venv) $ FLASK_APP=pgAdmin4.py flask db revision  
 This will create a file in: $PGADMIN4_SRC/web/migrations/versions/ .
Add any changes to the 'upgrade' function.
Increment the SCHEMA_VERSION in $PGADMIN4_SRC/web/pgadmin/model/ init .py file. 
 There is no need to increment the SETTINGS_SCHEMA_VERSION. 
  Support     
 See  https://www.pgadmin.org/support/  for support options. 
  Security Issues     
 If you would like to report a security issue with pgAdmin, please email
 security (at) pgadmin (dot) org . 
 Note that this address should only be used for reporting security issues
that you believe you've found in the design or code of pgAdmin, pgAgent,
and the pgAdmin website. It should not be used to ask security questions. 
  Project info     
 A GitHub project for pgAdmin 4 can be found at the address below: 
  https://github.com/pgadmin-org/pgadmin4  
 Please submit any changes as Pull Requests against the  master  branch of the
 pgadmin-org/pgadmin4  repository. 
 If you wish to discuss pgAdmin 4, or contribute to the project, please use the
pgAdmin Hackers mailing list: 
  pgadmin-hackers@postgresql.org

      Title: Matched Capabilities, Different Behaviors: A Controlled Study of MCP and CLI Interfaces for Language Agents 
      Authors:  Zhenning Shi ,  Liang Pang ,  Yongqi Li               View a PDF of the paper titled Matched Capabilities, Different Behaviors: A Controlled Study of MCP and CLI Interfaces for Language Agents, by Zhenning Shi and 2 other authors 
     View PDF 



     
             Abstract: Language agents increasingly act through external tools and interactive environments, making the interface between the model and its executable capabilities part of the decision process. Model Context Protocol (MCP) and command-line interfaces (CLI) can expose the same semantic operations through markedly different model-facing representations. We study whether these representational differences change agent behavior when executable capabilities are matched. We introduce Matched Interface Comparison and Analysis (MICA), which renders MCP and CLI from a shared semantic action contract and routes decoded actions through the same runtime. Across six models and three interactive environments, matched interfaces produce substantial differences in task performance and interaction cost. These effects extend beyond surface validity to semantic action selection, failure pathways, and recovery. Matched-state probes localize sensitivity to capability presentation, realization, and feedback. Paired natural trajectories reveal structured divergence in 94.3% of 2,004 episodes and show that early differences propagate through subsequent interaction. This analysis identifies interface realization as a direct intervention boundary. We therefore introduce Decoupled Action Realization and Targeted Repair (DART), which preserves validated semantic commitments while repairing interface-specific realization. DART improves benchmark score in all six evaluated settings by up to 9.0 points and reduces MCP token cost in all three environments by up to 27.1k tokens per task. Together, these results establish interface representation as part of the closed-loop decision environment shaping agent behavior.

      Title: Multi-Token Prediction Done Right 
      Authors:  Jayden Teoh               View a PDF of the paper titled Multi-Token Prediction Done Right, by Jayden Teoh 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) is now a common ingredient in language-model pre-training, as it improves downstream performance and enables faster inference through speculative decoding. We identify a flaw in standard MTP training, in which a residual component of the MTP gradient interferes with both next-token and multi-token learning, increasingly so with scale. Specifically, the MTP cross-entropy gradient can be decomposed exactly into a KL self-distillation term that pulls each MTP head toward the model's own next-token prediction (NTP) distribution and improves speculative decoding, and a residual that has a low signal-to-noise ratio and buries the useful KL signal. We introduce the KL gradient-recovery trick: when two distributions share a linear output head, the gradient of their KL divergence can be recovered exactly by combining their cross-entropy gradients through straight-through gradient routing. Unlike minimizing the KL directly, this trick requires no vocabulary-sized logit matrices and is compatible with standard fused cross-entropy kernels. This enables Soft Multi-Token Prediction (Soft-MTP), a one-line code change to MTP that removes the noisy residual and backpropagates only the KL self-distillation signal by reusing the existing NTP and MTP cross-entropy computations. Soft-MTP supports both DeepSeek- and Meta-style MTP, adds no parameters, and incurs no measurable overhead. From 167M to 1.2B parameters, Soft-MTP improves over standard MTP with lower NTP perplexity, faster speculative decoding and higher zero-shot accuracy at every scale, lower MTP perplexity from 689M onward, and stronger math and code reasoning after fine-tuning at 1.2B. Soft-MTP also matches, if not exceeds, direct KL divergence minimization on most metrics. Soft-MTP is, in effect, a free lunch for MTP optimization. Our code can be found at  this https URL .

Unlimited OCR Works

Pioneering the OCR-3.0 Era: From Long- to Unlimited-Horizon Parsing.

## Release - [2026/10/28] Thanks to the [ms-swift community](https://github.com/modelscope/ms-swift) for supporting training of **Unlimited OCR 2**. - [2026/10/27] 📊 We release [**MarathonDocBench**](https://huggingface.co/datasets/baidu/MarathonDocBench), a new benchmark for ultra-long document parsing. - [2026/10/27] 🤝 Thanks to the [ModelScope community](https://github.com/modelscope) for their support. Our model is now available at [ModelScope](https://modelscope.cn/models/PaddlePaddle/Unlimited-OCR-2). - [2026/10/27] 🤝 Thanks to the Baidu Cloud team for their support. Our model is now available on [Baidu Cloud](https://cloud.baidu.com/doc/OCR/s/fmr1p39gb). - [2026/10/27] 🤝 Thanks to [AK](https://x.com/_akhaliq) for creating a new demo for us. Try it at [Unlimited-OCR-2](https://huggingface.co/spaces/baidu/Unlimited-OCR-2). - [2026/10/27] 🚀 We release [**Unlimited OCR 2**](https://github.com/baidu/Unlimited-OCR), achieving unlimited-horizon parsing with SR-SWA. - [2026/07/21] 🤝 Thanks to the [ms-swift community](https://github.com/modelscope/ms-swift) for their support, our model now supports training with [ms-swift](https://github.com/modelscope/ms-swift). - [2026/07/03] 🤝 Thanks to the Baidu Cloud team for their support. All pages of a document are parsed in one request, so the model can use cross-page context. The output contains one `` per input page, in the same order as `image_files`. **Single-page inference** (`infer`). A single page is encoded with dynamic tiling (gundam mode) by default: ```python text = model.infer(tokenizer, image_file="your_doc/page_1.jpg", output_path="output/single", save_results=True) ``` ### SGLang Set up the environment (uv-managed virtualenv, Python 3.10) and install the customized SGLang wheel `sglang-0.5.20.dev13+g75b9b06b02-py3-none-any.whl`, plus PyMuPDF for PDF-to-image conversion: ```shell uv venv --python 3.10 source .venv/bin/activate uv pip install wheel/sglang-0.5.20.dev13+g75b9b06b02-py3-none-any.whl uv pip install pymupdf==1.27.2.2 uv pip install fastokens==0.3.2 ``` Start the SGLang server: ```shell # Page-window scheduling for very long documents (the KV tail of the previous window is reused). export SGLANG_UOCR_EANABLE_DOC_LIMIT=1 # 1 = enable, 0 = whole document in one window export SGLANG_UOCR_DOC_GUNDAM_PAGE_WINDOW=10 # pages per window (gundam mode) export SGLANG_UOCR_DOC_BASE_PAGE_WINDOW=10 # pages per window (base mode) export SGLANG_UOCR_MAX_PAGE_TOKENS=20000 # per-page output cap; must be > 0 # Chunk cap for the SAM attention bias. A smaller one makes oversized batches fall back to eager; a larger one is never used and only wastes capture memory. * `--cuda-graph-config`'s `full_prefill_max_req` is the request-slot count for the full-prefill CUDA graph. The default (8) makes 16/32 concurrency fall back to eager. * A smaller page window lowers peak memory but hurts cross-page merging, since blocks that continue across a window boundary lose their context. To parse a whole document in one window instead (`SGLANG_UOCR_EANABLE_DOC_LIMIT=0`). Send requests to the OpenAI-compatible API: ```python import base64 import json import os import tempfile import fitz import requests from sglang.srt.sampling.custom_logit_processor import DeepseekOCRNoRepeatNGramLogitProcessor server_url = "http://127.0.0.1:10000" NGRAM_PROCESSOR = DeepseekOCRNoRepeatNGramLogitProcessor.to_str() session = requests.Session() session.trust_env = False def pdf_to_images(pdf_path, dpi=300): doc = fitz.open(pdf_path) tmp_dir = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="pdf_ocr_") mat = fitz.Matrix(dpi / 72, dpi / 72) image_paths = [] for i, page in enumerate(doc): image_path = os.path.join(tmp_dir, f"page_{i + 1:04d}.png") page.get_pixmap(matrix=mat).save(image_path) image_paths.append(image_path) doc.close() return image_paths def encode_image(image_path): ext = os.path.splitext(image_path)[1].lower() mime = "image/jpeg" if ext in (".jpg", ".jpeg") else f"image/{ext.lstrip('.')}" with open(image_path, "rb") as f: data = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode("utf-8") return {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": f"data:{mime};base64,{data}"}} def build_content(image_paths): prompt = "" * len(image_paths) + "Multi page parsing." return [encode_image(path) for path in image_paths] + [{"type": "text", "text": prompt}] def generate(image_paths, crop_mode=True, tokens_per_page=8000): # A wider n-gram window for multi-page documents, as in our evaluation setup. window_size = 1024 if len(image_paths) > 1 else 128 payload = { "model": "Unlimited-OCR-2", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": build_content(image_paths)}], # Must be positive: it is the global output budget for the whole document. "max_tokens": tokens_per_page * len(image_paths), "temperature": 0, "skip_special_tokens": False, "images_config": {"crop_mode": crop_mode}, # True = gundam (tiles), False = base "custom_logit_processor": NGRAM_PROCESSOR, "custom_params": { "ngram_size": 35, "window_size": window_size, "page_token_id": 128827, # marker id (= sparse_attention_config.page_token_id) "eos_token_id": 1, # = eos_token_id in config.json "max_page_tokens": 20000, # per-page output cap, <= 0 disables the page guard }, "stream": True, } response = session.post( f"{server_url}/v1/chat/completions", headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}, data=json.dumps(payload), timeout=6000, stream=True, ) response.raise_for_status() chunks = [] for line in response.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True): if not line or not line.startswith("data:"): continue data = line[len("data:"):].strip() if data == "[DONE]": break event = json.loads(data) choices = event.get("choices") or [] # the final chunk carries usage only if not choices: continue delta = (choices[0].get("delta") or {}).get("content") or "" if delta: print(delta, end="", flush=True) chunks.append(delta) return "".join(chunks) # Multi page: all pages of a document, parsed in one request pages = [f"your_doc/page_{i}.jpg" for i in range(1, 8)] generate(pages) # Single page generate(["your_doc/page_1.jpg"]) # PDF generate(pdf_to_images("your_doc.pdf", dpi=300)) ``` ## Evaluation `infer.py` is the batch client we use for MPDocBench / MarathonDocBench: it sends each document to the SGLang server above as a single request and saves the raw output, which `utils/process_unlimitedOCR2.py` then converts to the evaluation Markdown. ```shell python infer.py --url 127.0.0.1:10000 --benchmark MPDocBench \ --dataset-root /path/to/MPDocBench --all --raw-dir raw --concurrency 4 python utils/process_unlimitedOCR2.py --infer-dir raw --out-dir pred ``` See [utils/README.md](utils/README.md) for the output format, the merging rules and the post-processing details. ## Visualization Unlimited-horizon parsing in action: a full-length book parsed in a single request (replay).

# sanstun

A sans-IO, performance-oriented user-space implementation of the WireGuard® protocol.

## History

Its roots are a fork of [BoringTun](https://github.com/cloudflare/boringtun) in [firezone/boringtun](https://github.com/firezone/boringtun).
For a long time, the fork retained 100% API-compatibility with upstream to make cherry-picking and usage by other projects easier.

The fork at [firezone/boringtun](https://github.com/firezone/boringtun) is now deprecated in favor of `sanstun`.

## Scope

The `sanstun` project combines our experience of operating WireGuard in production in a sans-IO setting.
It features a re-designed API and internals that are tuned for maximizing throughput whilst making it easy and safe to use.

- Fully sans-IO, including time and RNG seeds
- No internal buffering
- No locks or atomic counters in the protocol state
- Multi-core friendly API: Encapsulating and decapsulating packets performs only the minimal book-keeping necessary.
  The actual crypto operations can be deferred to other threads and thus parallelized when processing packets in batches.

## Out-of-scope

Being a sans-IO library, `sanstun` does not perform any kind of IO for you, neither towards the user via a TUN device nor on the network to other peers via UDP.
It needs an event loop to do something useful.

The API design of `sanstun` makes it easy for you to use it correctly.
Nevertheless, there are some things it cannot do for you by virtue of being sans-IO.

### Cryptokey routing

A decrypted packet only proves which peer sent it.
It is your responsibility to verify that the packet came from an allowed IP.

Similarly, `Tunnel` allows you to encrypt packets towards any peer.
It is your responsibility to pick the correct `Tunnel` based on the destination IP.

### Handshake routing

A handshake initiation is routed by the initiator's static public key, via `HandshakeInitiation::peer_static_public`.
`Interface::receive` authenticates it and, for keys you created a `Tunnel` for, rejects replayed initiations.
Anyone can generate a key pair though, so do not create a `Tunnel` for an unknown key based on it.

### Inner IP packet validation

You must parse the decrypted buffer and verify that it contains a valid IP packet.
The buffer may still be padded.

### Randomness

It is your responsibility to supply a seed with enough entropy.
Being sans-IO means the library is fully deterministic including all cryptography operations.
Supplying identical seeds will produce **the same keys, nonces, cookies etc**.
This is great for testing but needs to be taken seriously for production usecases.

With great power comes great responsibility.

### Time

The time passed in needs to be monotonically increasing, otherwise other peers might reject handshakes as replays.

## Security

For a WireGuard implementation to be secure, it is not enough to just use sound & audited cryptography primitives.
The API of `sanstun` is designed to guide you towards using it in a safe manner by enforcing many aspects through the type-system.
For example, it is not possible to directly create a `Tunnel`.
Instead, `Interface` serves as a factory for new tunnels and derives all key material from a seed.
It is also not possible to handle inbound traffic in `sanstun` without going through a rate limiter.
This ensures expensive crypto operations like DH cannot be triggered arbitrarily by remote peers.

While we have taken great care to design and implement `sanstun` as secure as possible, it has not received a formal security audit.
Use it at your own risk.

## License

The project is licensed under the [Apache License, Version 2.0](LICENSE).

Introducing sanstun: sans-IO WireGuard | Firezone Blog                                                Open main menu        Product       Solutions      Docs    Pricing    Blog    Support                 Book a demo                 Admin portal  Book a demo                    Thomas Eizinger    October 31, 2026     Introducing sanstun: A sans-IO, parallel-friendly, userspace WireGuard implementation in Rust    Today, we are announcing   sanstun  : a sans-IO Rust implementation of the WireGuard® state machine, optimized for ease of use, security and performance through a parallel-friendly and idiomatic API. 
  What is sans-IO?  
 sans-IO is the idea that you design your system such that IO and side-effects are cleanly separated from the state and "business logic".
The IO in sans-IO doesn't just mean file or network IO.
It also includes things like time and randomness! 
 Due to their lack of side-effects, sans-IO components compose very well and are relatively easy to test.
The design also avoids problems like function coloring and plays well with Rust's ownership rules. 
 The code examples and references in this post are in Rust but sans-IO isn't Rust-specific at all.
Its patterns and ideas can be applied in any language.
For a more in-depth explanation, our  sans-IO post  is a good place to start. 
  History  
 When we first built Firezone, we reached for   boringtun   as our WireGuard implementation.
 boringtun  more or less did what we wanted, but over time, we found ourselves patching our fork over and over with bug fixes as well as API additions.
The goal was to allow these patches to still be upstreamed, so we always kept the existing API working the way it was. 
 What we found was that retaining 100% API compatibility with upstream was increasingly difficult as our product requirements evolved.
One of the first big changes we made to  boringtun  was to make it fully sans-IO with regard to time handling ( firezone/boringtun#5 ).
This meant adding new APIs for everything with a  _at  suffix that would take an  Instant .
sans-IO time handling is very important if you want to accurately simulate an entire system.
See  this blog post  to learn more about how we do that. 
 Another thing we feature-flagged was internal buffering.
At first, it seems convenient that  boringtun  establishes a session automatically if you don't have one yet (or anymore) and you are trying to send a packet.
Internal buffering, however, comes with several problems: 
 
 At some point, the buffer needs to be drained.
 boringtun  solves this by requiring you to call  decapsulate  with a zero-length datagram.
Rather unintuitive. 
 It incurs additional allocations (at least in the way it was implemented in  boringtun ). 
 Buffer sizes should be configurable / tunable. 
 
 All of these problems point at the same solution: Just don't buffer in the library.
It simplifies the interface and the implementation on both sides. 
 The  full list  of patches and fixes is pretty long.
Even excluding dependency bumps, that is more than 70 PRs.
Several of them are fixes for edge-cases we discovered.
Others add new APIs or make certain aspects configurable. 
 After more than 2 years of using and patching  boringtun , we had a pretty good idea of what the overall API of a userspace WireGuard implementation should be.
Now it exists as  sanstun . 
  A better sans-IO API  
 The core building blocks of the sans-IO API are now: 
 
 Handling inbound packets: 
 
  Tunnel::handle_handshake_initiation  
  Tunnel::handle_handshake_response  
  Tunnel::handle_cookie_reply  
  Tunnel::begin_decapsulate  &  Tunnel::commit_decapsulate  
 
 
 Handling outbound packets:  Tunnel::begin_encapsulate  
 Handling timer updates:  Tunnel::handle_timeout  &  Tunnel::poll_timeout  
 Handling events:  Tunnel::poll_event  
 
 Without internal buffering, there is no API contract that requires you to call certain APIs in a loop, which fits much better into the overall sans-IO model.
To send a packet, you call  Tunnel::begin_encapsulate .
It is up to you to buffer the packet if you don't have a session yet.
Creating a new session means sending a handshake.
You can initiate a new handshake at any point with  Tunnel::initiate_handshake . 
 The design of these APIs is very deliberate and will make more sense if we quickly recap the WireGuard protocol. 
  WireGuard protocol  
 WireGuard's message format supports 4 types of messages: handshake init, handshake response, cookie reply and encrypted data. 
 Every WireGuard session starts with a Diffie-Hellman key exchange which is a moderately expensive operation.
WireGuard's design ensures that exposing an endpoint doesn't open up a DoS opportunity. 
 Anyone who knows the endpoint's public key can easily create bogus handshake initiations and forge the source IP of the incoming UDP packet.
The receiving WireGuard implementation has to run its half of the DH operations before it can tell that the supplied handshake data is bogus.
But at that point, the CPU resources have already been spent.
Send enough handshake initiations and the receiving end will spend all its CPU cycles on handling irrelevant handshakes. 
 To prevent this, WireGuard specifies a cookie mechanism that forces the remote to prove ownership of its claimed source IP, which in turn allows rate-limiting handshakes per source IP. 
 These rate limits apply to an entire WireGuard interface and not just to a single tunnel. 
 Once a handshake has been completed, both peers can exchange encrypted data packets with a symmetric cipher.
As part of the handshake, the peers also exchange their locally-chosen session indices.
These indices enable de-multiplexing of tunnels as well as multiple sessions within a tunnel. 
  Mapping protocol invariants to API design  
 If you are working in a language like Rust, chances are you enjoy using types.
And using types well means enforcing invariants at compile-time such that you can't even ship a certain bug in the first place.
For example, forgetting to apply the rate limiter to a message would be pretty bad because it doesn't show up under normal operation.
Similarly, routing an incoming packet to the wrong tunnel is something that will only show up in production. 
 A good API design makes it impossible to build things that are broken and also guides you along in understanding how the protocol works. 
  One interface, many tunnels  
 A WireGuard interface is identified by a single key and a tunnel is a connection between two interfaces.
Any time we want to send a packet, we therefore need to specify which tunnel it should be sent on and when we receive a packet, we need to figure out which tunnel it belongs to. 
 In  sanstun , these concepts directly map to the  Interface  and  Tunnel  types.
All inbound packets go through  Interface::receive .
That is the only public API that parses a raw datagram.
It parses the packet, applies rate limits and hands you back a  ReceivedMessage  with one enum variant per WireGuard message type, or a cookie reply to send back if the interface is under load.
These then map directly to the corresponding functions on a  Tunnel :  Tunnel::handle_handshake_initiation , etc.
Handshake initiations are routed by the initiator's static public key.
All other messages expose  which   Tunnel  they should be dispatched to, identified by a  TunnelId . 
     Every inbound datagram has to go through   Interface::receive .  
 Under the hood,  sanstun  does a lot of things for you here.
It parses the tunnel index and extracts the upper 24 bits, it applies rate limits, generates cookie replies and validates handshake messages. 
 Crucially, the constructors for types like  HandshakeInitiation  are all crate-private.
Even though  Tunnel  exposes a public  handle_handshake_initiation  function, the only way to call that is by going through  Interface::receive  first to obtain such a type.
And  Interface::receive  protects your application by applying the rate limiter, all without you having to think about it. 
  Parallel crypto  
 One of the best features of  sanstun  is its parallel-friendly API for encrypting and decrypting packets. 
 On a protocol level, WireGuard doesn't share any state between tunnels.
Therefore, parallelizing a WireGuard implementation across peers is very easy. 
 But what about parallelizing work within a single tunnel?
WireGuard operates on layer 3, and thus a single session with another peer carries the traffic of many individual network flows.
Even if we handle tunnels to different peers on different threads, all network flows (i.e., unique 5-tuples) toward the same host or subnet will be processed sequentially, effectively bounded by how fast the CPU is at ChaCha20-Poly1305, WireGuard's cipher for data packets.
To protect against replay by malicious on-path observers, WireGuard data packets have a monotonically increasing packet counter.
This counter is scoped to a single session and therefore would require synchronization if we were to access this state from multiple threads simultaneously. 
 To avoid this,  sanstun  separates the bookkeeping from the actual encryption and decryption.
Calling  Tunnel::begin_encapsulate  doesn't in fact encrypt anything.
It checks for the current session, reserves a packet counter, advances timer state and then hands you a  PendingEncapsulate : 
    impl   PendingEncapsulate  {
     pub   fn   encrypt < 'a >( self , plaintext: &[ u8 ], dst: & 'a   mut  [ u8 ])  ->   Result <DataMessage< 'a >, Error> {
         // ... 
    }
}
   
  PendingEncapsulate  implements  Send  and can thus be transferred to another thread to perform the bulk of the work.
Running  cargo bench data_path  in the  sanstun  repository showcases the effect of this split: 
   data_path/64B/begin_encapsulate
                        time:   [20.785 ns 20.828 ns 20.869 ns]
data_path/64B/encrypt   time:   [226.15 ns 226.22 ns 226.29 ns]
data_path/64B/begin_decapsulate
                        time:   [37.600 ns 37.675 ns 37.744 ns]
data_path/64B/decrypt   time:   [205.78 ns 205.83 ns 205.87 ns]
data_path/64B/commit_decapsulate
                        time:   [17.486 ns 17.529 ns 17.575 ns]

data_path/1280B/begin_encapsulate
                        time:   [20.785 ns 20.828 ns 20.869 ns]
data_path/1280B/encrypt time:   [933.49 ns 933.54 ns 933.59 ns]
data_path/1280B/begin_decapsulate
                        time:   [37.606 ns 37.681 ns 37.751 ns]
data_path/1280B/decrypt time:   [914.81 ns 914.89 ns 914.97 ns]
data_path/1280B/commit_decapsulate
                        time:   [17.657 ns 17.707 ns 17.764 ns]
   
 As expected, the bookkeeping parts ( begin_encapsulate ,  begin_decapsulate  and  commit_decapsulate ) do not scale with packet size.
What does scale with packet size are the  encrypt  and  decrypt  functions.
At a packet size of 1280 bytes, the bookkeeping part of encrypting a new packet is only 2%.
If we move the actual encryption to another thread, this hints at a potential speedup of more than 45x! 
 An effective speedup of 45x is hard to achieve in practice because it ignores the cost of passing  PendingEncapsulate  to another thread and assumes no other overhead is introduced.
Nevertheless, being able to offload the crypto to worker threads allows for some great throughput improvements. 
     The owner thread only does the bookkeeping, while encryption and decryption run on worker threads.  
 Being a sans-IO library,  sanstun  doesn't concern itself with how exactly you want to parallelize your crypto.
If you want to keep it simple, you can also just call  encrypt  and  decrypt  inline and not bother with parallelization at all. 
 The key thing we wanted to achieve with  sanstun 's API design was to enable parallel crypto while keeping everything around  Interface  single-threaded.
This lets the internal rate limiter work without locks or atomic counters and take advantage of Rust's borrow checker, all while combining state from multiple tunnels. 
  Closing  
 With  sanstun , our fork at   firezone/boringtun   is now deprecated.
If you are building on top of WireGuard, whether that's a VPN, a mesh network or something else entirely, we hope  sanstun  makes your life a little easier.
It is available on  crates.io . 
  sanstun  is open source under the Apache 2.0 license.
Check it out on  GitHub ; issues and pull requests are welcome!   Note:  This repository contains Anthropic's implementation of skills for Claude. For information about the Agent Skills standard, see  agentskills.io . 
 
     
  Skills     
 Skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Claude loads dynamically to improve performance on specialized tasks. Skills teach Claude how to complete specific tasks in a repeatable way, whether that's creating documents with your company's brand guidelines, analyzing data using your organization's specific workflows, or automating personal tasks. 
 For more information, check out: 
 
  What are skills?  
  Using skills in Claude  
  How to create custom skills  
  Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills  
 
  About This Repository     
 This repository contains skills that demonstrate what's possible with Claude's skills system. These skills range from creative applications (art, music, design) to technical tasks (testing web apps, MCP server generation) to enterprise workflows (communications, branding, etc.). 
 Each skill is self-contained in its own folder with a  SKILL.md  file containing the instructions and metadata that Claude uses. Browse through these skills to get inspiration for your own skills or to understand different patterns and approaches. 
 Many skills in this repo are open source (Apache 2.0). We've also included the document creation & editing skills that power  Claude's document capabilities  under the hood in the   skills/docx  ,   skills/pdf  ,   skills/pptx  , and   skills/xlsx   subfolders. These are source-available, not open source, but we wanted to share these with developers as a reference for more complex skills that are actively used in a production AI application. 
  Disclaimer     
  These skills are provided for demonstration and educational purposes only.  While some of these capabilities may be available in Claude, the implementations and behaviors you receive from Claude may differ from what is shown in these skills. These skills are meant to illustrate patterns and possibilities. Always test skills thoroughly in your own environment before relying on them for critical tasks. 
  Skill Sets     
 
  ./skills : Skill examples for Creative & Design, Development & Technical, Enterprise & Communication, and Document Skills 
  ./spec : The Agent Skills specification 
  ./template : Skill template 
 
  Try in Claude Code, Claude.ai, and the API     
  Claude Code     
 You can register this repository as a Claude Code Plugin marketplace by running the following command in Claude Code: 
   /plugin marketplace add anthropics/skills
   
 Then, to install a specific set of skills: 
 
 Select  Browse and install plugins  
 Select  anthropic-agent-skills  
 Select  document-skills  or  example-skills  
 Select  Install now  
 
 Alternatively, directly install either Plugin via: 
   /plugin install document-skills@anthropic-agent-skills
/plugin install example-skills@anthropic-agent-skills
   
 After installing the plugin, you can use the skill by just mentioning it. For instance, if you install the  document-skills  plugin from the marketplace, you can ask Claude Code to do something like: "Use the PDF skill to extract the form fields from  path/to/some-file.pdf " 
  Claude.ai     
 These example skills are all already available to paid plans in Claude.ai. 
 To use any skill from this repository or upload custom skills, follow the instructions in  Using skills in Claude . 
  Claude API     
 You can use Anthropic's pre-built skills, and upload custom skills, via the Claude API. See the  Skills API Quickstart  for more. 
  Creating a Basic Skill     
 Skills are simple to create - just a folder with a  SKILL.md  file containing YAML frontmatter and instructions. You can use the  template-skill  in this repository as a starting point: 
   --- 
 name :  my-skill-name 
 description :  A clear description of what this skill does and when to use it 
 --- 

 #  My Skill Name  

 [ Add your instructions here that Claude will follow when this skill is active ] 

 ##  Examples  
 -  Example usage 1
 -  Example usage 2

 ##  Guidelines  
 -  Guideline 1
 -  Guideline 2  
 The frontmatter requires only two fields:

      Title: The Real Cost of Context: Predicting Compute Time and Energy Consumption in LLM Prefill and Decode Phases 
      Authors:  Lars Krupp ,  Daniel Geißler ,  Francisco M. Calatrava-Nicolas ,  Stefan Gerd Fritsch ,  Paul Lukowicz ,  Jakob Karolus               View a PDF of the paper titled The Real Cost of Context: Predicting Compute Time and Energy Consumption in LLM Prefill and Decode Phases, by Lars Krupp and 5 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into agentic architectures has substantially increased token consumption, raising concerns about their energy footprint. Yet, estimating the energy consumption of proprietary API-based models remains challenging, and existing approaches focus primarily on generated output tokens while overlooking the impact of the large input contexts characteristic of agentic workflows. To address this gap, we systematically profile compute time and energy consumption across a wide range of prefill (input) and decode (output) token lengths. Using generalized linear models, we show that decode compute time and energy scale linearly with output length, whereas prefill compute time and energy exhibit both linear and quadratic scaling with input length. These findings demonstrate that input context becomes a relevant factor for large-context workloads. Furthermore, we show that compute time serves as a reliable proxy for energy consumption when direct energy measurements are unavailable. Our mapping framework enables precise energy estimation and supports more sustainable deployment decisions for agentic AI.
