      Title: Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins 
      Authors:  El Mustapha Mansouri ,  Eikichi Kimura ,  Masato Koga ,  Keigo Arai               View a PDF of the paper titled Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins, by El Mustapha Mansouri and 3 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: An autonomous research laboratory could conduct an entire study, from formulating questions to preparing manuscripts. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers one route towards this goal. Recent AI systems take on several research roles, but may draw conclusions that the evidence does not support. Here, we present an autonomous research laboratory in which agents based on large language models assess one another's work and can stop or redirect investigations. They can generate and reject research questions, require separate theoretical checks and conduct experiments designed to challenge their claims. We demonstrate these capabilities by investigating ensembles of quantum spins in diamond. The agents derived the minimum number of calibration settings needed to predict responses to a defined family of microwave pulse sequences. They checked the result computationally and designed experiments to distinguish competing predictions. An initial experiment agreed with the theoretical predictions, but repeated reference measurements showed that the signal was drifting during data collection. The agents therefore treated the result as inconclusive and revised the measurement protocol without relaxing the acceptance criteria. The revised experiment met those criteria and supported the theoretical predictions. This study demonstrates that collaborating AI agents can select research questions, derive theoretical results and test their predictions experimentally.

--- license: apache-2.0 language: - en - zh library_name: transformers pipeline_tag: text-generation tags: - llm - sparkx2_5 base_model: - XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B-Base --- # Spark-X2.6-4B: Advancing the Frontier of On-Device Agents for Real-World Tasks
[![Slack](https://img.shields.io/badge/Slack-Join-4A154B?logo=slack&logoColor=white)](https://join.slack.com/t/tokenspark/shared_invite/zt-432qf8l2f-5~dLyXv8uETr0P0UuC07nw) [![Discord](https://img.shields.io/badge/Discord-Join-5865F2?logo=discord&logoColor=white)](https://discord.gg/kTDE2Hg8aw) [![YouTube](https://img.shields.io/badge/YouTube-Subscribe-FF0000?logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://www.youtube.com/@SparkLLM) [![dev.to](https://img.shields.io/badge/dev.to-Follow-0A0A0A?logo=devdotto&logoColor=white)](https://dev.to/sparkllm) [![Bluesky](https://img.shields.io/badge/Bluesky-Follow-0285FF?logo=bluesky&logoColor=white)](https://bsky.app/profile/sparkllm.bsky.social) [![X](https://img.shields.io/badge/X-Follow-000000?logo=x&logoColor=white)](https://x.com/sparkllm) [![Zhihu](https://img.shields.io/badge/Zhihu-Follow-0084FF?logo=zhihu&logoColor=white)](https://www.zhihu.com/people/zhiikz7qh7m) [![WeChat](https://img.shields.io/badge/WeChat-Join-07C160?logo=wechat&logoColor=white)](images/xhtoken-wechat.jpg)
> [!Note] > This repository contains model weights and configuration files for the post-trained model in the Hugging Face Transformers format.

## Introduction A little over a month has passed since Spark-X2.5. In the rapidly evolving world of AI agents, that is enough time to rethink, refine, and move the frontier forward. Building on the Spark-X2.5-4B, we introduce **Spark-X2.6-4B**, the latest generation of our compact, general-purpose language models for on-device deployment. Spark-X2.6-4B retains exactly the same architecture as Spark-X2.5-4B, achieving its capability gains through improved post-training. It delivers substantial improvements in coding, agent, long-context, multilingual, reasoning, etc. These advances enable more capable and practical on-device AI for developers and users tackling real-world tasks. **Technical Highlights**: - **Stronger Coding, Agentic, and Long-Context Capabilities**: The models deliver substantial improvements in agentic workflows involving complex tool use, multi-step planning, and software engineering. They achieve state-of-the-art performance among similarly sized open-source models, matching or even surpassing models with approximately 9B parameters. - **Controllable Thinking Budget**: The models provide three configurable thinking levels—none, low, high—allowing applications to balance reasoning quality, latency, and inference cost dynamically. ## Benchmarks We evaluate our models and compare them with leading on-device models of similar size across a broad range of tasks, including agent, code, math, general and knowledge. Spark-X2.6-4B achieves best-in-class performance among models of comparable size, while matching or exceeding the performance of larger 9B models on several benchmarks.

## Edge Inference Spark-X2.6-4B delivers inference efficiency on par with or better than comparable on-device models, including Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma-E4B. It combines this efficiency with stronger capabilities, making it a practical choice for responsive, resource-conscious on-device AI.

## Quickstart ### Transformers Install the required version with `pip install transformers==4.57.1`. ```python from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_id = "XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, trust_remote_code=True, torch_dtype="auto", device_map="auto", ) messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of Anhui Province?"}] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt", ).to(model.device) outputs = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens=131072, do_sample=True, temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=0, ) print(tokenizer.decode(outputs[0][inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]:], skip_special_tokens=True)) ``` ### SGLang The examples below serve a local Spark-X2.6-4B checkpoint. Set `MODEL_PATH` to its absolute path before starting a container: ```bash export MODEL_PATH=/absolute/path/to/Spark-X2.6-4B ``` #### Install SGLang Use the pre-built image that tracks the Spark-X2.6 runtime: ##### For NVIDIA GPUs: ```bash docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-cu13-20260827-20621aa1 ``` ##### For Ascend NPUs: ```bash # A3 daily build export SGLANG_IMAGE=quay.io/ascend/sglang:main-cann9.0.0-a3 # A2 daily build (use this instead on A2 hardware) export SGLANG_IMAGE=quay.io/ascend/sglang:main-cann9.0.0-910b docker pull "$SGLANG_IMAGE" ``` #### Run Inference The following commands start an OpenAI-compatible API server configured for a maximum context length of 1,048,576 tokens. This setting requires sufficient device memory; reduce `--context-length` when necessary. #### Server ##### NVIDIA GPU: ```bash docker run --rm -it \ --gpus '"device=0"' \ --ipc=host \ -p 30000:30000 \ -v "$MODEL_PATH:/root/Spark-X2.6-4B:ro" \ lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-cu13-20260827-20621aa1 \ python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path /root/Spark-X2.6-4B \ --served-model-name spark2.6 \ --tool-call-parser spark25 \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 \ --tp-size 1 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.8 \ --context-length 1048576 \ --chat-template /root/Spark-X2.6-4B/chat_template.jinja \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 30000 ``` ##### Ascend NPU: ```bash docker run -it --rm -e ASCEND_USE_FIA=1 --network=host --ipc=host --shm-size=16g \ --device=/dev/davinci0 --device=/dev/davinci1 --device=/dev/davinci2 --device=/dev/davinci3 \ --device=/dev/davinci4 --device=/dev/davinci5 --device=/dev/davinci6 --device=/dev/davinci7 \ --device=/dev/davinci8 --device=/dev/davinci9 --device=/dev/davinci10 --device=/dev/davinci11 \ --device=/dev/davinci12 --device=/dev/davinci13 --device=/dev/davinci14 --device=/dev/davinci15 \ --device=/dev/davinci_manager \ --device=/dev/devmm_svm \ --device=/dev/hisi_hdc \ --volume /usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/sbin \ --volume /usr/local/Ascend/driver:/usr/local/Ascend/driver \ --volume /usr/local/Ascend/firmware:/usr/local/Ascend/firmware \ --volume /etc/ascend_install.info:/etc/ascend_install.info \ --volume /var/queue_schedule:/var/queue_schedule \ --volume ~/.cache/:/root/.cache/ \ --volume "$MODEL_PATH:/root/Spark-X2.6-4B:ro" \ --entrypoint=python \ "$SGLANG_IMAGE" \ -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path /root/Spark-X2.6-4B \ --served-model-name spark2.6 \ --tool-call-parser spark25 \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 \ --tp-size 1 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.8 \ --context-length 1048576 \ --chat-template /root/Spark-X2.6-4B/chat_template.jinja \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 30000 ``` #### Client Thinking is enabled by default by both the chat template and the Qwen3 reasoning parser. To disable thinking for a specific request, set `"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}`. ```bash curl -s http://localhost:30000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "spark2.6", "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": "安徽的省会在哪里？" } ], "max_tokens": 131072, "temperature": 1, "top_k": -1, "top_p": 0.95, "repetition_penalty": 1, "presence_penalty": 0, "frequency_penalty": 0 }' ``` ### vLLM #### Deploy vLLM vLLM provides an official Docker image for NVIDIA GPU deployment: ```bash docker run --rm --gpus all \ --ipc=host \ -p 30000:30000 \ -v "$MODEL_PATH:/models/Spark-X2.6-4B:ro" \ vllm/vllm-openai:latest \ --model /models/Spark-X2.6-4B \ --port 30000 \ --trust-remote-code \ --served-model-name spark25 \ --tensor-parallel-size 1 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.7 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --chat-template /models/Spark-X2.6-4B/chat_template.jinja ``` For Ascend NPUs, choose an official image for the fastest setup. ##### Ascend A2: ```bash export IMAGE=quay.io/ascend/vllm-ascend:nightly-main docker pull "$IMAGE" export DEVICE=/dev/davinci0 export MODEL_CACHE="${HOME}/.cache" mkdir -p "$MODEL_CACHE" docker run --rm \ --name vllm-ascend \ --shm-size=1g \ --device "$DEVICE" \ --device /dev/davinci_manager \ --device /dev/devmm_svm \ --device /dev/hisi_hdc \ -v /usr/local/dcmi:/usr/local/dcmi \ -v /usr/local/bin/npu-smi:/usr/local/bin/npu-smi \ -v /usr/local/Ascend/driver/lib64/:/usr/local/Ascend/driver/lib64/ \ -v /usr/local/Ascend/driver/version.info:/usr/local/Ascend/driver/version.info \ -v /etc/ascend_install.info:/etc/ascend_install.info \ -v "$MODEL_CACHE:/root/.cache" \ -p 8000:8000 \ -it "$IMAGE" bash ``` ##### Ascend A3: ```bash export IMAGE=quay.io/ascend/vllm-ascend:nightly-main-a3 docker pull "$IMAGE" export DEVICE0=/dev/davinci0 export DEVICE1=/dev/davinci1 export MODEL_CACHE="${HOME}/.cache" mkdir -p "$MODEL_CACHE" docker run --rm \ --name vllm-ascend \ --shm-size=1g \ --device "$DEVICE0" \ --device "$DEVICE1" \ --device /dev/davinci_manager \ --device /dev/devmm_svm \ --device /dev/hisi_hdc \ -v /usr/local/dcmi:/usr/local/dcmi \ -v /usr/local/bin/npu-smi:/usr/local/bin/npu-smi \ -v /usr/local/Ascend/driver/lib64/:/usr/local/Ascend/driver/lib64/ \ -v ``` ##### Ascend 950DT: ```bash export IMAGE=quay.io/ascend/vllm-ascend:nightly-main-a5 docker pull "$IMAGE" export MODEL_CACHE="${HOME}/.cache" mkdir -p "$MODEL_CACHE" docker run --rm \ --name vllm-ascend \ --net=host \ --shm-size=1g \ --device /dev/davinci0 \ --device /dev/davinci_manager \ --device /dev/devmm_svm \ --device /dev/hisi_hdc \ -v /usr/local/dcmi:/usr/local/dcmi \ -v \ -v "$MODEL_CACHE:/root/.cache" \ -it "$IMAGE" bash ``` Install the Spark plugin inside the container: ```bash pip install uv uv venv ~/spark2_6 source ~/spark2_6/bin/activate git clone https://github.com/XHToken/Spark-plugin.git cd ./Spark-plugin uv pip install . ``` #### Server ```bash vllm serve "/models/Spark-X2.6-4B" \ --port "30000" \ --trust-remote-code \ --served-model-name spark25 \ --tensor-parallel-size 1 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.7 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --chat-template /models/Spark-X2.6-4B/chat_template.jinja ``` #### Client ```bash curl -s http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "spark25", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of Anhui Province?"}], "temperature": 1.0, "top_k": -1, "top_p": 0.95 }' ``` ### MLX Spark-MLX-LLM runs the original Spark-X2.6 Hugging Face checkpoints locally. It supports Apple silicon GPU, Linux CPU, and NVIDIA CUDA on Linux. No GGUF conversion is required. #### Installation ```bash git clone https://github.com/XHToken/Spark-MLX-LLM.git cd Spark-MLX-LLM python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate # Apple silicon python -m pip install -e . # Linux CPU python -m pip install -e '.[cpu]' # Linux with CUDA 12 python -m pip install -e '.[cuda12]' # Linux with CUDA 13 python -m pip install -e '.[cuda13]' ``` #### Run Inference ```bash spark-mlx-generate \ --device gpu \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --model XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B \ --prompt "What is the capital of Anhui Province?" \ --max-tokens 512 \ --temp 0 ``` ### llama.cpp > [!NOTE] > Native `spark2_5` support requires [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/) `b10828` or later. Run the model in the CLI: ```bash llama cli -m /path/to/Spark-X2.6-4B-GGUF ``` Launch the OpenAI-compatible API server: ```bash llama serve -m /path/to/Spark-X2.6-4B-GGUF ``` ### Ollama 1. Download and install Ollama from [ollama.com](https://ollama.com/download) (v0.34.1 or later). 2. Run the model: ```bash ollama run SparkLLM/Spark-X2.6-4B ``` ### LM Studio 1. Download and install LM Studio from [lmstudio.ai](https://lmstudio.ai/download) (0.4.0 or later). 2. Search for "Spark-X2.6" in LM Studio and download the model. 3. Load the model and start chatting. #### Run with the lms cli ```bash # List available models lms ls # Run chat with Spark-X2.6 lms chat spark-x2.6 ``` ### Unsloth [Download Unsloth Studio](https://unsloth.ai/) > [!NOTE] > The latest Unsloth Studio supports native Spark-X2.6 GGUF inference. ### WebGPU (Community) Run Spark-X2.6-4B locally in your browser with the community WebGPU demo contributed by [Mohd Mahmodi](https://huggingface.co/mohdmahmodi). 1. Open the [WebGPU demo](https://huggingface.co/spaces/mohdmahmodi/Spark-X2.6-WebGPU) in a WebGPU-compatible browser. 2. Download the model through the demo and start chatting. Inference runs on your local GPU. [ONNX model files](https://huggingface.co/mohdmahmodi/Spark-X2.6-4B-ONNX-WebGPU) · [Source code and validation](https://github.com/mohdmahmodi/Spark-X2.6-4B-onnx-webgpu) > [!NOTE] > This community implementation uses the official Spark-X2.6-4B-INT4 weights and requires no local installation. Tested by the contributor on Windows with an NVIDIA GPU. > ### Fine-Tuning We recommend using [Llama-Factory](https://github.com/XHToken/LlamaFactory) to fine-tune the model. ## License The Spark-X2.6 model series is licensed under the [Apache 2.0 License](LICENSE). ## Citation If you find our work helpful, feel free to give us a cite. ```bibtex @misc{sparkx2.6, title = {Spark-X2.6-4B&1.7B: Advancing the Frontier of On-Device Agents for Real-World Tasks}, author = {SparkLLM Team}, year = {2026} } ```

      Title: Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm 
      Authors:  Yuda Song ,  Alvin Zhang ,  Fahim Tajwar ,  Daman Arora ,  Jeff Schneider ,  Daniel Khashabi ,  Ruslan Salakhutdinov ,  J. Andrew Bagnell ,  Aarti Singh ,  Andrea Zanette               View a PDF of the paper titled Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm, by Yuda Song and 9 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Foundation models are typically trained in stages: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL), with changes in both data and learning algorithms. We show that this algorithmic separation is not fundamental. By deriving suitable RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, we place all of these stages under a single likelihood-based training algorithm, unified training. This perspective turns the foundation-model training lifecycle into a problem of choosing which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with conventional staged training as a special case. We instantiate this framework in a unified training system that mixes static data and RL generations within a single trainer. Across controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy-compute tradeoff and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities, and provides a stronger starting point for continual learning. This work lays the groundwork for a unified science of foundation-model training, connecting mathematical principles, training infrastructure, and the development of model capabilities.

# Mistral Large 4 - Le Chonk

Mistral Large 4 is our largest and most capable model to date: a 1 trillion-parameter natively multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model with 49 billion active parameters per token (52 billion including embeddings and output layers), trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral's own datacenters in Europe.

Mistral Large 4 unifies instruction following, reasoning, coding, and agentic workflows in a single set of weights. While a generalist model, it shows especially good performance on workloads such as cybersecurity, finance, and law, and it surpasses frontier closed models on visual grounding. It is natively fluent in 160+ languages, including every official language of the European Union.

Find more information on our [blog](https://mistral.ai/news/mistral-large-4-oss/). The model is also served on the [Mistral API](https://docs.mistral.ai/models/mistral-large-4-0) as `mistral-large-4`.

> [!Note]
> The checkpoint ships with an embedded DSpark speculative decoding draft head — see [Speculative decoding (DSpark)](#speculative-decoding-dspark).

> [!Note]
> A quantized [NVFP4 checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-NVFP4) is also available, with a smaller memory footprint, faster inference and same performance. It targets Blackwell GPUs and supports vLLM and SGLang.

## Key Features

Mistral Large 4 includes the following architectural choices:

- **~1T total / ~52B active parameters**: granular Mixture-of-Experts with 128 routed experts (4 active per token) and 1 shared expert.
- **1M context length**, for long-context workloads.
- **Multimodal input**: accepts text and image input, with text output. Pixtral-style vision encoder trained to handle variable image sizes and aspect ratios.
- **Instruct and Reasoning functionalities** with function calls, reasoning effort configurable per request.

Mistral Large 4 offers the following capabilities:

- **Reasoning Mode**: three reasoning efforts — `low`, `medium`, `high` (default) — so the same model can answer a quick chat reply or work through a complex agentic run.
- **Vision**: analyzes images, charts, technical drawings, and documents, with state-of-the-art visual grounding among open weights.
- **Multilingual**: natively fluent in 160+ languages, including all official languages of the European Union.
- **System Prompt**: strong adherence and support for system prompts.
- **Agentic**: native function calling, JSON output, and strict JSON schema enforcement.
- **Cybersecurity**: state of the art among open-weight models for security work, while refusing malicious requests.
- **Large Context Window**: supports a 1M context window.

We release this model under the [**Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License**](https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B/blob/main/LICENSE): a modified version of the MIT license, for both commercial and non-commercial use — operating a Model-as-a-Service business requires a separate commercial license with Mistral.

## Recommended Settings

- **Reasoning Effort**:
  - `'low'` / `'medium'` / `'high'` — default is `'high'`.
  - Use `reasoning_effort="high"` for complex prompts and agentic usage, `'low'` for fast chat replies and `'medium'` for day to day usage.
- **Sampling**: for all reasoning efforts, we recommend the following sampling parameters:
  - `temperature=1.0`
  - `top_p=0.95`
- **System Prompt**: define a clear environment and use case, including guidance on how to effectively leverage tools in agentic systems.
- **Tools**: keep the set of tools well-defined and limit their number to the minimum required for the use case.
- **Context**: the checkpoint supports a 1M context window.

## Benchmarks

We compared Mistral Large 4 with recent open-weight models. We report results on agentic coding and global intelligence here; for more benchmarks, especially on cybersecurity, finance and law, see our [blog post](https://mistral.ai/news/mistral-large-4-oss/).

### Agentic Coding

Mistral Large 4 delivers frontier coding performance with significantly fewer tokens, making sophisticated coding agents more economical to run at scale.

On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, ML4 scores **48%**, effectively tied with the leading open-weight model, GLM-5.3, while using **47%** fewer tokens per task on average.

![Artificial Analysis - Coding Agent Index](images/coding_index.png)

### Global Intelligence

On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, Mistral Large 4 scores **26**, the highest among western open-weight models. The leading open-weight models from China score higher on this aggregate index, but Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong on coding and cybersecurity, as shown in our [blog post](https://mistral.ai/news/mistral-large-4-oss/).

![Artificial Analysis - Intelligence Index v5](images/intelligence_index.png)

## Demo Gallery

[Le Chonk Gallery](https://mistralai-ml4-le-chonk-gallery.hf.space/) is a live gallery of demo Spaces built with Mistral Large 4, from us and from the community: coding, vision and grounding, tool calls, JSON schema, multilingual, and more. Any Space tagged `Le_chonk` appears there.

Official demos run on the Mistral API with a small shared free budget per visitor for the first week of the release, so you can try the model without paying. You can also use your own Mistral API key.

To build a demo, we recommend [Mistral Vibe](https://github.com/mistralai/mistral-vibe), our coding agent powered by Mistral Large 4.

## Usage

You can find Mistral Large 4 support on multiple libraries for inference and fine-tuning.

We **thank** all the ecosystem folks who helped us throughout this release to integrate Le Chonk into their frameworks.

The model can be deployed with:

- [`vllm (recommended)`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm): See [here](#vllm-recommended) or [vLLM's recipes](https://recipes.vllm.ai/mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B).
- [`SGLang`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang): See [here](#sglang) or SGLang’s [cookbook](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/Mistral/Mistral-Large-4).
- [`transformers`](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers): See [here](#transformers) or [Hugging Face’s blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/mistral-large4).
- [`llama.cpp`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp): See GGUFs and instructions [here](https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-GGUF).

Fine-tune the model via:

- [`Axolotl`](https://github.com/axolotl-ai-cloud/axolotl): See [here](https://docs.axolotl.ai/docs/models/mistral-large-4.html).
- [`Unsloth`](https://unsloth.ai/): See [here](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/mistral-large-4) for a guide and [here](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-GGUF) for their GGUFs.
- [`TRL`](https://github.com/huggingface/trl): See [here](https://huggingface.co/blog/mistral-large4#fine-tuning-with-trl).

> [!Note]
> For optimal performance, we recommend using the Mistral AI API if local serving is subpar.

## vLLM (Recommended)

We recommend using Mistral Large 4 with the [vLLM library](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm) for production-ready inference.

See also the [vLLM recipe for Mistral Large 4](https://recipes.vllm.ai/mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B) for ready-made serving configurations.

### Installation

Use the official vLLM Docker image, which includes support for Mistral Large 4:

```bash
docker pull vllm/vllm-openai:mistral-large-4
```

### Serve the Model

We recommend a server/client setup:

```bash
docker run --runtime nvidia --gpus all \
  -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \
  -p 8000:8000 \
  --ipc=host \
  vllm/vllm-openai:mistral-large-4 \
  --model mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --tool-call-parser mistral \
  --reasoning-parser mistral \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85
```

Key parameter notes:

- `--tool-call-parser mistral` and `--reasoning-parser mistral`: required for tool usage and to separate reasoning from content in responses.
- If you run short of GPU memory, lower `--max-model-len` and/or `--max-num-seqs` (concurrency). See the [vLLM guide on conserving memory](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/configuration/conserving_memory/#context-length-and-batch-size).

### Ping the Server

`max_completion_tokens` includes reasoning tokens as well as visible output tokens.

```py
openai_api_key = "EMPTY"
openai_api_base = "http://localhost:8000/v1"

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=openai_api_key,
    base_url=openai_api_base,

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=model,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Write me a sentence where every word starts with the next letter in the alphabet - start with 'a' and end with 'z'.",
        }
    ],
    reasoning_effort="low",  # Increase with 'medium' or 'high'.
    temperature=1.0,
    top_p=0.95,
    max_completion_tokens=4096,
)

print("REASONING")
print("~~~~~~~~~")
print(response.choices[0].message.reasoning)
print("CONTENT")
print("~~~~~~~")
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

<details>
<summary>Strict JSON Schema</summary>

Mistral Large 4 enforces response formats natively, including strict JSON schemas.

```py
from openai import OpenAI

# Modify OpenAI's API key and API base to use vLLM's API server.
openai_api_key = "EMPTY"
openai_api_base = "http://localhost:8000/v1"

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=openai_api_key,
    base_url=openai_api_base,
)

model = client.models.list().data[0].id

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=model,
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "What is 1 + 1? Answer as JSON."}
    ],
    reasoning_effort="medium",
    temperature=1.0,
    top_p=0.95,
    response_format={
        "type": "json_schema",
        "json_schema": {
            "name": "arithmetic_answer",
            "strict": True,
            "schema": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {"answer": {"type": "string"}},
                "required": ["answer"],
                "additionalProperties": False,
            },
        },
    },
    max_completion_tokens=16384,
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Vision and Tool Call</summary>

Let's solve some equations thanks to our simple Python calculator tool.

```py
import json

from openai import OpenAI

# Modify OpenAI's API key and API base to use vLLM's API server.
openai_api_key = "EMPTY"
openai_api_base = "http://localhost:8000/v1"

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=openai_api_key,
    base_url=openai_api_base,
)

model = client.models.list().data[0].id

image_url = "https://math-coaching.com/img/fiche/46/expressions-mathematiques.jpg"

def my_calculator(expression: str) -> str:
    return str(eval(expression))

tools = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "my_calculator",
            "description": "A calculator that can evaluate a mathematical expression.",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "expression": {
                        "type": "string",
                        "description": "The mathematical expression to evaluate.",
                    },
                },
                "required": ["expression"],
            },
        },
    }
]

messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {
                "type": "text",
                "text": "Thanks to your calculator, compute the results for the equations that involve numbers displayed in the image.",
            },
            {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": image_url}},
        ],
    }
]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=model,
    messages=messages,
    tools=tools,
    tool_choice="auto",
    reasoning_effort="high",
    temperature=1.0,
    top_p=0.95,
)

tool_calls = response.choices[0].message.tool_calls

results = []
for tool_call in tool_calls:
    function_name = tool_call.function.name
    function_args = tool_call.function.arguments
    if function_name == "my_calculator":
        result = my_calculator(**json.loads(function_args))
        results.append(result)

messages.append({"role": "assistant", "tool_calls": tool_calls})
for tool_call, result in zip(tool_calls, results):
    messages.append(
        {
            "role": "tool",
            "tool_call_id": tool_call.id,
            "name": tool_call.function.name,
            "content": result,
        }
    )

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=model,
    messages=messages,
    reasoning_effort="high",
    temperature=1.0,
    top_p=0.95,
)

print("REASONING")
print("~~~~~~~~~")
print(response.choices[0].message.reasoning)
print("CONTENT")
print("~~~~~~~")
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

</details>

### Speculative decoding (DSpark)

The checkpoint ships a DSpark draft head next to the target weights: 3 dense MLA draft layers in BF16 that propose a block of 3 tokens with a recurrent Markov head.

To enable it, add the following argument to the serving command above:

```bash
--speculative-config '{"method": "dspark", "num_speculative_tokens": 3}'
```

`num_speculative_tokens` is set to 3, the depth of the draft block.

DSpark speeds up decoding without changing the target model's outputs: we measured up to **1.9x** higher throughput than serving the target model alone. Actual gains depend on hardware and workload.

## SGLang

Serve Mistral Large 4 with the [SGLang library](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang) for production-ready inference. See also SGLang's [cookbook](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/Mistral/Mistral-Large-4).

### Installation

Use the official SGLang Docker image, which includes support for Mistral Large 4:

```bash
docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:mistral-large-4
```

### Serve the Model

```bash
sglang serve \
  --model-path mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B \
  --tp-size 8 \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \
  --speculative-algorithm DSPARK \
  --max-running-requests 64 \
  --reasoning-parser auto \
  --tool-call-parser auto \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 30000
```

> [!Note]
> Speculative decoding (DSpark) is on and this recipe pins `--max-running-requests` to **64**. Adjust it to match your target concurrency — if you remove the flag, SGLang falls back to **48**.

Key parameter notes:

- `--speculative-algorithm DSPARK`: enables the embedded DSpark draft head, which proposes blocks of 3 tokens. Remove this flag to serve without speculation.
- `--tp-size 8`: example tensor-parallel size for a node of 8 GPUs; adjust to your topology.
- `--reasoning-parser auto` and `--tool-call-parser auto`: let SGLang pick the reasoning and tool-call parsers for this model.

## Transformers

For more details, check [Hugging Face’s blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/mistral-large4).

Install Transformers from `main`:

```bash
uv pip install git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers
```

<details>
<summary>Python Inference Snippet</summary>

Save the following as `script.py`:

```py
import os
from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM, DistributedConfig

distributed_config = DistributedConfig(
    tp_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]),
    ep_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]),
)

model_id = "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B"
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    distributed_config=distributed_config,
    dtype="auto",
)

# only text
text_messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": "Who are you?"
    }
]

# text + image
messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {
                "type": "image",
                "image": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/cats-image/resolve/main/cats_image.jpeg",
            },
            {
                "type": "text",
                "text": "How many cats are in the image?",
            },
        ],
    },
]

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages, # text_messages
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
    reasoning_effort="medium", # low, medium, high
).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)
input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=100)
if int(os.environ["RANK"]) == 0:
    print(processor.decode(outputs[0][input_len:], skip_special_tokens=False))
```

Then run it on 8 GPUs with `torchrun`:

```bash
torchrun --nproc-per-node 8 script.py
```

</details>

## Mistral-Vibe

Use Mistral Large 4 with [Mistral Vibe](https://github.com/mistralai/mistral-vibe), our open-source CLI coding assistant.

### Installation

Install Vibe with the one-line installer (Linux and macOS):

```bash
curl -LsSf https://mistral.ai/vibe/install.sh | bash
```

Or with `uv` or `pip`:

```bash
uv tool install mistral-vibe
# or
pip install mistral-vibe
```

Then run `vibe` in your project. On first launch it asks for your Mistral API key and saves it to `~/.vibe/.env`. To use Mistral Large 4 through the Mistral API, select `mistral-large-4` as the model.

### Local server

To use a local vLLM server instead, add this to `~/.vibe/config.toml`:

```toml
display_name = "Mistral Large 4 (local vLLM)"
description = "Mistral Large 4 mode using local vLLM"
safety = "neutral"

active_model = "mistral-large-4" # Make sure this is the only active_model entry
[[providers]]
name = "vllm"
api_base = "http://<your-host-url>:8000/v1"
api_key_env_var = ""
backend = "generic"
api_style = "reasoning"

[[models]]
name = "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B"
provider = "vllm"
alias = "mistral-large-4"
thinking = "high"
thinking_levels = ["low", "medium", "high"]
temperature = 1.0
supports_images = true
max_context_length = 1048576
auto_compact_threshold = 800000

[tools.bash]
default_timeout = 1200
```

**Notes**:

- Replace `<your-host-url>` with your server's URL.
- Other inference backends are also supported. Please look at [Mistral Vibe repo](https://github.com/mistralai/mistral-vibe) for more info.

           Published
					October 29, 2026          Update on GitHub                  Upvote  51                                                                 +45                                                merve      merve                  Follow                                      Alvaro Bartolome      alvarobartt                  Follow                                      Rémi Ouazan Reboul      ror                  Follow                                      Cyril Vallez      cyrilvallez                  Follow                                      Quentin Gallouédec      qgallouedec                  Follow                                      Enrique Hernández Calabrés      ehcalabres                  Follow                                      Juan Julián      juanjucm                  Follow                                      Xuan-Son Nguyen      ngxson                  Follow                                      Pedro Cuenca      pcuenq                  Follow                                      ben burtenshaw      burtenshaw                  Follow                                      Aritra Roy Gosthipaty      ariG23498                  Follow                                   :last-child]:mb-0">                   Table of Contents           What is new with Mistral Large 4        Cybersecurity Capabilities              Architecture        Vision encoder              Benchmark Results           Inference Support        Transformers           vLLM           Llama.cpp              Fine-tuning with TRL           Inference Endpoints           Dell Enterprise Hub           Try it out                    
 Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about  1T total, 49B active parameter , and a context window of  1M tokens . 
 The model is released in two official variants: 
 
  FP8  
  NVFP4  
 
 There are also  GGUFs  created by  Unsloth  and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings). 
 Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more! 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Table of Contents

		What is new with Mistral Large 4
	 
 
  Mistral Large 4  combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a  Pixtral  vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions. 
 You can find all the checkpoints in the  Mistral Large 4 collection . 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Cybersecurity Capabilities
	 
 
 Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for. 
 Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model. 
 For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with  TRL you could fine-tune  smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description. 
 In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community. 
 
 We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model,  you can watch it here . 
 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Architecture
	 
 
     
 Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query. 
     For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers. The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token. 
 Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses  LeRope , a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency. 
     
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Vision encoder
	 
 
 Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below. 
     
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Benchmark Results
	 
 
 Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index. 
 On coding, ML4 achieves  61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1 ,  59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA , and  28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4 . Its combined  Coding Agent Index score of 49.8%  places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max. 
 Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with  59.9% on AutomationBench  and  1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase , which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks. 
 Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance: 
 
  Artificial Analysis Cyber Index:  ML4 ranks among the  top five models globally  on this independent evaluation of models’ ability to find and fix software vulnerabilities.   
  Vulnerability reproduction and patching:  It achieves  82% , the highest reported score on this test within the index. The task requires reproducing a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patching it, testing both investigation and remediation.   
  Cybench:  ML4 solves  93%  of a suite of  40 challenges drawn from security competitions , demonstrating strong performance on hands-on security problems. 
 
 Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates  93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark , adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation. 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Inference Support
	 
 
 Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the  llama.cpp team . We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers. 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Transformers
	 
 
 The Transformers implementation provides  AutoModelForMultimodalLM , with  AutoProcessor  preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take  low ,  medium ,  high  as reasoning effort. The default is  high , and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using  reasoning_effort :  none  would still use  high . 
 To run the model, upgrade the transformers package 
  pip install --upgrade transformers
  
   import  os
 from  transformers  import  AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM, DistributedConfig

distributed_config = DistributedConfig(
    tp_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]),
    ep_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]),
)

model_id =  "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B" 
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    distributed_config=distributed_config,
)

 # only text 
text_messages = [
    {
         "role" :  "user" ,
         "content" :  "Who are you?" 
    }
]

 # text + image 
multimodal_messages = [
    {
         "role" :  "user" ,
         "content" : [
            {
                 "type" :  "image" ,
                 "image" :  "https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/cats-image/resolve/main/cats_image.jpeg" ,
            },
            {
                 "type" :  "text" ,
                 "text" :  "How many cats are in the image?" ,
            },
        ],
    },
]

 for  messages  in  [text_messages, multimodal_messages]:
    inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
        messages,
        add_generation_prompt= True ,
        tokenize= True ,
        return_dict= True ,
        return_tensors= "pt" ,
        reasoning_effort= "medium" ,
    ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)
    input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ]

    outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 100 )
     if   int (os.environ[ "RANK" ]) ==  0 :
         print (processor.decode(outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], skip_special_tokens= False ))
  
 You can run the script above by saving it in a python file  script.py  and then run 
  torchrun --nproc-per-node 8 script.py
  
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		vLLM
	 
 
 vLLM supports the high-quality NVFP4 Mistral Large 4 checkpoint, which has a smaller memory footprint and requires NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. The model also ships with a DSpark drafter for additional speed-ups with vLLM. Launch the server like this: 
  vllm serve mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-NVFP4 \
  --config-format mistral \
  --load-format mistral \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --decode-context-parallel-size 8 \
  --enable-expert-parallel \
  --dtype bfloat16 \
  --max-model-len 131072 \
  --max-num-seqs 16 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 2048 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --enforce-eager \
  --mm_processor_cache_gb 0.0
  
 Once the server is up and running, you can run the following. 
  curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions -H  'Content-Type: application/json'  \
  -d  '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is 17*23?"}],"max_tokens":512}' 
  
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Llama.cpp
	 
 
 Llama.cpp and  Llama App  already support Mistral Large 4. 
 You can install Llama App with the following command: 
  curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh
  
 Then you can start the server as follows, indicating the quant suffix after the model ID: 
  llama serve -hf ggml-org/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-GGUF:Q2_K
  
  Here’s the repository  with the  quants derived from the FP8 checkpoint, and  this is the NVFP4 one , converted from the official NVFP4 repo. 
 Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat using the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever. You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out  the API reference  for multimodality, tool calls and more. 
  curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
    -H  "Content-Type: application/json"  \
    -d  '{ 
         "messages": [ 
             {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."}, 
             {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"} 
         ] 
     }' 
  
 You can run image-text inference as follows. 
  curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
    -H  "Content-Type: application/json"  \
    -H  "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>"  \
    -d  '{ 
         "model": "muse-spark-open", 
         "messages": [ 
             { 
                 "role": "user", 
                 "content": [ 
                     { 
                         "type": "text", 
                         "text": "What is in this image?" 
                     }, 
                     { 
                         "type": "image_url", 
                         "image_url": { 
                             "url": "data:image/png;base64,..." 
                         } 
                     } 
                 ] 
             } 
         ], 
         "temperature": 0 
     }' 
  
 The llama.cpp team ships the following quants:  IQ2_XXS ,  Q2_K ,  Q4_K_M ,  NVFP4 ,  Q8_0 , and  BF16  for further conversions. The 2-bit quants run on a single Apple Silicon Ultra computer with 512 GB of unified RAM. The others require distributed inference. You can also run on multiple NVIDIA or AMD cards. 
 Running  Q2_K  on a single M3 Ultra, we got a prefill throughput of about 90 tokens per second, and a generation speed of 15 tok/s. On 4 x RTX6000 Pro, we observed the following results: 
 
 NVFP4: 32K context size, prefill 130-590 t/s, gen speed ~10 t/s   
 IQ2_XXS: 800K context size. At short context sizes, prefill is 500 tok/s and generation runs at 30 tok/s. However, using long contexts performance drops to 129 tok/s (prefill) and 3 tok/s (generation). 
 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Fine-tuning with TRL
	 
 
 We also ship day 0 support of fine tuning Mistral Large 4 using TRL. All you have to do is upgrade to the latest version of  transformers ,  trl  and  peft . 
  pip install --upgrade transformers trl peft
  
 In the following example we train the model to perform multilingual thinking. The fine tuned model would be able to reason in the language the system prompt asks for! 
 The script runs on the FP8 variant on a node of 8xB300s. The full example, with a Slurm launcher, is in  TRL's examples . 
   # torchrun --nproc-per-node 8 sft.py 
 import  os

 from  datasets  import  load_dataset
 from  peft  import  LoraConfig
 from  transformers  import  AutoModelForImageTextToText, DistributedConfig
 from  trl  import  SFTConfig, SFTTrainer

world_size =  int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ])
model_id =  "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B" 
model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    distributed_config=DistributedConfig(fsdp_size=world_size, ep_size=world_size),
    dtype= "auto" ,
)

dataset = load_dataset( "HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking" , split= "train" )
 # the assistant turns carry reasoning, so render them in reasoning mode 
dataset = dataset. map ( lambda  x: { "chat_template_kwargs" : { "reasoning_effort" :  "high" }})

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    args=SFTConfig(
        packing= True ,
        max_length= 4096 ,
        assistant_only_loss= True ,
        learning_rate= 1e-4 ,
        lr_scheduler_type= "cosine" ,
        warmup_steps= 10 ,
    ),
    train_dataset=dataset,
    peft_config=LoraConfig(
        r= 16 ,
        lora_alpha= 32 ,
        target_modules= r".*language_model.*\.(q_proj|kv_a_proj_with_mqa|kv_b_proj|o_proj|gate_proj|up_proj|down_proj)" ,
    ),
)
trainer.train()
  
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Inference Endpoints
	 
 
 Mistral Large 4 is also available on Inference Endpoints, with a ready-to-deploy recipe on 8 x NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The recipe runs vLLM with the FP8 weights split across all eight GPUs using tensor and expert parallelism, and uses the model's built-in DSpark draft head for faster generation through speculative decoding. It serves up to 131K tokens of context and processes up to 16 requests at a time, and we observed the following results: 
 
 Single request: time to first token of about 0.6 seconds for a 1K-token prompt, and a generation speed of ~65 tok/s, reaching 120–138 tok/s on chat prompts where DSpark's drafts are accepted.   
 Long prompts: 16K-token prompts, four at a time, are prefilled at about 4,300 tok/s in total, with a time to first token of 8–9 seconds.   
 Under load: about 480 tok/s of total generation across 1,000 ShareGPT conversations. 
 
 You can deploy it with the  hf  CLI as follows: 
  hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B --name mistral-large-4
  
 Once the endpoint is running, you can query its OpenAI-compatible API, using the endpoint URL and your Hugging Face token. The  reasoning_effort  field controls how much the model reasons before answering, and can be set to  low ,  medium , or  high  (default). 
  curl  " $(hf endpoints describe mistral-large-4 --json | jq -r .status.url) /v1/chat/completions"  \
    -H  "Authorization: Bearer  $(hf auth token 2>/dev/null) "  \
    -H  "Content-Type: application/json"  \
    -d  '{ 
         "model": "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B", 
         "messages": [ 
             {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"} 
         ], 
         "reasoning_effort": "medium" 
     }' 
  
 The answer comes back in  choices[0].message.content , and the reasoning in  choices[0].message.reasoning . The endpoint also supports tool calls, structured outputs, image inputs, and streaming through the standard Chat Completions fields. 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Dell Enterprise Hub
	 
 
 The easiest way to get up and running with your Dell AI Servers (NVIDIA H200, B200, GB200 or GB300) is by installing the  dell-ai  CLI: 
  pip install dell-ai && dell-ai login
  
 And use it to run an optimized recipe for Mistral Large 4 on e.g., a NVIDIA B300 node. 
  dell-ai models deploy --model-id mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-NVFP4 \
    --engine docker \
    --platform-id xe9780-nvidia-b300 \
    --gpus 4
  
 You can find more about this release in the  Dell Enterprise Hub (DEH) . 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Try it out
	 
 
 Grab the weights from the  Mistral Large 4 collection , run them locally with the  GGUFs , or deploy them with Inference Endpoints. We can't wait to see what you build with Le Chonk. Share your fine-tunes, quants and other artefacts on the Hub!

       GitLab Docs    Use GitLab    Release notes    GitLab 19    GitLab 19.2    19.2.8         GitLab Critical Patch Release: 19.4.2, 19.3.5, 19.2.8    On October 12, 2026, we released versions 19.4.2, 19.3.5, 19.2.8 for GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE).       19.3.4 had a bug that affected merge request pages when the Ona integration was enabled. This is fixed in 19.3.5.     These versions contain important bug and security fixes, and we strongly recommend that all self-managed GitLab installations be upgraded to
one of these versions immediately. GitLab.com is already running the patched version.
All GitLab Dedicated tenants were patched using an internal release before this patch
release was published.  GitLab releases fixes for vulnerabilities in patch releases. There are two types of patch releases:
scheduled releases and ad-hoc critical patches for high-severity vulnerabilities. Scheduled releases are released twice a month on the second and fourth Wednesdays.
For more information, please visit our  releases handbook  and  security FAQ .
You can see all of GitLab release blog posts  here .  For security fixes, the issues detailing each vulnerability are made public on our
 issue tracker 
90 days after the release in which they were patched.  We are committed to ensuring that all aspects of GitLab that are exposed to customers or that host customer data are held to
the highest security standards. To maintain good security hygiene, it is highly recommended that all customers
upgrade to the latest patch release for their supported version. You can read more
 best practices in securing your GitLab instance  in our blog post.  Recommended Action  We  strongly recommend  that all installations running a version affected by the issues described below are  upgraded to the latest version as soon as possible .  When no specific deployment type (omnibus, source code, helm chart, etc.) of a product is mentioned, it means all types are affected. Compiler impacts GitLab CE/EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server via a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration, due to insufficient regular expression validation.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  10.0 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H  )  Thanks  joaxcar  for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program.  Detecting  CVE-2026-97229  Exploitation Attempts  GitLab security has released six threat detections to support customers with self-managed instances, listed below. GitLab-managed infrastructure, including GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated, remains patched.    Onigmo native worker crash    Graphql cilint hostile regexp    ci regexp oversized non ascii path    ci regexp guard rejection    ci lint workhorse worker crash    ci lint scripted client error burst     CVE-2026-92883  - Cross-site Scripting issue in syntax highlighting impacts GitLab CE/EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the context of other users’ browser sessions via a specially crafted repository, due to improper sanitization of HTML attributes in syntax-highlighted output.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 19.1 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  8.7 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N  )  Thanks  a0xnirudh  for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program.   CVE-2026-16301  - Improper Authorization issue in downstream pipeline creation service impacts GitLab CE/EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user with Developer role to execute CI/CD pipelines on protected branches without authorization due to improper authorization checks in the downstream pipeline creation service.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 18.7 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  8.5 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:H/A:N  )  Thanks  sim4n6  for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program.   CVE-2026-14814  - Permissive Regular Expression issue in repository file access impacts GitLab CE/EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed a user to poison cached responses for raw repository files, causing targeted users’ CI/CD pipelines to execute specially crafted content and potentially exposing protected environment variables, due to improper validation of repository references.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab CE/EE: all versions before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  8.2 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N  )  Thanks  ahacker1  for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program.   CVE-2026-81839  - Incorrect Authorization issue in scheduled pipeline execution policy impacts GitLab EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user to execute arbitrary CI/CD pipelines in a transferred project with the new group’s privileges due to improper cleanup of scheduled pipeline execution policy records.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab EE: all versions from 18.1 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  7.7 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N  )  Thanks  no_01  for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program.   CVE-2026-96893  - Improper Neutralization of Input Used for LLM Prompting issue in GitLab Duo Agent Platform impacts GitLab EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user to inject specially crafted content into AI agent instructions, potentially causing unintended command execution attributed to other users, due to improper neutralization of special elements in AI conversation context construction.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab EE: all versions from 19.1 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  7.3 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N  )  This vulnerability has been discovered internally by GitLab team member Mert Coskuner.   CVE-2026-101168  - Sensitive Information Exposure issue in GitLab Pages impacts GitLab CE/EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user with access to GitLab Pages log data to obtain access tokens and other secrets, due to insertion of sensitive request data into log files and error tracking events.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 12.0 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  6.2 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N  )  This vulnerability has been discovered internally by GitLab team member RJ Coleman.   CVE-2026-7767  - Open Redirect issue in Kubernetes proxy impacts GitLab CE/EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user controlling a Kubernetes agent to cause sensitive authentication tokens to be sent to an unintended server due to improper redirect validation in the Kubernetes proxy.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 13.11 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  5.8 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N  )  Thanks  joaxcar  for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program.   CVE-2026-16275  - Incorrect Authorization issue in GraphQL notes widget impacts GitLab CE/EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to read confidential notes on public projects due to incorrect authorization checks.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 17.4 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  5.3 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N  )  Thanks  jaykp  for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program.   CVE-2026-84284  - Incorrect Authorization issue in GraphQL work item hierarchy impacts GitLab CE/EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to read work item contents from private groups and projects due to incorrect authorization checks.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 17.11 before 19.2.8, all 19.3 versions, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  5.3 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N  )  Thanks  modhanami  for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program.   CVE-2026-85529  - Incorrect Authorization issue in GraphQL scope impacts GitLab CE/EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to read internal notes and confidential system notes on public projects due to improper authorization in the GraphQL API.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  5.3 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N  )  Thanks  silaen_space  for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program.   CVE-2026-100755  - Page cache poisoning via improper cache key construction in merge requests impacts GitLab CE/EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain deployment configurations, could have allowed an authenticated user to poison cached page content served to other users due to improper cache key construction.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 16.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  4.6 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L  )  This vulnerability has been discovered internally by GitLab team member Peter Arts.   CVE-2026-14552  - Incorrect Authorization issue in work items GraphQL API impacts GitLab CE/EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user with Guest access to read confidential epic content meant to be restricted by external authorization, due to incorrect authorization checks.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 17.0 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  4.3 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N  )  Thanks  3nvz  for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program.   CVE-2026-6567  - Missing Authorization issue in merge request accessibility report comparison endpoint impacts GitLab CE/EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user with reporter role to access restricted CI artifact report content they were not authorized to, due to missing authorization checks.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 13.8 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  4.3 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N  )  Thanks  se1en  for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program.   CVE-2026-104661  - Incorrect Privilege Assignment issue in custom roles impacts GitLab EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user holding a custom role with compliance framework administration permissions to configure and execute a specially crafted compliance pipeline across group projects due to improper privilege assignment.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab EE: all versions from 17.0 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  4.3 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N  )  This vulnerability has been discovered internally by a GitLab team member.   CVE-2026-14210  - Insufficient Granularity of Access Control issue in project label management impacts GitLab CE/EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user with a project-scoped fine-grained Personal Access Token to permanently delete or modify group-level labels, due to incorrect authorization logic on label ownership scope validation.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 18.11 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  4.3 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N  )  Thanks  bate5a  for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program.   CVE-2026-105458  - Governance Control Bypass issue in Duo Agent Platform impacts GitLab EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user holding a specific granular permission to obtain a GitLab Duo Agent Platform token that bypasses governance controls, due to reliance on untrusted input in a security decision.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab EE: all versions from 19.1 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  4.3 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N  )  This vulnerability has been discovered internally by GitLab team member Rahul Barnwal.   CVE-2026-5954  - Incorrect Authorization issue in package registry impacts GitLab CE/EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed a user to download package files from a public project due to improper authorization checks.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 15.1 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  4.2 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N  )  Thanks  rogerace  for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program.   CVE-2026-92528  - Incorrect Authorization issue in merge request approval eligibility check impacts GitLab EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user to approve a merge request despite having contributed commits to it, due to improper identity resolution.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab EE: all versions from 16.11 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  4.2 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N  )  This vulnerability has been discovered internally by GitLab team member Kenneth Chu.   CVE-2026-78335  - Incorrect Authorization issue in fine-grained personal access tokens impacts GitLab CE/EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user holding a project-scoped fine-grained Personal Access Token to modify integrations belonging to a group outside the token’s scope, due to incorrect authorization checks.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 19.1 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  4.2 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N  )  Thanks  mahoraga007  for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program.   CVE-2026-100104  - Server Side Request Forgery (SSRF) issue in repository import impacts GitLab CE/EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user to perform server-side request forgery and reach internal network resources due to a time-of-check to time-of-use race condition in URL validation during repository import operations.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 10.3 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  3.5 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:N/A:N  )  This vulnerability has been discovered internally by GitLab team member Félix Veillette-Potvin.   CVE-2026-82632  - Incorrect Authorization issue in project import impacts GitLab CE/EE  GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user with a fine-grained Personal Access Token scoped only to user-boundary import permissions to import projects into group namespaces beyond the token’s intended scope, due to incorrect authorization of the import target namespace.   Impacted Versions:  GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 18.9 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  3.1 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N  )  Thanks  aur0r4_glyph  for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program. Impacted Versions:  GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 17.6 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2  CVSS  2.7 (  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N  )  This vulnerability has been discovered internally by a GitLab team member.  Regexp compilation fixes related to GitLab's CVE-2026-89078, CVE-2026-93577, CVE-2026-97229 and CVE-2026-110264 



         
           Posted by  k0kubun  on 23 Oct 2026 

           We have released Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12 and 3.3.13. They fix several bugs in Ruby’s regular expression engine (Onigmo) that GitLab found could be used for remote code execution on GitLab servers. GitLab published four CVEs for these issues, and the Ruby releases contain the fixes for the underlying bugs in Ruby. 

 Background 

 GitLab compiles regular expressions supplied by its users, such as patterns in CI configuration, with  Regexp.new . GitLab found that specially crafted patterns could corrupt memory while Ruby compiles them, and that this could be turned into remote code execution on GitLab servers. GitLab addressed these issues in its own releases by patching the Ruby it ships, and assigned the following CVE identifiers: 

 
    CVE-2026-89078 : Double Free issue in Regular Expression Parser ( GitLab 19.4.1 ) 
    CVE-2026-93577 : Integer Overflow issue in Regular Expression Compiler ( GitLab 19.4.1 ) 
    CVE-2026-97229 : Integer Overflow issue in CI/CD Regular Expression Compiler ( GitLab 19.4.2 ) 
    CVE-2026-110264 : Integer Overflow issue in Regular Expression Compiler ( GitLab 19.5.1 ) 
 

 Fixes in Ruby 

 The following table shows the change in Ruby that fixes the bug behind each CVE, and the first release of each series that contains it. 

 
   
     
       GitLab CVE 
       Bug in Ruby 
       Change 
       Ruby 4.0 
       Ruby 3.4 
       Ruby 3.3 
     
   
   
     
       CVE-2026-89078 
       Double free when parsing a pattern fails after an alternation 
        #13332  
       4.0.0 
       3.4.12 
       3.3.13 
     
     
       CVE-2026-93577, CVE-2026-97229 
       Integer overflow in the size of a compiled pattern 
        #19020  
       4.0.8 
       3.4.12 
       3.3.13 
     
     
       CVE-2026-110264 
       Overflow of internal IDs in a pattern with many repeats 
        #16801  
       4.0.9 
       3.4.12 
       3.3.13 
     
   
 

 Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12 and 3.3.13 contain all of these fixes. 

 Who is affected 

 These bugs are reached only when an application compiles a regular expression from a string that an attacker controls, for example by passing it to  Regexp.new ,  Regexp.union  or  Regexp.compile , or by interpolating it into a regexp literal such as  /#{input}/ . Applications that only use regular expressions written by their own developers are not affected. 

  Regexp.timeout  does not protect against these bugs. Limiting the length of patterns does not reliably protect against them either, because some of them can be triggered by short patterns. 

 Recommended action 

 We recommend upgrading to Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12 or 3.3.13 or later. 

 If you cannot upgrade, please avoid compiling regular expressions from untrusted input. 

 Ruby 3.3 is in the security maintenance phase, in which we normally release only fixes for vulnerabilities. Ruby 3.3.13 includes these fixes as an exception, because GitLab assigned CVEs to issues that rely on them. 

 About CVE identifiers 

 We have not requested CVE identifiers in Ruby for these fixes, at least for now. 

 Ruby has generally considered it unsafe to compile and use a regular expression created from untrusted input. We stated this in the advisory for  CVE-2022-28738 , where we nevertheless treated a double free in Regexp compilation as a vulnerability after a comprehensive assessment. We did the same for  CVE-2024-27282 . 

 However, the  Regexp documentation  currently discusses untrusted patterns only in terms of denial of service, and recommends a timeout for them. It does not clearly say whether compiling an untrusted pattern is a use case that Ruby supports. We plan to discuss how to document this, and whether we treat this kind of issue as a vulnerability in Ruby, including whether to request CVE identifiers for these fixes. If we request any, we will update this page. 

 In the meantime, please refer to GitLab’s CVE identifiers listed above when you track these issues, for example in a security scanner. 

 Credits 

 Thanks to Johan Carlsson ( joaxcar ) for discovering the integer overflow fixed by  #19020  through GitLab’s bug bounty program, and to GitLab for reporting these issues to us and coordinating the fixes.
