Chained PHP2Shell Exploit Roots 25 Servers | Dream Research                             
 
  
    
 
             A New Reality - Read the CEO's Post >            About  Careers  Research & News  Manifest  Contact Us       Contact Us          October 26, 2026  Chained PHP2Shell Exploit Roots 25 Servers, including US Government Servers  Dream Research           Updated: October 29, 2026.    Since this discovery, the Dream research team has been sharing updates and collaborating on an investigation with Palo Alto Networks, the vendor of the firewall in question. More information is available  on the Palo Alto Networks website . Additional details are now included in the post itself.    Custom PHP2Shell Exploit Chained with Kernel LPE to Root Versions of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS Firewalls in the Wild   On October 25, Dream researchers uncovered artifacts of what appeared to be a Chinese AI-assisted campaign that rooted 25 servers, including systems in a US government-affiliated environment. The attacker combined PHP2Shell with a kernel privilege-escalation exploit to compromise exposed systems.  The affected devices run specific versions of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS.  The exploited surface is the PAN-OS management web server, which also fronts the GlobalProtect portal. Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 has independently verified the attacker’s tooling and results, and Palo Alto Networks is releasing fixed PAN-OS versions across the affected branches.  After rooting the firewalls, the attacker launched attacks against Active Directory. The recovered artifacts confirm credential extraction and directory enumeration.  The operation illustrates how an exposed management interface can become a path into an organization’s identity infrastructure. For government defenders, vulnerability discovery is just the beginning, after which the real challenge extends from identifying vulnerable systems to understanding and containing the access a compromise makes possible.   The research below was conducted with proactive threat hunting using Dream’s autonomous cyber research product,  Hero .   Discovery  Dream researchers identified a complete attack operation that included a custom weaponization of the PHP2Shell exploit chain (CVE-2026-109618/CVE-2026-109619) paired with the Fragnesia kernel privilege escalation (CVE-2026-46300), target lists, exploitation logs, and approximately 40 custom post-exploitation scripts.  This included artifacts of a campaign that had rooted 25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. Once rooted, the attacker zeroed in on three specific servers in a US government-affiliated environment.  The discovered artifacts revealed an operation that began with exploit development in a lab environment and ended with persistent access to a US government organization's internal Active Directory domain.  AI Usage in Attack  We also observed some evidence of AI-assisted tooling in the attack infrastructure:   Claude Code had been installed  An AI-powered offensive security platform called aiscan was configured with Chinese LLMs DeepSeek and Kimi  API keys for the Chinese reconnaissance platform FOFA were present   While we have no direct evidence that the AI tools were specifically used to write the exploit or the post-exploitation scripts, the code structure, commenting style, and consistency across ~40 scripts suggest AI-assisted development. That said, this operation does not appear to be a  fully autonomous nation-state attack .  The Exploit: Two Vulnerabilities Chained Into One Request  The attacker developed two separate exploits and chained them together to achieve root access on any internet-facing PAN-OS firewall running a vulnerable build in a single HTTP request without any credentials.  PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619) — Remote Code Execution  The implementation we recovered is a custom, non-public build, not a copy of any known public exploit for PHP2Shell. It follows the same underlying concept but appears to have been independently developed and tailored specifically for PAN-OS.  The vulnerability targets PHP's  session.upload_progress  mechanism on the PAN-OS management web server (appweb). PAN-OS uses PHP 8.0.30 with a high memory limit that enables the memory corruption stages of the attack.  The attack works in four orchestrated stages:    A1 — Memory Exhaustion (~383MB):  The attacker floods the server with crafted multipart POST requests, each containing massive filenames and session progress data. This pushes PHP's memory allocator to its limits, forcing the system into a predictable memory layout.   B1 — Information Leak:  A second request forges the stale session ID length from A1, forcing an out-of-bounds read. The server's  Set-Cookie  response header carries the leaked pointer value — giving the attacker the base address of  libphp.so  in the running process.   A2 — Stale Reference Setup (~500MB):  Another round of memory pressure initializes a session, leaving  http_session_vars  as a live  zend_reference , then triggers a second OOM that leaves  mod_data=NULL  — creating a stale reference the attacker can forge in B2.   B2 — Code Execution:  The final request forges a PHP HashTable entry in the freed memory region. The forged entry's  pDestructor  callback points to  zif_system  (PHP's  system()  function), and its data points to a shell command string. When PHP's cleanup handler walks the HashTable, it calls the forged destructor — executing arbitrary commands as the  nobody  user.   Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300) — Kernel Privilege Escalation  Getting code execution as  nobody  isn't enough since SELinux confines  httpd_t  from modifying system files. In order to complete the root, the attacker chained in a second exploit: a Linux kernel vulnerability in the XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem.  Fragnesia uses page-cache writes to overwrite  /etc/pam.d/su  — replacing its authentication rules with  pam_permit.so  (accept all). Because the PAM file is only 774 bytes, the exploit uses a per-byte splicing variant to write it precisely. After the overwrite,  su root  succeeds without a password.  Both exploits run in a single B2 HTTP request. The total chain — from unauthenticated HTTPS connection to persistent root webshell — completes in under 15 minutes.  The Lab: Version Profiling at Scale  The exploit is not a single fire-and-forget payload. It requires precise memory offsets that differ between PAN-OS versions — the address of  zval_ptr_dtor , the address of  zif_system , HashTable structure sizes, and memory geometry parameters that control the heap layout during each stage.  Among the recovered artifacts, we found 11 JSON version profile files — one for each PAN-OS version that had been tested:   
   
   
      PAN-OS branch  PHP  Profiles  Notes  
   
         11.1  7.4.33  2 provisional  PHP 7.4 — RCE as nobody verified in lab, but full chain not calibrated (base build plus one hotfix variant)        12.1, 12.2  8.0.30  1 calibrated, 8 provisional  One base profile fully lab-tested; the others inherit its geometry or share offsets with neighboring builds     
   
   Each profile contains the exact offsets extracted from the  libphp.so  binary of that version — with SHA256 hashes of each library, ELF build IDs, and precise memory geometry parameters (chunk sizes, fill counts, drain counts, spray offsets) tuned through lab testing.  The difference between "calibrated" and "provisional" profiles is notable — calibrated means the attacker tested the exploit against a running VM of that version and confirmed the memory geometry works. Provisional means they calculated offsets from the binary but haven't verified on a live instance.  The Campaign Funnel: From 19,000 Discovered to 25 Exploited        Figure 1: Operational timeline of the campaign, from setup on October 8 through exploitation, the pivot into the internal network, and post-exploitation on October 24.     With the exploit ready and profiles for 9 exploitable versions, the attacker launched a targeting campaign that followed a clear funnel:  Stage 1: Global Discovery (19,000 targets)  Using FOFA — a Chinese internet asset search engine similar to Shodan — the attacker identified approximately 19,000 internet-facing PAN-OS firewalls worldwide. These were devices with management interfaces exposed to the internet, discoverable through certificate fingerprints and HTTP response signatures.  Stage 2: Version Fingerprinting (5,000 alive)  A custom version scanner ran with 200 concurrent threads against all 19,000 targets, identifying which devices were actually online and what PAN-OS version they were running. Approximately 5,000 responded with version information.  Stage 3: Geographic and Version Filtering (240 targets)  From the 5,000 alive devices, the attacker filtered to servers located in only United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. They then further filtered to versions matching their exploit profiles (the PAN-OS 12.1 and 12.2 branches running PHP 8.0.30). This produced a final target list of 240 firewalls.  Since US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea are the four primary strategic adversaries and intelligence targets for Chinese state-aligned cyber operations in the Pacific theater, this indicates potential nation-state adversary efforts.  Stage 4: Automated Exploitation (24 rooted)  The 240 targets were fed into an automated batch runner that exploited them five at a time, with an 1800-second (30-minute) timeout per target. For each success, the batch:   Ran the full PHP2Shell + Fragnesia chain  Planted a 103-byte PHP root webshell in a publicly accessible directory on the firewall ( /unauth/php/change_password.php )  Verified root by executing  id  through the webshell  Logged the target's hostname and IP to a success CSV  Moved to the next target   At this point, 24 firewalls had been successfully rooted.  Stage 5: Triage (2 firewalls prioritized)  For 22 of the 24 rooted firewalls, the attacker did nothing beyond planting the webshell. No persistence, no tunnels, no post-exploitation tools. The servers were effectively  owned and parked , allowing the attacker to return through the webshell at any time.  Two servers seemingly associated with one target progressed beyond this stage. Both appeared to belong to a US government-affiliated environment.  Stage 6: The Pivot (Shifting from Firewall to Domain)  Among the 24 rooted firewalls, two belonged to a US government-affiliated organization. The running configuration extracted from the first firewall revealed an environment with characteristics suggesting government affiliation: CAC (Common Access Card) authentication, a specific naming prefix, and standardized government-style asset naming. The configuration file contained the organization's complete internal network topology: domain controllers, a central firewall management server, a Keycloak SSO server, a GitLab instance, GlobalProtect VPN gateways, and the Active Directory domain.  The first firewall was rooted on Oct 23 at 18:14 UTC during the automated batch. But it crashed shortly after — likely from the ~900MB of exploit traffic — and never came back online. The attacker monitored it with 240 automated probes over two hours, waiting for it to recover. It didn't. The second firewall, whose certificate data definitively linked it to the target organization, had timed out during the original batch.  Recognizing the organization's value from the first firewall's configuration, the attacker created a separate, dedicated campaign and successfully exploited it on Oct 24 at 10:09 UTC.  Within hours, the attacker:   Built a persistent tunnel into the internal network.   An 8-port reverse SSH tunnel connected the compromised firewall back to the operator's infrastructure, forwarding access to:   Domain controllers (LDAP, LDAPS, RDP)  The internal firewall management server  GlobalProtect VPN infrastructure  A SOCKS5 proxy for arbitrary internal network access   The tunnel was wrapped in a systemd service and an  rc.local  boot hook, both launching scripts from  /usr/local/lib/.panops/  — it survives reboots and automatically reconnects.   Exploited the management server through the tunnel.  At 11:35 UTC, less than 90 minutes after rooting the second firewall, the attacker used the newly gained server access and the same PHP2Shell + Fragnesia chain against a third government server - the internal firewall management server that was only reachable through the tunnel. This server centrally manages all of the organization's firewalls. Compromising it gave the attacker access to every managed firewall's configuration, credentials, and network settings. This brought the total number of servers exploited to 25.   Launched an AD attack campaign from the management server.  Because the management server already had LDAP connectivity to Active Directory (it needs it to authenticate VPN users), the attacker used it as their launch platform for domain attacks:   Decrypted the LDAP service account password — the device config stores it encrypted, but with root access the attacker has the master key. They extracted it in plaintext and hardcoded it into every subsequent script.  Enumerated every user and group in the domain via LDAP queries.  Sprayed passwords against every user account using organization-themed passwords. The domain had  lockoutThreshold=0  — meaning no account lockout, allowing unlimited spray attempts.  Attempted to create backdoor AD accounts — both a user account (tried in every OU) and a machine account (exploiting the default  MachineAccountQuota  setting).  Analyzed AD ACL chains for privilege escalation paths.  Attempted SAML signing key extraction from the Keycloak IdP configuration.  Probed Keycloak SSO for authentication bypass.   The attack results — whether the password spray found valid credentials, whether the backdoor accounts were created, whether SAML keys were extracted — stayed on the management server's local filesystem and were not among the artifacts we recovered. This means we cannot determine the full extent of the compromise.        Figure 2: The attack path. PHP2Shell and Fragnesia root the perimeter firewall, a reverse SSH tunnel reaches the internal management server, and the decrypted LDAP service account opens Active Directory.     Management Server → Active Directory   
   
   
      Status  Activity  
   
         ✓  LDAP password decrypted from config        ✓  Full user & group enumeration        ?  Password spray (all users, no lockout)        ?  Backdoor user + machine account creation        ?  SAML signing key extraction     
   
   What the Attacker Has Now  From the recovered artifacts, we can confirm the attacker possesses:   Persistent remote access to the organization's internal network via a boot-surviving reverse tunnel and SOCKS proxy — likely still active  Root webshells on two firewalls and the firewall management server — likely still active  The full Active Directory user and group listing — a complete organizational blueprint  Decrypted LDAP service account credentials — enabling direct AD queries at any time  Private keys harvested from the PAN-OS firewall filesystem — HA replication keys, SSL/TLS certificate keys, and device authentication keys  Complete network topology — every IP, hostname, subnet, server role, and VPN gateway  SAML IdP configuration with weak security settings ( validate-idp-certificate: no )  22 additional parked firewalls across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea — ready for exploitation at any time   What we cannot determine is whether the password spray, backdoor account creation, or SAML key extraction succeeded. If any of these attacks worked, the compromise extends far beyond the perimeter firewalls into the organization's identity infrastructure.  Attribution Indicators  We do not attribute this activity to a named threat actor. Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 tracks this activity as CL-UNK-1280 and attributes it to a Chinese-speaking attacker in the UTC+8 time zone. However, multiple indicators point to a Chinese-nexus operation:   
   
   
      Indicator  Detail  
   
         Target selection  US, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea exclusively. These are the primary strategic intelligence targets for Chinese state-aligned operations in the Pacific.        FOFA  The internet reconnaissance platform used to discover targets is a Chinese service.        iox  A Chinese-developed tunneling utility observed among the recovered tools.        DeepSeek and Kimi  The LLMs configured in the aiscan offensive security platform are Chinese language models.        UTC+8 timestamps  The infrastructure's clock ran on China Standard Time, confirmed by comparing log timestamps against HTTP Date: response headers from targets.        Chinese-language prompts  The aiscan session logs contain user messages in Chinese.     
   
   Conclusion  This operation demonstrates a level of preparation and capability that sets it apart from opportunistic exploitation. The attacker invested significant effort into vulnerability research — obtaining PAN-OS firmware, decrypting it, extracting PHP libraries, building precise memory profiles for 9 different software versions, and calibrating exploit geometry through lab testing. The exploitation itself was automated and efficient: 240 targets attempted in a single batch, with version-specific profiles selected automatically.  There was a clear-cut focus on government targets.  The attacker scanned 19,000 firewalls, rooted 24, and immediately identified the two that mattered. Within hours of compromising a US government-affiliated firewall, they had tunneled into the internal network, compromised a third server using the same PHP2Shell exploit, and launched a full Active Directory attack campaign — all through a chain that started with a single unauthenticated HTTPS request to a management interface that should never have been exposed to the internet.  The 22 other rooted firewalls remain parked with active webshells. The persistent tunnel into the US government organization is likely still running. And the attacker still has 19,000 fingerprinted targets they can revisit as they develop profiles for additional PAN-OS versions. Palo Alto Networks device telemetry shows continued exploitation attempts against exposed PAN-OS devices.  See the  Palo Alto Networks website  for full guidance and indicators of compromise.  Closing the Gap Between Discovery and Defense  For governments and critical infrastructure, finding a vulnerability is only the beginning. Defenders need to identify exposed systems, establish what attackers can exploit, and act before a foothold becomes a wider compromise.  Dream addresses that challenge through two complementary cyberdefense platforms:    Sphere scales national cyber defense.  It maps exposure, prioritizes risks, and detects and responds to attacks across government networks, tailored to each nation’s threats and infrastructure.   Hero scales cyber research.  Its autonomous research agents help experts investigate threats, discover and validate vulnerabilities—including in software without source code—and develop remediation guidance and patches. This is the tool that was used by Dream researchers to conduct the investigation detailed in this post.      26 Oct 2026 
      Updated PHP Windows builds for Brotli security fix  
   
   
      
     
       
        The PHP team announces updated Windows builds:
         PHP 8.5.12-1, 8.4.27-1, 8.3.36-1 and 8.2.35-1 .
        These builds include Brotli 1.2.1, which fixes
         CVE-2026-111497 ,
        an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Brotli decompression.
       
       
        In PHP Windows builds, the vulnerable decoder can be reached through the
        cURL extension when automatic HTTP response decompression is enabled.
        This is disabled by default in cURL, but applications and HTTP client
        libraries can enable it.
       
       
        The  -1  suffix identifies a Windows package rebuild with updated
        dependencies. These builds use the same PHP source releases, and the PHP
        runtime versions remain unchanged.
       
       
        The updated packages are available on the
         downloads page .
       
     
  
   
 
 
   
     23 Oct 2026 
      Informational advisory: Session upload progress  
   
   
      
     
       
        We suggest you set  session.upload_progress.enabled=0  until the
        next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector.
        This setting was already listed as a mitigation in the
         GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp 
        advisory for CVE-2026-109619 published on Oct 21st, 2026. If you applied it
        then, keep it in place and no further action is needed.
       
       
        The issue can only occur under an unusual combination of configuration and
        application code. An application must set
         session.serialize_handler  to  php_binary  or
         php_serialize  in its configuration and then switch it to
         php  at runtime with  ini_set()  before calling
         session_start() . Session upload progress must also still be
        enabled. Applications that never change the serialize handler at runtime can
        keep the feature enabled. Since this setup is unlikely in practice, we are
        handling it in the regular release cycle and will publish a full advisory for
        CVE-2026-115560 with the next release.
       
     
  
   
 
 
   
     21 Oct 2026 
      Security advisory: Critical remote code execution vulnerabilities, update now  
   
   
      
     
 
 PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fix two critical vulnerabilities that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately. 
 

  Who is at risk:  all PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. We consider the risk highest for mod_php, with a demonstrated exploit where an unauthenticated request can trigger the attack before any application code runs. 

  The vulnerabilities:  

 
  RCE via OOM corruption , CVE-2026-109618 ( GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w ): out-of-memory
handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat the invalid data as valid. 
  RCE via stale global state , CVE-2026-109619 ( GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp ): request-owned
internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it. 
 

  How to update:  

 
 Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35. Source downloads are on our  downloads page . Windows source and binaries are  on the same page . 
 Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches in advance, so check your vendor for updated packages. 
  PHP 8.1 and older  no longer receive updates from the PHP project. Some distributions and LTS vendors provide backported fixes, so contact your vendor for details, or upgrade to a supported version. 

 Given the severity of these vulnerabilities, the PHP security team provided minimal source-backports for  PHP 7.4 ,  PHP 8.0 , and  PHP 8.1  to help people building from source or without access to an LTS vendor.
 
 

  If you cannot update immediately:  while only an update is a complete solution, the following measures reduce exposure to specific attack paths but do not make an installation safe. 

  RCE via OOM corruption (CVE-2026-109618):  

 
 Set  memory_limit=-1 , preferably in a way applications can't override, such as  php_admin_value  in the FPM pool or Apache configuration, and check that no pool, directory or application setting puts a finite limit back. This removes the controllable PHP memory limit failure, but an underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path. 
 Set a low  post_max_size . For applications that don't require file uploads, set  post_max_size = 8M . If file uploads are necessary, set  post_max_size = 32M . Keep  upload_max_filesize  below  post_max_size .
Consider enforcing limits at the web server or proxy level for decoded request size, input field count, multipart part count, header count, and nesting depth. These
limits must also cover requests without a usable  Content-Length . 
 Use a container or cgroup limit as an availability boundary, preferably with a policy that kills only the affected worker. Do not substitute  RLIMIT_AS  or
 RLIMIT_DATA , as these can cause the vulnerable allocation failure. 
 

  RCE via stale global state (CVE-2026-109619):  

 
 Set  session.upload_progress.enabled=0  and restart every worker. Use  php.ini , an FPM pool or server
configuration that applies before request parsing. Do not rely on  ini_set()  or FPM  .user.ini . This blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants. 
 On PHP 8.5, set  fatal_error_backtraces=0  and restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed fatal backtrace path only. 
 Remove invalid or deprecated settings applied per request that emit diagnostics before initialization. Hiding diagnostics with  error_reporting ,  display_errors 
or  @  does not help. 
 Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and execution timeouts, including failures in callbacks, upload or import processing and cleanup. 
 

 The advisories linked above have the full technical details.

The self-driving agent platform

## Introduction Agno is a self-driving agent platform. Build agents for your company, product, or customers. Run them as durable services on AgentOS. Put them to work automating company operations. - **Build** agents with the Agno, Claude Agent, or Codex SDKs. Combine agents into teams and workflows. - **Run** agents as durable services with built-in API and MCP. AgentOS handles authentication, role-based access, resume/replay, human approvals, scheduling, and durable execution. - **Automate** company operations with Company OS. Give agents responsibilities, organize work into projects and tasks, and configure recurring routines. People set direction and review results; agents own and execute. Agno provides the orchestration and service layer around your agents, making them available in: 1. **Your product:** using the REST API. 2. **Claude and ChatGPT:** using the MCP server. 3. **Chat apps like Slack:** using Agno Interfaces. Run your platform in your own cloud and keep your data in your control. Review conversations, inspect traces, manage knowledge, and track your agent activity using the [AgentOS UI](https://os.agno.com). ## Get started Agno is built for coding agents. Start with a pre-built template and give this prompt to your coding agent: ```text Help me set up my agent platform and build my first agent. Clone https://github.com/agno-agi/agentos-railway into a folder called agent-platform, cd into it, and follow .agents/skills/setup-platform/SKILL.md. ``` The setup skill runs your platform locally and helps you build your first agent. You get: - An API server and MCP server. - PostgreSQL storage for conversations, memory, and platform activity. - OS Manager to help build and manage your platform. - Claude and Codex engineers to work on your code. - Skills for building, evaluating, and improving agents. - A Company workspace for organizing ongoing work, with a daily maintenance routine that reviews your codebase and Agno releases and proposes platform improvements. Connect your platform to [os.agno.com](https://os.agno.com) to start using it. Build agents with code, use the no-code UI, or chat with the OS Manager. Start improving your agents and platform with the `/improve` skill. Keep useful changes and regression tests so each round builds on the last. When you're ready, configure scheduled improvement runs in a sandbox that return pull requests for review. ## Templates for every cloud Choose a template for your cloud: [Docker](https://github.com/agno-agi/agentos-docker) · [Railway](https://github.com/agno-agi/agentos-railway) · [AWS](https://github.com/agno-agi/agentos-aws) · [GCP](https://github.com/agno-agi/agentos-gcp) · [Azure](https://github.com/agno-agi/agentos-azure) · [Fly.io](https://github.com/agno-agi/agentos-fly) · [Render](https://github.com/agno-agi/agentos-render) · [Modal](https://github.com/agno-agi/agentos-modal) · [Helm](https://github.com/agno-agi/agentos-helm) ## What's included | Capability | What you can do | | --- | --- | | **[Agents](https://docs.agno.com/agents/overview) and [teams](https://docs.agno.com/teams/overview)** | Build agents that use tools, delegate work, and collaborate. | | **[Workflows](https://docs.agno.com/workflows/overview)** | Control execution with routing, conditions, loops, and parallel steps. | | **[Memory](https://docs.agno.com/memory/overview) and [knowledge](https://docs.agno.com/knowledge/overview)** | Remember users across sessions and retrieve answers from your data. | | **[Tools and integrations](https://docs.agno.com/tools/overview)** | Connect agents to APIs, databases, and MCP servers. | | **[Durable execution](https://docs.agno.com/agent-os/background-execution/durable-queue)** | Persist background jobs and track their status across restarts. | | **[Human approval](https://docs.agno.com/hitl/overview)** | Review sensitive actions before they run, then approve and continue. | | **[Observability](https://docs.agno.com/agent-os/tracing/overview)** | Trace runs, inspect tool calls, and diagnose failures. | | **[Scheduling](https://docs.agno.com/agent-os/scheduler/overview)** | Run agents, teams, and workflows on recurring schedules. | | **[Security](https://docs.agno.com/agent-os/security/overview)** | Control access with authentication, roles, and per-user data isolation. | | **[Coding agents](https://docs.agno.com/agent-platform/harness-agents)** | Run Claude and Codex in sandboxes to implement and test changes. | | **Company OS** | Organize work into products, projects, tasks, and recurring routines. | ## Tutorials First, [add Agno to your coding agent](https://docs.agno.com/coding-agents) so it can read the tutorials as you build. Then, learn how to: - [Build your agent platform](https://docs.agno.com/agent-platform/overview) - [Serve agents as an API](https://docs.agno.com/tutorials/agents-as-api) - [Serve agents over MCP](https://docs.agno.com/tutorials/agents-as-mcp) - [Run Claude and Codex as services](https://docs.agno.com/tutorials/harnesses-as-a-service) - [Read the documentation](https://docs.agno.com) ## Community Follow [Agno on X](https://x.com/AgnoAgi) for releases and demos, or subscribe to [The Agno Loop](https://www.agno.com/the-agno-loop-newsletter). See the [contributing guide](CONTRIBUTING.md) to contribute. ## License Agno is distributed under the [Apache 2.0 license](LICENSE). ## Telemetry Agno sends a telemetry event per agent so we know which model providers to prioritize. Prompts, messages, and outputs are never sent. Disable by setting `AGNO_TELEMETRY=false`.

                                     [Security] PandasTools: RCE via model-controlled pandas function selection (read_pickle)     #8699               New issue          Copy link              New issue          Copy link             Open        #8713             Open      [Security] PandasTools: RCE via model-controlled pandas function selection (read_pickle)   #8699         #8713           Copy link                         Description             bogdancherniy11-sudo    opened    on Jul 2, 2026               Issue body actions          Summary 
  PandasTools  selects the pandas callable to run from a  model-controlled string  and then calls it with model-controlled keyword arguments: 
   getattr ( pd ,  create_using_function )( **  function_parameters )  
 Because  create_using_function  and  function_parameters  come from the agent/LLM tool call, a prompt-injection–controlled model can choose  read_pickle , which deserializes attacker-supplied data with  pickle  →  remote code execution  on the host running the agent. The same dispatch also allows arbitrary local file read (e.g.  read_csv / read_json  on any path), with the contents returned to the model. 
 Affected code 
  libs/agno/agno/tools/pandas.py  (v2.6.20,  main  @  07fe6b2 ) 
 
  create_pandas_dataframe() :
   # create_using_function / function_parameters are model-controlled tool args 
 dataframe   =   getattr ( pd ,  create_using_function )( **  function_parameters )
 if   dataframe   is   None : ...
 if   not   isinstance ( dataframe ,  pd . DataFrame ): ...    # type check runs AFTER the call   
 
  run_dataframe_operation()  has the same pattern ( getattr(dataframe, operation)(**operation_parameters) ) — a secondary sink that also exposes e.g.  query / eval  and  to_pickle . 
 
 Both tools are registered by default ( enable_create_pandas_dataframe  /  enable_run_dataframe_operation  default to  True ). 
 Root cause 
  getattr(pd, <model string>)(**<model kwargs>)  is an unrestricted dispatch to any top-level  pandas  callable.  pandas.read_pickle()  runs  pickle.load , which executes a payload's  __reduce__  during deserialization → code execution. The  isinstance(..., pd.DataFrame)  guard runs only  after  the call, so it cannot prevent execution. 
 Preconditions / attacker model 
 
 An agent is configured with  PandasTools  (a standard toolkit). 
 Tool arguments are influenced by untrusted input — a user message or  indirect prompt injection  (e.g. a document or web page the agent ingests). 
 Default configuration; no unsafe/non-default option required.  read_pickle  accepts local paths  and URLs , so the payload can be remote. 
 
 Impact 
 
  Critical:  remote code execution on the agent host via  read_pickle  of an attacker-controlled payload. 
 Additional: arbitrary local file read (credential/secret files) returned to the model; outbound fetch to model-chosen URLs. 
 
 Steps to reproduce (mechanism) 
 
 Instantiate an agent/toolkit with  PandasTools . 
 Cause a tool call equivalent to: 
 create_pandas_dataframe(dataframe_name="x", create_using_function="read_pickle", function_parameters={"filepath_or_buffer": <attacker-controlled path or URL>}) . 
  pandas.read_pickle  deserializes the target; a pickle carrying a  __reduce__  payload executes on load — before the DataFrame type check. 
 
 I have a  minimal, local-only PoC  (temporary files, fake data, no external hosts) that demonstrates both code execution and the arbitrary-file-read variant, plus a regression test. To avoid publishing a working exploit I have not inlined the payload here — I can share the full PoC privately. (Private Vulnerability Reporting appears to be disabled for this repo and I could not find a  SECURITY.md ; please enable PVR or provide a security contact.) 
 Expected vs actual 
 
  Actual:  the model can invoke any pandas reader, including  read_pickle  (RCE) and readers that open arbitrary paths/URLs. 
  Expected:  only a fixed set of safe DataFrame constructors should be reachable;  read_pickle  (untrusted deserialization) must never be reachable from model-controlled input. 
 
 Suggested fix 
 Restrict  create_using_function  to an allowlist of safe constructors and refuse everything else; harden  run_dataframe_operation  against private attributes and code-executing methods. Verified locally: after the change  read_pickle  is rejected (no deserialization, no code execution) while  read_csv  and normal operations still work. 
   --- a/libs/agno/agno/tools/pandas.py 
 +++ b/libs/agno/agno/tools/pandas.py 
 @@ -9,6 +9,26 @@ 
     raise ImportError("`pandas` not installed. Please install using `pip install pandas`.")
 
 
  + # Safe pandas top-level constructors PandasTools may dispatch to from model-controlled 
  + # input. read_pickle / read_hdf are intentionally excluded: they deserialize untrusted 
  + # data (pickle) and lead to remote code execution. 
  + _ALLOWED_CREATE_FUNCS = { 
  +     "DataFrame", 
  +     "read_csv", 
  +     "read_json", 
  +     "read_excel", 
  +     "read_parquet", 
  +     "read_table", 
  +     "read_html", 
  +     "read_feather", 
  +     "read_orc", 
  +     "read_xml", 
  + } 
  +  
  + # DataFrame methods that execute code or (de)serialize to arbitrary locations. 
  + _BLOCKED_DF_OPERATIONS = {"query", "eval", "to_pickle", "to_hdf"} 
  +  
  +  
 class PandasTools(Toolkit):
     def __init__(
         self,
 @@ -50,8 +70,20 @@ 
             if dataframe_name in self.dataframes:
                 return f"Dataframe already exists: {dataframe_name}"
 
  +             # Only allow a fixed set of safe constructors. This blocks reaching 
  +             # `pd.read_pickle` (untrusted deserialization -> RCE) and other 
  +             # non-constructor callables via model-controlled input. 
  +             if create_using_function not in _ALLOWED_CREATE_FUNCS: 
  +                 return ( 
  +                     f"Unsupported function '{create_using_function}'. " 
  +                     f"Allowed functions: {sorted(_ALLOWED_CREATE_FUNCS)}" 
  +                 ) 
  +             func = getattr(pd, create_using_function, None) 
  +             if not callable(func): 
  +                 return f"Unsupported function '{create_using_function}'." 
  +  
             # Create the dataframe
  -             dataframe = getattr(pd, create_using_function)(**function_parameters) 
  +             dataframe = func(**function_parameters) 
             if dataframe is None:
                 return f"Error creating dataframe: {dataframe_name}"
             if not isinstance(dataframe, pd.DataFrame):
 @@ -85,9 +117,18 @@ 
 
             # Get the dataframe
             dataframe = self.dataframes.get(dataframe_name)
  +             if dataframe is None: 
  +                 return f"Dataframe not found: {dataframe_name}" 
  +  
  +             # Reject private/dunder attributes and code-executing / arbitrary-write methods. 
  +             if operation.startswith("_") or operation in _BLOCKED_DF_OPERATIONS: 
  +                 return f"Unsupported operation: {operation}" 
  +             op = getattr(dataframe, operation, None) 
  +             if not callable(op): 
  +                 return f"Unsupported operation: {operation}" 
 
             # Run the operation
  -             result = getattr(dataframe, operation)(**operation_parameters) 
  +             result = op(**operation_parameters) 
 
             log_debug(f"Ran operation: {operation}")
             try:  
 Environment tested 
 
 agno  2.6.20 , latest  main  (commit  07fe6b2 ), Python 3.12. Local-only reproduction; fake data only. 
 
 Duplicate / publicness check 
 Searched issues/PRs ( read_pickle ,  PandasTools ,  pandas ) and published advisories — no existing report for this deserialization sink; the only  PandasTools  hit is an unrelated non-security bug. Distinct from the published  eval() / field_type  RCE advisory (different sink).                  Activity                 bogdancherniy11-sudo   added a commit that references this issue   on Jul 2, 2026          [fix] PandasTools: restrict create_pandas_dataframe to safe construct…       ...         This issue will close once commit adbafb0 is merged into the 'main' branch.      adbafb0                            akavlabs   commented   on   Sep 28, 2026            akavlabs      on Sep 28, 2026                More actions          Confirmed. The core problem is  getattr(pd, create_using_function)(**function_parameters)  (and the  run_dataframe_operation  analogue against  getattr(dataframe, operation) ) is an open dispatch to any attribute on the module/object, not just DataFrame constructors. The post-hoc  isinstance  check is irrelevant to RCE since  pickle.load  executes on deserialization, before any return value exists to check. 
 Fix should be an allowlist, not a blocklist — enumerate the specific pandas constructors you actually intend to expose (e.g.  read_csv ,  read_json ,  read_excel ,  DataFrame ) and reject anything not in that set before the call, rather than trying to blacklist  read_pickle / to_pickle / eval / query . Blocklists on  getattr  dispatch are brittle — pandas adds/renames methods, and  eval / query  alone are a separate injection vector even without pickle. 
 Concretely for  create_pandas_dataframe : 
   ALLOWED_CONSTRUCTORS   =  { "read_csv" ,  "read_json" ,  "read_excel" ,  "read_parquet" ,  "DataFrame" }
 if   create_using_function    not   in    ALLOWED_CONSTRUCTORS :
  raise   ValueError ( f"Unsupported constructor:   {  create_using_function  }  " )  
 and for  run_dataframe_operation , allowlist against  pd.DataFrame 's public API minus anything that executes code ( eval ,  query ,  apply  with arbitrary callables,  to_pickle ) or does I/O to arbitrary paths. 
 Also worth constraining  function_parameters / operation_parameters  — even with an allowlisted  read_csv , a model-controlled  filepath_or_buffer  is unrestricted local file read/SSRF via URL. That needs its own scoping (fixed base dir, no URLs) separate from the RCE fix. 
 Since both toolkits are enabled by default, this affects any agent shipping  PandasTools  out of the box with untrusted input in the loop — indirect prompt injection via a fetched document is enough, no direct user cooperation needed. 
 Disclosure: I maintain agentsentry-gateway, a proxy that sits in front of the agent and flags/blocks this class of thing (unusual tool-arg patterns like  read_pickle / eval  selection, injected instructions in tool outputs) — but that's a mitigating layer at best, not a substitute for fixing the dispatch here. The allowlist is the actual fix.                           sattyamjjain   added a commit that references this issue   on Oct 30, 2026          feat(guards): refuse dispatch names and unsafe OAuth metadata URLs ( #402        ...          b21aec7                   Sign up for free       to join this conversation on GitHub. # Tabularis Tabularis is an open-source desktop SQL workspace with 3 built-in database drivers and 26 shipped driver plugins, including DuckDB, ClickHouse, Redis and Firestore. Its built-in MCP server lets Claude, Cursor and Devin (formerly Windsurf) read your schema and run queries in the same app you already use.

Everything else is on the [bounty board](https://tabularis.dev/plugins/bounties): claim one, sponsor one, or [request a database](https://github.com/TabularisDB/tabularis/discussions). ## Installation ### Windows **WinGet (Recommended)** ```bash winget install Debba.Tabularis ``` **Direct Download** Download the installer from the [Releases page](https://github.com/TabularisDB/tabularis/releases) and run it: ``` tabularis_x.x.x_x64-setup.exe ``` Follow the on-screen instructions to complete the installation. ### macOS **Homebrew (Recommended)** ```bash brew install --cask tabularis ``` [![Homebrew](https://img.shields.io/badge/Homebrew-Repository-orange?logo=homebrew)](https://github.com/debba/homebrew-tabularis) **Direct Download** Builds from **v0.13.1** onward are signed and notarized by Apple, so they open without any extra steps.
Notes for releases before v0.13.1
The notes below only apply to **older releases (before v0.13.1)** downloaded directly: - You need to allow accessibility access (Privacy & Security) to the tabularis app. If you are upgrading and already have tabularis on the allowed list, remove it manually before accessibility access can be granted to the new version. - You may need to run `xattr -c /Applications/tabularis.app` after copying the app to the Applications directory.
### Linux (Snap) ```bash sudo snap install tabularis sudo snap connect tabularis:password-manager-service # allow keychain access for saved credentials ``` > [!IMPORTANT] > The `password-manager-service` interface is not auto-connected by the Snap Store yet. Without it, saving a connection fails with a `Platform secure storage failure` error. [![Snap Store](https://img.shields.io/badge/snap-tabularis-blue?logo=snapcraft)](https://snapcraft.io/tabularis) ### Linux (Flatpak) ```bash flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists flatpark https://dl.flatpark.org/flatpark.flatpakrepo flatpak install flatpark dev.tabularis.Tabularis ``` [![Flatpak (Flatpark)](https://img.shields.io/badge/flatpak-tabularis-4A90D9?logo=flatpak&logoColor=white)](https://flatpark.org/apps/dev.tabularis.Tabularis/) ### Linux (AppImage) Download the `.AppImage` file from the [Releases page](https://github.com/TabularisDB/tabularis/releases), make it executable and run it: ```bash chmod +x tabularis_x.x.x_amd64.AppImage ./tabularis_x.x.x_amd64.AppImage ``` ### Arch Linux (AUR) ```bash yay -S tabularis-bin ``` ## Updates Tabularis checks for updates automatically on startup and notifies you when a new version is available. You can also download the latest version directly from the [Releases page](https://github.com/TabularisDB/tabularis/releases). ## Discord Join our [Discord server](https://discord.com/invite/K2hmhfHRSt) to talk with the maintainers, share feedback, suggest features, or get help from the community. ## Changelog Every release is documented in [CHANGELOG.md](./CHANGELOG.md). ## Features ### Connection Management [Full reference on tabularis.dev →](https://tabularis.dev/wiki/connections) - Support for **MySQL/MariaDB**, **PostgreSQL** (with multi-schema support) and **SQLite**, with multi-database selection per connection. - Save, manage, and clone connection profiles, with optional secure password storage in the system **Keychain**. - **SSH Tunneling** with automatic readiness detection. - **Per-Connection Appearance:** override the icon ([Lucide](https://lucide.dev/icons/), emoji, or custom image) and accent color of each saved connection. ### Database Explorer [Full reference on tabularis.dev →](https://tabularis.dev/wiki/schema-management) - **Tree View:** Browse tables, columns, keys, indexes, views, and stored routines, with inline editing from the sidebar. - **ER Diagram:** Interactive Entity-Relationship visualization (pan, zoom, layout) with selective table diagram generation. - **Context Actions:** Show data, count rows, modify schema, duplicate/delete tables. - **SQL Dump & Import:** Export and restore databases with a single flow. ### SQL Editor [Full reference on tabularis.dev →](https://tabularis.dev/wiki/editor) - **Monaco Editor** with syntax highlighting and auto-completion, in a tabbed interface with isolated connections per tab and resizable **split view**. - **Multi-Statement Execution:** Run All, Run Selected, or pick individual queries. Results appear in separate tabs with independent pagination. - **Smart Query Splitting:** Correctly handles stored procedures, functions, and `$$`-delimited blocks. - **SQL Files:** Open, edit, and save `.sql`, `.psql`, and `.pgsql` files in editor tabs without executing them. - **Saved Queries** and an **AI assist overlay** directly in the editor. ### SQL Notebooks [Full reference on tabularis.dev →](https://tabularis.dev/wiki/notebooks) - **Multi-Cell Workspace:** Combine SQL and Markdown cells in a single document, with inline results and bar/line/pie charts. - **Cross-Cell Variables:** Reference another cell's full result as a table with `{{cell_N}}` (expanded to a CTE at run time), plus global `@paramName` parameters. - **Run All:** Sequential execution with stop-on-error option and completion summary. - **Persistence & Export:** Auto-saved as `.tabularis-notebook` files; export as HTML, CSV, or JSON. - Outline panel, drag & drop cell reordering, and AI-generated cell names. ### Keyboard Shortcuts [Full reference on tabularis.dev →](https://tabularis.dev/wiki/keyboard-shortcuts) - **Built-in shortcuts** for navigation, editor, and data grid actions, platform-aware (`Cmd` on macOS, `Ctrl` on Windows/Linux). - **Fully customizable:** Remap any non-locked shortcut from **Settings → Keyboard Shortcuts**; overrides persist to `keybindings.json`. - Hold `Ctrl+Shift` in the sidebar to reveal numbered badges (1–9) for instant connection switching. ### Visual Query Builder [Full reference on tabularis.dev →](https://tabularis.dev/wiki/visual-query-builder) - **Drag-and-Drop:** Build queries visually with ReactFlow. - **Visual JOINs:** Connect tables to create relationships. - **Advanced Logic:** WHERE/HAVING filters, aggregates (COUNT, SUM, AVG), sorting, and limits. - **Real-time SQL:** Instant code generation. ### Visual EXPLAIN [Full reference on tabularis.dev →](https://tabularis.dev/wiki/visual-explain) - **Interactive Plan Graphs:** Inspect execution plans as navigable node graphs instead of raw text. - **Table, Raw, and AI Views:** Switch between exact node metrics, original database output, and optional AI-assisted analysis. - **Cross-Database Support:** Works with PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, and SQLite using the best available `EXPLAIN` format per driver. - **Faster Optimization Loops:** Spot expensive scans, estimate gaps, join behavior, and optimizer choices without leaving the editor. ### Data Grid [Full reference on tabularis.dev →](https://tabularis.dev/wiki/data-grid) - **Inline & Batch Editing:** Modify cells and commit multiple changes at once; create, delete, and multi-select rows. - **Export:** Save results as CSV or JSON, or copy selected rows straight to the clipboard. - **JSON & JSONB Cells:** Syntax-highlighted in the grid, with a dedicated editor window (Tree / Monaco / Raw modes). - **Spatial Data:** Initial GEOMETRY support for MySQL. ### Plugin System [Full reference on tabularis.dev →](https://tabularis.dev/wiki/plugins) Tabularis is **hackable with an external plugin system**. Plugins are standalone executables that communicate with the app over **JSON-RPC 2.0 via stdin/stdout**, and can be written in any language. - **Install Plugins:** Browse and install community drivers from **Settings → Available Plugins**, no restart required. - **Manage Drivers:** View all registered drivers (built-in and plugins) in **Settings → Installed Drivers** and uninstall plugins with one click. - **Any Database:** Add support for DuckDB, MongoDB, or any other database by writing or installing a plugin. - **Plugin Registry:** Official plugins are listed in [`plugins/registry.json`](./plugins/registry.json). - **Developer Guide:** See [`plugins/PLUGIN_GUIDE.md`](./plugins/PLUGIN_GUIDE.md) to build your own driver in any language. - **Declarative themes (development):** **Settings → Appearance** supports local packages (**Import theme → Local package**), previews and personal/VS Code imports without executable plugin activation. See the [theme author guide](./packages/create-plugin/THEMES.md) for the separate `tabularis-theme` CLI, packaging and release gates; public runtime/tooling rollout is not implied by this development feature. ### Logging - Real-time log viewer in Settings, with level filtering and export to `.log` files. - Automatically expand and inspect SQL queries in logs. - **CLI Debug Mode:** Start with `tabularis --debug` for verbose logging from launch. ### Configuration Storage [Full reference on tabularis.dev →](https://tabularis.dev/wiki/configuration) Configuration is stored in `~/.config/tabularis/` (Linux), `~/Library/Application Support/tabularis/` (macOS), or `%APPDATA%\tabularis\` (Windows): connection profiles, saved queries, app settings (`config.json`), custom themes, and per-connection editor preferences. You can move this folder from **Settings > Storage** (or with the `TABULARIS_DATA_DIR` environment variable), for example to an iCloud Drive or Dropbox folder to sync connections across machines; installed plugins always stay local. Tabs and queries are restored when you reopen a connection. The wiki covers the full file layout and every `config.json` option, including custom AI model overrides.
How Follow System works on Linux
On Linux, **Follow System** reads the XDG desktop settings portal's `org.freedesktop.appearance/color-scheme` preference and follows its live updates, including GNOME's dark-mode toggle with the standard Adwaita GTK theme. The resolved light/dark theme is applied explicitly to GTK window decorations and the webview. A portal value of `0` (no preference) resolves to light, so switching back to the desktop default cannot reuse the app's previously forced dark theme. If the portal is unavailable or returns an unsupported value, Tabularis falls back to the native window theme, then the browser media query. The default window capability grants `core:window:allow-set-theme` to allow native theme changes. macOS and Windows use native theme notifications. See [the portal specification](https://flatpak.github.io/xdg-desktop-portal/docs/doc-org.freedesktop.portal.Settings.html). Portal command reads reuse one cached D-Bus connection, while the live watcher keeps its own connection. Failed reads discard the cached connection so the next request can reconnect; failed connection attempts are not cached. The existing two-second command timeout also bounds concurrent requests waiting for the cache.
### AI Features (Optional) [Full reference on tabularis.dev →](https://tabularis.dev/wiki/ai-assistant) Optional Text-to-SQL and query explanation powered by **OpenAI**, **Anthropic**, **MiniMax**, **OpenRouter**, **Requesty**, **Ollama** (local models, no API key, full privacy), and any **OpenAI-compatible API** (Groq, Perplexity, Azure OpenAI, LocalAI, ...). Model lists are fetched from your provider and cached locally; custom models can be configured per provider. ### MCP Server: AI Agent Integration [Full reference on tabularis.dev →](https://tabularis.dev/wiki/mcp-server) Tabularis includes a built-in **MCP (Model Context Protocol) server** that lets AI agents read your database schema and execute queries directly from their chat interface. ```bash tabularis --mcp ``` **One-click setup** for Claude Desktop, Cursor, and Windsurf: open **Settings → MCP Server Integration**, click **Install Config** next to your client, and restart it. Manual configuration is covered in the wiki. #### Available tools Once connected, your AI agent can: | Tool | Description | | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- | | `list_connections` | List all saved database connections | | `list_databases` | List all databases available for a connection | | `list_tables` | List tables in a connection (with optional schema filter) | | `describe_table` | Get full schema: columns, indexes, foreign keys | | `run_query` | Execute any SQL query and return results | Every tool accepts an optional `output_format` argument. JSON is the default, preserving the existing response format for all clients. You can choose JSON or [TOON](https://toonformat.dev/) as the default under **Settings → MCP Server Integration**; a tool call's `output_format` argument overrides that preference. TOON is especially compact for tabular query results passed to an LLM. MCP transport remains JSON-RPC in either mode; only the text inside the tool result changes. #### Example prompts > "Show me all tables in my production database and describe the `orders` table" > "Write and run a query to find the top 10 customers by total order value this month" > "Check if there are any missing indexes on the `users` table" ## Tech Stack | Layer | Stack | | -------- | ------------------------------------- | | Frontend | React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4 | | Backend | Rust, Tauri v2, SQLx | ## Development **Setup** ```bash pnpm install pnpm tauri dev ``` **Build** ```bash pnpm tauri build ``` ## Roadmap - [ ] [Better PostgreSQL Support](https://github.com/TabularisDB/tabularis/issues/16) ## Contributing Contributions are welcome, see [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md). Good places to start: - [UI design system & visual identity: call for contributors](https://github.com/TabularisDB/tabularis/issues/195) - Write a driver plugin in any language with the [Plugin Guide](./plugins/PLUGIN_GUIDE.md) ## Sponsors and supporters - **[turboSMTP](https://www.serversmtp.com/?utm_source=tabularis&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsor)** — Professional SMTP relay that delivers your emails straight to the inbox, never to spam - **[Kilo Code](https://www.kilo.ai/?utm_source=tabularis&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsor)** — Open source AI coding agent to build, ship, and iterate faster with 500+ models - **[OpenAI](https://openai.com/codex/?utm_source=tabularis&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsor)** — Supporting Tabularis through the Codex for Open Source program. - **[Anthropic](https://claude.com/programs/startups?utm_source=tabularis&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsor)** — Supporting Tabularis through the Claude for Startups program. - **[Neon](https://neon.com/?utm_source=tabularis&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsor)** — Managed Postgres with database branching, supporting Tabularis through the Neon Open Source Program. - **[Blacksmith](https://www.blacksmith.sh/?utm_source=tabularis&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsor)** — Faster, cheaper GitHub Actions runners, powering the CI behind Tabularis. - **[DigitalOcean](https://m.do.co/c/f6ab3d158275?utm_source=tabularis&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsor)** — Simple, predictable cloud infrastructure for developers and growing teams. - **[Vercel](https://vercel.com/?utm_source=tabularis&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsor)** — The platform for the modern web: ship, preview, and scale frontend apps with zero config. - **[Usero](https://usero.io/?utm_source=tabularis&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsor)** — Feedback becomes code.    Description 
 

 
   
      Summary  
 SQL Injection in the SQLite driver's schema-introspection functions in TabularisDB/tabularis (main branch, commit  54d9eae2122a197d76be79f337def3f2de52a5a2 ) allows an MCP client (e.g. an AI agent driven by attacker-controlled/untrusted content it is processing) to execute arbitrary stacked SQL statements against a user's SQLite database via the  describe_table  MCP tool's  table_name  argument, completely bypassing Tabularis's MCP read-only-mode and write-approval security controls. 
  Product  
 TabularisDB/tabularis (desktop SQL workspace, built-in MCP server for Claude/Cursor/Devin) 
  Tested Version  
 Commit  54d9eae2122a197d76be79f337def3f2de52a5a2  (main branch, cloned 2026-08-04) 
  Estimated CVSS v3.1  
  CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H  —  7.8 (High)  
 
  AV:L  — the vulnerable code runs inside the Tabularis MCP server subprocess, reached over local stdio JSON-RPC from an MCP client (Claude Desktop, Cursor, etc.), not over a network socket. 
  UI:R  — exploitation requires a user's AI agent session to actually issue the  describe_table  tool call with the malicious  table_name  (e.g. because the agent was steered by untrusted content it was asked to process — the realistic trigger for a security control whose entire purpose is to contain an AI agent that isn't fully trusted). 
  PR:N  — no privilege beyond ordinary MCP tool access is needed; critically, this bypasses the  additional  privilege boundary (read-only mode / write-approval) the product itself advertises for MCP connections. 
  C:H / I:H / A:H  — stacked statements can read out arbitrary table contents, and can  INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE / DROP  freely (demonstrated with a  DROP TABLE ), fully bypassing read-only mode. 
 
  Details  
 Tabularis's SQLite driver builds several schema-introspection queries by directly string-interpolating the caller-supplied  table_name  into a  PRAGMA  statement, with no escaping and no parameter binding: 
 
  src-tauri/src/drivers/sqlite/mod.rs:67  ( get_columns ):  let query = format!("PRAGMA table_info('{}')", table_name);  
  src-tauri/src/drivers/sqlite/mod.rs:123  ( get_foreign_keys ):  let query = format!("PRAGMA foreign_key_list('{}')", table_name);  
  src-tauri/src/drivers/sqlite/mod.rs:160  ( get_all_columns_batch ): same pattern, per table in a loop 
  src-tauri/src/drivers/sqlite/mod.rs:200  ( get_all_foreign_keys_batch ): same pattern, per table in a loop 
  src-tauri/src/drivers/sqlite/mod.rs:239  ( get_indexes ):  let list_query = format!("PRAGMA index_list('{}')", table_name);  
 
 Each resulting string is passed straight to  sqlx::query(&query).fetch_all(&pool) . sqlx's SQLite backend ( sqlx-sqlite  0.8.6, pinned in  src-tauri/Cargo.toml:31 ) executes  every  statement it finds in that string, not just the first:  ExecuteIter::next()  ( sqlx-sqlite-0.8.6/src/connection/execute.rs ) repeatedly calls  statement.prepare_next(self.handle)  on the remaining tail returned by  sqlite3_prepare_v2  and steps each one, so a  table_name  value containing a closing quote/paren followed by  ;  and a second statement causes that second statement to execute for real. This differs from the codebase's own  mysql / postgres   get_columns  ( src-tauri/src/drivers/mysql/mod.rs:277 ,  src-tauri/src/drivers/postgres/mod.rs:109 ), which correctly use bound parameters ( ?  /  $1,$2 ) for the identical lookup — the SQLite driver is the outlier. 
 None of these functions validate  table_name  against the database's actual table list before use, and  SqliteDriver 's  DatabaseDriver  trait implementation forwards the argument unmodified: 
 
  src-tauri/src/drivers/sqlite/mod.rs:1101  ( get_columns  trait impl) →  get_columns(params, table).await  
  src-tauri/src/drivers/sqlite/mod.rs:1110  ( get_foreign_keys  trait impl) →  get_foreign_keys(params, table).await  
  src-tauri/src/drivers/sqlite/mod.rs:1119  ( get_indexes  trait impl) →  get_indexes(params, table).await  
 
  Reachability via the MCP server (the security-relevant path):  the built-in MCP server's  describe_table  tool takes  table_name  directly from the caller's JSON-RPC arguments with no validation and passes it straight to the driver: 
 
  src-tauri/src/mcp/mod.rs:907-961  ( tool_describe_table ): extracts  table_name  at line 919-926, resolves the driver at line 931, then calls  driver.get_columns(&db_params, table_name, effective_schema)  (and  get_foreign_keys / get_indexes ) at lines 942-945 inside a  tokio::join! . 
 
 Tabularis advertises a read-only mode and a write-approval gate specifically to let a database be safely exposed to an AI agent over MCP ( src-tauri/src/mcp/mod.rs:999-1021 ,  config::is_connection_readonly  +  mcp_approval_mode ). That enforcement is implemented  only  inside  tool_run_query  ( src-tauri/src/mcp/mod.rs:963-1193 ), by classifying the  query  argument's SQL kind.  tool_describe_table ,  tool_list_tables , and  tool_list_databases  never call  config::is_connection_readonly  or the approval flow at all — so for a SQLite connection, the injection above is a complete bypass of that control: an AI agent that only ever calls  describe_table  (a tool with no destructive-sounding name, and no approval prompt) can be made to run arbitrary writes/drops. 
  Proof of Concept  
 I could not compile the actual Tauri/Rust binary in this sandbox (no C linker and no passwordless sudo to install one), so the mechanism was verified in two complementary ways rather than by running the shipped binary directly: 
 
  Source trace  of the pinned  sqlx-sqlite = "0.8.6"  dependency (fetched from crates.io, inspected at  ~/.cargo/registry/src/.../sqlx-sqlite-0.8.6/src/connection/execute.rs ), confirming  ExecuteIter::next()  loops over every statement  prepare_next()  finds in a query string and steps (executes) each one — the exact mechanism  sqlx::query(&query).fetch_all(&pool)  relies on in the vulnerable code above. 
  Dynamic reproduction  against the real  libsqlite3  C library (the same library  sqlx-sqlite 's FFI layer binds) via a Python  ctypes  script that faithfully replicates that prepare-tail/step loop, fed the exact SQL string the vulnerable Rust code constructs. 
 
 Script:  ~/engagements/tabularis/evidence/ctypes_poc.py  (full source embedded/commented with file:line references to the vulnerable code; real run transcript saved alongside at  ~/engagements/tabularis/evidence/poc_run_transcript.txt ). Payload used, matching the  get_columns  code path: 
   table_name = "nonexistent'); DROP TABLE secret;--"
query = "PRAGMA table_info('{}')".format(table_name)
# -> PRAGMA table_info('nonexistent'); DROP TABLE secret;--')
   
 Real transcript from running the script against a fresh SQLite DB containing a  secret  table: 
   === Setting up victim DB (mirrors a real Tabularis-managed SQLite file) ===
Tables before: ['secret']

=== Injected SQL sent through sqlx::query(&query).fetch_all() equivalent ===
PRAGMA table_info('nonexistent'); DROP TABLE secret;--')

=== Executing via prepare-tail loop (matches sqlx ExecuteIter) ===
  -> statement #1 executed, sqlite3_step rc=101
  -> statement #2 executed, sqlite3_step rc=101

Tables after: []

RESULT: CONFIRMED — stacked 'DROP TABLE secret' executed via the unescaped
table_name interpolated into a PRAGMA statement.
   
 In the real product this same string arrives as the  table_name  argument of an MCP  tools/call  request: 
  { "jsonrpc" :  " 2.0 "  , "id" : 1 , "method" :  " tools/call "  , "params" :{
   "name" :  " describe_table "  ,
   "arguments" :{
     "connection_id" :  " <sqlite-connection-id> "  ,
     "table_name" :  " nonexistent'); DROP TABLE secret;-- "  
  }
}}  
  Impact  
 For any SQLite connection reachable through the Tabularis MCP server, an attacker who can influence the  table_name  an AI agent passes to  describe_table  (the realistic route is indirect prompt injection — untrusted content the agent is asked to summarize/process steering it into making this tool call) can: 
 
 Read arbitrary data from other tables by stacking a  SELECT  (rows from a stacked statement are collected into the same result set  fetch_all  returns). 
 Modify or delete arbitrary data ( UPDATE / DELETE / INSERT ). 
 Destroy schema/data ( DROP TABLE , demonstrated above). 
 
 ...all while the connection is configured in Tabularis's  read-only mode  or set to require  write approval  — because that enforcement never runs for this tool. This defeats the specific safety control the product ships to make MCP-exposed databases safe to hand to an AI agent. 
  Weaknesses  
 
 CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection') 
 CWE-863: Incorrect Authorization (read-only mode / write-approval gate is bypassable for this tool) 
 
  Remediation  
 
 Bind  table_name  as a query parameter instead of interpolating it. SQLite's  PRAGMA  statements don't accept  ?  bind parameters directly, so the standard fix is to validate  table_name  against the actual table list (e.g.  SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' AND name = ?1 ) before using it, or to quote it as an identifier (double-quotes, doubling any embedded  " ) rather than as a string literal — never as a bare single-quoted literal — for all five sites listed above ( get_columns ,  get_foreign_keys ,  get_indexes ,  get_all_columns_batch ,  get_all_foreign_keys_batch ). 
 Apply  config::is_connection_readonly  / the MCP approval gate to every MCP tool that reaches a driver ( describe_table ,  list_tables ,  list_databases ), not only  run_query  — or, at minimum, ensure none of those tools can execute more than the single intended statement regardless of input. 
 Consider switching to a query builder/prepared-statement API consistently across all three built-in drivers (mysql/postgres already do this correctly) instead of  format!() -built SQL strings for identifier-bearing introspection queries.

  Tabularis     
 Tabularis is an open-source desktop SQL workspace with 3 built-in database drivers and 26 shipped driver plugins, including DuckDB, ClickHouse, Redis and Firestore. Its built-in MCP server lets Claude, Cursor and Devin (formerly Windsurf) read your schema and run queries in the same app you already use.

 How Follow System works on Linux

The resolved light/dark theme is applied explicitly to GTK window decorations and the webview. A portal value of  0  (no preference) resolves to light, so switching back to the desktop default cannot reuse the app's previously forced dark theme. If the portal is unavailable or returns an unsupported value, Tabularis falls back to the native window theme, then the browser media query. The default window capability grants  core:window:allow-set-theme  to allow native theme changes. macOS and Windows use native theme notifications. See  the portal specification . 
 Portal command reads reuse one cached D-Bus connection, while the live watcher keeps its own connection. Failed reads discard the cached connection so the next request can reconnect; failed connection attempts are not cached. The existing two-second command timeout also bounds concurrent requests waiting for the cache.
