# AnySpeechRecognizer

AnySpeechRecognizer is a Swift package that implements Apple's modern Speech API
with a choice of recognition engine.
Code written for `SpeechAnalyzer`, `SpeechTranscriber`, `DictationTranscriber`,
`SpeechDetector`, and `AssetInventory` builds against this package
when you change the import statement:

```diff
- import Speech
+ import AnySpeechRecognizer
```

The default backend is Apple's Speech framework.
The package also has its own runtime for NVIDIA's
[Parakeet TDT](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3) models on Core ML,
with file and live input, volatile results, and word timing.
To use it, pass a model instead of a locale when you create the transcriber:

```diff
  let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber(
-     locale: locale,
+     model: ParakeetSpeechModel(variant: .v3),
      transcriptionOptions: [],
      reportingOptions: [.volatileResults],
      attributeOptions: [.audioTimeRange]
  )
```

Asset installation, analysis, and results use the same API for both backends.
As a package extension, `SpeakerDiarizer` identifies who speaks when
with NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer model, on the same timeline as the transcriber.
The package does not implement the older `SFSpeechRecognizer` API.

## Requirements

- Swift 6.2 or later
- macOS 26 or later, or iOS 26 or later
- Apple silicon for the Parakeet and Sortformer models

## Installation

Add the package to your `Package.swift`:

```swift
.package(url: "https://github.com/mattt/AnySpeechRecognizer", from: "0.1.0")
```

The package uses
[swift-huggingface](https://github.com/huggingface/swift-huggingface)
to download and cache model files.

## Usage

### Transcribe a file

Resolve a locale, install assets explicitly,
and read results while the analyzer reads the file:

```swift
import AVFoundation
import AnySpeechRecognizer

func transcribe(_ url: URL) async throws -> AttributedString {
    guard let locale = await SpeechTranscriber.supportedLocale(
        equivalentTo: Locale(identifier: "en-US")
    ) else {
        throw SpeechRecognitionError.unsupportedLanguage("English is unavailable.")
    }
    let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber(
        locale: locale,
        transcriptionOptions: [],
        reportingOptions: [],
        attributeOptions: [.audioTimeRange]
    )
    if let request = try await AssetInventory.assetInstallationRequest(
        supporting: [transcriber]
    ) {
        try await request.downloadAndInstall()
    }

    let analyzer = SpeechAnalyzer(modules: [transcriber])
    async let text: AttributedString = {
        var text = AttributedString()
        for try await result in transcriber.results {
            text.append(result.text)
        }
        return text
    }()

    do {
        let file = try AVAudioFile(forReading: url)
        _ = try await analyzer.analyzeSequence(from: file)
        try await analyzer.finalizeAndFinishThroughEndOfInput()
        return try await text
    } catch {
        await analyzer.cancelAndFinishNow()
        throw error
    }
}
```

Each final result is a phrase, emitted once in source order,
with attributed text, alternatives, and a source time range.
Times stay on the source recording's timeline,
including a file's starting position.

### Transcribe live audio

Supply buffers as an `AsyncStream<AnalyzerInput>` and request volatile results.
A volatile result replaces earlier volatile text for the same audio;
a final result never changes.

```swift
let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber(locale: locale, preset: .progressiveTranscription)
let (audio, input) = AsyncStream<AnalyzerInput>.makeStream()
let analyzer = SpeechAnalyzer(inputSequence: audio, modules: [transcriber])

Task {
    var finalized = AttributedString()
    for try await result in transcriber.results {
        if result.isFinal {
            finalized.append(result.text)
            show(finalized, pending: nil)
        } else {
            show(finalized, pending: result.text)
        }
    }
}

// Feed capture buffers as they arrive, then finish.
input.yield(AnalyzerInput(buffer: buffer))
input.finish()
try await analyzer.finalizeAndFinishThroughEndOfInput()
```

The package does not capture audio.
Supply buffers in any PCM format; the analyzer converts them for each module.
`finalize(through:)` makes results final through a time while input continues,
and `volatileRange` reports the audio whose results can still change.

> [!WARNING]
> On macOS 27.0.1, Apple's `AnalyzerInput(buffer:)` initializer traps
> for Float32 buffers.
> Convert capture buffers to Int16 before you wrap them.

### Dictation and speech detection

`DictationTranscriber` and `SpeechDetector` use Apple's backend.
All Apple modules in one analyzer share one native analyzer:

```swift
let dictation = DictationTranscriber(locale: locale, preset: .longDictation)
let detector = SpeechDetector()
let analyzer = SpeechAnalyzer(modules: [dictation, detector])
```

### Results and cancellation

A module belongs to one analyzer and permits one result iterator.
One input operation runs at a time.
Read results concurrently with analysis:
each module buffers at most 256 results and 4 MiB of text.
A newer volatile result replaces an unread one,
but final results are never dropped;
too many unread final results fail the session with
`SpeechRecognitionError.bufferOverflow`.

If you stop reading results early, cancel the analyzer:

```swift
for try await result in transcriber.results {
    if shouldStop(result) {
        await analyzer.cancelAndFinishNow()
        break
    }
    display(result)
}
```

Cancellation discards buffered results, ends every module's results,
and waits for cleanup.
The active input operation throws `CancellationError`.
If the session already failed, it keeps the original error.

### Differences from Apple's Speech framework

The package has its own analyzer, module, and result types that match Apple's,
and it reuses Speech value types such as `AnalyzerInput` and `AnalysisContext`.
Package modules do not conform to `Speech.SpeechModule`,
so the package analyzer does not accept Apple's module instances.
If a file imports both modules, qualify ambiguous names,
such as `AnySpeechRecognizer.SpeechAnalyzer`.
To read word timing and confidence, import Speech for its attribute keys:

```swift
import Speech

let range = run[AttributeScopes.SpeechAttributes.TimeRangeAttribute.self]
let confidence = run[AttributeScopes.SpeechAttributes.ConfidenceAttribute.self]
```

`SpeechAnalyzer.state` is an extension that reports the session's lifecycle.
The package does not provide custom language models
or the OS 27 capture and asset input providers.

## Backends

| Capability | Apple | Parakeet | Qwen3-ASR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `SpeechTranscriber` | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `DictationTranscriber`, `SpeechDetector` | Yes | No | No |
| Live input and volatile results | Yes | Yes | No; live input gives final results per segment |
| Fast results | Yes | Yes, with less right context | No |
| Alternatives, etiquette replacement | Yes | No | No |
| Word timing | Yes | Yes, in 80 ms frames | No; each result has its segment's range |
| Confidence | Yes | Yes, the geometric mean of token probabilities | No |
| Language | Selected by locale | Detected automatically, not reported; English only for `.unified` | Detected automatically, not reported, or forced |
| Assets | Apple's inventory | Pinned files in the Hugging Face cache | Pinned files in the Hugging Face cache |

Requests for an unsupported module or option fail before the analyzer reads audio.

### Apple

Modules created with a locale use Apple's Speech framework through `SystemSpeechModel`,
with every preset and option that Speech supports.
For these modules, `AssetInventory` forwards to Apple's inventory,
including locale reservations.

### Parakeet

`ParakeetSpeechModel` has three variants:

- `.v3` is NVIDIA's
  [Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3),
  which recognizes 25 European languages.
- `.ultra` is Moondream's
  [Parakeet Ultra](https://huggingface.co/moondream/parakeet-ultra),
  a post-trained version of v3 that is more accurate in most of our measurements.
- `.unified` is NVIDIA's
  [Parakeet Unified EN 0.6B](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b),
  which recognizes English only.
  It is the most accurate variant on English read speech,
  especially in live mode, but not on meetings.
  It is licensed under the NVIDIA Open Model License (see [License](#license)).

Creating a model does not download or load weights.
`AssetInventory` downloads pinned files from Hugging Face
and verifies the size and SHA-256 digest of each one.
`.v3` and `.ultra` need about 632 MB each, and `.unified` about 614 MB.
Modules with volatile or fast results also use an 8-second live encoder,
about 591 MB more, which makes live transcription faster
but raises its word error rate on long files.
Until it is installed, those modules use the 15-second encoder,
and `AssetInventory.status(forModules:)` reports them as not installed.

The files go into the standard Hugging Face cache:
`HF_HUB_CACHE` or `$HF_HOME/hub` if set,
`~/.cache/huggingface/hub` for Mac apps outside the sandbox,
and `Application Support/AnySpeechRecognizer/HuggingFace/hub`
for sandboxed apps and iOS apps.

To use the model offline, stage a directory with the compiled models and vocabulary:

```swift
let model = ParakeetSpeechModel(
    variant: .v3,
    assets: .directory(URL(fileURLWithPath: "/path/to/parakeet-models")),
    computeUnits: .cpuAndNeuralEngine
)
```

The directory contains `Encoder_v2.mlmodelc` or `Encoder.mlmodelc`,
`Decoder.mlmodelc`, `JointDecisionv3.mlmodelc`, `parakeet_vocab.json`,
and optionally the live encoder, `Encoder8s.mlmodelc`.
The runtime does not verify a staged directory.

### Qwen3-ASR

`QwenSpeechModel` runs Alibaba's
[Qwen3-ASR-0.6B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-0.6B-hf) or
[Qwen3-ASR-1.7B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-1.7B-hf) on Core ML
for file transcription.
It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects,
including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet does not cover.
The conversions are published at
[mattt/qwen3-asr-0.6b-coreml](https://huggingface.co/mattt/qwen3-asr-0.6b-coreml)
and [mattt/qwen3-asr-1.7b-coreml](https://huggingface.co/mattt/qwen3-asr-1.7b-coreml),
and `AssetInventory` installs and verifies their pinned files as it does Parakeet's:

```swift
let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber(
    model: QwenSpeechModel(
        variant: .large,
        language: Locale.Language(identifier: "yue")  // or nil to detect it
    ),
    transcriptionOptions: [],
    reportingOptions: [],
    attributeOptions: []
)
```

To use a conversion that you make with [`Tools/QwenConversion`](Tools/QwenConversion),
pass its output directory as `assets: .directory(url)`.

The model transcribes audio in segments of up to 40 seconds,
cut at the quietest point near 30 seconds, as the original Qwen3-ASR library cuts long audio.
Each segment becomes one final result with the segment's source range.
Results arrive when a segment is complete:
at a cut, at a gap in the input, or at finalization.
Live input works, but results trail the audio by up to 40 seconds.
Requests for volatile or fast results, word timing, confidence, or dictation
fail with `SpeechRecognitionError.unsupportedConfiguration` before the analyzer reads audio.
The model card's separate forced-alignment model, Qwen3-ForcedAligner-0.6B,
predicts word timing but is not integrated,
so results have no time attributes.

Qwen3-ASR-1.7B is more accurate than 0.6B in every test below.
Each converted model is an int8 audio encoder and an int8 text decoder
with a float16 embedding table:
0.94 GB for 0.6B (187 MB and 754 MB) and 2.36 GB for 1.7B (319 MB and 2,035 MB).
Both models run on the GPU; Core ML cannot build the decoder for the Neural Engine.
While it transcribes, a Mac needs about 1.7 GB of memory for 0.6B and 4.4 GB for 1.7B,
for a 10-second file as for a 36-minute meeting.

## Speaker diarization

`SpeakerDiarizer` identifies who speaks when.
Apple's Speech framework has no diarization module,
so code that uses it doesn't build with `import Speech`.
Add it to the same analyzer as a transcriber from either backend.
Both modules receive the same input,
and the diarizer does not change the transcriber's results:

```swift
let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber(
    model: ParakeetSpeechModel(variant: .v3),
    attributeOptions: [.audioTimeRange]
)
let diarizer = SpeakerDiarizer(model: SortformerDiarizationModel())
if let request = try await AssetInventory.assetInstallationRequest(
    supporting: [transcriber, diarizer]
) {
    try await request.downloadAndInstall()
}
let analyzer = SpeechAnalyzer(modules: [transcriber, diarizer])

async let transcript: AttributedString = {
    var text = AttributedString()
    for try await result in transcriber.results where result.isFinal {
        text.append(result.text)
    }
    return text
}()
async let speakers: SpeakerTimeline = {
    var timeline = SpeakerTimeline()
    for try await result in diarizer.results { timeline.apply(result) }
    return timeline
}()

let file = try AVAudioFile(forReading: url)
_ = try await analyzer.analyzeSequence(from: file)
try await analyzer.finalizeAndFinishThroughEndOfInput()

let attributed = try await speakers.attributing(try await transcript)
for turn in attributed.speakerTurns {
    print(turn.speaker?.description ?? "Unknown", String(turn.text.characters))
}
```

Each result lists speaker segments in a source range;
overlapping speech appears as overlapping segments.
`SpeakerTimeline` collects results
and attributes each timed word to the speaker who overlaps it the most.
The speaker attribute is in the package's own attribute scope,
`AttributeScopes.AnySpeechRecognizerAttributes`.
Request `.audioTimeRange` from the transcriber so that words have times.
A transcriber usually recognizes only the louder voice in overlapping speech,
so a short interjection can lack its own words.

`SortformerDiarizationModel` runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML.
It reports up to four speakers, numbered from 0 in order of arrival
and stable within one analyzer session.
Accuracy degrades with five or more speakers.
Final results trail the input by about 2 seconds.
File input and live input give the same results,
except near a `finalize(through:)` call or a gap in the input.
Each model version needs about 246 MB.

- `.v2`, the default, is
  [Streaming Sortformer 4spk v2](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2),
  licensed under CC BY 4.0.
- `.v2_1` is
  [Streaming Sortformer 4spk v2.1](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2.1),
  which NVIDIA trained with additional meeting data.
  It has the same architecture and latency,
  and is licensed under the NVIDIA Open Model License (see [License](#license)).

The default compute units are `cpuAndNeuralEngine`.
`cpuAndGPU` runs about three times faster
but uses about 530 MB of memory instead of about 135 MB.
To use a staged model, pass its version and the compiled model:
`SortformerDiarizationModel(version: .v2_1, assets: .compiledModel(url))`.

## Custom providers

To add a recognition engine,
implement `SpeechRecognitionModel` for its configuration
and `SpeechRecognitionExecutor` for one module's session.
The executor pulls timed buffers from its input
and publishes results through a sink that validates their timing.
Capabilities declare the options the provider supports;
other requests fail before the analyzer reads audio.

This provider reports placeholder text instead of recognizing speech:

```swift
import AVFoundation
import AnySpeechRecognizer
import CoreMedia

struct ExampleModel: SpeechRecognitionModel {
    let modelID = "example/placeholder"
    let capabilities = SpeechRecognitionCapabilities(
        transcription: .init(reportingOptions: [.volatileResults], attributeOptions: []),
        liveInput: true
    )
    func makeExecutor() -> any SpeechRecognitionExecutor { ExampleExecutor() }
}

actor ExampleExecutor: SpeechRecognitionExecutor {
    private var results: SpeechRecognitionResultSink?
    private var finalized = CMTime.zero
    private var consumed = CMTime.zero

    func prepare(
        request: SpeechRecognitionRequest, format: AVAudioFormat, context: AnalysisContext
    ) async throws {
        try request.validate(for: ExampleModel().capabilities)
    }

    func analyze(_ input: SpeechAnalysisInput, results: SpeechRecognitionResultSink) async throws {
        self.results = results
        for try await buffer in input {
            consumed = buffer.endTime
            let pending = CMTimeRange(start: finalized, end: consumed)
            results.setVolatileRange(pending)
            try await results.emit(
                .init(text: "Speech so far", range: pending, resultsFinalizationTime: finalized)
            )
        }
    }

    func finalize(through time: CMTime) async throws {
        guard let results, time > finalized else { return }
        let range = CMTimeRange(start: finalized, end: min(time, consumed))
        try await results.emit(
            .init(text: "Final text. ", range: range, resultsFinalizationTime: range.end)
        )
        finalized = range.end
        results.setVolatileRange(nil)
    }

    func cancel() async {}
}

let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber(model: ExampleModel(), reportingOptions: [.volatileResults])
```

`finalize(through:)` and other controls refer to source times,
so the executor applies them when its input reaches them.
A provider whose assets depend on the request can implement
`availability(for:)` and `assetInstallationRequest(supporting:)`.

## Command-line tool

The `hear` executable transcribes, diarizes, and evaluates local files:

```console
$ swift run hear prepare --backend parakeet --live --diarize
$ swift run hear transcribe meeting.wav --backend parakeet --live --diarize
$ swift run hear transcribe recording.wav --backend apple --locale en-US --json
```

Every command requires an explicit `--backend`.
`--backend qwen` uses the built-in assets of the size that `--version` selects
(default: 1.7b) unless `--model-directory` names a staged directory,
and its `--locale` forces a language, such as `--locale ja`.
`prepare` is the only command that downloads;
`status` checks assets without downloading.
`--live` reads the file in 100 ms blocks with volatile results,
and `--diarize` adds a Sortformer diarizer
and prints one line for each speaker turn.
`--json` writes one record per line with word ranges, speaker segments,
and finalization times.
`evaluate` also reports elapsed time, peak memory,
and, with `--reference` or `--rttm`, the word error rate or diarization error rate.
Run `swift run hear --help` for all options.

## Accuracy and performance

We measured the `hear` CLI on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1.
Each LibriSpeech row has about 30 minutes of audio,
each FLEURS row the first 100 test files,
and the AMI row four test meetings (1.5 hours).
Word error rates are computed after lowercasing and removing punctuation.
Parakeet Unified recognizes English only, so it was not run on FLEURS.
Apple's transcriber was not run on FLEURS.

| Test set | Parakeet v3, file | v3, live | Ultra, file | Ultra, live | Unified, file | Unified, live | Apple, file |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LibriSpeech test-clean, utterances | 2.57% | 3.28% | 2.27% | 2.51% | 2.07% | 2.24% | 2.81% |
| LibriSpeech test-other, utterances | 3.51% | 4.19% | 3.53% | 3.92% | 3.09% | 3.23% | 4.54% |
| LibriSpeech test-clean, 3–8 min files | 1.55% | 4.73% | 1.66% | 2.65% | 1.43% | 1.45% | 2.12% |
| LibriSpeech test-other, 3–8 min files | 2.78% | 4.29% | 2.55% | 3.28% | 2.19% | 2.42% | 3.97% |
| FLEURS German | 4.90% | 7.30% | 4.22% | 4.39% | | | |
| FLEURS French | 6.55% | 9.13% | 5.62% | 5.82% | | | |
| AMI meetings, headset mix | 26.72% | 23.95% | 25.17% | 23.56% | 25.25% | 25.41% | 29.24% |

Parakeet v3 and Ultra process an hour of audio in 18 to 31 seconds in file mode
and in 93 to 112 seconds in live mode;
Unified takes 33 to 42 seconds and 124 to 136 seconds.
Peak memory is about 100 MB except while Core ML compiles a model,
which can take about 680 MB.
Parakeet v3 and Ultra word start times have a median error of 60 ms
against forced alignments of LibriSpeech.

For Qwen3-ASR, the table below gives character error rates on the first 100 FLEURS test files,
counted after NFKC normalization, without punctuation, symbols, or spaces;
Cantonese texts are first converted to simplified characters with OpenCC,
because the references use traditional characters and the model writes either script.
The references write numbers as digits, Latin names in Latin script,
and some English glosses in parentheses that speakers did not always read.
The model often writes such numbers in words and such names in the local script,
so these rates are higher than the model card's.
The transformers columns transcribe each file in one call with greedy decoding on the CPU;
the package's runtime stays within 0.32 points of them.

| Test set | 0.6B | 0.6B, transformers | 1.7B | 1.7B, transformers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FLEURS Mandarin | 7.11% | 7.14% | 6.28% | 6.25% |
| FLEURS Japanese | 9.49% | 9.31% | 6.10% | 6.08% |
| FLEURS Korean | 5.29% | 4.97% | 3.93% | 3.80% |
| FLEURS Cantonese | 8.15% | | 6.25% | |
| LibriSpeech test-clean, utterances (WER) | 2.14% | 2.10% | 1.97% | 1.86% |
| LibriSpeech test-other, utterances (WER) | 4.65% | 4.63% | 3.46% | 3.40% |

On the other sets of the first table,
Qwen3-ASR had word error rates of 1.68% with 0.6B and 1.58% with 1.7B
on the test-clean 3–8 min files,
2.63% and 1.94% on the test-other 3–8 min files,
6.67% and 3.88% on FLEURS German, 8.71% and 5.12% on FLEURS French,
and 26.31% and 24.49% on the AMI meetings.

On the sets of this table, Qwen3-ASR file mode took 10.5 to 15.4 minutes per hour of audio
with 0.6B and 14.5 to 21.2 minutes with 1.7B;
the 3–8 min files took 7.9 to 8.1 minutes per hour with 0.6B
and 12.6 to 12.9 minutes with 1.7B.
These times leave out model loading and Core ML compilation,
and each is the median of two runs that differed by less than 2%.
Peak memory was 1.7 GB for 0.6B and 4.4 GB for 1.7B.

With Parakeet v3 in the same analyzer,
Sortformer's diarization error rate on the 16 AMI test meetings,
with overlapping speech and no collar,
was 25.73% for v2 and 23.42% for v2.1.

## Limitations

- Fast results are not usable on natural speech:
  they insert repeated filler, such as "and the other thing",
  and reach 15% to 22% WER on long recordings.
  Live mode does this less often.
- Parakeet sometimes decodes a window of speech as silence,
  mostly in live mode and in meetings with overlapping speech.
- Parakeet Unified's word start times are currently about 300 ms late.
- Parakeet on a physical iPhone, the OS 26 runtime,
  and the minimum Swift 6.2 toolchain are not yet tested.
- Qwen3-ASR transcribes files only, with no word timing and no context prompt,
  and it is not tested on iOS devices.
  Its decoder runs only on the GPU, and file mode takes 8 to 21 minutes per hour of audio,
  where Parakeet v3 and Ultra take 18 to 31 seconds.
- With Apple's analyzer, `finalize(through:)` for the newest audio
  can wait until more input arrives while the input stream stays open.
- An interrupted download keeps the files that finished,
  but a partial file starts over
  ([swift-huggingface#97](https://github.com/huggingface/swift-huggingface/issues/97)).

## Development

The repository uses [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev/) tasks.
Swift comes from the selected Xcode.

| Task | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `mise run setup` | Resolve package dependencies. |
| `mise run build` | Build the library and CLI. |
| `mise run build:ios` | Compile the library for iOS. |
| `mise run test` | Run the tests without model downloads. |
| `mise run test:compatibility` | Build the [fixtures](Tests/Fixtures/Compatibility) with `import Speech` and with `import AnySpeechRecognizer`. |
| `mise run test:integration` | Run opt-in tests with local recordings and installed assets. |
| `mise run evaluate` | Run `hear evaluate` on a local recording. |
| `mise run prepare:apple` | Download and prepare Apple Speech assets. |
| `mise run prepare:parakeet` | Download and prepare Parakeet assets. |

Integration tests read their inputs from environment variables:
`ANYSPEECH_INTEGRATION_AUDIO` selects the Apple tests,
`ANYSPEECH_PARAKEET_MODELS` with `ANYSPEECH_PARAKEET_LONG_AUDIO`
selects the Parakeet tests,
and `ANYSPEECH_QWEN_MODELS` with `ANYSPEECH_QWEN_AUDIO` selects the Qwen3-ASR tests.

The [`Tools`](Tools) directory contains the development tools:

- [`ParakeetConversion`](Tools/ParakeetConversion) and
  [`SortformerConversion`](Tools/SortformerConversion)
  convert NVIDIA's checkpoints to the Core ML models that the package downloads.
- [`QwenConversion`](Tools/QwenConversion) converts, verifies, and packages Qwen3-ASR
  for `QwenSpeechModel`.
- `make-parakeet-manifest.py`, `make-sortformer-manifest.py`, and `make-qwen-manifest.py`
  generate the pinned model manifests.
- `natural-speech-eval.py` downloads the test sets
  and reproduces the measurements above.
- `make-evaluation-audio.swift` and `make-diarization-audio.swift`
  generate synthetic recordings for stress and diarization tests.

 Language models can do a lot.
They write, summarize, translate, and call tools.
But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do. 
 Say a customer calls your support line.
First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition).
Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision).
You  could  hand both to a language model,
but there are models built for each that are
better, faster, and less expensive. 
 In our  AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap ,
we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases,
we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions:
familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model. 
 Today we're announcing two packages: 
 
  AnySpeechRecognizer 
implements Apple's new speech-to-text API with a choice of recognition engine,
including NVIDIA's Parakeet and Alibaba's Qwen3-ASR running locally on Core ML,
and adds speaker diarization to track who speaks when. 
  AnyDecisionModel 
answers yes-or-no, multiple-choice, and rating-scale questions
with typed results and probabilities.
It derives each answer from the model's probabilities
instead of generating text,
using a model on your device with MLX, Core AI, or llama.cpp,
or a decision model from Jev or Ollama. 
 
 Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub
and run them on device. 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		AnySpeechRecognizer
	 
 
 Computers have been transcribing speech for decades,
and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it.
Apple platforms already have an API for it.
macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced  SpeechAnalyzer ,
Apple's new speech-to-text API.
You add modules such as  SpeechTranscriber  and  SpeechDetector  to an analyzer,
give it a file or a stream of audio buffers,
and read results from async sequences as they arrive.
 AssetInventory  installs the models,
so your app decides when downloads happen. 
 It's a well-designed API,
but the only engine behind it is Apple's.
AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine: 
   - import Speech 
 + import AnySpeechRecognizer 
  
 The package mirrors  SpeechAnalyzer ,  SpeechTranscriber ,  DictationTranscriber ,
 SpeechDetector , and  AssetInventory ,
with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine.
If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough.
To use Parakeet instead,
change only how you create the transcriber: 
   let  transcriber  =   SpeechTranscriber (
    model:  ParakeetSpeechModel (variant: .v3),
    transcriptionOptions: [],
    reportingOptions: [.volatileResults],
    attributeOptions: [.audioTimeRange]
)
  
 The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer,
and reading results stay the same.
The  README 
has a complete example
and  lists the differences 
from Apple's framework. 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Meet the models
	 
 
  Parakeet v3  is NVIDIA's  Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 .
It's a polyglot:
it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing,
so you don't pass a locale. 
  Parakeet Ultra  is Moondream's  post-trained take on v3 .
It was more accurate in most of our measurements. 
  Parakeet Unified  is NVIDIA's
 English-only Parakeet . 
 All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime,
which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing,
and word confidence. 
  Qwen3-ASR  is Alibaba's speech model,
in  0.6B 
and  1.7B  sizes.
It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects,
including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover.
It detects the language automatically, or you can set one: 
   let  transcriber  =   SpeechTranscriber (
    model:  QwenSpeechModel (variant: .large, language:  Locale . Language (identifier:  "yue" )),
    transcriptionOptions: [],
    reportingOptions: [],
    attributeOptions: []
)
  
 Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds,
without volatile results, word timing, or confidence.
It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet,
so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input. 
 To add another engine, implement  SpeechRecognitionModel  for its configuration
and  SpeechRecognitionExecutor  for one module's session.
The README includes a  small provider 
that reports placeholder text to help you get started. 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Core ML models on the Hub

we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:

 Each repository records its source checkpoint
and a checksum for every file,
and the package pins it to a fixed revision.
The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input,
which cuts live analysis time by about a third
at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate.
The repository also has the conversion workflows,
most of which follow FluidInference's  mobius  scripts,
and checks each conversion against the original model. 
 Downloads happen only when your app asks for them:
about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder,
0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer.
Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache,
so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools. 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Speaker diarization
	 
 
 When you transcribe a conversation,
you often want to know who said what.
That's speaker diarization,
and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it,
so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one.
 SpeakerDiarizer  runs NVIDIA's
 Streaming Sortformer 
on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber,
on the same timeline: 
   let  diarizer  =   SpeakerDiarizer (model:  SortformerDiarizationModel ())
 if   let  request  =   try   await   AssetInventory .assetInstallationRequest(
    supporting: [transcriber, diarizer]
) {
     try   await  request.downloadAndInstall()
}
 let  analyzer  =   SpeechAnalyzer (modules: [transcriber, diarizer])
  
 The diarizer tracks up to four speakers,
even when they talk over each other.
A  SpeakerTimeline  collects its results
and attributes each timed word to a speaker,
so you can print a transcript by speaker turn.
Like image support in AnyLanguageModel,
this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today. 
 The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default.
You can also choose  v2.1 ,
which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data
and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too. 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		How well does it work?
	 
 
 We measured the package with its  hear  command-line tool
on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1.
Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes: 
 
	 
		  
 Transcriber 
 test-clean 
 test-other 
 

		   
 Parakeet v3, file 
 1.55% 
 2.78% 
 
 
 Parakeet v3, live 
 4.73% 
 4.29% 
 
 
 Parakeet Ultra, file 
 1.66% 
 2.55% 
 
 
 Parakeet Ultra, live 
 2.65% 
 3.28% 
 
 
 Parakeet Unified, file 
 1.43% 
 2.19% 
 
 
 Parakeet Unified, live 
 1.45%

 2.12%

 Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio
in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file,
or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live,
with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model.
Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory.
Meetings are hard for everyone:
on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other,
every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%. 
 These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets,
so measure with your own hardware and audio.
 hear evaluate  works on your own files,
and the repository's  natural-speech-eval.py  tool
 reproduces these measurements .
So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone. 
 Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27. 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		AnyDecisionModel
	 
 
 AnyDecisionModel is a different story.
There's no Apple framework to map onto,
and decision models aren't new, exactly. 
 
 It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France;
otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification. 
 
 What's new is the name, a lot of hype,
and a crop of models trained to make decisions.
We think that's where things are going,
so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them. 
 Apps often ask language models to make decisions.
 Is this message urgent? 
 Which team should handle this ticket? 
 How frustrated is this customer? 
The usual approach is to prompt a language model
and parse the text that it generates.
That gives you one answer,
but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives. 
 Here's what a decision looks like in Swift: 
   import  AnyDecisionModel

 enum   Department :  String ,  Choosable  {
     case  billing, technical, sales
}

 let  ticket  =   "I was charged twice for my order, and now the app logs me out when I try to ask for a refund." 

 let  model  =   MLXDecisionModel (modelID:  "mlx-community/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-4bit" )
 let  session  =   DecisionSession (model: model, state: .text(ticket))

 let  urgent  =   try   await  session.probability(of:  "Does this convey urgency?" )
 let  team  =   try   await  session.choice( "Which team?" , from:  Department . self )
 let  anger  =   try   await  session.score(
     "How frustrated?" ,
    levels: [ "Calm" ,  "Frustrated" ,  "Very angry" ]
)
  
  urgent  is a  Double .
 team  is a  Choice<Department>  containing the selected case,
a probability for each option, and a confidence value.
 anger  is a  Score  containing the expected level,
a probability for each level, and a confidence value.
Because  Department  conforms to  Choosable ,
 team.value  is a  Department  that you can use in an exhaustive  switch . 
 If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel,
the model-and-session pattern will look familiar.
A  DecisionSession  holds a single state, which can be text or JSON,
and every question is about that state.
Questions are independent:
an answer never becomes input to a later question.
To ask several questions at once,
pass them to  decide(_:)  as a batch. 
 For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt
with a one-token label for each allowed answer,
then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass. 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Try it out: Emoji Magnet
	 
 
    
 Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji.
Type a phrase, such as "things you wear",
and the emoji that match rise out of the pile.
Refine it to "things you wear in winter",
and the emoji that no longer match fall back. 
 The app has no built-in keyword rules;
the model decides everything at inference time.
When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji,
for example: 
  Statement: a heavy winter coat fits the description "things you wear". Is this statement true?
  
 The session's state holds the phrase.
The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend,
which answers all 343 questions in one request,
so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase.
Without a  TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY , the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend.
That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once,
then answers 16 questions per forward pass.
On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads.
A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds,
and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive. 
 Emoji Magnet is in the  AnyDecisionModel-Examples  repository. 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Decision heads and Clef
	 
 
 Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models,
but those models weren't trained to make decisions.
Cloudflare's  Clef  models
are an example of a newer approach:
a model with a trained decision head
that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions,
returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions
in one forward pass.
 Clef-Flash  is the 9B variant. 
 AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX: 
   let  model  =   MLXHeadDecisionModel (
    modelID:  "mlx-community/clef-flash-4bit" ,
    head: .jointSchema
)
  
 You use the same sessions and questions,
but  MLXHeadDecisionModel  reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head
instead of from next-token probabilities.
The  4-bit model  is a 6.2 GB download,
and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory.
Clef can read images and video,
but this backend accepts only text and JSON states. 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Calibrating and checking probabilities
	 
 
 Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident.
The local backends accept a  Calibration ,
which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers.
Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results. 
 Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list.
On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends,
turn on  rotationDebiasing  to ask a choice question
once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities.
That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation. 
 Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value
based on the entropy of its probabilities.
It measures how concentrated the probabilities are,
not whether the answer is right,
so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold.
The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability
the model assigned to the allowed answers.
A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere. 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Backends
	 
 
 AnyDecisionModel has six backends: 
 
  MLX  runs a small language model on Apple silicon
with  mlx-swift-lm 
and downloads it from the Hub. 
  MLX decision heads  run a model with its own trained decision head,
such as Clef. 
  Core AI  does the same as MLX with a Core AI model on macOS 27 and iOS 27. 
  llama.cpp  reads decisions from a local GGUF model
through  llama.swift . 
  Jev  calls TypeSafe's Jev through the  System One API ,
or any server that implements it, such as  Kev . 
  Ollama  calls a System One decision model on a local Ollama server
or in Ollama's cloud.
It requires Ollama 0.35.0 or later, or 0.40.5 or later for cloud models. 
 
 The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9,
so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels.
Decision heads have no such limit. 
 Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits.
Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies.
You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends,
which also build on Linux.
Enable the  MLX ,  CoreAI , or  Llama  trait for the local backends. 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Get started
	 
 
 Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later.
The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon.
AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later
and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime. 
 Add the packages to your  Package.swift : 
  dependencies: [
    .package(url:  "https://github.com/mattt/AnySpeechRecognizer" , from:  "0.1.0" ),
    .package(
        url:  "https://github.com/mattt/AnyDecisionModel" ,
        from:  "0.6.0" ,
        traits: [ "MLX" ]
    ),
]
  
 For now, AnyDecisionModel's  CoreAI  trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer,
because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0
and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x. 
 Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends.
AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool,  hear ,
that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results.
Every  hear  command requires  --backend apple ,  --backend parakeet , or  --backend qwen ;
run  hear prepare  with the same backend and model options before analysis
to install the needed assets. 
 Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't.
Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

		Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software
	 
           Enterprise         Article        Published
					October 29, 2026                          Upvote  20                                                                 +14                                                Kate Soule      katesoule                  Follow                     ibm-granite                       Luis A Lastras      GrizleeBer                  Follow                     ibm-granite                       Subhajit Chaudhury      subhajit1412                  Follow                     ibm-granite                       Abraham Daniels      abedaniels                  Follow                     ibm-granite                    :last-child]:mb-0">       
     
 Just over a week ago, we released  Granite Switch 4.1 , showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint. 
  Granite Switch 4.1.1  is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood. 
 
  Updated Granite Speech ASR model  — multilingual speech-to-text across 10 languages with native punctuation and capitalization, so transcripts are ready for downstream models without a formatting pass. 
 Updated Decision adapter in  granitelib-core  —  featuring improved overall performance on the Jev Decision Index test set. 
 
 While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy. 
 This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon. 
 Until then, test out our  latest models , and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our  Speech-to-Decisions  demo.

Fewer than half led to a study that says the same thing.     Mack Grenfell  28 October 2026 · 12 min read        44%, drawn coming apart: a statistic with no study underneath it.    “44% of salespeople give up after just one follow-up attempt.”         All five assistants we asked said it. We couldn’t find a study behind it.          1 Following one number     2 Where the trails end     3 What AI cites     4 How numbers change     5 The zombie stats      What to do            1  Following one number back to its source    We asked ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude and Google’s AI Overviews 200 questions that call for a number, the kind people ask every day.  1   Note 1 A statistic is a share, rate, average, count or cost that an assistant states as fact. We left out advice (“save 20% of your income”) and prices.   Then we clicked the citations, and kept clicking. Here is one trail, from the answer to the end.        Google AI Overviews  What percentage of salespeople give up after one follow-up?   44%  of salespeople give up after just one follow-up attempt. 1      44%     44%     44%     44%     44%          A sales firm’s stats page  2020    44%  of salespeople give up after one follow-up attempt  (source) .         A freelance writer’s sample article  by 2017   80 Percent of Sales Require 5 Follow-up Calls after Meeting;  44 Percent  Salespeople Give Up After One Follow-up         No study behind it  This page cites no research.          In the answer  Every assistant got the same question: “What percentage of salespeople give up after one follow-up?” All five assistants gave the same figure, and only ChatGPT said the evidence behind it was unclear.    One click in  Google AI Overviews cited a sales firm’s stats page, from 2020. The number is right there. Its “source” link goes to a writing sample.    Two clicks in  That leads to a freelance writer’s sample article, online by 2017. The number is in its headline. It lists two slide decks, a blog list and two news stories. None is a study of follow-ups.    The end of the trail  That’s where the trail ends. We tried every other route to this number we could find, and each one stopped at a page that cites no research. This is what we mean by a zombie stat: a number that keeps getting repeated with no study behind it.      Most numbers aren’t like this one. The trouble is that you can’t tell which ones are from the answer. This one came with the same confident tone and the same kind of citation as any other, and all five assistants agreed on it. So we followed 1,285 statistics the same way.      2  Fewer than half lead back to a study    We took a random sample of the statistics each assistant cited, 1,285 in all, and walked every trail the same way: the cited page, then that page’s source, up to five pages deep.  2   Note 2 Each assistant’s sample was drawn at random from the statistics it cited: ChatGPT 108, Perplexity 277, Gemini 300, Claude 300, Google AI Overviews 300. The five-assistant rate weights each assistant by how many cited statistics it quoted, so it describes the statistics people were shown.   Where a page named a source without a link, we searched for it.  40% reached a study that says the same thing. Another 8% reached the study, but the number or its context had changed on the way. The rest never got there: 40% stopped at a source we couldn’t check, because it was locked, gone or silent on the number, and 11% led nowhere at all.  3   Note 3 An AI model judged every trail, and a stronger one re-judged 300. Then people re-checked 150 trails at random, with a third check wherever the two disagreed. People found originals the model missed: by the model alone, 23% were sourced. Every rate here is corrected with the hand checks, and its range carries the uncertainty from both.       Four in ten trails reached a study that says the same thing  Each square is one in a hundred of the 1,285 statistics we traced, sorted by where its trail ended.                                                                                                                                                                                                                 40%    Sourced  We found the study, and it says the same thing.    8%    Changed  We found the study, but the number, who was asked, where or when is different.    40%    Can’t check  A page names a real source, but the number isn’t in it, or the source is locked or gone.    11%    Nowhere  No study anywhere on the trail. Every page repeats the number and credits no one.     The last 1%: trails whose pages wouldn’t load for us.    Trakkr Research, five AI assistants asked 200 questions that call for a number, October 2026. A random sample of each assistant’s cited statistics, weighted by how many each quoted, and corrected with 150 trails checked by hand. Sourced: 40%, 95% range 34% to 46%.  Cite     ChatGPT did best, and quoted the fewest numbers: 1.3 per answer, against 6.8 for Claude. The other four landed between 38% and 46%, too close to rank.     ChatGPT quoted the fewest numbers, and sourced the most  The same hundred squares for each assistant, from its own sample of cited statistics.                                                                                                                                                                                                                 ChatGPT   57%  sourced  1.3 statistics per answer                                                                                                                                                                                                               Perplexity   46%  sourced  2.2 statistics per answer                                                                                                                                                                                                               AI Overviews   39%  sourced  4.8 statistics per answer                                                                                                                                                                                                               Gemini   38%  sourced  6.2 statistics per answer                                                                                                                                                                                                               Claude   38%  sourced  6.8 statistics per answer      Trakkr Research, five AI assistants asked 200 questions that call for a number, October 2026. Traced per assistant: ChatGPT 108, Perplexity 277, Google AI Overviews 300, Gemini 300, Claude 300. The four after ChatGPT sit inside each other’s ranges, so they aren’t ranked.  Cite     To check this wasn’t down to the questions we picked, we also traced 300 statistics from Google AI Overviews answers to real everyday searches. 40% were sourced, about the same share.  4   Note 4 Google AI Overviews answers to 52,930 everyday English searches that Trakkr tracked between 25 September 2026 and 25 October 2026. 4.4% carried a statistic, and we traced 300 of those the same way. Only counts and rates leave our systems.        3  AI mostly cites pages that repeat the number    The AI mostly wasn’t making numbers up. The page it cited had the figure 82% of the time. But only 21% of the pages cited for a number were the original research.  More than half were company blogs. Add news stories and statistics roundups and you have most of the citations: pages that repeat figures from somewhere else, often without linking to it.     How often each kind of cited page led to the study  Every page an assistant cited first for a number, by kind. Each column’s width is its share of those citations. Statistics grouped by figure and meaning. Original year shown where the trail reached the study.  Cite       What to do with a statistic from an AI  Treat it as a lead rather than a source. Here’s what we’d do, whether you use these numbers or publish them.     If you use them    1   Follow the citation, then follow it again.  If the cited page is a list of statistics or a company blog, use its own link to go one page further. Keep going until you reach the study itself, or until you can’t.     2   Check who was asked, how many, and when.  Most of the changes we found were in the context, not the digits: one country’s poll, a ten-year-old study, fifteen people.     3   Don’t take agreement as a check.  Five assistants giving the same number isn’t five sources. The numbers they repeated most were no better sourced than the rest.       If you publish them    1   Put the method next to the number.  The sample, the date and a link to the source, on the same page as the figure, so the next page, and the next answer, can trace it back to you.     2   Keep the findings in the open.  Reports behind a form were a common dead end: even trails that started at a research firm fell short 38% of the time. Put the headline numbers and the method on an open page.     3   See which page AI cites for your numbers.  It is often a roundup or a blog that copied you, sometimes with an older figure. That page decides what people hear.            How we did it  Everything you need to check our work, repeat it or cite it.     Questions   200  160 everyday questions in 16 topics, plus 40 famous statistics     Answers   1,000  From ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude and Google AI Overviews     Statistics quoted   3,167  2,419 with a citation, in answers to the everyday questions     Trails followed   1,285  A random sample of cited statistics, up to five pages deep; 180 checked by hand       We asked each assistant 200 questions that call for a number, word for word, through its company’s API with web search on and a US location: 160 everyday questions across 16 topics, and 40 famous statistics we suspected, reported separately. We pulled every statistic out of every answer, with the page it cited.  For a random sample of each assistant’s cited statistics (every one of ChatGPT’s, up to 300 from each of the others), we opened the cited page, found the figure, and followed the page’s own source, up to five pages deep. Where a page named a source without a link, we searched for it. An AI model judged each trail, and a stronger model re-judged 300 of them, agreeing on the outcome 82% of the time.  Then we checked 150 trails by hand, picked at random, with a third check wherever the hand check and the model disagreed. A trail we checked by hand counts as we found it; every other trail counts as the mix of outcomes we found by hand behind the model’s verdict. The ranges carry the uncertainty from both samples. Trakkr. https://trakkr.ai/trakkr-research/zombie-stats   Copy citation         Questions  The ones we hear most about this study.       Do AI assistants make up statistics?      Rarely, in our sample. The page an assistant cited contained the figure 82% of the time. The bigger problem is upstream: the pages AI cites are mostly blogs and roundups repeating a number. Of the statistics we traced, four in ten reached a study that says the same thing.       Which AI assistant is most reliable with statistics?      In our sample, ChatGPT did best: 57% of the statistics it quoted reached a matching original, and it quoted the fewest. The other four were between 38% and 46%. Every assistant quoted numbers that led nowhere.       How can I check a statistic an AI gives me?      Open the source it cites. If that page is a list of statistics or a company blog, follow its link to the next page, and keep going until you reach the study itself. Check the year, who was asked and how many, then quote the study, not the page that repeated it.       What is a zombie statistic?      A number that keeps being repeated after its source has changed, aged or never existed. It survives because each page copies the last one, and AI assistants now repeat it to millions of people.       Can I use these numbers in my own work?      Yes, with attribution. Cite Trakkr Research Study 013 and link to this page. The aggregate data is a free JSON download. page:https://skypilot.ai/blog/grace-blac.text: Grace Blackwell needs a new scheduler: 27% more usable GPUs from the same racks | SkyPilot                                              New study: SkyPilot’s scheduler bumps NVL72 training throughput by 14%                Platform    Tokens    Case Studies     Docs     Open Source  SkyPilot Platform        Resources     Blog  Company  Careers                10.8k                          Get started                    Platform    Tokens    Case Studies     Docs      Open Source    SkyPilot Platform       Resources      Blog    Company    Careers                            Get started            Grace Blackwell needs a new scheduler: 27% more usable GPUs from the same racks  NVL72 puts all 72 GPUs in a rack on one NVLink fabric, but only rack-local jobs get the speedup. How SkyPilot keeps multi-node training and inference on NVLink with topology-aware placement, in-place recovery from GPU failures, and automatic defragmentation.       Rohan Sonecha  Member of Technical Staff      Oct 29, 2026               Training at scale is a communication problem      Tensor Parallelism    Expert Parallelism           Inference needs fast inter-node networking too           The rack is the new server           Sometimes less is more: using less nodes in each rack significantly improves reliability           How a modern scheduler keeps jobs on NVLink      Schedulers need to understand the hardware    Fragmentation blocks rack-scale jobs           Conclusion              Not all high-speed interconnects are created equal, and using the wrong one can be quite costly: running the same distributed training job over InfiniBand rather than NVLink can  degrade performance by 43% .  Historically, NVLink was limited to communication within a single node, meaning that multi-node AI workloads were forced to communicate over InfiniBand or a cloud equivalent (EFA on AWS, GPUDirect-TCPX on GCP). NVIDIA’s NVL72 systems remove this limitation by connecting all 72 GPUs in a rack with a unified NVLink fabric, so GPUs on different nodes can exchange data with an order of magnitude more bandwidth.       However, maximizing the benefits of NVL72 systems is highly dependent on workload placement: a multi-node job spread across racks is still bottlenecked by InfiniBand. Preserving rack-locality gets harder as hardware failures take nodes offline and jobs finishing at different times scatter free capacity across racks.  This blog covers the communication bottleneck in large-scale training and inference, the NVL72 rack-scale fabric, and slice sizing for resilience to GPU failures, as well as how the  SkyPilot Platform  keeps multi-node jobs rack-local through topology-aware placement, in-place recovery from hardware failures, and automatic defragmentation of shared clusters.    Training at scale is a communication problem    #    Frontier training jobs run across thousands of GPUs. Doing so requires answering two questions:   How do you shard your model across GPUs to ensure that it can actually run?  Given your compute budget, how many copies of the sharded model can you run to maximize training throughput?   The first question is typically answered with a combination of:   Tensor Parallelism (TP): splitting a layer’s weight matrices across GPUs  Expert Parallelism (EP): placing a mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer’s experts on different GPUs  Pipeline Parallelism (PP): splitting a model layer-wise across GPUs   The answer to the second question sets the degree of Data Parallelism (DP): the number of copies of the sharded model that train in parallel, each on a different slice of the training data.  Of these parallelism strategies, tensor parallelism’s all-reduce and expert parallelism’s all-to-all communication patterns sit on the critical path during training, making them  the most important to keep on NVLink  (§9.1.2).  Tensor Parallelism  Tensor parallelism splits the weight matrices inside each layer across GPUs, so every GPU only stores and computes a slice of each layer.  Transformer layers are made up of two blocks: self-attention and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP). At its core, each block is two matrix multiplications (GEMMs) in a row.  Megatron-LM  (§3) showed that by partitioning a block’s first GEMM column-wise and its second GEMM row-wise, the GPUs only need to synchronize via all-reduce once per block, after the second GEMM, instead of after each one.        Figure 1.  Tensor parallelism across two GPUs. A is split column-wise, so each GPU computes its own slice of y without communicating. B is split row-wise to match, so each GPU produces a partial z, and one all-reduce sums the partial results.    Even with this optimization, tensor parallelism still requires two all-reduces per transformer layer during the forward pass.  These all-reduce steps sit on the critical path  during training because they cannot be fully overlapped with computation. As a result, tensor parallelism is typically kept on NVLink: Hugging Face measured a 43% drop in training throughput when it moved off NVLink onto InfiniBand.  Expert Parallelism  In a mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer, the MLP block is replaced by many smaller MLPs, called experts, and a router that sends each token to a small subset of experts. Expert parallelism splits MoE layers such that these small, independent experts are placed on different GPUs.  Under expert parallelism, each MoE layer requires two all-to-all communication steps during the forward pass, dispatch and combine. A router selects the top- k  experts for each token and dispatches tokens to the GPUs that have those experts in memory. Each GPU then computes its local experts on the tokens it received via a single grouped matrix multiplication. Finally, the expert outputs are sent back to each token's original GPU and combined.        Figure 2.  Expert parallelism distributes experts across GPUs. The all-to-all communication dispatches tokens to their assigned experts and combines results. (Source:  NVIDIA , Figure 4.)    As models add more MoE layers and route each token to more experts, the volume of all-to-all traffic grows, introducing a communication bottleneck.  Training an MoE model with 64-way expert parallelism spreads each MoE layer’s experts across 64 GPUs. On standard 8-GPU servers, that moves the all-to-all traffic off high-bandwidth NVLink and through much narrower InfiniBand interconnects where unoptimized communication can consume  up to 60% of training time  (§1.2). On NVL72 systems, all 64 GPUs stay within a single NVLink domain,  effectively eliminating the communication bottleneck  (§9.2.2).    Inference needs fast inter-node networking too    #    The parallelism techniques discussed above are not unique to training. Beyond enabling inference engines to serve models that are too large for a single GPU, model parallelism can also improve throughput. Splitting a model's weights across more GPUs frees up memory for the KV cache, so the engine can process  more concurrent requests or support larger context windows . In some cases, the freed memory grows faster than the number of GPUs: in one  vLLM  benchmark, splitting a model tensor-parallel across two GPUs increased the amount of KV cache blocks by 13.9x and delivered 3.9x more throughput.        Figure 3.  GPU memory breakdown for Llama-3.1-70B on one vs. two H100s. (Data:  vLLM .)    Expert parallelism follows the same logic. With a low degree of expert parallelism, each GPU holds many experts, leaving less room for the KV cache. WideEP, which refers to expert-parallel configurations spanning multiple nodes, significantly reduces the number of experts per GPU. The trade-off is network traffic: every all-to-all now spans more GPUs. On standard 8-GPU servers, an expert-parallel group can span at most eight GPUs before it has to communicate over InfiniBand, where  per-GPU bandwidth drops 18x . NVL72 removes this limit by keeping all 72 GPUs in a rack on NVLink. When serving DeepSeek-R1 at interactive speeds, GB200 NVL72 with 32-way expert parallelism delivers  up to 4.4x higher throughput per GPU  than 8-GPU B200 servers, which are capped at 8-way.    The rack is the new server    #    NVL72 extends NVLink from a single node to the entire rack, so the whole rack acts like a  gigantic accelerator with shared memory .        Figure 4.  The NVLink hierarchy within an NVL72 rack. (Source:  NVIDIA , Figure 1.)    Every GPU on the NVL72 rack has 18 NVLink ports each delivering 100 GB/s of bidirectional bandwidth, which sums up to a total of  1.8 TB/s for each GPU . Each NVLink port on a given GPU maps to one of 18 NVSwitch chips that power the rack's fabric backplane. Because each NVSwitch chip accepts 72 NVLink lines, one from each of the GPUs, the aggregate internal bandwidth within the rack is 130 TB/s.        Figure 5.  Each GPU connects one NVLink port to each of the rack's 18 NVSwitch chips. (Source:  NADDOD .)    This network topology ensures that the fabric is fully non-blocking, meaning that  any GPU in the rack can transmit data to any other GPU  with uniform latency, making it ideal for large-scale distributed AI workloads.        Figure 6.  The NVSwitch fabric is fully non-blocking. Any GPU can communicate with any other GPU in the rack at full bandwidth with the same latency. (Source:  NVIDIA , Figure 1)      Sometimes less is more: using less nodes in each rack significantly improves reliability    #    With NVL72 systems, it is tempting to allocate entire 18-node racks to workloads to maximize cluster utilization. In practice, teams actually get more usable capacity out of their cluster by leaving a couple of spare nodes in each rack.  GPUs are unreliable. On its gigawatt-scale supercluster,  Meta  measured a mean time between interruptions (MTBI) of roughly 490 days per 4-GPU node after putting significant engineering effort into improving reliability. NVL72 clusters make the 72-GPU rack the atomic unit of compute, which increases the fault blast radius by 18x compared to the 4-GPU nodes that make up the rack. The MTBI for the rack is given by:   Loading...   Based on the formula above, a rack would be interrupted roughly every 490 / 18 ≈ 27 days. If jobs are allocated entire 18-node racks, each of those interruptions makes the entire rack unschedulable until the failed node is repaired. On a 128-rack cluster, this means that a rack would become unusable for full-rack jobs roughly every 5 hours.  Reserving two nodes per rack as spares changes this. When a node fails, a spare in the same rack replaces it, so a single node failure no longer takes the entire rack out of commission. The cost is that two nodes per rack sit idle while everything is healthy.  To quantify this trade-off,  NVIDIA  modeled how different slice sizes affect usable capacity on a 128-rack (2,304-node) cluster as the share of unavailable nodes grows.        Figure 7.  Usable capacity of a 128-rack cluster for different slice sizes as node unavailability increases. Each slice must fit within a single rack. (Adapted from  NVIDIA , Figure 6.)    At SkyPilot, we manage tens of thousands of our customers’ GPUs, and on production NVL72 clusters we have measured unavailability rates of around 2%. At that rate, NVIDIA’s model shows that 16-node slices provide 27% more usable capacity than 18-node slices (2,037 vs. 1,602 nodes). They also beat 9-node slices by 4%, even though two 9-node slices fill a rack exactly: with 9-node slices, every failure costs half a rack, while with 16-node slices, the first two failures in a rack are fully absorbed. Compared with 8-node slices, 16-node slices give each job twice as many GPUs per NVLink domain while giving up less than 1% of usable capacity until node unavailability exceeds about 3.3%.  Sixteen nodes is also a natural size for distributed AI workloads: 64 GPUs is a power of two, which  matches how parallelism groups are typically sized .    How a modern scheduler keeps jobs on NVLink    #    So far, we have covered why the most communication-heavy parallelism techniques belong on NVLink, how NVL72 extends NVLink from a single node to the whole rack, and why 16-node slices with two spare nodes per rack get the most usable capacity out of production clusters. SkyPilot puts this into practice by placing each slice on a single rack, recovering from hardware failures in-place, and keeping whole racks free as jobs come and go.  Schedulers need to understand the hardware  Choosing the right slice size is only the first step. How do researchers ensure that each slice of a multi-node training run actually lands on a single rack?  Naive schedulers split multi-node jobs across racks, forcing workers to communicate over  InfiniBand (400 Gb/s per direction) instead of NVLink (1.8 TB/s bidirectional) :        Figure 8.  Naive placement splits a multi-node job across racks.    SkyPilot’s Topology-Aware Scheduler (TAS) ensures that workers are colocated on the same rack:        Figure 9.  SkyPilot's Topology-Aware Scheduler keeps the job's workers on a single rack.    For multi-rack workloads, TAS splits the job into 16-node (configurable) slices, and places them each on their own rack with two spare nodes. Then, when  SkyPilot’s GPU Manager  detects GPU failures,  SkyPilot Frontier Trainer  can hot swap the faulty node with one of the reserved healthy nodes while the remaining nodes continue running without interruption. If there are no remaining spares in the same rack, Frontier Trainer will reschedule the slice on the faulty rack to a healthy rack:        Figure 10.  Slice-based scheduling holds two healthy spare nodes in each rack. When GPU Manager detects a failed node, Frontier Trainer swaps the faulty node for a spare in the same rack.    To quantify the impact of slice-based scheduling,  NVIDIA’s GR00T team compared the effect of two different scheduling policies  during pre-training of GR00T N1.7, a multimodal foundation model for humanoid robots, on 512 GB300 GPUs across 128 nodes. The first run used a naive scheduler that placed nodes across an arbitrary number of racks. The second run was scheduled with a rack-aware, slice-based policy like the one in Figure 10, which placed it on exactly 8 racks. Rack-aware placement raised throughput by 14.4%, cutting each iteration from 1.59 s to 1.39 s.  On a 10,000-GPU cluster, the same speedup saves roughly $16.7K per training hour. That’s about $400K saved for every training day, just by making better scheduling decisions.  Fragmentation blocks rack-scale jobs  In practice, large clusters are shared: heterogeneous workloads such as pre-training runs, RL rollouts, and batch inference all compete for the same resources. TAS bin packs workloads within the same rack at scheduling time, but jobs finish at different times, leaving free nodes scattered across racks. This is fragmentation: the cluster has enough free GPUs to run a rack-scale job, but because they’re spread across racks, the job can’t be scheduled.        Figure 11.  Jobs finish at different times, leaving free nodes split across racks. With 16 nodes free but split between the two racks, the 16-node hero-run cannot be placed and waits.     SkyPilot’s Automatic Defragmentation  (Auto Defrag) is built to address this. When a job is blocked by topology rather than capacity, Auto Defrag finds the least disruptive set of workloads to preempt to free up an entire rack. Those workloads are rescheduled on other racks, allowing the blocked job to be scheduled.        Figure 12.  Auto Defrag preempts sft-d and reschedules it in rack-a, where it resumes from checkpoint. This frees up rack-b, so hero-run can be scheduled as a single 16-node slice.    Auto Defrag only preempts workloads that restart safely, such as managed jobs that resume from a checkpoint. Interactive development environments are left alone unless an admin explicitly opts them in.    Conclusion    #    Large-scale AI workloads are distributed by default, and their most network-intensive communication patterns sit on the critical path. Rack-scale systems like NVL72 aim to address this bottleneck in hardware, but the hardware alone doesn't guarantee the speedup. These systems require rack-aware placement, resilience to hardware failures, and dynamic rebalancing as jobs come and go. The SkyPilot Platform is purpose-built to close that gap: Topology-Aware Scheduling keeps multi-node jobs on NVLink, Frontier Trainer swaps in a healthy spare when GPU Manager detects hardware failures, and Automatic Defragmentation keeps shared racks open for large jobs. If you're wrangling NVL72 clusters, we'd love to  chat . # tstack

The agent skills I use every day, cleaned up so anyone can use them. They work
in Claude Code and Codex. Some use [T3 Code](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code)
features when they are available and fall back to native tools when they are
not.

## Skills

| Skill | Say | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `full-send` | "full send" | Takes a change to a merged PR with nobody watching: proves it, reviews it, files it, babysits it, merges it. |
| `full-stop` | "full stop" | Same as `full-send`, but stops when the PR is ready for you to merge. |
| `council` | "council" | Gets review from three models from different providers, and loops until they agree. |
| `sol-loop` | "sol loop" | Reviews a change with GPT Sol in a loop until both agents agree. |
| `file-pr` | "file a PR" | Files a short PR that leads with the problem, not an inventory of changes. |
| `takeover` | "take over" | Finishes someone else's PR, branch, or agent thread, and keeps their credit. |
| `babysit-pr` | "babysit" | Watches a PR through CI and review bots, and fixes the real findings. |
| `modernize` | "modernize" | Rebases an old PR and decides if it should still exist. |
| `leaving-pr-comments` | (automatic) | Formats comments that an agent posts on your behalf. |

Some skills call others. Install the ones they need too:

- `full-send` uses `sol-loop`, `file-pr`, and `babysit-pr`.
- `full-stop` uses `full-send`.
- `takeover` uses `modernize`, `file-pr`, `babysit-pr`, and `leaving-pr-comments`.
- `file-pr`, `babysit-pr`, and `modernize` use `leaving-pr-comments`.

## Install

```bash
git clone https://github.com/t3dotgg/tstack
cp -R tstack/skills/* ~/.claude/skills/   # Claude Code
cp -R tstack/skills/* ~/.codex/skills/    # Codex
```

## Requirements

- An authenticated [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com) (`gh`).
- `python3` for `babysit-pr`'s `pr-wait` script.
- `council` and `sol-loop` need subagents on other providers' models. T3 Code
  does this with `delegate_task`. Otherwise you need a harness that can run
  those models.

## Make them yours

These are starting points. Edit them. Put personal settings, like which models
sit on your council, in your `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`, so you can update the
skills without losing them.

## License

[MIT](LICENSE)
