# GPU unlock 1.1.1 — RTX 4090 and experimental Ada GPUs

New to this project? Start with the [copy-paste Quick Start](QUICKSTART.md).

This Linux kernel module enables the SM speed-select override before the stock
NVIDIA driver starts. RTX 4090 (`10de:2684`, AD102) support has demonstrated
approximately **2× FP16 and BF16 tensor throughput with FP32 accumulation**:

| Mode | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| FP16 → FP32 accumulate | 165.6 TF/s | 331.6 TF/s |
| BF16 → FP32 accumulate | 165.5 TF/s | 330.6 TF/s |

The override survived PCIe Function Level Reset (FLR), stock NVIDIA `615.78.08`
initialization and CUDA benchmarks. INT8, `dp4a` and scalar FP32 stayed near their
baseline rates. The original transaction preceded the repository cleanup; see
the [technical report](rtx4090-register-report.md) and
[original evidence](docs/evidence/rtx4090/README.md).

An independent owner run of revision `8855e7b` also completed the RTX 4090
transaction and NVIDIA driver handoff on Linux `7.2.11-arch1-1`. Matched
stock/unlocked measurements with NVIDIA `615.78.08` and the same 450 W cap
found FP16/FP32 instruction throughput **160.4 → 320.4 TF/s** and BF16/FP32
**159.7 → 320.2 TF/s**. All exercised numerical checks passed. Real cuBLAS
GEMM median throughput varied by shape: FP16 gained 12–34%, BF16 gained
16–20% at two shapes and was essentially unchanged at 4096³. These are one
matched run pair with the desktop active, not whole-application speedups or
an extended stability test. See the [matched evidence and limits](docs/evidence/rtx4090-pr1-matched/README.md)
and [testing workflow](docs/testing.md).

A modified 48 GB RTX 4090 (`10de:2684`, AD102) on Ubuntu 26.04 with Linux
`7.0.0-38-generic` and NVIDIA `610.57.04` open kernel modules also completed the
transaction and driver handoff on 2026-10-25: `fmla32` went from `1` to `0`,
FP16/FP32 instruction throughput **164.9 → 328.9 TF/s**, BF16/FP32
**164.8 → 328.7 TF/s**, with INT8, `dp4a` and scalar unchanged and no Xid. A
quantized mixture-of-experts serving workload on the same card showed **no**
gain (8K prefill 0.983×), which is consistent with quantized matmuls not
consuming the FP32-accumulate tensor path. That is one card, one cold boot and
one workload. See the [modified-card evidence and limits](docs/evidence/rtx4090-48g-modded/README.md).
Further matched owner reproductions used NVIDIA [610.57.04](docs/evidence/rtx4090-610.57.04/README.md)
and [595.91.07](docs/evidence/rtx4090-595.91.07/README.md).

A separate cold test of the Ada port on one RTX 4070 Ti SUPER
(`10de:2705`) with NVIDIA `580.178.04` measured FP16/FP32 tensor issue rate
at **95.0 → 189.9 TF/s** and BF16/FP32 at **95.0 → 189.7 TF/s** under the
same 240 W power cap. INT8 stayed at 379.5 TOP/s. The stock driver loaded,
the NVIDIA RM getter reported full FMLA32 rate, deterministic FP16/BF16 GEMM
outputs matched exactly, and owner mining recovered with fresh accepted shares.
A second matched instruction benchmark found **TF32/FP32 47.49 → 94.51 TF/s**
(1.99×), with its FP16/FP32 control also near 2×. Unsigned INT4/INT32 stayed
at approximately **754.8 TOP/s** in both states. These are register-resident
issue rates, not application GEMM or inference speedups.
A matched, verified E4M3 FP8/FP32 CUTLASS GEMM measured **59.326 TF/s stock →
59.495 TF/s unlocked** on this card, a 0.3% difference. That kernel reaches only
about 17% of this card's FP8 peak, so it cannot resolve an issue-rate change.
Other measurements do put FP8 in the affected group: an 8192³ E4M3 GEMM on a
Windows RTX 4080 SUPER measured **199.4 → 310.4 TF/s (+55.7%)** and
**199.4 → 298.7 TF/s (+49.8%)** in two runs (see
[goldlionren/gpu-unlock-4080s](https://github.com/Goldlionren/gpu-unlock-4080s);
its author flags FP8 variance and keeps FP8 out of that repo's own pass/fail
gate), and register-resident E4M3 probes read **603.1 TF/s** unlocked on the
modified 48 GB RTX 4090 (see [that evidence directory](docs/evidence/rtx4090-48g-modded/README.md))
and **165.45 → 323.95 TF/s (1.96×)** on a Windows RTX 4070 Ti SUPER (see
[A-XIANGQAQ/rtx4070tis-ad103-tensor-unlock](https://github.com/A-XIANGQAQ/rtx4070tis-ad103-tensor-unlock)).
The 4090 figure is 91% of its 660.6 TF/s full FP8 rate; NVIDIA rates a stock
RTX 4090 at 330.3 TF/s for FP8 with FP32 accumulate and 660.6 with FP16
accumulate.
So FP8 does move at the issue-rate level; a matched AD103 pair is 1.96×. At a
fixed power limit the application GEMM stays below that: an
unlocked RTX 4090 peaked at 346 W against 313 W stock and spent both MMA and
GEMM passes under SW Power Cap (see
[the 610.57.04 evidence](docs/evidence/rtx4090-610.57.04/README.md)).
This is one card; the unlock succeeded on two cold boots and two ordinary
warm reboots, the last from a persistent EFI default. Throughput was measured
on the first cold boot. See the [2705 canary report](docs/ada-2705-report.md)
and its [sanitized raw benchmark output](docs/evidence/ada2705/README.md).

The AD102 payload and its debug-booter analysis come from
**[TOTORONG/AD103_win_unlocker](https://huggingface.co/TOTORONG/AD103_win_unlocker)**.
This fork integrates that published payload into
**[Zagitta/gpu-unlock](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock)**'s Linux module,
firmware generation and boot packaging. The payload is essential to the result.

## Experimental Windows contribution — Latence.app

A separate [MSI RTX 4070 Ti AD104 Windows UEFI reference port](windows/ad104-msi/README.md)
records one successful manual boot with NVIDIA 616.56 and matched cuBLAS FP16/FP32
**+80.1%**, BF16/FP32 **+76.4%** measurements. It is tied to one captured MSI Z490
profile; it does **not** add AD104 admission to the Linux module. See the
[report and limitations](docs/ad104-windows-latence-app.md). No firmware/Windows/ROM
binaries or automatic boot installer are distributed. Contribution by **Latence.app**;
original upstream credits and licences are retained.

## Supported targets

The module selects the AD102 firmware and payload automatically for RTX 4090
`10de:2684`. The original GeForce/CMP GA102/GA104 device list and GA102 payload
are retained, along with the newer GA103/GA106 device list. Upstream reported
RTX 3090 success; this branch does not revalidate every legacy board.
GA107 RTX 3050 6GB (`10de:2584`) uses the same GA102 Booter path and was
unlocked on one card ([2584 report](docs/ga107-2584-report.md)).

### Experimental Ada targets

Each ID below needs its own opt-in flag. Rows marked *exact* must also be
named by their exact PCI address in `gpu_unlock.targets=`, alone or in a
comma-separated list, and `targets=all` never selects them. All of them use the RTX 4090's pinned
AD102-family firmware and payload. Results come from one or a few cards per ID;
other boards, memory configurations and laptop models remain unverified.
`tools/print_boot_option.py` prints the exact option for any card listed here.

| PCI ID | Card | Die | Opt-in | Tested | Details |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `2685` | RTX 4090 D | AD102 | `rtx4090d_experimental` | eight cards in one host | [#7](https://github.com/JustAResearcher/gpu-unlock-ada/pull/7) |
| `2689` | RTX 4070 Ti SUPER | AD102 | `rtx4070tis_ad102_experimental`, exact | one card, 30-minute soak | [#19](https://github.com/JustAResearcher/gpu-unlock-ada/pull/19) |
| `2702` | RTX 4080 SUPER | AD103 | `ad103_experimental`, exact | one card, matched mma and cuBLAS, alongside a 2704 in one host | [matched evidence](docs/evidence/ada2702-ada2704-matched/README.md), [#53](https://github.com/JustAResearcher/gpu-unlock-ada/issues/53) |
| `2704` | RTX 4080 | AD103 | `rtx4080_experimental`, exact | one modified 32 GiB card; a second card in [matched evidence](docs/evidence/ada2702-ada2704-matched/README.md) | [report](docs/rtx4080-hardware-report.md) |
| `2705` | RTX 4070 Ti SUPER | AD103 | `ad103_experimental`, exact | one card, matched stock/unlocked | [report](docs/ada-2705-report.md) |
| `2709` | RTX 4070 | AD103 | `ad103_experimental`, exact | one card, matched | [report](docs/ada-2709-report.md) |
| `2757` | RTX 4090 Laptop GPU | AD103M | `ad103m_experimental`, exact | Clevo: unlocked, no throughput change; Lenovo: 2× on two cold boots | [report](docs/ada-2757-report.md), [Lenovo](https://github.com/JustAResearcher/gpu-unlock-ada/issues/4#issuecomment-6397961415) |
| `2782` | RTX 4070 Ti | AD104 | `ad104_experimental`, exact | one card in a VFIO guest, matched; one bare-metal owner report | [report](docs/ada-2782-report.md), [#15](https://github.com/JustAResearcher/gpu-unlock-ada/pull/15) |
| `2783` | RTX 4070 SUPER | AD104 | `ad104_experimental`, exact | one card, matched | [report](docs/ada-2783-report.md) |
| `2786` | RTX 4070 | AD104 | `ad104_experimental`, exact | one card; three owner reports | [report](docs/ada-2786-report.md), [#11](https://github.com/JustAResearcher/gpu-unlock-ada/pull/11) |
| `2803` | RTX 4060 Ti | AD106 | `ad106_experimental`, exact | one 16 GB card, matched; two more boards in #34 | [report](docs/ada-2803-report.md), [#34](https://github.com/JustAResearcher/gpu-unlock-ada/pull/34) |
| `2805` | RTX 4060 Ti 16GB | AD106 | `ad106_experimental`, exact | one card, no matched throughput run | [report](docs/ada-2805-report.md) |
| `2882` | RTX 4060 | AD107 | `ad107_experimental`, exact | one card, matched cuBLAS; cold boot and warm reboot | [report](docs/ada-2882-report.md) |
| `28a0` | RTX 4060 Laptop GPU | AD107 | `ad107_experimental`, exact | one card, unlocked state only | [report](docs/ada-28a0-report.md) |
| `28e0` | RTX 4060 Laptop GPU | AD107 | `ad107_experimental`, exact | one owner report | [#10](https://github.com/JustAResearcher/gpu-unlock-ada/pull/10) |
| `28e1` | RTX 4050 Laptop GPU | AD107 | `ad107_experimental`, exact | one laptop, matched | [report](docs/ada-28e1-report.md) |

Laptops differ in VBIOS ROM exposure, embedded-controller power rails and FLR
handling, so a result on one model does not carry over to another. Other Ada
IDs, professional RTX A-series and data-centre parts are not accepted. Shared
firmware across Ada chips does not establish support for untested cards.

The RTX 4090 path runs the signed firmware, checks the payload's completion marker and
required permissions, writes SS0 `0x88888888` and SS1 `0x8`, then performs FLR
before the unmodified NVIDIA driver binds. It requires the expected
effective speed-select readout before and after FLR. No patched NVIDIA driver or UEFI
application is needed. The payload uses instruction addresses derived from
published decrypted debug-booter analysis; the production booter is authenticated
and decrypted inside the GPU.

## Build and install

Clone the GPL-2.0-only source and build the packages locally so the pinned
NVIDIA firmware is downloaded and generated on your own machine:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/JustAResearcher/gpu-unlock-ada.git
cd gpu-unlock-ada
make install
```

`make install` detects the supported distribution family. Its explicit targets
are:

```sh
make install-arch   # makepkg -sif
make install-deb    # apt-get build-dep, dpkg-buildpackage, apt-get install
make install-rpm    # dnf builddep, rpmbuild, dnf install
```

`make arch`, `make deb` and `make rpm` build without installing. Packages are
built from the committed `HEAD`; Debian and RPM outputs go to `build/deb` and
`build/rpm`. Kernel headers and a working DKMS toolchain are required.

Builds fetch the pinned NVIDIA `610.43.03` source and binary inputs over HTTPS
and verify their SHA-256 hashes. `make inputs` prepares the cache;
`make firmware` generates assets from cached inputs; `make assets` does both.
The default cache is `$HOME/.cache/gpu-unlock` and can be overridden with
`CACHE=`, `INPUTS=` and `ASSETS=`. A clean-chroot Debian build needs
`GPU_UNLOCK_INPUTS` pointing to the input cache because `dpkg-buildpackage`
does not fetch inputs itself.

The source archive produced by `make dist`, the Debian source package and the
`.nosrc.rpm` contain no NVIDIA archives or generated firmware. See
[firmware/README.md](firmware/README.md) for the input and asset layout.
Prebuilt firmware packages are not distributed by this repository.

## Enable at boot

The package installs the module and firmware into the initramfs so the unlock
runs before NVIDIA binds the card. It remains inactive unless the kernel
command line opts in:

```text
gpu_unlock.targets=0000:03:00.0
gpu_unlock.targets=0000:03:00.0,0000:04:00.0
gpu_unlock.targets=all
gpu_unlock.targets=0000:01:00.0 gpu_unlock.ad103_experimental=1
```

These PCI addresses are examples. Use the full PCI names printed by `lspci -D`.
`all` selects every accepted unbound card, including legacy GA102/GA104 targets;
an explicit address is useful when selecting one RTX 4090. Do not mix `all` with
addresses. Every experimental Ada target requires its own flag from the
[experimental target table](#experimental-ada-targets), and the exact ones must
be named by their exact PCI address; `all` never selects them. Invalid entries
are logged and ignored.

The packages support these initramfs generators:

- **mkinitcpio:** `/etc/mkinitcpio.conf.d/zz-gpu-unlock.conf` puts `gpu_unlock`
  immediately before `nvidia` in `MODULES`, or last if NVIDIA is absent. Images
  are rebuilt on installation. A custom configuration selected with `-c` or a
  preset `_config` does not read drop-ins; add `gpu_unlock` before `nvidia` in
  that configuration's `MODULES` yourself.
- **initramfs-tools:**
  `/usr/share/initramfs-tools/modules.d/gpu-unlock.conf`.
- **dracut:** `/usr/lib/dracut/dracut.conf.d/gpu-unlock.conf`.

There is no `softdep nvidia pre:` rule because kmod uses only the first matching
soft dependency line, which can conflict with other packages.

**Power the machine off and start it again for the first attempt.** The module
needs a card whose firmware state is fresh before NVIDIA loads. A warm reboot
is not guaranteed to provide that state: it did on the tested
RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, where the pre-firmware WPR2 readback returned to zero and
the unlock succeeded again without an AC cut. Other boards may retain WPR2;
the module refuses to rerun the firmware sequence in that state. It also skips
cards that are already bound or powered down. If board firmware left bus
mastering enabled, the module clears it and verifies that it stayed cleared;
the later WPR2 check still rejects an already initialized card.
Loading the module manually after NVIDIA has bound the card cannot unlock it.

After validating a cold boot and a one-time warm reboot on the exact card, a
persistent bootloader entry can select the same early initramfs and exact
`gpu_unlock.*` options on every boot. A one-shot entry by itself does not
persist. Keep an unmodified stock entry available, and verify
`gpu_unlock: unlocked`, the rate readback and GPU health after each boot.
The tested canary uses a kernel-version-specific image; regenerate and
revalidate that image before removing its pinned kernel during an upgrade.

Avoid `nvidia-smi`, CUDA, NVML and `nvidia-modprobe` before a manual cold-card
attempt: they can load NVIDIA by name. Ordinary modprobe blacklist rules do not
block explicit named loads. The packaged initramfs flow avoids the need for
manual firmware staging and research parameters.

The original display-card handoff is retained: the firmware framebuffer is
removed just before FLR, and the display stays blank until `nvidia-drm` takes
over. Display handoff and multi-card operation were not part of the RTX 4090
validation.

## Check and disable

Inspect the kernel log after boot:

```sh
journalctl -k -b | grep gpu_unlock
lspci -nnk -s 0000:03:00.0  # replace the example address
```

A loaded module or successful `modprobe` return alone does not prove an unlock:
look for the selected card's `gpu_unlock: unlocked` message and the payload,
selector and post-FLR checks. The report describes independent register and
performance confirmation. The optional read-only sampler lives in
`diagnostics/peek`; the CUDA instruction benchmark is in `diagnostics/bench`.
Never load a second BAR0 sampler while `gpu_unlock` is performing its firmware
transaction.

If the module reports that firmware did not stop and its DMA buffers are being
kept, power off before trying again. The module intentionally retains buffers
that firmware may still use. Do not force-unload it in this state.

Remove `gpu_unlock.targets=` from the kernel command line to disable future
attempts. It can be removed for one boot in the bootloader editor. Removing the
packages removes the module and initramfs integration; power off to return to a
fresh hardware state.

## Development and credits

`make test` runs the host-side suite without accessing a GPU. Missing generated
firmware is reported as an explicit skip of the full transaction tests. After
`make assets`, use `make test-full` for a strict check that requires both the
pinned source and all generated assets. Override `ASSETS=` and `NVIDIA_SOURCE=`
for inputs built elsewhere. These tests mock firmware execution and device
behavior; they do not replace a hardware repeat.
See [testing and interpreting results](docs/testing.md) for the validation
levels, matched benchmark commands and recorded hardware evidence.

The kernel verifies each loaded asset against its pinned SHA-256 before claiming
the card or starting firmware DMA, including files staged into an initramfs.
The kernel's SHA-256 library (`CONFIG_CRYPTO_LIB_SHA256`) must be available.
`make -C kernel/gpu_unlock` builds against the running kernel's headers; use
`LLVM=1` when those headers support a Clang build.

The Linux module and packaging derive from
[Zagitta/gpu-unlock](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock). The AD102 four-PLM
payload derives from
[TOTORONG/AD103_win_unlocker](https://huggingface.co/TOTORONG/AD103_win_unlocker),
including its published payload generator and debug-booter analysis. The GA102
V67 chain derives from
[WildFlash1st/cmp90hx-unlock](https://github.com/WildFlash1st/cmp90hx-unlock).
The earlier CMP unlock work, NVIDIA's published loader code, Nouveau and
[envytools](https://github.com/envytools/envytools) also underpin the loader and
investigation.

The kernel module, packaging and payload integration are GPL-2.0-only. NVIDIA
firmware remains under its own terms. See [firmware/NOTICE.md](firmware/NOTICE.md)
and [licenses/](licenses/) for provenance and preserved license notices.

      Title: h1: A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving 
      Authors:  Skander Moalla ,  Ahmad Rammal ,  Niket Patel ,  Remi Munos ,  Julia Kempe               View a PDF of the paper titled h1: A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving, by Skander Moalla and 4 other authors

             Abstract: While progress in informal mathematics has come largely from scaling the chain-of-thought and agentic reasoning of frontier language models, formal theorem proving has increasingly relied on human-designed workflows around these models, such as planning, decomposition, and orchestrating specialized provers. This raises a bitter-lesson question: can a simple agentic loop that scales test-time compute match these workflows? The answer matters as formal verification must scale to keep up with frontier models producing research mathematics, yet new workflows rarely settle it, as their gains are often confounded with stronger models or more compute. We study this question with h1, a simple harness that gives a model an efficient interface to Lean 4 and keeps it working through verifier feedback and self-reflection, without imposing a decomposition or search structure. h1 reaches state-of-the-art results on PutnamBench, FATE-X, and FormalConjectures100-Solved, settles eight open problems in FormalConjectures, and, at matched models, matches or outperforms specialized workflows such as Goedel-Architect and AlphaProof Nexus, surprisingly showing that a single attempt (pass@1) can often scale to solve open problems. Through ablations and matched-model comparisons with Claude Code and AxProverBase, we find that simplicity alone is not enough: an efficient Lean interface largely determines cost and solve rate. We thus recommend that future work evaluate frontier models with efficient execution feedback before prescribing workflows, at the risk of bitter lessons.

  Abstract 
    
 While progress in informal mathematics has come largely from scaling the chain-of-thought and agentic reasoning of frontier language models, formal theorem proving has increasingly relied on human-designed workflows around these models, such as planning, decomposition, and orchestrating specialized provers.
This raises a bitter-lesson question: can a simple agentic loop that scales test-time compute match these workflows?
The answer matters as formal verification must scale to keep up with frontier models producing research mathematics, yet new workflows rarely settle it, as their gains are often confounded with stronger models or more compute.
We study this question with  h1 , a simple harness that gives a model an efficient interface to Lean 4 and keeps it working through verifier feedback and self-reflection, without imposing a decomposition or search structure.
 h1  reaches state-of-the-art results on PutnamBench,  FATE-X , and FormalConjectures100-Solved, settles eight open problems in FormalConjectures, and, at matched models, matches or outperforms specialized workflows such as Goedel-Architect and AlphaProof Nexus, surprisingly showing that a single attempt (pass@1) can often scale to solve open problems.
Through ablations and matched-model comparisons with Claude Code and AxProverBase, we find that simplicity alone is not enough: an efficient Lean interface largely determines cost and solve rate.
We thus recommend that future work evaluate frontier models with efficient execution feedback before prescribing workflows, at the risk of bitter lessons. 
  
   †    †  date:  October 25, 2026     †    †  correspondence:  Skander Moalla at  skander.moalla@epfl.ch    
 
  
        
    
   Figure 1 :   (Left) Simple scaling Pareto-dominates specialized systems.  On PutnamBench (672 competition problems),  h1  with DeepSeek V4 Flash Pareto-dominates Goedel-Architect’s best of four runs (pass@4) seeded with natural-language proofs.
With GPT-5.5, it solves every solvable problem, as Humanfia and Aleph Prover do, at lower cost.
 (Middle) Longer attempts can outperform repetition.  On five open Erdős problems, a single  h1  attempt (pass@1) beats three attempts of AlphaProof Nexus’s basic agent (APN basic, pass@3) at lower mean cost per success, can be cheaper than repeating  h1  itself, and Pareto-dominates the full APN system.
 (Right) Simple harness design is important for scaling efficiency and effectiveness.  On a 100-problem PutnamBench subset, Gemini 3 Flash trails Opus 4.5 in the AxProverBase loop but overtakes it in  h1  at matched budget through more efficient tool use and caching.
   
 
 
  1  Introduction 

 
 The bitter lesson predicts that general methods which scale with computation ultimately outperform approaches built around human domain knowledge  ( Sutton, 2019 ) .
However, while progress in informal mathematics has come from scaling frontier models’ chain-of-thought and agentic reasoning  ( OpenAI, 2024 ;  Guo et al., 2025 ;  Shang et al., 2025 ;  Feng et al., 2025 ) , progress in formal proving has increasingly relied on human-designed workflows around those models.
Indeed, formal proof assistants such as Lean  ( Moura and Ullrich, 2021 )  express mathematical statements and proofs in a precise language that can be checked mechanically.
This includes intermediate proof steps, which naturally supports structured search that can be encoded as part of a workflow in a  harness : the tools, context, and control loop around a model.
Recent formal proving harnesses exploit this structure by orchestrating specialized provers or prescribing planning, decomposition, and proof refinement  ( Varambally et al., 2026 ;  Chung et al., 2026 ;  Li et al., 2026a ;  Isenbaev and Hanin, 2026 ;  Math Inc., 2026b ) .
Only very recently has interest grown in  simple  loops that use the harness  only  to provide Lean feedback and sustain work  ( Requena et al., 2026 ;  Tsoukalas et al., 2026 ;  Humanfia, 2026 ;  Kabra et al., 2026 ) . 
 
 
 Formal mathematics thus raises a bitter-lesson question for harness design: with frontier models already capable of reasoning and agentic test-time scaling, can a simple test-time scaling loop match specialized workflows?
And what should a simple harness provide to make that scaling effective and efficient?
Do these simple methods offer better performance for the same cost?
These questions matter increasingly as frontier models generate research mathematics whose informal arguments are difficult to verify.
Indeed, scaling automated theorem proving (ATP) to produce mechanically checked proofs has become a necessary component of automated discovery  ( Tsoukalas et al., 2026 ;  OpenAI, 2026b ;  OpenAI, 2026a ;  Patel et al., 2026 ) .
Yet new workflows are often presented alongside stronger models and more compute, or compared to baselines that scale poorly.
This leaves unclear whether their gains hold against an efficient simple loop given enough test-time compute. 
 
 
 We tackle these questions with  h1 , a simple harness with an efficient interface to Lean 4 that imposes no decomposition or search structure.
This loop keeps a model working until success or a cost cap stops it by iterating between a multi-turn block of reasoning and tool-calling, submission to a formal validator, and a reflection that compacts the transcript into a new context for the next iteration.
Each additional iteration is akin to appending “Wait” to a model’s thinking in s1  ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ) , extending the computation available at test time.
We evaluate cost–success curves across benchmarks and open problems, accounting for inference cost and matching models where possible.
Our findings are threefold: 
 
 
 
  •  
 
  A bitter lesson for specialized harnesses: simple test-time scaling reaches frontier results without prescribed workflows  (Sections   3.1   and   3.2  ).
A simple loop often matches or Pareto-dominates specialized systems at matched models and comparable budgets, while reaching state-of-the-art results on PutnamBench  ( Tsoukalas et al., 2024 ) , FATE-X  ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) , and FormalConjectures100-Solved  ( Firsching et al., 2026 )  and settling eight open Formal Conjectures problems, and variants of Erdős 138  ( Bloom, 2026a )  and 337  ( Bloom, 2026b ) .
At matched models,  h1  surpasses Goedel-Architect  ( Chung et al., 2026 )  at lower estimated cost; on five open Erdős problems, it Pareto-dominates full AlphaProof Nexus (APN)  ( Tsoukalas et al., 2026 )  with the same LLM. 
  
  •  
 
  Longer attempts can be more efficient than repetition  (Section   3.3  ).
With sequential test-time scaling, pass@1 traces a budget-dependent curve that can Pareto-dominate pass@   k  k   : on five Erdős problems, extending  h1  can cost less than repeating  h1  or APN basic  ( Tsoukalas et al., 2026 ) . 
  
  •  
 
  A simple harness still needs efficient interaction, reliable feedback, and sustained progress  (Section   4  ).
Among simple loops, harness design produces large differences in solve rates and cost. Controlled ablations and comparisons with AxProverBase  ( Requena et al., 2026 ) , Claude Code  ( Anthropic, 2026a ) , and Humanfia  ( Humanfia, 2026 )  show the value of a reliable and efficient interface to Lean with search tools, a loop that sustains repair and reflection, and efficient reasoning and cache reuse. 
  
 
 
 
 Our results show that a simple harness can match or outperform more complex systems, extending the bitter lesson to harness design in ATP and plausibly other structured environments.
Frontier models keep improving their reasoning and adaptation to execution feedback, and harnesses should help these capabilities scale through efficient interaction with the environment rather than impose workflows.
Future work should thus evaluate frontier models with efficient execution feedback before prescribing workflows, or risk a bitter lesson. 
 
 
 
  2  Methods 

 
 We first introduce the formal-proving task, benchmarks, and baselines, and explain how we evaluate test-time scaling. We then describe  h1 ’s tools and interaction loop, which let the model work efficiently and sustain progress as its inference budget grows. 
 
 
  2.1  Experimental setup 

 
 Formal proving. 

 
 In Lean  ( Moura and Ullrich, 2021 ) , a formal statement specifies a mathematical claim and its assumptions; the agent must complete its proof in a source file.
Mathlib  ( The mathlib Community, 2020 )  is a shared library of formalized mathematics that provides definitions and previously proved results.
Compiling the file checks the proof and returns errors.
During proof development,  open goals  list what remains to be proved.
Additionally, formal validation tools such as SafeVerify  ( GasStationManager, 2024 )  allow checking the final proof against the original statement, rejecting placeholders for unfinished steps and added assumptions. 
 
 
 
 Benchmarks. 

 
 We evaluate on formal statements of increasing difficulty.
PutnamBench  ( Tsoukalas et al., 2024 )  contains 672 problems from the past Putnam undergraduate competitions; for controlled comparisons, we use Putnam100, the same 100-problem subset used by AxProverBase  ( Requena et al., 2026 ) .
We also use the 12 problems of the 2025 Putnam competition, formalized both in PutnamBench and by Numina  ( Liu et al., 2026b ) .
IMO 2026 contains the 6 problems of the 2026 International Mathematical Olympiad, the leading competition for high-school students, as formalized by Axiom  ( Axiom Math, 2026a ) .
FATE-X  ( Jiang et al., 2026 )  contains 100 algebra problems at PhD qualifying-exam level or beyond, and FormalQualBench  ( Math Inc., 2026a )  23 theorems at PhD qualifying-exam level.
Formal Conjectures  ( Firsching et al., 2026 )  collects formalized research conjectures; we evaluate on FC100-solved, a random sample of 100 problems with known informal solutions, and on open targets.
Appendix   C.1   records benchmark source revisions and Lean/Mathlib versions.
We omit older benchmarks such as miniF2F  ( Zheng et al., 2022 ) , which modern models essentially saturate.
PutnamBench mainly tests efficiency, while FATE-X, FormalQualBench, and FC100-solved remain unsaturated at our scale.
Putnam 2025 and IMO 2026 are recent enough to be unseen by the models released before them (Appendix   E.10  ).
Open conjectures, such as those in Formal Conjectures  ( Firsching et al., 2026 ) , test progress beyond problems with known solutions. 
 
 
 
 Models and baselines. 

 
 We evaluate frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, alongside open-weight DeepSeek V4 Flash  ( DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026 )  and Leanstral 1.5  ( Kabra et al., 2026 ) .
We select baselines representing the most competitive results on our benchmarks as of August 27, 2026, alongside simple loops that help isolate the contribution of harness design.
All state-of-the-art (SOTA) claims use this comparison cutoff (Appendix   C.2  ).
To compare with human-designed workflows, we include systems that enforce planning, decomposition, or agent roles in code: Goedel-Architect  ( Chung et al., 2026 ) , MerLean  ( Li et al., 2026a ) , and full AlphaProof Nexus  ( Tsoukalas et al., 2026 ) .
OpenGauss  ( Math Inc., 2026b )  instead prescribes a plan–review workflow to a general coding agent through instruction files (skills), while Numina  ( Liu et al., 2026b )  gives a general coding agent optional tools that consult a natural-language (informal) prover and other models, and prescribes a subagent workflow for its hardest problem.
Comparisons with other simple loops test interaction efficiency and persistence; these include Humanfia  ( Humanfia, 2026 ) , APN basic  ( Tsoukalas et al., 2026 )  (AlphaProof Nexus’s single-agent loop), and our same-model reruns of both AxProverBase  ( Requena et al., 2026 )  and Claude Code  ( Anthropic, 2026a ) .
We also report the published scores of trained provers, such as Seed-Prover 1.5  ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , where they still define the SOTA.
Appendix   A   discusses additional related work. 
 
 
 
 Measuring test-time scaling with cost per task. 

 
 Prior work very rarely compares systems at matched inference compute.
Earlier theorem-proving work focused on training better models, with evaluation emphasizing solve rates rather than inference cost.
As improvements increasingly come from inference-time search, repair, and orchestration, these reporting conventions have persisted even as an attempt has come to mean very different amounts of computation.
For example, on PutnamBench, one Goedel-Architect attempt permits up to 16 revisions of its proof plan  ( Chung et al., 2026 ) , while one AxProverBase attempt permits 50 agent iterations  ( Requena et al., 2026 ) .
Both papers report these as pass@1, but matching attempt counts do not match inference budgets; Appendix   C.4   gives further examples.

(Table   9  ).
As inference-time methods drive more of the progress, accounting for their cost should become standard practice.
We compare inference cost, holding the model fixed to compare harnesses or the harness fixed to measure model progress.

  2.2   h1 : a simple harness for efficient test-time scaling 

 
     
  
   Figure 2 :   h1 : a simple harness that scales. 
An LLM agent edits a Lean file through reasoning and tool calls (ReAct;   Yao et al., 2023  ) until it submits or reaches the    T  T   -turn limit, forcing submission. An external validator then checks the proof. On failure, a reflection LLM compacts the transcript and feedback for the next iteration. The loop provides Lean tools without prescribing a proof search structure. Search uses LeanExplore  ( Asher, 2025 ) , Loogle  ( Breitner, 2023 ) , and grep; proof fragments run in the Lean read–eval–print loop (REPL)  ( leanprover-community, 2023 ) ; the language server (LSP) reports goals and definitions; SafeVerify  ( GasStationManager, 2024 )  performs validation.
    
 
 
  h1  keeps a model working on a Lean proof until an external validator accepts it or the budget runs out (Figure   2  ).
In each  iteration , the model reasons and calls tools in a ReAct loop  ( Yao et al., 2023 )  for at most    T  T     turns , editing a persistent working file; every edit is compiled and returns errors and open goals.
The iteration ends when the model submits the file, which an external validator then checks against the original statement, also accepting checked disproofs where supported (Appendix   C.2  ).
If the validator rejects the submission, a reflection LLM compacts the transcript and feedback into verified progress, lessons from failed attempts, and useful lemma names, and discourages giving up, as in Reflexion  ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) , Self-Refine  ( Madaan et al., 2023 ) , and AxProverBase  ( Requena et al., 2026 ) ; the model then continues from the current file with this summary.
The loop builds on APN basic  ( Tsoukalas et al., 2026 ) , AxProverBase, and the  Ralph  loop from software engineering  ( Huntley, 2025 ;  Macedo, 2026 ) . 
 
 
 A simple loop with an efficient interface. 

 
  h1  imposes no decomposition, planning, or search structure.
Instead, it gives the model an efficient interface to Lean, with targeted edits rather than rewritten proofs, immediate compiler feedback, and a context that grows and is cached within an iteration.
Optional tools let the model search Mathlib, inspect definitions, and test proof fragments, and the model decides which to use and how to develop the proof.
Section   4   shows that these choices matter for both cost and success, and Appendix   B   details tools and prompts. 
 
 
 
 
 
  3  Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results 

 
 We first show that frontier models in  h1  reach state-of-the-art results across competition and research mathematics.
We then show that simple scaling often matches or outperforms specialized workflows at matched models and comparable inference costs, and that, even on open research problems, extending a single attempt can be more efficient than repetition.

All these results use a single run per problem, without repetition or parallelism.
Reaching state-of-the-art performance with a recent frontier model required only a larger inference budget, as the model keeps iterating, adjusting proofs and changing approaches without a prescribed workflow.

  3.2  The bitter lesson for specialized workflows 

 
 We show that, at matched models, simple test-time scaling recovers much of the performance of specialized workflows, often at lower inference cost, and that repetition (pass@   k  k   ) or a newer frontier model in the same loop usually closes any remaining gap (Figure   1  ; Table   2  ). 
 
 
 Simple test-time scaling can match specialized systems at lower cost. 

 
 On PutnamBench, one extended  h1  attempt surpasses Goedel-Architect’s blueprint-based search, which assigns separate agents to prove the lemmas in a dependency graph.
With the same DeepSeek V4 Flash model,  h1  first matches its pass@1 score at comparable cost, then reaches 598 solves against 597 at pass@4 with informal proof seeding, at an estimated $1.08 versus $1.47 per problem  ( Chung et al., 2026 )  (Figure   1  , left).
Goedel-Architect’s tool-integrated reasoning baseline reaches only 54.5% at pass@32 on a 200-problem subset, compared with  h1 ’s 89.0% at pass@1 on the full benchmark with the same model.
With Gemini 3.1 Pro alone,  h1  also matches Goedel-Architect’s July leaderboard result of 642 solves, which pairs Gemini 3.1 Pro with the cheaper DeepSeek V4 Pro, at a similar cost ($6.32 versus $5.80 per problem).
The much stronger performance of a simple harness with the same model illustrates how a weak simple baseline can overstate the need for specialized workflows (Figure   6  ). 
 
 
 
 A simple loop solves the problem that needed a hand-designed workflow. 

 
 A single model in  h1  also recovers the result of Numina-Lean-Agent, which reserved a specialized workflow for the hardest problem of Putnam 2025.
Numina runs Opus 4.5 in Claude Code, a general coding agent, with optional tools that call other models: an informal prover built as a Gemini 3 Pro generator–verifier loop, and a discussion partner  ( Liu et al., 2026b ) .
For that problem, A5, the authors switch to a coordinator that delegates blueprint decomposition, sketching, and proving to subagents, seeded with a GPT-5.2 hint and a $1,000 budget.
On the same statements, GPT-5.2 alone solves all twelve in  h1 , including A5, in a single run per problem and without such a workflow, spending $81.52
on A5 against Numina’s $1,000 budget (Table   2  ).
Also note that with Opus 4.5 alone,  h1  solves seven problems against four for Numina without its informal prover, consistent with our finding that Claude Code, on which Numina builds, scales less effectively than  h1  with the same model (Section   4  ). 
 
 
 
 Repetition closes most remaining gaps. 

 
 When a single  h1  run falls short, rerunning the unsolved problems from a fresh context (residual pass@   k  k   ) closes most remaining gaps.
Like  h1  itself, repetition prescribes no workflow; it simply adds independent attempts, though often at a higher cost than extending a single run (Section   3.3  ).
As long as that cost is counted, including failed attempts, repetition therefore belongs to the simple baseline against which specialized workflows should be tested.
On Putnam 2025,  h1  with Opus 4.7 solves eleven against MerLean’s twelve; retrying the remaining problem recovers all twelve within six attempts.
On full PutnamBench, extra attempts on the last two problems let  h1  with GPT-5.5 match Aleph Prover’s  ( Logical Intelligence, 2026 )  final 672/672 coverage at an estimated $17.86 versus about $74 per problem, counting the cost of failed attempts (Appendix   C.4  ).
On FormalQualBench  ( Math Inc., 2026a ) , OpenGauss  ( Math Inc., 2026b )  instructs Claude Code to cycle through planning, proving, review, and replanning, generating several candidate proofs per open goal and extracting helper lemmas when a goal is stuck.
The best of four  h1  runs with Opus 4.6 matches its eight solves under the same four-hour limit.
On these benchmarks, the only remaining exception after scaling and repetition is MerLean on FormalQualBench with Opus 4.7, which retains a one-problem advantage with or without the four-hour cutoff (Appendix   E.1  ).

 The next frontier model closes the rest. 

 
 In some rare cases, such as on FormalQualBench with MerLean  ( Li et al., 2026a ) , we find that repetition does not close the gap between  h1  and the other methods.
However, even in this case, replacing Opus 4.7 with its direct successor, Opus 4.8, is enough for  h1  to overtake MerLean, with 13 against 10 solves at $49.46 rather than $118.35 per solve, and with GPT-5.6 Sol,  h1  also solves the one problem that only MerLean had proved (Table   2  ).
MerLean would likely also improve with Opus 4.8 or GPT-5.6 Sol, but we expect this gap to keep shrinking as newer models internalize the strategies that workflows prescribe.
We see this as the bitter lesson at work, as newer models convert more training compute into capabilities that an unchanged simple loop directly benefits from. 
 
 
 
 
  3.3  Persisting can beat repetition, even on open problems 

 
 When an attempt can keep going, pass@1 is no longer a single number but a curve that grows with budget: within one run, the model can abandon an approach and try another.
The question becomes whether spending more on one attempt beats spending the same on several.
AlphaProof Nexus (APN)  ( Tsoukalas et al., 2026 )  found that its basic agent, a simple loop like  h1 , can Pareto-dominate its full system, which evolves proof sketches with LLM raters, parallel provers, and AlphaProof, but only through repetition: at pass@   k  k    for large enough    k  k   .
APN reports each pass@   k  k   , including pass@1, as a single point at a fixed budget, leaving open whether a single attempt given more budget can do what repetition does. 
 
 
 We evaluate  h1  on the six open Erdős problems that APN reports individually, using the same model, Gemini 3.1 Pro.
Following APN, we report mean cost conditional on success, charging each group its members’ summed cost up to the first accepted proof.
This metric is undefined for a problem with no successful attempts, so Figure   1   (middle) compares the five problems that all three systems solve at least once.
For  h1 , we show how pass@1 changes as the budget grows, rather than reporting a single point.
As the budget grows, it matches APN basic’s pass@1 at lower cost, then exceeds both APN basic’s pass@3 (75.4% at $191) and full APN (76% at $317), reaching 82.5% at $121.
On these five problems, giving one  h1  attempt more time achieves a higher solve rate at lower cost than three attempts of APN basic.
Full APN retains an advantage over both APN basic and  h1  on the remaining problem, Erdős 125, where all sixteen  h1  attempts end in Lean timeouts (Appendix   E.6  ). 
 
 
 APN’s conditional metric gives a first view of this depth–breadth trade-off, but omits spending on groups with no accepted proof (Appendix   E.6  ).
To account for these costs and separate compute allocation and isolate differences between harnesses, we also compare longer attempts with repetition within  h1 , using mean spend across all successful and failed groups (Figure   12  ).
On the same five problems, pass@1 reaches 82.5% at $138 in mean spend including failures, whereas pass@3 needs $202 to reach at least that rate.
Thus, the advantage of longer attempts at these budgets persists when failed searches are charged.
Repetition reaches higher success rates at larger budgets.
The right balance between depth (longer attempts) and breadth (more attempts) therefore depends on the budget and problem and is hard to set in advance.
The bitter lesson suggests leaving this choice to the model rather than to hand-set budgets.

 Leaving the proof workflow to the model does not make the harness irrelevant: with the same model, simple loops differ several-fold in solve rate and cost.
We explain these differences, and what makes  h1  a state-of-the-art harness and an effective Lean baseline, by pairing comparisons with other simple loops with ablations on  h1  that vary its tools, prompts, reflection, turns between reflections, and reasoning effort.
The resulting lessons concern the interface, persistence, and context management, and should transfer beyond the automated theorem proving domain, to agents that work against a verifier in rich environments allowing structured development and retrieval, such as software verification and coding in large libraries and codebases. 
 
 
 An efficient, reliable interface lets the model act in small steps and look things up. 

 
 In  h1 , the model edits a persistent working file over many turns, sees compiler feedback after every edit, and can search the library or test a proof fragment at any point.
AxProverBase  ( Requena et al., 2026 )  instead makes one round of tool calls, then regenerates a complete proof after each round of feedback.
With the same Gemini 3 Flash model and a $20 budget, it solves 18 Putnam100 problems against  h1 ’s 69, and trails in all six settings we compare (Figure   , left).
A reliable interface also removes avoidable failures by construction: 42.2% of AxProverBase’s failed compilations stop at an invalid library import, which cannot occur in  h1  because its file already imports all of Mathlib (Figure   19  ).
Likewise,  h1  retries transient API failures and restores the file after a Lean timeout, whereas some Claude Code runs failed through API errors and repeated timeouts even after restarts (Appendix   E.9  ).
Library search, which AxProverBase found the least useful of its components, matters much more when the model can act on its results over many turns: without search tools, the REPL, or the language server,  h1  solves 49 Putnam100 and 49 FATE-X problems, against 69 and 63 with all tools (Figure   21  ).
Any single search tool or the REPL recovers most of this gain, and removing any one tool from the full set costs at most four solves: what matters is the ability to look up and check, not a particular tool.
Other simple loops with less efficient interfaces reach  h1 ’s solve rates only at higher cost.
APN basic  ( Tsoukalas et al., 2026 )  lacks dedicated search tools; on the five-problem Erdős subset, extending a single  h1  attempt can be more efficient than repeating APN basic (Section   3.3  ).
Humanfia  ( Humanfia, 2026 )  checks proofs only through shell commands and restarts its coding agent in a fresh session each round, carrying over only the proof file and reviewer feedback; with GPT-5.5, it spends five times more than  h1  for the same 670 PutnamBench solves.
A harness should thus support the model by offering a persistent workspace edited in small steps, immediate feedback, ways to retrieve and check what the model needs, and robust handling of predictable failures, leaving their use to the model. 
 
 
 
 The loop, not the model, decides when to stop. 

 
 Test-time compute helps only if the harness turns a larger budget into continued work.
With Opus 4.8, native Claude Code  ( Anthropic, 2026a )  solves 63 FATE-X problems; giving it our prompt and our Lean tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), in place of its built-in shell and file tools, raises this to 73, while  h1  reaches 83 (Figure   , right; 81, 95, and 99 on Putnam100).
Access to verification helps, but the model can still stop without calling the validator or give up after a rejection; in  h1 , a rejection starts another iteration with the working file, the feedback, and a reflection summary (Appendix   E.9  ).
Within  h1 , the system prompts matter most on open problems. Unlike one-line prompts, our detailed prompts describe the tools, set rules for statement integrity and disproofs, and tell the prover not to give up because a problem is open and the reflection LLM not to endorse such a decision (Appendix   B.2  ). On six Erdős problems, a single attempt with them outperforms six attempts with one-line prompts at the same $150 cap per attempt (Figure   4  , left).
Reflection, which carries verified progress and lessons into the next iteration, raises  h1  with DeepSeek V4 Flash from 554 to 598 PutnamBench solves, consistent with AxProverBase’s findings (Figure   6  ).
None of these tells the model how to prove: the harness decides whether the model keeps going, not how. 
 
 
 
 Reuse context, reset it before it degrades, and think more per turn. 

 
 Each turn in a continuing context rereads it from cache, typically ten times cheaper than uncached input and a hundred times cheaper than output, whereas each restart discards it.
AxProverBase sits at one extreme: output accounts for 89% of its $17.39 per problem, against 34% of  h1 ’s $9.00, and it reuses at most 0.5% of its input from cache, against 74–94% for  h1  (Figure   17  ).
Varying the number of turns between reflections in  h1  exposes the same trade-off (Figure   4  , right).
With one turn,  h1  solves 50 Putnam100 and 39 FATE-X problems, against 72 and 65 with ten turns, and pays roughly twice as much per solve.
With 200 turns instead of one, the cached share of input rises from 0.2% to 86%, yet solves drop to 60 and 52 (Figure   28  ): caching makes long contexts cheap but not productive, consistent with context rot  ( Hong et al., 2025 ) .
Thinking more per turn is a better use of budget.
AxProverBase found that raising the thinking budget from 10k to 32k tokens gains as much as doubling the number of iterations, at lower cost.
In  h1 , higher reasoning effort solves more at lower total cost: with Gemini 3.1 Pro, it solves 89 Putnam100 problems at $20.63 each with low effort and 99 at $5.34 with high effort, needing far fewer compilations (Figure   27  ).
In short, a harness for long-horizon agents should let the model work in one context long enough to reuse it, compact that context before it degrades, and favor reasoning over repeated failed attempts. 
 
 
 
 
  5  Conclusion, limitations, and discussion 

 
 Conclusion. 

 
 We asked whether harnesses for frontier models should prescribe hand-designed workflows or give the model a simple loop and a larger budget.
With  h1 , a simple loop with an efficient interface to Lean, test-time compute alone reaches state-of-the-art results and matches or surpasses hand-designed workflows at the same model and comparable cost. We find that a single longer attempt in this loop can even outperform repetition on open problems.
Getting the details of the harness right still matters: its interface, persistence, and context management determine how efficiently compute turns into progress.
Before designing a workflow, one should thus carefully try a frontier model in a simple loop at a realistic budget. 
 
 
 
 Limitations and discussion. 

 
 We acknowledge that most frontier models are black boxes, and that we cannot measure the extent to which benchmark exposure during training could narrow the gap between specialized workflows and a simple loop, but where possible we used models that predate the problems or their solutions, such as Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.2 for Putnam 2025 and GPT-5.6 Sol for IMO 2026 (Appendix   E.10  ).
Across the 707 benchmark problems on which we compare the simple loop with a specialized workflow, we find only two exceptions where the specialized harness is able to solve a problem we are not  3    3 
               3 
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            Full APN solves Erdős 125, where all sixteen  h1  attempts end in Lean timeouts, and MerLean with Opus 4.7 proves  BurnsidePrimeDegree , which  h1  with Opus 4.8 does not prove in our run, although  h1  with GPT-5.6 Sol does (Appendix   E.1  ).   . 
 
 
 Regarding scale,  h1  works on a single file, whereas formalizations that exceed a context window, such as those of Fermat’s Last Theorem  ( Anthropic, 2026b )  or entire textbooks  ( Rammal et al., 2026 ) , require dependency management across files, and codebase-level validation, as well as parallel agents that share intermediate results to complete the task in reasonable time: in OpenAI’s Navier–Stokes resolution, about 10,000 agents exchanged millions of messages over 88 hours  ( OpenAI, 2026a ) .
Our tools also cover only Lean, not numerical computation, simulation, visualization, or web search.
What makes a simple loop efficient and effective at that scale is the natural next question.
Following the bitter lesson, parallel agents, codebase management, and richer tools should be added without prescribing their use, for instance by letting agents communicate freely rather than through a fixed hierarchy. 
 
 
  h1 ’s interface and tools are themselves hand-designed, which the bitter lesson might discourage.
Yet human design and leveraging computation need not run counter to each other  ( Sutton, 2019 ) ; the question is where each helps most first.
In formal mathematics, spending compute on the reasoning of frontier models, and using human effort on the interface currently works best.
Further ahead, a model could build and deploy its own harness for a problem and become more efficient than the human-designed interfaces.

  Appendix A  Related Work 

 
 Trained provers. 

 
 Neural provers began with tactic prediction inside proof search  ( Polu and Sutskever, 2020 ;  Lample et al., 2022 ;  Polu et al., 2023 ;  Yang et al., 2023 ;  Kumarappan et al., 2025 ;  Song et al., 2025 ;  George et al., 2025 ;  Lin et al., 2025a ;  Xin et al., 2025b ) , reaching olympiad level with AlphaProof’s reinforcement learning and search  ( Hubert et al., 2026 ) .
Later models generate whole proofs  ( First et al., 2023 ;  Xin et al., 2025a ;  Ren et al., 2025 ;  Wang et al., 2025 ;  Dong and Ma, 2025 ;  Lin et al., 2025b ;  Lin et al., 2026 )  or are trained for agentic, tool-integrated proving  ( Chen et al., 2025a ;  Wang et al., 2026 ;  Ma et al., 2026 ) .
These systems contribute trained models rather than a harness around a given model, so we compare against their reported scores where available (Section   3.1  ). 
 
 
 
 Harnesses around generalist models. 

 
 Following informal-to-formal sketching  ( Jiang et al., 2023 )  and early agentic loops  ( Thakur et al., 2024 ;  Ospanov et al., 2025 ) , recent systems add proof-specific structure around generalist models: auxiliary lemmas and informal reasoners  ( Baba et al., 2026 ;  Liu et al., 2026a ) , multi-agent proving  ( Breen et al., 2026 ) , recursive decomposition  ( Zhou et al., 2025 ;  Varambally et al., 2026 ;  Li et al., 2026a ) , blueprints  ( Chung et al., 2026 ) , optional informal-prover and multi-model tools  ( Liu et al., 2026b ) , and evolutionary search over proof sketches in full APN  ( Tsoukalas et al., 2026 ) ; Seed-Prover  ( Chen et al., 2025b )  and Aristotle  ( Achim et al., 2025 )  build such structure around their own trained provers.
We compare with several of these using the same model (Section   3.2  ).
  Rögnvaldsson et al. (2026)   reduce the compute such workflows spend on failed attempts with a learned controller; we instead remove the workflow.
Among simple loops, we compare with AxProverBase  ( Requena et al., 2026 ) , Claude Code  ( Anthropic, 2026a ;  Math Inc., 2026a ) , Humanfia’s loop with reviewer feedback  ( Humanfia, 2026 ) , and APN basic  ( Tsoukalas et al., 2026 )  (Section   4  ).
AxProverBase demonstrates the strength of minimal agents and self-reflection for retaining lessons  ( Requena et al., 2026 ) .
We extend this evidence to open problems and compare harnesses using the same models and accounting for inference cost.
These agents use Lean interfaces including the REPL  ( leanprover-community, 2023 ) , Pantograph  ( Aniva et al., 2025 ) , the Kimina server  ( Santos et al., 2025 ) , and lean-lsp-mcp  ( Dressler, 2025 ) . 
 
 
 
 Autoformalization systems. 

 
 Aleph  ( Isenbaev and Hanin, 2026 ) , AxiomProver  ( Axiom Math, 2025 ;  Axiom Math, 2026a ) , and OpenGauss  ( Math Inc., 2026b )  target formalization more broadly, as do efforts on major results  ( Anthropic, 2026b ) , corpora  ( Rammal et al., 2026 ) , and research mathematics  ( Zhang et al., 2026 ;  Moakhar et al., 2026 ) .
OpenGauss prescribes its planning and review workflow through skill instructions, whereas Goedel-Architect enforces its blueprint search in code.
We compare with Aleph, AxiomProver, and OpenGauss only on proof completion for fixed statements, which evaluates part of what they do; our results say nothing about their value in open-ended formalization (Section   5  ). 
 
 
 
 Test-time scaling and simple loops. 

 
 Inference compute scales through repeated sampling  ( Brown et al., 2024 ;  Snell et al., 2025 )  and longer reasoning  ( OpenAI, 2024 ;  Guo et al., 2025 ) ;  h1  extends s1’s budget forcing  ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 )  from one chain of thought to an agent’s iterations.
For agents, test-time scaling has been studied in general  ( Zhu et al., 2025 )  and in coding  ( Kim et al., 2026 ;  Ding and Zhang, 2026 ) ;   Li et al. (2026b)   find sequential scaling limited by context and parallel scaling by verification, the two limitations addressed by  h1 ’s reflection and verifier.
Rather than hand-crafting test-time scaling strategies,   Zheng et al. (2026)   have an agent discover them.
 h1  combines ReAct  ( Yao et al., 2023 )  with self-reflection  ( Shinn et al., 2023 ;  Madaan et al., 2023 ) , and enforces external validation, which LLMs need to self-correct  ( Huang et al., 2024 ;  Kambhampati et al., 2024 ) .
In software engineering  ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , interfaces matter  ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , simple pipelines and minimal agents compete with complex ones  ( Xia et al., 2025 ;  SWE-agent Team, 2025 ) , and the Ralph loop runs an agent until verification succeeds  ( Huntley, 2025 ;  Macedo, 2026 ) .
Following   Kapoor et al. (2025)  , we evaluate accuracy jointly with cost (Section   2.1  ). 
 
 
 
 Benchmarks and validation. 

 
 Beyond earlier benchmarks  ( Zheng et al., 2022 ;  Ying et al., 2024 ;  Yu et al., 2025 ;  Ravi et al., 2026 ;  Letson et al., 2026 ) , we evaluate on PutnamBench  ( Tsoukalas et al., 2024 ) , FATE  ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) , FormalQualBench  ( Math Inc., 2026a ) , and Formal Conjectures  ( Firsching et al., 2026 ) , accepting proofs through a formal validator  ( GasStationManager, 2024 ;  Lean FRO, 2025 ;  Axiom Math, 2026b )  since compilation alone need not prove the intended statement.

  C.2  Formal validation 

 
 A compiling file need not prove the intended theorem: it may contain  sorry ,
change assumptions, or introduce axioms. We use SafeVerify  ( GasStationManager, 2024 )  to compare
compiled submissions with an immutable challenge, check target declarations and permitted
axioms, and replay new declarations through Lean’s kernel. Imported modules remain part
of the trusted environment. 
 
 
 Comparator  ( Lean FRO, 2025 )  also checks statement agreement, permitted axioms,
and kernel acceptance, and integrates sandboxed compilation of the challenge
and submission. AXLE’s  verify_proof  tool  ( Axiom Math, 2026b )  offers similar checks, including optional verification of a statement’s negation, through a hosted API. SafeVerify instead takes already-compiled  .olean  files,
so the harness must isolate compilation and protect the challenge and imported
dependencies  ( GasStationManager, 2024 ) . We chose SafeVerify for its disproof support,
which allows a fixed conjecture to be settled by proving it or its negation,
and because Comparator’s Landlock/landrun sandbox was not supported in our
execution environment.
We built SafeVerify against each
benchmark’s toolchain and implemented the isolated compilation procedure in
Table   8  . 
 
 
   Table 8 :   Independent validation of submitted source.  The same boundary applies to API provers and coding agents. Only the designated source file crosses from the agent workspace into validation; the agent’s compiled artifacts are never trusted.

  Compile the original statement with fixed Lean and library versions in an isolated environment; retain its compiled artifact in storage inaccessible to the prover.

  C.3  Inference budgets and cost curves 

 
 An attempt can denote a single model call, an iterative repair session, or a complete
multi-stage pipeline. For example, Goedel-Architect allows up to 16 blueprint refinements
within one PutnamBench attempt  ( Chung et al., 2026 ) . Matching attempt counts
therefore need not match inference cost. Total token counts are also insufficient:
uncached input, cached input, and output have different costs, with output tokens
costing up to     100  ×   100\times    as much as cached input in our price cards.
Ideally, we would compare inference
FLOPs directly, but closed-model providers rarely disclose the information needed
to measure them. We therefore use inference cost as a practical proxy and compare
cost with the model held fixed to assess
harness differences; input, cached input, cache writes, and output are priced separately
using the reference rates in Table   9  , including applicable
long-context rates. These API-equivalent costs quantify token usage under a

 To compare with published results, we follow the corresponding benchmark’s
reporting conventions where needed. In Table   2  , costs are campaign totals for Putnam 2025, per-problem means
for PutnamBench and IMO, and means over successful problems for FormalQualBench.

only API time. Putnam 2025 uses Numina’s statements, whereas the PutnamBench 2025 slice
uses separate formalizations. Our FormalQualBench Opus 4.6 result is the best of four
seeds (7, 6, 8, and 6 solves); the leaderboard model attribution to Opus 4.6 is inferred.

seed can reach among six attempts; its cost counts successful attempts only. We report it
next to pass@1 and pass@4, and the four FormalQualBench seeds individually, so that the
spread is visible; we draw no conclusion from the best seed alone.
The cost measure therefore changes across tables and figures: to compare with a published
number, we adopt that work’s convention, such as campaign totals, budget caps, or cost
conditional on success. Wherever our data allow, we also report the full cost including
failed attempts, and we claim comparable or lower cost at matched models rather than
uniform cost dominance across systems.

  C.6  Statistical significance and uncertainty 

 
 Many comparisons in this paper rest on a single run per configuration. Repeating every
run would multiply an already large inference cost, and we judge single runs sufficient
for the claims they support, because most of them are existence claims: that a simple
loop  can  reach a given score at a given cost. Since every accepted proof is formally
verified, one run establishes such a claim; for example, a single run shows that  h1 
with GPT-5.5 can solve 670 of the 672 PutnamBench problems. Where a claim requires statistical significance, we repeat runs or resample problems and report 95% confidence intervals, as in the
tool ablation (Figure   21  ), the Erdős prompt comparison
(Figure   4  ), and the reflection-input costs
(Table   16  ).

witnesses satisfying the intended mathematical constraints, and exclude exact-answer targets when that transformation

  E.1  Remaining advantages of specialized systems 

 
 Among 707 problems, two fixed-model exceptions stood out: the group-theoretic  BurnsidePrimeDegree  and the density problem Erdős 125 (Appendix   E.4  ).
On FormalQualBench with Opus 4.7, MerLean leads  h1  by one solve with or without the four-hour cutoff (Table   2  ).
MerLean proves  BurnsidePrimeDegree  in 3h12m with a 32-node decomposition  ( Li et al., 2026a ) ; eleven  h1  attempts fail despite a combined $6,000 and 255 hours.
With Opus 4.8, we stopped our FormalQualBench run by hand after 17 hours because of time and compute limits (Appendix   C.3  ); it had not proved  BurnsidePrimeDegree  by iteration 19 ($195), so that run’s 13/23 is a lower bound.
With GPT-5.6 Sol, however,  h1  proves  BurnsidePrimeDegree  (Table   2  ).
On Erdős 125, full APN reaches 50% at pass@1, basic reaches only 10% at pass@10, and all sixteen  h1  attempts end in unrecoverable Lean REPL timeouts, an interface limitation (Appendix   C.3  ; Figure   8  ; Appendix   E.4  ). 
 
 
 Specialized harnesses may still reduce time to a solution, even when  h1  matches their solve rate at lower cost.
Numina solves twelve in less summed time than  h1  with GPT-5.2, possibly helped by faster constituent models (Table   2  ).
Multi-agent parallelization could further reduce elapsed time, a capability orthogonal to  h1 ’s simple sequential search that we discuss in Section   5  .

 We selected the six Erdős problem instances in Figure 3 of   Tsoukalas et al. (2026)   for direct comparison: 12(i), 12(ii), 26, 125, 138, and 152. 
 
 
 AlphaProof Nexus operates on Lean files with explicitly marked editable regions:  EVOLVE-BLOCK  regions contain proof code, while  EVOLVE-VALUE  regions allow the agent to determine values within the statement, including a conjecture’s truth value  ( Tsoukalas et al., 2026 , Section 2 and Appendix A.2) .
We reconstruct our tasks from the statements and edit boundaries in APN’s public GitHub release,  4    4

This preserves the fixed parts of each statement.
We interpret these released specifications as corresponding to the tasks underlying APN’s reported comparison results, although the paper does not explicitly confirm the initial files used for those experiments. 
 
 
 We run these experiments in an isolated environment without internet access or access to existing solutions on the host filesystem.
After observing attempts to use the Lean REPL to explore the filesystem, we also explicitly inform the model of this isolation to discourage such attempts and avoid wasting inference budget (Table   5  ).
The reflection LLM also redirects the prover away from these attempts and toward mathematical work in the next iteration.
This is part of the effective repair loop that supports  h1 ’s efficiency (Section   4  ): carrying lessons from unproductive attempts into the next iteration helps direct additional inference budget toward sustained progress.

  E.9  Additional comparisons with Claude Code and analysis of failed attempts 

 
 With the same Claude model, native Claude Code (with its built-in shell and file tools), Claude Code with our prompt and Lean tools through MCP (which replace the built-in tools),
and  h1  solve 81/95/99 PutnamBench subset problems and 63/73/83 FATE-X problems,
respectively (Figures   5   and   , right). The tools expose Lean
feedback and SafeVerify rejection within the session;  h1  additionally enforces
validation and another repair round after rejection. 
 
 
 Relative to native Claude Code, exposing final-proof validation addresses a
frequent failure mode. Of 30 problems solved by  h1 
where native Claude Code stops normally without an accepted proof, 28 end with
an artifact rejected by SafeVerify. Adding our Lean tools to Claude Code solves
20 of these problems.  h1  uses multiple rounds on 21 of the 30. 
 
 
 Relative to Claude Code with MCP tools,  h1  additionally controls how execution
continues after failures. On FATE-X problem 19, Claude Code with our tools
resubmits an unchanged file 170 times, whereas  h1  edits after
each of 17 negative outcomes and succeeds. 
 
 
 The MCP integration also leaves API-call retries under Claude Code’s control.
Some Claude Code runs fail through API-call errors and repeated
timeouts. We took care to give these baselines their strongest showing: we restarted
affected runs from scratch, and reran configurations whose wall-time limit was binding
with a larger allowance. Exposing
Lean tools through MCP does not give the experimenter the same control over
Claude Code’s internal retries and failure handling as implementing the harness
directly. In  h1 , these policies are explicit: transient connection failures can
retry the same call, while verifier failures return feedback for further edits.

      Title: What Outcome RL Buys: Finishing, Reliability, Rarely Reach 
      Authors:  Shan Yang               View a PDF of the paper titled What Outcome RL Buys: Finishing, Reliability, Rarely Reach, by Shan Yang 
     View PDF

             Abstract: Outcome RL raises pass@1 but not pass@k at large k (Yue et al., 2025). But every pass@1 is scored under a token budget. Every recipe also trains under one. On physics and math problems at fixed token budgets, we compare the pass@1 of 20 released RL models (1.5B to 32B) with that of the thinking models they started from. We ask whether each pass@1 gain is changed behaviour or new knowledge. We divide each change in pass@1 into three parts. Finishing measures answering before the budget runs out. Reliability measures being right once finished. Reach measures problems RL solves that its base answered wrongly in all eight tries, minus problems the base solves that RL answered wrongly in all eight. We find four things. (1) Where the base often hits the token budget before answering, most of the change, gain or loss, is finishing (82% at 4k and 8k). Given more tokens, the base closes most of the finishing gap itself. (2) Where the base has enough tokens, the gain is reliability: the RL model is graded right more often, even on problems both finish. (3) By our definition, RL rarely solves what its base cannot. Reach adds at most 2.1 percentage points on any of our four physics and math sets. We checked 144 physics problems that only the RL model solved. Of these, 3.5% hold up when resampled or read. In a random sample, nine of ten new RL steps a human confirmed also appear in the base's samples. (4) In a small-scale RL run on an 8B model, the gain on new problems is finishing, with reliability flat. Supplying each problem's physical setup was not shown to improve on plain RL.
