  Affiliation:  Individual Researcher
 
  Correspondence to:   alexyangshan@gmail.com 
     

  Abstract 
    
 Outcome RL raises pass@1 but not pass@   k  k    at large    k  k     ( Yue et al., 2025 ) . But every pass@1 is scored under a token budget. Every recipe also trains under one. On physics and math problems at fixed token budgets, we compare the pass@1 of    20  20    released RL models (   1.5  1.5   B to    32  32   B) with that of the thinking models they started from. We ask whether each pass@1 gain is changed behaviour or new knowledge. We divide each change in pass@1 into three parts.  Finishing  measures answering before the budget runs out.  Reliability  measures being right once finished.  Reach  measures problems RL solves that its base answered wrongly in all eight tries, minus problems the base solves that RL answered wrongly in all eight. We find four things. (1) Where the base often hits the token budget before answering, most of the change, gain or loss, is finishing (    82  %   82\%    at    4  4   k and    8  8   k). Given more tokens, the base closes most of the finishing gap itself. (2) Where the base has enough tokens, the gain is reliability: the RL model is graded right more often, even on problems both finish. (3) By our definition, RL rarely solves what its base cannot. Reach adds at most    2.1  2.1    percentage points on any of our four physics and math sets. We checked    144  144    physics problems that only the RL model solved. Of these,     3.5  %   3.5\%    hold up when resampled or read. In a random sample, nine of ten new RL steps a human confirmed also appear in the base’s samples. (4) In a small-scale RL run on an    8  8   B model, the gain on new problems is finishing, with reliability flat. Supplying each problem’s physical setup was not shown to improve on plain RL. 
  
 
 
 Keywords:  reinforcement learning, reasoning, language models, physics
 
 
 Project page:  https://shanyang.me/what-outcome-rl-buys/ . Code and released tables:  https://github.com/shanyang-me/outcome-rl-buys . 
 
 
  1  Introduction 

 
      reliability    P  P        reach, net of its mirror              
  
  Figure 1:  Outcome RL’s pass@1 gain on physics and competition math, split into finishing, reliability and net reach. Each bar is the mean over the recipes in its group. Recipes are grouped by how often their base finishes at the training cap on that set, with their number in parentheses. Reliability is measured on each model’s own finished derivations. A part left of zero lowers the score: the RL model hits the budget before answering more often (finishing), is right less often once finished (reliability), or solves fewer problems alone than the base does (reach). 
 
 
 
              
     
  finishing term    F  F         reliability term    P  P         reach, net of its mirror  
 
  Figure 2:  What outcome RL buys at each recipe’s own training cap and at the next budget above it, in pass@1 on physics. Each row is one recipe, split as in Figure   1  . Parts left of zero read as in Figure   1  . The number at the right of each row is the change, with the budget read. Red  parts        <  0.005   <0.005    marks a row whose parts are all below    0.005  0.005   , too small to read. Rows are sorted by how often the base finishes at the cap on physics, least first. The lone-win panels count physics problems that only the RL model solves (black, right) or only the base (grey, left), while the other model finished all eight samples.  † : the cap is not exact. DeepMath trains at a    24  24   k cap but penalizes length from    20  20   k. STILL-3 trains at    29  29   k and is read at    28  28   k. 
 
 
 Outcome RL, which rewards only a correct final answer, is a standard way to train reasoning models. Its gains are reported as pass@1. Whether such a gain is new knowledge or changed behaviour matters. New knowledge widens what a model can solve. Changed behaviour only helps it use what it already knows. The two are hard to tell apart. Every pass@1 is scored under a token budget, so one number mixes answering in time, answering right and solving new problems.   Yue et al. (2025)   found that outcome RL adds no reasoning the base cannot already produce. Pass@   k  k    is the chance that at least one of    k  k    samples is right. Once    k  k    reaches the hundreds, the base scores higher than the RL model. The problems the RL model solves are nearly a subset of those its base solves. Prior work calls this narrowing  sharpening   ( Huang et al., 2024 ;  Qin et al., 2025 ;  Wu et al., 2025c ) . We ask whether RL changes behaviour or knowledge at     k  =  1   k=1   , the score every report rests on. Finishing in time and being right more often change behaviour. Solving problems the base cannot points to new knowledge. We count a gain as new knowledge only when the base finishes all eight samples on the problem and gets every one wrong. We count any other gain as changed behaviour, since the base either answers the problem right at least once or does not finish every sample. 
 
 
 Our first question asks of released models: how much of a pass@1 gain is finishing within the token budget, and is the rest reliability or reach? Every recipe is also trained under a budget. If part of a gain is the model fitting its answer into the budget, comparisons between recipes, or between a recipe and its base, partly measure how long each model writes rather than how well it reasons. We ask the first question of thinking models on physics and math. A bounded second question follows: can training install knowledge the model does not use on its own, when it is supplied? 
 
 
 Our main study answers the first question by reading twenty released RL models against their bases at fixed budgets. All twenty start from thinking bases, which distillation has already widened.   Yue et al. (2025)   leave thinking bases open. Once the budget suffices, reliability rises on physics wherever the base already finishes. Reach stays small. 
 
 
 The second question tests the obvious remedy for sharpening: hand the model the knowledge its derivations lack (a hint, a teacher’s derivation, or a question about the setup). We train an    8  8   B thinking model with outcome RL on physics, supplying in five ways the physical setup of problems its base almost never solves. At this small scale, the supplied setup changes the model during training but is not shown to carry over to held-out problems beyond plain RL. Reward raises a problem’s solve rate only once the model samples a success on that problem (§  5  ). Released recipes that use the remedy, QuestA and KnowRL, reach only a little further. Their net reach is at most    0.018  0.018    (§  4.3  ). 
 
 
 Contributions. 

 
 (1)  A budget-aware split of the pass@1 gain  into finishing, reliability and reach (Eqs. (  1  )–(  5  )). Unlike pass@   k  k   , it separates answering in time from answering right. The split also nets reach against the reverse. (2)  A read of twenty released pairs on thinking bases , the case   Yue et al. (2025)   leave open, at each recipe’s own training cap and the next budget above it (§  4  ). (3)  A comparison rule : compare a recipe with its base at or above its training cap. (4)  A controlled probe  that supplies an    8  8   B model, in five ways, the setup of physics problems its base almost never solves, and tests transfer to their text-only twins (§  5  ). 
 
 
 
 
  2  Related Work 

 
  What RL with verifiable rewards changes.  Prior work disagrees on what outcome RL changes. None splits the measured gain into finishing and the rest. On pass@   k  k    curves, RL raises pass@1, but the base wins at large    k  k     ( Yue et al., 2025 ;  Wu et al., 2025b ) . RL stays within what the base can sample.   Yue et al. (2025)   count the problems only the RL model solves at    0  0   –    1  %   1\%    on AIME24 and MATH500, at    k  k    up to    1,024  1{,}024   . Follow-ups trace this lost coverage to hard prompts whose rare successes drop out of small sample groups  ( Zhou, 2026 )  and to winner-take-all reinforcement of what the base already finds likely  ( Nguyen et al., 2025 ) . Others trace part of reported gains to budget mismatch and attempt inflation  ( Wu et al., 2025a ;  Yang & Chen, 2026 ) . Studies of derivations say RL narrows the policy where fine-tuning broadens it  ( Matsutani et al., 2025 ) , acts on a few tokens where derivations branch  ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , and amplifies habits the base already has  ( Gandhi et al., 2025 ) . Power sampling, entropy minimisation and even spurious rewards reproduce much of RL’s gain  ( Karan & Du, 2025 ;  Agarwal et al., 2025 ;  Shao et al., 2025 ) . One training example recovers most of a full data set’s gain  ( Wang et al., 2025d ) . A second RL stage shortens derivations at no cost in accuracy  ( Fatemi et al., 2025 ) . Both results say RL moves behaviour more than content. Prolonged training, by contrast, is reported to expand the solvable set  ( Liu et al., 2025a ) . Decompositions find RL improves execution within a fixed coverage  ( Qin et al., 2025 ) . Fine-tuning, not RL, moves knowledge  ( Wu et al., 2025c ) . All this evidence is observational: no work supplies the missing content and tests whether RL learns it. Our reliability term is the execution gain of   Qin et al. (2025)   with finishing removed. We compare reliability with finishing at each budget. Our reach is a term of an exact split of the pass@1 gain, counted per problem at     k  =  8   k=8   . The base-only count in reach controls for sampling noise. Problems only one model solves are resampled and read. Unlike budget corrections of reported gains  ( Wu et al., 2025a ) , we split the gain at a fixed budget. We also read each recipe at its own cap. 
 
 
  Objectives, samplers and replay.  Other work changes how RL credits rare successes. We use one such method, replay. Pass@   k  k    objectives reshape the group advantage  ( Chen et al., 2025d ;  Walder & Karkhanis, 2025 ;  Liu et al., 2025b ) . VinePPO branches continuations to estimate credit  ( Kazemnejad et al., 2024 ) . RLEP replays past successes into the group  ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) . Replay shows what reward teaches once a success is sampled. 
 
 
  Measuring RL on thinking models.  Length and answer rate are known confounds  ( Liu et al., 2025b ;  Yu et al., 2025b ;  Aggarwal & Welleck, 2025 ;  Hou et al., 2025 ) . For a fixed thinking model, accuracy at a cap rises with the cap  ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ;  Qwen Team, 2025 ) . Any change to derivation length therefore changes the score. We separate the two with the finishing decomposition. We also fix a held-out set before training and measure its noise floor. 
 
 
 
  3  Experimental Setup 

 
 This section gives the study’s scope, the three metrics that split pass@1 under a budget (§  3.1  ) and the protocol for reading the twenty released pairs (§  3.2  ). 
 
 
  Scope: thinking bases.  We study thinking bases because they give RL the most to change: how long the model reasons, when it commits to an answer and how often that answer is right, not only whether it answers. A token budget makes each change visible in the score. Practice uses thinking bases too. The strongest open models on math and science, DeepSeek-R1 and its distills and Qwen3, ship in this thinking mode. Every recipe we study starts from one of them. All models studied are thinking models: the five bases (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B and 7B, Qwen3-1.7B and 4B in thinking mode, OpenMath-Nemotron-1.5B), the    14  14   B and    32  32   B bases added later, and our controlled run’s Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking. Models that answer in a few hundred tokens are out of scope, except one pair read for contrast: Qwen2.5-7B and its outcome-RL version, Open-Reasoner-Zero-7B (§  4.1  ). 
 
 
  Scope: physics and math.  To tell changed behaviour from new knowledge, we read every pair in two domains. Math is the recipes’ own domain: all twenty recipes we study train on competition math and report math results. A gain on math shows what RL buys where it was trained. A gain on physics shows what RL buys outside that domain. Physics is at most about     1  %   1\%    of the RL training data of every recipe that states its mix, except ProRL v2, whose mix includes STEM. Skywork-OR1-Math-7B does not state its mix. Physics problems also need modelling, which math problems rarely exercise. A physics derivation first picks the governing principle and decides which quantities and effects matter, and only then does the algebra. A wrong setup is not repaired by careful algebra later. Once they finish at    16  16   k, the five bases are right on    85  85   –    91  %   91\%    of their MATH-500 derivations but only    21  21   –    56  %   56\%    of their physics ones. The modelling also makes physics derivations long, so the token budget binds more often than on math (§  4.1  ). 
 
 
  Test sets.  Each domain has a main set and a check. The main physics set is    300  300    text-only problems from the training corpus of our controlled run (§  5  ), so both questions share one audited answer checker. The set keeps only problems the controlled run’s base solves at least sometimes, so pass@1 can move. Filtering on the base caps how much reach can show, so    671  671    unfiltered physics problems check the reach result (Appendix   A.6  ). On math, the main set is MATH-500, the recipes’ standard benchmark. The math check is    276  276    recent contest problems, below MATH-500’s ceiling, some released after every model (Appendix   A.7  ). We call it competition math. 
 
 
 
 
     
             
  finishing    F  F         reliability    P  P         reach, net of its mirror    
  Figure 3:  What outcome RL buys at each recipe’s own training cap on competition math, the recipes’ own domain. Rows are split as in Figure   2  . Parts left of zero read as in Figure   1  . Rows are sorted by how often the base finishes at the cap, least first.  
 
 
  3.1  Metrics 

 
 We split a pass@   k  k    gain under a token budget    B  B    into three parts:  finishing     F  F   , answering in time;  reliability     P  P   , answering right once finished; and  reach , reach@    k  ⁡   (  B  )    k(B)   , solving problems the base leaves unsolved in    k  k    samples.   3.2  Protocol for Reading the Released Pairs 

 
 We read twenty released outcome-RL models, each against the thinking base it was trained from (Table   6  ). Eighteen are of up to    7  7   B. The other two are a    14  14   B and a    32  32   B pair. Each RL model and its base are sampled the same way, with one prompt and one answer checker, the matcher. Each model writes     k  =  8   k=8    answers per problem at temperature     T  =  0.6   T=0.6   . Budgets:    4  4   k,    8  8   k and    16  16   k; the recipe’s training cap; and the next budget above the cap on a fixed grid up to    64  64   k. The split is read at     k  =  1   k=1   , per sample. fin@1    (  B  )   (B)    is the share of derivations that finish within    B  B   . pass@1    (  B  |  fin  )   (B\,|\,\text{fin})    is pass@1 on finished derivations. Reach is read at     k  =  8   k=8   , as reach@8 and reach  ≥4  @8 (    k  =  32   k=32    in Appendix   A.5  ). We  registered  predictions for ten pairs at    4  4   k and    8  8   k, committing them before any of their outputs existed. Reads at the cap and the next budget above it were not registered.

The reward explains why. An unfinished derivation scores zero whatever it contains, so at a tight budget the first thing group-relative credit can tell apart is whether a sample finished. The finishing share is larger on MATH-500 than on physics, because a finished base derivation on MATH-500 is already usually right.   Outcome RL moves derivation length toward what earns most reward within its cap.  The effect on finishing therefore depends on where the base starts. At a short cap, RL teaches a thinking base to fit its derivations inside the cap, as ProRL v2 does at    8  8   k. At a long cap, RL teaches longer derivations. The RL model then finishes less often, as Polaris-1.7B does even at its own cap. Across recipes, the change in derivation length tracks the change in finishing (Table   1  ). RL lengthens derivations on a short-answer base too, and the RL model then finishes less at a tight budget (Open-Reasoner-Zero-7B  ( Hu et al., 2025 ) ; Table   1  ). 
 
 
  Finishing is not hidden knowledge.  A base that cannot finish within    B  B    tokens might not know how to derive the answer. Two results argue against this reading. First, the extra tokens go to hesitation, not derivation. In our controlled run (§  5  ), RL halves the backtracking words (“wait”, “actually”) per derivation. Reliability on problems finished both before and after training does not move. Second, given more tokens, the base solves most of the problems on which RL, at a tight budget, finishes more often and scores higher. We pick those problems with four of the eight samples, then score them on the other four and on a separate    64  64   k base run. At    64  64   k the base passes the RL model on the problems picked at    4  4   k and closes most of the gap on those picked at    8  8   k (Table   1  ). The gap the base does not close counts as reliability, not finishing. Finishing and knowledge are not fully separable, since committing to the right approach is a skill. Our claim is narrower: RL adds few steps the base does not already write (§  4.3  ). Finishing still pays at a tight deployment budget, as ProRL v2 at    8  8   k shows.

  Whether the base still hits the training cap before answering decides which part grows.  RL can buy finishing only where the base fails to finish (Figure   2  ). A recipe is  cap-bound  when its base still often hits its cap before answering. Four recipes are cap-bound: ProRL v2, Open-RS3, e3 and JustRL-DeepSeek. For ProRL v2 and e3 on physics, finishing is the whole gain (Table   8  ). JustRL-DeepSeek gains about a third by reliability, half under the matched split. Open-RS3’s score does not measurably change at its cap. The split of Eqs. (  2  )–(  3  ) can hide a reliability gain, because the problems RL newly finishes are harder and pull its reliability down.  Matched  reliability, measured only on problems both models finish, avoids that pull (§  3.1  ). With matched reliability, the four recipes gain some reliability as well. Across all twenty recipes, the more the base leaves unfinished at the cap, the larger the finishing share. 
 
 
  Where the base already finishes, reliability rises in every recipe.  The sixteen recipes that are not cap-bound train at caps where the base already finishes    93  93   –    100  %   100\%    of its derivations. In all sixteen, reliability rises on physics. By size, reliability is the larger part in fourteen of them (Figure   2  ). Averaged by base, reliability exceeds finishing on all seven bases, and is larger by size on six (Table   2  ). Finishing moves either way: seven of the sixteen finish less than their base. Math shows the same rise, on MATH-500 and on competition math, a separate set of    276  276    recent contest problems (Figure   3  ). One recipe goes the other way: e3’s reliability falls on MATH-500, although its base finishes there. 
 
 
  Reliability still rises on problems both models finish.  Matched reliability still rises in all sixteen recipes, clear of zero in twelve (Table   8  ). The Polaris pairs finish less than their bases, and their matched rise is smaller than their plain rise. On competition math, the matched split narrows the gap between the two parts in both groups of Figure   1  , without changing which is larger (Table   2  ). A registered prediction that the rise would stay under    0.03  0.03    held with both benchmarks pooled but failed on physics alone (Appendix   A  ). 
 
 
  On problems where RL is right more often, the step behind its win is one the base already writes.  To test whether RL’s reliability gain adds a step the base lacks, we drew    40  40    problems at random where the base finishes all eight samples at    16  16   k but is right in only one to four, and the RL model is right more often. A language-model reader, blind to which model wrote which, named the step that makes the RL derivation right and the base derivation wrong. A second reader looked for that step in the base’s other samples. On    12  12    of the    40  40    problems, the two derivations differ only in answer form or grading. None of the    26  26    steps judged decisive on the other    28  28    is missing from the base (Table   2  ). The base’s own wrong samples state the step too, but on    17  17    of the    26  26    they do not carry it through. The reverse search, for the base’s steps in the RL model’s samples, finds no step missing either. At the caps of    13  13    of the    16  16    recipes that are not cap-bound, the check finds no RL step missing where the base is right five to seven times. RL uses, more reliably, a step its base already has. 
 
 
  Across all twenty recipes, reliability is the part of the gain that rises consistently.  At the cap, reliability is the largest part of the mean physics gain (Table   2  ). Across recipes, reliability and reach are clear of zero. Finishing is not, because it moves either way. Resampling the seven bases instead of problems widens the intervals of the two shares until they overlap (Appendix   A  ). At the next budget above the cap, reliability rises in more recipes than finishing does (Table   2  ). Our reads cannot explain why some recipes gain more reliability than others. The recipes differ in data, steps and algorithm at once.

  Of what RL solves on physics, its base already solves     𝟖𝟓  %   85\%   .  Problems only one model solves,  lone wins , are about as common in each direction (Table   3  ). In two thirds of them, the losing model left at least one sample unfinished. The rest, where the losing model finished all eight and got all eight wrong, are the candidates for new knowledge. 
 
 
  A lone win can be chance.  Eight samples can miss a problem a model solves with low probability. Given    24  24    more samples, each model solves a similar share of the problems the other got wrong in all eight (Table   3  ). 
 
 
  Of    𝟏𝟒𝟒  144    lone wins we checked,    𝟓  5    are real physics.  A lone win is real physics if the base’s answers are wrong in substance in every sample we have, not only in form such as an option letter. On four bases at    16  16   k, the base solves    87  87    of RL’s    121  121    lone wins in    56  56    more samples (Table   4  ). On the other    34  34   , we read new samples of both models that keep the full text. Three are real physics. Reading    23  23    lone wins at the caps, without resampling, finds two more. 
 
 
  Reach stays at or below    0.021  0.021    on all four sets.  The bound holds on our physics set, on a harder, unfiltered physics set, on MATH-500 and on competition math (Table   4  ). 
 
 
  A tenth to a third of the gain falls on problems the base never gets right but leaves some samples unfinished.  Eq. (  4  ) needs all eight base samples to finish, so it counts such a problem toward finishing and reliability. At the cap on the    16  16    regenerated pairs, these problems carry about a tenth of the gain for the recipes that are not cap-bound and about a third for the cap-bound ones (Table   4  ). Given    64  64   k tokens, the bases solve under half of the ones RL gets right. Counted as unsolved, these problems would lift net reach above    0.02  0.02    only for ProRL v2 at its    8  8   k cap (Table   4  ). Our definition counts this part as behaviour. On    56  56    of the    57  57    such problems checked where a step decides, the base’s own samples write RL’s deciding step (Appendix   A.1  ). 
 
 
  In a random sample, nine of ten new RL steps a human upheld are already in the base’s samples.  On problems an RL model gets right and its base gets wrong, language-model readers compared the winning RL derivation with a failed base one. Read blind, each derivation has a step the other lacks about as often. In a random sample of    50  50    pairs, an author upheld under half of these claims on each side (Table   3  ). Nine of the ten upheld RL steps appear in the base’s own samples. A reader then searched four other samples of the model whose derivation lacked the step. On physics, the search finds RL-side steps in the base’s samples about as often as the reverse (Table   3  ). 
 
 
  Recipes built to add knowledge solve few new problems.  QuestA puts a partial reference solution in every training prompt. KnowRL adds knowledge-point hints to about four prompts in five. ProRL v2 trains    3,000  3{,}000    steps on data that includes physics. At its cap, each of the three robustly solves at most three problems its base gets wrong in all eight (Table   4  ). On the harder, unfiltered physics set, QuestA and KnowRL lead the twenty recipes in net reach (Table   11  ). Read one by one,    13  13    of their    19  19    robust wins there stand, and none is answer form (Appendix   A.6  ). KnowRL trains on QuestA’s problems, so the lead may come from those problems rather than the hints. Training length does not predict reach (Table   4  ). 
 
 
  Larger bases split the same way, and four of the five show more reach.  The three    7  7   B recipes split like the smaller ones. The    14  14   B and    32  32   B recipes train at long caps, so at    4  4   k and    8  8   k they finish less often than their bases and score lower. At its cap, the    32  32   B recipe gains mostly reliability (Table   4  ). For four of the five recipes from    7  7   B up, net reach at the cap is higher than for any smaller recipe. Part of this extra reach is answer form, which the matcher rejects more often for larger models. Six of the    32  32   B recipe’s nine robust wins on physics are answer form. A more lenient answer judge removes most of the    32  32   B recipe’s net reach. The judge does not lower the    7  7   B recipes’ reach, so for them the answer-form reading rests only on their robust counts (Table   10  ). Whether real reach grows with scale is open.

  At this scale, reward raises reliability only on the problems it lands on. Beyond those problems, the planned test finds a gain whose part beyond finishing is not robust.  To see whether outcome RL installs knowledge it is given, we supply it ourselves, at small scale. We train Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking  ( Bai et al., 2025 )  with group-relative outcome RL (GSPO;   Zheng et al., 2025 ;  Shao et al., 2024  ) on physics at a    12  12   k-token cap, for up to sixty updates, one seed per treated arm and two for the control. Plain RL repeats the result of §  4  : its held-out gain comes from finishing, with reliability flat (Appendix   B.1  ). The knowledge supplied is the  setup : the physical modelling a problem needs before any algebra. The base solves at most    16  16    of the    160  160    hard training problems at least once in eight samples. A gain on problems the base finishes and still gets wrong would count as new knowledge. Five  channels  supply the setup, from a hint in the prompt to a teacher’s full derivation. Each channel changes the model during training (Table   5  ). None of the four channels we could evaluate is shown to carry over to held-out problems beyond plain RL. The test would detect a gain a third the size of plain RL’s. A smaller gain could go undetected, such as the hint’s lead over the second control seed (Table   14  ). The fifth channel, a setup reward, taught the policy to game its scorer, so its held-out effect could not be measured. 
 
 
  Reward works where it lands.  Training again and again on    60  60    hard problems,  revisiting , raises their solve rate from    0.10  0.10    to    0.28  0.28    (Table   5  ). Revisiting moves neither the other    293  293    hard problems nor the held-out set. On the training problems the control earned reward on, finishing and reliability both rise, so finishing’s share of the gain depends on the order of the split (Table   5  ). 
 
 
  Transfer beyond those problems is not shown.  We call a training problem  credited  when the control earned reward on it in updates    31  31    to    60  60   . Each hard training problem has a text-only  twin : the same physics and method on a new, much easier surface. On the planned mean score, credited problems’ twins gain more than other twins, clear of zero (Table   5  ). The other planned measure, solving a twin at least once in eight samples, includes zero. Over the two control seeds and the three orders of the split, finishing is    26  26   –    62  %   62\%    of that excess. The base finishes credited twins less often than other twins. The rest is not clear of zero under any order for the first control seed, and only in Eq. (  2  )’s order for the second (Appendix   B.13  ). Credited problems also differ in kind: a supervised fine-tune never trained on them shows part of the same excess. Two adjustments added after the full read, for the base and for problem kind, each leave the excess including zero. A last test, chosen after a first look, finds no difference on twins both models finish. A partial transfer cannot be excluded. Even the control’s own gains are not shown to transfer beyond finishing. The probe cannot tell whether the channels failed or supplied knowledge does not transfer this way. 
 
 
 
  6  Discussion and Limitations 

 
  The two questions, answered.  On the released models, RL’s gain is changed behaviour by our definition, not new knowledge. Where the budget binds, finishing is most of the change (    82  %   82\%    at    4  4   k and    8  8   k). Where it no longer binds, the gain is reliability, from steps the base already writes or from answer form. New knowledge, measured as reach, is rare. At our probe’s scale, supplied knowledge is not shown to transfer beyond the problems reward lands on. ProRL v2, trained fifty times as long as our probe, holds two of the five real physics wins. A much larger scale may matter. 
 
 
  What this means in practice.  Report pass@1 at a budget together with fin@1    (  B  )   (B)    at that budget. Otherwise a model that stops sooner will look like one that reasons better. Compare a recipe with its base at or above its training cap. Below the cap, a recipe trained long looks worse than it is. QuestA and the two Polaris recipes score below their bases on physics at    16  16   k and no longer do at their own caps (Table   8  ;    16  16   k cells released). On MATH-500, QuestA still loses    0.07  0.07    at its cap. 
 
 
  Limitations.  The released-pair study and the controlled run are bounded in scale, sampling and grading, and cover thinking bases only. Each limit below names what we checked. 
 
 
  The probe.  The controlled run has one seed per treated arm, one model family and one domain. The run’s held-out set was chosen on base-model samples. The channels ran at up to the control’s scale, about two visits per problem. Prolonged training is untested. Supervised distillation at scale, known to transfer  ( Yue et al., 2025 ) , is untested too. 
 
 
  Sampling.  The released pairs are read with eight samples per problem (   32  32    or    64  64    on lone-win problems). The budgets are three fixed ones, the cap and the next budget above it, up to    64  64   k. Only Polaris evaluates higher, at    90  90   k. The pairs are read at temperature    0.6  0.6   , where nine recipes report at    0.7  0.7    to    1.4  1.4   . The eight pairs re-read at their authors’ temperatures split the same way (Appendix   A.3  ). A second generation of    16  16    pairs, three of them cap-bound (Table   9  ), moves each term at the cap by at most    0.007  0.007   , inside every interval. 
 
 
  Reach.  Our definition counts as behaviour the tenth to third of the gain on problems the base never gets right but leaves some samples unfinished (§  4.3  ). Filtering the physics problems on the controlled run’s base caps how much reach they can show. On MATH-500, neither model was resampled on the problems it alone fails. The MATH-500 mirror may therefore hold real losses of coverage. On both physics sets, both models were resampled (Appendices   A.5   and   A.6  ). Physics is at most about     1  %   1\%    of the recipes’ stated RL data but may be in the bases’ pretraining. We did not check our problems against any recipe’s training set. 
 
 
  Grading.  The answer matcher is strict, and stricter for larger models. On the    40  40    reliability problems checked by language-model readers,    12  12    RL wins over the base differ only in answer form or grading. Part of the measured reliability gain therefore reflects which answer forms the matcher accepts. Regraded under the fixed judge protocol of Appendix   C.2  ,    3  3   –    6  %   6\%    of the matcher-rejected physics answers become right for the    1.5  1.5   B and    1.7  1.7   B models, and    10  10   –    17  %   17\%    for the    4  4   B to    32  32   B models. On the eight pairs with stored texts and the    16  16    regenerated pairs, the judge raises pass@1    (  B  |  fin  )   (B\,|\,\text{fin})    for base and RL alike. On the    16  16    regenerated pairs, the judge lowers the reliability term at the cap by    0.003  0.003    on average, about     8  %   8\%    of it. The judge moves net reach by less than    0.01  0.01    (Table   9  ). Closed models were trace readers (Claude Opus 5.5) and setup grader (Claude Sonnet 5). The trace readings are by one language model. One author checked the model’s claimed new steps. No human checked the step checks’ finds. Only the new-step comparison (   143  143    pairs) and the step checks were read blind.

  A.1  How the traces were read 

 
  Protocol.  We read up to twelve problems per recipe that the RL model solves and its base, despite finishing, does not. Two language-model readers (Claude Opus 5.5) see both derivations with model and grade labels, so the reading is not blind. The readers mark whether the RL derivation states a principle, method or reading the base’s never states. A third reader settles disagreements. Of the    195  195    wins,    42  42    are grading or answer-form artifacts (full table in the released repository). 
 
 
  Blind reading.  A blind, shuffled re-read of    143  143    pairs asks whether each side states a step the other never does. Weighted to the    195  195    wins, it finds a new step on the RL side in     46  %   46\%    and on the base side in     50  %   50\%   , assuming the    60  60    unmarked pairs read stand for the other    112  112   . A failed derivation lacks steps as often as the winning one, so the labelled count measures attention as much as content. 
 
 
  A human check of the new steps.  One author, blind to side, checked the claimed new steps in    50  50    of the    143  143    pairs, drawn at random with a fixed seed. Of    45  45    decided claims (   12  12    unsure),    19  19    hold. There is no detectable difference between sides:    10  10    of    26  26    for RL (   0.38  0.38    [   0.22  0.22   ,    0.57  0.57   ]),    9  9    of    19  19    for the base (   0.47  0.47    [   0.27  0.27   ,    0.68  0.68   ]). The readers overcount on both sides, so the counts above are upper bounds. The symmetry the reuse finding rests on survives. The check tests only claims made, so it gives no    κ  \kappa   . 
 
 
  Repertoire check.  A step missing from one base sample may still be in the model, so checkers searched four other base samples on the same problem. Of the    83  83    steps flagged in the unblinded reading (   37  37    from the first eight recipes,    46  46    from the ten added),    77  77    appear in one,    37  37    used correctly. Six appear in none. Two of the    77  77    were found only weakly and no finds were re-examined, so the count may lean toward finding them. Of the    10  10    RL-side steps the human check upheld, the base’s samples hold    9  9   . Of the    80  80    blind RL-side steps, the search finds    58  58   ,    32  32    of them used correctly in a base sample that then abandons them. The search misses    13  13   , and    9  9    were not searched because their base samples were not stored.   A.6  A harder, unfiltered physics set 

 
  Reach stays rare on problems the filter never touched.  The paper’s    300  300    physics problems were filtered to ones the controlled run’s base solves sometimes, so reach there is a lower bound. On two further sets without that limit, all twenty pairs split the same way (Table   11  ). Net reach at the cap is     −  0.006   -0.006    to     +  0.018   +0.018   , clear of zero for seven pairs, touching zero for four and below zero for one. Bases leave two to three times more problems finished in all eight samples but never solved than on the paper’s sets (Table   10  ). Even so, the RL model solves at least four of eight on at most    10  10    of them. 
 
 
  The sets.  The  harder set  has    471  471    closed-form problems from OlympiadBench, PHYBench, PHYSICS’s olympiad tier and FrontierScience. The  unfiltered set  has    200  200    random problems from the paper’s pools, excluding its    300  300   . On AceReason-Nemotron-7B the judge leaves net reach unchanged. 
 
 
  Far from ceiling, the split is the same.  The gain is small and mostly reliability where both models finish, and finishing for recipes trained at    16  16   k or below. Reach counts only finished samples, so QuestA and Polaris-1.7B, which finish less, could show less reach. At the next budget above the cap, where both finish more, their filtered-set net reach falls (released tables). 
 
 
  The two knowledge-guided recipes’ robust wins hold up when read.  QuestA and KnowRL have    10  10    and    9  9    robust wins on this set at their caps, on    13  13    distinct problems. For each win, a language-model reader compared the base’s eight answers and the RL model’s eight with the gold. No base answer agrees with the gold, so none of the    19  19    is answer form. On three wins, two of QuestA’s and one of KnowRL’s, the RL answers the judge credited do not agree with the gold. On three more, one credited answer is wrong, which leaves three right in eight. The other    13  13    stand. Without the wrongly credited answers, net reach is about    0.016  0.016    for QuestA and    0.014  0.014    for KnowRL, still the largest. Other recipes’ wins were not read this way. 
 
 
  The filter did not hide reach.  Scored by the matcher alone, net reach at the cap is     −  0.009   -0.009    to     +  0.014   +0.014    on the unfiltered    200  200   , against     −  0.007   -0.007    to     +  0.013   +0.013    on the filtered    300  300    (full table in the released repository). Net reach on OlympiadBench (February    2024  2024   , before every base) is no larger than on FrontierScience (December    2025  2025   , after every model) (    −  0.013   -0.013    to     +  0.027   +0.027    against     −  0.005   -0.005    to     +  0.035   +0.035   ), so there is no contamination signature.

Over the    19  19    pairs resampled, six of them only in part, the base solves    244  244    of    448  448    RL wins (    54  %   54\%   ). The RL model solves    187  187    of    289  289    base wins (    65  %   65\%   ). After both are resampled, the RL model solves    162  162    of its wins again in its new samples while the base still fails them, and the base does the same on    70  70    of its own, a net of    92  92   , about five per pair.

  A.7  A competition-math set 

 
  Reach stays rare in domain.  Physics is out of domain for every recipe that states its mix except ProRL v2, and MATH-500 is near ceiling, so we read every pair at its cap on    276  276    MathArena final-answer problems (Table   12  ). Of these,    213  213    are from 2025 and    63  63    from AIME and HMMT February 2026, after every model. Net reach is     −  0.002   -0.002    to     +  0.021   +0.021   , clear of zero for nine pairs and touching or straddling zero for eleven. The judge moves net reach by at most     +  0.001   +0.001   . 
 
 
  Registered predictions.  Before any output existed we registered five. P1: every base finishes less than on physics, and finishing leads for the four cap-bound recipes. P2: reliability rises clear of zero, leading in most, in at least three quarters of recipes whose base finishes     90  %   90\%    or more. P3: net reach within     [    −  0.02   ,   +  0.03    ]   [-0.02,+0.03]   , clear of zero for at most half the pairs, robust reach at most    0.02  0.02   . P4: no more reach on 2026 than on 2025. P5: AIME 2025 pass@1 within    0.08  0.08    of the authors’ comparable numbers. P2 to P5 held. P1 failed on Open-RS3, where neither model finishes more than     6  %   6\%    at    4  4   k, leaving too few finished samples to split. 
 
 
  Far from finishing, which term leads depends on the estimator.  For the five recipes on R1-Distill-1.5B, whose base finishes    0.74  0.74    to    0.80  0.80   , finishing carries more of the gain than on physics. Under the matched split, reliability is larger for four of the five. The matched finishing term is a remainder that also carries accuracy changes outside the matched set. 
 
 
  Reliability leads where the base finishes.  In all nine recipes whose base finishes     90  %   90\%    or more, reliability rises clear of zero and leads under either split. On matched problems, where selection cannot act, pass@1    (  B  |  fin  )   (B\,|\,\text{fin})    still rises clear of zero for every such base. For QuestA and KnowRL it rises     +  0.109   +0.109    and     +  0.129   +0.129   , against     +  0.245   +0.245    and     +  0.188   +0.188    over all. Selection therefore accounts for part of each gain. A gain clear of zero remains. 
 
 
  Contamination.  P4, a test of base contamination, holds for every pair (full table in the released repository). More reach on 2025, the sign of recipe contamination, is clear of zero only for STILL-3 and Skywork-OR1-7B. With only    11  11    and    13  13    finished-but-unsolved problems in their 2026 strata, contamination and chance cannot be told apart. 
 
 
  The harness reproduces the authors’ AIME 2025 numbers.  Where authors report pass@1 at our temperature and within one budget step of the cap, our read is within    0.040  0.040    for all five models. The other gaps (    −  0.160   -0.160    to     −  0.011   -0.011   ) are budget or temperature effects. 
 
 
  With    𝟐𝟒  24    samples the base solves about three fifths of the RL model’s lone wins.  The base solves    99  99    of    159  159    (    62  %   62\%   ). The RL model solves    31  31    of the    60  60    base wins. After both are resampled, the RL model solves    44  44    of its wins again in its new samples while the base still fails them, and the base does the same on    17  17    of its own, a net of    27  27   , about    1.4  1.4    per pair.

  Appendix B  The controlled run 

 
  Privileged information for hard groups.  Partial solutions  ( Li et al., 2025 ;  Amani et al., 2025 ) , answer-derived hints  ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , scaffolds  ( Zhang et al., 2025c ;  Wang et al., 2025c ) , reverse curricula  ( Xi et al., 2024 ) , hint reweighting  ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ) , expert traces  ( Zhou et al., 2025 ;  Yan et al., 2025 )  and trained hinters  ( Xia et al., 2026 ;  Han et al., 2026 ;  Liao et al., 2026 )  report the deployed score, not whether content was learned. These methods do not control finishing. Our channels belong to these families and claim no algorithmic novelty. Process rewards  ( Wang et al., 2023 ;  Chen et al., 2026 ;  Xie et al., 2026 ;  Zhang et al., 2025b )  need a target step, which on all-fail problems only a reference solution gives. Answer-conditioned rationales  ( Zelikman et al., 2022 ;  Phan et al., 2023 )  and hindsight relabelling  ( Zhang et al., 2023 )  leak the reward. We supply a setup, not an answer. 
 
 
  B.1  The probe in full 

 
  The run.  The  control  is Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking  ( Bai et al., 2025 )  trained with outcome RL (GSPO;   Zheng et al., 2025 ;  Shao et al., 2024  ) on PhysReason  ( Zhang et al., 2025d )  and UGPhysics  ( Xu et al., 2025 ;  Yang, 2026 )  at a    12  12   k-token cap. Each  arm  adds a  channel  supplying the  setup , the physical modelling before any algebra: a reward, the prompt, hinted derivations, a policy-written setup, or a stronger model’s questions. 
 
 
  Two hard sets.  The  held-out hard set  is    87  87    PhysReason problems the base solves at most once in eight, never trained on, frozen before any arm under one registered protocol. A fresh base read scores    0.16  0.16   , above what selection implies, so arms are compared with the control. The  training hard set  is    160  160    problems the control never solved in its first thirty steps. As in §  4  , the control’s held-out score rises from    0.16  0.16    to    0.26  0.26    almost all by finishing (fin@1    (  B  )   (B)        0.39  →  0.69   0.39\to 0.69   ; pass@1    (  B  |  fin  )   (B\,|\,\text{fin})    flat at    0.38  0.38   ). 
 
 
  The missing fact is often in the model, which does not ask for it.  The right question, without the answer, nearly triples the training hard set’s share solved at least in part in eight samples (    0.062  →  0.175   0.062\to 0.175   ; gold setup    0.350  0.350   ). A stronger model’s questions written without the reference setup give    0.200  0.200   , so the gain is not only leakage. At    64  64    samples,     41  %   41\%    is solved only with help and     34  %   34\%    under no condition we tried. The model’s own questions do no better than a generic checklist. 
 
 
  No channel raises the held-out score clear of zero.  Only a pilot of the reward gave a valid read, since at full scale the policy gamed its scorer (§  B.2  ; Appendices   B.6  –  B.10  ). The setup hint leads the two control seeds by     +  0.009   +0.009    and     +  0.019   +0.019   , below the detection floor (Table   14  ). Hinted derivations move it     −  0.05   -0.05   , beyond the seed gap. The policy-written setup moves it     −  0.03   -0.03   , near the detection floor. A     +  2.4   +2.4   -point hint-arm lead on an earlier corpus did not hold at the    16  16   k read. The held-out problems mostly carry figures but are given as text. 
 
 
  Content is detected only where trained.  The control lifts the training hard set’s pass@8 from    0.056  0.056    to    0.344  0.344    (§  B.2  ). On the held-out set, drawn from another source, the control’s gain is almost all finishing. On the    160  160    easier text-only twins of its training problems it gains mostly by finishing. Content transfer is neither shown nor excluded (Appendix   B.13  ). The channels’ failure may therefore not be specific to them. Whether recurring techniques explain why guidance gains on competition mathematics is untested here.

The count is taken visit by visit during training, over the first thirty updates of each run. The curves are with and without the policy’s own earlier successes replayed into the group (§  B.2  ). Replayed rows are excluded from the count. 
 
 
  The policy rarely samples a success.  The base solves     24  %   24\%    of the training hard set in    64  64    samples (    44  %   44\%    at a    16  16   k cap), still rising (Figure   5  , left). At a few percent per sample, a group of sixteen sees a success less than half the time. At least a quarter are within reach but need a long, improbable derivation. Gains follow a     p  ⁡   (   1  −  p   )    p(1-p)    shape:     +  0.16   +0.16    to     +  0.18   +0.18    next visit when solved one to six times in eight,     +  0.05   +0.05    and     +  0.02   +0.02    at the ends. 
 
 
  Finishing carries because every prompt shares it.  Finishing explains     48  %   48\%    of within-group reward variance early and     21  %   21\%    once saturated. Finishing’s gradient adds up across the batch. Problem-specific content is not detected to carry. 
 
 
  Each channel moves only what the policy already samples.  At full scale the setup reward taught unit-appending for the answer matcher, a gain that was not real. Derivations hinted with the setup lean heavily on the hint (   400  400   –   580  580    nats; Appendix   B.11  ), so the bound of   Xia et al. (2026)   gives no reason to expect transfer. A teacher’s derivation lifts touched problems from     12  %   12\%    to     59  %   59\%   , not their neighbours. Self-written setups succeed equally often (intraclass correlation    0.03  0.03   ), so rewarding them changes only format. Questioner samples that ask solve no more often. 
 
 
  Once a success is sampled, credit installs it, but only on that problem.  On    60  60    of    353  353    hard training problems, read after training at    16  16   k with eight samples, the solve rate goes from    0.10  0.10    to    0.28  0.28   , or    0.31  0.31    with replay  ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) . Replay only shortens the wait (Figure   5  , right). The held-out set and the    293  293    unrevisited problems do not move. These problems are rarely solved, so spread to sometimes-solved problems is not excluded. Twins bear on it weakly: on the    16  16    of the    60  60    with twins, the revisit arm does no better than the control (Appendix   B.13  ). The held-out bottleneck is the first success.

The committed plan compares credited and other twins’ gains over the base in mean score and any-solve@8. The split below, with its matched contrast as the content-transfer test, was chosen after a first look at    113  113    of the    160  160    problems. 
 
 
  On the credited originals, finishing’s share of the gain depends on the order of the split.  Finishing and reliability both rise there (Table   17  ), so the term they make together is large. Eq. (  2  ) gives that term to finishing, which then makes up     71  %   71\%    of the control’s gain (    73  %   73\%    for the second seed). Splitting the term evenly gives finishing     50  %   50\%    (    51  %   51\%   ). Giving it to reliability leaves finishing     29  %   29\%    (also     29  %   29\%   ). 
 
 
  On the planned measure, the credited twins gain more,    𝟐𝟔  26   –    𝟔𝟐  %   62\%    of it by finishing.  The mean-score excess is     +  0.096   +0.096    [    +  0.008   +0.008   ,     +  0.182   +0.182   ], and     +  0.115   +0.115    [    +  0.029   +0.029   ,     +  0.202   +0.202   ] for the second seed, whose credit does not define the groups. The any-solve@8 excess,     +  0.095   +0.095    [    −  0.054   -0.054   ,     +  0.242   +0.242   ], includes zero. Of the pass@1 excess,     +  0.093   +0.093    [    +  0.005   +0.005   ,     +  0.181   +0.181   ], finishing makes up    0.058  0.058    under Eq. (  2  ),    0.048  0.048    with the cross term split evenly and    0.038  0.038    with it given to reliability. The rest is     +  0.035   +0.035    [    −  0.011   -0.011   ,     +  0.078   +0.078   ],     +  0.045   +0.045    [    −  0.021   -0.021   ,     +  0.108   +0.108   ] and     +  0.055   +0.055    [    −  0.032   -0.032   ,     +  0.140   +0.140   ] under the three orders. For the second seed, finishing makes up    56  56   ,    41  41    and     26  %   26\%    of     +  0.110   +0.110   , and the rest is     +  0.048   +0.048    [    +  0.004   +0.004   ,     +  0.090   +0.090   ],     +  0.065   +0.065    [    −  0.001   -0.001   ,     +  0.128   +0.128   ] and     +  0.081   +0.081    [    −  0.007   -0.007   ,     +  0.169   +0.169   ]. Mean score per finished sample falls on both groups. Regrouping by the second seed’s credit is a weak check, since the credited sets share    53  53    of    74  74    problems. 
 
 
  The split of Eqs. (  1  ) and (  4  ) finds no content gain on the twins, and cannot exclude one  (Table   17  ). Where both models finish at least seven times in eight, the credited-minus-other reliability contrast is     −  0.003   -0.003    [    −  0.048   -0.048   ,     +  0.037   +0.037   ] (second seed:     −  0.008   -0.008    [    −  0.043   -0.043   ,     +  0.021   +0.021   ]). That interval is as wide as the originals’ contrast,     +  0.039   +0.039    [    +  0.006   +0.006   ,     +  0.081   +0.081   ], on only    5  5    and    10  10    problems. 
 
 
  A never-credited model and an adjusted contrast leave the excess unresolved.  The questioner fine-tune (E), never trained on these problems, shows a credited-minus-other twin difference of     +  0.035   +0.035    [    −  0.020   -0.020   ,     +  0.091   +0.091   ] from the problems alone. Finishing little more than the base, E is not a clean control. The control’s difference less E’s is     +  0.061   +0.061    [    −  0.029   -0.029   ,     +  0.149   +0.149   ]. Adjusting for the base’s finishing and score gives     +  0.077   +0.077    [    −  0.004   -0.004   ,     +  0.160   +0.160   ] on the twins, against     +  0.186   +0.186    [    +  0.132   +0.132   ,     +  0.237   +0.237   ] on the originals. Neither check is clear of zero. Both checks were added after the full read. 
 
 
  The twins are easier than their originals  (Table   17  ), partly perhaps from answer form, since only twins whose gold the reward can match were kept. With the base finishing under half the twins, finishing dominates (§  4.1  ). Content needed only on the hardest problems would not show. 
 
 
  No channel beats the control on the twins  (full table in the released repository). On credited twins the hint (B) is level, the revisit arm (§  B.2  ) within noise, and the teacher’s derivation (C), D and E lower. C’s interval includes zero. Channels are compared on all twins, not only those of problems they touched. 
 
 
  In the twins read, the base solves    𝟏𝟔  16    of the    𝟏𝟔𝟎  160    originals at least once , against    9  9    in the earlier read. At such low rates the solved set varies by read.

The change in pass@1 splits into finishing    F  F   , reliability    P  P    and net reach as in Eq. (  4  ). Matched    P  P    is reliability on the    n  n    problems both models finish at least seven times in eight, weighted as    P  P    is. The groups are defined by the first seed’s credit in steps    31  31   –   60  60   . Splitting the twins’ change this way was chosen after a first look at    113  113    of the    160  160    problems. 
 
 
 
  B.14  Why the finishing signal transfers 

 
  Credit splits into a finishing term and a content term.  Write rewards      r  j   =    f  j   ​   c  j     r_{j}=f_{j}c_{j}    (    f  j   f_{j}   : finished inside the budget;     c  j   c_{j}   : correct once finished). The group-relative step is proportional to     Cov  ⁡   (   r  j   ,     ∇  log   ⁡  π   ​   (   y  j   )    )    \mathrm{Cov}(r_{j},\nabla\log\pi(y_{j}))   , which scales with     p  ⁡   (   1  −  p   )    p(1-p)   . By the law of total covariance, 
 

  
  
       Cov  ⁡   (  r  ,    ∇  log   ⁡  π   )    =    Cov  ⁡   (   f  ​  𝔼  ​   [   c  ∣  f   ]    ,    ∇  log   ⁡  π   )    +   𝔼  ⁡   [   f  ​  Cov  ​   (   c  ,    ∇  log   ⁡  π    ∣  f  )    ]      .   \mathrm{Cov}(r,\nabla\log\pi)=\mathrm{Cov}(f\,\mathbb{E}[c\mid f],\nabla\log\pi)+\mathbb{E}[f\,\mathrm{Cov}(c,\nabla\log\pi\mid f)].    
    
 
 Finishing is shared by every prompt, so its term adds across a batch and carries to held-out prompts. Content adds only where a problem recurs, so it installs success on its own problem, as replay shows. 
 
 
 
 
  Appendix C  Instruments 

 
  C.1  Setup readout rubric 

 
  Each item is a problem, its mined setup claims and one trimmed rollout.  The grader (Claude Sonnet 5) marks each claim  established ,  contradicted  (an incompatible setup) or  absent , judging only the setup, not the arithmetic or the answer. 
 
 
 
  C.2  The judge protocol 

 
  Protocol v2 fixes the matching rules in code.  Graders disagree mostly on whether a bare number matches a gold with a unit. Giving units tracks training: models trained with and without the benchmark’s split give units     97.2  %   97.2\%    and     64.0  %   64.0\%    of the time. A deterministic checker decides    43  43   –    55  %   55\%    of items. A model given the same rules decides the rest. 
 
 
  Differences between systems are grader-invariant; absolute scores are not.  Regrading six systems on PhysReason held-out (    n  =  526   n{=}526   ) under v2 with a pinned Qwen3-32B is    6.7  6.7   –   8.9  8.9    points stricter on every system. The margin between systems agrees to    0.11  0.11    points.

ATTO(1)                 NetBSD General Commands Manual                 ATTO(1)

   NAME   
      atto  -- simple modeless text editor

   SYNOPSIS   
      atto  [ -C ]  file ... 

   DESCRIPTION   
      atto  is a screen-based text editor.  It serves as an alternative to  vi(1) 
     for users who are not accustomed to text editors with separate insertion
     and editing modes, and includes support for editing UTF-8 text.

     Perhaps all that needs to be known to use  atto  at a basic level is that
     holding the control key, pressing x, then pressing w will write the cur-
     rently open file, and holding the control key, pressing x, then pressing
     c will exit the editor.

     The options are as follows:

      -C           Use colours, if available, for basic language-unaware syntax
                 highlighting.

    Cursor movement commands 
     C is used as an abbreviation for the control key, commonly rendered as
     "ctrl" on English language keyboards.

     Arrow keys or the navigation cluster can also be used to move the cursor
     when the keyboard has such features.

           C-a        move cursor to beginning of current line (i.e. "home")
           C-b        move cursor back one character (i.e. "left")
           C-e        move cursor to end of current line (i.e. "end")
           C-f        move cursor forward one character (i.e. "right")
           C-n        move cursor to next line (i.e. "down")
           C-p        move cursor to previous line (i.e. "up")
           C-v        move cursor to next page of text (i.e. "page down")
           Esc-b      move cursor back one word
           Esc-f      move cursor forward one word
           Esc-g      jump to a specific line number in the file
           Esc-v      move cursor to previous page of text (i.e. "page up")
           Esc-<      jump to the start of the file
           Esc->      jump to the end of the file

    Text editing commands 
           C-d        delete character under cursor (i.e. "del")
           C-h        move cursor backwards and delete previous character
                      (i.e. "backspace")
           C-g        abort at prompts (cancel task when asked a question)
           C-i        insert tab character
           C-j        insert newline character (i.e. "enter", "return")
           C-k        cut text up to the end of the line (i.e. "kill line")
           C-l        refresh the screen
           C-m        insert carriage return character
           C-r        search for text backwards, jump to next result
           C-s        search for text forwards, jump to next result
           C-y        paste the text in the cut buffer (i.e. "yank")
           Esc-r      search for text and replace it

    Buffer commands 
      atto  supports multiple editing buffers, allowing users to edit multiple
     files from a single instance of the program.

           C-x C-c    close all open buffers and exit  atto , prompting if
                      changes would be discarded
           C-x C-f    open a file into a new buffer
           C-x C-k    close the current buffer, prompting if changes would be
                      discarded (i.e. "kill")
           C-x C-s    save current buffer to disk, overwriting the file
           C-x C-w    save current buffer to disk, prompting for file name
                      ("write")
           C-x n      cycle to next buffer
           C-x i      read another file and insert it into the current buffer
           C-x =      display cursor position in current buffer

    Region commands 
     As well as cutting text on a line basis (i.e. C-k), a region can be
     selected by setting a mark at the beginning of the region, and then mov-
     ing the cursor to the end of the region.

           C-space    set the beginning of the region at the current position
           C-w        cut the marked region
           Esc-w      copy the marked region without deleting it

    Window management commands 
     Simple split-screen window management is included.  For more advanced use
     cases, consider using  tmux(1) .

           C-x 1      delete windows except the currently active one
           C-x 2      split current window into two windows
           C-x o      switch to the next open window

   SEE ALSO   
      ed(1) ,  ex(1) ,  vi(1) ,  xedit(1) 

   STANDARDS   
      atto  is not the standard editor.

   AUTHORS   
      atto  was written primarily by Hugh Barney, and was originally based on
     public domain code from Anthony Howe's editor (commonly known as
     Anthony's Editor).

     It has been modified for inclusion in NetBSD, including with enhanced
     option handling.

The IDE you know, rebuilt in Rust.

Download  ·  Benchmark  ·  Build  ·  Discord

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/234dd54c-1255-4b3a-b35c-533d78d737c0 OpenIDEA brings the IntelliJ IDEA way of working — its keymap, its tool windows, its search-everything habits — to a native app with a Rust core. Editor, code insight, debugger, Git, terminal, database and HTTP clients, for 60+ languages. Builds for macOS, Windows and Linux. ## Benchmark Opening [freqtrade](https://github.com/freqtrade/freqtrade) (Python, ~770 files) with warm caches, median of 5 runs: | | OpenIDEA | IntelliJ IDEA 2026.2.3 | | --------------------------- | ----------------- | ---------------------- | | Window with the project | **0.9 s** | 3.1 s | | Ready (CPU settled) | **1.1 s** | 13.2 s | | Memory (USS, all processes) | **169 MB** | 2011 MB | | CPU time until ready | **2.4 s** | 47.9 s | | Idle CPU | **4 %** of a core | 7 % of a core | | Quit | **0.3 s** | 5.9 s | A release build of OpenIDEA from `main` and IDEA with default settings and plugins, on Windows 11, 32-core AMD, 62 GB RAM. IDEA analyses Python more deeply, so "ready" doesn't mean the same work on both sides. Both are measured from the outside, the same way: see [`perf/compare`](perf/compare) to run it on your machine and projects. ## Build ```sh pnpm install pnpm tauri dev ``` Rust 1.96, Node 22, pnpm and the [Tauri prerequisites](https://v2.tauri.app/start/prerequisites/). Native notebook execution tests are opt-in and need two distinct Python environments with `ipykernel` installed: ```sh OPENIDEA_TEST_PYTHON=/first/env/bin/python \ OPENIDEA_TEST_PYTHON_SECOND=/second/env/bin/python \ cargo test -p ide-notebook --test kernel_runtime -- --ignored --test-threads=1 ``` ## License [Apache 2.0](LICENSE). Bundled third-party assets are listed in [`THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md`](THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md). Not affiliated with JetBrains. IntelliJ IDEA is a trademark of JetBrains s.r.o.

   Description 
 

 
   
     Generated-code injection through three additional OpenAPI fields 
 Prepared for private maintainer triage on October 19, 2026. Execution results below are the saved October 16 evidence; today’s work was source, documentation and report review only. The tested version is not asserted to be the latest supported release. 
 Tested version: github.com/oapi-codegen/oapi-codegen/v2 2.8.0. Earlier and later affected versions have not been established by this review. 
 Scope and limitations 
 The victim must generate, build and execute code from a supplied OpenAPI document without catching the change in code review. Please assess severity and consolidate with related generated-code advisories as appropriate. 
 I would like to report 3 code-injection issues in oapi-codegen v2.8.0 (tested October 16, 2026). Found with AploSec, our security scanner, and confirmed by execution. 
 They are the same class as  GHSA-rjwr-m7qx-3fjr  (server description, fixed in 2.7.1) but in other spec fields that the fix did not cover. The project requires review of generated code before execution. The parent advisory currently lists Moderate 6.1; this report leaves severity to maintainer triage. 
 Affected 
 v2.8.0, pkg/codegen templates: 
 
 (a) templates/server-urls.tmpl:6,7,58,59: .GoName from servers[].x-go-name (needs generate: server-urls: true) 
 (b) templates/echo/echo-register.tmpl:50: .MiddlewareKey from the raw operationId, placed between literal quotes (echo-server, no opt-in). The same pattern may exist in the other server templates; not checked. 
 (c) templates/constants.tmpl:16: {{$value}} for enum entries when ValueWrapper is empty, i.e. a non-string schema type (default models output) 
 
 Root cause 
 Untrusted spec strings reach text/template without escaping or quoting. ValidateSpec does not walk spec.Servers or operationId, and its enum check only rejects control characters. The payloads contain no newlines, and gofmt/imports accept the result as valid Go. 
 Reproduction (golang image, Docker, --network none; each generated package imported by a small main) 
   ##### A-control
main start (importing gen only)
##### A-attack
PWNED-A
PWNED-A
main start (importing gen only)
##### B-control
main start
main end
##### B-attack
main start
PWNED-B
main end
##### C-control
main start (importing gen only)
##### C-attack
PWNED-C
main start (importing gen only)
   
 A: the generated file contains an injected top-level func init() { println("PWNED-A") }. B: router.GET(options.BaseURL+"/p", ...) is followed by an injected println("PWNED-B") statement inside RegisterHandlers. C: a type: integer enum with a string entry emits func init() { println("PWNED-C") } after the const block (the schema must be referenced from a path, or skip-prune set). 
 Impact 
 A malicious or tampered OpenAPI document gives code execution in the generated package: at import time for (a) and (c), at server start for (b). The victim has to generate and build without reviewing the diff. 
 Suggested fix 
 (a) validate x-go-name and server variable names with token.IsIdentifier and walk spec.Servers in ValidateSpec. (b) render keys with strconv.Quote / toGoString. (c) when ValueWrapper is empty, require the value to parse as a number or bool, or quote it. 
 Source review and coordination 
 The parent advisory recognizes generated-code injection despite the review-before-execution requirement. Its current severity is Moderate 6.1, correcting the draft’s “parent low” assertion. Saved generated-package execution covers three other fields. 
 Reviewed sources:

  https://github.com/oapi-codegen/oapi-codegen/security

  oapi-codegen  is a command-line tool and library to convert OpenAPI specifications to Go code, be it  server-side implementations ,  API clients , or simply  HTTP models . 
 Using  oapi-codegen  allows you to reduce the boilerplate required to create or integrate with services based on  OpenAPI 3.0  and  OpenAPI 3.1 , and instead focus on writing your business logic, and working on the real value-add for your organisation. 
 With  oapi-codegen , there are a few  Key Design Decisions  we've made, including: 
 
 idiomatic Go, where possible 
 fairly simple generated code, erring on the side of verbose code over complex modular code 
 supporting as much of OpenAPI 3.0 and 3.1 as is possible, alongside Go's type system 
 
  oapi-codegen  is one part of a wider ecosystem, which can be found described in further detail in the  oapi-codegen organisation on GitHub .

  Installation     
  Action Required: The repository for this project has changed     
 As announced in  May 2024 ,
we have moved the project from the Deepmap organization to our own organization, and you will need to update your
import paths to pull updates past this point. You need to do a recursive search/replace from
 github.com/deepmap/oapi-codegen/v2  to  github.com/oapi-codegen/oapi-codegen/v2 . 
   Important   oapi-codegen  moved to its new home with the version tag  v2.3.0 . 
 
 If you are using  v2.2.0  or below, please install like so: 
    #  for the binary install 
go install github.com/deepmap/oapi-codegen/v2/cmd/oapi-codegen@v2.2.0  
 If you are using  v2.3.0  or above, please install like so, using the new module import path: 
    #  for the binary install 
go install github.com/oapi-codegen/oapi-codegen/v2/cmd/oapi-codegen@latest  
  Installing     
  oapi-codegen  requires Go 1.25+ to build and install. Note that the  generated  code has its own, lower requirements — see  Supported Servers . 
 It is recommended to use   go tool  support  for managing the dependency of  oapi-codegen  alongside your core application. 
 To do this, you run  go get -tool : 
  $ go get -tool github.com/oapi-codegen/oapi-codegen/v2/cmd/oapi-codegen@latest
  #  this will then modify your `go.mod`   
 From there, each invocation of  oapi-codegen  would be used like so: 
   //go:generate go tool oapi-codegen -config cfg.yaml ../../api.yaml   
 Alternatively, you can install it as a binary with: 
  $ go install github.com/oapi-codegen/oapi-codegen/v2/cmd/oapi-codegen@latest
$ oapi-codegen -version  
 Which then means you can invoke it like so: 
   //go:generate oapi-codegen --config=config.yaml ../../api.yaml   
  Pinning to commits     
 While the project does not ( yet ) have a defined release cadence, there may be cases where you want to pull in yet-unreleased changes to your codebase. 
 Therefore, you may want to pin your dependency on  oapi-codegen  to a given commit hash, rather than a tag. 
 This is  officially recommended  for consumers of  oapi-codegen , who want features/bug fixes that haven't yet been released. 
 We aim to keep the default branch ready-to-release so you should be able to safely pin. 
 To do so, you can run: 
    #  pin to the latest version on the default branch
