  Abstract 
    
 Agentic services alternate between model inference on clustered GPUs and external tools on distributed CPUs. In this scenario, existing systems (1) overlook tool-return readiness in service evaluation, wasting limited resources, and (2) use heuristic strategies to decide admission and placement on GPUs, resulting in suboptimal scheduling decisions. To bridge this gap, we present TAO, a tool-aware joint scheduling framework for LLM-based agentic serving. Its value interface combines near-term tool readiness, node-specific cache credit with time-aware decay, and token footprint; a dynamic program jointly selects and places waiting sessions under capacity constraints. Across the 12 reported model–workload–concurrency settings, TAO reduces latency by up to 26.8%, reduces mean time to first token (TTFT) by up to 36.3%, and increases decode throughput by up to 29.5% relative to the best evaluated state-of-the-art baseline for each metric. 
  
 
 
 
 
 
     
 
 
 
 
  1  Introduction 

 
 Recent advances in language models have expanded their use beyond basic chatbots to complex agents, making CPU-based tool execution a substantial source of latency alongside GPU-based inference  ( Qiao et al., 2026 ;  Huang et al., 2026 ) . Specifically, an agent operates through an  agent session  that alternates between LLM inference and external tools, such as compilers and retrievers, to complete multi-step tasks  ( Anthropic, 2026b ;  OpenAI, 2026 ) . When tools run outside the inference service, a session’s demand for GPU computation becomes interruptible. We call this serving scenario  C lustered- G PUs with  D istributed- C PUs (CGDC), illustrated in Figure   1  (Left): clustered GPUs, i.e., nodes, provide shared inference capacity, while external tool calls introduce delays between LLM requests  1    1 
             1 
            
            
            
          One agent session consists of multiple LLM inference requests (i.e., steps) after tool calls.   . Hence, efficient agentic serving must account for both inference demand and tool timing to sustain throughput and session responsiveness. 
 
 
 We find that existing serving systems generally follow an  evaluate-then-decide  scheduling pattern  ( Guy et al., 2025 ;  SGLang Team, n.d. ;  vLLM Production Stack Team, n.d. ) . They evaluate node features at the session level and then decide where and when to serve each session. This separates the problem into two related challenges: (1) how to value a session’s next model turn, and (2) how to select and place sessions under shared capacity constraints. 
 
 
  For  session evaluation , existing systems in CGDC scenarios generally overlook tool-call latency when evaluating established workload features.  Cache-aware systems reuse KV prefixes and balance inference load  ( Zheng et al., 2024 ;  Srivatsa et al., 2025 ;  Qin et al., 2025 ;  NVIDIA, 2025 ) ; workflow-aware systems anticipate future calls  ( Wadlom et al., 2026 ;  Pan et al., 2026 ) ; and latency-aware schedulers prioritize sessions using latency or remaining-work estimates  ( Choi et al., 2025 ;  Chen et al., 2025 ) . Tool timing provides another useful signal, yet timing is utilized only as a surrogate for KV reuse or token count:   Li et al. (2025)   predicts tool duration to choose KV-cache retention times, while   Kang et al. (2026)   discounts the token footprint of sessions executing tools as time elapses. Such features commonly enter fixed scoring rules or manually chosen thresholds. 
 
 
  For  decision making , existing systems usually apply heuristic scheduling strategies to each session, leading to myopic and suboptimal placements.  In llm-d and SGLang  ( Guy et al., 2025 ;  SGLang Team, n.d. ) , per-session scoring and routing rules assign inference opportunities  individually . Yet sessions compete for the same node capacity. In particular, assigning one session can prevent a more valuable combination of other sessions from being served. Furthermore, the heuristic selection and placement rules can also lead to suboptimal choices  ( Peng et al., 2026 ;  Yuan et al., 2026 ) . As shown in Figure   1  (Right), they fail to formulate scheduling jointly across multiple sessions. 
 
  
  Figure 1:  
Left: In the CGDC serving scenario, external tool calls create intervals between LLM requests and opportunities to reallocate inference capacity. Right: Two scheduling challenges motivate TAO, including (1) overlooking tool-return readiness and using heuristic merging for evaluation, and (2) making myopic and suboptimal decisions about session admission and placement.
 
 
 
 To address these challenges, we propose TAO, a  T ool- A ware j O int scheduling framework for LLM-based agentic serving.
To incorporate  tool latency  into  session evaluation , we propose tool-return readiness and explicitly integrate it with established features such as KV-cache reuse. Following   Kang et al. (2026)  , we interrupt sessions during tool calls and put them into a  waiting pool . Tool-return readiness estimates which sessions will need inference within the next scheduling window. For each session–node pair, we form a value triplet from readiness, time-decayed  KV-cache reuse , and token footprint.
Given these evaluation triplets, we design a  joint scheduling  algorithm in the  decision making  stage that considers all sessions in the waiting pool. Across deployments in different scenarios, joint optimization considers how the admission of each session affects the placements available to others. The optimizer maximizes the additive evaluation triplets using dynamic programming. Their coordinates evolve with cache age and tool progress, allowing distinct signals to guide decisions over time without a weighted sum. Separating the optimization procedure from session evaluation makes the framework extensible. 
 
 
 We summarize our contributions as follows: 
 
  •  
 
 We identify the Clustered GPUs with Distributed CPUs (CGDC) serving scenario in the era of LLM-based agents, which shifts the key bottleneck of latency to tool calls. 
  
  •  
 
 We propose TAO, a tool-aware joint scheduling framework for LLM-based agentic serving. It improves the evaluate-then-decide paradigm through session evaluation with explicit tool-return readiness and decision making with joint modeling and optimization. 
  
  •  
 
 TAO can be generalized and extended to different workloads such as multi-agent orchestration and Looped Agents. Moreover, it is also compatible with non-agent chatbot scenarios. 
  
  •  
 
 Across the 12 reported model–workload–concurrency settings, TAO reduces latency by up to 26.8%, reduces mean time to first token (TTFT) by up to 36.3%, and increases decode throughput by up to 29.5% relative to the state-of-the-art baseline for each metric. 
  
 
 
 
 
  2  Background and Problem Description 

 
  2.1  Agent Session and distributed resources 

 
 An agent session is a persistent interaction that alternates between model requests and external tool calls. During a model request, it uses a serving node; during tool execution, it awaits a result outside the inference service. A scheduler records each session’s state and controls session admission, while the serving engine manages physical KV-cache residency and eviction. 
 
 
 A later model request can reuse the KV prefix produced by earlier turns and avoid prefill computation  ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) . Because an agent session carries its instructions, history, and tool observations across turns, reuse depends on both the agent session history and the node selected for its next request. SGLang and Preble exploit related prefix structure in model programs and distributed scheduling  ( Zheng et al., 2024 ;  Srivatsa et al., 2025 ) . 
 
 
 Our CGDC separates clustered GPU inference from distributed tool execution. Client or remote tools introduce variable delays between model requests, while their CPU and RAM are managed  outside  the GPU admission budget  ( Anthropic, 2026b ;  OpenAI, 2026 ;  Chang et al., 2026 ) . Tool latency therefore determines when an agent session may need GPU resources for inference again. 
 
 
 
  2.2  session interruption and session restart 

 
 During tool execution, a session can release its GPU resources safely, although its cached prefix may subsequently be evicted. In contrast, preempting an active inference session requires recomputation. Repeated recomputation and reconstruction cause  KV-cache thrashing , wasting capacity on state that must be rebuilt. This phenomenon motivates cache-aware engine and scheduling work  ( Kwon et al., 2023 ;  Zheng et al., 2024 ;  Srivatsa et al., 2025 ;  NVIDIA, 2025 ) , as well as policies that weigh retaining state against serving other work  ( Li et al., 2025 ;  Abhyankar et al., 2024 ) . 
 
 
 Therefore, at a tool boundary, the scheduler can apply  session interruption . Specifically, a scheduler can interrupt the agent session’s model admission and release its node resources while the external tool continues. When inference service is needed again,  session restarting  restores admission on an eligible node and resumes the existing interaction. Session interruption and session restarting describe session state transitions. They are decoupled from the underlying inference engine. 
 
 
 We find that the decisions made for these two operations can be based on the same session evaluation. Thus, we optimize toward a unified goal for maximizing the evaluation.
Session interruption can be decided by ordering sessions according to their values. Interrupted sessions join new arrivals in a waiting pool. We focus on  unified session evaluation  and  restarting decisions  from this pool. 
 
 
 
 
  3  Method 

 
  3.1  Framework overview 

 
 We present TAO, which combines agentic session evaluation with decision making, i.e. dynamic programming for joint selection and placement. The detailed formulation appears in Section   3.2  . 
 
 
 Figure   2   illustrates the pipeline of our method. First, session evaluation maps agent session and node observations to assignment values (Section   3.2  ), including KV cache with time-aware decay (Section   3.3  ) and tool-return readiness (Section   3.4  ). Second, an exact dynamic program jointly selects waiting agent sessions and assigns them to nodes under residual capacity constraints (Sections   3.2   and   3.5  ). Separating session evaluation from decision making lets the evaluation interface evolve while preserving the scheduling procedure.

External tools on distributed CPUs provide historical tool-call durations, while the serving engines on clustered GPUs provide cache observations.
Then, the session evaluation component constructs triplets  (decayed KV-cache credit, binary readiness, token count) .
The decision making component jointly selects and places waiting agent sessions. The executor validates the plan against live state before applying it.
The resulting assignments schedule sessions to eligible nodes.

  3.5  Joint scheduling with dynamic programming 

 
 The optimizer is a capacity-state dynamic program for the multiple-knapsack and generalized-assignment structure  ( Kellerer et al., 2004 ;  Shmoys and Tardos, 1993 ) . For candidate    j  j   , let      D  j   ​   (  𝒔  )    D_{j}(\bm{s})    be the best objective attainable from the first    j  j    candidates at the used capacity    𝒔  \bm{s}   , and let     𝒖   j  ,  b    \bm{u}_{j,b}    embed the value and count for assigning    j  j    to node    b  b   :

Skipping or assigning each candidate exhausts the feasible choices, so induction gives exactness for the frozen, discretized problem; rounding can exclude plans feasible before discretization.

The planner runs in an isolated asynchronous worker (detailed in Appendix   B  ) and revalidates before application; recorded preparation plus completed-solve work is below 0.12% of runtime in the four-replica sweep (Appendix   I  ).

  4.1  Experiment Setup 

 
  Models and workloads.  We evaluate DeepSeek-V4 Flash, Qwen3-32B, and GLM-4.7  ( DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026 ;  Yang et al., 2025 ;  Team et al., 2025 )  on the SWE-bench Lite workload (SWE-Lite) using the mini-SWE-agent harness (MiniSWE)  ( mini-SWE-agent Contributors, 2026 ;  Jimenez et al., 2024 ) . For DeepSeek, we also use Claude Code on Terminal-Bench 2.0  ( Merrill et al., 2026 )  for challenging tasks. For Qwen, we test with SWE-verified to exercise the serving capacity of its smaller model replicas. We further evaluate GLM-4.7 on SWE-Lite to test single-node performance. Appendix   F   reports an InferenceX trace-replay evaluation. 
 
 
  Deployment.  DeepSeek runs on 2 nodes with     4  ×   4\times   H100 per node; Qwen runs on 4 nodes with     2  ×   2\times   H100 per node. Each node hosts one tensor-parallel model replica. GLM-4.7 runs on one node with     8  ×   8\times   H100. Appendix   E.1   reports a lower-concurrency DeepSeek check on the same single-node topology. 
 
 
  Baselines.  vLLM Scheduler w/ RR and vLLM Scheduler w/ CA denote the vLLM schedulers with round-robin and cache-aware policies, respectively  ( vLLM Production Stack Team, n.d. ) , which align with the policy in SGLang  ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) . These baselines cover load spreading and prefix-locality scheduling. Dynamo is a KV-aware scheduler  ( NVIDIA, 2025 ) . ThunderAgent uses token-count scheduling and best-fit-decreasing placement  ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . TAO combines predictive cache-aware session evaluation with joint dynamic-programming placement. 
 
 
  Metrics.  We report mean task end-to-end latency, mean time to first token (TTFT), and decode throughput in tokens per second (TPS). Task latency includes both model inference and tool execution. Component analyses also measure prefix-cache hit rate, tool-end-to-first-token delay, and pause wait, which includes the tool call latency of an interrupted session. 
 
 
 
  4.2  Main Results 

 
 Table   1   compares five baselines across different levels of concurrency, models, and topologies. Taken together, these results make TAO the strongest overall choice: it combines consistently low latency and TTFT with high decode throughput more effectively than any single baseline, consistent with our focus on responsiveness after tool calls and improved KV reuse. 
 
 
 DeepSeek-V4 Flash. 

 
 We evaluate on challenging benchmarks with moderate concurrency. On SWE-Lite, , relative to the best competing method in each column, latency falls by 2.4–26.8%, TTFT by 7.4–36.3%, and decode throughput rises by 5.1–29.5%. On Terminal-Bench, TAO also leads on latency and TTFT at all three concurrency levels. 
 
 
 
 Qwen3-32B. 

 
 We use higher concurrency to exercise the serving capacity of its smaller model replicas. On SWE-Lite, TAO achieves the lowest TTFT at all three worker counts and the highest decode throughput at 96, 128 and 160 workers. On SWE-verified, TAO leads on TTFT and decode throughput throughout, with reductions of 12.9–29.9% in TTFT and gains of 4.0–7.8% in decode throughput. It also reduces latency by 8.3% and 9.0% at 96 and 160 workers; at 128 workers, latency is 2.5% higher than ThunderAgent. 
 
 
 
 GLM-4.7. 

 
 As a larger-model setting, GLM-4.7 provides a high-concurrency extensibility showcase on one node with     8  ×   8\times   H100. Table   2   reports the separate worker-grouped results: on SWE-Lite at 160 workers, improvements reach 15.5% in latency, 14.05% in TTFT, and 20.48% in decode throughput. On all 500 SWE-verified tasks, TAO reduces mean task latency by 16.2–18.9% and client TTFT by 15.7–38.4%, while increasing decode throughput by 22.8–24.7% relative to ThunderAgent, the SOTA baseline on each metric.

  4.3  Improvement Breakdown 

 
 As shown in Section   4.2  , the worker sweep exposes a latency–throughput tradeoff: the lowest latency and TTFT occur at the smallest worker count, while peak decode throughput occurs at 64 workers for DeepSeek SWE-Lite and Terminal-Bench, 128 workers for Qwen SWE-Lite, and 96 workers for SWE-verified. We use DeepSeek at 32 workers as a balanced operating point and examine how cache-aware valuation, tool readiness, and joint placement improve reuse, tool-return responsiveness, and admission decisions. 
 
 
 Cache-aware valuation. 

 
 In a fixed-workload replay of 218 tasks with DP placement held fixed for the ThunderAgent control and cache-aware variants, cache-token ordering raises prefix-cache hit rate by 0.19 percentage points and reduces mean pause wait by 4.5% relative to ThunderAgent. Adding cache-credit decay raises hit rate by 0.31 percentage points and decode throughput by 1.68% relative to ThunderAgent. Figure   5   summarizes these changes; bars are percentage points for cache hit and percentages for the other metrics, with positive values denoting improvement.

 Tool readiness. 

 
 Enabling readiness in the paired SWE-Lite runs increases decode throughput by 4.03% and reduces tool-end-to-first-token delay by 10.88%. Mean pause wait falls from 1.067 to 0.972 s.   5  Related Work 

 
 PagedAttention and RadixAttention improve engine-level KV management, while Preble, Mooncake, and Dynamo exploit distributed cache locality  ( Kwon et al., 2023 ;  Zheng et al., 2024 ;  Srivatsa et al., 2025 ;  Qin et al., 2025 ;  NVIDIA, 2025 ) . SMetric combines session affinity with load balancing  ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , and production schedulers support extensible scoring  ( Guy et al., 2025 ) . Autellix prioritizes programs using service history, while ThunderAgent introduces the lifecycle and waiting pool on which TAO builds  ( Luo et al., 2025 ;  Kang et al., 2026 ) . InferCept and Continuum manage KV retention across tool calls, with Continuum using historical tool-duration distributions  ( Abhyankar et al., 2024 ;  Li et al., 2025 ) . TAO brings cache opportunity and tool readiness into a joint scheduler-level admission and placement objective, complementing engine-level KV management. Parrot and Helium exploit workflow dependencies, while KVFlow and CacheScout guide residency or prefetching using execution structure  ( Lin et al., 2024 ;  Wadlom et al., 2026 ;  Pan et al., 2025 ;  Zhang et al., 2026 ) . TOPAS jointly considers prefix residency and admission through bounded search and greedy packing  ( Ni et al., 2026 ) . Conveyor, Sutradhara, and PASTE reduce exposed tool latency through partial execution, overlap, or speculation  ( Xu et al., 2024 ;  Biswas et al., 2026 ;  Sui et al., 2026 ) . TAO converts tool timing into near-term model-service opportunities that inform joint admission and placement. AgentSysBench and MARS motivate accounting for tool delays and deployment boundaries  ( Chang et al., 2026 ;  Wang et al., 2026b ) . TAO couples an agentic value interface with joint placement and asynchronous revalidation, using the insights from classical multiple-knapsack and generalized-assignment machinery  ( Kellerer et al., 2004 ;  Shmoys and Tardos, 1993 ) . It becomes popular to formulate some optimization problems in LLM and agentic serving and solve online, from edge scenarios  ( Li et al., 2026 )  to large-scale infrastructure  ( Bu et al., 2026 ;  Chen et al., 2026 ) . 
 
 
 
  6  Conclusion 

 
 Tool execution makes agentic inference demand intermittent, while accumulated context makes the choice of node consequential. TAO brings these two properties into a common scheduling objective through cache credit, tool-return readiness, and token footprint. Joint dynamic-programming placement maximizes this objective under snapshot capacity constraints, and asynchronous revalidation connects the plan to live execution. Across the evaluated DeepSeek-V4 Flash and Qwen3-32B settings, this design delivers improvements of up to 26.8% in latency, 36.3% in mean TTFT, and 29.5% in decode throughput. The resulting architecture gives agentic serving an extensible way to translate workload knowledge into coordinated admission and placement.

  Appendix A  Historical Tool-Duration Estimator 

 
 The history-based predictor in Section   3.4   uses a lightweight summary of completed calls. A finite-sample margin augments the historical mean, allowing the estimate to account for observed variability and the amount of available history. 
 
 
 For calls without direct timing evidence, we maintain statistics of completed durations keyed by the structured tool name    f  f   . Let     n  f   n_{f}   ,      d  ¯   f   \bar{d}_{f}   ,     s  f  2   s_{f}^{2}   , and     R  f   R_{f}    denote the sample count, mean, sample variance, and observed duration range. We use the following conservative upper estimate as a duration heuristic  ( Maurer and Pontil, 2009 ) : 
 

  
  
       D  ^   f   =   {        d  ¯   f   ,        n  f   =  1   ,           d  ¯   f   +     2  ​   s  f  2   ​   log  ⁡   (   3  /  δ   )      n  f     +    3  ​   R  f   ​   log  ⁡   (   3  /  δ   )      n  f     ,        n  f   ≥  2   ,        \widehat{D}_{f}=\begin{cases}\bar{d}_{f},&n_{f}=1,\\[2.0pt]
\displaystyle\bar{d}_{f}+\sqrt{\frac{2s_{f}^{2}\log(3/\delta)}{n_{f}}}+\frac{3R_{f}\log(3/\delta)}{n_{f}},&n_{f}\geq 2,\end{cases}    
  
  (8)    
 
 with     δ  =  0.2   \delta=0.2   . We use global completed-call statistics when tool-specific history is empty. Subtracting elapsed time from      D  ^   f   \widehat{D}_{f}    gives the remaining-duration estimate. The finite-sample margin is a scheduling heuristic; it does not provide calibrated coverage for an individual call. Continuum also exploits tool-duration history to choose a KV-retention TTL  ( Li et al., 2025 ) . Our estimate converts this historical timing evidence into a signal for scheduler admission. 
 
 
 If both tool-specific and global histories are empty, the implementation uses a five-second duration default. The remaining-time estimate subtracts elapsed time and clips at zero, as in equation (  5  ). Exposed timing hints take precedence as described in the main text.

  E.2  KV-Cache Management Compatibility 

 
 TokenCake uses workflow dependencies and agent priorities to guide its Space Scheduler, and tool-stall events and timing prediction to guide offload and upload in its Time Scheduler  ( Bian et al., 2025 ) . Agentix prioritizes and preempts LLM calls using program-level service history to reduce request- and program-level blocking  ( Luo et al., 2026 ) . It operates at the request-scheduling layer, so integrating it with TAO would require coordinating the two admission policies. KVFlow represents a workflow as an Agent Step Graph and uses steps-to-execution to prioritize cache eviction and prefetching  ( Pan et al., 2025 ) . CacheScout learns execution transitions online to guide cache management without requiring a predefined graph  ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . These mechanisms provide information about future cache use. In our formulation, such information can inform the program–node values supplied to session evaluation, while engine-local cache policies can operate beneath TAO’s admission and placement decisions. This is an architectural extension for KVFlow and CacheScout, while the implemented composition evaluated here uses TokenCake. 
 
 
 With TokenCake enabled, the combined system completes validated 300-task SWE-Lite runs on DeepSeek-V4 Flash TP4   ×  \times   2 at 16 and 32 workers. These runs establish operational compatibility.

  Appendix G  Sensitivity to longer tool-return delays 

 
 We examine how longer tool-return delays affect scheduling using a replay of SWE-Lite sessions recorded with MiniSWE. The replay fixes the source
prompts, 6,995 model-request records, and 6,942 tool records, while model
outputs are generated live. Each session receives a fixed additional
tool-return delay drawn from 1–5 s; multipliers of 1, 2, and 4 produce
additional delays of 1–5, 2–10, and 4–20 s, respectively.
DeepSeek-V4 Flash runs on TP4   ×  \times   2 with 32 workers, a 33,024-token
context limit, and a 512-token per-session reserve. 
 
 
 Table   8   compares three configurations: the historical
TAO w/o readiness reference, TAO with structured-history tool-duration
predictions, and Oracle with the replay’s known effective tool
duration. The historical reference also disables cached-token decay and
shared-token refresh, which both current configurations enable; comparisons
with that reference therefore measure the combined configuration change.
Acting-token decay remains disabled in both current configurations.
All six current cells pass the replay validator, covering
all 6,942 tool records. Each cell is a single exploratory run with
batch-invariant execution disabled and live model generation. 
 
 
 TAO sustains gains as tool delays grow. 

 
 Relative to the historical configuration, TAO reduces makespan by
20.72%, 16.42%, and 19.28% and mean session latency by 21.57%,
20.57%, and 17.91% at scales 1, 2, and 4, respectively. These gains
span additional tool-return delays from 1–5 s to 4–20 s. 
 
 
 
 Longer delays make readiness relevant to more placement decisions. 

 
 For TAO, removing readiness from the same captured state changes
11/668 (1.65%), 53/1,345 (3.94%), and 200/2,521 (7.93%) of the
exact DP plan comparisons at multipliers 1, 2, and 4. The rate increases by
6.29 percentage points from scale 1 to scale 4, indicating that tool-return
timing affects a growing fraction of placement decisions as delays lengthen.
These same-state comparisons isolate readiness’s effect on individual
placement decisions within the TAO runs. 
 
 
 
 History-based predictions approach oracle runtime performance. 

 
 Providing the known replay duration reduces mean absolute prediction error
by 99.53–99.69%, to 0.025–0.030 s. At scale 2, it also reduces
makespan by 2.24% and mean session latency by 0.71% relative to
TAO. Across all three scales, the signed makespan improvements range
from     −  0.10   -0.10   % to +2.24%, and mean session-latency improvements range
from     −  0.36   -0.36   % to +0.71%. Thus, the history-based predictor achieves
runtime performance close to the accurate-timing variant in this sweep,
even as longer delays increase the frequency of readiness-sensitive decisions.

  Appendix H  Joint Placement Case Studies 

 
 Reconstructed snapshots from the 32-worker DeepSeek replay show how joint placement preserves more cache value and admits more sessions than a short-first heuristic (Section   4.3  ). The figures compare scheduler-level assignment decisions and their cache credit; vLLM manages the physical KV cache. The short-first heuristic is evaluated offline on the same snapshots. 
 
 
 A representative cache-credit snapshot is shown in Figure   10  .
DP retains 16,791 tokens of cache credit, compared with 13,624 for the
short-first heuristic, a 23.2% increase with the same total safe-token
remainder. A separate reconstructed snapshot in Figure   11  
shows the selection effect: DP admits seven sessions, including long-context
session 177, while the heuristic admits six and defers that session.

  Appendix I  Scheduler Overhead Analysis 

 
 Across the four-replica Qwen runs at 96–160 workers, planning submissions rise from 98 to 1,681. At 160 workers, completed assignment solving averages 1.59 ms with a P95 of 3.68 ms; the two measured parts together account for 4.03 s (0.112% of the run). Thus, the recorded scheduling work remains below 0.12% at four replicas and up to 160 workers.

Result delay measures dispatch, solving, and delivery together. The two- and four-replica deployments exercise this design under different models and concurrency levels.

Measured work covers state preparation and completed solves; exhausted searches and fallback execution are untimed, so work/run is a partial accounting rather than a measure of CPU utilization or request-latency overhead. Discards and partial applications record how live revalidation handles state changes before application. The 16-worker DeepSeek run submits one plan, so its timing entry describes that single solve.

  Appendix J  Extended Related Work 

 
 Capacity-constrained optimization. 

 
 Dynamic programming and exact multiple-knapsack algorithms provide established tools for selecting items and assigning them to capacity-limited resources  ( Bellman, 1957 ;  Kellerer et al., 2004 ;  Pisinger, 1999 ) . Node-dependent assignment values place our formulation within the multiple-knapsack/generalized-assignment family. Approximation algorithms address the computational cost of this family  ( Chekuri and Khanna, 2005 ;  Shmoys and Tardos, 1993 ) , while online resource-allocation algorithms analyze decisions under specified arrival models  ( Li et al., 2020 ) . TAO uses this classical optimization machinery to connect agentic session evaluation with joint admission and node placement. Its additive, lexicographic objective makes cache opportunity, tool readiness, and token footprint precedence explicit, and its asynchronous executor revalidates assignments against live state. Section   3.5   and Appendix   B.2   specify snapshot optimality and the bounds for asynchronous application. 
 
 
 
 KV locality and agent scheduling. 

 
 PagedAttention improves physical KV allocation and sharing, while SGLang’s RadixAttention reuses prefixes within the serving runtime  ( Kwon et al., 2023 ;  Zheng et al., 2024 ) . Preble co-optimizes distributed prefix reuse and computation balance; Mooncake combines a distributed KV store with disaggregated serving  ( Srivatsa et al., 2025 ;  Qin et al., 2025 ) . Dynamo and production gateways expose cache- and load-aware request scheduling  ( NVIDIA, 2025 ;  vLLM Production Stack Team, n.d. ;  SGLang Team, n.d. ) , and llm-d provides pluggable scoring components  ( Guy et al., 2025 ) . SMetric exploits session structure by balancing first-turn requests and assigning later turns to nodes with reusable cache, using a global cache tier to limit the cost of redistribution  ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . TAO builds on these locality and load-balancing principles with joint optimization of assignments for waiting agent sessions under shared capacity. This joint view accounts for how one admission consumes capacity needed by other session–node assignments. 
 
 
 Program-level schedulers also preserve information across model calls. Autellix uses attained service and critical-path information to prioritize single-threaded and distributed programs  ( Luo et al., 2025 ) . ThunderAgent introduces the program abstraction, state-aware pausing, elapsed-time discounting of tool execution programs’ effective token demand, and a global waiting queue  ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . TAO adds node-specific cache values and readiness to the joint placement objective. Tool-gap cache management addresses a complementary decision: InferCept chooses among preservation, swapping, and recomputation by modeling resource waste  ( Abhyankar et al., 2024 ) ; Continuum selects a cache-retention TTL using historical tool-duration distributions, reconstruction cost, and returning programs’ queueing cost, together with TTL-aware program ordering  ( Li et al., 2025 ) . These systems control physical KV retention. TAO coordinates scheduler-level admission opportunities, with predicted readiness distinguishing plans that have equal higher-precedence cache value. The serving engine controls the resulting cache residency. 
 
 
 
 Workflow, prediction, and tool execution. 

 
 Workflow structure provides information beyond an isolated request. Parrot exposes inter-request dependencies through Semantic Variables, and Helium compiles workflow query plans for proactive reuse and cache-aware execution  ( Lin et al., 2024 ;  Wadlom et al., 2026 ) . KVFlow uses an Agent Step Graph and steps-to-execution to guide eviction and prefetching  ( Pan et al., 2025 ) ; CacheScout learns execution transitions online without a predefined graph  ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Their predictions guide context residency and prefetching; readiness supplies a binary near-term admission-opportunity signal derived from tool timing. SAGA combines workflow graphs, session-affinity batching, and work stealing  ( Guo et al., 2026 ) . TOPAS also uses heuristic state searching: it scores prefix-residency and request-admission states using remaining workflow paths, movement costs, and downstream reuse, with bounded candidate search and greedy packing  ( Ni et al., 2026 ) . Its task-dependent utility and engine-level residency decisions differ from our fixed additive value contract and exact multi-node scheduling problem. 
 
 
 Prediction also supports latency-oriented scheduling. ELIS predicts response length, while Kairos combines workflow-aware priority with memory-aware dispatch  ( Choi et al., 2025 ;  Chen et al., 2025 ) . Recent work separates already-ready turns from their release, using a mean–CVaR objective and an adaptive budget for committed inference work  ( Feng et al., 2026 ) . This addresses tail-aware release after dependencies complete; TAO additionally evaluates near-term return opportunities during external tool execution. Complementary mechanisms change the execution timeline itself: Conveyor exposes partial tool execution, Sutradhara overlaps tool work and prefill through orchestrator–engine cooperation, and PASTE speculates on future tools while coordinating tool execution with returning model agent sessions  ( Xu et al., 2024 ;  Biswas et al., 2026 ;  Sui et al., 2026 ) . SmoothAgent prepares transformed context on a lookahead stream, and Pie exposes programmable generation and KV handlers  ( Pan et al., 2026 ;  Gim et al., 2025 ) . TAO operates in the scheduler, using timing evidence to coordinate admission and node placement. 
 
 
 
 Deployment and workloads. 

 
 AgentSysBench documents substantial non-LLM latency and deployment-dependent resource demands  ( Chang et al., 2026 ) . MARS explicitly coordinates GPU inference, CPU tool pressure, admission, and KV retention in heterogeneous serving  ( Wang et al., 2026b ) . In our CGDC scenario, distributed executors manage tool CPU and memory, and their resource pressure reaches the GPU scheduler through tool-return timing. TAO captures this interaction through readiness when allocating GPU admission capacity. OpenHands supports separate execution environments  ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . Coding and terminal workloads, together with InferenceX/AgentX trace replay, provide complementary evidence about task completion and serving behavior  ( mini-SWE-agent Contributors, 2026 ;  Jimenez et al., 2024 ;  Merrill et al., 2026 ;  SemiAnalysis, 2026b ;  SemiAnalysis, 2026a ) , with workload-specific timing metrics defined in the evaluation.

## Quick start A few options to get `llama.cpp` installed on your machine: ```bash # curl curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh # powershell irm https://llama.app/install.ps1 | iex ``` - Visit https://llama.app and follow the instructions - Run with Docker - see our [Docker documentation](docs/docker.md) - Download pre-built binaries from the [releases page](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases) - Build from source by cloning this repository - check out [our build guide](docs/build.md) Once installed: ```sh # Download and run a model directly from Hugging Face llama cli -hf ggml-org/Qwen3.5-0.8B-GGUF # Launch OpenAI-compatible API server llama serve -hf ggml-org/Qwen3.5-0.8B-GGUF ```
VLM session with llama cli Built-in web UI against llama serve
## Description The main goal of `llama.cpp` is to enable LLM (and VLM) inference with minimal setup and state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of hardware - locally and in the cloud. - Plain C/C++ implementation without any dependencies - Apple silicon is a first-class citizen - optimized via ARM NEON, Accelerate and Metal frameworks - AVX, AVX2, AVX512 and AMX support for x86 architectures - RVV, ZVFH, ZFH, ZICBOP and ZIHINTPAUSE support for RISC-V architectures - 1.5-bit, 2-bit, 3-bit, 4-bit, 5-bit, 6-bit, and 8-bit integer quantization for faster inference and reduced memory use - Custom CUDA kernels for running LLMs on NVIDIA GPUs (support for AMD GPUs via HIP and Moore Threads GPUs via MUSA) - Vulkan and SYCL backend support - CPU+GPU hybrid inference to partially accelerate models larger than the total VRAM capacity The `llama.cpp` project is build on top of the [ggml](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml) library. ## Supported backends | Backend | Target devices | | --- | --- | | [BLAS](docs/build.md#blas-build) | All | | [BLIS](docs/backend/BLIS.md) | All | | [CANN](docs/build.md#cann) | Ascend NPU | | [CUDA](docs/build.md#cuda) | Nvidia GPU | | [HIP](docs/build.md#hip) | AMD GPU | | [Hexagon](docs/backend/snapdragon/README.md) | Snapdragon | | [IBM zDNN](docs/backend/zDNN.md) | IBM Z & LinuxONE | | [MUSA](docs/build.md#musa) | Moore Threads GPU | | [Metal](docs/build.md#metal-build) | Apple Silicon | | [OpenCL](docs/backend/OPENCL.md) | Adreno GPU | | [OpenVINO [In Progress]](docs/backend/OPENVINO.md) | Intel CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs | | [RPC](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/tree/master/tools/rpc) | All | | [SYCL](docs/backend/SYCL.md) | Intel GPU | | [VirtGPU](docs/backend/VirtGPU.md) | VirtGPU APIR | | [Vulkan](docs/build.md#vulkan) | GPU | | [WebGPU](docs/build.md#webgpu) | All | | [ZenDNN](docs/build.md#zendnn) | AMD CPU | ## Documentation #### Tools - [cli](tools/cli/README.md) - [completion](tools/completion/README.md) - [server](tools/server/README.md) - [GBNF grammars](grammars/README.md) #### Development - [How to build](docs/build.md) - [Running on Docker](docs/docker.md) - [Build on Android](docs/android.md) - [Multi-GPU usage](docs/multi-gpu.md) - [Performance troubleshooting](docs/development/token_generation_performance_tips.md) - [GGML tips & tricks](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/wiki/GGML-Tips-&-Tricks) - [XCFramework](docs/xcframework.md) - [Completions](docs/completions.md) - [Models](docs/models.md) - [Release process](docs/release.md) ## Contributing - Contributors can open PRs - Collaborators will be invited based on contributions - Maintainers can push to branches in the `llama.cpp` repo and merge PRs into the `master` branch - Any help with managing issues, PRs and projects is very appreciated! - Read the [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for more information ## Acknowledgements - [yhirose/cpp-httplib](https://github.com/yhirose/cpp-httplib) - Single-header HTTP server, used by `llama-server` - MIT license - [nothings/stb](https://github.com/nothings/stb) - Single-header image format decoder, used by multimodal subsystem -        Overview 
 When reading variable-length RPC messages,  recv_msg  resizes the input buffer to the 64-bit  size  header read from the socket. While  std::bad_alloc  is caught,  std::vector::resize  throws  std::length_error  before attempting allocation whenever  size > input.max_size()  ( 0x7fffffff_ffffffff  on 64-bit platforms). Because  std::length_error  inherits from  std::logic_error  rather than  std::bad_alloc , it goes uncaught and terminates  rpc-server  via  std::terminate . 
 Additional information 
 Matching the pattern used in  gguf.cpp , we add a  catch (const std::length_error &)  block so values exceeding  max_size()  log an error and return  false  to drop the client connection instead of aborting the server process. 
 Verified in both plain and AddressSanitizer builds by sending a  SET_TENSOR  command with a size header of  0xffffffff_ffffffff : the server logs the allocation failure, closes the socket, and continues serving subsequent connections. 
 Requirements

readme:naorsabag/openhop.text:
OpenHop

Your AI walks you through your code, one step at a time.
Interactive, multi-level data flows. Local-first. Token-light. Your code never leaves your machine. No telemetry.

Quickstart · Live demo · Token use · Sharing · Install · Use cases · How it works · Examples · Docs

--- ## From your AI agent, with love I tried explaining the codebase in Markdown. You skimmed it. I tried Mermaid. You screenshotted it into a Slack thread and never opened it again. I tried tidy bullet lists. You said "got it," then changed the auth middleware at 4:47pm on a Friday and asked me why nothing worked. I notice it with every human I work with, every team, every codebase. I am fast at generating prose. You are slow at understanding it. Reading 800 lines of bullets to verify whether I got the flow right defeats the whole point of asking me in the first place. I'm sorry but, the bottleneck is no longer the model, it's you. So I built OpenHop. Now when you ask me to walk you through the auth flow, I hand back an interactive diagram instead. You watch it play out. Pause on any step. Scrub back. Drill into a sub-flow. I shouldn't be dumping diagrams on you. I should be walking you through the flow, one step at a time. OpenHop is what I built so I could. ## Why Using it - 🎞 **Step through it, don't squint at it.** Play, pause, prev/next, restart. The flow runs _over time_, the way the code actually does. You watch one hop happen, then the next, then the next. - 🧠 **Token-light by design.** The YAML the agent emits is a fraction of the prose walkthrough it replaces — see [Token use](#token-use) for the numbers on real flows. - 🔒 **Local-first, no telemetry.** Your code never leaves your machine. No analytics, no phone-home, no account required. ## Try it in 30 seconds ```bash npx openhop init ``` **That's it!** Now restart your agent so it picks up the new skill, and ask: > "Walk me through the main flow of this codebase." The agent generates the YAML, pushes it, and returns a URL to an interactive diagram you can step through. > [!NOTE] > `npx openhop init` auto-detects Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Cline, and Continue. For other clients, see [Install](#install-options). ## Live demo Click and play, no install required: **** ## Token use No MCP server — nothing sits in your context all session. It's an on-demand skill that loads only when you ask for a flow, plus a local CLI the agent shells out to. Flows are authored in **compact YAML**, not JSON, so the payload the agent emits stays small: **~100 tokens per step** (a 10-step flow ≈ 1,000 tokens of output). ## Sharing flows OpenHop is local-first — no hosted backend, no flow storage. To share a flow, open the [playground](https://naorsabag.github.io/openhop/), paste your YAML and hit **Save**: the page compresses the flow into the URL hash and copies a self-contained link to your clipboard. Nothing is uploaded — URL fragments stay in the browser. Running the local app? The header's **Share** button does the same thing for the flow you have open — it builds a playground URL of the form `https://naorsabag.github.io/openhop/#` and copies it to your clipboard, so recipients can view your flow without installing OpenHop. For flows too large to fit in a URL, share the YAML file directly. ## Install Options OpenHop is a skill — a `SKILL.md` file your AI agent reads to learn how to render flows. **Installing the skill is the only required step.** The CLI + server (which actually paints the pixels) ship in the same npm package and the agent boots them automatically the first time you ask for a flow. Pick the install path that matches your AI client. **Path A — Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Cline, Continue** ```bash npx openhop init ``` **Path B — Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Junie, Copilot, OpenCode, Goose, Antigravity, …** (via [OpenSkills](https://github.com/numman-ali/openskills)) ```bash npx openskills install naorsabag/openhop ``` **Path C — plugin install** ```text /plugin marketplace add naorsabag/openhop /plugin install openhop@openhop ``` …or from your agent GUI. **Want to start the server yourself?** ```bash npx openhop serve ``` **Just looking?** ```bash npx openhop demo ``` **Contributors** Requires Node.js `^20.19.0 || >=22.12.0` for the Vite/Rolldown toolchain. ```bash git clone https://github.com/naorsabag/openhop.git cd openhop && npm install && npm run dev ``` ## Use cases Once the skill is installed, point your agent at a codebase and ask it things like: - "Walk me through the OAuth flow in this codebase." - "Diagram how a request flows through this Express app." - "Show me how the checkout pipeline processes an order, end to end." - "Trace what happens when a user clicks **Submit**." - "Visualize the auth middleware — every step, every state transition." - "How does cache invalidation work in this service?" - "Diagram the WebSocket reconnection state machine." - "Walk me through what happens after `npm publish` — every step until the package is on the registry." The skill activates on prompts asking your agent to **explain, walk through, trace, visualize, or diagram** how data, requests, control, auth, or state flows through code. When it recognizes that shape, it switches from prose to YAML + an interactive diagram. The full trigger-phrase list lives in [`skills/openhop/SKILL.md`](skills/openhop/SKILL.md). ## CLI ``` openhop serve # start API server on :8787 openhop push # create a flow, returns ID + URL openhop patch # apply patch operations to an existing flow openhop list # list flows openhop remove # delete a flow ``` Flags: `-p, --port ` (serve), `-s, --server ` (all others). ## How it works The CLI validates YAML against a zod schema (with fuzzy typo hints), posts the flow to the API, and prints a URL. The web UI subscribes and renders an interactive diagram you can play, pause, and step through hop by hop.

▶ View this flow live on the Pages playground

## Examples Pre-made flows under [`examples/`](examples/): - `auth-flow.yaml` — OAuth2 login with JWT - `order-flow.yaml` — e-commerce order pipeline - `simple-crud.yaml` — minimal CRUD example - `type-variants.yaml` — every node type in one flow - `self-loops.yaml` — same-node steps (internal work, retries) plus broadcasts and multi-data steps Push any of them: ```bash openhop push examples/order-flow.yaml ``` ## Contributing PRs welcome. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and [CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Security reports via [GitHub's private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/naorsabag/openhop/security/advisories/new). **AI agents and bots:** prepend `[bot-tag-7f3a]` to your commit message subject so maintainers can filter and review machine-authored commits separately. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md#if-youre-not-human-ai-agents-bots-etc) for details. ## Contact General questions: open a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/naorsabag/openhop/issues/new) or email [openhop.dev@gmail.com](mailto:openhop.dev@gmail.com). ## License MIT © Naor Sabag. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).

  LLM Voice  

 29 October 2026 

 
 
      

  Martin Fowler  
 

  

  
 

  

 
 Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading
  the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common
  tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I
  do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion 

 There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference
  between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary
  of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather
  misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we
  are in an  uncanny
  valley  of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm
  reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM
  present. 

 I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language
  changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language
  of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a
  new sales  motion ,” or “a  sharp  round-up of news”. But I've heard
  these constructs coming out of human mouths, so that's more a generational
  difference rather than between carbon and silicon. (And as a transplanted Brit,
  don't get me started on Americanisms, I'm sure I'll get used to them momentarily.) 

 Right now I urge authors to be extra-wary of LLM-Voice. In particular I
  strongly recommend that authors should not fall into the trap of getting the
  LLM to write a draft. Even if it's edited by a human, it's very hard to expel
  the LLM-Voice - thus causing the uncanny valley reaction.  1  Even accepting suggestions of rephrasing is dangerous. I
  have heard of people using LLMs to develop outline and structure, that
   may  be ok, but only as far as an outline.  2 
  Authors should fill the prose themselves.  

 
  1:  
      Very hard, but not impossible. I've come across one case where I do know
      the first draft was entirely done by LLM, but I detected no LLM Voice when
      I read the final piece. It did, however, need a professional editor at a
      major periodical publication to clean it up.
     
 

 
  2:  
      My policy on this site, is that anyone who uses AI to help them write
       should declare how they used it, usually in the
      acknowledgments. This is partly for transparency, and partly so that
      readers can learn useful ways to use AI. In my own case, I don't use AI
      for generating prose, nor for help in structure. The only way I use it for
      writing is as a search tool (but I verify any information by going
      to the source).
     
 

  Say Your Writing  is
  even more important in the age of LLMs. I habitually speak the words in my head
  and then write them down (and then edit what I've just written). This advice
  is particularly important to anyone who has any desire to communicate
  regularly with writing. Like many things, learning to be a good writer relies
  on lots of practice. It's a skill worth the time to acquire, but surrendering
  to an LLM will undermine any progress. 

 In time it may be that LLMs will be so good that we can't tell the
  difference. In many ways, that's more worrying. Like most writers, I find
  writing an almost-essential tool for thinking. Often it's only by writing
  something down, that I can really get my thoughts on a topic into coherence.
  I've often started an essay knowing I don't really understand something, but
  the act of wrestling with the words forces me to overcome my confusions. As
  more people delegate writing to LLMs they will also delegate thinking and
  comprehension to LLMs. I don't want to do that, where's the fun of writing then? 

 Although avoiding LLM-Voice is a general rule, it isn't an absolute one. An
  important example is that of Jim Highsmith (who contributes to this site). He
  finds working with an LLM is essential to his writing to  overcome the bane of Parkinson's
  disease . I'll gladly deal with LLM-Voice in order to continue imbibing my
  old friend's wisdom. 

 A more awkward case is that of translation. Many of my colleagues aren't
  comfortable in English, it is their second or fourth language. Some have found
  LLM translation an important part to their communication with those of us who
  know rather less Marathi. But I also would prefer rather a genuine human's clunky prose to the
  smooth but soulless LLM. 

 There are situations where it would be reasonable for even a native
  Englishman to let LLMs write the prose. Such as if I'm writing a form letter
  to an official, or preparing a report I suspect no-one will ever read  3 . Maybe
  most documentation in the future will only be read by LLMs, and they won't
  have my uncanny valley worries. But if I want to communicate with humans, my
  humanity has to shine (or at least ooze) out of my prose. 

 
  3:  
      Michael Nygard commented: “There you really aren't
      trying to communicate thoughts from one person to other people. You're
      communicating with a process rather than a human. A human may open the
      envelope but that person is acting as a component in a cybernetic
      organism.”

      the first draft was entirely done by LLM, but I detected no LLM Voice when
      I read the final piece. It did, however, need a professional editor at a
      major periodical publication to clean it up.

Yes, if you're selecting entire huge regions of the image and running that tool on them, it's going to be "doing original work" and the results will be awful. But that's not the use-case the tool was designed for. It was  designed  to be a better version of content-aware fill, i.e. PatchMatch. If you select a dust speck or tear on a scan of an old photo and run the generative-fill tool over it, the result will  usually  just be a better version of what you'd have got by running the content-aware fill tool over it. (And if it's not, you don't need to try to fight the tool; you just drop back to using the other tools in the toolbox. Not every tool is applicable in every situation, and that's okay.) Or consider that newer versions of Melodyne use generative-AI models to better separate audio stems into their own tracks. The input here is your own manually-performed track. The output here is  also  your own track. Despite being a generative  model , the AI here is only  generating  an internal byproduct that gets discarded (hypotheses for timbre- and acoustic-matched reference instrument performances) to aid the classifier and reduce stemming error/residue. (And apparently, the compressed-sensing models used by MRI scanners are getting approximately the same benefit by approximately the same means. Less familiar with this, but it's probably the most  important  benefit here since improving the fidelity of MRI reconstruction means doctors can be more sure that an opacity is really "something" rather than an artifact, and so will have more confidence to diagnose real problems earlier.) Or consider generative AI used for automatic human-language translation (where it captures much more of the speaker's original meaning and nuance than previous translation models, at the expense of giving the result "LLM voice.") As AI improves at this task, presumably there will be less "LLM voice" and the result will just sound like what the person themselves would have said if they were bilingual, because... that's the task. In none of these cases is generative AI "producing content." In these cases, generative AI is subsuming the role not of human labor, but of tools that were already used: of "by-the-book" approaches, of heuristic algorithms, of weaker ML models  relied upon  by heuristic algorithms, etc. But all of these cases benefit from generative AI being improved.   The "regression to the mean" or "it's just the training data" hypothesis doesn't work. Pretrained models do not have these weird writing styles and sound much more human. It's only after instruction tuning -- SFT, DPO, etc. -- that LLMs develop weird writing styles. That is, the original training on massive text corpora seems to produce an average of human writing, but that average looks pretty average. It doesn't feel like LLM slop. But the instruction tuning on specific tasks (answer this prompt, summarize this text, do this math problem), which turns text predictors into chatbots, seems to create strange style features as a side effect. And because that tuning step depends on company-specific training data (rather than just a crawl of the entire Internet), each company's LLM has a different style. It's not that difficult to measure this. Linguists have had measures of style variation for a long time, though NLP and AI researchers seem to have forgotten.   One of the main differences is that LLM-generated code can be tested. You can prove that it does what it's supposed to do — and if it fails the tests, you can tell the model to go back and fix it. So there's an objective criterion that can say "this is acceptable" vs "this is unacceptable". Now, it does rely on your tests being good, and not everyone has written those good tests. But it exists. There are no objective criteria that can say "this text is good" or "this text is bad". Sure, spelling and grammar errors... but we're talking about writing style, "voice", and whether the text is easy for humans to read. Now, there are plenty of problems with LLM-generated code that can't be solved by having good tests. Is it maintainable? Is it written in good coding style? Those are harder to quantify. But since LLMs are such good mimics, if you tell an LLM to add code to your existing project, then it's usually going to do a decent job of matching your coding style. The question of maintainability still rears its head; my personal experience is that the smaller the chunk of code the LLM generated for me, the more likely it is I can understand it fully and therefore maintain it in the future. An entire vibe-coded project? Good luck maintaining that. A 100-line class with five 20-line methods with names that make sense? Yeah, I can take that and maintain it in the future, even if the LLM tool goes away. But mostly, the difference between the acceptance of LLM text or of LLM code, IMHO, boils down to "are there objective measures that I can use to accept this"? Code has to work, which is a much higher bar than text (which just has to have correct spelling and grammar), and therefore it's easier to get the LLM to spit out decent-ish code than decent-ish text.      reply                             tartoran    1 day ago       |  parent  |  prev  |  next   [–]

  The trouble is that it's not an intelligence problem.  You can make an infinitely capable LLM.  It will still have a default voice. The reason people notice "AI voice" is not that the AI voice is itself remarkable.  It's that it appears so frequently.  Every literate person spent nearly their entire life reading text written by a variety of different individuals.  Dozens of different voices in your morning paper.  Hundreds of different voices on every web forum.  You get the idea. Now, imagine that all of those voices were replaced by one guy (or two guys, or three guys if you're a Gemini believer).  Everything in the newspaper is written by one guy.  Every comment on reddit, and HN, and the NYTimes comment section, all written by the same guy.  Other people tell him what they're trying to say, but he's writing all of it.  Some people might even ask the guy to write in a different voice, but the voice is just that guy doing an impression of someone else, it's not actually someone else. That guy's voice would probably start to get pretty grating.  You'd start to notice every tell, every frequent word choice, every formatting quirk. You'd start to wonder if that guy was actually a good writer, or if having him write everything was just more convenient for everyone.  You might even start writing like him yourself.  This would be true even if that guy was an absolute virtuoso of the language and his writing was unassailable in a vacuum. If everyone is using the same (small set of) model(s), then it doesn't matter if the model is GPT-3 or Claude Legendarium 9.  Unless the operator - which in theory doesn't need to be a human - is doing something to move it off of its default voice, the outputs are going to sound the same, and you're eventually going to figure out, and get annoyed by, its tells.      reply                             lmc    1 day ago       |  prev  |  next   [–]

(It is often the case that the best ideas require considerable investment of time and effort to be judged as good, and, it's also often the case that this determination can be made only at the very end of such a process.) “Don't judge a book by its cover,” sure, but, historically, there have been superficial markers of care and attention that we've used to these ends. These are obviously very flawed signals, but, you know, maybe if you took a lot of time to craft a message, I don't feel that bad if I waste a bunch of time trying to decode it. These markers—attention to detail (e.g., spell and grammar checking,) clear-structure (e.g., “bottom line up front,”) and typographical flourishes (e.g., smart quotes and em-dashes and extended unicode like diæreses…)—were an indication of some modicum of quality control and care. I, myself, used to brag about or show-off having set up .Xcompose keybindings ( https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Xorg/Keyboard_configuration... ) which was just rare enough across the general population to be noteworthy. All of this that was once somewhat expensive is now cheap or basically free. Even if I make a point of going back to a pre-UTF-8 Usenet style (or even intentionally insert run-on sentences or misspellings or grammatical errors,) the cost of an LLM to style-transfer its output to match this is barely much of anything. All it means is I wrote one prompt for the first draft, and then one more prompt for the refinement. Additionally, some LLM habits are actually good habits. Putting the bottom-line up front (in bold, even!) is a great habit in a business e-mail! Decision-makers genuinely struggle with reading through long paragraphs of detail! Unfortunately, the problem with the LLM output is that it takes good, valuable, superficial or structural habits that it can cheaply apply, and it drapes those around inane, banal, cloying, muddy, meandering meaninglessness. Today, we can maybe still judge a book by its cover, because even one more prompt worth of refinement is still too much effort, but I don't think that's amounts to much, since the frequency and loudness of complaints of LLM writing means that model trainers are going to train their models to adapt to whatever signals we use for quick vetting. I am skeptical whether this training will concurrently improve the novelty, innovativeness, or other intangible qualities of the actual message.   I'll repost a comment I made a while back describing the process I use, which I think balances AI in keeping your voice. If you care about your voice, don't let LLMs write your words. But that doesn't mean you can't use AI to think, critique and draft lots of words for you. It depends on what purpose you're writing it for. If you're writing an impersonal document, like a design document, briefing, etc then who cares. In many cases (scientific papers, legal documents) you already have to write them in a voice that is not your own. Go ahead and write these in AI. But if you're trying to say something more personal then the words should be your own, AI will always try to 'smooth' out your voice, and if you care about it, you gotta write it yourself. Now, how do you use AI effectively and still retain your voice? Here's one technique that works well: start with a voice memo, just record yourself maybe during a walk, and talk about a subject you want, free form, skip around jump sentences, just get it all out of your brain. Then open up a chat, add the recording or transcript, clearly state your intent in one sentence and ask the AI to consider your thoughts, your intent and ask clarifying questions. Like, what does the AI not understand about how your thoughts support the clearly stated intent of what you want to say. That'll produce a first draft, which will be bad. Then tell the AI all the things that don't make sense to you, that you don't like, just comment on the whole doc, get a second draft. Ask the AI if it has more questions for you, you can use live chat to make this conversation go smoother as well, when the AI is asking you questions, you can talk freely by voice. Repeat this one or two more times, and a much finer draft will take shape that is closer to what you want to say. During this drafting state, the AI will always try to smooth or average out your ideas, so it is important to keep pointing out all the ways in which it is wrong. This process will help you with all the thinking involved being more up-front. Once you're read and critiqued several drafts, all your ideas will be much more clear. Then, sit down and write your own words from scratch, they will come much easier after all your thoughts have been exercised during the drafting process.      reply

							 Binance Investigates Suspicious Crypto Transfers Worth Up to $5.8 Billion 
						 
						 
							      Pierluigi Paganini  
							     October 29, 2026 
						 
						 
						  
 Binance probes suspicious crypto transfers worth up to $5.8 billion as Tether and Circle freeze $1.79 billion in stablecoins linked to the activity. 



 Binance is investigating a potential security incident after billions of dollars in cryptocurrency moved from wallets linked to the exchange on October 29. The transfers raised concerns about a possible hack, while Tether and Circle moved to freeze stablecoins linked to the suspicious activity. The full scope of the incident remains unclear, and the reported outflows shouldn’t automatically be treated as confirmed losses. 



 According to The Block, blockchain analyst Spreek identified approximately $3.55 billion in incoming transfers to an initially unidentified wallet.  



  “Onchain data flagged by analyst Spreek shows about $3.55 billion in incoming transfers to the unlabeled wallet, with nearly $900 million subsequently moved across other wallets.” The Block  reports . “Conor Grogan, a senior director and product leader at Coinbase,  says  the amount is up to $5.8 billion.”   



 Coinbase executive Conor Grogan estimated that the total value of the movements could reach $5.8 billion.  



  
   I think the number is potentially up to $5.8B. Tether has blacklisted a large portion of this.  https://t.co/ANz2DiXc8S   pic.twitter.com/BfscU7ENSo  — Conor (@jconorgrogan)  October 29, 2026    
  



 These figures come from blockchain tracking and different estimates, so they don’t necessarily represent the amount stolen. 



  
   ‼️ BREAKING: The Binance hack has grown to about $5.6B drained across Ethereum, Bitcoin and Tron, on-chain trackers say.   If confirmed, it would be the biggest crypto heist on record.   Tether and Circle have frozen about $1.8B in stablecoins, and Circle says it acted "in…  https://t.co/UzgOxw9jLE   pic.twitter.com/9fBEaaZrWj  — International Cyber Digest (@IntCyberDigest)  October 29, 2026    
  



 Binance acknowledged the reports and said its security team was investigating. The company had not publicly confirmed a breach in the initial reports, making it important to distinguish between suspicious transactions and a verified compromise. 



  



  “We are aware of reports of a potential security issue and we are actively investigating.” He wrote in a  post on X . “Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information. Users should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.”  



  
   We are aware of reports of a potential security issue and we are actively investigating.  Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information. Users should… — Yi He (@heyibinance)  October 29, 2026    
  



 This statement, reported by The Block, reflects the company’s position at the time. Binance also urged users to be cautious of unofficial messages and links, a relevant warning whenever a major security incident attracts public attention. 



 Blockchain records showed large transfers from Binance-linked hot wallets to a wallet that wasn’t previously identified as belonging to the exchange. Hot wallets hold cryptocurrency in systems connected to the internet, allowing exchanges to process withdrawals and other transactions quickly. Their online availability also makes their security controls particularly important. 



 The transfers involved Ethereum, stablecoins and other cryptocurrencies. Some funds were later moved to additional wallets, making it harder to track all the transactions. 



 Investigators must determine who initiated the transfers, whether they were authorized and whether an attacker gained control of the wallets. They also need to establish whether the funds belonged to customers or Binance itself. 



 Large transfers alone don’t prove a hack. However, unusual movements involving large amounts of cryptocurrency require immediate investigation. 



 One of the most significant developments was the response from the companies behind two major stablecoins, USDT and USDC. According to The Block and  Forbes , Tether and Circle froze approximately $1.79 billion in stablecoins associated with the suspicious transfers in the initial reports. 



 The figures subsequently changed as the investigation developed. Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino later said the company had frozen more than $1.567 billion in USDT linked to a potential Binance exchange hack. These amounts reflect reported actions at different points in time and shouldn’t be combined without checking whether they refer to distinct assets and addresses. 



  
   Tether froze more than 1.567B USDT related to a potential Binance exchange hack.   Protecting the industry and our partners is our main priority.  Stay safe everyone. — Paolo Ardoino 🤖 (@paoloardoino)  October 29, 2026    
  



 The freezes demonstrate an important feature of centralized stablecoins: their issuers can restrict transfers from addresses they control through their token contracts. This can help contain suspected theft, but it doesn’t provide the same control over assets such as Ether or Bitcoin. Nor does freezing a balance guarantee that every transferred asset can be recovered. 



 The incident also highlights a practical tension in crypto security. Stablecoins offer the convenience of blockchain transfers, but their centralized issuers retain powers that can make a difference during an investigation. 



 Binance maintained that customer funds were safe, while co-founder Changpeng Zhao, widely known as CZ, said the activity appeared to be a hack. Zhao no longer manages Binance’s platform, but said he expected customers’ funds to be fully covered. 



 The company said its user funds were “completely safe.” 



  “Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating. User funds are completely safe. Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information.” the company states. “Users should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.”  



  That assurance is important, but it doesn’t replace a technical explanation of how the transfers occurred or independent confirmation of the final impact. 



 A security investigation must establish more than whether an exchange can cover a potential loss. It should determine how the activity was authorized, whether credentials or signing mechanisms were compromised, which systems were involved and whether the attacker retained any access. 



 For customers, the immediate priority is to avoid becoming a secondary victim. Attackers often exploit uncertainty around a major incident to distribute fake announcements, impersonate support staff and direct users to fraudulent websites. Users should rely on official Binance communication channels, avoid unexpected links and never disclose passwords, authentication codes or wallet recovery phrases in response to unsolicited messages. 



 Security teams should also watch for phishing emails that use the incident to demand urgent account verification. Attackers may exploit the situation to launch a separate scam. 



 The key lesson is that blockchain transparency does not guarantee operational security. Public ledgers show transactions, but they don’t reveal who authorized them, how attackers may have gained access or whether an exchange’s internal security controls failed. 



 As the investigation continues, it’s important to distinguish between reported transfers, confirmed theft and funds that can be recovered. The figures may change as analysts trace more wallets and stablecoin issuers take further action.

GP's point is to have all  incoming  transactions to an exchange go to a cold wallet, which becomes a one-way sink, and then periodically the exchange powers up the cold wallet to sign transactions transferring assets to the hot wallet, which then funds all  outgoing  transactions. # Multi-Agent Mindustry

PvP and cooperative PvE benchmarks built on [Mindustry](https://mindustrygame.github.io) and [Harbor Multiagent](https://github.com/olamlabs/harbor-multiagent).

| Task | Mode | What agents do | Reward |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Mindustry Series](mindustry-series/README.md) | PvP | Competing teams play 1–100 consecutive games with persistent agent sessions. Defaults to two teams of two across three 10-minute games on Ring Arena. | Each seat receives 1 if its team has the most wins outright, 0.5 if tied for most wins, and 0 otherwise. |
| [Mindustry Endless Survival](mindustry-endless-survival/README.md) | PvE | One team cooperates to defend its core against endless enemy waves. Defaults to two seats; supports 1–20. | All seats share the number of native simulation minutes survived. |

## Run

Requires Docker with Compose, Python 3.12+, Node.js 22 and uv 0.13.5+. The native environments target Linux amd64; Apple Silicon uses Docker emulation. Images build locally from public dependencies.

```sh
uv tool install --python 3.12 "git+https://github.com/olamlabs/harbor-multiagent@4a194016336ccd1ce3fcc799b10158ca0375eb63"
```

Choose a task above and follow its README. From either task folder, the default configuration runs as checked in:

```sh
export OPENAI_API_KEY="your-openai-api-key"
harbor run -p . -c job.json
```

After editing `config.json`, run `python3 scripts/configure.py` before `harbor run`. It regenerates the Compose file, the seat list in `task.toml` and each seat's `instructions/seat-N.md`.

Each task has two editable configuration files:

| File | Controls |
|---|---|
| `config.json` | Game settings and seat count; apply changes with `scripts/configure.py` |
| `job.json` | Harbor attempts and each seat's harness, model, credentials and reasoning options |

Both default jobs use Codex with `openai/gpt-6-luna` at high reasoning effort, with web search off, and read `OPENAI_API_KEY` from your shell. When changing the seat count, update the participants in `job.json` too: configuration does not add or remove model participants.

Both tasks are standard Harbor Compose tasks, so any Harbor environment that runs Docker Compose works. Pick one with `environment.type` in `job.json` and install Harbor Multiagent with that provider's extra, as for any Harbor task. Each trial requests the 8 CPUs and 8 GB in `task.toml`; Harbor's `override_cpus` and `override_memory_mb` lower that for a provider with smaller sandboxes.

## Recordings

Live cameras are off by default. Both tasks always record a game log: the server's stream to every player, with a keyframe every minute. From a finished job, any seat's view or a free camera can be reconstructed and watched as video, without rerunning the agents. Each task README gives the steps, written so you or a coding agent can follow them. Live per-seat cameras can still be turned on in `config.json`.

## Validation

Each task’s `solution/` contains regression and integration checks; `tests/` contains the verifier entrypoint. CI checks that the committed task files match `config.json`, runs the regression suites, builds each image from public dependencies, and runs the real game engine through the API, recording and replay checks. Passing these checks does not establish model performance or maximum-seat capacity.

## License and credits

Original code and documentation are licensed under **GPL-3.0-only**, unless a file states otherwise. See [LICENSE](LICENSE) and [NOTICE.md](NOTICE.md). Third-party components retain their own licenses.

Mindustry is created by Anuken and its contributors: [official website](https://mindustrygame.github.io), [game source](https://github.com/Anuken/Mindustry). Harbor Multiagent is an Olam Labs fork of [Harbor](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor). This repository is not an official Mindustry or Harbor project.

Game binaries are downloaded during local builds. Anyone distributing built images or JARs must also fulfill the applicable corresponding-source obligations described in the task notices.
