items                    minecraft-agent-harness     
 LLM agents that play Minecraft. 
 
     
     
     
     
 
 
     
 
 
   Quickstart  ·
   Configuration  ·
   Tools  ·
   Teams  ·
   Bed Wars example 
 
 Point an LLM at a Minecraft server and give it something to do. It plays through
 Mineflayer , so it walks, mines, crafts, builds, fights and chats like a
regular player.  pi  handles the model session. We've run Bed Wars matches with it,
and a survival server with 50 agents on it at once. 
 What's in here: 
 
 Claude, GPT, Gemini, OpenRouter, or your own endpoint if it speaks the OpenAI Responses API 
 Sessions that survive restarts. Kill an agent, start it again under the same name, and it carries on 
 A shell for every agent (Docker, E2B or a plain local folder). Agents keep notes there and write little scripts that
call their own game tools 
 Teams from a single JSON file, with DMs between agents and an optional shared machine 
 Vision, if you want it (experimental) 
 
  Quickstart     
 You'll need Node 22.19+, an API key for some model provider, and a Minecraft server. If you don't have a server, the
repo comes with a dev one, which needs Java 21. 
  npm ci
cp .env.example .env      #  add the API key for your model provider 
npm run server            #  Paper 1.21.6 on localhost:25565, offline mode   
 Then in a second terminal: 
  npm start -- --objective   " Gather wood and build a small shelter near spawn "    
 That's it. The default model is GPT-6.1 Terra, and  Configuration  covers the other providers
and how to switch. 
 Join  localhost:25565  from Minecraft 1.21.6 if you want to watch, and  /tell Agent <message>  to talk to it. Its
output and tool calls stream to the terminal.  Ctrl+C  stops it. Everything it knows lives in
 .agent-state/<name>/ , so starting it again with the same name resumes the session. 
  Your own server     
  npm start -- --host play.example.net --port 25565 --objective   " Mine iron "    
 Online-mode servers need  --auth microsoft  (you'll get a sign-in prompt). Agents assume survival; pass  --game-mode 
if your server puts them in something else. 
  Docker     
 Fill in  .env  as above, then: 
  docker compose up  
 You get a Paper server on  localhost:25565  and one agent. Change what it does with  AGENT_OBJECTIVE  in  .env . State
goes in the  agent-state  volume. 
 Already have a server? Just run the agent image: 
  docker build -t minecraft-agent  . 
docker run --rm -it --env-file .env -v agent-state:/data minecraft-agent --host play.example.net -o   " Mine iron "    
  Teams     
  npm start -- team examples/team.json  
 Starts three agents who can message each other.  Team config  has the details. For
something with rules and a referee, look at the  Bed Wars example . 
  Configuration     
 Flags, environment variables ( .env  works) or a JSON file via  --config . Flags win over env vars, env vars win over
the file. 
 A heads-up about the shell: agents get one by default. That's E2B if  E2B_API_KEY  is set, otherwise Docker if it's
running, otherwise a local folder, and local means commands run as you. Use  --sandbox none  if you'd rather they
didn't have one. 
 More docs: 
 
  Configuration : models, auth, sandboxes, vision, where files go 
  Tools : everything an agent can do 
  Architecture : how the code fits together 
 
  Development     
  npm run check     #  lint, format, tests   
  CONTRIBUTING.md  covers the rest. 
  License     
 MIT. Some of the skill library comes from  Mindcraft  and the renderer worker
from  prismarine-viewer ; their licenses are in
 THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md .

 PvP and cooperative PvE benchmarks built on  Mindustry  and  Harbor Multiagent . 
  
 
 
 Task 
 Mode 
 What agents do 
 Reward 
 
 
 
 
  Mindustry Series  
 PvP 
 Competing teams play 1–100 consecutive games with persistent agent sessions. Defaults to two teams of two across three 10-minute games on Ring Arena. 
 Each seat receives 1 if its team has the most wins outright, 0.5 if tied for most wins, and 0 otherwise. 
 
 
  Mindustry Endless Survival  
 PvE 
 One team cooperates to defend its core against endless enemy waves. Defaults to two seats; supports 1–20. 
 All seats share the number of native simulation minutes survived. 
 
 
  
  Run     
 Requires Docker with Compose, Python 3.12+, Node.js 22 and uv 0.13.5+. The native environments target Linux amd64; Apple Silicon uses Docker emulation. Images build locally from public dependencies. 
  uv tool install --python 3.12   " git+https://github.com/olamlabs/harbor-multiagent@4a194016336ccd1ce3fcc799b10158ca0375eb63 "    
 Choose a task above and follow its README. From either task folder, the default configuration runs as checked in: 
   export  OPENAI_API_KEY=  " your-openai-api-key "  
harbor run -p  .  -c job.json  
 After editing  config.json , run  python3 scripts/configure.py  before  harbor run . It regenerates the Compose file, the seat list in  task.toml  and each seat's  instructions/seat-N.md . 
 Each task has two editable configuration files: 
  
 
 
 File 
 Controls 
 
 
 
 
  config.json  
 Game settings and seat count; apply changes with  scripts/configure.py  
 
 
  job.json  
 Harbor attempts and each seat's harness, model, credentials and reasoning options 
 
 
  
 Both default jobs use Codex with  openai/gpt-6-luna  at high reasoning effort, with web search off, and read  OPENAI_API_KEY  from your shell. When changing the seat count, update the participants in  job.json  too: configuration does not add or remove model participants. 
 Both tasks are standard Harbor Compose tasks, so any Harbor environment that runs Docker Compose works. Pick one with  environment.type  in  job.json  and install Harbor Multiagent with that provider's extra, as for any Harbor task. Each trial requests the 8 CPUs and 8 GB in  task.toml ; Harbor's  override_cpus  and  override_memory_mb  lower that for a provider with smaller sandboxes. 
  Recordings     
 Live cameras are off by default. Both tasks always record a game log: the server's stream to every player, with a keyframe every minute. From a finished job, any seat's view or a free camera can be reconstructed and watched as video, without rerunning the agents. Each task README gives the steps, written so you or a coding agent can follow them. Live per-seat cameras can still be turned on in  config.json . 
  Validation     
 Each task’s  solution/  contains regression and integration checks;  tests/  contains the verifier entrypoint. CI checks that the committed task files match  config.json , runs the regression suites, builds each image from public dependencies, and runs the real game engine through the API, recording and replay checks. Passing these checks does not establish model performance or maximum-seat capacity.

 Mindustry is created by Anuken and its contributors:  official website ,  game source . Harbor Multiagent is an Olam Labs fork of  Harbor . This repository is not an official Mindustry or Harbor project. 
 Game binaries are downloaded during local builds. Anyone distributing built images or JARs must also fulfill the applicable corresponding-source obligations described in the task notices.

readme:langflow-ai/langflow.text: [![Release Notes](https://img.shields.io/github/release/langflow-ai/langflow?style=flat-square)](https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/releases) [![PyPI - License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-orange)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT) [![PyPI - Downloads](https://img.shields.io/pypi/dm/langflow?style=flat-square)](https://pypistats.org/packages/langflow) [![Twitter](https://img.shields.io/twitter/url/https/twitter.com/langflow-ai.svg?style=social&label=Follow%20%40Langflow)](https://twitter.com/langflow_ai) [![YouTube Channel](https://img.shields.io/badge/Subscribe-red?logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://www.youtube.com/@Langflow) [![Discord Server](https://img.shields.io/discord/1116803230643527710?logo=discord&style=social&label=Join)](https://discord.gg/EqksyE2EX9) [![Ask DeepWiki](https://deepwiki.com/badge.svg)](https://deepwiki.com/langflow-ai/langflow) [Langflow](https://langflow.org) is a powerful platform for building and deploying AI-powered agents and workflows. It provides developers with both a visual authoring experience and built-in API and MCP servers that turn every workflow into a tool that can be integrated into applications built on any framework or stack. Langflow comes with batteries included and supports all major LLMs, vector databases and a growing library of AI tools. ## ✨ Highlight features - **Visual builder interface** to quickly get started and iterate. - **Source code access** lets you customize any component using Python. - **Interactive playground** to immediately test and refine your flows with step-by-step control. - **Multi-agent orchestration** with conversation management and retrieval. - **Deploy as an API** or export as JSON for Python apps. - **Deploy as an MCP server** and turn your flows into tools for MCP clients. - **Observability** with LangSmith, LangFuse and other integrations. - **Enterprise-ready** security and scalability. ## 🖥️ Langflow Desktop Langflow Desktop is the easiest way to get started with Langflow. All dependencies are included, so you don't need to manage Python environments or install packages manually. Available for Windows and macOS. [📥 Download Langflow Desktop](https://www.langflow.org/desktop) ## ⚡️ Quickstart ### Install locally (recommended) Requires Python 3.10–3.14 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) (recommended package manager). #### Install From a fresh directory, run: ```shell uv pip install langflow -U ``` The latest Langflow package is installed. For more information, see [Install and run the Langflow OSS Python package](https://docs.langflow.org/get-started-installation#install-and-run-the-langflow-oss-python-package). #### Run Official release packages and tagged source archives disable automatic login by default. Set `LANGFLOW_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD` before starting Langflow, then sign in with the username `langflow` (or your configured `LANGFLOW_SUPERUSER`). Development branches retain automatic login by default. See [authentication configuration](https://docs.langflow.org/api-keys-and-authentication#start-a-langflow-server-with-authentication-enabled). To start Langflow, run: ```shell uv run langflow run ``` Langflow starts at http://127.0.0.1:7860. That's it! You're ready to build with Langflow! 🎉 ## 📦 Other install options ### Run from source If you've cloned this repository and want to contribute, run this command from the repository root: ```shell make run_cli ``` For more information, see [DEVELOPMENT.md](./DEVELOPMENT.md). ### Docker Set and export a strong password before starting the container (Bash): ```shell read -rsp "Langflow administrator password: " LANGFLOW_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD; echo export LANGFLOW_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD docker run -p 7860:7860 -e LANGFLOW_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD langflowai/langflow:latest ``` Langflow is available at http://localhost:7860/. Sign in as `langflow` with the password you entered. Official Docker images require authentication by default. If you already have an auto-login installation, follow the [upgrade instructions](https://docs.langflow.org/api-keys-and-authentication#upgrade-from-auto-login) before switching defaults. For configuration options, see the [Docker deployment guide](https://docs.langflow.org/deployment-docker). ## 🛡️ Security For security information, see our [Security Policy](./SECURITY.md). ## 🚀 Deployment Langflow is completely open source and you can deploy it to all major deployment clouds. To learn how to deploy Langflow, see our [Langflow deployment guides](https://docs.langflow.org/deployment-overview). ## ⭐ Stay up-to-date Star Langflow on GitHub to be instantly notified of new releases. ![Star Langflow](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/03168b17-a11d-4b2a-b0f7-c1cce69e5a2c) ## 👋 Contribute We welcome contributions from developers of all levels. If you'd like to contribute, please check our [contributing guidelines](./CONTRIBUTING.md) and help make Langflow more accessible. --- [![Star History Chart](https://api.star-history.com/svg?repos=langflow-ai/langflow&type=Timeline)](https://star-history.com/#langflow-ai/langflow&Date) ## ❤️ Contributors [![langflow contributors](https://contrib.rocks/image?repo=langflow-ai/langflow)](https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/graphs/contributors)

     Security Bulletin: Langflow OSS is affected by multiple vulnerabilities 
 


     
    
  
    
             
          
 
   
                 
   
     
       
       
         
         
         
                   Security Bulletin 
                   
           
          
          
          
          
          
   
         Summary 
                      Langflow OSS is affected by multiple vulnerabilities involving code execution, server-side requests, access controls, file handling, and a development workflow. Depending on the affected feature and deployment configuration, an attacker could execute code, disclose sensitive information, access or modify other users' data, or disrupt service.

                       IBM strongly recommends addressing the vulnerability now by upgrading  Langflow OSS to version 1.12.5.  
 For Langflow OSS versions 1.0.0 - 1.12.4, follow the  Prepare to upgrade instructions and release-specific configuration changes , including backing up your existing installation, then follow the  Langflow OSS installation instructions  to install version 1.12.5 and test your flows. For deployments using MCP stdio, also apply the configuration controls in Workarounds and Mitigations. 
 This bulletin also discloses fixes delivered in prior releases: CVE-2026-107366 was fixed in version 1.9.0; CVE-2026-18894 was fixed in version 1.11.2; and CVE-2026-77817 was fixed in version 1.11.5. Version 1.12.5 includes these fixes.  
           

          
   
         Workarounds and Mitigations 
                       IBM strongly recommends applying the following configuration controls to deployments using MCP stdio in addition to upgrading Langflow OSS to version 1.12.5. These controls do not replace the upgrade. 
 Set  LANGFLOW_MCP_SERVER_INTERPRETER_HARDENING=true  to reject direct shell-script execution, and set  LANGFLOW_CUSTOM_COMPONENT_ADMIN_ONLY=true  to block non-admin MCP stdio access. Restart the Langflow service after updating its environment configuration. These restrictions can require changes to existing MCP server launch configurations and limit which users can use MCP stdio. 
 For public workflows, retain the default restriction on custom components. Explicitly enabling  LANGFLOW_ALLOW_PUBLIC_CUSTOM_COMPONENTS  permits custom component execution and changes the default protection described for CVE-2026-18894. 
 For CVE-2026-77817, upgrading prevents the identified secret disclosure in new flow and project exports. Revoke or rotate any credentials exposed in previously exported files; upgrading does not remove secrets from copies already exported.

     Security Bulletin: Langflow OSS is affected by multiple vulnerabilities 
 


     
    
  
    
             
          
 
   
                 
   
     
       
       
         
         
         
                   Security Bulletin 
                   
           
          
          
          
          
          
   
         Summary 
                      Langflow OSS is affected by multiple vulnerabilities that could allow a remote attacker to bypass authentication controls, execute arbitrary code, expose application programming interface (API) credentials, or disclose information through vulnerable dependencies. Issues include an incomplete remediation of an auto-login security control, agentic code execution via a third-party library, operator-injected API key exposure reachable without intended authorization, and unauthenticated remote code execution exploitable through model context protocol tool enumeration. Additionally, several open-source dependencies included in the product contain known vulnerabilities. 
           

          
          
          
          
          
          
          
          
          
          
          
          
          
   
         Vulnerability Details 
                        CVEID:     CVE-2026-93680    DESCRIPTION:    Langflow OSS could allow a remote attacker to bypass security restrictions due to improper authentication.  CWE:     CWE-287: Improper Authentication   CVSS Source:    IBM  CVSS Base score:    9.8  CVSS Vector:    (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H)    CVEID:     CVE-2026-110193    DESCRIPTION:    Langflow OSS could allow a remote attacker with a low-privileged authenticated account to cause the Agentic Assistant to generate or submit component code using these unblocked patterns, resulting in arbitrary operating system command execution on the server. CWE:     CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')   CVSS Source:    IBM  CVSS Base score:    9.8  CVSS Vector:    (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H)    CVEID:     CVE-2026-84363    DESCRIPTION:    Hono is a Web application framework that provides support for any JavaScript runtime. Prior to 4.13.5, Hono's query helpers treat a question mark after a literal hash fragment as the start of a query string, so the application can read request parameters that browsers, new URL(), reverse proxies, filtering rules, parameter allow and deny lists, access logging, request validation, and other middleware do not observe. The Cache Middleware removes the fragment when building its cache key, allowing a response influenced by parameters inside the fragment to be stored under a key that omits those parameters and later served to other users. This can bypass filtering and auditing, poison cached responses, and enable stored cross-site scripting when an affected parameter is reflected into cached HTML without escaping. Exploitation requires a runtime and intermediary path that passes a literal hash character through to the request URL; Cloudflare Workers and intermediaries that strip fragments are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 4.13.5.  CWE:     CWE-444: Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests ('HTTP Request/Response Smuggling')   CVSS Source:    security-advisories@github.com  CVSS Base score:    5.9  CVSS Vector:    (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N)    CVEID:     CVE-2026-84364    DESCRIPTION:    Hono is a Web application framework that provides support for any JavaScript runtime. Prior to 4.13.5, when parseBody() expands dot-separated form field names into nested objects with dot-notation parsing enabled, it does not limit the nesting depth or the total number of intermediate objects created. Empty segments are preserved, so one deeply dotted field name can encode one nesting level per byte, while a large number of shallowly dotted fields can create the same amplification across a request. A request body within a normal size limit can therefore allocate an object graph far larger than the request after the body has already been accepted. An unauthenticated attacker who can reach an affected endpoint can send concurrent requests that exhaust the JavaScript heap, terminate the server process, and leave the service unavailable until restart. Dot-notation parsing is not enabled by default, and applications using the default behavior are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 4.13.5.  CWE:     CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption   CVSS Source:    security-advisories@github.com  CVSS Base score:    5.3  CVSS Vector:    (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L)    CVEID:     CVE-2026-84365    DESCRIPTION:    Hono is a Web application framework that provides support for any JavaScript runtime. From 4.12.12 until 4.13.5, the fix released for CVE-2026-39408 does not cover every traversal sequence, and toSSG() can still write files outside the configured output directory when a route parameter contains consecutive parent-directory segments. Static site generation builds each output path from the route path and values supplied through ssgParams, then verifies that the result stays inside the output directory using the same normalization routine that built the path. That routine does not fully collapse runs of consecutive parent-directory segments, allowing a path that the check accepts to resolve outside the output directory, and the check also treats output directories that differ in how they are rooted as equivalent. This arises when an application generates a static site from route parameter values it does not fully control, such as slugs from a CMS, API, or user submission.                        IBM strongly recommends addressing these vulnerabilities now by upgrading Langflow OSS installations running versions 1.0.0 - 1.12.8 to Langflow OSS 1.13.0. 
 Review the  Langflow OSS 1.13.0 release notes  and follow the installation instructions for your deployment: 
  Python package: install  Langflow 1.13.0 from PyPI  with  pip install --upgrade "langflow==1.13.0" , following the  installation instructions .  Docker: use  langflowai/langflow:1.13.0  and follow the  Docker upgrade instructions  to pull the image and restart the deployment while preserving its persistent data.  
 Before upgrading, back up the database, secret key, and uploaded files. If the deployment uses automatic login, prepare the existing account for password sign-in as described in the installation and Docker upgrade instructions. These preparation steps accompany the product upgrade; no separate interim workaround is provided.

Description             andersk    opened    on Mar 6, 2019               Issue body actions           markdown.markdown('[' * 13000)  takes about a minute (in 3.0.1 and master), with the time increasing by about a factor of four every time the length is doubled.                  Activity   Next                  waylan   commented   on   Mar 6, 2019            waylan      on Mar 6, 2019           Member       More actions          I expect this is because the link processor allows for nested brackets. On the bright side, it doesn't crash (many such things raised recursion errors back in version <2.0). The fact is, performance is not a high priority for us. If you are providing such a unrealistic input, then I don't really care that it is slow. Although, I'm curious how different this is for version 2.x as we changed the bracket parsing in 3.0.                           facelessuser   commented   on   Mar 6, 2019            facelessuser      on Mar 6, 2019           Collaborator       More actions          Makes sense to me. I'm sure it's running through the entire algorithm for each  [ . And for each  [ , it runs to the end of the chain of  [ . So, if you double the size of the string, it goes through the entire string trying to resolve all the  [ . This allows you to nest  [[]] , which is a good thing. 
 Currently, I see no problem with this behavior as the current compliant is based on an unrealistic situation. A document consisting of a chain of 13,000  [  is not a good argument for changing anything. To me it seems like an academic exercise to show you can construct documents that take a long time to parse. 
 Before, we used regular expression which failed miserably when tasked with nested  [] . The new algorithm allows it to handle as much nesting as needed. As far as performance is concerned, I would say it behaves as one would expect. 
 If we are just concerned someone could create a document that freezes up the parser, we could add nested bracket limit just to prevent the parser from getting tied up in ridiculously large nested situations.                           andersk   commented   on   Mar 6, 2019            andersk      on Mar 6, 2019           Contributor  Author       More actions          Thanks for the quick response. 
 My perspective is that I’m concerned about denial of service attacks on applications parsing user input as Markdown. This isn’t an academic exercise—this very comment is user input that GitHub is parsing as Markdown, and you can imagine that they’d be really sad if I could easily cause their parser to spin for minutes or hours, whether maliciously or by accident. In an even less hypothetical sense, I’m filing this issue in the aftermath of a real denial of service attack that actually took down a  large application  via a complexity attack on Python-Markdown. 
 Now, obviously, you’re under no obligation to support my use case. You are free to decide that Python-Markdown is not designed for use on untrusted input. Part of the reason I’m filing this is that I’d like to know how these kinds of issues will be handled. Should I file more of them, or should I work on finding a Markdown library that better suits my requirements?        👍   React with 👍 2    Reacted by  LouisNitag and Seongchul Ahn                         facelessuser   commented   on   Mar 6, 2019            facelessuser      on Mar 6, 2019            Last edited by  facelessuser             Collaborator       More actions          
 I’m filing this issue in the aftermath of a real denial of service attack that actually took down a large application via a complexity attack on Python-Markdown. 
 
 Context is important, and I think pointing this out is important when filing such an issue. 
 I suspected near the end of my reply that the act of a hanging parser might have been the direction you were heading in, which is why I also suggested the possibility of limiting the recursion.  There are two quadratic scan functions in inlinepatterns.py, reachable by six different 
payload shapes. On most of them the work is discarded, so it is pure waste. One line of 
input is enough. 
 Scanner one: LinkInlineProcessor.getText, inlinepatterns.py:884 
   def getText(self, data: str, index: int) -> tuple[str, int, bool]:
    """Parse the content between `[]` of the start of an image or link
    resolving nested square brackets.
    """
    bracket_count = 1
    text = []
    for pos in range(index, len(data)):
        c = data[pos]
        if c == ']':
            bracket_count -= 1
        elif c == '[':
            bracket_count += 1
        index += 1
        if bracket_count == 0:
            break
        text.append(c)
    return ''.join(text), index, bracket_count == 0
   
 Two things combine. 
 When the brackets never balance the loop runs all the way to len(data), one Python level 
text.append(c) per character. There is no early exit for the case where there is no "]" 
left in the input at all, so an unmatched "[" always costs a full scan of everything after 
it. 
 And the result is then thrown away. handleMatch at :934 does: 
   text, index, handled = self.getText(data, m.end(0))
if not handled:
    return None, None, None
   
 So the multi thousand character list that was just built and joined is discarded, and the 
pattern is retried at the next "[". N unmatched brackets cost N full scans. 
 getText is inherited by six processors: Link, Reference, ShortReference, Image, 
ImageReference and ShortImageReference. Each one calls it on the same data. 
 Scanner two: BacktickInlineProcessor.find_code_spans, inlinepatterns.py:445 
 This one makes no getText calls at all, so it is independent. 
   def find_code_spans(self, start: int, text: str) -> tuple[int, int] | None:
    last = len(text)
    ...
    i = start
    while i < last:
        span_length = 0
        while i < last and text[i] == '`':
            span_length += 1
            i += 1
        ...
        if max_ticks == span_length:
            return start, i - span_length
        if span_length > longest_span:
            longest_span = span_length
            end = i
   
 Same shape. When no span of matching length exists, "while i < last" runs to the end of the 
text, and it is re-entered once per backtick position.

   python3 -c "import markdown,time; p='['*30000; t=time.perf_counter(); markdown.Markdown().convert(p); print(time.perf_counter()-t)"

 The uncaught exception, which is a different defect class 
 Before the measurement, your own documented goal. docs/index.md lists this FIRST under 
Goals, and the parenthetical is the relevant part: 
   Maintain a Python library (with an optional CLI wrapper) suited to use in web
server environments (never raise an exception, never write to stdout, etc.) as
an implementation of the markdown parser that follows the syntax rules and the

 "Never raise an exception", for "web server environments". That is the property the next 
measurement refutes, and it is also the reason this belongs in a security report rather 
than an issue: you have told people they can point this library at a web request, and the 
goal that makes that safe is the one that does not hold. 
 With def_list loaded, or with extra, which bundles it: 
   496 definition entries, 5,345 B -> renders fine
497 definition entries, 5,356 B -> RecursionError

python3 -c "import markdown; print(markdown.Markdown(extensions=['extra']).convert(chr(10).join(f't{j}{chr(10)}:   d' for j in range(497))))"
   
 The RecursionError propagates straight out of md.convert(). I checked: it is not caught and 
converted into anything, it escapes. Default recursion limit here is 1000, and the threshold 
is sharp at 497, which is consistent with about two frames per entry. 
 So 5.4 KB of entirely ordinary looking markdown, a definition list with 497 terms, crashes 
the renderer. For anything rendering user supplied markdown in a request that is a 500 
rather than a slow response. 
 I am including it here because you already treat this class as a security issue in this 
library:  CVE-2025-69534  is "Python-Markdown has an Uncaught Exception", where malformed HTML 
like sequences raised an unhandled AssertionError, fixed in 3.8.1. This is the same shape 
with a different trigger. 
 Suggested fix 
 The cheap guard handles the worst case in getText. Before the loop, if there is no "]" 
anywhere after index then the brackets cannot balance: 
   if data.find(']', index) == -1:
    return '', index, False
   
 That turns "[" * n from quadratic into linear. 
 It does not fix every shape, because bracket_balanced and ref_open do contain closing 
brackets and are still quadratic. The complete fix is to stop rescanning from scratch at 
every candidate, for instance by hopping with str.find instead of a per character Python 
loop, and by not building text until the match is known to resolve. Building a string that 
gets discarded on the failure path is waste regardless of the complexity question. 
 find_code_spans needs the same treatment: it can precompute the backtick run positions once 
per text rather than rescanning from each opener. 
 Because five of the six shapes funnel through one function, a fix in getText covers most of 
this at once. 
 I tested the same payloads against cmark-gfm, and they are linear there 
 This is not theoretical, and it is the reason I think the fix is worth doing rather than 
documenting as a known limit. 
 Earlier in the same work I swept cmark-gfm, compiled to WebAssembly, over 26 payload shapes 
at sizes from 250 bytes to 256,000 bytes. The shapes included open bracket runs, bracket 
pairs, unclosed links, backtick runs, nested blockquotes, nested lists and many reference 
definitions, which is the same family I am reporting here. 
 Every one was linear. Per byte cost stayed flat across a 1,000x size range. 
 So a C markdown parser handles these exact inputs in linear time, after it was hit by 
CVE-2023-22486 and added dedicated quadratic fuzzers in 2023. The inputs are not 
pathological in some unavoidable way, they are pathological for this implementation. 
 Prior art 
 I checked before writing. The same mechanism has a CVE in two sibling projects: 
 Mistune,  CVE-2026-49851 , fixed in 3.3.0: "Under specific conditions involving dense, 
unmatched nesting of opening square brackets, the parser fallback loops degrade from linear 
execution time to a worst-case quadratic complexity." 
 cmark-gfm, CVE-2023-22486, fixed in 0.29.0.gfm.7: "Quadratic complexity bug in 
handle_close_bracket may lead to a denial of service." 
 The python-markdown CVE I could find,  CVE-2025-69534 , is a different bug: malformed HTML 
like sequences causing an unhandled AssertionError in html.parser, fixed in 3.8.1. I could 
not find any python-markdown advisory for quadratic bracket or backtick parsing. 
 Honest limits 
 CPU only. Peak memory stays between 0.3 and 0.6 MB on every arm. 
 Severity depends on the consumer's input cap and the library has none of its own, so I 
cannot give you a single number. I found this while measuring Zulip, where messages are 
capped at 10,000 characters and rendering is wrapped in a 5 second timeout, so there it 
burns the budget and gets killed. Applications without a cap or a timeout are worse off, and 
30 KB is a perfectly ordinary document size. 
 The payloads are visually obvious, a line of "[" or backticks, so a content check could 
block these exact shapes. That does not fix the complexity. 
 Measured on Python 3.13.14 on Windows with Markdown 3.11 from PyPI. Absolute times will 
differ on other platforms. The scan/n^2 constants are character counts, so those do not 
depend on the platform. 
 Thanks, 
furkan 
 -- 
 A 30,001 byte document consisting of "[" characters takes 126.99 seconds to render on 
current 3.11. The output is the same size as the input, so the parser spends two minutes 
and produces nothing. Fitted exponent across the range is 2.06, so it is quadratic, and I 
measured that rather than projecting it. 
 There are two independent quadratic scanners behind this and six payload shapes that reach 
them. The worst per byte is "![[" repeated, which persuades all six inline processors to 
scan the remaining text, giving 9 times n squared characters scanned. 
 I instrumented the scanners and counted. The characters scanned come to exactly 1.50, 3.00, 
5.00 or 9.00 times n squared depending on the shape, with the constant being simply how 
many processors the payload triggers. On five of the six shapes every single call fails to 
resolve, so 100% of the scanning and string building is thrown away. At n=4,000 that is 
24,006,041 list appends. 
 How bad this is depends on the consumer, and I want to be straight about that, because the 
library has no input size limit of its own. The ceiling is whatever the application 
accepts. 30 KB is an ordinary README. A wiki page, a pull request description, a docs 
build, or a comment field with no cap gets the full quadratic. Zulip, where I found this, 
caps messages at 10,000 characters and wraps rendering in a 5 second timeout, so there an 
attacker burns the whole budget and the request is killed, which is a much softer landing 
than an uncapped consumer gets. 
 This is CPU only. Peak memory stays under 1 MB on every arm, so it is not memory 
exhaustion. 
 Two more things from the same sweep. 
 The first one goes against your own stated goal, which is why I am leading with it. Your 
docs/index.md lists this first under Goals: 
 "Maintain a Python library (with an optional CLI wrapper) suited to use in web server 
environments (never raise an exception, never write to stdout, etc.)" 
 With def_list loaded, or with extra which bundles it, a definition list of 497 terms in 
5,356 bytes makes md.convert() raise an uncaught RecursionError. 496 terms renders fine, so 
the threshold is sharp. That is a crash rather than a slowdown, a 500 for anything rendering 
user markdown in a request, and it is the same class as  CVE-2025-69534  which you already 
fixed as a security issue. I am not reading "never raise an exception" as a promise you broke 
on purpose, I am pointing out that the goal and the deployment context it names are exactly 
what makes this a security issue rather than a bug report. 
 Second, the toc extension has a quadratic worse in absolute terms than anything else here: 
8,000 ATX headers in 64 KB takes 64.2 seconds, against 0.239 seconds for the same document 
with no extensions loaded. 
 The bracket mechanism already has a CVE in two sibling projects. Mistune fixed it in 3.3.0 as 
 CVE-2026-49851 , described as "dense, unmatched nesting of opening square brackets" 
degrading "to a worst-case quadratic complexity". cmark-gfm fixed it in 0.29.0.gfm.7 as 
CVE-2023-22486, "Quadratic complexity bug in handle_close_bracket". python-markdown looks 
like the one that did not get the fix, and I checked that directly rather than inferring it: 
I ran the same payloads through cmark-gfm from 250 bytes to 256,000 bytes and every one was 
linear.                  Activity                 kedi   commented   on   Oct 13, 2026            kedi      on Oct 13, 2026           Author       More actions          One thing I should have led with, now that I have looked at how you handled the last one of 
these. 
  CVE-2025-69534  was an uncaught exception raised while parsing untrusted markdown, reported 
through issue  #1534  and fixed in 3.8.1. I think the RecursionError above is the same class 
with a different trigger, and it is still present in 3.11. 
 A definition list of 497 terms, 5,356 bytes, makes md.convert() raise an uncaught 
RecursionError. 496 terms renders fine, so the threshold is sharp at a single entry. It 
propagates out of md.convert() rather than being caught and converted, so for anything 
rendering user markdown inside a request it is a 500 rather than a slow response. 
 python3 -c "import markdown; markdown.Markdown(extensions=['extra']).convert( 
chr(10).join(f't{j}{chr(10)}:   d' for j in range(497)))" 
 The quadratic parsing in the report above is a separate problem and I am not trying to merge 
the two. This one is the crash. 
 So the ask is just this: do you consider the RecursionError in scope for the same treatment as 
 #1534 ? A yes or no is enough for me to know whether to keep working on it.                           facelessuser   commented   on   Oct 13, 2026            facelessuser      on Oct 13, 2026           Collaborator       More actions          This is a massive wall of text, and to be honest, each individual case should have been its own issue instead of lumping them all together. 
 Admittedly, some recent changes in the library can allow us to refactor a number of these inline cases, allowing us to scan once and avoid rescanning; we just need to rewrite those inline processors to do exactly this. 
 I would duplicate link discusion to  #798 . This should be able to more intelligently handled once refactored to take advantage of some our recent changes to the inline treeprocessor. We just need to get around to the refactor. 
 While backticks were improved some recently, as stated previously, with some of the recent changes, we should be able to properly scan and avoid rescanning with another refactor, once we get around to doing that work. 
 While it was stated that emphasis is linear, there are absolutely pathological cases in this area which  #1632  will help to address. 
 I stopped looking after that. 
 This is my personal opinion, but I'd like to not see issues filed like this in the future. Each individual case should be its own issue so we can tackle them individually.

      Title: Accuracy is not compatibility: two Evo 2 checkpoints hinge on one FP8 matrix multiplication 
      Authors:  Xun Ding  (Independent researcher),  Ziyuan Qin  (Emory University)              View a PDF of the paper titled Accuracy is not compatibility: two Evo 2 checkpoints hinge on one FP8 matrix multiplication, by Xun Ding (Independent researcher) and 1 other authors

             Abstract: FP8 formats specify how values are stored, not how products are summed; this gap can break checkpoints. Evo 2, a DNA language model, documents a Hopper FP8 requirement for its 1B and 40B checkpoints. On two Blackwell (sm_120) GPUs both fail the developers' forward test (the 7B passes); on an RTX 5070 Ti the 40B's next-base accuracy is 25.7%, near guessing. Greater accuracy breaks them, as BioNeMo saw for the 40B on Hopper: natively, 99.996% of one projection's outputs are correctly rounded (H100: about 30%), and fp32 accumulation of the same operands fails. Our H100 FP8 GEMM emulator, mmaemu (bit-exact on captured 1B projections), localises the dependence to the 1B's first projection (of 21), where exact sums fail but pass when shrunk by the H100's 1.4% (measured in-sample), not 2.1%. The 40B fails with only its first projection native. Emulating only that projection, weights unchanged, raises 40B BRCA1 variant-classification AUROC from 0.434 to 0.869 (H100: 0.868) on the RTX 5070 Ti, despite a narrow forward-test miss, and 0.481 to 0.867 on an RTX PRO 6000. We tested one model family but not training origin; releases should specify reference arithmetic.

 Accuracy is not compatibility: two Evo 2 checkpoints hinge on one FP8 matrix multiplication 
 
 
 Xun Ding
   †    †  thanks:  ORCID 0000-0001-7719-7268. Correspondence:
 dxun1@alumni.jh.edu      
  Affiliation:  Independent researcher
    
     
 Ziyuan Qin
   †    †  thanks:   zqin30@emory.edu      
  Affiliation:  Emory University, United States of America
     

  Abstract 
    
 FP8 formats specify how values are stored, not how products are summed; this gap can break
checkpoints. Evo 2, a DNA language model, documents a Hopper FP8 requirement for its 1B and 40B
checkpoints. On two Blackwell (sm_120) GPUs both fail the developers’ forward test (the 7B passes); on an
RTX 5070 Ti the 40B’s next-base accuracy is 25.7%, near guessing. Greater accuracy breaks them, as BioNeMo
saw for the 40B on Hopper: natively, 99.996% of one projection’s outputs are correctly rounded (H100: about
30%), and fp32 accumulation of the same operands fails. Our H100 FP8 GEMM emulator, mmaemu (bit-exact
on captured 1B projections), localises the dependence to the 1B’s first projection (of 21), where exact sums
fail but pass when shrunk by the H100’s 1.4% (measured in-sample), not 2.1%. The 40B fails with only its
first projection native. Emulating only that projection, weights unchanged, raises 40B  BRCA1 
variant-classification AUROC from 0.434 to 0.869 (H100: 0.868) on the RTX 5070 Ti, despite a narrow forward-test
miss, and 0.481 to 0.867 on an RTX PRO 6000. We tested one model family but not training origin;
releases should specify reference arithmetic. 
  
 
 
  1  Introduction 

 
 When a released low-precision checkpoint runs on a new GPU or kernel, which arithmetic properties must the new
implementation preserve? The number format does not say: the OCP FP8 specification defines how values are
encoded and excludes arithmetic on them from its scope  [ 1 ] . Tensor cores differ in how many bits
they keep while accumulating FP8 products, 13 fraction bits on measured Hopper and Ada GPUs against 25 on the
B200 and RTX PRO 6000  [ 2 ] , and libraries choose how partial sums are split and combined
 [ 3 ] . That extra intermediate precision can change a program’s results is well known
 [ 4 ] , and changing the GPU version can change the outputs of large language models
 [ 5 ] . More accurate FP8 accumulation is a sound choice in training
 [ 6 ] ; we ask whether a checkpoint with fixed weights keeps its
function when its accumulation changes, even towards greater accuracy. 
 
 
 Evo 2 is a substantial contribution to long-context genomic modelling  [ 7 ] . The Arc Institute and its collaborators share weights, inference software, tests
with explicit tolerances and evaluation notebooks  [ 8 ] , and variant effects can be scored
zero-shot from changes in sequence likelihood  [ 9 ,  10 ,  7 ] . The inference
code uses FP8 input projections in the Hyena blocks of StripedHyena 2
 [ 11 ,  12 ,  13 ] . The README lists FP8 on a Hopper GPU as a
requirement for the 1B, 20B and 40B checkpoints and advises validating outputs after hardware changes
 [ 8 ] ; our experiments explore portability beyond that documented requirement. 
 
 
 Public reports describe failures of these upstream tests on consumer Blackwell GPUs and B200s, alongside a passing 7B
 [ 14 ,  15 ] . NVIDIA’s BioNeMo documentation notes that enabling more accurate accumulation breaks the original
40B even on Hopper and reports the original 1B working on
a B300 under its own stack and evaluation  [ 16 ] . A fine-tuning project attributes 20B/40B
failures to Hopper accumulation and localises a dependence to block 23  [ 17 ] . The phenomenon
is therefore known; missing is a controlled path from an arithmetic change to a localised dependence and back
to recovery with the weights fixed. 
 
 
 We call the upstream Transformer Engine (TE) FP8 path  official , and the H100 PCIe and RTX 4060 running
it our  reference GPUs ; on one measured projection their outputs lean towards zero, consistent with
truncating accumulation. mmaemu  [ 18 ] , our emulator of their FP8 matrix
multiplications (GEMMs), lets us change the arithmetic of chosen projections while the executing GPU, weights
and FP8 operands stay fixed: in effect, bisecting a model by arithmetic. Unlike instruction-level models such as
MMA-Sim  [ 19 ] , mmaemu emulates whole library GEMM calls. Five findings follow: the more accurate GEMM is the incompatible one; one early
projection carries most of the dependence; in the 1B, that projection passes with a slight shrinkage like the
reference’s, not with exact sums or more accumulator bits; downstream of it, the native difference collapsed the
1B but matched-size random perturbations did not; and restoring that projection alone recovers variant scoring
on two GPUs. Beyond Evo 2,
the case shows that operator agreement, model function and application agreement can disagree, and suggests a
cheap screen, untested elsewhere, for other FP8 checkpoints: rerun their tests accumulating the same operands
in fp32 (a pass does not rule dependence out). The study
concerns one model family, and whether training produced the dependence is not tested. 
 
   
  Figure 1:   Arithmetic accuracy and checkpoint compatibility are different targets. 
 a , Evo 2 1B. Left: share of the 11,796,480 outputs of block 0’s FP8 projection on one 2,048-bp window
that equal the correctly rounded bf16 value (one GEMM, whose rows embed only four distinct tokens: 23,040 distinct dot products; other projections and windows were not analysed). Right:
next-base accuracy of the whole model over the four upstream test prompts (printed by the test; not its pass
criterion). The comparison is across devices: the reference GPUs ran the official Transformer Engine path,
whereas the RTX 5070 Ti’s native FP8 projections called  torch._scaled_mm ; panel b’s fp32 rows are the
within-device control.
 b , Each square is one FP8 input projection, in model order; the first is block 0’s. All runs used the
RTX 5070 Ti, with every other operation native. Emulated squares are live mmaemu  hopper-te ; the hatched
square is a lookup table of emulated  hopper-te  block-0 outputs; fp32 squares accumulate the same E4M3
operands in IEEE fp32. Filled circles pass the upstream forward test (within 0.001 of the expected loss),
crosses fail, and the open circle lies 0.0011 from the expected value, just outside the tolerance; with the other
40B projections in bf16 the table gives 0.2168, within it (Table   1  ). Each loss is a mean of four bf16
per-prompt values, so distinct runs can print identical means (e.g. 1.2480).
 c , 40B AUROC on 500  BRCA1  variants (111 LoF), with conditional 95% variant-bootstrap
intervals. Within each native/table pair the GPU, weights, software stack and cohort are fixed and only
block 0’s FP8 projection changes; on the PRO 6000, native is the unmodified upstream path. The dashed line is the
H100 reference (cu128), so comparing the PRO 6000 (cu13) column with it changes both device and stack; the dotted
line marks 0.5. AUROCs are not ranked, and recovered variant scoring does not certify the forward or generation
tests. 
 
 
 
  2  Results 

 
  2.1  A more accurate GEMM breaks two checkpoints 

 
 Two of the three tested checkpoints fail on both sm_120 GPUs. We ran the published weights on the reference
GPUs and on an RTX 5070 Ti (sm_120), varying only the FP8 input projections (21 GEMMs in the 1B, 42 in the
40B) and leaving all other computation native (Methods). The upstream forward test passes if the mean
next-base cross-entropy over four prompts lies within 0.001 of an expected value. With native FP8 (the GPU’s own kernels), the
RTX 5070 Ti gave 1.2480 for the 1B and 1.4023 for the 40B, 2.5 and 6.5 times the expected 0.5020 and
0.2159; the H100 passed both.
The 40B predicted the next base correctly 25.7% of the time, close to the 25% of guessing among four bases,
against 91.6% on the same GPU with mmaemu’s emulation of the H100’s TE path ( hopper-te ) and 91.7% on
the H100. The 1B’s accuracy roughly halved (Fig.   1  a), and it
failed the generation test (32.65% identity against     68.0  ±  3   68.0\pm 3   ). Running bf16 GEMMs, which change operand quantisation
as well as accumulation, failed (Table   1  ). The 7B, whose input projections also use
FP8, passed natively (0.3477). An RTX PRO 6000 running the unmodified upstream path under a separate CUDA 13 (cu13)
stack showed the same pattern (Table   1  ; the 7B passed both tests), as did a public 1B report from
another RTX 5070 Ti  [ 14 ] . 
 
 
 At the measured projection, the native GEMM was the more accurate one (Fig.   1  a). For
the 1B’s first projection on one 2,048-bp window, the RTX 5070 Ti returned the correctly rounded bf16 value for
99.996% of outputs, against about 30% on either reference GPU, whose deviations lean towards zero. We then kept each projection’s E4M3 operands, scales and output epilogue fixed and
accumulated the products in IEEE fp32 or, for the 1B, also in float64 rounded once to fp32. Both gave the native
loss of 1.2480 in the 1B, and fp32 accumulation gave the native 1.4023 in the 40B: more
accurate accumulation of the same operands, with no FP8 kernel involved, reproduces the failure
(Fig.   1  b). Emulating the H100’s more accurate slow-accumulation mode (Methods) at block 0 also failed (1.2275), consistent with BioNeMo’s note  [ 16 ] . 
 
 
 Exact agreement with one reference GPU was not needed either. The H100 and RTX 4060 differed on every one of
the 21 captured projections of this window, yet both supported the expected model behaviour (the RTX 4060 by
fp32 loss and AUROC); their tensor cores accumulate in blocks of different sizes
 [ 2 ] . For the tested first-projection calls, a truncating chain retaining 25 fraction bits
matched the RTX 5070 Ti’s native outputs bit for bit; this is not a general model of sm_120. 
 
 
 The failure reached a scientific application. Following the upstream notebook, we scored a seeded subset of
500  BRCA1  variants, classified by a genome-editing assay  [ 20 ]  (111 loss-of-function,
LoF), by the change in mean sequence log-probability between
variant and reference windows (Table   1  ). The 1B’s area under the receiver operating characteristic
curve (AUROC) was 0.733 on the H100 and 0.738 on the RTX 4060, but 0.559 with native FP8. The 40B gave 0.868 on
the H100 and 0.434 natively, below 0.5 (95% interval 0.373–0.497; we do not interpret the direction), with
per-variant scores essentially uncorrelated with the H100’s (Pearson     −  0.032   -0.032   ; 50.4% same sign).

  2.2  Swapping one projection’s arithmetic localises the dependence 

 
 mmaemu computes the scaled FP8
GEMM of a named reference platform, a specific H100 PCIe or RTX 4060 configuration, on another CUDA GPU
 [ 18 ] . Its profiles model the tensor-core accumulation chain, the library’s split-K behaviour
and the output epilogue. It reproduces bit for bit all 168 captured H100 outputs of the 1B’s 21 projections (two
output types, two accumulation modes, two APIs; Methods), and a
rule for combining split-K partial sums, fitted on an initial probe, matched all 2,416 split calls of a later
sweep at the splits the H100 used. Longer windows and all 40B projections rely on the validated model rather
than direct H100 captures. With either profile ( hopper-te , or  ada-te  for the RTX 4060’s TE path), both checkpoints
passed the upstream forward test on the RTX 5070 Ti (Table   1  ).
Whole-model logits still differed from the reference GPUs’, because convolutions, attention, bf16 GEMMs and
normalisation ran natively. 
 
 
 We then changed individual projections (Fig.   1  b) under a locally hashed, self-attested
analysis plan (PLAN_C; Methods). With only block 0’s
projection computed by  hopper-te  and the other 20 native, the 1B passed its forward test (0.5027); with
block 0 native and the other 20 emulated, it failed (1.2500). The 1B’s block 23, whose H100 outputs shrink more
(least-squares gain against exact outputs 0.982, against 0.986 at block 0), stayed native in the passing configuration. Block 0’s
projection sees the normalised embedding of a single token, so its outputs for all 512 token ids (plus zero pad
rows) fit in a lookup table, which matched live emulation on every call. With this table and every other
projection native, the 1B also passed the generation test (70.95% against     68.0  ±  3   68.0\pm 3   ). 
 
 
 The same projection mattered in the 40B. With block 0 native and the other 41 projections emulated, it failed
(1.4277). With block 0’s table and every other projection native, it gave 0.2170, a deviation of 0.0011 from the
expected value against a tolerance of 0.001; with the others in bf16 it gave 0.2168, within tolerance
(Table   1  ). In both checkpoints, native arithmetic at this
projection is enough to cause failure, and in the 40B restoring it alone comes close to restoring the forward
test. The fine-tuning project’s block-23 localisation  [ 17 ]  uses other criteria and GPUs.

  2.4  Matched-size random changes after block 0 did not collapse the model 

 
 In captures from a separate 35-run study under a locally hashed plan, block 0’s residual addition largely
cancels its branch output: across it, the native-minus-F13 discrepancy kept its absolute size but grew
12.5–13.4-fold in relative size, so the sum is about that much smaller in norm than the branch. The study
asked whether size alone explains the collapse, perturbing the residual stream after this addition and before block 0’s MLP
(Fig.   2  d). Injecting the full native-minus-F13 residual difference gave a mean fp32 loss of 1.2488.
Five Gaussian directions whose realised per-token L2 norms matched it within 1% gave 0.5023–0.5027 and passed
the test’s bf16 criterion; at amplitude 0.75 (   λ  \lambda   , the injected fraction), one
random direction narrowly missed it and the native-shaped target also missed it. Splitting the observed branch
difference into components parallel and orthogonal to the reference branch gave fp32 losses of 0.5094 and
0.5033 separately, both missing the bf16 criterion but far below their combination’s 1.2488. At this node and on these prompts,
the structured native difference collapsed the model while matched-norm random changes did not; direction,
channel structure and cross-token correlation were not separated. 
 
 
 
  2.5  One projection’s emulated outputs restore variant scoring on two GPUs 

 
 For the 1B’s 500 variants, full  hopper-te  emulation and the H100 had score-change Pearson correlation
0.988 and 86.0% sign agreement, compared with 0.987 and 84.2% between the two reference GPUs; paired bootstrap
differences included zero and AUROC intervals overlapped, which shows agreement, not equivalence or rank. The
block-0 table with all other projections native gave AUROC 0.735, Pearson 0.986 and 86.0% sign
agreement against the H100, not distinguishable from the reference pair at this sample size. 
 
 
 For the 40B on the RTX 5070 Ti, the table raised AUROC from 0.434 to 0.869 (paired difference 0.435, 95%
interval 0.360–0.507), with Pearson correlation 0.997 and 97.4% sign agreement against the H100
(Figs.   1  c and   3  e,f); full  hopper-te  emulation gave 0.998 and 97.4%
(no 40B reference-pair band exists: the RTX 4060 ran out of memory). The table’s forward loss of 0.2170
still misses tolerance (Section   2.2  ): application agreement is distinct from forward-test
compatibility. 
 
 
 Within the PRO 6000 configuration (cu13), the same intervention raised AUROC from 0.556 to 0.721 for the 1B and
from 0.481 to 0.867 for the 40B on the same 500 variants (Fig.   3  a–d); the 40B’s paired
improvement was 0.385 (0.306–0.463). The 40B’s per-variant correlation with the earlier H100 reference rose from
    −  0.082   -0.082    to 0.997 (Table   1  ), but that comparison changes both device and software stack, whereas the
within-PRO intervention holds both fixed.

  3  Discussion 

 
 For fixed weights, the more accurate GEMM was the incompatible one, as BioNeMo observed on Hopper
 [ 16 ] . These experiments trace this change to one projection, to a candidate property in the
1B, and back to recovery with the weights unchanged. The lesson
is not that less accurate arithmetic is safer: a larger shrinkage and round-to-nearest at reference precision
failed as surely as exact sums. Rather, a fixed checkpoint can depend on specific properties of its reference
arithmetic. We do not estimate how common such dependence is among low-precision models; even within Evo 2, the
7B passes. 
 
 
 Validation should separate operator agreement, model function and application agreement, which disagreed here.
The two reference GPUs differ in every projection’s bits yet both support the expected behaviour; full emulation
passes the forward tests with logits that differ from the H100’s; the 40B table restores AUROC while missing the
forward tolerance. Repeated runs of the tested calls were bit-identical on each platform, and on the tested
fixed-operand calls the two sm_120 GPUs matched bit for bit under the same cu13 stack, whereas the RTX 5070 Ti’s native outputs
for the first projection differed from both reference GPUs’: determinism is not compatibility. The two
reference GPUs also agreed on the sign of only 84.2% of 1B variant effects; all disagreements involved effects
below four times the mean cross-GPU difference in    Δ  \Delta    (computed for this paper). Scientific analyses should retain execution provenance and read small score changes against measured
platform variation. 
 
 
 Evo 2’s upstream tests exposed this dependence.
Releases could add application reference outputs and tolerances, together with the GPU configuration, software
stack and effective accumulation mode. Libraries could expose the mode actually used: cuBLAS documents its
fast-accumulation flag as taking effect only on Ada and Hopper  [ 3 ] , and on the
RTX 5070 Ti the flag changed none of the tested outputs. Substituting emulated reference GEMMs one projection at a time could then
localise such dependence; like the fp32 screen (Introduction), it is untested beyond Evo 2. Where a sensitive layer’s input depends only on the token id, its
reference outputs can be tabulated: on the RTX 5070 Ti, an 8,192-bp 1B forward pass took 16% longer with the
table than natively (medians; table construction excluded), whereas full emulation took 2.2 times as long; with
native FP8 elsewhere, the 40B table missed the forward tolerance. Fine-tuning offers another route, with native kernels and changed weights
 [ 16 ] ; BioNeMo’s original 1B working on a B300, under another stack and evaluation, is an
important boundary case that these experiments do not explain. 
 
 
 Training could compensate for an arithmetic effect whose later removal changes the model’s function: if
    r  =   x  +   α  ​  w  ​  x     r=x+\alpha wx    (input    x  x   , GEMM gain    α  \alpha   , weight    w  w   ) is fitted to a small target     ϵ  ​  x   \epsilon x   , replacing

 Limitations. 

 
 We tested one model family on two sm_120 GPUs; the 20B, B200 and B300 were not run, and the 7B has no reference-GPU comparison. Reference evidence is one H100 PCIe and one RTX 4060
configuration. The PRO follow-up changes software as well as hardware relative to the original experiments. There are no direct
H100 captures of 40B projections or tests above 8,192 projection rows. The 40B table misses the forward
tolerance on the RTX 5070 Ti, the PRO table’s forward loss was not recorded, and 40B generation was not tested
under emulation or with the table. Biology is one assay and one 500-variant cohort; bootstrap intervals are
conditional on the recorded runs and model neither overlapping-window dependence nor run-to-run variation. The
gain is in-sample, and no rescaling correction was tested. Mechanism controls use four previously studied
prompts. mmaemu does not
support bias, row-wise scales, autograd or CUDA graphs. 
 
 
 
 
  4  Methods 

 
 Models and software. 

 
 We used the Evo 2 checkpoints  evo2_1b_base  and  evo2_40b   [ 7 ] , and  evo2_7b  (PLAN_C and PRO 6000, below). The 1B has 21 FP8 input projections with     K  =  1,920   K=1{,}920    and     N  =  5,760   N=5{,}760   ; the 40B has 42, with     K  =  8,192   K=8{,}192   
and     N  =  24,576   N=24{,}576   . Original reference runs used evo2 0.6.0, vtx 1.1.0
 [ 11 ] , torch 2.7.1+cu128  [ 21 ]  and Transformer Engine 2.3.0; the RTX 5070 Ti ran the same
stack without Transformer Engine, its native FP8 projections calling  torch._scaled_mm . The original Evo 2 runs with
mmaemu  [ 18 ]  predate
its 0.1.0 tag ( ada-te : development build 0.1.0.dev0, 14–15 October;  hopper-te : commit fa0fd90, 16 October); with
the released code, the upstream tests (1B with both profiles; 40B with  hopper-te ) and 40  BRCA1 
windows gave bit-identical outputs. Later runs used the
release. 
 
 
 
 Platforms. 

 
 The reference platforms are an NVIDIA H100 PCIe (sm_90, 114 SMs, driver 570.148.08) and a GeForce RTX 4060 (sm_89,
24 SMs, driver 572.16), both with cuBLASLt 12.8.3.14. The H100 was rented four times on 14–16 October 2026. The RTX 5070 Ti (sm_120, 70 SMs, 16 GB,
driver 610.88) runs mmaemu but is not a reference platform. 
 
 
 
 Execution modes. 

 
 On the RTX 5070 Ti, bf16 mode runs the original weights in a bf16 GEMM, and mmaemu uses kernels h4
( hopper-te ) and v4 ( ada-te ). The 40B, too large
for the GPU, runs one block at a time from host memory (offload). On the 1B, offload gave the resident model’s logits
exactly on every test window checked. The official 40B runs,
and the H100’s 1B test losses, ran the upstream blocks one at a time with Transformer Engine; on the 1B this gave the
upstream model’s logits bit for bit on both reference GPUs. 
 
 
 
 PRO 6000 follow-up. 

 
 The follow-up used an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (sm_120, 188 SMs, 96 GB), driver 580.178.04,
torch 2.14.1+cu130, cuBLASLt 13.1.1 and Transformer Engine 2.20.2, with the same Evo 2/vtx versions and
released mmaemu tree. Its plan and package hashes preceded GPU measurements; the plan was informed by earlier
results and was not externally preregistered. All three checkpoints passed full-file SHA-256 checks before loading. Models stayed resident. For operator comparisons, the RTX 5070 Ti ran the same torch and cuBLASLt. 
 
 
 The same exported cohort supplied 435 reference and 500 variant windows to the upstream scoring API,
with batch size one and no BOS. The table substitution was gated by bit-identical patched-native and official
logits on one prespecified reference window, then matched live emulation on every substituted block-0 call.
New AUROC intervals and paired differences use the existing variant-bootstrap procedure, computed post hoc. 
 
 
 The unmodified forward and generation tests ran in fresh processes. After the original resident 40B generation
test exhausted memory during Hyena FFT cache prefill, a dated supplement reran it through the public API with
 force_prompt_threshold=128 , keeping weights, prompts, seed and scoring but changing prefill scheduling;
the native FP8 40B on the PRO 6000 reached 23.95% identity against     91.15  ±  3   91.15\pm 3    expected. The supplement is reported separately
from the original matrix, which completed 13 of 14 application cells. 
 
 
 
 Evaluation and statistics. 

 
 The upstream test ( test_evo2.py ) averages the bf16 next-base cross-entropies (natural logarithm) of four
prompts and passes within     10   −  3    10^{-3}    of the expected loss (1B 0.501953125; 7B 0.3476563; 40B 0.2159424). It also
prints next-base accuracy (argmax agreement), which is not part of its pass rule; guessing among four bases gives
25%. The generation test greedily continues the first half of each prompt for 500 bases and passes within 3
points of the expected identity with the true continuation (1B 68.0%, 7B 89.25%, 40B 91.15%).
We followed the upstream notebook’s  BRCA1  scoring procedure on a subset selected by
 sample(n=500, random_state=0) : 500 of 3,893 variants, including 111 LoF variants.
These AUROCs are not comparable with full-set values. Windows of 8,192 bp are centred on the
variant, and    Δ  \Delta    is the variant window’s mean next-base log-probability minus the reference window’s. The AUROC
of     −  Δ   -\Delta    for LoF has a 95% percentile bootstrap interval (2,000 unstratified variant resamples; NumPy
 default_rng(0) ). Functional and intermediate variants form the negative class. Paired comparisons use resamples shared across runs.
These intervals are conditional on the recorded inference runs and do not quantify uncertainty across genomic
regions, assays or GPU runs. 
 
 
 A later cu128 follow-up extended five RTX 5070 Ti 40B configurations from 100 to 500 variants on
20–21 October 2026. The first-100 outcomes were known; inputs and scripts were locally hashed before measurement.
Each configuration rescored 935 windows. All 198 first-100 window scores matched
their historical files bit for bit in every configuration; all 935 table calls matched live  hopper-te . 
 
 
 
 Arithmetic model. 

 
 mmaemu models a tensor-core FP8 GEMM as chains of block fused multiply-adds, each adding a block of products to
an incoming accumulator in one operation  [ 22 ,  2 ,  23 ,  24 ] ,
with blocks of 16 ( ada ) or 32 ( hopper ) products. Each block aligns its products and incoming
accumulator to a common exponent, truncates the aligned terms towards zero to 13 fraction bits, sums them exactly,
then truncates the result to 13 fraction bits relative to its own leading bit. Slow accumulation sums 128-element
chains in round-to-nearest fp32. Split-K deals 64-wide    k  k   -tiles to the splits in turn on the RTX 4060. On the H100, each
split takes contiguous 128-wide tiles and the partial sums are added serially. The epilogue computes
    bf16  ⁡   (    RN  32   ​   (    𝑎𝑐𝑐  ⋅   RN  32    ​   (    s  a   ​   s  b    )    )    )    \mathrm{bf16}(\mathrm{RN}_{32}(\mathit{acc}\cdot\mathrm{RN}_{32}(s_{a}s_{b})))   . For the 168 H100 comparisons,
full outputs were stored for three of the 21 projections and the first 256 rows for the other 18. 
 
 
 
 Additional runs for this paper. 

 
 Runs A7, A9, A11 and A12 on the RTX 5070 Ti were specified, with their criteria and readings, in a plan hashed (self-attested) on 17
October 2026 before any of them started; all use tag  v0.1.0 .
 A7  recomputed the first 1B projection natively from the recorded operands; as a gate, it reproduced the
recorded difference count. It then compared all outputs with the exact product, accumulated in
float64 (exact at     K  =  1,920   K=1{,}920   ), scaled and rounded once to bf16.
 A9  (accumulation control) dequantises the E4M3 operands exactly, accumulates them in IEEE fp32 (TensorFloat-32
off) or in float64 rounded once to fp32, and applies mmaemu’s epilogue. An amendment, hashed before the A9 runs, adds the 40B upstream test
with fp32 accumulation; a smoke test of both modes on two 1B windows had finished about one minute earlier, and
whether its output had been seen is not recorded. A second amendment dropped a planned 40B  BRCA1  run before
it started.  A11  timed native  torch._scaled_mm  and kernels h4 and v4 with CUDA events on synthetic
operands of Evo 2 GEMM shapes; full emulated calls took 21.8–27.7 (h4) and 23.0–28.5 (v4) times
as long as native.
 A12  rescored 40 windows of the  hopper-te  1B  BRCA1  pass, which had run through offload, on the
resident model. 
 
 
 
 Localisation runs (PLAN_C). 

 
 The single-projection runs of Sections   2.1  –  2.2  , the runs of Section   2.3  , the block-0 tables,
the generation test and the 7B were specified, with classes, gates and readings, in an analysis plan (PLAN_C) frozen by SHA-256 on 18 October 2026 at
16:20 PDT, before any of its GPU runs. The hash is self-attested, not deposited with a third party before the runs, and the plan
text did not change. A ten-entry deviation log records re-hashed code fixes and run-setting changes, errata, an
analysis note, amendments for another plan and run-order changes; the timing step, initially deferred, completed on
19 October with the frozen command. The analysis scripts were not frozen before the runs; the  BRCA1  statistics script was
written after the scores existed. Classes: strict, the upstream pass criterion; broken, above 1.0. The block-0
diagnostics, not fixes, were: the exact sum times    g  g   , or (Ea) times the H100’s least-squares gain against it,
    a  =  0.985869   a=0.985869   , fitted on one of six evaluated windows (in-sample);  hopper-te ’s accumulator divided by    a  a   
(Ha) or times     1  +   σ  ​  z    1+\sigma z    (   z  z    standard normal per output, fixed per distinct input row;     σ  =  0.016   \sigma=0.016    or
0.0104; three seeds); and truncating Hopper-structured chains with 13–16 or 25 fraction bits (13 equals
 hopper-te , 25 native, bit for bit) or 13 bits rounded to nearest. The 40B analogues Ea40 and Ha40 use a gain
fitted likewise to  hopper-te ’s block-0 outputs over the test’s own token rows. Distances are
token-weighted relative L2 distances, normalised by the exact outputs; a post hoc CPU recomputation agreed. Cells were grouped after the runs by precedent recorded before them (the same or an
analogous observation). Retests: for the 1B, the test losses of native, bf16 and full emulation, the block-0 localisation and
tables, the exact sum (    g  =  1   g=1   , equal to float64 accumulation), the 13- and 25-bit chains (equal to  hopper-te  and native; that the 25-bit chain equals native bit for bit, gate G3, was new), native’s generation failure (issue #132), the fast-accumulation flag (another software environment),
and block 23, slow accumulation and the table’s  BRCA1  scores (exploratory runs below); for
the 40B, native, full emulation and the table; for the 7B, native (issue #157; an exploratory
bf16 run). All other cells had no recorded precedent, including the scaled and perturbed block-0 outputs
(    g  ≠  1   g\neq 1   , Ea, Ha, noise), the 14–16-bit and round-to-nearest chains, the fp32 residual additions, the generation
tests of the table and of full emulation, and the other 40B and 7B cells. The 7B also passed with full emulation
(0.3481) and the table (0.3477); the 1B’s fp32 residual additions changed no class. 
 
 
 
 Matched residual interventions. 

 
 A subsequent locally hashed plan, informed by PLAN_C and not externally preregistered, specified 35
fresh-process 1B cells using the same cu128 stack and four prompts. We captured the actual biased branch    h  h    and bf16
residual sum    r  r    on the local F13 and native paths, with the other 20 FP8 projections native.
Residual replay and decomposition endpoints reproduced baseline logits bitwise. Five fixed Gaussian seeds were
evaluated at amplitudes 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1, with a shared zero-amplitude reference. Realised post-bf16 per-token
perturbation norms matched the corresponding native-shaped injection within 1% for every token (maximum
relative mismatch 0.166%). Neither labels nor losses entered matching. Branch decomposition used one inner product
per complete prompt. The relative capture ratio of native-minus-F13 discrepancies is
     (    ∥   δ  ​  r   ∥   /   ∥  r  ∥    )   /   (    ∥   δ  ​  h   ∥   /   ∥  h  ∥    )    (\lVert\delta r\rVert/\lVert r\rVert)/(\lVert\delta h\rVert/\lVert h\rVert)   . 
 
 
 
 Exploratory runs. 

 
 Runs on the RTX 4060 on 10–11 October 2026, before mmaemu’s first commit and without criteria fixed in advance,
had shown most retested effects. A quantise–dequantise bf16 stand-in for block 0’s FP8 GEMM gave a high 1B test
loss (1.081), whereas stand-ins for block 23 or the 19 others left it low. A table of block 0’s Transformer Engine
outputs with bf16 elsewhere passed the 1B test, gave a 40B fp32 loss of 0.2165 and gave 1B  BRCA1     Δ  \Delta   
correlating at 0.988 with the official RTX 4060 run. With all 21 projections accumulated in
fp32, or in  torch._scaled_mm  with fast accumulation off, the 1B gave high fp32 losses, but not with the
table and fp32 accumulation elsewhere; fast accumulation on matched Transformer Engine in every recorded digit. The
fp32 runs’ code is not preserved, and the  torch._scaled_mm  runs’ script version is not established. 
 
 
 
 
 Code and data availability 

 
 mmaemu 0.1.0 is free software under the Apache License 2.0, at  https://github.com/astding/mmaemu , on PyPI as
 mmaemu . The v0.1.0 release is archived at  https://zenodo.org/records/23440103 
(version DOI  10.5281/zenodo.23440103 )  [ 18 ] . Documentation:
 https://astding.github.io/mmaemu/ . Repository paths refer to commit  ab37ab1 , which differs from the tag
 v0.1.0  only in documentation and citation metadata.
The release’s validation logs under  docs/validation_logs/  contain the original hardware-validation and Evo 2
inference logs, result files and per-variant  BRCA1  scores.  docs/validation.md  summarises them. The official RTX 4060 Evo 2 1B
outputs are in  examples/data/ , and  examples/evo2_blackwell.ipynb  and  examples/evo2_offload.py 
run Evo 2 with mmaemu. Continuous integration replays committed subsets of the RTX 4060 and H100 recordings.
Larger hardware recordings and later datasets, including runs A7, A9, A11 and A12, PLAN_C with its deviation log,
the matched residual interventions, the RTX PRO 6000 and RTX 5070 Ti 40B 500-variant follow-ups, the exploratory
RTX 4060 probes, a ledger tracing each reported number to its source file, post hoc analyses and figure scripts, are
deposited with SHA-256 manifests at Zenodo (DOI  10.5281/zenodo.23740390 ).
Evo 2 checkpoints are the Arc Institute’s releases on Hugging Face; the  BRCA1  data are those of Findlay et
al.  [ 20 ] , as read by the evo2 notebook.
