readme:SheepSeb/tinyworldformer.text: Using 2 small neural networks to generate and play the game at the same time on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W. The first one creates the game: given the current frame and the action, it predicts the next frame and the reward. The second one plays that game: it uses the generated frame and picks an action. | | | | | |---|---|---|---| | ![](docs/media/dream_breakout.gif) | ![](docs/media/dream_doomlite.gif) | ![](docs/media/dream_flappy.gif) | ![](docs/media/dream_pong.gif) | Every frame above was sampled by the world model network, and the actions were taken by the actor network. ## Why I got interested in looped transformers, where one transformer block is applied several times with the same weights instead of stacking different layers. Reusing weights is cheap on memory, so I wanted to see if a looped world model could be small enough to run on a microcontroller. I picked the Pico 2 W because it is cheap and has an FPU, and small games because I could write the real versions directly into numpy and check every generated frame against them. Later I added a streaming RL agent so the board could also learn to play inside its own dream. Contents: [the two networks](#the-world-model-and-the-actor) · [the games](#the-games) · [the world model](#how-the-world-model-works) · [the agents](#the-agents-stream-x) · [quantization](#quantization-and-the-pico) · [on the chip](#on-the-chip) · [flashing](#flashing-a-game-and-an-agent) · [browser](#in-the-browser) · [reproduce](#reproduce) · [code layout](#code-layout) ## The world model and the actor ![the world model and the actor](docs/media/explain_twonetworks.gif) | | network 1: the world model | network 2: the actor | |---|---|---| | job | frame + action → next frame + reward | frame → action | | architecture | looped transformer, q int8 | MLP with two hidden layers, float32 | | size | 26k–131k parameters | 9k–16k parameters | | cost per frame | 2–8M multiply-adds | 9k–16k multiply-adds | | trained | on recorded real games ([how](#how-the-world-model-works)) | with stream-x, in the real game or inside the dream ([how](#the-agents-stream-x)) | The size depends on the game, some games require more parameters to learn them to be playable, we tried to get to keep the number of the parameters small enough. On the chip neither network ever uses the real game: the actor only sees frames the world model, and the world model only gets actions from the actor. Both run on core 1 of the RP2350, while core 0 handles USB and the display. The pretrained actor can be swapped for a fresh stream-x agent that learns from scratch on the board. And any button press hands control to you, so you can play the dream yourself. ## The games Each game is a few hundred lines of numpy in `src/tinyworldformer/games/`. It renders to a small grid of token ids, and one frame always holds the whole game state, so hidden state has to be drawn into the frame: the ball's heading is part of its token, and Doom-lite has a minimap. | game | frame | rules | random event | world model | exact frames, 2 loops | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Breakout | 20×16 | paddle, ball, 56 bricks, 5 lives | the serve after a miss | 26k params, 4.3M MACs | 99.99% | | Doom-lite | 32×32 | raycast first-person view of an 8×8 maze; an enemy walks shortest paths to you; you shoot | the enemy's respawn | 55k params, 4.2M MACs | 83.6% (see below) | | Flappy Bird | 24×24 | gravity, flaps, scrolling pipes | the next gap height | 46k params, 2.0M MACs | 100% | | Pong | 20×32 | you against a CPU paddle that reacts late, first to 5 | the serve after a point | 46k params, 2.3M MACs | 99.45% | | Pac-Man lite | 48×48 | 23×21 maze, 249 pellets, two ghosts on shortest paths, 3 lives | the ghosts' respawn | 131k params, 8.2M MACs | 86.4% | "Exact frames" is the share of held-out transitions where every cell of the predicted frame matches the real game. Frames right after a random event are left out, since those can only be sampled, not predicted. Doom-lite's 3D view has 768 cells and a single shaded wall pixel off counts the whole frame as wrong, so its number looks worse than it plays; the game state is almost always right (see [checking the dream](#checking-the-dream)). You can play the real games in a terminal: `uv run python -m tinyworldformer.games.play --game pacman` (or `breakout`, `doomlite`, `flappy`, `pong`). ## How the world model works ### Frames split into tokens ![patches](docs/media/explain_patches.gif) The frame is cut into square patches: 2×2 cells in Breakout, 4×4 in Doom-lite, Flappy Bird and Pong, 6×6 in Pac-Man. That gives 36 to 80 tokens per game. A patch's embedding is the sum of one learned vector per cell, with a separate table for each position inside the patch so the cell order isn't lost. Every token also gets a position vector and the action's vector. ### Looped Transformer ![loop](docs/media/explain_loop.gif) The model is a single transformer block (attention plus a ReLU MLP) with one set of weights, applied 1 to 4 times, with the input added back before every pass. The output after every pass is trained against the next frame, so at run time the loop count trades speed for accuracy. On the Pico to keep a decent frame rate we use uses two loops. The animation shows one held-out Doom-lite step. After one pass the model draws an enemy that isn't there, and each further pass removes part of it: 92, 35, 12, then 0 wrong cells. The bars on the right are the share of held-out frames each loop count gets exactly right. Here is a dreamed Doom-lite step decoded after 1, 2, 3 and 4 loops, with red boxes on cells that differ from the real rules: ![loops](docs/media/loops_doomlite.gif) Exact held-out frames by loop count: | loops | Breakout | Doom-lite | Flappy Bird | Pong | Pac-Man | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | 99.68% | 59.8% | 99.99% | 98.47% | 79.6% | | 2 | 99.99% | 83.6% | 100% | 99.45% | 86.4% | | 3 | 100% | 85.9% | 100% | 99.60% | 85.7% | | 4 | 99.96% | 84.7% | 100% | 99.53% | 84.4% | ### Decoding ![decode](docs/media/explain_decode.gif) The model outputs a score for every cell and every token. Turning those scores into a frame turned out to matter almost as much as the model, and it ended up as three rules (shown above on Pong): 1. Background cells (walls, bricks, pellets, floor) each take their most likely token independently. 2. Singletons (the ball, the player, each ghost) are placed with one choice over all (cell, token) pairs, so there is always exactly one of each. After a random event the choice is sampled among candidates within 2.2 logits of the best, so the world model samples a new serve or respawn instead of averaging them. 3. Pac-Man and the ghosts are 2×2 sprites, but only one cell of each carries state (the mouth holds the heading; the ghost's lower-left cell holds whether a pellet is underneath). The other three cells are stamped from it instead of predicted. We implemented Rule 2 because the first Breakout model drew two balls at once; one global choice took exact frames from 91.6% to 99.7%. ### Checking the world model Accuracy on recorded data wasn't enough. An agent drives the dream into states the data never had, and any mistake there is something it can exploit. So the main check runs while an agent plays: read the game state back off the dreamed frame (`games/.py: read`), apply the real rules to that state and the agent's action, and compare the result with the next dreamed frame and reward. ![check](docs/media/check_doomlite.gif) 5,000 dreamed steps per game at 2 loops, with the shipped agent (`training/evalwm.py --agent`): | game | wrong game states | wrong rewards | wrong cells per step | |---|---|---|---| | Breakout | not read back; 0 frames with impossible tokens | 6 (paid without a brick breaking) | – | | Doom-lite | 1 | 0 | 1.50 | | Flappy Bird | 0 | 0 | 0.00 | | Pong | 1 | 0 | 0.00 | | Pac-Man | 742 | 38 | 0.39 | ### Training First, agents play the real game and every step is recorded as one example (frame, action, next frame, reward), 1–3 million per game. Some episodes start from unusual states, like bricks with holes or random positions, so the data covers more of the game. ![data](docs/media/explain_data.gif) Then the world model learns to predict the next frame with a per-cell cross-entropy loss: 30k steps, with the first 3–4k steps run in float, then int8 rounding switches on ([QAT](#quantization-and-the-pico)). ![training](docs/media/explain_training.gif) The int8 weights are written into Rust source with every float stored as its exact bits. We check them with `cargo test` to reproduces the Python integer spec bit for bit, and then the firmware runs on the Pico. ![deploy](docs/media/explain_deploy.gif) An agent trained in the world model reaches states the recorded data never had, so record real games with that agent and fine-tune the world model on everything. The agent in different games stated exploiting them so those are some fixes to it: - Weighting the loss by "this cell changed" biased the model toward predicting change, so it drew two balls and broke two bricks. Weighting by where things can happen in the input frame, plus the global singleton choice, fixed it. - A Breakout agent in the dream got 154 points with 26 bricks left, because the world model didn't remove bricks from the corner when it were hit. Doom-lite agents learned to snipe from 5 cells away. - Agents trained only in the dream scored 210 there (the real maximum is 56) and 28 in the real game, as *World Models* (Ha & Schmidhuber) predicts. Each collect-and-fine-tune round closed the exploit that agent had found. - The Doom-lite dream sometimes lost the enemy sprite and never drew it again: the model copied the previous view instead of redrawing it from the minimap. Noise augmentation fixed it (`train --noise 0.3`, as in GameNGen): input views get random pixels and sometimes lose the sprite. - `d=32` couldn't absorb the wider Breakout data and `d=48` could. Pac-Man's 48×48 frame needed `d=64`. ## The agents: stream-x ![stream-x](docs/media/explain_streamx.gif) The agents use Stream AC(λ) (Elsayed, Vasan & Mahmood, 2024), which learns from one transition at a time: no replay buffer, no batches, no target network. Eligibility traces carry credit back in time, and ObGD shrinks any step that would overshoot the TD target. The policy and value networks each have two hidden layers of 64 units (32 on the Pico) with LayerNorm. The input is a feature vector read off the frame (`training/streamx.py: observe_*`, mirrored in Rust in `tinyworldformer-rs/src/agent.rs`). For example, the ball's row, column and heading in Breakout, or in Pac-Man, for each direction, the shortest-path distance to the nearest pellet and how close each ghost is. Below is one training run per game (real game, 500k steps) at six stages: untrained, the end, and the snapshots where the score has covered 25, 50, 75 and 95% of the way. Each panel plays greedily from the same start and skips a few steps per frame. "try" counts the episodes played so far, so you can see the crashes. **Breakout** ![](docs/media/progress_breakout.gif) **Doom-lite** ![](docs/media/progress_doomlite.gif) **Flappy Bird** ![](docs/media/progress_flappy.gif) **Pac-Man lite** ![](docs/media/progress_pacman.gif) **Pong** ![](docs/media/progress_pong.gif) Greedy return in the real game, mean of 10 episodes, at snapshots of the same run: | game | 0 | 1k | 2k | 5k | 10k | 20k | 50k | 100k | 150k | 250k | 500k | max | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Breakout | 8.2 | 17.0 | 15.9 | 21.9 | 29.9 | 29.9 | 29.9 | 31.1 | 35.0 | 39.9 | 45.6 | 56 | | Doom-lite | −5.0 | −5.0 | −5.0 | −5.0 | −5.0 | 59.5 | 69.9 | 78.1 | 81.8 | 82.1 | 82.9 | – | | Flappy Bird | −1.0 | −1.0 | −1.0 | 1.9 | 24.6 | 24.9 | 96.2 | 123.7 | 309.2 | 332 | 332 | 332 | | Pac-Man | 7.0 | 3.8 | 17.0 | 17.7 | 8.2 | 46.8 | 72.9 | 138.9 | 146.6 | 190.3 | 217.4 | 249 | | Pong | −4.3 | −3.9 | −3.9 | −3.9 | −1.7 | −2.0 | −0.3 | 1.1 | 1.7 | 1.1 | 1.1 | 5 | Without shaping, Doom-lite agents camp in the start corner and fire, because the enemy always comes to them. `--idle-penalty 0.1` costs 0.1 for each step spent in a cell visited more than 6 times in the last 20 steps. The position is read off the minimap, so the penalty works inside the dream too. With it the agent patrols and gets twice the kills. `tinyworldformer-rs/src/learner.rs` is the same algorithm in `no_std` Rust, with the backward pass written by hand. It matches 200 PyTorch updates to within 3.5e-6. On the host, a fresh agent inside the Rust int8 Flappy Bird dream averages 6 pipes per episode after 25k steps, 121 after 100k, and 300+ after 250k. ## Quantization and the Pico ![quantization](docs/media/explain_quantize.gif) Every matrix in the world model is int8 with one scale per output row (`scale = max|w| / 127`). Activations are int8 too, with one scale per tensor and per loop index, since the loops see different ranges. Matmuls sum int8 × int8 into int32 (two multiply-adds per `SMLAD` instruction on the RP2350) and then apply one float multiply by the two scales. Softmax uses a 1024-entry exp table, with probabilities stored as uint8. Norms, residuals and embeddings stay in float32, since the RP2350 has an FPU. Training applies the same rounding (QAT with a straight-through estimator), so the int8 model is the model that was trained. `rustexport/intref.py` is the int8 model in numpy with every float operation in a fixed order; the Rust engine reproduces it bit for bit, and `cargo test` checks golden vectors for every exported env. ![sizes](docs/media/sizes.png) | game | int8 weights | float32 (embeddings, norms, scales) | game data | agent (float32) | firmware flash | firmware RAM | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Breakout | 19.7 KB | 31.6 KB | 1.1 KB | 54.1 KB | 361 KB | 299 KB | | Doom-lite | 33.9 KB | 91.9 KB | 12.0 KB | 61.3 KB | 471 KB | 357 KB | | Flappy Bird | 30.1 KB | 69.5 KB | 10.1 KB | 50.8 KB | 409 KB | 227 KB | | Pong | 30.1 KB | 70.4 KB | 10.9 KB | 52.6 KB | 414 KB | 244 KB | Flash and RAM are measured from the firmware ELF (`size -A`), built with the Display Pack driver, so they include the code, USB, the display driver and the on-device learner. The Pico 2 W has 4 MB of flash and 520 KB of SRAM, 512 KiB of it in the main memory map. The float32 embedding tables are the largest part and could be int8 too. `src/tinyworldformer/rustexport/` imports only numpy and torch (a test keeps it that way), so other projects can reuse the export: build a model from `rustexport.qat` (`QLinear`, `LoopedBlock`), train it with `ActQuant.enabled = True` after a float warm-up, convert it with `rustexport.convert.looped_model`, then write the Rust source with `int_model_arrays`, `mlp_arrays` and `codegen.write_module`. `rustexport.Golden` writes the vectors a Rust test checks. ## On the chip The firmware (`tinyworldformer-rs/firmware`) is `no_std` Rust on embassy. Nothing is allocated at run time: the weights are `static` arrays in flash, and every buffer is a fixed-size `static` in RAM. Core 1 runs the game. One pass of its loop (`dream_loop` in `firmware/src/main.rs`) is one frame: 1. The actor reads features off the current frame (`agent::observe`) and runs its MLP to pick a button. If on-device learning is on, the learning agent picks instead; if you are pressing buttons, your press is used. 2. The int8 transformer runs 2 loops over the frame and the button (`Engine::forward`), and decoding turns its scores into the next frame: background argmax per cell, each singleton placed once (sampled for random events with an xorshift RNG), then the sprite stamps. The reward is the argmax of the reward head; lives and episode ends are counters on top. 3. If learning is on, the learner updates from this one transition and then forgets it. 4. The frame goes to core 0 through a two-slot channel. If core 0 is still busy with the previous frame, this one is dropped, so core 1 never waits for the screen. When you play, core 1 slows down to a playable speed (66–150 ms per frame, depending on the game). The agent runs as fast as the chip allows. Core 0 runs embassy async tasks for everything else. Over USB serial, each frame goes out as coloured ANSI text with a status line (model time, actor time, fps, env and agent names), and keys come back in. The optional Display Pack (`--features display`) is a 320×240 ST7789 over SPI at up to 62.5 MHz, and only cells that changed since the last frame are redrawn. Its buttons are polled every 20 ms. The two cores share only the frame channel and a few atomics: who is playing, the pressed key, learning on/off, and the loop count. Where the memory goes: | | in flash | in RAM | |---|---|---| | world model | int8 matrices, float32 embeddings, norms and scales, the game's opening frames and colours (52–138 KB) | scratch buffers for one forward pass: activations for 36–80 tokens, the int8 copies the matmuls read, and the per-cell scores of the next frame (114 KB for Flappy Bird up to 368 KB for Pac-Man, whose per-cell scores alone take 184 KB) | | actor | float32 MLP weights and feature normalization (51–61 KB) | its features and hidden layers (about 1 KB) | | on-device learner | code only | weights, eligibility traces and normalization for two 32-unit networks (49 KB for Pac-Man up to 106 KB for Doom-lite; it scales with the number of input features) | | firmware | code, USB, display driver (about 150 KB) | stacks (16 KB for core 1), USB buffers, frame channels | Every game fits in the 4 MB of flash and 512 KiB of SRAM. Breakout uses 361 KB of flash and 299 KB of SRAM; Pac-Man, the largest, uses 600 KB and 460 KB. Most of the time goes into int8 dot products (`dot_i8` in `src/lib.rs`). One 32-bit load fetches 4 weights, `SXTB16` unpacks bytes 0/2 and 1/3 into 16-bit halves, and `SMLAD` does two multiply-adds in one instruction. Attention multiplies uint8 probabilities by int8 values, so it uses `UXTB16` instead. Norms, the exp table lookup and the final per-output scale stay in float32 on the FPU. A frame at 2 loops is 2–4M multiply-adds (8.2M for Pac-Man); on a desktop CPU the same Rust code dreams a frame in 0.7 ms (Flappy Bird) to 1.5 ms (Breakout). I haven't measured the frame rate on the Pico itself yet. The board boots with a fresh agent learning on the device. Press `l` over USB, or hold B for 1 s on the Display Pack, to switch to the pretrained actor, and again to switch back. ## Flashing a game and an agent Every export sits side by side in the crate: world models in `tinyworldformer-rs/models/envs//`, agents in `models/agents///`. You pick both at build time. ```bash cd tinyworldformer-rs ./flash.sh --list # what is exported ./flash.sh --env doomlite --agent doom_agent_roam_p0.3 # build and flash (hold BOOTSEL while plugging in) ./flash.sh --env breakout --display # with the Display Pack ./flash.sh --env pong --host # play it in this terminal ./flash.sh --env flappy --default # make it the default for plain cargo TWF_ENV=doomlite TWF_AGENT=doom_agent_roam_p0.1 cargo test --release # golden tests for that pair ``` Without `--agent`, the agent for the env's game listed in `models/default` is used if there is one, otherwise the first by name. An agent for a different game is refused with a list of the valid ones. The status line on screen shows which env and agent are running. Keys over USB: Breakout a/d/s, Doom-lite w/a/d/space/s, Flappy space, Pac-Man w/a/s/d, Pong w/s. Then `g` hands back to the agent, `1`–`4` set the loop count, `l` toggles on-device learning and `r` restarts it. ## In the browser The same `no_std` int8 engine also compiles to WebAssembly (`tinyworldformer-rs/web/`). The module has no imports and no wasm-bindgen, and it runs the firmware's loop: dream, agent, and stream-x learning on the fly. A static page draws the frames on a canvas. ```bash rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown # once cd tinyworldformer-rs/web ./build.sh # one module per env into www/ (or ./build.sh pong flappy) python3 -m http.server -d www # open http://localhost:8000, ?env=pacman picks a game ``` With the same seed, the wasm build dreams the same episodes as the native build, frame for frame, at 1–5 ms per frame depending on the game. Each module carries its game's default agent; `TWF_AGENT=... ./build.sh ` picks another. The keys are the same as on the Pico, plus arrow keys and on-screen buttons, and `f` runs the dream as fast as it can, which helps while learning (`l`). ## Reproduce ```bash uv sync G=pong # breakout, doomlite, flappy, pacman, pong uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.data --game $G --transitions 2000000 --varied 0.3 # -> data/$G uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.train --data data/$G --d 48 --heads 3 --ff 96 --out models/${G}_wm.pt uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.streamx --env real --game $G --out models/${G}_agent.pt uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.evalwm --ckpt models/${G}_wm.pt --agent models/${G}_agent.pt # check the dream uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.streamx --env dream --wm models/${G}_wm.pt --out models/${G}_dream_agent.pt uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.export --ckpt models/${G}_wm.pt uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.streamx --out models/${G}_agent.pt --export tinyworldformer-rs cd tinyworldformer-rs && TWF_ENV=$G cargo test --release && TWF_ENV=$G cargo run --release ``` Settings that differ per game: | game | settings | |---|---| | Breakout | 1M transitions, `--miss-penalty 5`, then collect with the agent (`data --learned --holes 0.5 --out data/breakout_learned`) and fine-tune on all of it (`train --init ... --data data/breakout data/breakout_learned --steps 15000 --warmup-float 0 --lr 1e-3`), four rounds | | Doom-lite | `--varied 0.5`, `train --noise 0.3`, `streamx --max-ep-steps 500 --idle-penalty 0.1` | | Flappy Bird | `streamx --max-ep-steps 3000` | | Pac-Man | 1.2M transitions, `--varied 0.4`, `train --d 64 --heads 4 --ff 128 --steps 40000 --warmup-float 4000`, `streamx --miss-penalty 5 --max-ep-steps 1500` | | Pong | `streamx --max-ep-steps 5000` | ## Code layout | path | contents | |---|---| | `src/tinyworldformer/games/` | the five games (rules, rendering, `read`), the `Game` registry, scripted agents, terminal play | | `src/tinyworldformer/training/` | data, world model, training, dream checks, stream-x, export to the Rust crate | | `src/tinyworldformer/rustexport/` | reusable PyTorch → `no_std` Rust export: QAT layers, the int8 spec, conversion, code generation | | `tinyworldformer-rs/` | `no_std` int8 engine, dream loop, agent and learner; host demo (`src/main.rs`) | | `tinyworldformer-rs/firmware/` | Pico 2 W firmware | | `tinyworldformer-rs/web/` | WebAssembly build and the browser page (`www/`) |

        any step that would overshoot the TD target. The policy and value networks each have two hidden layers of 64
        units (32 on the Pico) with LayerNorm. 
       The input is a feature vector read off the frame ( training/streamx.py: observe_* , mirrored in Rust
        in  tinyworldformer-rs/src/agent.rs ). For example, the ball's row, column and heading in Breakout,
        or in Pac-Man, for each direction, the shortest-path distance to the nearest pellet and how close each ghost is.
       
       Below is one training run per game (real game, 500k steps) at six stages: untrained, the end, and the snapshots
        where the score has covered 25, 50, 75 and 95% of the way. Each panel plays greedily from the same start and
        skips a few steps per frame. "try" counts the episodes played so far, so you can see the crashes. 
        Breakout

       Without shaping, Doom-lite agents camp in the start corner and fire, because the enemy always comes to them.
         --idle-penalty 0.1  costs 0.1 for each step spent in a cell visited more than 6 times in the last 20
        steps. The position is read off the minimap, so the penalty works inside the dream too. With it the agent
        patrols and gets twice the kills.
       
        tinyworldformer-rs/src/learner.rs  is the same algorithm in  no_std  Rust, with the
        backward pass written by hand. It matches 200 PyTorch updates to within 3.5e-6. On the host, a fresh agent
        inside the Rust int8 Flappy Bird dream averages 6 pipes per episode after 25k steps, 121 after 100k, and 300+
        after 250k. 
       Quantization and the Pico 
         
       Every matrix in the world model is int8 with one scale per output row ( scale = max|w| / 127 ).
        Activations are int8 too, with one scale per tensor and per loop index, since the loops see different ranges.
        Matmuls sum int8 × int8 into int32 (two multiply-adds per  SMLAD  instruction on the RP2350) and then
        apply one float multiply by the two scales. Softmax uses a 1024-entry exp table, with probabilities stored as
        uint8. Norms, residuals and embeddings stay in float32, since the RP2350 has an FPU. 
       Training applies the same rounding (QAT with a straight-through estimator), so the int8 model is the model that
        was trained.  rustexport/intref.py  is the int8 model in numpy with every float operation in a fixed
        order; the Rust engine reproduces it bit for bit, and  cargo test  checks golden vectors for every
        exported env.

       Flash and RAM are measured from the firmware ELF ( size -A ), built with the Display Pack driver, so
        they include the code, USB, the display driver and the on-device learner. The Pico 2 W has 4 MB of flash and 520
        KB of SRAM, 512 KiB of it in the main memory map. The float32 embedding tables are the largest part and could be
        int8 too. 
        src/tinyworldformer/rustexport/  imports only numpy and torch (a test keeps it that way), so other
        projects can reuse the export: build a model from  rustexport.qat  ( QLinear ,
         LoopedBlock ), train it with  ActQuant.enabled = True  after a float warm-up, convert it
        with  rustexport.convert.looped_model , then write the Rust source with
         int_model_arrays ,  mlp_arrays  and  codegen.write_module .
         rustexport.Golden  writes the vectors a Rust test checks.
       
       On the chip 
       The firmware ( tinyworldformer-rs/firmware ) is  no_std  Rust on embassy. Nothing is
        allocated at run time: the weights are  static  arrays in flash, and every buffer is a fixed-size
         static  in RAM.
       
       Core 1 runs the game. One pass of its loop ( dream_loop  in  firmware/src/main.rs ) is
        one frame: 
       
         The actor reads features off the current frame ( agent::observe ) and runs its MLP to pick a
          button. If on-device learning is on, the learning agent picks instead; if you are pressing buttons, your press
          is used. 
         The int8 transformer runs 2 loops over the frame and the button ( Engine::forward ), and decoding
          turns its scores into the next frame: background argmax per cell, each singleton placed once (sampled for
          random events with an xorshift RNG), then the sprite stamps. The reward is the argmax of the reward head;
          lives and episode ends are counters on top. 
         If learning is on, the learner updates from this one transition and then forgets it. 
         The frame goes to core 0 through a two-slot channel. If core 0 is still busy with the previous frame, this
          one is dropped, so core 1 never waits for the screen. 
       
       When you play, core 1 slows down to a playable speed (66–150 ms per frame, depending on the game). The agent
        runs as fast as the chip allows. 
       Core 0 runs embassy async tasks for everything else. Over USB serial, each frame goes out as coloured ANSI text
        with a status line (model time, actor time, fps, env and agent names), and keys come back in. The optional
        Display Pack ( --features display ) is a 320×240 ST7789 over SPI at up to 62.5 MHz, and only cells
        that changed since the last frame are redrawn. Its buttons are polled every 20 ms. The two cores share only the
        frame channel and a few atomics: who is playing, the pressed key, learning on/off, and the loop count. 
       Where the memory goes: 
       
         
           
             
                
               in flash 
               in RAM 
             
           
           
             
               world model 
               int8 matrices, float32 embeddings, norms and scales, the game's opening frames and colours (52–138 KB)
               
               scratch buffers for one forward pass: activations for 36–80 tokens, the int8 copies the matmuls read,
                and the per-cell scores of the next frame (114 KB for Flappy Bird up to 368 KB for Pac-Man, whose
                per-cell scores alone take 184 KB) 
             
             
               actor 
               float32 MLP weights and feature normalization (51–61 KB) 
               its features and hidden layers (about 1 KB) 
             
             
               on-device learner 
               code only 
               weights, eligibility traces and normalization for two 32-unit networks (49 KB for Pac-Man up to 106 KB
                for Doom-lite; it scales with the number of input features) 
             
             
               firmware 
               code, USB, display driver (about 150 KB) 
               stacks (16 KB for core 1), USB buffers, frame channels 
             
           
         
       
       Every game fits in the 4 MB of flash and 512 KiB of SRAM. Breakout uses 361 KB of flash and 299 KB of SRAM;
        Pac-Man, the largest, uses 600 KB and 460 KB. 
       Most of the time goes into int8 dot products ( dot_i8  in  src/lib.rs ). One 32-bit load
        fetches 4 weights,  SXTB16  unpacks bytes 0/2 and 1/3 into 16-bit halves, and  SMLAD  does
        two multiply-adds in one instruction. Attention multiplies uint8 probabilities by int8 values, so it uses
         UXTB16  instead. Norms, the exp table lookup and the final per-output scale stay in float32 on the
        FPU. A frame at 2 loops is 2–4M multiply-adds (8.2M for Pac-Man); on a desktop CPU the same Rust code dreams a
        frame in 0.7 ms (Flappy Bird) to 1.5 ms (Breakout). I haven't measured the frame rate on the Pico itself yet.
       
       The board boots with a fresh agent learning on the device. Press  l  over USB, or hold B for 1 s on
        the Display Pack, to switch to the pretrained actor, and again to switch back. 
     
     Code, weights and the full reproduction steps:  github.com/SheepSeb/tinyworldformer

  > Also, it's the same model for all the games, right It's a bit unclear but it looks like different models, since they all have different parameter and MAC counts. It would be much more impressive with a single world model that could maybe dream up new games inbetween the games in the training set.      reply                             sheepseb    1 day ago       |  parent  |  prev  |  next   [–]

The fixed was add some noise to the input frame and keep the target clean.      reply                             noduerme    20 hours ago       |  root  |  parent  |  next   [–]       
  Not the poster you responded to... Your Singleton hack was clever. In some ways it brings game design back into the equation, in that it mirrors the special cases that most game code has to deal with. You alluded to something in the docs that I was curious about, which is state. From reading it, I gathered that both agents interpret the direction of the Pac Man based on the position of its mouth in the previous frame. And one of your graphics seems to imply that the Doom state of where you are and which direction you're facing is magically grokked by the agent reading the map in the corner. Is that so? In that case, I wanted to ask, in pong or breakout, what is it using to figure out the direction and velocity of the ball? Faded prior shadows in other cells, maybe?      reply                             sheepseb    18 hours ago       |  root  |  parent  |  next   [–]       
  No, not shadows. I use the heading as a token, in Doom the minimap has a player token and the facing (the current 3D view), I tried using only the frame but it was harder to learn only from the wall patterns. So the agent isn't magically grokking position, its using the map. As for the Pac Man, it's based on mouth and has tokens for "keep going" or N/E/S/W direction. For breakout it uses 4 ball tokens, one per diagonal and it moves one cell per step in that diagonal, and for pong the ball has 6 tokens (combiantion between [up, level, down] with [left, right], e.g up right, level down)      reply                             mervikhaums    13 hours ago       |  prev  |  next   [–]

  I honestly believe that these neat projects (smallest possible, locally run LLMs) are the real future of AI on the long run.      reply                             Coill    16 hours ago       |  parent  |  next   [–]       
  There is still immense potential for optimization. Future local intelligence on your phone.      reply                             nater5000    1 day ago       |  prev  |  next   [–]       
  Honestly fascinating. I almost feel like you'd be better off avoiding any discussion of the fact that this runs on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W because it takes away from the crazy world model capabilities (of course, the fact that this  does  run on a Pico 2 makes the whole thing much more impressive). There's gotta be a good way to incorporate this logic into a larger, more "traditional" game in a meaningful way. # ElementaryUI - A Swift Frontend Framework [![](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https%3A%2F%2Fswiftpackageindex.com%2Fapi%2Fpackages%2Felementary-swift%2Felementary-ui%2Fbadge%3Ftype%3Dswift-versions)](https://swiftpackageindex.com/elementary-swift/elementary-ui) [![](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https%3A%2F%2Fswiftpackageindex.com%2Fapi%2Fpackages%2Felementary-swift%2Felementary-ui%2Fbadge%3Ftype%3Dplatforms)](https://swiftpackageindex.com/elementary-swift/elementary-ui) ElementaryUI brings the declarative approach of [Elementary](https://github.com/elementary-swift/elementary), the server-side HTML rendering library, to reactive Swift applications running directly in the browser. ## Features - 🌐 **Swift in the Browser** - Run declarative Swift applications natively in the browser with WebAssembly - 🎨 **SwiftUI-inspired APIs** - Familiar and intuitive syntax for building web UIs - ⚡ **Built-in Reactivity** - Automatic state management with `@State`, `@Environment`, and `@Reactive` - 📦 **Tiny Binaries** - Full Embedded Swift support means kB-sized wasm bundles instead of MB - ✨ **Magical Animations** - Powerful CSS-based animation system including automatic FLIP transitions - 🚀 **Vite-Powered Development** - Fast dev server with hot reload for rapid iteration - 🧩 **Web Components** - Publish ElementaryUI views as typed custom elements with the optional `ElementaryWebComponents` library
```swift @View struct Counter { @State var count = 0 var body: some View { div { p { "Count: \(count)" } button { "Increment" } .onClick { count += 1 } } } } ``` ## Guides & Documentation - **Guide & Get Started**: [elementary.codes](https://elementary.codes) - **API docs**: [Swift Package Index](https://swiftpackageindex.com/elementary-swift/elementary-ui/documentation) > [!NOTE] > ElementaryUI is an actively developed passion project in its early days. > Expect sharp edges, APIs may change, and things may break as I balance performance, ergonomics, and feature set. > > The ambition is simple: make Swift a first-class option for building serious web applications, and keep the project healthy for the long run.

Thank you to everyone supporting this open‑source project financially.
Please consider joining them by sponsoring ElementaryUI.

## Example [Check out the "Swiftle" demo app](/Examples/Swiftle/) ## 🚧 Work In Progress 🚧 Based on the [swift.org WebAssembly SDKs](https://forums.swift.org/t/swift-sdks-for-webassembly-now-available-on-swift-org/80405), [JavaScriptKit](https://github.com/swiftwasm/JavaScriptKit), and [Elementary](https://github.com/elementary-swift/elementary). Swift 6.4 or later with matching *Swift SDKs for WebAssembly* from [swift.org](https://www.swift.org/install) is required. ### Things to figure out - ~~identity system and list-diffing~~ - ~~lifecycle events and proper "unmounting" (currently nodes are just "dropped")~~ - ~~@State system~~ - ~~typed event handlers~~ - ~~@Environment system~~ - ~~dependencies on versioned packages (i.e., build without unsafe flags)~~ - ~~fix DOM not child-diffing to preserve animations/nodes (the current solution based on `replaceChildren` will not work, it seems)~~ - ~~"model-bindings" for inputs (i.e., bind a @Binding to a text box, or bind a @Binding to a checkbox)~~ - ~~view value comparing (generated comparing and custom equatable support)~~ - ~~different handling of environment (individual reactivity needed)~~ - ~~transitions and animations (ideally CSS-based, probably svelte-like custom easing functions applied through WAAPI)~~ - ~~better control over animations~~ - ~~somehow migrate over to "var body" instead of "var content" (what was I thinking....)~~ - ~~automatic FLIP animations for certain layout changes (child-layout after changes, maybe size of containers)~~ - ~~fix those Foundation imports, review thread-local + mutex usage~~ - ~~basic phaseAnimator implementations~~ - implement auto-flip animation for custom CSS values (on value triggers) - maybe add "animateContainerLayout" modifier with value trigger (eg: to animate changes without child-changes) - multi-select bindings (options, radio-buttons, tagged check boxes, ...) - support for combined and reversible transitions - more unit testing (FLIP handling, animations, reactivity, ...) - more built-in animatable CSS modifiers (colors, borders) (maybe in extra module with more SwiftUI shims?) - implement @ViewEquatableIgnored - ~~split out JavaScriptKit stuff in separate module to contain spread, maybe one day we can switch to faster interop somehow~~ - ~~add basic docs, a good intro readme, and push a 0.1 out the door! (probably best to wait for Swift 6.2 to drop)~~ - a router implementation (probably in extra module?) - maybe conditionally support @Observable for non-embedded builds? - ~~figure out why `@Environment` with optional `ReactiveObject` does not build in embedded~~ - preference system (i.e., bubbling up values) - ~~embedded-friendly Browser APIs (Storage, History, maybe in swiftwasm package with new JavaScriptKit macros)~~ - ~~think about how to deal with the lack of `Codable` in embedded (wait for new serialization macros)~~ - ~~make printing work without WASI (maybe pipe putchar through to JavaScript?)~~ - isolation and @MainActor stuff for reusable types (server-side rendering and client apps - probably never quite possible to have same types render "multi-threaded" server side and stay single-threaded client side....) - ~~decide whether the current idea of `Views` flattening themselves into renderable types is even necessary, or if views should just "apply" themselves into the reconciler - might be a bit messier, but maybe faster and more flexible~~ - ~~move all elementary repos under one project roof and use a traits-based, single "ElementaryUI" top-level package (or similar)~~ ### Embedded Swift for WASM waitlist - Codable 2.0 (we need JSON handling for embedded, on [the horizon](https://forums.swift.org/t/the-future-of-serialization-deserialization-apis/78585)) - ~~simple build with SwiftPM (wasm-ld)~~ - ~~\_Concurrency module (Task)~~ - ~~Synchronization (Mutex)~~ ## License and Derived Code This package is generally licensed as [Apache 2](LICENSE). The `Reactivity` module is inspired by the Swift stdlib's `Observation` framework. Some code in this repo is derived from Swift.org projects: - `ReactivityMacros` from [ObservationMacros](https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/tree/main/lib/Macros/Sources/ObservationMacros) in the Swift repo - `Sources/ElementaryUI/_Shims/MutableRef.swift` from [Swift Collections](https://github.com/apple/swift-collections/blob/1.7.1/Sources/InternalCollectionsUtilities/MutableRef.swift) Find a copy of the Swift.org open source project license [here](LICENSE-swift_org.md). This repo also contains the [BrowserRuntime](BrowserRuntime) JavaScript package which bundles source code from [JavaScriptKit](https://github.com/swiftwasm/JavaScriptKit) (see [license](./BrowserRuntime/LICENSE.md)) --- *SwiftUI is a trademark of Apple Inc. This project is not affiliated with or connected to Apple in any way.*

  ElementaryUI - A Swift Frontend Framework     
    
    
 ElementaryUI brings the declarative approach of  Elementary , the server-side HTML rendering library, to reactive Swift applications running directly in the browser. 
  Features     
 
 🌐  Swift in the Browser  - Run declarative Swift applications natively in the browser with WebAssembly 
 🎨  SwiftUI-inspired APIs  - Familiar and intuitive syntax for building web UIs 
 ⚡  Built-in Reactivity  - Automatic state management with  @State ,  @Environment , and  @Reactive  
 📦  Tiny Binaries  - Full Embedded Swift support means kB-sized wasm bundles instead of MB 
 ✨  Magical Animations  - Powerful CSS-based animation system including automatic FLIP transitions 
 🚀  Vite-Powered Development  - Fast dev server with hot reload for rapid iteration 
 🧩  Web Components  - Publish ElementaryUI views as typed custom elements with the optional  ElementaryWebComponents  library 
 
 
   @ View  
 struct   Counter   { 
     @ State    var    count    =   0 
    
     var    body   :   some   View   { 
         div   { 
             p   {   "  Count:   \( count )  "   } 
             button   {   "  Increment  "   } 
                 .  onClick   {  count  +=   1   } 
         } 
     } 
 }   
  Guides & Documentation     
 
  Guide & Get Started :  elementary.codes

   Note  ElementaryUI is an actively developed passion project in its early days.
Expect sharp edges, APIs may change, and things may break as I balance performance, ergonomics, and feature set. 
 The ambition is simple: make Swift a first-class option for building serious web applications, and keep the project healthy for the long run.

      Title: RetroChessBench: A Benchmark for Reconstructing and Proving Chess Histories 
      Authors:  Tidor-Vlad Pricope               View a PDF of the paper titled RetroChessBench: A Benchmark for Reconstructing and Proving Chess Histories, by Tidor-Vlad Pricope 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Frontier language models such as GPT 6 Astra have contributed to research mathematics, demonstrating substantial reasoning capabilities. Yet serious reasoning failures persist even in tasks governed by explicit rules. We demonstrate this in retrograde chess which is a playground for pure reasoning, where solvers reconstruct legal histories and distinguish possible events from forced ones. We introduce RetroChessBench, a 12-task benchmark covering exact-length constructions, unique endings, and exhaustive answer sets, with references, rubrics, and a terminal-reward environment. In two trials per task and condition, GPT 6 Astra High fails to produce the required final answer in 22/24 attempts without tools and 18/24 with code execution; mean terminal RL rewards are 14.75% and 27.19%, respectively. The examples identify faulty deductions: failed responses reject legal histories and treat temporary obstructions as permanent. Online retrograde archives often provide puzzles and final move sequences without detailed derivations. We hypothesize that limited exposure to these missing explanations in web-derived training data contributes to the observed reasoning failures. This questions how far frontier mathematical reasoning really generalizes beyond familiar solution patterns. Claims of general intelligence require evidence that models can transfer learnt principles to areas with few worked examples.

  RetroChessBench: A Benchmark for
 
Reconstructing and Proving Chess Histories  
  Pricope Tidor-Vlad  
 Poindexter Labs 
  27 October 2026  
 
  
 
  Abstract 
    
 Frontier language models such as GPT 6 Astra have contributed to research mathematics, demonstrating substantial reasoning capabilities. Yet serious reasoning failures persist even in tasks governed by explicit rules. We demonstrate this in retrograde chess which is a playground for pure reasoning, where solvers reconstruct legal histories and distinguish possible events from forced ones. We introduce RetroChessBench, a 12-task benchmark covering exact-length constructions, unique endings, and exhaustive answer sets, with references, rubrics, and a terminal-reward environment. In two trials per task and condition, GPT 6 Astra High fails to produce the required final answer in 22/24 attempts without tools and 18/24 with code execution; mean terminal RL rewards are 14.75% and 27.19%, respectively. The examples identify faulty deductions: failed responses reject legal histories and treat temporary obstructions as permanent. Online retrograde archives often provide puzzles and final move sequences without detailed derivations. We hypothesize that limited exposure to these missing explanations in web-derived training data contributes to the observed reasoning failures. This questions how far frontier mathematical reasoning really generalizes beyond familiar solution patterns. Claims of general intelligence require evidence that models can transfer learnt principles to areas with few worked examples. 
  
 
 
 1  Introduction 

 
 A chess position records where the surviving pieces stand. It omits the moves that brought them there, the pieces that disappeared, and the promotions that may have occurred. Retrograde analysis reconstructs this missing history under the ordinary rules of chess. The scientific question is whether a model can reason consistently over these hidden histories and distinguish what  could  have happened from what  must  have happened. 
 
 
 The distinction changes the standard of proof. An exact-length proof game needs one legal witness. A unique-ending problem needs an argument covering every compatible history. A problem with several possible last moves needs a feasible history for each answer and an exclusion of all others. These obligations remain different even when their final answers fit on one line. A six-move ending can depend on a promotion or capture budget established much earlier in the game. 
 
 
 These tasks put a basic expectation of general reasoning under pressure: known rules should remain usable when the question changes from choosing a future move to establishing a necessary past event. The solver must keep track of hypothetical states, revise assumptions, and distinguish constraints that hold in one candidate history from constraints that hold in all of them. Fluent reconstruction can conceal a failure at precisely this distinction. 
 
 
 A concrete failure illustrates the issue. In P0292, a model constructs a legal 47-ply game and concludes that the requested 45-ply game is impossible. Its bound treats a pawn on g6 as an unavoidable obstruction to a bishop’s route. A replayable 45-ply construction sends the bishop through g6  before  the pawn arrives. The model has found one possible history and mistaken its schedule for a necessary constraint. Table   1   isolates the error; Appendix   D   gives the full counterexample. 
 
 
 We introduce  RetroChessBench  (also on  Hugging Face ), a 12-task benchmark comprising seven exact-length games, four unique suffixes, and one exhaustive two-answer task. These tasks were selected from a  48-task candidate pool  drawn from  StrateGems  compositions, including two adaptations. References, prompts, board images, responses, rubrics, and replay checks accompany the tasks. A  terminal-reward interface  accepts alternative valid constructions and scores analytical obligations separately. 
 
 
 We evaluate GPT 6 Astra High twice per task without tools and twice with hosted code execution. Final answers are correct in 2/24 and 6/24 attempts. The code condition produces two valid constructive games and four correct suffixes; three of those suffix answers still lack complete proofs. Five construction tasks fail in all four attempts. These are descriptive outcomes on a set selected using observed failures, not an unbiased estimate of retrograde-chess ability or a causal estimate of tool benefit. 
 
 
 OpenAI reported a Navier–Stokes solution on 8 September 2026  ( OpenAI, 2026d ) . Four weeks later, on 6 October, it released hundreds of mathematical research manuscripts with varying verification status  ( OpenAI, 2026c ;  OpenAI, 2026b ) . Both releases concern internal models; OpenAI describes the Navier–Stokes model as more capable than Astra, whose separate mathematical contributions include prime-gap results  ( OpenAI, 2026a ) . ChessBench’s 27 October 2026 snapshot lists Astra at 1745 Elo for XHigh and 1531 for High  ( ChessBench, 2026a ) . These reports motivate broader tests of reasoning. The question is whether mathematical progress brings reliable construction and exclusion across other domains. 
 
 
 Backward reasoning is already studied in language-model planning, and reverse chess appears in LongCoT  ( Ren et al., 2024 ;  Motwani et al., 2026 ) . Our source compositions and answers are public, but availability does not establish training exposure. A leading hypothesis is limited exposure to worked retrograde explanations. The source archive gives P0292’s game with a short theme description and R0185’s ending with a compact rejected branch  ( The Retrograde Analysis Corner,  ) . A game certifies existence but need not teach discovery; a suffix sequence alone does not establish uniqueness. Detailed treatments do exist  ( Volet, 2003 ) ; the hypothesis concerns explanatory coverage in training, which we have not measured. If such coverage is sparse, can a model assemble familiar rules into historical deductions without abundant demonstrations of the method? 
 
 
 Our contribution operationalizes these established proof obligations in hidden chess histories through distinct answer contracts, executable witness checks, recorded proof assessments, and inspectable counterexamples to failed arguments. The benchmark and auditable pilot motivate controlled tests of local rule knowledge, candidate discovery, state representation, and proof verification (Section   9  ). Those tests can distinguish missing techniques from failures to coordinate techniques the model already possesses. 
 
 
 
 
 
  P0292, code run 1  
 
 
  Observable argument and counterexample  
   
 
 
 
  Invalid inference  
 
 
  A pawn on g6 prevents Be8-h5, so the required construction needs at least 47 plies.  
   
 
  Legal counterexample  
 
 
  The 45-ply reference contains 6.e8=B+ Ke6 7.Bh5 g6 8.g5 gxh5: the bishop traverses g6 before it is occupied.

 2  Related work 

 
 Chess play and state tracking. 

 
 Chess offers several distinct evaluation targets.   Toshniwal et al. (2022)   study piece tracking and legal-move prediction from move sequences, finding that explicit state information helps with limited training data.   Harang et al. (2025)   evaluate inferred chess states through the actions those states permit.   Kolasani et al. (2025)   examine reasoning and instruction following during extended forward play. ChessBench derives ratings from game outcomes using an anchored Monte Carlo Elo procedure  ( ChessBench, 2026b ) . These settings test following or choosing a continuation from a supplied history. RetroChessBench instead asks the solver to recover unobserved events, including captures and promotions, and sometimes to prove that other histories cannot change the answer. A forward-play rating motivates comparison but supplies no calibration for historical proof difficulty. 
 
 
 
 Reverse reconstruction and classical planning. 

 
 LongCoT is the closest benchmark predecessor: its reverse-chess task reconstructs a legal alternating move sequence consistent with a terminal board, side to move, and specified move fragments  ( Motwani et al., 2026 ) . This shares the existential objective of our proof games. The unique-suffix and exhaustive-answer tasks add universal exclusions over legal histories. PlanBench provides systematic tests of planning and reasoning about actions and change using domains from automated planning  ( Valmeekam et al., 2023 ) . It establishes a broader methodological precedent for explicit transition rules and checkable plans.   Ren et al. (2024)   study directional planning biases and combine forward and backward search with verification. Together these studies motivate separating discovery from checking, rather than treating all backward reasoning as one capability. 
 
 
 
 Abduction and missing premises. 

 
 Recovering history is a form of reasoning from effects to possible causes. ART asks models to choose or generate plausible explanations of narrative observations  ( Bhagavatula et al., 2020 ) . Plausibility is a different criterion from chess legality, and neither entails uniqueness. ProofWriter generates implications, proofs, and abductive statements over explicit natural-language theories  ( Tafjord et al., 2021 ) .   Sprague et al. (2022)   interleave forward deduction and backward abduction to infer missing premises, using round-trip validation to filter candidates. RetroChessBench shares the need to propose hidden events and check their consequences, but the missing objects are time-indexed states and piece identities under a fixed transition system. An explanation must fit a complete legal history; a uniqueness claim must survive every alternative explanation admitted by that system. 
 
 
 
 Proof search, quantifiers, and generalization. 

 
 PrOntoQA makes generated reasoning steps amenable to formal analysis.   Saparov and He (2023)   find that valid individual deductions can coexist with failures to explore alternative proof steps.   Saparov et al. (2023)   separately test depth, width, and compositional generalization, including hypothetical subproofs. These results motivate our distinction between knowing a local chess rule and coordinating it across a branching historical argument; they do not establish the cause of Astra’s errors. SATBench evaluates constraint satisfaction and unsatisfiability on generated logical puzzles  ( Wei et al., 2025 ) , a related separation of witnesses from exclusion. RetroChessBench adds capture identities, alternating turns, and hidden event order, while retaining the need to distinguish an existential solution from a universal claim. 
 
 
 
 Mathematics, constructions, and robustness. 

 
 MathArena evaluates recent competition mathematics, and Proof or Bluff examines proof quality on olympiad problems  ( Balunović et al., 2025b ;  Petrov et al., 2025 ) . MathConstruct accepts automatically checkable mathematical constructions  ( Balunović et al., 2025a ) ; the same principle governs our exact-length games: any valid witness earns full credit. Those results provide context for asking about transfer, rather than a measurement of transfer in this study. GSM-Symbolic probes mathematical robustness through template variations  ( Mirzadeh et al., 2025 ) . Its later re-evaluation identifies numerical-distribution and statistical confounds and reports model-specific failure profiles  ( Długosz et al., 2026 ) . The methodological lesson is relevant here: a performance gap requires controlled explanation. Counterfactual-task evaluations  ( Wu et al., 2024 )  and chess-prior interventions  ( Pleiss et al., 2026 )  offer complementary ways to test dependence on familiar representations. RetroChessBench keeps orthodox rules fixed; future transfer tests must additionally control the inference demanded and the solution budget. 
 
 
 
 Classical retrograde analysis and assessment. 

 
 The compositions and source solutions predate this benchmark and remain credited to their authors  ( The Retrograde Analysis Corner,  ) . Generalized retrograde reachability on growing boards is PSPACE-complete  ( Brunner et al., 2020 ) ; this does not classify the difficulty of our fixed     8  ×  8   8\times 8    instances. Specialist software such as Jacobi already solves proof games  ( Labelle,  ) . Our claim concerns language-model evaluation, not the impossibility of algorithmic reconstruction. Natural-language uniqueness proofs introduce a different assessment problem. Known limitations of model judges  ( Zheng et al., 2023 )  require separate records for deterministic witness checks, rubric credit, and proof review. A reference receiving full credit is a calibration control, not independent evidence that the proof or judge is correct.

 3.4  Why a standard chess engine is insufficient 

 
 Stockfish searches forward for strong continuations  ( Stockfish developers,  ) . Historical reconstruction requires additional information: the identity of captured pieces, earlier promotions, and the times at which squares were available. A best-move query does not supply it. Undoing a recorded move also differs from generating every possible predecessor of an arbitrary board. 
 
 
 Code can still help.  python-chess  provides move generation, legality checks, notation handling, and replay  ( Fiekas,  ) . Custom search, constraint solvers, and proof-game programs can reconstruct histories. Our code condition supplies general hosted execution; it does not supply a complete retrograde solver. Historical reconstruction also differs from computing game-theoretic endgame tablebases backward from terminal states. 
 
 
 
 
 4  Benchmark construction 

 
 4.1  From the source archive to the benchmark 

 
 We audited 82 primary problem entries in  StrateGems  Nos. 52–58 and documented their variants. Eligible tasks asked for prior moves or an orthodox proof game. We excluded piece-addition tasks, position release alone, and fairy-chess stipulations. The resulting 58 task instances each received two no-code runs. At least one run failed on 47 instances. We removed P0299 because its analytical completeness proof remained unresolved. The remaining 46 instances and two adaptations form a 48-task candidate pool. 
 
 
 RetroChessBench contains 12 tasks with completed grading and recorded secondary review of all 48 solver responses. Ten were selected using observed results, with R0178 and the easier R01 adaptation included to broaden suffix coverage. The final inventory and attempt slots are frozen, but the selection process was adaptive: it first retained no-code failures and subsequently used code outcomes and proof coverage to select the benchmark tasks. The reported no-code trials include the same attempts used for screening. This creates an asymmetric comparison: screening for no-code failure can make subsequent code trials look better through selection and regression to the mean, even without a tool effect. Later selection on code failures adds another dependency. The retained snapshots document the filtering stages and final task IDs, not a preregistered selection rule. We report a challenge-set baseline and give the selection ledger in Appendix   A  . A causal tool comparison requires a frozen task set and fresh trials in  both  conditions. 
 
 
 
 4.2  Composition, adaptations, and attribution 

 
 The benchmark comprises seven constructive tasks, four unique-suffix tasks, and one two-alternative task. Constructive lengths range from 35 to 60 plies; suffix lengths are 5, 6, 36, and 40 plies. Table   7   credits every composer and source issue. 
 
 
 R01 adapts Andrey Frolkin’s R0185 ( StrateGems  No. 56, 2011). We ask for the last six single moves instead of eight because this shorter ending retains the central reasoning challenge; proving its uniqueness still requires looking further back. We also relocate White’s rook from h8 to g8, leaving every other piece in place. The rook remains to the right of Qd8, preserving its role in the eighth-rank obstruction used by the proof. The relocation deliberately changes the original diagram to reduce reliance on exact diagram memorization, should the source have appeared in training. It does not establish absence from pretraining data or measure a reduction in memorization. 
 
 
 R02 adapts Nikolai I. Beluhov’s R0176 ( StrateGems  No. 53, 2011). The diagram is unchanged; the only task modification is to request the last five single moves instead of forty. This keeps the exposition manageable while preserving the central trap, which arises near the start of the backward analysis. Establishing those five moves still requires excluding a tempting continuation whose failure becomes apparent only further back in the history. 
 
 
 Both adaptations retain the central proof mechanism under the prompt’s legal-reachability premise. R02 and R0176 share a position and much of their reasoning; Section   7   reports a family-weighted sensitivity analysis.

 4.3  What the artifact contains 

 
 Tasks include prompts, FENs, board images, attribution, reference proofs, answer specifications, and versioned rubrics. Evaluation records contain responses, request metadata, criterion judgments, sequence checks, reviews, and hashes. Each solver rollout is an episode; its trajectory receives a terminal reward and feedback based on the final answer and justification. Intermediate messages and tool calls receive no separate process rewards. This supports reinforcement learning; we evaluate without training a policy. 
 
 
 The  benchmark website  provides task documents, paired results, and evidence;  PDL-Bench on Hugging Face  hosts the 12-task  retro_chess  subset. The  RL environment  is available as a  tested Docker build bundle , also on  Hugging Face , with  setup instructions  and a  validation report . Researchers can export solver inputs, check references, and grade new trajectories against the frozen tasks and rubrics. The paper bundle includes scripts that reproduce the reported tables and aggregate scores from archived judgments. Appendices   B   and   A   specify the protocol and archived release. 
 
 
 References and rubrics were developed with AI assistance. The author manually reviewed the solutions on a physical chessboard. A Codex agent performed the recorded secondary reviews. The artifact records these roles and retains attribution for the original compositions and solutions. 
 
 
 
 
 5  Reward design and grading 

 
 5.1  Separate answer correctness from proof quality 

 
 The evaluator reports final-answer correctness, categorical proof status, and terminal reward separately. A final-answer failure means the required game, suffix, or complete answer set was not produced. Terminal reward scores the task’s full objective. A correct ending with an incomplete proof can earn less than 100%; sound deductions can earn partial credit despite a wrong ending. The public dashboard calls a final-answer failure a “stump.” The primary scientific outcomes are exact-answer success and whether the applicable proof obligation is complete. Aggregate reward is an environment-specific summary, not a percentage of reasoning ability or of tasks solved. 
 
 
 The binary answer metric uses verified sequence status, not full sequence-criterion credit. Omitting or mislabeling  +  or  #  does not turn an otherwise verified game, suffix, or complete answer set into a final-answer failure. Such defects can reduce analytical sequence credit and hence reward; they do not reduce the binary constructive witness reward. Required move order, promotion identities, and captured-piece alternatives remain substantive constraints. All 48 retained verdicts agree with this rule, and none of the 40 failures is notation-only (Appendix   E  ).

 5.4  Calibration and corrections 

 
 All 12 reference controls (the “golden answers”) score 100%. Because those references were used to develop the rubrics, this checks calibration rather than independent judge accuracy. Solver and judge also use the same model family, leaving room for correlated errors. 
 
 
 Secondary audits cover all 48 answers and 12 controls. One retained score changed: R0178 code run 1 rose from 82.5% to 88% after review found inconsistent credit for a valid blocker-exclusion argument. The record preserves both scores and the correction. R0171 required a reference repair: an earlier grading bundle loaded an obsolete incomplete draft. We synchronized the completed reference, versioned its task and rubric, and regenerated its five grades. That reference includes both full feasibility witnesses and the analytical exclusion argument. 
 
 
 
 
 6  Experimental setup 

 
 We evaluate GPT 6 Astra High using RetroChessBench’s terminal-reward RL environment. The study uses 48 archived Azure solver rollouts, subsequently scored as episodes: 12 tasks, two runs, and two solver tool presets. Each trajectory’s final answer and written justification determine its terminal reward     r  ∈   [   0  ,  1   ]    r\in[0,1]   , alongside separate final-answer and proof-status assessments. Analytical tasks allow partial reward; constructive games use the binary witness reward (Section   5  ). Intermediate messages and tool calls receive no process rewards, and this study performs no policy updates. 
 
 
 Calls were made on 26–27 October 2026 through Azure with deployment alias  gpt-6-astra  and reasoning effort  high . We call this configuration GPT 6 Astra High. The response metadata identifies the alias, not an immutable weight snapshot. Separate ChatGPT XHigh experiments are excluded. 
 
 
 The two solver presets share task and reward definitions:  no code  supplies no tools;  code enabled  supplies Azure’s hosted code interpreter with an automatically provisioned 4 GB container. The grading pipeline is the same in both presets. The system prompt specifies only a JSON object containing one  solution  string and adherence to the task. All four runs for a task receive identical text after newline normalization, including FEN, and the same high-detail board image. Solvers receive no reference, rubric, or chess strategy. Web search is unavailable. Requests leave seed, temperature, and maximum output tokens unset, using provider defaults. 
 
 
 All selected responses completed, and every code-enabled rollout invoked the tool. The archive records 219 completed code calls and none in the no-code preset. It retains code payloads but no console outputs, so we cannot confirm library installation, useful verifier feedback, or whether a solver used or ignored that feedback. In particular, the record does not establish successful Stockfish use. 
 
 
 Median output-token usage, including reasoning tokens, is 42,295 without code and 58,443 with code. Compute is therefore unmatched; tool access, token usage, and search behavior vary together. The comparison uses the frozen completed pair for each task. Technical retries, two later R01 no-code runs, and separate ChatGPT outputs remain outside the 48-episode analysis. 
 
 
 The analysis pins task IDs, answer hashes, references, rubrics, and reviewed grades. A local script regenerates every numerical summary, task table, and plot. It also replays the constructive references and successful model games, checking legality, length, final placement, and premature automatic termination. Analytical proofs retain their separate rubric assessments.
