 7.4  Sensitivity and interpretation 

 
 The R0178 correction changes the code mean from 26.96% to 27.19%, a 0.23-point increase. To reduce double weighting of the R02/R0176 position, we average their task means and give each of the resulting eleven families equal weight. The means become 12.52% without code and 26.33% with code. Dropping R02 gives 10.82% and 26.80%; dropping R0176 gives 14.23% and 25.86%. The aggregate contrast survives each adjustment. 
 
 
 Omitting any one task gives a code-minus-no-code difference between 7.82 and 15.98 percentage points. This is a sensitivity range, not a confidence interval. Two runs per task, shared source families, and selection on observed performance prevent a precise population interpretation. 
 
 
 Reward design has a larger effect than the grading correction. Substituting diagnostic rubric credit for binary construction reward raises the means to 20.06% and 32.88%. That measures a different objective. We retain binary reward for construction because the requested deliverable is a valid exact-length witness, and keep diagnostic credit available for studying partial progress. 
 
 
 
 
 8  Failure mechanisms 

 
 Saved answers make the failures inspectable. Each case below identifies the disputed claim and the move or history that defeats it. The analysis concerns observable arguments; it does not infer hidden model states or estimate the frequency of each mechanism outside this set. 
 
 
 8.1  R01: applying king safety to the wrong time step 

 
 The six-move ending is 
 

  
  
          Kb6  ×  Bb7   ,    c7  −  c8   =   B  +    ,   Kb7  −   b8  +     ,          Bc8  −   b7  +    ,   Kb8  ×  Bb7   ,   a5  −   a6  #     .      \begin{gathered}\mathrm{Kb6}\times\mathrm{Bb7},\quad\mathrm{c7-c8}=\mathrm{B}^{+},\quad\mathrm{Kb7-b8}^{+},\\
\mathrm{Bc8-b7}^{+},\quad\mathrm{Kb8}\times\mathrm{Bb7},\quad\mathrm{a5-a6}^{\#}.\end{gathered}    
    
 
 Code run 1 rejects b8 as the origin of Black’s penultimate king move because White’s queen attacks it. The king can legally  start  its turn in check, then capture the bishop on b7 to escape. The rule concerns safety after the move. Applying it before the move leads to a false impossibility claim. The response earns 7.5% for a sound preliminary pawn-provenance argument. 
 
 
 No-code run 1 makes the same kind of error earlier. Black vacates b7, opening the bishop’s a8–b7–c6–d5 diagonal against White’s king. White then plays Bc8-b7, blocking that check and uncovering a queen check against Black. The response declares the intermediate check impossible instead of testing White’s reply. Its capture accounting earns 22.5%; its no-history conclusion is false. 
 
 
 The reference required a related repair. To exclude a  knight  as the earliest b7 victim, it is insufficient to observe that White was in check before a hypothetical Nc5-b7: that move could block the check. The corrected proof examines whether Black’s preceding move could have created it. The grader must enforce the same temporal standard on the reference and the submission. 
 
 
 
 8.2  R02: a temporary lock mistaken for a permanent constraint 

 
 The required five moves are 
 

  
  
       Bc6  −  a4   ,   b3  −  b2   ,   Ba4  −  c2   ,    b2  −  b1   =  B   ,   Rf2  ×   Nf3  +     .   \mathrm{Bc6-a4},\quad\mathrm{b3-b2},\quad\mathrm{Ba4-c2},\quad\mathrm{b2-b1}=\mathrm{B},\quad\mathrm{Rf2}\times\mathrm{Nf3}^{+}.    
    
 
 Code run 2 derives useful capture and promotion constraints, including the final promotion/capture pair. It then declares the central group locked until an earlier pawn capture is undone, missing a release through a knight-screen exchange. It also fixes capture squares from the white pawns’  final  ranks without establishing their ranks at the time. These assumptions create a false shortage of turns. The answer concludes that the position is impossible and earns 47% for its valid deductions. 
 
 
 The release moves the bishop away from c2, routes the a6 knight backward through b4 and c2 to e1, and coordinates the restored f3 knight. Each step depends on squares becoming available at the right time. A shortest geometric knight route is only a candidate; it must fit the alternating turns. Those deadlines force the early bishop moves in the answer. 
 
 
 
 8.3  P0292: a near witness does not establish a lower bound 

 
 Both code runs reach the board legally in 47 plies; the task requires 45. Run 1 claims that 47 is minimal because a bishop cannot travel from e8 to h5 through the pawn on g6. The reference sends the newly promoted bishop through g6  before  g7-g6, then plays g6   ×  \times   Bh5. The supposed obstruction exists only after the route has been used. 
 
 
 Replay confirms the proposed 47-ply games. It cannot certify the claimed lower bound. The 45-ply reference refutes that claim directly and is printed in Appendix   D  . Any valid 45-ply alternative would earn full credit; the submitted games fail the length requirement. 
 
 
 
 8.4  R0171 and R0178: a final answer is not a proof certificate 

 
 R0171’s answers are b7   ×  \times   Rc8=R# and b7   ×  \times   Nc8=R#. Writing b7   ×  \times   Xc8=R# identifies the mechanism but leaves the victim identities and completeness unresolved. The reference supplies legal histories for both the rook and knight branches and excludes the other victims. The two-move answer set carries both existence and exclusion obligations. 
 
 
 Both code runs on R0178 give the correct ending and omit parts of its uniqueness proof. One reaches the 90% incompleteness cap. Retaining the final-answer check alongside the reward makes this distinction visible. 
 
 
 
 
 9  Validation priorities and follow-up tests 

 
 The archived responses expose failures of temporal consistency and historical exclusion. Establishing their cause requires validated references and controlled comparisons; the present pilot supplies neither a causal tool effect nor a transfer estimate. 
 
 
 Complete witness coverage and assess the grader. 

 
 The remaining reference-evidence work is to supply a legal start-to-diagram witness for each suffix position (Table   14  ). A separate blinded evaluation of the grader should assess solver answers, valid alternative proofs, and minimally corrupted proofs without model or condition labels. Report criterion-level disagreement, false acceptance, false rejection, and adjudication; retain unresolved cases as such. Full-score reference controls establish calibration and cannot replace these checks. 
 
 
 
 Separate discovery from justification. 

 
 The most direct diagnostic compares free solving with a condition that supplies the correct suffix and asks whether it is forced. This holds the position fixed and removes answer discovery; a separate incorrect-candidate arm tests automatic endorsement. Persistent exclusion errors with the true ending supplied would locate a failure beyond discovery. Complement this with unrelated local-rule probes and blinded proof-verification trials. Score final answers and proof validity separately, and keep assisted results outside the unassisted benchmark score. 
 
 
 
 Test explanatory coverage. 

 
 Compare an unadapted baseline with adaptation on final-answer sequences or fully worked proofs for the same training tasks. Match total training tokens and compute; test fresh composition families and new combinations of mechanisms. Measure answer recovery and proof completion separately. Gains from worked proofs would establish their usefulness, not their absence from the original training corpus. 
 
 
 
 Test mechanism-specific predictions. 

 
 Appendix   F   specifies the interventions and safeguards for state tracking, search, and compositional transfer. A transfer claim requires demonstrated source competence, a defined target shift, and improvement from a targeted intervention that does not reveal the answer. Architectural explanations additionally require controlled comparisons with comparable training and inference budgets; improvement from an external state ledger alone would not isolate architecture. Freeze fresh composition families and primary outcomes before evaluation. These are proposed experiments, not results of this study. 
 
 
 
 
 10  Limitations and Reproducibility 

 
 Selection and scale. 

 
 The 12 tasks were selected using the model results reported here, including no-code screening trials retained in the comparison. This asymmetry can favor code without a causal tool benefit. Composers, mechanisms, and the repeated R02/R0176 position create dependencies. Two runs per condition and unmatched compute support descriptive scores, not population success rates or a causal estimate of code’s benefit. A broader evaluation needs tasks fixed in advance, more runs, multiple model families, and matched budgets. 
 
 
 
 Ground truth and grading. 

 
 Complete constructive witnesses can be replayed. The author manually reviewed the solutions, including the analytical uniqueness and exclusion arguments, on a physical chessboard. These arguments are presented as natural-language proofs rather than formal certificates. The four suffix references additionally lack full reachability witnesses in this bundle; their arguments are conditional on the prompt premise. Solver and judge may share errors. Reference controls calibrate the rubric; they do not measure independent judge accuracy. The recorded reference repair and score correction show why versioned evidence and review matter. 
 
 
 
 Exposure and adaptation. 

 
 Source problems and answers are public. We have measured neither the volume of public worked explanations nor Astra’s exposure to them. Changing a rook square or suffix length cannot guarantee that a task is absent from training. Future splits should keep shared position families together and include newly composed problems with documented creation dates. We also lack a matched mathematics evaluation of this deployment. The results do not identify memorization, an architectural limit, or a general-intelligence boundary as the cause of failure. 
 
 
 
 RL environment and replication. 

 
 Researchers can download the 12-task benchmark and tested RL environment from  https://app.poindexterlabs.net/docs/retro-chess  or  PDL-Bench on Hugging Face , under  retro_chess . The  Docker ZIP , also  mirrored on Hugging Face , contains build files, all 12 tasks, board images, reference solutions, rubrics, and the grading runtime. Follow the  setup instructions  to build the container, run offline checks, export solver inputs, and grade new model trajectories with provider credentials. The paper bundle’s analysis scripts reproduce the reported tables and aggregate scores from archived judgments. Appendix   B   specifies the experimental settings; the  validation report  records the Docker and grading checks. Replication should record the downloaded release hash and actual grading provider. 
 
 
 
 Provenance and attribution. 

 
 The manuscript bundle preserves the prompts, diagrams, references, rubrics, answer evidence, scoring scripts, and analyses used here; the  candidate pool  records selection provenance. Composition attribution and applicable third-party rights must accompany redistribution. The bundle does not grant a blanket license to the original compositions. 
 
 
 
 
 11  Conclusion 

 
 RetroChessBench tests three obligations: constructing a legal history, proving a forced ending, and identifying every possible answer. On this selected challenge set, Astra High gives correct final answers in 2/24 attempts without code and 6/24 with code. Mean terminal rewards from the RL environment are 14.75% and 27.19%, respectively. The benchmark remains far from saturated in both solver presets, even with code execution. 
 
 
 We expect the  three hardest tasks  to resist reliable solution for some time, while the others approach saturation as models improve. Progress requires both better answers and complete proofs: only one of the four correct code-enabled suffix answers receives full proof credit under the archived review. 
 
 
 The model rules out legal histories for the wrong reasons. It rejects a king for starting its turn in check even though it can escape legally, excludes a route because a square is occupied later, and uses a valid construction to claim a false lower bound. A restriction on one moment or candidate does not establish a claim about every legal history. 
 
 
 Limited exposure to worked retrograde proofs is a leading hypothesis to test. Generality requires evaluating how efficiently a model learns from such explanations and transfers the method to new compositions. Matched tests must distinguish missing domain instruction from failures to combine familiar rules. Claims of artificial general intelligence require evidence of reliable reasoning across new, independently validated problems, beyond saturation of a fixed public set. The standard is a legal construction when one history suffices, and rigorous exclusion when every history matters.

 Intended use. 

 
 The benchmark supports final-response evaluation and terminal-reward experiments on reconstruction, analytical proofs, and tool use. It is a selected challenge set. Training on its references or rewards must be disclosed when reporting results on these tasks.

 A task consists of a diagram, stipulation, output requirement, and reference version. Changing the suffix length creates a different task from the same source problem.  Selection provenance. 

 
 The coverage audit and  exploration_selection_final.json  record source-level inclusion decisions.  exploration_summary.json  records the 58-task screen.  selection.json  preserves an earlier snapshot with answer hashes;  frozen_selection.json , current task references, and  grading.json  govern the paper. Earlier evidence strings can predate the R0171 reference repair and must not override the current version. Table   8   records the verifiable stages without treating an adaptive process as an independent test split. The 22/24 and 18/24 failure counts use archived comparison trials, not new post-selection reruns. 
 
 
 
 Reference scope. 

 
 Constructive references supply replayable games and explanations of their mechanisms. Suffix references prove the ending under the prompt’s legal-reachability premise. R0171 includes full histories of 167 and 189 plies for its two branches; these establish feasibility without a minimum-length claim. Analytical exclusions remain natural-language proofs. 
 
 
 
 Version and packaging. 

 
 The paper analysis pins the 12-task selection recorded on 27 October 2026 and the subsequently synchronized reference/grade bundle. The environment build-source ZIP archived with this manuscript has SHA-256 
  1ec140391c6df9e44825e65e4f43ed51b2d988714f761e8715ae71402beae63e
  
 and is 646,079 bytes. It contains the runtime, tasks, images, references, and rubrics, with no model weights or API credentials. New model-based grades in this archived runtime require Azure access. Recomputing scores from saved judgments is offline. The  current public release , mirrored in  PDL-Bench on Hugging Face , has been built and tested in Docker, as documented in its  validation report ; its 48 frozen task, reference, rubric, provenance, and image files match the archived release byte for byte. The public ZIP has its own release hash and must not be identified by the archived hash above. 
 
 
 
 
  Appendix B  Exact solver protocol and replication 

 
 The system prompt is the following two-sentence format instruction: 
 
  Return your response as a JSON object with one string field named solution. Follow the task’s instructions within that field.  
 
 The strict response schema requires one string field,  solution , and permits no others. The user message contains the task text and one base64-encoded board image with  detail=high . Content hashes verify the four inputs for each task; R01’s raw text differs only in newline formatting. The system prompt adds no task identifier, reference, or rubric.

 Replication files. 

 
 Start from  RetroChessBench on Poindexter Research Docs  or the  retro_chess  subset of  PDL-Bench on Hugging Face . Download the  tested RL environment Docker bundle  from the website or its  identical Hugging Face ZIP . The  website setup instructions  and  Hugging Face quick start  cover building the image, running offline checks, and exporting prompts and board images for a solver. Release validation covers native ARM64 and emulated AMD64 Docker builds and runs, all 12 reference-sequence checks, 60 regression tests, and live grading checks ( validation report ). Keep reference answers and rubrics in the evaluator. New model-based grading needs provider credentials; pin the Azure route when reproducing the study’s provider condition. The newer runtime also supports an OpenAI route and fallback, whose results have separate provenance. 
 
 
 The bundle includes the exact prompts at  data/prompts/<task>/<mode>/run_1.txt  and  run_2.txt , final answers, sanitized metadata, task configurations, and grades. Full API responses remain in the original archive; the bundle retains their hashes and extracted usage/tool metadata. Credentials and private reasoning traces are excluded. 
 
 
  analysis/analyze.py  regenerates the attempt CSV, summary statistics, plots, and counterexample table using local data. It makes no model calls and never executes solver code. The collection script records evidence provenance. Original workspace paths are archival metadata, not build dependencies. 
 
 
 
 Boundaries of the tool audit. 

 
 All 219 code calls have completed status and saved payloads; none retains console output. Some attempt a chess-library import or engine lookup, which does not establish availability. A replication should preinstall dependencies, retain outputs, and record network permissions alongside tool settings. 
 
 
 
 
  Appendix C  Concrete analytical rubrics

 Sequence partial credit. 

 
 The deterministic R01/R02 policy awards half of C1 only for the explicitly specified near-complete cases, including at least four correct moves in their chronological slots; R02 additionally permits a specified single ordering repair. It does not convert a different final conclusion into the expected sequence. Missing identity or annotation details may prevent full notation credit even where the underlying moves agree. The full JSON policy distinguishes these cases. 
 
 
 
 Judge input and feedback. 

 
 The judge receives the task, reference proof, expected answer or set, rubric, and submission as separate inputs. Credited reasoning requires evidence in the submission. The environment checks the quoted evidence and computes scores locally. Anchoring verifies that the text exists; judging its logic remains a separate responsibility. Instructions embedded in a submission must be treated as answer data.

 Proof-status derivation. 

 
  analysis/reviewer_audit.py  maps the 20 archived analytical grades and review comments to Table   4  , retaining submission/reference hashes. It changes no rewards and requests no new judgments. The 28 constructive answers use the replay categories above: a valid witness suffices. Partial reasoning credit is not a proof-validity probability. 
 
 
 
 Notation and headline counts. 

 
  analysis/notation_audit.py  checks all 48 retained verdicts against archived sequence status: accepted answers are exactly those marked verified. None of the 40 failures is notation-only. Two P0295 answers have a check/mate-marker defect, but both supply 48 plies instead of the required 46. Thirteen annotation-removal checks on reference strings using the archived runtime retain verified status; analytical sequence credit can fall from full to half. The audit records these checks without new model calls or changes to the saved scores. It does not validate global reachability or analytical proofs. 
 
 
 
 Why 27.5% diagnostic credit can coexist with zero reward. 

 
 P0332 no-code run 1 reaches the target legally in 46 plies; the task requires 44. Route, check, and material deductions earn 27.5% diagnostic credit. Terminal reward remains zero because the construction misses the move budget. The artifact preserves both values so that analysis of partial progress can use the diagnostic without changing the exact-task score. 
 
 
 
 Reference-control interpretation. 

 
 All 12 current references score 100%. Full-game replay verifies the constructive controls. Analytical controls satisfy the calibrated rubric under the current judge and review. R01 includes the expanded earliest-knight exclusion; R0171 uses its completed v2 reference. Reproduction must use those versions. 
 
 
 
 One explicit correction. 

 
 Review raised R0178 code run 1 from 82.5% to 88%: its tracked position and argument excluded competing c8 blockers, meeting the standard accepted in run 2. Other omissions prevent full credit. Run 2 totals 95.5% before the incomplete-proof cap reduces it to 90%. Raw judgments, caps, and overrides are stored separately. 
 
 
 
 What an independent replay checks. 

 
 Replay starts from the standard position and checks UCI moves for legality, exact length, final placement, and premature automatic termination. All seven constructive controls and both successful model games pass. Replay can establish these properties of a supplied witness. Lower bounds and complete exclusions require additional arguments. 
 
 
 
 
  Appendix F  Controlled follow-up study 

 
 Following the validation priorities in Section   9  , freeze fresh tasks and keep composition families within one split. Use the same model snapshot and explicit token/tool budgets across paired conditions. Predefine source competence, target shift, and primary outcomes; report uncertainty over families. The interventions below are proposed controls, not completed experiments. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  Candidate explanation  
  
 
 
  Intervention and control  
  
 
 
  Discriminating outcome / safeguard  
   
 
 
 
 
 
  Missing rule knowledge  
  
 
 
  Probe check escape, promotions, capture budgets, and event order on unrelated positions; compare with a rules primer.  
  
 
 
  Local failure identifies prerequisite gaps. Do not reveal the target history.  
   
 
 
 
  Answer discovery  
  
 
 
  Compare free solving with correct-suffix assistance and a separate incorrect-candidate arm.  
  
 
 
  Proof failure despite a supplied answer extends beyond discovery. Keep assisted scores separate.  
   
 
 
 
  Proof verification  
  
 
 
  Compare valid proofs with minimal corruptions in blinded, randomized trials; request error location and repair.  
  
 
 
  Measure false acceptance and rejection; a binary label alone does not show the critical step was checked.  
   
 
 
 
  State tracking  
  
 
 
  Render boards and capture ledgers from the solver’s own candidates; use an equal-budget text control.  
  
 
 
  Improvement tests representation. Supplying true intermediate states leaks the answer.  
   
 
 
 
  Insufficient search  
  
 
 
  Add locally legal predecessor enumeration to the same legality checker.  
  
 
 
  More witnesses with residual exclusion errors separates search from proof. Global reachability filtering is oracle assistance.  
   
 
 
 
  Explanatory coverage / transfer  
  
 
 
  Compare no adaptation, answer-only examples, and worked proofs on the same training tasks; test disjoint families and new mechanism combinations.  
  
 
 
  Match token and compute budgets; establish source competence. Separate answer recovery from proof completion. Gains do not reveal original training exposure.  
   
 
 
 
  Quantifier confusion  
  
 
 
  Match feasible unique, multiple-answer, and impossible instances with certified labels.  
  
 
 
  Require witnesses or exclusions for the contract; match geometry and proof burden.  
   
 
 
 
 
 Tool records. 

 
 Preinstall and smoke-test supplied libraries. Retain code, standard output/error, package versions, network policy, timeouts, and tool-call limits. Report provider-default use separately from matched-budget comparisons; identify any specialist proof-game solver or global reachability oracle explicitly.

[![Github release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/picocss/pico?color=0172ad&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/picocss/pico/releases/latest) [![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@picocss/pico?color=0172ad)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@picocss/pico) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-%230172ad)](https://github.com/picocss/pico/blob/master/LICENSE.md) [![X (formerly Twitter)](https://img.shields.io/twitter/url/https/twitter.com/picocss.svg?style=social&label=Follow%20%40picocss)](https://x.com/picocss) ## Pico CSS is no longer maintained [v2.1.1](https://github.com/picocss/pico/releases/tag/v2.1.1) is the final release. **Why**
Today, AI can generate lightweight, standalone, accessible HTML with just the CSS it needs, so a Minimal CSS Framework for Semantic HTML matters less than it used to. To stay relevant, Pico CSS would need a full rewrite: plain modern CSS instead of Sass, built on features it doesn't use today (OKLCH colors, cascade layers, Popover, anchor positioning) with fallbacks for older browsers, and a native compiler that strips unused CSS and makes customization easy. That would be a different project. Pico CSS stays as it is. **What this means** - Nothing breaks. [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@picocss/pico), the [jsDelivr CDN](https://www.jsdelivr.com/package/npm/@picocss/pico) and [picocss.com](https://picocss.com) stay online for the long term. - The repositories are archived. No new issues, PRs or releases. - Pico CSS is [MIT licensed](LICENSE.md). You're free to fork it and take it further. See [community forks](https://github.com/picocss/pico/forks). - The Pico CSS name and logo are not covered by the MIT license. Please give your fork its own name, so users don't confuse it with the original. **Thank you**
What started as a small side project ended up powering thousands of websites. Thank you to everyone who used it, opened issues, sent pull requests and wrote kind messages over the years. --- ## Minimal CSS Framework for Semantic HTML A minimalist and lightweight starter kit that prioritizes semantic syntax, making every HTML element responsive and elegant by default. Write HTML, Add Pico CSS, and Voilà! ## What’s new in v2? Pico v2.0 features better accessibility, easier customization with SASS, a complete color palette, a new group component, and 20 precompiled color themes totaling over 100 combinations accessible via CDN. [Read more](https://picocss.com/docs/v2) ## A Superpowered HTML Reset With just the right amount of everything, Pico is great starting point for a clean and lightweight design system. - Class-light and Semantic - Great Styles with Just CSS - Responsive Everything - Light or Dark Mode - Easy Customization - Optimized Performance ## Table of contents - [Quick start](#quick-start) - [Class-less version](#class-less-version) - [Limitations](#limitations) - [Documentation](#documentation) - [Browser Support](#browser-support) - [Contributing](#contributing) - [Copyright and license](#copyright-and-license) ## Quick start There are 4 ways to get started with pico.css: ### Install manually [Download Pico](https://github.com/picocss/pico/archive/refs/heads/main.zip) and link `/css/pico.min.css` in the `` of your website. ```html ``` ### Usage from CDN Alternatively, you can use [jsDelivr CDN](https://www.jsdelivr.com/package/npm/@picocss/pico) to link pico.css. ```html ``` ### Install with NPM ```shell npm install @picocss/pico ``` Or ```shell yarn add @picocss/pico ``` Then, import Pico into your SCSS file with [@use](https://sass-lang.com/documentation/at-rules/use): ```SCSS @use "pico"; ``` ### Install with Composer ```shell composer require picocss/pico ``` ### Starter HTML template ```HTML Hello world!

Hello world!

``` ## Class-less version Pico provides a `.classless` version. In this version, `
`, `
`, and `
` inside `` act as containers to define a centered or a fluid viewport. Use the default `.classless` version if you need centered viewports: ```html ``` Or use the `.fluid.classless` version if you need a fluid container: ```html ``` Then just write pure HTML, and it should look great: ```html Hello, world!

Hello, world!

``` ## Limitations Pico CSS can be used without custom CSS for quick or small projects. However, it’s designed as a starting point, like a “reset CSS on steroids”. As Pico does not integrate any helpers or utilities `.classes`, this minimal CSS framework requires SCSS or CSS knowledge to build large projects. [Read more](https://picocss.com/docs/usage-scenarios) ## Documentation **Getting started** - [Quick start](https://picocss.com/docs) - [Version picker `New`](https://picocss.com/docs/version-picker) - [Color schemes](https://picocss.com/docs/color-schemes) - [Class-less version](https://picocss.com/docs/classless) - [Conditional styling `New`](https://picocss.com/docs/conditional) - [RTL](https://picocss.com/docs/rtl) **Customization** - [CSS Variables](https://picocss.com/docs/css-variables) - [Sass](https://picocss.com/docs/sass) - [Colors `New`](https://picocss.com/docs/colors) **Layout** - [Container](https://picocss.com/docs/container) - [Landmarks & section](https://picocss.com/docs/landmarks-section) - [Grid](https://picocss.com/docs/grid) - [Overflow auto `New`](https://picocss.com/docs/overflow-auto) **Content** - [Typography](https://picocss.com/docs/typography) - [Link](https://picocss.com/docs/link) - [Button](https://picocss.com/docs/button) - [Table](https://picocss.com/docs/table) **Forms** - [Overview](https://picocss.com/docs/forms) - [Input](https://picocss.com/docs/forms/input) - [Textarea](https://picocss.com/docs/forms/textarea) - [Select](https://picocss.com/docs/forms/select) - [Checkboxes](https://picocss.com/docs/forms/checkboxes) - [Radios](https://picocss.com/docs/forms/radios) - [Switch](https://picocss.com/docs/forms/switch) - [Range](https://picocss.com/docs/forms/range) **Components** - [Accordion](https://picocss.com/docs/accordion) - [Card](https://picocss.com/docs/card) - [Dropdown](https://picocss.com/docs/dropdown) - [Group `New`](https://picocss.com/docs/group) - [Loading](https://picocss.com/docs/loading) - [Modal](https://picocss.com/docs/modal) - [Nav](https://picocss.com/docs/nav) - [Progress](https://picocss.com/docs/progress) - [Tooltip](https://picocss.com/docs/tooltip) **About** - [What’s new in v2?](https://picocss.com/docs/v2) - [Mission](https://picocss.com/docs/mission) - [Usage scenarios](https://picocss.com/docs/usage-scenarios) - [Brand](https://picocss.com/docs/brand) - [Built With](https://picocss.com/docs/built-with) ## Browser Support Pico CSS is designed and tested for the latest stable Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari releases. It does not support any version of IE, including IE 11. ## Contributing Contributions are closed. This repository is archived. ## Copyright and license Licensed under the [MIT License](https://github.com/picocss/pico/blob/master/LICENSE.md).

          v2.1.1  is the final release. 
  Why  
Today, AI can generate lightweight, standalone, accessible HTML with just the CSS it needs, so a Minimal CSS Framework for Semantic HTML matters less than it used to. To stay relevant, Pico CSS would need a full rewrite: plain modern CSS instead of Sass, built on features it doesn't use today (OKLCH colors, cascade layers, Popover, anchor positioning) with fallbacks for older browsers, and a native compiler that strips unused CSS and makes customization easy. That would be a different project. Pico CSS stays as it is. 
  What this means  
 
 Nothing breaks.  npm , the  jsDelivr CDN  and  picocss.com  stay online for the long term. 
 The repositories are archived. No new issues, PRs or releases. 
 Pico CSS is  MIT licensed . You're free to fork it and take it further. See  community forks . 
 The Pico CSS name and logo are not covered by the MIT license. Please give your fork its own name, so users don't confuse it with the original. 
 
  Thank you  
What started as a small side project ended up powering thousands of websites. Thank you to everyone who used it, opened issues, sent pull requests and wrote kind messages over the years.

  Pico CSS is no longer maintained     
  v2.1.1  is the final release. 
  Why  
Today, AI can generate lightweight, standalone, accessible HTML with just the CSS it needs, so a Minimal CSS Framework for Semantic HTML matters less than it used to. To stay relevant, Pico CSS would need a full rewrite: plain modern CSS instead of Sass, built on features it doesn't use today (OKLCH colors, cascade layers, Popover, anchor positioning) with fallbacks for older browsers, and a native compiler that strips unused CSS and makes customization easy. That would be a different project. Pico CSS stays as it is. 
  What this means  
 
 Nothing breaks.  npm , the  jsDelivr CDN  and  picocss.com  stay online for the long term. 
 The repositories are archived. No new issues, PRs or releases. 
 Pico CSS is  MIT licensed . You're free to fork it and take it further. See  community forks . 
 The Pico CSS name and logo are not covered by the MIT license. Please give your fork its own name, so users don't confuse it with the original. 
 
  Thank you  
What started as a small side project ended up powering thousands of websites. Thank you to everyone who used it, opened issues, sent pull requests and wrote kind messages over the years. 
 
  Minimal CSS Framework for Semantic HTML     
 A minimalist and lightweight starter kit that prioritizes semantic syntax, making every HTML element responsive and elegant by default. 
 Write HTML, Add Pico CSS, and Voilà! 
  What’s new in v2?     
 Pico v2.0 features better accessibility, easier customization with SASS, a complete color palette, a new group component, and 20 precompiled color themes totaling over 100 combinations accessible via CDN. 
  Read more  
  A Superpowered HTML Reset     
 With just the right amount of everything, Pico is great starting point for a clean and lightweight design system. 
 
 Class-light and Semantic 
 Great Styles with Just CSS 
 Responsive Everything 
 Light or Dark Mode 
 Easy Customization 
 Optimized Performance

  Quick start     
 There are 4 ways to get started with pico.css: 
  Install manually     
  Download Pico  and link  /css/pico.min.css  in the  <head>  of your website. 
   <  link   rel =" stylesheet "  href =" css/pico.min.css " >   
  Usage from CDN     
 Alternatively, you can use  jsDelivr CDN  to link pico.css. 
   <  link   rel =" stylesheet "  href =" https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@picocss/pico@2/css/pico.min.css " >   
  Install with NPM     
  npm install @picocss/pico  
 Or 
  yarn add @picocss/pico  
 Then, import Pico into your SCSS file with  @use : 
   @use    " pico "  ;  
  Install with Composer     
  composer require picocss/pico  
  Starter HTML template     
   <!doctype html >  
 <  html   lang =" en " > 
   <  head  > 
     <  meta   charset =" utf-8 " > 
     <  meta   name =" viewport "  content =" width=device-width, initial-scale=1 " > 
     <  meta   name =" color-scheme "  content =" light dark " > 
     <  link   rel =" stylesheet "  href =" css/pico.min.css " > 
     <  title  > Hello world! </  title  > 
   </  head  > 
   <  body  > 
     <  main   class =" container " > 
       <  h1  > Hello world! </  h1  > 
     </  main  > 
   </  body  > 
 </  html  >   
  Class-less version     
 Pico provides a  .classless  version. 
 In this version,  <header> ,  <main> , and  <footer>  inside  <body>  act as containers to define a centered or a fluid viewport. 
 Use the default  .classless  version if you need centered viewports: 
   <  link 
   rel =" stylesheet "
   href =" https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@picocss/pico@2/css/pico.classless.min.css "
 />   
 Or use the  .fluid.classless  version if you need a fluid container: 
   <  link 
   rel =" stylesheet "
   href =" https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@picocss/pico@2/css/pico.fluid.classless.min.css "
 >   
 Then just write pure HTML, and it should look great: 
   <!doctype html >  
 <  html   lang =" en " > 
   <  head  > 
     <  meta   charset =" utf-8 " > 
     <  meta   name =" viewport "  content =" width=device-width, initial-scale=1 " > 
     <  meta   name =" color-scheme "  content =" light dark " > 
     <  link 
       rel =" stylesheet "
       href =" https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@picocss/pico@2/css/pico.classless.min.css "
     > 
     <  title  > Hello, world! </  title  > 
   </  head  > 
   <  body  > 
     <  main  > 
       <  h1  > Hello, world! </  h1  > 
     </  main  > 
   </  body  > 
 </  html  >   
  Limitations     
 Pico CSS can be used without custom CSS for quick or small projects. However, it’s designed as a starting point, like a “reset CSS on steroids”. As Pico does not integrate any helpers or utilities  .classes , this minimal CSS framework requires SCSS or CSS knowledge to build large projects.

# Herdr

Herdr is a desktop app for terminals and coding agents. Keep work in spaces, see which agents need you, and leave terminals running when you close the window.

## Install

### Linux and macOS

```sh
curl -fsSL https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.sh | sh
```

Linux needs a desktop session and a working Vulkan driver. macOS builds are available for Apple Silicon; Intel Mac users can [build from source](#build-from-source). Linux builds are x86-64 and ARM64.

The installer adds Herdr to your apps and puts the command in `~/.local/bin`.
Add that folder to your PATH if the installer asks.
On macOS the app lives in `~/Applications/Herdr.app`.
For drag-and-drop installation on Apple Silicon, download [Herdr.dmg](https://releases.herdr.dev/app/Herdr.dmg) and drag Herdr to Applications.

### Windows

Run in PowerShell on x64 Windows with curl and tar installed (Windows 10 1803 or newer):

```powershell
irm https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.ps1 | iex
```

Herdr appears in the Start menu. The installer adds `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\herdr-app` to your user PATH. Open a new terminal to pick it up.

Both installers download and run code. Read the [shell installer](distribution/install.sh) or [PowerShell installer](distribution/install.ps1) first if you prefer.
They also install [herdr-core](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr-core) if it is missing.
The app can help install or update a core it cannot use.

## Find your work

A **space** holds work on one machine, usually in one repo. Each space has **tabs**. Split a tab into **panes** to put terminals or mod panels beside each other.

An unnamed space follows its first terminal's folder. Name a space or tab when you want a label that stays.
New tabs start in the focused terminal's folder.

The agents sidebar brings agents from your spaces into one list, including workers started by another agent.
Agents that report status show as:

- **Working:** still busy.
- **Blocked:** waiting for you.
- **Done:** finished while you were looking elsewhere.
- **Idle:** not working, or a finished agent you have looked at.

Click an agent to see it. A worker without a pane opens in **peek**, over your tab. Keep it as a tab if you want it beside your other work.
Ctrl-click a live terminal address in terminal text to peek at it; use Cmd-click on macOS.
An address such as `t7` means a terminal on the same machine as the terminal showing it. `vps/t7` names one on another machine.

The window arranges terminals. The core runs them.
Closing the window leaves them running; closing a pane or tab ends its terminals.
After a reboot or core crash, kept panes get fresh shells in their last folders, not their old programs.

## Work on another machine

Add an SSH machine from Settings → Machines or the sidebar's Add machine action.
Pick a host from your SSH config or type how SSH reaches it.
Spaces on that machine run their terminals there, not on your computer.

Each machine keeps its spaces, tabs and splits in its core. Connected screens share that structure and the live terminals, but keep their own focus and zoom.
Remote work keeps running when your local window closes or your laptop sleeps, as long as the remote machine and core stay up.

## Make it yours

Open the command palette to find an action by name, or open Settings to change fonts, colors, sounds and other preferences.
The built-in layouts include Herdr, Terminals and Herdr 98.
A **layout** arranges the window. **Mods** are small JavaScript programs that draw its panels, menus and dialogs.

Duplicate a shipped layout or mod before changing its structure or code. Your copies stay yours; Herdr updates the shipped ones on start.
Save a personal layout, mod or key file and the window reloads it.
A broken edit keeps the last good version and reports the error.

Ctrl+Shift+P shows every command and its key (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS). Change any key in `keys.json`; see [the keys section](defaults/AGENTS.md#keys-keysjson) of the mod guide for the format.

[Layouts and mods](docs/mods.md) · [Commands](docs/commands.md)

## Updates and privacy

Installed releases check for updates in the background and download a new app beside the running one. It takes over when you quit and reopen, or choose the update action. Your terminals keep running in the core.
Settings → Updates shows what is available. What's New opens after an update; you can open it again from the command palette.
Builds from source do not update themselves.

Usage telemetry is on by default in releases. Turn it off in Settings → Privacy.
Mods are trusted code, not sandboxed extensions. Read [security and privacy](docs/security.md) before installing someone else's mod.

## For agents

```sh
herdr-app --skill
```

This prints the agent guide for driving the window. The herdr-core skill points agents here.
Use herdr-core for running and coordinating programs; use the app to change what you see.

```sh
herdr-app ls
herdr-app status
herdr-app commands
```

The first two inspect the open window. The command list also works without one.
See the [command reference](docs/commands.md) for arguments.

## Build from source

For bugs, mod API requests and code contributions, see [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md).

Clone this repo with its submodules. Use Rust 1.95.0 and Zig 0.16.0, the versions used in [CI](.github/workflows/ci.yml).
Linux needs the development packages listed in that workflow.

```sh
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr-app.git
cd herdr-app
just build
just test
just install
```

Install [just](https://github.com/casey/just) to use these recipes.
The platform installer builds a release and adds the app to your desktop.
On Linux it links to this checkout, so keep the checkout in place.
Quit and reopen Herdr to use the new build.

Documentation checks also need [Bun](https://bun.sh): `just docs-check` checks generated pages and CLI examples; `just docs-generate` refreshes the reference pages.

To compare drawing changes on Windows, Linux or macOS, run the same fixed workloads against each build:

```sh
python scripts/bench.py --bin <app executable> --set spinners --seconds 20
```

The runner requires `hc` on PATH and uses the Python executable running the script. It prints a unique artifact folder with the run settings, counters and results, then stops its private app, terminals and core. Both sets use Python fixture programs; the default set’s TUI workload replaces historical `btop` measurements. `--only spinners` measures just the quiet native spinner scenario. Keep the window visible and the display awake, and compare the same window activity and display settings; inactive windows may draw at a lower rate. Windows records visibility, foreground activity and display Hz at each measurement boundary; other platforms mark these observations unavailable. Visibility does not establish occlusion. Draws are window render calls. Render-to-paint elapsed time stops before scene finalization, backend drawing, uploads and presentation; it is separate from OS process CPU time. Neither measures physical presentation or the FPS HUD’s derived MAX FPS.

`python scripts/bench_compare.py ghostty --root <artifact folder>` reuses a run’s fake agent for the macOS comparison. Benchmark checks: `python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_bench.py`.

Herdr: made for your agents, remade by them             
 
            Herdr     App   Core   Layouts   Mods   Guide   Blog      Herdr TUI ↗  GitHub  Download               Made for your agents.  Remade by them.    Herdr is a native app for Claude Code, Codex and any other coding agent. Your agent can change any part of it.  Close it, they keep working.         Download for Mac   or install from the terminal:         macOS · Linux  Windows        $  curl -fsSL https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.sh | sh   Copy       $  powershell -c "irm https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.ps1 | iex"   Copy         Paste it in a terminal.    All downloads and what happens next →                      Ask your agent to change Herdr. Try one:      ❯               Customizing usually means picking colors. In Herdr it means everything.  Want your Linear issues next to your agents? A meter for how much of your plan is left? A git graph of the repo you're in? Tell your agent. It's your Herdr.          Your agents run agents.  And hear back.    Your agent can hand a review or a test run to another agent and keep working. When the helper finishes, its report shows up in your agent's input, so you never copy anything between windows.             It starts helpers  hc run --bg codex "review my diff. Done: hc send t1"  Any agent can start another, like Claude, Codex or a test script, and tell it where to report.     It steers them  hc send t3 "take another look"  While a helper works, your agent can change its task or answer its questions.     They report back  <hc from="t3 reviewer">  Reports, exits and requests for help go to your agent. You only see the result.            README.md    01 See who needs you    02 Close it, they keep working    03 Every machine in one sidebar    04 Change anything    05 Any agent    06 Open source    07 Questions          ## See who needs you   Each agent tells Herdr whether it's working, done or waiting on you. The sidebar and the tab show which one needs you, so you can stop checking the rest.   Use a  space  for each repo and a  tab  for each task.             ## Close it, they keep working   Your agents run in  herdr-core , a small server on your machine, not in the window. Quit the app, update it or let it crash, and every terminal is still where you left it.       More about herdr-core →         ## Every machine in one sidebar   Add any machine you can reach over SSH, like a server, a VM or a cloud sandbox. Its spaces and agents show up in the same sidebar under its name, and you start agents there the same way.         # or ask your agent: "add my server vps" 
hc machine add vps   Its agents keep running there while your laptop sleeps or the app is closed.        ## Change anything   Herdr keeps its layout, sidebar, tabs, keys and themes as plain files in  ~/.config/herdr-app . An  AGENTS.md  in there explains them to your agent. You say what you want and your agent writes it.    ~/.config/herdr-app/ 
├── AGENTS.md         what your agent can change 
├── settings.json     fonts, theme, sounds 
├── keys.json
├── layouts/
│   ├── main.json
│   └── board.json
├── mods/
│   ├── agents/main.js
│   └── tabs/main.js
└── themes/    ❯   put a timer on each tab: how long its agent has been working 

 ⏺   Update (mods/tabs/main.js)
   ⎿   Updated mods/tabs/main.js with  6 additions  and  1 removal 

⏺ Done. Each tab shows how long its agent has been at it.                  ## Any agent   Herdr runs real terminals, so your agents work the way they do now. Agents that support  OSC 7501 , an open status protocol, also show whether they're working, done or need you. Your own script can do it with one line.    # one line, and your own script is an agent too 
printf '\e]7501;state=blocked:app=my-agent\e\\'        ## Open source   The app, herdr-core and Herdr TUI are open source under Apache 2.0. You can read the code, change it, or build your own app on top of herdr-core.    herdrdev/herdr-app →     herdrdev/herdr-core →     herdrdev/herdr →         ## Questions     What is Herdr?   A native app for running coding agents. They run in herdr-core, so they keep going when you close the window, and your agent can change any part of the app.       How is it different from Herdr TUI?   Herdr TUI is the original Herdr: a terminal app with its own server. This is a new, separate program built on herdr-core. They don't share agents, so what runs in one doesn't show up in the other. Herdr TUI keeps working, and everything for it is at  herdr.dev/tui .       Which agents does it work with?   Anything that runs in a terminal. Agents that speak  OSC 7501 , an open protocol for reporting status, also show whether they're working, done or need you. An agent that doesn't speak it still runs, just without a status.       My agent doesn't show up in the agents list   The list shows agents that report their status through OSC 7501, so check these:     Older versions of an agent may not report it yet. Update the agent.   An agent running inside tmux within Herdr can't report through tmux. Run it in a Herdr pane directly.   Agents started in Herdr TUI live in its own server, so they don't show up in the app.         What happens when I quit, update or reboot?   Quitting or updating the app changes nothing: every agent keeps running in herdr-core. If the machine reboots or herdr-core stops, the programs stop too. Their panes come back with a shell in the same folder, but Herdr doesn't restart an agent or resume its work in progress. Start it again and carry on.       Which systems does it run on?   macOS (Apple silicon), Linux (x86_64 and arm64) and Windows (x86_64). Other machines join over SSH, whatever they run.       Is it free?   Yes. The app, herdr-core and Herdr TUI are all open source.                Made for your agents.  Remade by them.         Download for Mac   or install from the terminal:         macOS · Linux  Windows        $  curl -fsSL https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.sh | sh   Copy       $  powershell -c "irm https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.ps1 | iex"   Copy         Paste it in a terminal.    All downloads and what happens next →                            Herdr  Made for your agents. Remade by them.   2004 called. They want to return their disemvoweled penultimate "e". 2004 - The Big Bang (Flickr) - Co-founder Caterina Fake wants to buy Flicker.com, but an offline beer brewer refuses to sell it. Out of options, she suggests dropping the "e". It works, and Flickr is born, instantly setting a precedent that typos equal modernism. 2005–2006 - The YC Copycat Flood - Paul Graham launches Y Combinator, and the application form might as well have had a checkbox for "did you delete a vowel to look disruptive?" Scribd (YC S06) drops the E because buying a real dictionary noun requires actual revenue. Twitpic and Pixlr emerge to capture that sweet, sweet pre-seed funding. Even Twitter originally launches in 2006 as "Twttr" because the actual domain is owned by a bird enthusiast. (They buy the "e" back six months later once they realize they look ridiculous). 2007 - The Peak of Style - Tumblr launches, proving the vowel-less trend isn't a passing fad but the official language of the new internet. Dropping the "e" becomes shorthand for "we have venture capital, a minimalist mobile interface, and absolutely no monetization strategy." 2009 - The Aggressive Pivot - Grindr launches. The convention branches out of pure utility and enters cultural lifestyle apps, cementing "-r" as the universal suffix for a location-based mobile service. Every YC batch now features at least three "Uber for X" startups named after a mangled verb. 2011–2012 - The Saturation Point - Companies like Blendr and Fiverr continue the trend, but the public begins to push back. Every SaaS tool on Hacker News looks like a typo. Critics and users start pointing out how incredibly annoying it is to vocally explain a business name ("It's called Taskr... no, without the E"). 2015–2018 - The Death Kneel & Corrections - The joke gets old. Brand consultants begin labeling creative misspelling a "cardinal sin". Startups realize they are losing millions of organic visitors to the properly-spelled domains owned by domain squatters. The internet enters the "-ify" (Spotify, Shopify) and "-ly" (Bitly) eras, completely abandoning the broken suffix because pg wrote an essay saying missing vowels hurt your SEO. 2019–Present - The "Adult in the Room" Era - The trend is officially dead. Modern YC startups pivot toward ultra-literal names (The Browser Company) or aggressive, serious abstract words (OpenAI, CoreWeave) to pretend they are enterprise-ready AI infrastructure rather than a wrapper wrapper wrapper. Postscript - The Ultimate Regression - The convention reaches its absolute, braindead rock bottom with Elon Musk. After burning 44 billion dollars to buy Twitter just so he could unban literal Nazis and amplify white supremacist conspiracy theories to the front page, he rebranded the entire platform to "X.com". It turns out "X" is just "Ex" without the penultimate "e" -- a fittingly hollow, single-letter monument to a sociopathic tech bro who couldn't innovate a functional name if his taxpayer subsidies depended on it.      reply                             77ko    23 hours ago       |  prev   [–]


 Herdr is a desktop app for terminals and coding agents. Keep work in spaces, see which agents need you, and leave terminals running when you close the window. 
  Install     
  Linux and macOS     
  curl -fsSL https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.sh  |  sh  
 Linux needs a desktop session and a working Vulkan driver. macOS builds are available for Apple Silicon; Intel Mac users can  build from source . Linux builds are x86-64 and ARM64. 
 The installer adds Herdr to your apps and puts the command in  ~/.local/bin .
Add that folder to your PATH if the installer asks.
On macOS the app lives in  ~/Applications/Herdr.app .
For drag-and-drop installation on Apple Silicon, download  Herdr.dmg  and drag Herdr to Applications. 
  Windows     
 Run in PowerShell on x64 Windows with curl and tar installed (Windows 10 1803 or newer): 
  irm https: // releases.herdr.dev / app / install.ps1  |  iex  
 Herdr appears in the Start menu. The installer adds  %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\herdr-app  to your user PATH. Open a new terminal to pick it up. 
 Both installers download and run code. Read the  shell installer  or  PowerShell installer  first if you prefer.
They also install  herdr-core  if it is missing.
The app can help install or update a core it cannot use. 
  Find your work     
 A  space  holds work on one machine, usually in one repo. Each space has  tabs . Split a tab into  panes  to put terminals or mod panels beside each other. 
 An unnamed space follows its first terminal's folder. Name a space or tab when you want a label that stays.
New tabs start in the focused terminal's folder. 
 The agents sidebar brings agents from your spaces into one list, including workers started by another agent.
Agents that report status show as: 
 
  Working:  still busy. 
  Blocked:  waiting for you. 
  Done:  finished while you were looking elsewhere. 
  Idle:  not working, or a finished agent you have looked at. 
 
 Click an agent to see it. A worker without a pane opens in  peek , over your tab. Keep it as a tab if you want it beside your other work.
Ctrl-click a live terminal address in terminal text to peek at it; use Cmd-click on macOS.
An address such as  t7  means a terminal on the same machine as the terminal showing it.  vps/t7  names one on another machine. 
 The window arranges terminals. The core runs them.
Closing the window leaves them running; closing a pane or tab ends its terminals.
After a reboot or core crash, kept panes get fresh shells in their last folders, not their old programs. 
  Work on another machine     
 Add an SSH machine from Settings → Machines or the sidebar's Add machine action.
Pick a host from your SSH config or type how SSH reaches it.
Spaces on that machine run their terminals there, not on your computer. 
 Each machine keeps its spaces, tabs and splits in its core. Connected screens share that structure and the live terminals, but keep their own focus and zoom.
Remote work keeps running when your local window closes or your laptop sleeps, as long as the remote machine and core stay up. 
  Make it yours     
 Open the command palette to find an action by name, or open Settings to change fonts, colors, sounds and other preferences.
The built-in layouts include Herdr, Terminals and Herdr 98.
A  layout  arranges the window.  Mods  are small JavaScript programs that draw its panels, menus and dialogs. 
 Duplicate a shipped layout or mod before changing its structure or code. Your copies stay yours; Herdr updates the shipped ones on start.
Save a personal layout, mod or key file and the window reloads it.
A broken edit keeps the last good version and reports the error. 
 Ctrl+Shift+P shows every command and its key (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS). Change any key in  keys.json ; see  the keys section  of the mod guide for the format. 
  Layouts and mods  ·  Commands  
  Updates and privacy     
 Installed releases check for updates in the background and download a new app beside the running one. It takes over when you quit and reopen, or choose the update action. Your terminals keep running in the core.
Settings → Updates shows what is available. What's New opens after an update; you can open it again from the command palette.
Builds from source do not update themselves. 
 Usage telemetry is on by default in releases. Turn it off in Settings → Privacy.
Mods are trusted code, not sandboxed extensions. Read  security and privacy  before installing someone else's mod. 
  For agents     
  herdr-app --skill  
 This prints the agent guide for driving the window. The herdr-core skill points agents here.
Use herdr-core for running and coordinating programs; use the app to change what you see. 
  herdr-app ls
herdr-app status
herdr-app commands  
 The first two inspect the open window. The command list also works without one.
See the  command reference  for arguments. 
  Build from source     
 For bugs, mod API requests and code contributions, see  Contributing . 
 Clone this repo with its submodules. Use Rust 1.95.0 and Zig 0.16.0, the versions used in  CI .
Linux needs the development packages listed in that workflow. 
  git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr-app.git
 cd  herdr-app
just build
just  test 
just install  
 Install  just  to use these recipes.
The platform installer builds a release and adds the app to your desktop.
On Linux it links to this checkout, so keep the checkout in place.
Quit and reopen Herdr to use the new build. 
 Documentation checks also need  Bun :  just docs-check  checks generated pages and CLI examples;  just docs-generate  refreshes the reference pages. 
 To compare drawing changes on Windows, Linux or macOS, run the same fixed workloads against each build: 
  python scripts/bench.py --bin  < app executable >  --set spinners --seconds 20  
 The runner requires  hc  on PATH and uses the Python executable running the script. It prints a unique artifact folder with the run settings, counters and results, then stops its private app, terminals and core. Both sets use Python fixture programs; the default set’s TUI workload replaces historical  btop  measurements.  --only spinners  measures just the quiet native spinner scenario. Keep the window visible and the display awake, and compare the same window activity and display settings; inactive windows may draw at a lower rate. Windows records visibility, foreground activity and display Hz at each measurement boundary; other platforms mark these observations unavailable. Visibility does not establish occlusion. Draws are window render calls. Render-to-paint elapsed time stops before scene finalization, backend drawing, uploads and presentation; it is separate from OS process CPU time. Neither measures physical presentation or the FPS HUD’s derived MAX FPS. 
  python scripts/bench_compare.py ghostty --root <artifact folder>  reuses a run’s fake agent for the macOS comparison. Benchmark checks:  python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_bench.py .

Clover-35B-A3B-Preview

The first diffusion language model from DiffuSpace.

Introduction · Performance · Quick Start · Inference Backends · Fine-Tuning

## Introduction We introduce **Clover-35B-A3B-Preview**, the first model released by **DiffuSpace**. Clover delivers state-of-the-art performance among open-source diffusion language models at release on the benchmarks reported in our [launch blog](https://diffuspace.ai/blog/clover-35b/). Built on [Qwen3.6-35B-A3B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B), Clover combines a text-only mixture-of-experts backbone with block diffusion generation: - **35B total parameters, approximately 3B active per token.** A hybrid Gated DeltaNet (GDN) / full-attention MoE architecture. - **Bidirectional attention within each block.** Additional learned GDN parameters support block diffusion while preserving a causal prefix. - **128K context.** Up to 131,072 tokens across the prompt and generated response. ## Performance [![Clover agentic benchmark results](./benchmark.png)](https://diffuspace.ai/blog/clover-35b/#agentic-benchmarks) See the [launch blog](https://diffuspace.ai/blog/clover-35b/#agentic-benchmarks) for benchmark results, evaluation settings, and comparisons. ## Quick Start ### Hugging Face Transformers Install PyTorch with CUDA support, then the Hugging Face dependencies. This example uses Transformers 5.19.0 and PyTorch 2.10 or later. ```bash pip install "transformers==5.19.0" accelerate safetensors ``` The example runs on one GPU with enough memory for the BF16 weights (approximately 69 GB) plus inference state. ```python import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_id = "Diffuspace/Clover-35B-A3B-Preview" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, trust_remote_code=True, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="cuda:0", ).eval() messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "What is diffusion?"}] prompt = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=True, ) inputs = tokenizer( prompt, add_special_tokens=False, return_tensors="pt" ).to("cuda:0") output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=24576) completion = output[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:] print(tokenizer.decode(completion, skip_special_tokens=True)) ``` Generation defaults are included in the checkpoint. For decoding options and configuration details, see the [Hugging Face model card](https://huggingface.co/Diffuspace/Clover-35B-A3B-Preview#generation-controls). ## Inference Backends | Backend | Use case | Decoding | | --- | --- | --- | | [Hugging Face Transformers](#hugging-face-transformers) | Standalone Python inference and experimentation | Block diffusion denoising | | [SGLang](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/46927) | Serving and evaluation | Block diffusion denoising and Self-speculative decoding | | [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31306) | Local inference | Self-speculative decoding | ### SGLang and llama.cpp Our SGLang implementation supports both **Block diffusion denoising** and **Self-speculative decoding** for Clover. The llama.cpp implementation supports **Self-speculative decoding**. Backend code and setup guides will be added to this repository. > [!NOTE] > We recommend our official **SGLang implementation for serving and evaluation**. Small numerical differences between the Hugging Face implementation and SGLang's kernels can lead to different generated text. ## Supervised Fine-Tuning **Coming soon.** SFT code and training instructions will be released in [`sft/`](./sft/). ## License and Acknowledgments The model is distributed under **Apache-2.0**. See the [model license](https://huggingface.co/Diffuspace/Clover-35B-A3B-Preview/blob/main/LICENSE) and [attributions](https://huggingface.co/Diffuspace/Clover-35B-A3B-Preview/blob/main/ATTRIBUTIONS.md) for details. Clover builds on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. We thank the [Qwen](https://github.com/QwenLM), [Hugging Face Transformers](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers), [SGLang](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang), and [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp) communities for their open-source work.

# Clover-35B-A3B-Preview **Clover-35B-A3B-Preview** is the first model released by **DiffuSpace**, delivering state-of-the-art performance among open-source diffusion language models at release on the benchmarks reported in our [launch blog](https://diffuspace.ai/blog/clover-35b/). Clover combines a 35B-parameter mixture-of-experts backbone with approximately 3B active parameters per token, block diffusion generation, and a **128K context window**. [Blog](https://diffuspace.ai/blog/clover-35b/) · [Code & inference backends](https://github.com/DiffuSpace/Clover-35B-A3B-Preview) · [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/Diffuspace/Clover-35B-A3B-Preview) ## Performance [![Clover agentic benchmark results](https://diffuspace.ai/assets/blog/clover/agentic-benchmarks.jpg)](https://diffuspace.ai/blog/clover-35b/#agentic-benchmarks) See the [benchmark discussion](https://diffuspace.ai/blog/clover-35b/#agentic-benchmarks) for evaluation results, settings, and comparisons. ## Architecture and decoding Clover is a text-only model derived from [Qwen3.6-35B-A3B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B), retaining its hybrid Gated DeltaNet (GDN) / full-attention MoE backbone with 40 layers, 256 routed experts, top-8 token routing, and one shared expert per layer. - **Bidirectional block attention:** additional learned GDN parameters, including right-convolution weights and softmax controls, let tokens attend within a noisy block while preserving a causal prefix. - **128K context:** up to 131,072 tokens for the prompt and generated response together. - **Block diffusion with LowConfidence decoding:** this Hugging Face implementation starts each block with masked tokens and resolves confident positions in parallel. Positions with confidence above the threshold are filled; if none qualify, the most confident position is filled to ensure progress. Once resolved, the block becomes part of the prefix for the next block. Defaults are `block_size=32` and `threshold=0.95`. For **self-speculative decoding** with our SGLang and llama.cpp implementations, see the [official code repository](https://github.com/DiffuSpace/Clover-35B-A3B-Preview). ## Quick start Install PyTorch with CUDA support, then the Hugging Face dependencies. The example below uses Transformers 5.19.0 and PyTorch 2.10 or later. ```bash pip install "transformers==5.19.0" accelerate safetensors ``` Use a GPU with enough memory for the BF16 weights (approximately 69 GB) plus inference state. ```python import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_id = "Diffuspace/Clover-35B-A3B-Preview" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, trust_remote_code=True, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="cuda:0", ).eval() messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "What is diffusion?"}] prompt = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=True, ) inputs = tokenizer(prompt, add_special_tokens=False, return_tensors="pt").to("cuda:0") output = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens=24576, block_size=32, threshold=0.95, do_sample=False, ) completion = output[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:] print(tokenizer.decode(completion, skip_special_tokens=True)) ``` You can also set `model_id` to a local model directory. Generation defaults are loaded automatically from `generation_config.json`; keyword arguments to `generate()` override them. Requests exceeding the 128K context limit are rejected, including space needed to resolve the final full block. ## Generation controls We observe that very long generations can sometimes become repetitive. The model includes repetition controls and gradual biases toward ending the response or thinking phase. **The defaults are already configured**, so no extra arguments are needed for normal use. They also apply during greedy decoding. | Parameter | Default | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | `presence_penalty` | `0.9` | Discourages tokens that have already appeared in the generated response. | | `frequency_penalty` | `0.0` | Penalizes tokens in proportion to their occurrence count; disabled by default. | | `repetition_penalty` | `1.05` | Reduces the preference for previously generated tokens; `1.0` disables it. | | `dllm_length_penalty` | `10.0` | Gradually increases the preference for end-of-response tokens. | | `dllm_think_end_bias` | `10.0` | Gradually encourages `` to close the thinking phase. | Length control begins at `dllm_length_penalty_start=8192` response tokens and reaches its full strength over `dllm_length_penalty_window=8192` more tokens. Thinking control uses `dllm_think_end_start=4096` and `dllm_think_end_window=4096`. These are soft controls; `max_new_tokens` sets the hard output limit. Repetition controls operate on generated response history, excluding the prompt. ## Expert selection During block denoising, Clover can restrict routing to a shared subset of experts for each block. This reduces the number of distinct experts used across the block. The relevant model configuration settings are: | Setting | Default | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | `moe_block_coreset_enabled` | `true` | Enables block-level expert selection during denoising. | | `moe_block_coreset_top_p` | `0.9` | Sets the cumulative routing-mass threshold used to select the expert subset. | The selector aggregates the routing scores of each token's top-8 candidate experts across the block, ranks experts by their aggregate score, and keeps enough to cover the requested fraction of that mass. A value of `0.9` means **90% of the aggregated routing mass**, not 90% of all experts. Lower values generally select fewer experts, with a possible quality tradeoff. This setting is separate from token-sampling `top_p` and does not reduce the size of the stored or loaded model weights. ## Serving and evaluation The Hugging Face implementation provides a standalone PyTorch inference path. Small numerical differences between its operations and SGLang's kernels can lead to different generated text, even with the same decoding settings. **We recommend our official SGLang implementation for serving and evaluation.** Setup instructions and supported decoding modes are available in the [official repository](https://github.com/DiffuSpace/Clover-35B-A3B-Preview). ## Upstream attribution and modifications Clover is derived from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Upstream model assets are Copyright 2026 Alibaba Cloud and distributed under Apache-2.0; the accompanying [LICENSE](LICENSE) preserves the upstream license and copyright statement. The model implementation derives from the Hugging Face Transformers Qwen3.5-MoE implementation used for the Qwen3.6 architecture, Copyright 2025 The Qwen Team and The HuggingFace Inc. team. Clover adds text-only block diffusion inference, bidirectional GDN parameters, and generation controls. See [ATTRIBUTIONS.md](ATTRIBUTIONS.md) for file-level provenance and modification notices.
