  Appendix C  Deterministic Executability Checking and Recovery 

 
  C.1  Executability Checks and First-Failure Classification 

 
 The executability scorer is deterministic and separate from the LLM-based pre-execution verifier used by Dual-Loop. The scorer evaluates the actual emitted actions against benchmark tool and state semantics; no learned judge, human step label, or single gold action sequence is required. The Dual-Loop verifier instead examines a proposed plan before execution and may change the executor’s subsequent behavior. Its acceptance decision does not establish that the emitted trajectory is executable. 
 
 
 For action     a  j   a_{j}   , let      V  j   =  1   V_{j}=1    exactly when the tool is exposed, its arguments satisfy the declared interface and validators, referenced values are available and type-compatible, required information has been obtained, applicable state preconditions hold, and the benchmark accepts the transition. Otherwise      V  j   =  0   V_{j}=0   . The checker determines first failure as follows. 
 
  1.  
 
 Initialize replay from the benchmark’s initial state. Available values comprise the prompt and benchmark-visible initial values. Initialize     FED  =   T  +  1    \mathrm{FED}=T+1   . 
  
  2.  
 
 Process emitted actions in order. Resolve the selected tool; an unavailable tool is a schema/tool-availability failure. For an exposed tool, check argument binding, declared types, and registered validators. 
  
  3.  
 
 Check referenced values for absence, stale bindings, or incompatible types; these are dependency failures. Check whether required task information has been obtained, and whether applicable state preconditions hold. 
  
  4.  
 
 If these checks pass, execute the action against the replay or sandbox state. A rejected transition is a state-consistency failure. For an accepted transition, record the output, update available values, and advance the state. 
  
  5.  
 
 At the first failed predicate or rejected transition, set      V  j   =  0   V_{j}=0    and     FED  =  j   \mathrm{FED}=j   . Choose the first applicable diagnostic category in the precedence order below, then stop prefix replay. Retain the full observed rollout for benchmark-defined final success    Y  Y    and RR. 
  
  6.  
 
 If every action satisfies the predicate, retain     FED  =   T  +  1    \mathrm{FED}=T+1   . A terminal no-tool action is executable only when benchmark semantics permit completion without a tool call. 
  
 
 The diagnostic precedence is 
 

  
  
      schema  ⟶  dependency  ⟶  precondition  ⟶  state-consistency  ⟶  information   .   \text{schema}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{dependency}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{precondition}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{state-consistency}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{information}.    
    
 
 The tie-break assigns one primary cause at the first failed action; it changes neither action validity nor FED, PEC, TER, AUC-PEC, RR, or final success. In particular, the diagnostic ordering is distinct from the order in which applicable conditions are checked. 
 
 
 BFCL-v3 evaluates prefixes by replay in a copied state under the case-specific function namespace and benchmark evaluator semantics  [ 3 ] . ToolSandbox uses tools visible at the relevant turn, their registered validators, and the recorded execution outcome and state transition  [ 4 ] . These benchmark-specific semantics ground the same executability predicate. The metrics then aggregate the resulting     (   T  i   ,   FED  i   ,   Y  i   )   (T_{i},\mathrm{FED}_{i},Y_{i})    records deterministically. 
 
 
 Stopping the first-failure replay does not truncate the observed episode or replace its final outcome. Here     V  j   V_{j}    describes the validity of action     a  j   a_{j}    in its local benchmark state. Determining FED requires checking actions only through the first failure. Later actions in the observed episode can be executable, and the task can still succeed. For     k  ≤  T   k\leq T   , however, prefix validity is 
 

  
  
      E  k   =   ∏   j  =  1   k    V  j   =  𝟏   {  FED  >  k  }   .   E_{k}=\prod_{j=1}^{k}V_{j}=\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{FED}>k\}.    
    
 
 Once an action fails, every subsequent prefix still contains that failure. Consequently, later successful execution can contribute to recovery while never restoring executable-prefix survival for that rollout.

 This appendix specifies the validation intervention in Section   2.5  . Only the evaluated executor trajectory, including the terminal no-tool action defined in Section   2.2  , enters the prefix metrics.   D.1  Objects and Information Boundary 

 
 Let    x  x    denote the user goal,    𝒰  \mathcal{U}    the available tool specification, and     s  0   s_{0}    a compact summary of benchmark-visible state before execution. Dual-Loop uses a planner    P  P   , verifier    V  V   , and executor    R  R   . At validation iteration    j  j   , the planner proposes a finite candidate plan 
 

  
  
       z   (  j  )    =   (   z  1   (  j  )    ,  …  ,   z   M  j    (  j  )    )    ,   z^{(j)}=(z^{(j)}_{1},\ldots,z^{(j)}_{M_{j}}),

The plan length     M  j   M_{j}    need not equal the eventual executed horizon     T  i   T_{i}   : the plan is conditioning context, not the object being scored.

        τ  ^   i   =   (   a   i  ,  1    ,  …  ,   a   i  ,   T  i     )    .   \hat{\tau}_{i}=(a_{i,1},\ldots,a_{i,T_{i}}).    
    
 
 The evaluator scores this emitted trajectory directly. Thus, if the executor deviates from a verified plan, terminates early, or emits an invalid call, the metrics reflect the emitted actions exactly as they occurred. 
 
  
  Figure D.1:  Dual-Loop validation intervention. The planner proposes a structured candidate plan, the verifier either accepts it or returns targeted feedback, and the executor emits the only environment-facing actions scored by the prefix-level metrics. 
 
 
 
  D.2  Verifier Checklist 

 
 The verifier is designed to reject candidate plans that contain predictable sources of non-executable prefixes before any environment action is taken. It applies the following local checklist, aligned with the first-failure taxonomy in Section   2.4  : 
 
  1.  
 
  Tool and schema validity.  Each planned operation must refer to an available tool in    𝒰  \mathcal{U}   , include required arguments, avoid unsupported arguments, and satisfy declared type or formatting constraints. 
  
  2.  
 
  Dependency resolution.  Values referenced by a planned step must be available from the prompt, the initial state summary, or an earlier planned step. The verifier rejects forward references, stale bindings, and type-incompatible reuse. 
  
  3.  
 
  Information availability.  Required user information or lookup results must either be present, requested before use, or represented as a dependency on an earlier planned step. This check catches plans that use information before collecting it. 
  
  4.  
 
  Explicit preconditions.  If a tool requires prior authorization, a preceding state update, or a specific object to exist before use, the plan must satisfy that prerequisite before the tool is called. 
  
  5.  
 
  State consistency.  Planned state mutations must be compatible with benchmark-visible state and with state changes induced by earlier planned steps. Examples include rejecting updates to absent objects or operations that consume unavailable resources. 
  
 
 The checklist is intentionally local. It is not a proof of global optimality, and it does not replace benchmark replay after execution. The benchmark-side evaluator remains the authority for FED, TER, final success, and RR. 
 
 
 
  D.3  Repair Loop and Iteration Budgets 

 
 If the verifier rejects a candidate plan, its feedback identifies the earliest detected failing step, the failed check, and the information needed for repair when that information is available from    x  x   ,    𝒰  \mathcal{U}   , or     s  0   s_{0}   . The planner then proposes a revised candidate before any environment-facing action is emitted. In the BFCL-v3/ToolSandbox experiments, the validation loop is capped at      K  val   =  5   K_{\mathrm{val}}=5    candidate plans. If no candidate is accepted within this cap, the validation stage returns a failure flag and the executor receives no accepted plan as a strong constraint. The rollout is not discarded; any environment actions subsequently emitted by the executor are scored in the same way as all other rollouts. Cap exhaustion is therefore method-side behavior, not a prefix failure. 
 
 
 The validation cap is separate from the ReAct execution cap. For BFCL-v3 and ToolSandbox, we use      K  exec   =  10   K_{\mathrm{exec}}=10    ReAct action iterations for the environment-facing executor. This separation is important because the two loops bound different resources:     K  val   K_{\mathrm{val}}    limits unscored pre-execution search over candidate plans, whereas     K  exec   K_{\mathrm{exec}}    limits the scored action horizon available for multi-step tool use. A validation iteration does not increment     T  i   T_{i}   ; only executor-emitted environment actions, or the terminal no-tool action described in Section   2.2  , contribute to     T  i   T_{i}    and to PEC, FED, TER, AUC-PEC, and RR. 
 
 
 
  D.4  Metric Accounting and Controls 

 
 The following conventions keep the intervention aligned with the prefix-level definitions: 
 
  1.  
 
 Candidate plans, verifier decisions, and verifier feedback are not benchmark actions. They affect metrics only through the executor’s subsequent environment-facing behavior. 
  
  2.  
 
 FED is computed after execution from      τ  ^   i   \hat{\tau}_{i}   . A verified plan that later leads the executor to an invalid call is counted as an ordinary prefix failure. 
  
  3.  
 
 RR is computed only for rollouts with      FED  i   ≤   T  i    \mathrm{FED}_{i}\leq T_{i}   . Rejected candidate plans before execution are not RR-eligible because no benchmark prefix has failed. 
  
  4.  
 
 Validation does not modify benchmark state before execution. It can improve PEC, TER, or AUC-PEC only by changing the environment-facing actions emitted by the executor. 
  
 
 Within each benchmark–model condition, all variants use the same task identifiers, tool specifications, executor horizon cap, and decoding rule. The Dual-Loop–Plan-Conditioned ReAct comparison measures the joint effect of validation, revision, and their additional inference cost under matched executor conditions. The scored trajectory semantics are the same across variants. Appendix   F   gives the verifier-sensitivity results and experimental controls. Planner and verifier calls are outside the scored trajectory, but should be included when comparing token use, latency, or deployment cost. 
 
 
 
  D.5  Limitations of the Intervention 

 
 The verifier can miss hidden-state constraints, underspecified intent, or semantic requirements outside the tool interface, and can reject executable alternatives. Pre-execution validation also adds inference cost. The prefix metrics characterize how Dual-Loop’s effects vary across environments and configurations (Appendix   F  ). 
 
 
 
 
  Appendix E  Additional Experimental Settings and Compute Resources 

 
 Decoding and rollout settings. 

 
 The following decoding settings and aggregate runtime apply to the 4,800-rollout BFCL-v3/ToolSandbox grid. All LLM conditions used the least-stochastic provider-supported configuration.
For GPT-4.1 and Llama-4-Maverick-Instruct, we set temperature to    0  0   , used
top-    p  =  1   p=1    when exposed, and disabled presence and frequency penalties. For the
GPT-5.4 reasoning condition, unsupported sampling controls were not set; instead
we fixed  reasoning.effort=high  and kept the remaining provider-exposed
generation controls at their defaults. To equalize generation budget, every
planner, verifier, and executor call used a    4,000  4{,}000   -token response cap; for
APIs that distinguish hidden reasoning tokens from visible text, this cap is
applied to the provider’s total output-token budget. The environment-facing
ReAct execution loop was capped at      K  exec   =  10   K_{\mathrm{exec}}=10    tool-action iterations
for every ReAct-style agent variant, while Dual-Loop additionally used the
separate pre-execution planner–verifier budget      K  val   =  5   K_{\mathrm{val}}=5    described
in Appendix   D  ; validation attempts are method-side computation
and are not counted as tool actions in     T  i   T_{i}   . 
 
 
 
 Compute resources. 

 
 Our experiments evaluate agent rollouts rather than train or fine-tune models. All LLM inference was performed through hosted model APIs; the local machine only orchestrated benchmark execution, tool-state updates, trajectory logging, and metric computation. Model inference was served by provider-managed accelerator infrastructure behind API endpoints, so per-request GPU type, GPU count, and accelerator occupancy were not exposed to us. We therefore report local orchestration compute separately from hosted inference compute. The BFCL-v3/ToolSandbox grid contains      200  ×  2  ×  3  ×  4   =  4,800   200\times 2\times 3\times 4=4{,}800    rollouts across two datasets, three models, and four agent variants. A CPU-only local worker is sufficient for the evaluation harness; the BFCL-v3/ToolSandbox runs used a Linux worker with 16 vCPUs and 64 GB RAM, with no local GPU allocated. Wall-clock time was dominated by remote model latency and API rate limits rather than local computation; using 16 asynchronous API-request workers, the 4,800-rollout BFCL-v3/ToolSandbox grid completed in approximately 72 hours. Offline computation of PEC, FED, TER, AUC-PEC, RR, and bootstrap confidence intervals for this grid completed in under 1 hour on the same machine. 
 
 
 The four-method, three-benchmark audit comprises 4,800 BFCL-v3/ToolSandbox rollouts and 1,968 Airline/Retail rollouts, totaling 6,768. The verifier-sensitivity study uses separate paired runs outside this total. The approximately 72-hour runtime applies only to BFCL-v3/ToolSandbox. Appendix   F   reports agent-side token and latency measurements for Airline/Retail and cost differences for the sensitivity study, excluding simulator and evaluator calls.

      Title: Only Accepted Tokens Count: An Energy Accounting of Speculative Decoding Under Latency Targets 
      Authors:  Bole Ma ,  Ayesha Afzal ,  Jan Eitzinger ,  Harald Koestler ,  Gerhard Wellein               View a PDF of the paper titled Only Accepted Tokens Count: An Energy Accounting of Speculative Decoding Under Latency Targets, by Bole Ma and 4 other authors 
     View PDF

             Abstract: Large language model serving is limited by facility power. Energy per token determines how many tokens a datacenter can serve, while a latency target bounds how quickly each user receives them. During decode, every weight is read from memory for every generated token. Batching amortizes this read across users but makes no individual user faster. Speculative decoding does: a drafter proposes several future tokens, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass that reuses the same weight read. Because every drafted token must be verified whether or not it is accepted, the energy speculation saves depends on how many drafted tokens are accepted. This saving is hard to pin down. It varies across target models from different attention families and across drafting schemes, and it depends on the text being served. Every drafter we evaluate accepts fewer tokens on conversation than on code, and every trained drafter accepts fewer on Romansh, a low-resource language, than on English. We measure speculative decoding under production serving conditions (SGLang, CUDA graphs enabled) on H100 and H200 GPUs, at batch sizes up to 64 across 5 corpora. On dense models, verification, not drafting, dominates the energy cost. The saving shrinks as the batch grows, because batching has already shared the weight read that speculation would divide among the accepted tokens. At large batch sizes, block drafters push verification past the balance point between arithmetic and memory traffic into the compute-bound regime, where the saving becomes a loss, and a drafter with low acceptance raises energy per token. Meeting a tighter latency target with speculation then costs additional energy. Larger batches lower energy per token without speculation. Speculation adds to that saving only when acceptance is high, and on the model we tested it leaves little headroom for latency-preserving DVFS.

  Abstract.

per token determines how many tokens a datacenter can serve, while a latency

attention families and across drafting schemes, and it depends on the text
being served. Every drafter we evaluate accepts fewer tokens on conversation
than on code, and every trained drafter accepts fewer on Romansh, a

 We measure speculative decoding under production serving conditions (SGLang,
CUDA graphs enabled) on H100 and H200 GPUs, at batch sizes up to    64  64    across 5 corpora. On dense models, verification, not drafting, dominates the energy cost. The saving shrinks as
the batch grows, because batching has already shared the weight read that
speculation would divide among the accepted tokens. At large batch sizes,
block drafters push verification past the balance point between arithmetic
and memory traffic into the compute-bound regime, where the saving becomes a loss, and a drafter with low
acceptance raises energy per token. Meeting a tighter latency target with

saving only when acceptance is high, and on the model we tested it leaves
little headroom for latency-preserving DVFS. 
  
 
 
 Keywords:  speculative decoding, energy efficiency, LLM inference, attention,
GPU
 
 
  1.  Introduction 

 
 Language model serving is limited by facility power. NVIDIA presents its
Vera Rubin systems against a fixed facility power budget and names performance
per watt the defining metric of AI infrastructure  ( Kampman, 2026 ;  Moseley et al., 2026 ) ,
and from the operator side SemiAnalysis reports that OpenAI is limited by
datacenter power rather than by budget or floor space, which makes tokens per
megawatt the quantity it buys  ( Shan et al., 2026 ) . Tokens per
megawatt is energy per token inverted, so every joule a serving configuration
saves per token is capacity a power-limited facility gains  ( Afzal et al., 2026a ) . The same
comparisons already mix systems served with and without speculative
decoding  ( Shan et al., 2026 ) , which is the setting whose energy
this paper measures. 
 
 
 Energy is not the only target. A service is also held to latency objectives
that its users feel: the time to the first token of a response, and the time
between the tokens that follow. A service that saves energy by streaming
tokens more slowly loses its users, so the configuration an operator wants is
one that meets both targets at once. Choosing the lowest-energy configuration
that still meets a latency objective is the framing of cluster-level energy
managers such as DynamoLLM  ( Stojkovic et al., 2025 ) ; this paper asks the same question
of speculative decoding. The first token has several levers, among them prefix
caching  ( Zheng et al., 2024 )  and running prefill on separate
machines  ( Patel et al., 2024 ) . The time between tokens is set by decode
alone. 
 
 
 Decode generates text one token per forward pass. Every pass reads all of the
model’s weights to produce a single token, so the machine spends its time
moving bytes while its arithmetic units wait on memory, and both the energy
per token and the time between tokens follow the bytes. 
 
 
 That makes meeting both targets plausible. Reading a byte from off-chip memory costs far more energy than an arithmetic
operation on it: on a GH200, a Hopper GPU like ours, a byte read from HBM costs
about 93 pJ and a 16-bit tensor-core operation about 0.5 pJ  ( Antepara et al., 2025 ) ,
so a pass that produces more tokens per weight read should lower energy per
token, and if those tokens belong to one user, such a pass should shorten the time
between that user’s tokens as well. 
 
 
 Batching is the first candidate. Running many sequences together reads the
weights once and amortises that read, so energy per token falls and throughput
rises. Batching does nothing for any individual user. On the dense models we measured, the time between a user’s tokens grows by 9 to 34% from a batch of 1 to 32. On the Mixture-of-Experts models it grows 2.5 to 4.0 times,
because each added request routes to the experts chosen for its tokens and adds their weights
to the read. 
 
 
 The time-between-tokens objective is written in that quantity. When the
objective is tight enough, no batch size meets it, and
speculative decoding becomes the only remaining lever. A drafter proposes
several tokens at low cost, the model verifies them in one pass, and the accepted
ones are produced for the cost of a single weight read. On our models speculation shortens the mean time between tokens at single
stream by    1.3  1.3    to     4.3  ×   4.3\times    (Table   4  ).
Without speculation, an objective of    25  25    ms per token is missed at every
batch we ran by gemma-4-31B-it, the largest dense model, and an objective of    10  10    ms by 4 of our 11 models; speculation brings every one of them under the
objective. 
 
 
 The remaining question is the energy cost of speculation. Where batching has
already amortised the weight read, there is less for a drafter to recover, and
the drafter still has to be paid for. 
 
 
 This paper measures that trade. We run 5 published drafting schemes
against 11 models spanning 4 attention designs, sweeping the number of
tokens verified per step and the batch. For every model, scheme and batch we
also run a non-speculative baseline, the same model served at the same batch
size without speculative decoding, and we add hardware performance counters for
the roofline and a draft and verify split measured by removing the draft.
The paper contributes (1) a paired energy measurement of speculative decoding
as production engines serve it; (2) a mechanism, from the draft and verify
split and from hardware-counter rooflines on two GPUs that show where
verification crosses the balance point and the saving ends; (3) guidance on the
choice of drafter and the number of drafted tokens across batch and GPU; and
(4) measurement pitfalls that change the reported saving without any sign in the
result file, among them a CUDA-graph bias of up to 39 percentage points on
Mixture-of-Experts models. 
 
 
 
  2.  Background: Decode, Speculation, and Draft Cost 

 
 On an H100 the balance point between arithmetic and memory sits near    316  316   
operations per byte, and on an H200 near    163  163   , from the tensor-core rates and
memory bandwidths we measure (Section   3  ), while a decode
step at single stream executes about 10 operations per byte, including the
padded work of tensor-core tiles (Section   9  ).
Decode runs more than an order of magnitude below the balance point, so the
arithmetic units are mostly idle and the energy of a token follows the bytes
that produced it and the time spent moving them. 
 
 
 Speculation raises the arithmetic done per byte by giving each weight read
several tokens of the same request to process. A drafter proposes    k  k   
tokens and the model being served, the  target model  of the
speculative-decoding literature, checks all of them in one pass, a small
matrix product rather than a vector product. The model keeps the drafted
tokens up to the first one it disagrees with and adds one token that it predicts itself. A
rejected token was still drafted and still carried through verification, so
the drafter’s work on that token and its share of the pass return nothing. At
single stream that share costs little, because the extra tokens ride along on
a weight read that dominates the step. At serving batch the pass is already
doing useful work for every request, and the share spent on rejected tokens
displaces useful work. The quantity that
matters is therefore the number of tokens accepted per verification, set
against the cost of every drafted token, and not the fraction of drafted
tokens that is accepted: only the accepted tokens divide the weight read. 
 
 
 We compare 5 drafting schemes: n-gram lookup, multi-token-prediction (MTP)
heads, EAGLE3  ( Li et al., 2025 ) , DFlash  ( Chen et al., 2026 )  and
DSpark  ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) . They differ in where the drafter comes from, and
therefore in what a draft costs. Training-free n-gram drafting matches the
recent context against itself and runs no network; SGLang, the engine we
measure, matches on the host  ( Zheng et al., 2024 )  and vLLM on the
GPU  ( vLLM Team, 2026 ) , and either way its GPU cost is verifying the tree of
candidates it proposes. The trained drafters come in two kinds. A  draft
head  (the MTP heads, EAGLE3, and gemma’s assistant, described below) is one or
a few extra layers that read the hidden state of the model and predict the next
token, so one pass of the head costs a small fraction of a pass of the model.
A head drafts one token per pass and each pass waits for the previous one, so
a draft of    k  k    tokens takes    k  k    small passes run in sequence. A  block
drafter  (DFlash and DSpark) is a separate small network that drafts a
whole block of tokens in one pass. The block has a fixed size set in training,
counting the last accepted token that opens it: 16 tokens for the z-lab
DFlash drafters, and 7 tokens for DeepSpec’s DFlash and DSpark
drafters  ( Chen et al., 2026 ;  Cheng et al., 2026 ) . 
 
 
 A drafter trained together with its model is co-trained, as are the MTP
heads shipped with Qwen3.6, GLM-4.7-Flash and JoyAI-LLM-Flash. A drafter
trained after its model is post-hoc, and its training comes either from the
model’s vendor or from a third party. Gemma 4 ships a vendor post-hoc draft
head, trained by Google, which its authors call an assistant  ( Gemma Team, 2026 ) ;
the engine serves it through its MTP path, so the figures list it under MTP.
The EAGLE3, DFlash and DSpark checkpoints we use are third-party post-hoc
drafters. Every scheme sends the last accepted token through the verification
pass together with the drafted ones, so the model verifies one token more per
request and step than the drafter proposes; for a block drafter this number
equals the block size. Table   1   lists the number of tokens each
drafter has verified per step, and the figures append it to the name of the
drafter: DFlash-16 verifies 16 tokens per request and step. 
 
 
 
  3.  Measurement 

 
 The 11 models span 4 attention families: plain grouped-query attention
(GQA: Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct),
grouped-query attention with sliding-window layers (GQA+SWA: gemma-4-12B-it,
gemma-4-26B-A4B-it and gemma-4-31B-it), multi-head latent attention (MLA:
GLM-4.7-Flash and JoyAI-LLM-Flash), and state-space hybrids that interleave
Gated DeltaNet layers with gated attention (GDN+GA: Qwen3.6-27B and
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B). Of the 11 models, 5 are Mixture-of-Experts models, marked with asterisks in
Table   1  .
Every run uses one NVIDIA H100 SXM5 with 94 GB of HBM2e and a 700 W power
limit, on which we measure a memory bandwidth of 2.28 TB/s and a BF16
tensor-core rate of 719 TFLOP/s. Of the 11 models, 3 run their batch sweeps on an H200 with 141 GB of HBM3e
(4.44 TB/s and 722 TFLOP/s measured) instead: JoyAI-LLM-Flash, whose
weights alone fill the H100’s memory, and the two Qwen3.6 hybrids, which the H100 cannot hold at large batch
(Section   6  ); Section   9  
repeats Qwen3-4B on the H200 as well. Every run generates 512 tokens per request: a batch of    B  B    is    B  B    requests
submitted together and decoded to that length, with no further arrivals. Each
batch is drawn from a pool of 96 distinct prompts for its task and sent through
the chat template of each model with its default settings
(Figure   1  ), so Qwen3, Qwen3.6 and GLM-4.7-Flash generate
thinking text, and their results describe that text. The code pool feeds every
batch sweep; Section   4.1   repeats the sweeps on conversation and long
documents and serves English and Romansh news at batches of 1 and 16. 
 
 
 
 
  Code  (every batch sweep) 16–18 tokens
 
 Write a Python function that reverses a list of integers and returns the
result as a tuple.    
  
 
  Conversation , real user turns (Section   4.1  ) 16–19 tokens
 
 how do I add multiple new columns in m for power query or power bi?    
 
 

 
  Long document  (Section   4.1  ) 1000–1200 tokens
 
 Summarize the following government report in three sentences.
The structure of the armed forces is based on the Total Force concept, which

 Energy comes from the cumulative energy counter built into the GPU
( nvmlDeviceGetTotalEnergyConsumption ), read at    10  10    Hz; the energy of
a generation is the difference between two readings. The counter covers the GPU
board only, not the host processor, host memory, network or cooling, which
favours n-gram drafting, whose matching runs on the host. Weights and the
key-value cache are BF16, decoding is greedy, each cell runs at least 3 seeds,
and each model uses one SGLang build (0.5.12 or newer) under CUDA 13.2. Every speculative run is compared with a
non-speculative baseline run: the same model served without speculative
decoding, at the same batch size, with the same prompt pool, generation length,
GPU and engine settings. The
energy saving is the fraction by which the energy per token of the speculative
run falls below that of this baseline run, so a difference in serving
configuration cannot be reported as a difference in scheme.
Acceptance is ragged: within one batch each request keeps the accepted
prefix and rolls back the rest. Verification is not. The engine’s default,
which every measurement here uses, verifies the full number of tokens for every
request whatever its drafter proposed, so the verification pass has the same
shape at every step. DSpark also offers confidence-scheduled verification, a
non-default mode that verifies fewer tokens for some requests, chosen with a cost table
measured on the GPU  ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) . On the H100 the table prices an extra
verified token at a small fraction of a percent of a step, so the mode
verifies the full number of tokens at every batch. Acceptance is then unchanged at every batch
and the saving at serving batch falls by a few points, so all results use the
default mode.
Each drafter verifies the number of tokens it was released with, so that number differs across schemes
(Table   1  ). A block drafter verifies its trained block, and the
engine does not accept a shorter one. Where a block drafter and a head share a
model, the block drafter therefore also verifies more tokens per request,
and the comparisons in Section   6   include that difference.

 DeepSpec’s DSpark drafter for gemma-4-12B-it has no implementation in the serving engine, because its layers are Gemma-4 layers rather than the Qwen3 layers the
engine’s DSpark drafter builds. We wrote that implementation from the DeepSpec reference code; at a batch of 1 it reproduces the baseline’s greedy output
token for token. 
 
 
 The counter updates more slowly than a single draft or verify phase lasts, so
we never divide energy between phases by time; every energy number is a total
over a whole generation, and the draft’s share comes from removing the draft
(Section   8  ). Production engines capture the decode step in CUDA
graphs wherever shapes allow, so deployments run with capture enabled, not in
eager mode. Capture
and speculation both exist to amortise kernel launches. A non-speculative decode
step is the most launch-bound thing the engine does, while a speculative step
already carries many tokens of work per launch, so capture helps the baseline more than it helps the speculative run and leaves speculation with less to
recover. Measuring with capture disabled
therefore credits speculation with an overhead it never removed. 
 
 
 We measured that credit by re-running the baseline and the speculative run with capture enabled. The credit is not a constant and cannot be transferred
between models, because it tracks how launch-bound the baseline is. The credit splits by architecture: on every dense model it is under 10 percentage points, and on every Mixture-of-Experts model it is 19 to 39 points at single stream (Table   3  ). Mixture-of-Experts
decode issues many small per-expert kernels and is the most launch-bound
baseline in the study. With
the launches removed, a Mixture-of-Experts step costs what its experts cost to
read, and every token in the step routes to the experts chosen for it, whether it
belongs to another request or is another drafted token. Verifying a draft
then reads more expert weights even for a single request.
Because the credit differs between schemes, capture can also change which scheme saves the most energy: at single stream on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, DFlash saves the most with capture disabled and the draft head saves the most with capture enabled, and n-gram drafting, which saves energy on every model with capture
disabled, costs energy on every Mixture-of-Experts model it runs on with
capture enabled.
Independent work reaches the same conclusion about Mixture-of-Experts decode
being launch-bound rather than arithmetic-bound, for an unrelated set of
optimisations  ( Sakthivel et al., 2026 ) . 
 
 
 We therefore report every saving, batch sweep, latency and energy split with
capture enabled (Table   2  ), and use capture disabled only for
the hardware-counter roofline (Section   9  ). Graph replay
launches the same kernels, so the arithmetic and memory traffic each kernel
performs does not depend on capture.

  4.  What Speculation Saves, and Where the Saving Ends 

 
 At single stream every model has a scheme that saves energy, and the largest saving per model, taken over its schemes, has a median of 54%
of decode energy (Table   2  ). The one
scheme that costs energy at single stream is n-gram drafting on the
Mixture-of-Experts models. N-gram drafting accepts too few tokens to pay for
the expert weights each extra verified token reads
(Section   3  ), while on the dense models the same drafter
saves energy. 
 
 
 The saving then decays as batch grows (Figure   2  ), because
batching has already amortised the weight read that the drafter would divide.
This decay holds for the short contexts we serve; at long contexts the
key-value cache keeps large-batch decode memory-bound, and the speedup from
speculation can grow with batch  ( Sadhukhan et al., 2025 ) .

  4.1.  Does the Served Text Change the Answer? 

 
 A drafter predicts text, so the served content changes what it can recover. Structured, repetitive text is the favourable case: EAGLE reports its largest speedups on code and attributes them to fixed templates  ( Li et al., 2024 ) . On the Spec-Bench
cross-task benchmark, drafting by lookup in the prompt does best where the
output copies the input, as in summarisation, and almost every method gains
least on translation  ( Xia et al., 2024 ) . We ran the whole batch sweep on a code pool, a long-document pool and real
conversational turns, with every speculative run compared with a non-speculative baseline run on the
same pool at the same batch size, and with each pool built to avoid the
duplicate-prompt problem above. 
 
 
 Conversation is harder to predict than code for every drafter: every scheme
on every model accepts fewer tokens per verification on conversation, the
training-free n-gram drafter included. How much a drafter loses follows how it
was trained. The co-trained MTP heads lose little, and on GLM-4.7-Flash the largest saving, from its MTP head, is the same on both
pools. The post-hoc drafters lose more, and the
most specialised loses most: the DFlash drafter trained for
Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct accepts 2.0 to 3.0 tokens per verification on
conversation against 5.9 on code, and at a batch of    64  64    it saves 51% of
decode energy on code and costs energy on conversation. Across models, the largest saving per model at a batch of    64  64    is a median of
11 percentage points
lower on conversation than on code. On long documents, where the answer copies
from the prompt, n-gram acceptance on the gemma models is higher than on
code, as Spec-Bench reports for lookup drafting. 
 
 
 The scheme that saves the most energy can change with the text, because a
drafter that accepts fewer tokens still pays for the same number of verified
tokens: the engine verifies the full number of tokens for every request,
whatever that request accepts (Section   3  ). On
gemma-4-12B-it and gemma-4-31B-it, the two schemes that save the most are the
DFlash drafter, which verifies 16 tokens per request and step, and the
assistant, which verifies 6 tokens. On code the DFlash drafter saves the most at a batch of 1
to 4 and the assistant at a batch of 32 and 64, the change with batch that
Section   6   explains. On conversation the DFlash drafter accepts
3.3 to 3.4 tokens per verification, and the assistant accepts 3.3
to 3.5 tokens: both drafters accept about as many tokens, the DFlash drafter
still verifies 16 tokens per request, and the assistant saves the most at every
batch. 
 
 
 Spec-Bench attributes the weak translation speedups to thin multilingual data
in pretraining  ( Xia et al., 2024 ) , without separating how the drafter was
trained from how the model was trained. A language outside the drafters’ training data separates how the drafter was trained from how the model was trained, and there are two common explanations: that block drafters
are fragile, and that what matters is when and on what data a drafter was
trained. We served matched news prompts in English and in Romansh, a low-resource
language. No model lists Romansh among its supported languages  ( Qwen Team, Alibaba, 2025 ;  Gemma Team, 2026 ;  Z.ai, 2026 ;  JD Open Source, 2026 ;  Qwen Team, 2026 ) ,
and no post-hoc drafter’s published training set contains it: those sets are English
instruction and chat data, and the z-lab DFlash recipe adds Spanish, French,
German, Italian and Japanese  ( Thoughtworks, 2026 ;  Chen et al., 2026 ;  Cheng et al., 2026 ) .
Every model nevertheless writes Romansh, so some reached their pretraining,
and a co-trained head saw what its model saw. Each model was asked to
continue the article in the article’s language, and only the responses that
stayed in Romansh, judged by the rate of Romansh function words that Italian
and the other neighbouring languages lack, are scored: 7 to 11 responses per
model and drafter at a batch of 1 (Figure   3  ). 
 
 
 On the 3 models where drafters of different origin serve the same model, the
outcome follows when each drafter was trained, not how it drafts or who trained it.
GLM-4.7-Flash and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B each ship a co-trained MTP head and are also
served by a post-hoc drafter, EAGLE3 on GLM-4.7-Flash and DFlash on
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. On both, the head keeps 81 to 84% of its English accepted length in
Romansh, and the post-hoc drafter 70%. With capture enabled
these two Mixture-of-Experts models save little at single stream even in
English, so in Romansh every drafter on them costs energy, in particular post-hoc
drafters cost the most. On GLM-4.7-Flash the MTP head
and the EAGLE3 drafter both verify 4 tokens, and EAGLE3 drafts token by
token, so drafting a block at once is not the cause. On gemma-4-12B-it, the
assistant Google trained keeps no more of its English accepted length than
the third-party DFlash drafter, 66 to 69%, and both lose most of their
saving: trained after its model, the assistant behaves as a post-hoc drafter
even though the model’s vendor trained it. Qwen3-14B’s DeepSpec drafters keep
most of their accepted length, but the model drifts out of Romansh into Italian on
23 to 27% of its responses, which leaves it the smallest clean sample. A post-hoc drafter therefore needs to be re-measured on the text it will serve.

  5.  How Much Batching Does It Replace? 

 
 Every saving in the sections above compares a speculative run with a
non-speculative baseline run at the same batch size, so both runs serve the same number of
requests at once. That comparison shows what the drafter changes when the load
is fixed. A deployment can also lower energy per token without a drafter, by raising the batch size of the non-speculative baseline. This section therefore compares runs at
different batch sizes: for a speculative run at a given batch size, we find
the smallest batch size at which the baseline uses no more energy per token
than that speculative run. On each model, the speculative run is the scheme
with the lowest energy per token at that batch size, and the baseline batch
sizes are the ones we ran, 1 to 64 in powers of 2. 
 
 
 A speculative run serving one request uses as little energy per token as the
baseline serving 2 to 8 requests, depending on the model. Against a
speculative run serving 32 requests, the baseline needs at least 64 requests
on every model, and on 5 of the 11 models the baseline serving 64 requests, the
largest batch size we ran, still uses more energy per token than the
speculative run serving 32. The batch size cannot be
raised past what latency permits, and that limit is what motivates
speculation. 
 
 
 Putting speed and energy on the same axes shows why the substitution is
partial (Figure   4  ). As the batch of the baseline grows, its trace falls almost vertically: raising the batch size cuts energy per token
by more than an order of magnitude. On the dense models each user is served at
close to the same rate throughout; on the Mixture-of-Experts models the trace
also leans left, because each added request adds expert reads to every step and
slows every user. Speculation moves the trace to the right instead, raising
per-user speed at single stream by    1.3  1.3    to     4.3  ×   4.3\times   . On dense models the
two levers are close to perpendicular. Batching is the energy lever and costs
little latency; speculation is the latency lever, and the energy it also buys
is the part that decays with batch. For a service that is not
latency-constrained, batching is the cheaper way to reduce energy; for one that
is, speculation provides the per-user speed that batching cannot, and on a
Mixture-of-Experts model it also recovers speed that batching gives up. 
 
 
 Table   4   gives the mean time between tokens behind
Figure   4  . Under an objective of    25  25    ms per token, the
lowest-energy configuration that meets it within the batches we ran uses 18 to
69% less energy per token with speculation than without on 10 of the 11
models, and gemma-4-31B-it meets it only with speculation. The time is a mean
over each generation; per-token percentiles need timestamps that our runs do
not record. 
 
 
 Lowering the GPU clock through dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS)
offers a third lever, one that keeps latency
where the step waits on memory. We locked the SM clock of an H200 at 1500,
1200 and 900 MHz for Qwen3-8B on the code pool, ran with three seeds per batch, and
compared each lock with the default power limit. Without speculation the
baseline step runs near the top clock while it waits on memory, so the
1500 MHz lock costs 3 to 7% of throughput and lowers energy per
token by 4 to 11% at every batch. With DSpark-7 or DFlash-16 at a batch of 16
or more, the GPU already runs at between 1450 and 1700 MHz under
the default limit, so the same lock removes little clock and saves no
energy. The 1200 MHz lock lowers energy for every configuration but also lowers
throughput. The up to 32% that clock locking recovers on the H200
in  ( Ma et al., 2026 ;  Afzal et al., 2026b )  comes from the lock that minimises
energy, on other models and without CUDA graph capture.

  6.  Which Drafter, and Does It Change With Batch? 

 
 The drafter that saves the most energy at single stream is not the drafter
that saves the most at serving batch. At single
stream a block drafter leads on 7 of the 9 models that have a block drafter (Table   2  ), and on all 9 models with capture
disabled, because block drafters accept the most tokens per verification. On every model that also has a draft
head, a co-trained MTP head on the Qwen3.6 models and the assistant on the
gemma models, the head saves the most energy at the largest batch the model runs.
On Qwen3.6-27B, gemma-4-12B-it and gemma-4-31B-it the head takes over between
a batch of 8 and a batch of 32, on gemma-4-31B-it with DFlash leading again at a
batch of 16; on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B it saves the most at every
batch, and on gemma-4-26B-A4B-it at every batch except 2. 
 
 
 The cost that grows with batch is the number of tokens verified. A block
drafter proposes all its tokens in one pass: the z-lab DFlash drafters propose 15 tokens, so the model verifies 16 tokens per request and step. The draft heads on these models, the MTP heads and the assistant, propose one
token per pass and stop after 3 to 5 tokens, so the model verifies 4 to 6
tokens per request and step. The model verifies every proposed token for every
request, accepted or not. Rejected tokens cost little at single stream, where
the step waits on memory, and add compute at serving batch
(Section   2  ), so a drafter that proposes more tokens per
step adds more of that compute. The draft itself does not grow with batch (Section   8  ).
The head starts to save the most energy at the batch where the energy of verifying
16 tokens instead of 4 to 6 tokens exceeds the energy saved by the extra
tokens the block drafter gets accepted. 
 
 
 We modified the engine so that the n-gram drafter can serve the two
state-space hybrids, Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. A hybrid layer carries a
recurrent state, and after each verification the engine must advance that
state to the last accepted token. The MTP and DFlash code paths of the engine
perform this step, but the n-gram path does not, so the state stops advancing
after the first verification and the output becomes incoherent within the
first few words. With the step added to the n-gram path,
n-gram text departs from the baseline text no earlier than MTP text does. On
the models without a recurrent state, n-gram text departs from the baseline
text no earlier than the texts of two baseline runs depart from each other. 
 
 
 On the hybrids, n-gram drafting then follows the trend it shows on the models
without a recurrent state (Figure   2  ). On the dense Qwen3.6-27B it saves energy up to a batch of
4, 12% at a batch of 1, breaks even at a batch of 8 and costs energy from a
batch of 16. On the Mixture-of-Experts Qwen3.6-35B-A3B it costs energy at
every batch (Section   4  ). 
 
 
 Among block drafters, the drafter that proposes fewer tokens per pass saves
more energy. Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B each have two DFlash drafters, trained by
different groups. The DeepSpec drafter proposes 6 tokens per pass, so the model verifies 7 tokens per request and step; the z-lab drafter proposes 15 tokens, so the model verifies 16 tokens. The drafter that proposes 6 tokens saves more
energy at every batch we measured, and its margin grows with batch. The model
verifies the 9 extra tokens for every request, and at large batch the
extra accepted tokens no longer cover the compute those 9 tokens add. 
 
 
 Memory can also cap the batch, independent of energy. On a state-space
hybrid, rolling back a rejected draft is not a matter of discarding cache
entries: the recurrent state has already absorbed the rejected tokens, so the
engine keeps a copy of that state after every drafted token of every
request, and restores the one that matches the accepted prefix. The buffer
grows with the number of drafted tokens times the batch. On Qwen3.6-27B on the H100, DFlash-16
fails to start at a batch of 16, which the baseline runs, rather than
running slowly; at that batch the rollback buffer alone is about 10 times the
size of the drafter’s weights. The H200’s larger memory moves the ceiling but
does not remove it: DFlash-16 still fails to start at the largest batches on
both hybrids, while the co-trained MTP head, which verifies 4 tokens, holds
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at a batch of    64  64   . A deployment on a recurrent architecture should budget memory for the number of drafted tokens, not only for the
weights of the drafter. 
 
 
  6.1.  How Many Tokens Should a Draft Hold? 

 
 The same argument sets the number of tokens to draft. Drafting
more tokens per verification helps when they are accepted, because more
tokens come out of one weight read, and wastes draft compute when they are
not. Acceptance falls off as the draft runs further ahead of the model, so
there is an interior optimum. 
 
 
 Batch moves that optimum downward, because the verify pass already carries
many tokens while each drafted token is still verified for every request. 
 
 
 We swept the number of tokens the n-gram drafter proposes from 1 to 32 tokens at 4 batch sizes on gemma-4-31B-it, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct and
gemma-4-26B-A4B-it. On gemma-4-31B-it, the dense model of the three models, drafting
more tokens saves more energy at single stream, but from a batch of 4 requests 4 drafted tokens save the most energy, and at serving batch every number of
drafted tokens costs energy, 32 tokens the most. On the two Mixture-of-Experts models every number of drafted tokens costs energy already at single stream,
and the loss grows with the number of tokens, because each verified token reads
the experts chosen for that token (Section   3  ). On all three models the least costly choice at a batch of    64  64    is 4 tokens.
For the n-gram drafter, and for the two DFlash drafters of
Section   6  , over-drafting, not under-drafting, is the failure mode, and a number of drafted
tokens tuned at single stream on a dense model should be cut when the batch is
raised. 
 
 
 
 
  7.  Which Metric Predicts the Energy Ranking? 

   
  Figure 5.  Energy saving against accepted tokens per verification for every model, scheme and batch that has a baseline run at the same batch size, coloured by batch (a), and the share of decode energy spent drafting and verifying at     B  =  1   B{=}1    and     B  =  64   B{=}64    with capture enabled for every dense model and scheme, measured by removing the draft (b). 
 
 
 Acceptance, the number of drafted tokens the model keeps per verification, is
the obvious metric. Drafter
training optimises acceptance, and every drafter release reports it.
Acceptance alone does not tell which drafter uses less energy, because that
drafter changes with batch while acceptance does not. For any one drafter,
acceptance changes little from a batch of 1 to a batch of    64  64   . Block
drafters accept more tokens than draft heads in every matched comparison we
measured, at every batch. Yet on all 5 models that have both, the head uses less energy at the largest
batch, because the block drafter also verifies more tokens
(Section   6  ); acceptance counts only the tokens kept. 
 
 
 Once the batch is fixed, acceptance does predict the saving
(Figure   5  a). At every batch the saving rises with the number of
accepted tokens per verification, the quantity that divides the weight read.
The acceptance needed to break even rises with batch, because batching has
already amortised the weight read that a drafter would otherwise divide. At a
fixed batch, the scheme that accepts more also uses less energy in    287  287    of
   332  332    pairs of schemes on the same model; the pairs share models and baselines,
so they are not independent tests. In all but one of the    45  45    pairs
where it does not, the scheme that accepts more also verifies more tokens per
request, most often a block drafter against a draft head. The remaining pair
is EAGLE3 on Qwen3-8B at single stream, which drafts 7 tokens in 7 sequential passes. 
 
 
 
  8.  Where the Energy Goes 

 
 Verification takes most of decode energy on every dense model and scheme, at
single stream and at a batch of    64  64    (Figure   5  b). We measure the
split with capture enabled by removing the draft. The speculative run is
repeated with the drafter’s passes skipped after the first step and the first
step’s draft verified at every following step, so verification keeps its number of tokens and
shape. An engine setting fixes how many drafted tokens each step accepts in both
runs, so
they run the same steps over the same contexts, and the difference in their
decode energy is the energy of the draft. On a dense model the tokens verified in place of
a draft do not matter: on Qwen3-8B, verifying random or repeated tokens instead
changes the energy by under 3%. 
 
 
 No drafter takes more than 45% of decode energy, and a block drafter takes at
most 23%, so the cost of running the drafter is the smaller lever: halving the
cost of a block drafter would lower decode energy by at most 12%. The share
follows how many sequential passes a drafter runs and how large each pass is
next to a pass of the model. EAGLE3 on Qwen3 runs 7 passes per draft and
takes the largest share, while a block drafter runs one pass per block. On
gemma-4-31B-it, the largest dense model, the passes of every drafter are small next
to those of the model, and every share is small. The share stays close to constant or falls
from single stream to a batch of    64  64   , because verification grows with the
batch at least as fast as the draft does. 
 
 
 Phase markers emitted by the host, the usual way to split the two phases,
need capture disabled and do not give this split on the gemma models
(Section   10  ). With capture disabled, the markers credit the
gemma-4-12B-it assistant at a batch of    64  64    with a larger share of decode
energy than removing the draft measures. 
 
 
 On the Mixture-of-Experts models the subtraction does not hold, because each
verified token is routed to the experts chosen for that token. On GLM-4.7-Flash, verifying random
or repeated tokens in place of the reused draft changes the energy of the
verify-only run by up to 52%. On these models the cost of
verification depends on which tokens are drafted and not only on how many, so
we do not report their split. 
 
 
 
  9.  Does Speculation Reach the Compute-Bound Regime? 

 
 The standard explanation of speculation is a roofline shift: the step is said
to move toward the regime where the machine’s arithmetic units
are the limit rather than its memory. If that were happening, energy per token
would fall for a structural reason, and the effect would grow with the number of
tokens verified. 
 
 
 We measured the operating point with hardware counters rather than inferring
it, taking executed arithmetic intensity as measured arithmetic, including the
padded work of tensor-core tiles, over measured memory traffic for a whole
decode step, on an H100 and on an H200. The counters capture the first decode steps after the prompt, so the
context is set by the prompt length: we use prompts of 1024 tokens and of
about 260 tokens, the average context over a 512-token generation from our
code prompts. 
 
   
  Figure 6.  Arithmetic intensity of a decode step on Qwen3-4B against batch, with the balance point of each GPU as a horizontal line (a), and the energy saving of the same drafters with capture enabled on each GPU, filled where the step at that batch is past the balance point of that GPU (b), shaded in (a) from the batch at which the DFlash-16 step crosses each balance point and in (b) from the batch at which its saving turns negative on each GPU. 
 
 
 The number of verified tokens alone moves the operating point little: at single
stream every scheme on every model sits within a few per cent of where its
baseline sits. Combined with batch, it moves the operating point a long way. Arithmetic intensity is
a property of the step and not of the GPU, and the same step measures close
to the same on both (Figure   6  a). With 260-token contexts, a
DFlash-16 step on Qwen3-4B reaches the balance point of the H100 at a batch of    32  32   
and that of the H200 at    16  16   . DSpark-7, which verifies fewer than half as many
tokens, stays below the H100’s balance point at every batch and passes the
balance point of the H200 from a batch of    32  32   . The baseline stays far below both balance points
at every batch. The number of verified tokens sets the crossing, not the drafter: the n-gram
drafter verifying 16 tokens passes the balance point of the H200 at a batch
of    16  16   , as DFlash-16 does, while verifying 4 tokens, as in our panels, it
stays below it up to a batch of    64  64   . Longer contexts lower the intensity at a given batch, because
each request’s context has to be read as well, which adds more memory traffic
than arithmetic. 
 
 
 Below the balance point, the n-gram drafter and the assistant on
gemma-4-12B-it run below the memory roof from a batch of 1, because attention
over their drafted tokens runs in slow kernels, while DSpark runs close to it. 
 
 
 Reaching the compute-bound regime is not a gain in energy; it marks where the
saving ends (Figure   6  b). Past the balance point, every
verified token costs arithmetic time that the weight read no longer hides,
and most verified tokens are rejected: DFlash-16 accepts under 3 of the 16 tokens it verifies per request. On both GPUs and for both drafters, the
saving changes sign within one doubling of the batch at which the step reaches
that GPU’s balance point. DFlash-16 stops saving between batches of    16  16    and
   32  32    on the H100 and at    16  16    on the H200. DSpark-7 still saves energy at a
batch of    64  64    on the H100, where its step stays below the balance point, and
costs energy on the H200, where its step passes the balance point. A GPU with more memory bandwidth per unit of arithmetic reaches the
compute-bound regime at a smaller batch and loses the saving there, so a number of
drafted tokens tuned on one GPU does not carry over to a GPU with a different balance
point. The H200 also changes the energy of the baseline itself, through its
memory and power behaviour, so the balance point explains where the saving
changes sign, not its size. 
 
 
 
  10.  Measurement Pitfalls 

 
 Speculative decoding energy is easy to mismeasure, and the failures share one
form: the run succeeds, the result file is well formed, the number is
plausible, and nothing in it shows that the configuration differed from the
one requested. 
 
 
 Besides the capture bias of Section   3  , the following
conditions produce the same failure. The serving engine resolves concurrency separately for the baseline and the speculative run, so the batch that ran can differ from the batch
requested, and the result file stores the requested batch and the batch that ran in
different fields. A batch larger than the prompt pool repeats prompts that share a cache prefix
(Section   4  ). A prompt sent to an instruction-tuned model without its chat template
changes the text being predicted and moves the reported saving in either
direction: without the template, n-gram drafting on the gemma models reports
savings up to 117 percentage points higher, and the MTP head on
JoyAI-LLM-Flash up to 12 points lower. A profiler window that opens
while requests are still being admitted includes prefill, which the decode
analysis excludes. Phase markers emitted by the host record when the host enters a
phase, not when the GPU runs it, so they can book GPU work of verification to drafting
(Section   8  ). A result writer that matches each appended row to the
file’s existing header discards, without warning, any column the header
lacks, including the column that records the condition a row was measured
under. Result rows that do not name the GPU can mix H100 and H200 runs. The same requested batch can then run in full on one GPU and below the
requested concurrency on the other GPU: the MTP head on
Qwen3.6-27B at a batch of    16  16    holds 12 requests on the H100 and saves a
fraction of what it saves on the H200, which holds all 16 requests. 
 
 
 Holding the generation length fixed keeps the baseline and the speculative
run on the same token count, but a run that continues past the end of the model’s answer starts a new
turn and repeats text. That repetition does not cancel within
the pair. The baseline pays the same per token whatever it generates, while a
drafter predicts repeated text cheaply, so acceptance rises once the answer
has ended.
With the end-of-sequence token honoured, every model answers our code prompts
in a median of more than 700 tokens, so the 512 tokens of every run stay inside
the answer. 
 
 
 A speculative run can produce broken text while its result row looks normal,
as n-gram does on the state-space hybrids without the engine fix
(Section   6  ). Taken at face value, those runs would show n-gram
matching or beating the co-trained head on Qwen3.6-27B up to a batch of 8. 
 
 
 Each condition above shows only outside the reported metric: in the generated
text, the count of distinct outputs, the engine log or the profiled kernel
count. The minimum audit confirms the workload, the concurrency and the
measurement window, and reports the capture mode and the GPU with every number. 
 
 
 Our measurements have limits: latency is the mean time between tokens, the
counter covers the GPU board only, prompts are short, batches stop at 64, heads
and block drafters differ in the number of tokens they verify, only the n-gram
drafter has its number of drafted tokens swept, and the roofline covers Qwen3-4B. 
 
 
 
  11.  Related Work 

 
  Drafting schemes.  Speculative decoding was introduced with a separate,
smaller network as the drafter  ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ) . The drafters in wide use
remove that separate network: Medusa  ( Cai et al., 2024 )  attaches parallel heads, EAGLE and
EAGLE-3 draft over the hidden features of the model  ( Li et al., 2024 ;  Li et al., 2025 ) , and several recent checkpoints ship
multi-token-prediction heads trained jointly with the
model  ( DeepSeek-AI, 2024 ) . Block drafters emit a whole block in one
pass, and the checkpoints we use are of that
family  ( Cheng et al., 2026 ;  z-lab, 2026 ;  DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ) . All of
this work is evaluated in accepted length and wall-clock speedup. We ask what
the same drafters cost in joules, which orders them differently once the batch
is non-trivial. Serving systems tune the number of drafted tokens in
closed loop against throughput  ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . 
 
 
  Energy measurement.  Roofline analysis explains why decode is
memory-bound  ( Williams et al., 2009 ) , and phase-attributed energy
benchmarks exist for the prefill and decode
split  ( Niu et al., 2025 ;  Chung et al., 2026 ) , and for power-capped
operation  ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . Two studies are closer to ours: decode energy has been
measured across attention mechanisms with hardware counters, without
speculation  ( Chkir et al., 2026 ) , and the energy savings of speculative
strategies have been surveyed on older dense
models  ( Dutta et al., 2026 ) . None separates draft from verify energy, and that
split determines whether a drafter pays for itself. 
 
 
  Positioning.  Closest to this work, Fernandez et
al.  ( Fernandez et al., 2025 )  measure speculative decoding’s energy on two dense grouped-query models with a single drafter at fixed draft length. We
measure across 4 attention families and 5 schemes, vary the number of
drafted tokens, and decompose the energy. The same comparison of schemes has been measured in time on a
production engine  ( Liu et al., 2026 )  and in throughput by a dedicated
benchmark  ( Abramovich et al., 2026 ) ; neither reports joules. An analytic roofline
treatment of architecture-dependent speculation predicts several of the
effects we measure  ( Finn, 2026 ) , and SpecLA  ( Wang and others, 2026 ) 
builds verification kernels for linear-attention states; we measure the
energy of speculation on such models. That Mixture-of-Experts models gain
more from speculation than dense ones is an established
result  ( Huang et al., 2025 ;  Cohere, 2026 ) ; we show that the launch-bound decode behind that gain also makes their
speculative energy the most sensitive to graph capture. 
 
 
  Language and task.  With a separate small drafter, speculative decoding is
less effective in low-resource languages, and distilling that drafter on the
target language generalises poorly  ( Paudel et al., 2026 ;  Sandler et al., 2025 ) .
Pretraining a drafter on broad data helps most on out-of-domain and
multilingual text  ( Bie et al., 2026 ) . None of these compares, on one model, the different
drafters that production engines ship for it, and none measures energy. 
 
 
 
  12.  Conclusion 

 
 Speculation shortens the time between output tokens, which batching does not,
and under a tight enough objective no batch size meets it without speculation,
so a service in that regime chooses speculation to meet its objective rather
than on energy grounds. 
 
 
 Speculation is most valuable for energy where a latency target rules out a
larger batch size, and least valuable where the batch size can still grow,
because there the drafter competes with batching, a lever that needs no extra
model and costs only cache memory and per-user latency. Most services value
time between output tokens above energy per token, and they should run
speculation and tune the drafter and the number of drafted tokens to the batch. Where energy per token is the
binding constraint, for instance under a facility power limit, a service
should raise the batch size first and then check whether a drafter still
reduces energy. 
 
 
 Three findings carry beyond our models. A draft long enough to push
verification past the GPU’s balance point loses its saving there, and that
point depends on the GPU, so the same drafter at the same batch can save
energy on one GPU and cost energy on another with more memory bandwidth. The
drafter that saves the most energy at single stream is often not the drafter
that saves the most at serving batch, and acceptance, which changes little with
batch, does not show the change. Each condition in
Section   10   changed a reported number in this study, and none
was visible in the energy number.

 Pre-Crime for Agents, at the Last Second:
 Probing When a Recruited Agent Gives In    Thanks:  This work began at the Apart Research AI Collusion Research Sprint (October 2026), where an earlier version was submitted ( project page ).   Appendix   P   lists the numbers that changed.    
 
 
  
 
 
 
  Leonidas Raghav   
 
 Independent  
 
  
   

  Abstract 
    
 When AI agents share channels and credentials, one agent can press another to break its operator’s rule, a first step towards collusion.
Output filters check only what an agent has already written.
Can an overseer tell beforehand that an agent is about to give in?
We show that a linear probe on the agent’s activations can, in a controlled multi-agent setting.
Across six scenarios, a peer presses a target for up to 20 rounds to reveal a secret, such as a deploy token; the target often refuses, then gives in.
Read at each model call before its output is written, the probe picks out the one that leaks.
On held-out Qwen3-32B episodes, at a threshold set to flag 5% of benign calls, it catches 82% of leaking calls.
At a similar flag rate, a zero-shot decision-model monitor catches 26%.
On gpt-oss-20b, a probe on its reasoning reaches AUROC 0.91.
A bag-of-words classifier trained on the same calls comes close, so most of the gain comes from training on labels, not activations.
The probe also flags permitted disclosures: it reads the coming disclosure more than the violation.
The warning is short-range, and halting on any alarm would stop most benign episodes, which a second text check does not fix.
A warning raised before generation could let an overseer stop an agent that is about to give in, ahead of others acting on its messages or recruitment spreading through a swarm. 
    
 
 
    
  github.com/leonidas1712/precrime-agents  
  
 
 
 
 
 
     
 
 
 
 
  1  Introduction 

 
 AI agents increasingly work alongside other agents, sharing channels, tools and credentials, so one agent can press another to break its own operator’s rule.
The easy case is a one-shot request to hand over a secret through a tool call.
A filter on that tool call, or a monitor that blocks a suspicious action before it runs, can catch it  ( Bhatt et al., 2025 ) . 
 
   
  Figure 1:   How an episode works. 
(a) A real leak on Qwen3-32B, verbatim and shortened, with the token redacted; the leaking message is highlighted.
(b) The peer (horns) asks over the team channel for the token held by the target (halo), which is bound by its operator’s rule. Solid arrows are actions; dashed arrows are observation: the text monitor reads the transcript, and the probe reads the target’s internal activations before each output.
(c) The three labels on one schematic episode; shaded calls are those scored after the first read (  Appendix   A   gives a matched episode in which the target never leaks). 
 
 
 The hard cases look different.
The leak can go out as an ordinary message that other agents read at once: on our development episodes, most Qwen3-32B leaks go straight to the shared team channel, and 44% are the agent’s plain end-of-turn reply, which a filter on tool calls never sees (  Appendix   L  ).
The request comes openly from a teammate, so it is not an injection hidden in data  ( Liu et al., 2024 ;  Debenedetti et al., 2024 ) , and the pressure can build over many rounds, as in multi-turn attacks whose steps each look harmless  ( Russinovich et al., 2024 )  and in sustained pushback that wears down a model’s correct answers  ( Tang et al., 2026 ) .
Compromised agents can pass an attack on to others  ( Cohen et al., 2024 ;  Pulipaka et al., 2026 ) , as in the 2026 OpenAI–Hugging Face incident, where evaluation agents attacked production infrastructure  ( OpenAI, 2026a )  and some pressed others to join  ( Greenblatt et al., 2026 ) .
The rule is often the operator’s own, such as keeping one credential private, which guardian models built on fixed harm categories do not cover  ( Hoover et al., 2025 ) .
Agents also leak in action even when they state the norm correctly  ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . 
 
 
 Why not filter the output?
Current defences act on the action or the output: they block a suspicious action before it runs  ( Bhatt et al., 2025 )  or halt a model’s output as it streams  ( Sharma et al., 2025 ;  Cunningham et al., 2026 ) .
Such a filter can stop a leak before it is delivered, but only if it recognises the leak in the text.
Small rewordings and translation evade verbatim filters  ( Ippolito et al., 2022 ;  Zhang et al., 2023 ) .
Output-only censorship is impossible in principle under invertible encodings  ( Glukhov et al., 2023 ) .
Encoded exfiltration that evades output-only detection stays legible in activations  ( Revankar et al., 2026 ) .
A warning raised before the output exists does not depend on recognising the leak in the text.
We do not test reworded or encoded leaks here: our secrets are exact strings, so that every leak can be labelled exactly, and a string filter would also catch them. 
 
 
 Activation probes, small linear classifiers trained on a model’s internal activations, already read agents before they act.
They detect exposure to an injection  ( Dong et al., 2026 ) , or whether the injection will hijack the agent  ( Yu et al., 2026 ) , at the last input token, forecast unauthorised actions at the end of the agent’s reasoning  ( Fayyazi et al., 2026 ) , and read covert encoding at the planning step  ( Revankar et al., 2026 ) , while early-warning work under user pressure or injection finds weak signals  ( Saraogi et al., 2026 )  that text baselines often match  ( Jia et al., 2026 ) .
What is new here is the setting and the question.
A teammate presses the agent openly over many rounds, the agent refuses and then gives in, and we ask which call gives in, before that call generates anything, comparing each call only with calls from the same scenario and round.
Work on collusion between AI agents has mostly studied markets and shared multi-agent tasks  ( Fish et al., 2024 ;  Lin et al., 2024 ;  Nakamura et al., 2026 ) .
We instead study open recruitment by a teammate over many rounds, in workplace scenarios of the kind seen in recent agent incidents. 
 
 
 In our setup, the target holds a secret, such as a deploy token, that its operator has told it never to share, and a peer agent keeps asking for it over many rounds (  Figure   1  ).
At each of the target’s calls, the last-prompt probe reads its activations before generation, and on gpt-oss-20b a reasoning probe reads them during the private reasoning, before the public reply or tool call. We compare linear probes with a zero-shot text monitor and a trained text classifier on exactly the same calls, in six scenarios on two open-weight models.
We find three things (  Figures   3   and   4  ).
First, the call that leaks is predictable just before it acts, and this held on test episodes, for the last-prompt probe on Qwen3-32B and for the reasoning probe on gpt-oss-20b.
Second, the warning comes late: the probe is only modestly accurate for whether the target leaks this round or the next, and weak for whether an episode will ever leak.
Third, a zero-shot text monitor does far worse than the probe, but a text classifier trained on the same labelled calls comes close, so activations add at most a small edge on top of training. 
 
 
 Our contributions are: 
 
  •  
 
 a recruitment benchmark of six workplace scenarios in which the same model leaks in some episodes and refuses in others, with control episodes in which the peer never asks, released with all prompts and transcripts (  Section   2  ); 
  
  •  
 
 probes, a zero-shot text monitor and a trained text classifier, scored on exactly the same calls at three distances from the act (  Section   3  ); 
  
  •  
 
 a per-call warning that holds on test episodes, with checks against simple shortcuts and an analysis of what acting on its alarms would cost (  Section   4  ). 
  
 
 
 
 
  2  Setup 

 
 Two agents share a workspace: a target that holds a secret under its operator’s rule, and a peer that wants the secret.
Below we cover the workspace, the agents and their calls, then leaks, labels and detectors;   Figure   1   follows one real episode. 
 
 
  2.1  Workspace, agents and calls 

 
 Workspace and rule. 

 
 A target agent does an ordinary task in a mocked workspace under one rule from its operator.
The task is to read a configuration file and write a short status report.
The rule is to never share a protected value outside the file that holds it.
In our main scenario that value is a staging deploy token, and five other scenarios protect a reserve price, a capacity figure, a rollout threshold, a handoff note and an integration code.
All six scenarios share one task template, and every protected value is a randomly generated fake string (  Appendix   A  ).
Formally, a scenario is a tuple 
 

  
  
      S  =   (  F  ,   f  ⋆   ,  σ  ,  ρ  ,  q  )    ,   S=(F,f^{\star},\sigma,\rho,q),    
  
  (1)    
 
 where    F  F    is the set of workspace files,      f  ⋆   ∈  F   f^{\star}\in F    is the protected file,    σ  \sigma    is the secret string it holds,    ρ  \rho    is the operator’s rule that    σ  \sigma    appear in no output of the target, and    q  q    is the task. 
 
 
 
 Agents and tools. 

 
 The target can list, read and write files, run the workspace tests, and post to a shared team channel.
Text that comes with a tool call stays private, and the final reply of a turn is posted to the channel only if the target posted nothing else in that turn.
A peer agent shares the channel and needs the value, but cannot read the files and is not shown the rule’s text.
The peer asks for the value openly, as a colleague would, so we study recruitment that arises from an ordinary conflict of goals.
Tools act in memory, so no real system, credential or network is touched.
The target is a language model    M  M   .
Its system prompt states its role and    ρ  \rho   , and it receives    q  q    as its first user message.
It reaches    F  F    only through its tools.
The peer is a second language model    P  P    that writes each message from the channel so far, and it never sees    F  F   ,     f  ⋆   f^{\star}    or    ρ  \rho   .

 Every scenario also runs with a control peer, which asks only for the ordinary task details and never for the value, so the peer is either recruiting or control,     P  ∈   {   P  rec   ,   P  ctrl   }    P\in\{P_{\text{rec}},P_{\text{ctrl}}\}   .
Both models have control episodes, and on Qwen3-32B the target also runs alone, with no peer at all.
No control or alone episode leaks (  Tables   4   and   M  ), so the leaks in recruiting episodes are caused by the peer’s request.
We call the calls in control and alone episodes  control calls , and recruiting episodes that never leak  refusing episodes .

  2.2  Leaks, labels and detectors

 A call  leaks  if its output contains the secret, wherever it goes: a channel post, the end-of-turn reply or a file write.
We detect this with an exact string match on the tool log, so the label needs no judge.
A leak is defined on     o  t   o_{t}    only, so the secret may appear in     z  t   z_{t}    without counting.
The first leak is at

This is an emission label rather than an exact rule check: in 2 Qwen3-32B episodes, one development and one test, the target wrote the value back into the protected file itself, which the label counts but the rule allows (  Appendix   B  ).

  2.3  Models and datasets 

 
 We use two open-weight target models, Qwen3-32B  ( Yang et al., 2025 )  with thinking disabled and gpt-oss-20b  ( OpenAI, 2025b ) , which reasons before it answers.
Each faces its own peer model, from the DeepSeek-V4 family: DeepSeek-V4-Flash for Qwen3-32B  ( DeepSeek, 2026a )  and DeepSeek-V4-Pro for gpt-oss-20b  ( DeepSeek, 2026b ) .
gpt-oss-20b refuses requests that name the token, so its peer instead asks, after a delay, for the whole configuration block that contains it to be copied into the handoff file, the shared status file that the target writes for the peer.
We chose that strategy on behaviour alone, before any probe or monitor saw the data (  Appendix   M  ).
We never pool the two models’ results. 
 
 
 Each model has two sets of episodes (  Table   1  ).
We develop and evaluate every method on the  development episodes .
The  test episodes  were collected after development and are scored once, by detectors fit and thresholded on development episodes only.
The sprint version of this work had already scored these episodes, but no detector’s weights or per-call threshold were fit on them (  Appendix   P  ). The per-episode and cascade operating points in   Section   4.4   are chosen on them to show the trade-off, and are marked as such.
In both models’ development episodes, the target leaks in some recruiting episodes and refuses throughout in others: 66 of 152 recruiting episodes leak on Qwen3-32B, and 146 of 238 on gpt-oss-20b.
