In parallel we trained the same model on a B200 GPU with the same initialization, data, batch and learning-rate schedule. On 1,024 windows of FineWeb-Edu text that neither model ever saw , the NPU model reaches a loss of 0.7993 and the GPU model 0.7994 . The paired difference is -0.0001 with a standard error of 0.0007 . The NPU model is lower on 50.1% of windows. Both sets of weights and the evaluation script are public, so anyone can check this result in a few minutes: FINAL-Bench/VKORE-325M-NPU-Base . 1. Why this matters Accelerators sold for inference are now deployed in large numbers. They are cheaper and use less power than training GPUs, and their vendors ship them with a compiler and runtime built for one job: running a forward pass of a model that was trained somewhere else. The accepted view is that such chips cannot train. Not a LoRA fine-tune, and certainly not a pretraining run from zero. Training needs a backward pass, an optimizer state, and numerically stable updates over tens of thousands of steps, none of which an inference stack is built to provide. If that view is wrong, the consequences are practical. Organizations that already own inference hardware could adapt and even pretrain models on it, and new data centers could plan for one class of chip instead of two. We tested the view directly, in two steps: VKORE-46M-NPU (earlier): a 46M model trained on TinyStories. It showed that an inference-only NPU can run backpropagation at all. VKORE-325M-NPU-Base (this post): a model seven times larger, trained on real web text for 76k steps, with a GPU twin to measure the result against. 2. Experimental design: one variable A claim like "the NPU reached GPU quality" is only meaningful against a reference that differs in nothing but the hardware. We therefore trained the same model twice. Held fixed Value Initialization identical random seed and initial weights Training corpus the same 6.94 GB FineWeb-Edu byte file Batch 65,536 byte tokens per step Steps 76,293 (NPU run saved its final checkpoint at step 76,292) Optimizer AdamW, betas (0.9, 0.95), weight decay 0.1, gradient clipping at 1.0 Learning rate 500-step warmup to 3e-4, step down to 1.5e-4 at step 18,000, linear decay over the last 20% The only difference is the machine: a commercial inference-only NPU for run A, and a single B200 GPU for run B. 3. Model and data Item Value Parameters 325.6M Architecture decoder-only Transformer, RoPE (theta 1e5), RMSNorm, SwiGLU, grouped-query attention Layers 20 Hidden / FFN width 1024 / 3584 Attention 8 query heads, 2 key-value heads, head dimension 256 Vocabulary 256 (byte level: token id = byte value) Context length 256 Format on the Hub standard LlamaForCausalLM , loads with plain transformers Data. The training corpus is built from FineWeb-Edu sample/10BT . The parquet shards were read in repository order, each document was encoded as UTF-8 bytes, and documents were joined with a blank line. The corpus is the first two shards ( 000 and 001 ), 6.94 GB in total. Training drew random 257-byte windows from this file, so 5.0B training tokens correspond to about 0.72 passes over it. A byte-level vocabulary keeps the comparison clean: there is no tokenizer to tune, and the reported loss is cross entropy per byte, which converts directly to bits per byte. 4. What made this hard A backward pass is necessary but not sufficient. Our first long runs on the NPU trained correctly for thousands of steps and then diverged. Short tests did not reveal the problem; it only appeared in long runs checked against a GPU reference. Making long runs stable on an inference-only stack was the main engineering work between the 46M model and this one. The technique was developed in house and is under patent application, so this post does not describe it. What we can show is the result: the 325M run trained for 76,292 steps with no divergence and no loss spikes. The run was interrupted twice by process failures and resumed from saved checkpoints both times, which is visible in the logs and has no visible effect on the curve. 5. Results 5.1 Training curves The two curves overlap from the first thousand steps to the end. Both fall from about 5.8 to about 0.80. Small local wiggles differ because the two runs see their random windows in a different order; the trend is the same throughout. (The plotted NPU log runs to step 74,360; the final checkpoint is step 76,292.) 5.2 Loss on unseen text The decisive test is text that was not in the training corpus at all. We used FineWeb-Edu sample/10BT shard 013 , the last shard, which was never part of the training file, and evaluated both published models on 1,024 random 256-byte windows from it. We also report the 256 fixed windows from the end of the training corpus that were used during development. Model Loss, unseen text (1,024 windows) Bits per byte, unseen Loss, training-corpus windows (256) Inference-only NPU 0.7993 1.1531 0.8067 B200 GPU reference 0.7994 1.1533 0.8070 Because both models were evaluated on identical windows, we can compare them window by window. That removes the variation between windows and gives a much tighter test than comparing two averages. The paired difference is -0.0001 (NPU minus GPU) with a standard error of 0.0007, and the NPU model has the lower loss on 50.1% of windows. In other words, at this resolution the two models cannot be told apart. A note on evaluation hygiene: the first version of our model card called the 256 training-corpus windows a "held out" set. They are not strictly held out, because training sampled windows from the whole file. We corrected the card and added the unseen-shard evaluation above, which is the number we stand behind. 5.3 Samples Both models are small base models trained on 5B tokens, so they write fluent text with shaky facts. The point is that they behave alike. Sampling with temperature 0.7, top-p 0.9, repetition penalty 1.15, seed 0: Prompt NPU model B200 reference Photosynthesis is the process ...by which plants can produce oxygen from the air. It is a process by which carbon dioxide (CO2) is transferred... ...by which plants use sunlight and carbon dioxide to convert carbohydrates (carbon dioxide) into food energy... Climate change is caused by ...human activities and occurs in nature. The main reason for this problem is the continuing presence of carbon dioxide... ...human-caused greenhouse gas emissions. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is committed to cutting emissions... The heart is ...connected to the body. Blood pumps blood to the body and pumps blood to our body for oxygen... ...the most powerful organ in the body. It is also responsible for pumping oxygen to the blood... 6. Reproduce it Both models live in one repository. The B200 reference is in the b200_reference subfolder. from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM npu = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "FINAL-Bench/VKORE-325M-NPU-Base" ) gpu = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "FINAL-Bench/VKORE-325M-NPU-Base" , subfolder= "b200_reference" ) The unseen-text comparison in section 5.2 is one script, evaluate_unseen.py . It downloads shard 013 , draws the same 1,024 windows (seed 2026), and prints both losses and the paired difference. It uses only transformers , numpy and pyarrow . Generating text with the byte-level model: import torch prompt = "Photosynthesis is the process" ids = torch.tensor([ list (prompt.encode( "utf-8" ))]) out = npu.generate(ids, max_new_tokens= 200 , do_sample= True , temperature= 0.7 , top_p= 0.9 , repetition_penalty= 1.15 ) print ( bytes (out[ 0 ].tolist()).decode( "utf-8" , errors= "replace" )) 7. What we do not claim Not a capable assistant. This is a 325M base model trained on 5B tokens, released as a training-hardware result. Not a speed record. This post is about whether an inference-only NPU can carry a full pretraining run to GPU quality, not about how fast. Throughput is a separate engineering track. Not the method. The training loop and the stability technique are in house and under patent application. The weights, data recipe, hyperparameters and evaluation are fully open. 8. What comes next Larger models on the same hardware class, and longer token budgets. Fine-tuning and adaptation workloads on inference-only NPUs for customers who already own the hardware. A paper with the full method once the patent filing is complete. Links Model and B200 reference: FINAL-Bench/VKORE-325M-NPU-Base Previous model: FINAL-Bench/VKORE-46M-NPU Training data: HuggingFaceFW/fineweb-edu VIDRAFT. # Old Ideas, Novel Problems:
The Instability of LLM-Based Novelty Evaluation [![Arxiv](https://img.shields.io/badge/Arxiv-2610.02022-red?style=flat-square&logo=arxiv&logoColor=white)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02022) [![Python Versions](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.12-blue.svg?style=flat&logo=python&logoColor=white)](https://www.python.org/) [![Data](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97%20Data-Here-yellow?style=flat-square)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/novelty-judge-bench)

AI-based ideation systems are often evaluated on the novelty of their ideas, and that judgment is increasingly delegated to large language models. Such judges are typically built ad hoc and validated, if at all, on human-authored papers rather than on the generated ideas they are meant to score. So, how do novelty judges perform? Not well. We present a systematic controlled study of novelty evaluation design choices. We build an evaluation set automatically, mining OpenReview for passages where reviewers explicitly affirm or dispute a paper's originality and keeping only submissions with unanimous agreement at the extremes of their research area; we pair these with ideas from a vanilla LLM generator. Across six judges, we find that seemingly small prompt design choices have large consequences; e.g., simply telling the judge that reviewers found one idea novel and the other not can change its verdict on more than half of the identical idea pairs it is shown, shifting pairwise accuracy by over 50 points and occasionally pushing it below chance. The same change helps one judge and hurts another. Retrieval and larger reasoning budgets help little, and two purpose-built novelty evaluators are outperformed by our cheapest prompted baseline. These results raise questions about reported novelty gains of automated ideation systems, and call for robust novelty evaluation methods. ## Table of Contents - [Old Ideas, Novel Problems: The Instability of LLM-Based Novelty Evaluation](#old-ideas-novel-problems-the-instability-of-llm-based-novelty-evaluation) - [Table of Contents](#table-of-contents) - [Getting started](#getting-started) - [Setting up API keys](#setting-up-api-keys) - [Novelty Evaluation Data](#novelty-evaluation-data) - [🤗 Hugging Face](#-hugging-face) - [Expert Annotation of Judge Errors](#expert-annotation-of-judge-errors) - [Automatic Data Collection](#automatic-data-collection) - [Judge Evaluation](#judge-evaluation) - [Reproducing the Paper's Experiments](#reproducing-the-papers-experiments) - [Controlled study](#controlled-study) - [Retrieval's limitations](#retrievals-limitations) - [Dedicated novelty judges](#dedicated-novelty-judges) - [License](#license) - [Authors](#authors) - [Cite us!](#cite-us) ## Getting started 1. Clone this repository: ```bash git clone https://github.com/allenai/novelty-eval.git cd novelty-eval ``` 2. Create and activate a virtual environment: ```bash python3.12 -m venv myenv source ./myenv/bin/activate ``` 3. Install dependencies: ```bash pip install -r requirements.txt ``` 4. Point the code at the repository: ```bash export PYTHONPATH="$PWD/src" export SECRETS="$PWD/secrets.toml" export OUTPUT_DIR="$PWD/output" ``` If you plan to commit changes, register the notebook filter so that running a notebook (outputs, execution counts, kernel metadata) doesn't show up as a change (needs `jq`): ```bash git config filter.nbstrip.clean 'jq --indent 1 -f scripts/nbstrip.jq' git config filter.nbstrip.smudge cat git config filter.nbstrip.required true ``` ### Setting up API keys The judges and the benchmark-construction pipeline call external APIs. Keys go in a `secrets.toml` file at the project root (the location `$SECRETS` points at): ```toml openai_key = "your-openai-api-key" anthropic_key = "your-anthropic-api-key" semantic_scholar_key = "your-s2-api-key" # retrieval only ``` Rebuilding the benchmark from scratch additionally needs OpenReview credentials: ```bash export OPENREVIEW_USERNAME="your-openreview-email" export OPENREVIEW_PASSWORD="your-openreview-password" ``` ## Novelty Evaluation Data

Our benchmark consists of two data setups: **Human-Only** and **Human+Generated**. Both setups consist of two separate idea "pools": a **high-novelty pool `D_+`** and a **lower-novelty pool `D_-`**, where ideas from `D_+` can be assumed to be more novel than those in `D_-`. | Setup | `D_+` (novel) | `D_-` (lower-novelty) | |---|---|---| | **Human-Only** (`data/human-only/`) | 154 **validated-novel** | 145 **validated-lower-novelty** | | **Human+Generated** (`data/human-plus-generated/`) | 154 **validated-novel** | 154 **weakly-labeled-lower-novelty** | Where: * **validated-novel** (both setups) — ICLR 2026 submissions whose reviewers explicitly praised the originality of the contribution itself and none disputed it; accepted, in the top rating decile of their primary area, with an average contribution score >= 3.0. * **validated-lower-novelty** (Human-Only) — the mirror image: reviewers faulted the originality and none praised it; rejected, in the bottom rating decile of their primary area, with an average contribution score <= 2.0. * **weakly-labeled-lower-novelty** (Human+Generated) — ideas from Claude Sonnet 4.5, prompted simply to propose a novel idea with no scaffold, literature access, or tools. Each setup is instantiated in two evaluation formats: * **pointwise** — one idea per row, binary label: is this idea novel? * **pairwise** — one `D_+` idea against one `D_-` idea; which of the two is more novel? and in two idea formats: * **abstract** (default) — the idea as a free-form abstract. * **plan** (`*_plan` configs) — the same ideas normalized into a two-field *purpose* / *mechanism* research plan. `data/human-plus-generated/backbone-*/` regenerates `D_-` with other ideation backbones (`gpt-5`, `gpt-5.1`, `gpt-5.4`, `opus-4-5`) and is used in the negatives-source experiment. ### 🤗 Hugging Face Code in this repo is designed to work with the YAML files in `data`, but we also release the same instances on the Hub: [allenai/novelty-judge-bench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/novelty-judge-bench). ```python from datasets import load_dataset ds = load_dataset("allenai/novelty-judge-bench", "human-plus-generated_pointwise", split="test") ``` ### Expert Annotation of Judge Errors [`data/expert-annotations/judge_errors.csv`](data/expert-annotations/judge_errors.csv) holds 30 pairwise instances re-judged blind by a domain expert: 28 the LLM judge got wrong and 2 controls it got right. The expert sided with the benchmark's gold label on all 30, and explains each choice in `annotation_reasoning`. See [data/README.md](data/README.md#expert-annotations) for further information. ### Automatic Data Collection The same pipeline that produced these files can be re-run on a newer conference cycle. See instructions here: [**Rebuilding the benchmark**](src/novelty_eval/benchmark_data/README.md) ## Judge Evaluation [example_eval.yaml](src/novelty_eval/config/example_eval.yaml) runs a single judge over a single released benchmark file, under the baseline configuration of the paper: a verdict plus reasoning, three samples per decision, high reasoning effort, no tools, and no related work. ```bash python src/novelty_eval/run_benchmark.py \ --config src/novelty_eval/config/example_eval.yaml ``` ## Reproducing the Paper's Experiments

Every experiment takes three steps: 1. **Run** the controlled changes: `./scripts/eval/run_ablations.sh --skip-create --models ,,... --parallel-models --tracks ,,... --ablations ,,...`. Controlled changes (ablations) are defined in [ablations.yaml](src/novelty_eval/ablation/ablations.yaml). Adding `--batch` runs experiments in API batch mode (half the price). 2. **Merge** results for different controlled changes and compute statistical significance: `python src/novelty_eval/ablation/merge_ablation_runs.py --config `. The configs in [configs/merge/](src/novelty_eval/ablation/configs/merge/) list *our* run directories under `dirs:`, so replace them with yours. 3. **Plot** with the notebook listed below. In key and config names, `hvh` is **Human-Only** and `vanilla` is **Human+Generated**. ### Controlled study | Paper | `ablations.yaml` key | |---|---| | Reference configuration | `current` | | P1: Criteria without guardrails | `vague_criterion` | | P2: Criteria removed | `no_criteria_prompt` | | P3: "Which was judged novel?" | `ai_researcher_base` | | P4: "Which is novel?" | `ai_researcher_no_review` | | P5: "Which was judged more novel?" | `ai_researcher_comparative` | | + Related work (retrieval) | `retrieval` ¹ | | Reasoning effort = low | `low_judge_reasoning` | | Idea format | `convert_to_plan_form_{pairwise,pointwise}_{human,vanilla}` | | No verdict aggregation | `mec_k_1` ² | | D₋ source | `{gpt_5,gpt_5.1,gpt_5.4,opus-4-5}_backbone_{pairwise,pointwise}_vanilla` | ¹ Needs a retrieval cache first: [run_retrieve_candidates.sh](src/novelty_eval/retrieval/run_retrieve_candidates.sh) builds it for pairwise, and [flatten_retrieval_cache.py](src/novelty_eval/retrieval/flatten_retrieval_cache.py) derives the pointwise cache from it.
² Not a separate run. [derive_subrun_artifacts.py](src/novelty_eval/ablation/derive_subrun_artifacts.py) carves it out of the `current` runs. Merge with [merge_config_hvh.yaml](src/novelty_eval/ablation/configs/merge/merge_config_hvh.yaml) and [merge_config_vanilla.yaml](src/novelty_eval/ablation/configs/merge/merge_config_vanilla.yaml), then plot: | Figure / table | Notebook | |---|---| | Controlled-change results, plus the soft-accuracy and per-class F1 versions in the appendix | [two_track_figure.ipynb](src/novelty_eval/figures/two_track_figure.ipynb) | | Tie rates (figure and table) | [tie_rates_figure.ipynb](src/novelty_eval/figures/tie_rates_figure.ipynb) | | Effect of the lower-novelty ideas source | [negatives_source_figure.ipynb](src/novelty_eval/figures/negatives_source_figure.ipynb) | | Controlled-change results without verdict aggregation ³ | [sampling_depth_figure.ipynb](src/novelty_eval/figures/sampling_depth_figure.ipynb) | ³ Derive the single-sample version of every ablation with `derive_subrun_artifacts.py`, then merge with [configs/merge/mec_k1/](src/novelty_eval/ablation/configs/merge/mec_k1/). ### Retrieval's limitations * **Strong agentic RAG judge**: run `./scripts/eval/run_retrieval_faceoff.sh sample`, then `submit`, then `poll`. Plot with [retrieval_faceoff_figure.ipynb](src/novelty_eval/figures/retrieval_faceoff_figure.ipynb). * **Retrieval across ideation backbones** (appendix): run the `{gpt_5.1,gpt_5.4,opus-4-5}_backbone_retrieval_{pairwise,pointwise}_vanilla` ablations, merge with [configs/merge/retrieval_given_backbone/](src/novelty_eval/ablation/configs/merge/retrieval_given_backbone/), and plot with [retrieval_given_backbone_figure.ipynb](src/novelty_eval/figures/retrieval_given_backbone_figure.ipynb). ### Dedicated novelty judges We ran [AI-Scientist](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06292) and [Idea-Novelty-Checker](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22026) with the implementations released at [simra-shahid/idea_novelty_checker](https://github.com/simra-shahid/idea_novelty_checker). That code is not part of this repository. [cost_efficiency.ipynb](src/novelty_eval/figures/cost_efficiency.ipynb) draws the cost vs. macro-F1 figures and the pointwise results table. Point it at your run directories first. A file-by-file map of the codebase lives in [src/novelty_eval/README.md](src/novelty_eval/README.md). ## License The code is licensed under [Apache 2.0](LICENSE). The data in [`data/`](data/) is licensed under [ODC-BY 1.0](data/LICENSE); see [data/README.md](data/README.md#license) for the OpenReview attribution and model-output terms that apply to it. ## Authors - [Noy Sternlicht](https://noy-sternlicht.github.io/) — Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Allen Institute for AI - [Simra Shahid](https://sites.google.com/view/simra-shahid/home) — Microsoft - [Peter Jansen](https://cognitiveai.org/) — Allen Institute for AI, University of Arizona - [Daniel S. Weld](https://www.cs.washington.edu/people/faculty/weld/) — Allen Institute for AI, University of Washington - [Pao Siangliulue](https://paoponder.com/) — Allen Institute for AI - [Tom Hope](https://tomhoper.github.io/) — Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Allen Institute for AI ## Cite us! ```bibtex @misc{sternlicht2026oldideasnovelproblems, title={Old Ideas, Novel Problems: The Instability of LLM-Based Novelty Evaluation}, author={Noy Sternlicht and Simra Shahid and Peter Jansen and Daniel S. Weld and Pao Siangliulue and Tom Hope}, year={2026}, eprint={2610.02022}, archivePrefix={arXiv}, primaryClass={cs.CL}, url={https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02022}, } ```

Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel? Hugging Face Models Datasets Spaces Buckets Docs Enterprise Pricing Website Tasks HuggingChat Collections Languages Organizations Community Blog Posts Daily Papers Hardware Learn Discord Forum GitHub Solutions Team & Enterprise Hugging Face PRO Enterprise Support Inference Providers Inference Endpoints Storage Buckets Log In Sign Up Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel? Enterprise Article Published October 27, 2026 Upvote 14 +8 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai :last-child]:mb-0"> Building a benchmark for novelty judges Small changes can produce very different verdicts Toward more reliable evaluation of novel research 📄 Paper | 📊 Data | 💻 Code Today we’re releasing Old Ideas, Novel Problems , a new study of how reliably large language models can evaluate the novelty of scientific research ideas. Alongside the paper, we’re publishing a benchmark, data, and code for testing novelty judges, plus an automated pipeline researchers can use to build new evaluation sets. At Ai2, we’ve been developing AI systems that support different parts of scientific discovery. DataVoyager helps researchers explore and analyze structured data, AutoDiscovery generates and tests hypotheses, and Theorizer synthesizes evidence across large bodies of literature into candidate scientific theories. Together with Asta , these projects point toward systems that can help researchers move from understanding prior work to proposing, testing, and refining new ideas. But generating research ideas is only part of the challenge of automating scientific discovery. Those ideas also need to contribute something genuinely new, which means these systems need a way to distinguish a novel direction from one that mostly repackages existing work. That judgment is often handed to another LLM—what we call a novelty judge . Novelty judges assess whether a research idea is new relative to prior work, either on its own or in comparison with another idea. There’s no standard way to build one; research teams choose a model, prompt, evaluation format, reasoning budget, and sometimes a literature-retrieval system. Those choices can materially affect the verdict. Yet these judges are often validated only on human-written papers rather than the AI-generated ideas they are actually meant to evaluate. Our new benchmark results suggest novelty evaluation itself is far from reliable. Across six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – seemingly small changes to the evaluation setup produce dramatically different judgments of the same ideas. In one experiment, changing just a few words in a prompt shifts a model’s accuracy in identifying which of two ideas is more novel by more than 50 percentage points. Retrieval and additional reasoning do not consistently improve judgments, and two purpose-built novelty evaluation systems perform worse than a simple prompted Claude Opus 4.6 baseline. If AI is going to play a larger role in scientific discovery, we need more dependable ways to tell whether it is actually proposing something new. Our work provides tools for studying that problem, while showing how much remains unresolved. Building a benchmark for novelty judges To test how reliably novelty judges can distinguish more novel research ideas from less novel ones, we first needed examples where there was strong evidence about the originality of the underlying scientific contribution. So we built an automated pipeline around ICLR 2026 peer reviews. Rather than treating paper acceptance as a proxy for novelty, we mined the reviews themselves for passages where reviewers explicitly discussed a contribution’s originality. That distinction is key; a paper can be accepted without being particularly novel as long as it is strong enough in other aspects. Likewise, a rejected paper with an original contribution can have other weaknesses. We created a high-novelty pool of 154 human-authored research ideas by selecting accepted papers in the top-rated 10% of their ICLR research area whose reviewers positively identified novelty and where no reviewer disputed it. We applied the reverse criteria to build a lower-novelty pool : 145 ideas from rejected papers in the bottom 10% whose reviewers raised originality concerns without any reviewer positively identifying novelty. In a separate check of the review-mining process, an annotator agreed with the extracted novelty-signal polarity in 47 of 50 cases; none of the disagreements would have changed whether a reviewer was counted as praising or disputing the paper’s novelty. Together, these two pools form our first evaluation setting, Human-Only , which tests whether novelty judges can tell apart human-authored ideas with strong evidence of higher or lower novelty. But in practice, novelty judges are increasingly being used to evaluate AI-generated ideas. So we created a second setting, Human+Generated . For this pool, we paired the same 154 validated human ideas with 154 ideas produced by a simple LLM generator. We assumed the generated ideas were less novel than their human-authored counterparts; these are weak labels, not verified judgments for every idea. The generator received only a research area and an instruction to propose a novel idea, with no literature search, tools, iteration, or feedback. This gave us a conservative comparison between ideas from a basic generator and contributions from top-10% ICLR papers whose reviewers had explicitly endorsed their originality. As additional checks, an expert independently reviewed 30 Human+Generated pairs, heavily weighted toward cases our strongest judge got wrong, and we rewrote the human- and AI-generated ideas into a common structure to test whether judges were simply reacting to differences in writing style. The expert preferred the human idea in all 30 pairs and judged none of the generated ideas novel. Importantly, many of our core findings don’t depend on the labels at all. If two reasonable evaluation setups give opposite answers for the same pair of ideas, that disagreement itself reveals instability. Small changes can produce very different verdicts Using our collections of human-authored and AI-generated research ideas, we tested how well six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – could evaluate novelty through both pointwise (i.e., absolute novelty ratings) and pairwise (i.e., comparing two ideas to find the most novel) comparisons. We varied one factor at a time: the prompt, reasoning budget, whether the judge could see related papers, how the ideas were formatted, how many judgments were combined into a final verdict, and – for AI-generated ideas – which model generated them. The largest shifts in performance came from how we prompted the model to judge novelty. For example, we showed GPT-5.4 the same Human+Generated pairs – each containing one validated human-authored idea and one AI-generated idea – with two prompts. One prompt told the model that reviewers had found exactly one idea in each pair to be novel and asked it to identify which one; the other simply asked which idea was novel. When we switched to the simpler prompt, accuracy dropped from 93.5% to 40.9% – below chance – and the model changed its verdict on more than half of the same pairs. By contrast, the same prompt change shifted accuracy by only about seven percentage points on the Human-Only dataset, which pairs human-authored ideas with stronger and weaker evidence of novelty. That suggests a novelty judge can appear relatively stable on human-authored research but behave very differently on AI-generated ideas. That said, human-authored ideas weren’t immune. We saw substantial shifts on the Human-Only dataset as well; the same change moved Claude Opus 4.6 accuracy by 21 points. The shifts were just less severe than on the AI-generated ideas. There was also no universally better prompt. For example, when judging ideas individually, dropping an instruction that warned judges not to treat trivial or incremental contributions as novel improved accuracy for some judges while reducing it for others. A prompt that works well for one model may not transfer to another, in other words. We also tested a common use of novelty judges: comparing ideas from two AI generators. We paired ideas from Claude Opus 4.5 with Claude Sonnet 4.5, and GPT-5.4 with GPT-5.1. Across the tested prompt changes, roughly a quarter to a third of verdicts changed on average across six judges. This disagreement can be measured without assuming which generator produces more novel ideas, showing how the choice of judge prompt can affect comparisons between ideation systems. More search and reasoning didn’t necessarily produce better novelty judgments. We gave GPT-5.6 Sol an extra-high reasoning budget and live, iterative search restricted to arXiv, then compared it with standard-retrieval judges that each saw five pre-retrieved abstracts. (All judges in this comparison ran once per idea on Human+Generated .) The agentic judge scored 0.78 macro-F1 – 11 points behind Claude Opus 4.6 at 0.89, and in roughly the same range as simpler Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.4 setups – while costing roughly 10× more per decision at current API prices. (In this context, macro-F1 measures how well a judge identifies novel and non-novel ideas; higher is better.) Purpose-built evaluators weren’t more accurate either, despite costing substantially more. On the Human+Generated set, a simple Claude Opus 4.6 prompt using low reasoning and majority voting across three calls achieved 0.854 macro-F1 at a total evaluation cost of $2.59. By comparison, Idea Novelty Checker, a literature-grounded retrieval and reranking pipeline, scored 0.642 at $30.66, while Sakana AI’s AI Scientist, whose novelty evaluator iteratively searches Semantic Scholar, scored 0.772 at $82.05. (Both dedicated evaluators used Claude Opus 4.6, with one call per decision.) In other words, the simple prompted baseline was both more accurate and considerably cheaper than either purpose-built system. Taken together, these results suggest that novelty evaluation is particularly brittle on the AI-generated ideas these systems are increasingly being asked to judge. Toward more reliable evaluation of novel research Our results suggest that LLM-based novelty evaluation remains a major open problem. Judges that appear reliable on human-authored research may behave differently on AI-generated ideas; prompts that help one model can hurt another; and more search or compute does not necessarily produce more consistent judgments. Future work should test judges on the kinds of ideas they will actually evaluate, measure sensitivity across prompts and models, improve how prior literature is incorporated, and build benchmarks that can evolve as the scientific literature grows and AI systems improve. Our benchmark and reusable data pipeline are a starting point—researchers can apply them to new peer reviews, other scientific communities, and future generations of novelty judges. Automated ideation depends on more than generating plausible research directions; we also need ways to tell when those ideas are genuinely new. By making the weaknesses of current novelty judges easier to measure, we hope this release helps researchers build more robust ways to evaluate AI-generated research ideas. The finding that agentic search and complex evaluators underperform simpler baselines strongly resonates with what I observed in my own research: https://coronring.github.io/blog/stop-taking-ai-advice-on-where-to-submit/

\n

Earlier this month, I ran a complementary study asking current models (GPT-6 Luna and Claude Opus 5.5) where to submit 132 full, blinded AI papers from the 2026 cycle (NeurIPS, EMNLP, COLM, Findings, and workshops) strictly after the model knowledge cutoff date: Stop taking AI advice on where to submit your paper.

\n

While Novelty-Bench examines the idea-level novelty judge, evaluating full manuscripts revealed the exact same underlying failure modes:

\n
    \n
  1. \"Careful review\" degraded performance: Prompting the model to write a comprehensive program-committee review and estimate acceptance odds first dropped tier accuracy from 39% to 30%, mirroring your finding that heavier reasoning pipelines (like AI Scientist) fell behind simple prompted baselines.
    2. \n
  2. Superficial heuristics over substance: Just as your judges reacted to generator formatting styles, our evaluator followed venue topic stereotypes (NLP to EMNLP, vision to NeurIPS) and length. In fact, ranking papers by simple word count matched or outperformed the model's predicted acceptance odds across multiple tiers.
    3. \n
  3. 0 of 29 top contributions recognized: The model never once recommended aiming for an oral or spotlight, treating NeurIPS workshop papers and actual oral presentations with almost identical estimated probabilities (~2.5% vs 2.7%).
    4. \n
  4. Completely uncalibrated confidence: Confidence was virtually indistinguishable when the model was right (0.42) versus wrong (0.40).
    5. \n
\n

Your work provides the benchmark tools needed to quantify this at the ideation stage, and our results suggest the problem persists all the way downstream to full paper evaluation. Very glad to see rigorous attention brought to this issue and love to chat on it!

 AI-based ideation systems are often evaluated on the novelty of their ideas, and that judgment is increasingly delegated to large language models. Such judges are typically built ad hoc and validated, if at all, on human-authored papers rather than on the generated ideas they are meant to score. So, how do novelty judges perform? 
 Not well. We present a systematic controlled study of novelty evaluation design choices. We build an evaluation set automatically, mining OpenReview for passages where reviewers explicitly affirm or dispute a paper's originality and keeping only submissions with unanimous agreement at the extremes of their research area; we pair these with ideas from a vanilla LLM generator. Across six judges, we find that seemingly small prompt design choices have large consequences; e.g., simply telling the judge that reviewers found one idea novel and the other not can change its verdict on more than half of the identical idea pairs it is shown, shifting pairwise accuracy by over 50 points and occasionally pushing it below chance. The same change helps one judge and hurts another. Retrieval and larger reasoning budgets help little, and two purpose-built novelty evaluators are outperformed by our cheapest prompted baseline. These results raise questions about reported novelty gains of automated ideation systems, and call for robust novelty evaluation methods.

  Getting started     
 
 Clone this repository:
  git clone https://github.com/allenai/novelty-eval.git
 cd  novelty-eval  
 
 Create and activate a virtual environment:
  python3.12 -m venv myenv
 source  ./myenv/bin/activate  
 
 Install dependencies:
  pip install -r requirements.txt  
 
 Point the code at the repository:
   export  PYTHONPATH=  "  $PWD /src "  
 export  SECRETS=  "  $PWD /secrets.toml "  
 export  OUTPUT_DIR=  "  $PWD /output "    
 
 
 If you plan to commit changes, register the notebook filter so that running a notebook (outputs, execution counts, kernel metadata) doesn't show up as a change (needs  jq ): 
  git config filter.nbstrip.clean   ' jq --indent 1 -f scripts/nbstrip.jq '  
git config filter.nbstrip.smudge cat
git config filter.nbstrip.required  true   
  Setting up API keys     
 The judges and the benchmark-construction pipeline call external APIs. Keys go in a  secrets.toml  file at the project root (the location  $SECRETS  points at): 
   openai_key  =   " your-openai-api-key "  
 anthropic_key  =   " your-anthropic-api-key "  
 semantic_scholar_key  =   " your-s2-api-key "       #  retrieval only   
 Rebuilding the benchmark from scratch additionally needs OpenReview credentials: 
   export  OPENREVIEW_USERNAME=  " your-openreview-email "  
 export  OPENREVIEW_PASSWORD=  " your-openreview-password "    
  Novelty Evaluation Data     
 
     
 
 Our benchmark consists of two data setups:  Human-Only  and  Human+Generated . Both setups consist of two separate idea "pools": a  high-novelty pool  D_+   and a  lower-novelty pool  D_-  , where ideas from  D_+  can be assumed to be more novel than those in  D_- . 
  
 
 
 Setup 
  D_+  (novel) 
  D_-  (lower-novelty) 
 
 
 
 
  Human-Only  ( data/human-only/ ) 
 154  validated-novel  
 145  validated-lower-novelty  
 
 
  Human+Generated  ( data/human-plus-generated/ ) 
 154  validated-novel  
 154  weakly-labeled-lower-novelty  
 
 
  
 Where: 
 
  validated-novel  (both setups) — ICLR 2026 submissions whose reviewers explicitly praised the originality of the contribution itself and none disputed it; accepted, in the top rating decile of their primary area, with an average contribution score >= 3.0. 
  validated-lower-novelty  (Human-Only) — the mirror image: reviewers faulted the originality and none praised it; rejected, in the bottom rating decile of their primary area, with an average contribution score <= 2.0. 
  weakly-labeled-lower-novelty  (Human+Generated) — ideas from Claude Sonnet 4.5, prompted simply to propose a novel idea with no scaffold, literature access, or tools. 
 
 Each setup is instantiated in two evaluation formats: 
 
  pointwise  — one idea per row, binary label: is this idea novel? 
  pairwise  — one  D_+  idea against one  D_-  idea; which of the two is more novel? 
 
 and in two idea formats: 
 
  abstract  (default) — the idea as a free-form abstract. 
  plan  ( *_plan  configs) — the same ideas normalized into a two-field  purpose  /  mechanism  research plan. 
 
  data/human-plus-generated/backbone-*/  regenerates  D_-  with other ideation backbones ( gpt-5 ,  gpt-5.1 ,  gpt-5.4 ,  opus-4-5 ) and is used in the negatives-source experiment. 
  🤗 Hugging Face     
 Code in this repo is designed to work with the YAML files in  data , but we also release the same instances on the Hub:  allenai/novelty-judge-bench . 
   from   datasets   import   load_dataset 

 ds   =   load_dataset ( "allenai/novelty-judge-bench" ,  "human-plus-generated_pointwise" ,  split  =  "test" )  
  Expert Annotation of Judge Errors     
   data/expert-annotations/judge_errors.csv   holds 30 pairwise instances re-judged blind by a domain expert: 28 the LLM judge got wrong and 2 controls it got right. The expert sided with the benchmark's gold label on all 30, and explains each choice in  annotation_reasoning . See  data/README.md  for further information. 
  Automatic Data Collection     
 The same pipeline that produced these files can be re-run on a newer conference cycle. See instructions here: 
   Rebuilding the benchmark   
  Judge Evaluation     
  example_eval.yaml  runs a single judge over a single released benchmark file, under the baseline configuration of the paper: a verdict plus reasoning, three samples per decision, high reasoning effort, no tools, and no related work. 
  python src/novelty_eval/run_benchmark.py \
    --config src/novelty_eval/config/example_eval.yaml  
  Reproducing the Paper's Experiments     
 
     
 
 Every experiment takes three steps: 
 
  Run  the controlled changes:  ./scripts/eval/run_ablations.sh --skip-create --models <key>,<key>,... --parallel-models --tracks <key>,<key>,... --ablations <key>,<key>,... . Controlled changes (ablations) are defined in  ablations.yaml . Adding  --batch  runs experiments in API batch mode (half the price). 
  Merge  results for different controlled changes and compute statistical significance:  python src/novelty_eval/ablation/merge_ablation_runs.py --config <merge config> . The configs in  configs/merge/  list  our  run directories under  dirs: , so replace them with yours. 
  Plot  with the notebook listed below. 
 
 In key and config names,  hvh  is  Human-Only  and  vanilla  is  Human+Generated .

readme:mottopanikeiku/doomformer.text:
Neural networks computed by voodoo dolls inside DOOM maps.
Every value is read back and checked against NumPy. Tolerance 0.

Quick start · Walk a digit · The museum · How it works · What is checked · Films · Docs

| **10,000 / 10,000** | **1,355** | **0** | **4** | |:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:| | MNIST test digits exact | voodoo dolls in one MNIST map | mismatches in 20,000 fuzzed nets | other DOOM engines run the museum exactly |

## Quick start ```sh pip install git+https://github.com/mottopanikeiku/doomformer # Python 3.11+, Linux or macOS doomformer hello # 2 s: a small MLP, every value checked doomformer draw --digit 7 # 15 s: the marine walks a 7 and the level reads it ``` `doomformer doctor` checks your setup. It builds ACC, the ACS compiler, if it is missing. That needs git, cmake and a C compiler. On Fedora: `sudo dnf install git cmake gcc gcc-c++ make`. > [!TIP] > No install needed for the [Colab notebook](https://colab.research.google.com/github/mottopanikeiku/doomformer/blob/main/examples/doomformer_colab.ipynb). > Draw a digit in your browser and DOOM reads it. ## Walk a digit, DOOM reads it

The marine holds FIRE and inks the floor. Then he presses READ. 1,355 voodoo dolls in the same map run an MNIST network. The winning digit's doll crosses a line. That line lights the digit on the display. ```text ▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄ ▄████████████████ ████▀▀ ▀████▀ ▀▀▀ ▄███▀ ████ ███ ███ ███ ████ ███▀ ████ ▀███ DOOM reads: 7 (right) -- the winner's doll lit it on the 7-segment display EXACT: all 248 values DOOM computed [...] equal the NumPy integer reference (tolerance 0) READ pass: 273 game tics = 8 s of real-time DOOM at 35 tics/s, 3 s wall [...] ``` Python reads back 248 values and checks every one. With `--digit`, Python presses the keys for you. Without it, you walk and draw yourself. [Full output](docs/commands.md#doomformer-draw---digit-7) > [!NOTE] > EXACT means DOOM got the same numbers as the integer network. It does not mean the digit is right. | run | right | exact | |---|---|---| | first 100 MNIST test digits | 99 | 100 | | 1,000 sampled test digits, one map each | 966 | 1,000 | | all 10,000 test digits, tile maps | 9,716 (97.16 %) | 10,000 | The float model scores 97.58 %. The network also trained on the strokes the scripted marine walks. [Details](docs/drawpad.md) · [Film](https://mottopanikeiku.github.io/doomformer/#drawpad) ![eight MNIST test digits and what DOOM read: 7 2 1 0 4 9 6 3, all exact](https://github.com/mottopanikeiku/doomformer/releases/download/v0.1.0/mnist.png) ## The museum: rewire one connection

> [!TIP] > **Play it without Python.** Download [museum.wad](https://github.com/mottopanikeiku/doomformer/releases/download/v0.7.1/museum.wad) > ([sha256](https://github.com/mottopanikeiku/doomformer/releases/download/v0.7.1/museum_SHA256SUMS.txt)) and the free > [Freedoom](https://freedoom.github.io/download.html) IWAD. Then run `gzdoom -iwad freedoom2.wad -file museum.wad`. Step on seven floor pads to light a digit. Press READ. 136 voodoo dolls run a tiny network and light the answer. Press MUTATE and the level rewires one connection while it runs. The same 7 now reads as 1. You can watch it happen: one doll stops at its gate. ```text $ doomformer museum verify 7 pads abc w_7a +1 DOOM reads 7 scores [4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 3, 2, 7, 3, 4] EXACT (148 values; 744 tics; [...]) 7 after MUTATE pads abc w_7a -1 DOOM reads 1 scores [4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 3, 2, 5, 3, 4] EXACT (148 values; 744 tics; [...]) 7 after RESTORE pads abc w_7a +1 DOOM reads 7 scores [4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 3, 2, 7, 3, 4] EXACT (148 values; 744 tics; [...]) ``` A self-test version runs exactly in GZDoom, LZDoom, UZDoom and ZDoom 2.8.1. [Details](docs/museum.md) ## How it works Every part of a network becomes a part of the map: | in a neural network | in the DOOM map | |---|---| | a value of 5 | 5 voodoo dolls | | a weight | a line on the floor; each doll that crosses it adds the weight | | a sum | a sector's light level or floor height | | an activation (ReLU) | a staircase of gates the dolls must climb | | attention | dolls squeezing under ceilings that another value lowered | | a lesion | a closed door | One layer, from dolls to dolls: ```mermaid flowchart LR A["input value
= a crowd of dolls"] --> B["weight lines
each crossing adds w"] B --> C["the sum
= a light level or height"] C --> D["staircase of gates
= the activation"] D --> E["next layer's dolls"] ```

A matrix multiply. Each doll is one unit of a value. Each lava line it crosses adds a weight.
Attention. Dolls squeeze under ceiling gates. Counting who gets through is a multiply.
The engine has sharp edges, and the compiler works around them: - A floor mover ignores a second request while it is still moving. - A teleport cancels lines a doll crossed earlier in the same tic. - Things far from a BSP node can land in the wrong room, so every map fits in 32,000 units. `doomformer facts` checks these in about 10 s. [Engine facts](docs/HOW_IT_WORKS.md#engine-facts) · [Engine features it needs](docs/HOW_IT_WORKS.md#engine-features-it-needs) · [Other ports](docs/engine_limits.md#other-ports) Computers in DOOM maps are not new. [counter.wad](https://www.wad-archive.com/wad/8d0de31d8b392fc2d7fd817e933b3cf43bca799a) counts with voodoo dolls, [conway.wad](https://github.com/pwiecz/conway.wad) runs Game of Life, and [Danny Spencer's calculator](https://github.com/nukep/doom-calculator) adds numbers. New here: a compiler for neural networks, and an exact check on every value. [Related work](docs/related_work.md) ## What is checked

Every run compares each value the map exposes with NumPy. That proves the inputs that ran, nothing more. So the repo also attacks its own check: | attack | result | |---|---| | **Tamper** with one weight line | the check fails on exactly the inputs that cross it | | **Fuzz** 20,000 random nets at the range limits | 0 mismatches; CI fuzzes a fresh seed on every push | | **Mutate** one line of a map, 1,004 times | 297 caught; no survivor is proven harmless | | **Extract** the weights back out of the map, without DOOM | equal to the source net | | **Guard** every readout page with a poison value | a page that never runs cannot pass old values | The MNIST map exposes 248 values. It does not expose its 903 staircase counts and 1,351 gate comparisons. Those are checked only through the sums they feed. Fuzzing and tests found four bugs in the compiler. All are fixed. [Verification](docs/verification.md)
Who computes what | run | Python | voodoo dolls | |---|---|---| | `mnist`, `df.compile` | writes the inputs, waits, reads | every sum, activation, comparison and the choice | | `demo`, `ask` (tile maps) | writes tokens, copies values between maps, samples letters | every sum and activation | | `draw`, `--loop`, the marine's brain, the fly | only advances the clock and reads | everything, including the choice | | `machine` | loads the program, then advances the clock and reads | program counter and registers | | `museum`, played in GZDoom | nothing | every sum, comparison and the choice | ACS level scripts move gates, rewind the dolls, sense the world and copy results out. Two do more. `df.Agent` takes an argmax in ACS. `--opt 3` copies each layer's values into the next layer with a script. [Per demo](docs/HOW_IT_WORKS.md#who-does-what-per-demo) The maps need ZDoom (UDMF and ACS). This repo runs [ViZDoom](https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/ViZDoom) 1.3.2 with Freedoom assets.
## Commands | Command | What DOOM does | Time | Skill level | |---|---|---|---| | `doomformer hello` | a small MLP, 5 random inputs | 2 s | I'm too young to die | | `doomformer draw --digit 7` | the marine walks a 7, the level reads it | 15 s | Hey, not too rough | | `doomformer museum build` | a playable map that reads a digit | 1 s | Hey, not too rough | | `doomformer mnist` | reads 4 test digits, or your own image | 1.5 to 3 min | Hurt me plenty | | `doomformer demo` | a transformer writes a level name | 15 to 60 s | Hurt me plenty | | `doomformer machine subleq all` | a tiny computer runs three programs | about 5 min | Ultra-Violence | | `doomformer learn digits --classes 4 --steps 300` | a blank brain learns digits inside the map | about 5 min | Ultra-Violence | | `doomformer ask "what does iddqd do"` | answers from 189 DOOM facts | about 11 min | Ultra-Violence | | `doomformer demo --nightmare` | the 2-layer model, 106 tile maps | 3.5 to 7 min | Nightmare! | Times are from a 16-core arm64 Linux machine. [Every command](docs/commands.md) Some outputs are picked. DEMON CANYON, the name `--nightmare` writes, is one hand-picked sample. `ask` gets 94.7 % of its training questions right, and 35.4 % of new wordings. ## Bigger experiments

**His brain is the level.** The level senses the nearest demon. 1,345 voodoo dolls of the marine run his brain and pick an action. The level turns him and fires. Python only steps the clock and reads. 50 of 50 decisions are exact. [Film](https://mottopanikeiku.github.io/doomformer/#brain) · [Code](demos/brainlevel.py) > [!WARNING] > He is not playable. One decision takes 22 s of game time, and the demons are frozen while he thinks. With the demons > awake (`--live`), he dies in 5.5 s without a kill. [Live demons](docs/DEMOS.md#live-demons-what-the-latency-costs-him) | run it from a clone | what you see | |---|---| | `python -m demos.brainlevel` | his brain is the level | | `python -m demos.brainlevel --live` | the same brain against awake demons | | `python -m demos.brainlevel --lesion-when near` | the level closes neuron doors when a demon gets close | | `python -m demos.aimlearn` | a perceptron learns to aim inside one game | | `python -m demos.flyloop` | a fruit-fly circuit drives the marine | | `python -m demos.lobotomy` | lesions that turn him into a pacifist |

A transformer names a level. It writes DEMON CANYON. A Python generator builds the level.
One hand-picked sample.
A marine plays the level it named. Doors, two kills, exit. 102 decisions, all exact.
Python gives the compass. Seed 118 of 120, picked.

A perceptron learns inside one game. Its 38 weights are ceiling heights. Dolls raise and lower them.
Python gives the labels.
Lesions. A shotgun blast closes 7 neurons. The marine stops firing.
Picked from 3,000 random blasts.

A fruit-fly circuit. 255 neurons from the FlyWire connectome drive the marine.
Simplified dynamics.
A transformer in one map. No Python between layers. 3,548 dolls write SHIL.
A small model.

Generation without Python. The winner's doll writes the next letter. The level rewinds itself.
One model, one prompt.
A 4-layer transformer. It writes UNHOLY STRONGHOLD over 10,166 tile runs.
Runs share a pool of games.
[All demos, numbers and picked seeds](docs/DEMOS.md) ## Build your own Compile a network into a map. Let its outputs open doors, flash lights or shove the marine. This runs as pasted: ```python import numpy as np import doomformer as df # 2 inputs -> [a AND b, a OR b] -> 2 outputs, all integers net = df.MLP( weights=[np.array([[1, 1], [1, 1]]), np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1]])], biases=[np.array([-1, 0]), np.array([0, 0])], thresholds=[np.array([1]), np.array([1])], signed_input=False, ) with df.compile(net) as brain: for x in ([0, 0], [1, 0], [1, 1]): # computed by voodoo dolls; raises df.MismatchError on any difference from net.reference print(x, "->", brain(np.array(x)).tolist()) brain.record([np.array([0, 1]), np.array([1, 1])], "dolls.gif") # film the dolls doing it ``` `df.MLP.from_torch` converts a PyTorch model ([example 02](examples/02_pytorch_to_doom.py)). The `world` and `actions` hooks wire outputs to doors, lights and thrusts ([example 03](examples/03_brain_opens_doors.py)). [Guide](docs/BUILD_YOUR_OWN.md) · [12 examples](examples) · [Show and tell](https://github.com/mottopanikeiku/doomformer/issues/new/choose) ## Many games at once One map runs in one game, on one core. `df.run_many` spreads inputs over many games, or over a Ray cluster. A network can also be split into tile maps, one per layer. Then Python copies values between them. | run | digits | right | exact | time | |---|---|---|---|---| | one map, 14 games | 1,000 | 966 | 1,000 | 2 h | | 4 tile maps, 6 games | 10,000 | 9,716 | 10,000 | 23 min | ```sh doomformer mnist --tiles --all --workers 6 # all 10,000 digits as tile maps, about 23 min pip install "doomformer[ray]" ray start --head # other machines: ray start --address=HEAD:6379 doomformer mnist --all --ray --record mnist.json # all 10,000 digits, one map each, on a cluster ``` Budget one core and 1.3 GB of RAM per game. [Scaling](docs/scaling.md#scaling-out-many-games-many-machines) ## More | what | try | read | |---|---|---| | Faster schedules: MNIST in one map from 5,696 to 272 tics | `--opt 3` | [scheduling](docs/scheduling.md) | | A counter machine: 7 × 9 = 63 in 464 checked steps | `doomformer machine multiply 7 9` | [machine](docs/machine.md) | | A SUBLEQ machine with self-modifying code | `doomformer machine subleq all` | [machine](docs/machine.md) | | A blank brain learns digits in the map: 71 % held-out | `doomformer learn digits` | [learning](docs/learning.md) | | PyTorch import with BatchNorm, pooling and QAT | `MLP.from_torch` | [interop](docs/interop.md) | | A transformer that learned induction, exact in DOOM | `python -m demos.induction` | [induction](models/induction/EVAL.md) | | Patching, lesions and steering, checked in DOOM | `intref.forward(interventions=...)` | [interventions](docs/interventions.md) | | Speed per pass and throughput | `doomformer bench` | [scaling](docs/scaling.md) | ## Limits > [!IMPORTANT] > - **Slow.** A small MLP runs about 23,000 times slower than NumPy. Most of the time goes to idle conveyor belts. > [Speed](docs/HOW_IT_WORKS.md#speed) > - **Only the runs are checked.** Inputs that never ran are not covered. [Not covered](docs/verification.md#not-covered) > - **Integer models.** Attention is integer attention. No model has LayerNorm. > - **ViZDoom first.** Other DOOM engines ran only small maps. > - **No reinforcement learning.** The marine copies a scripted aimbot. > - **Finite machines.** Memory is bounded. Nothing here claims DOOM is Turing complete. > - **Picked samples.** Showcased seeds and names are picked. [The list](docs/DEMOS.md#seeds-and-selection) ## What's in the box | Path | What it holds | |---|---| | [`doomformer/`](doomformer) | the toolkit: map compiler, DOOM runtime, exact checks, CLI | | [`demos/`](demos) | research code: the marine's brain, the level generator, the fly circuit, the learning arena | | [`training/`](training) | training scripts for every model, with the data and sources | | [`models/`](models) | every trained model with its training log and evaluation | | [`examples/`](examples) | twelve one-file examples, most under 15 s | | [`tests/`](tests) | 496 tests; CI runs them against real headless DOOM on Linux and macOS | | [`docs/`](docs/README.md) | how it works, every demo with its numbers, the engine facts, the guide, [every command](docs/commands.md) | | [`CHANGELOG.md`](CHANGELOG.md) | what each release added | ## Licensing Code and docs: [MIT](LICENSE). Data keeps its own licence ([THIRD_PARTY.md](THIRD_PARTY.md)). The level-name lists come from the Doom Wiki (CC BY-SA 4.0) and id Software's source (GPL-2.0). The 100 sample MNIST digits are CC BY-SA 3.0. The fruit-fly circuits in `models/fly` come from the FlyWire connectome (CC BY-NC 4.0, non-commercial). Freedoom graphics are BSD-licensed. DOOM is a trademark of id Software / ZeniMax. This project is not affiliated with them.

DOOMFORMER: integer neural networks computed by voodoo dolls in ZDoom maps 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
     
   Integer neural networks compiled into ZDoom maps. Voodoo dolls do the arithmetic, and every value is checked against NumPy with tolerance 0. 
   
     tolerance 0 
     MIT 
   
   
     GitHub repository 
     Install 
     Films 
     How it works 
     Docs 
   
 

 

 
   A number is a crowd of voodoo dolls on a conveyor belt. An activation is a staircase they climb. A weight is a line
  they cross, and each crossing changes a light level or a floor height. When the dolls stop, Python reads the values
  back and compares each one with a NumPy integer reference. One value off by one and the run fails. 
 

 
   Walk a digit, DOOM reads it 
   
     
       
       drawpad.mp4 
     
     
       The marine holds FIRE to ink the floor, then presses READ. The level writes the 784 pixels into an MNIST
      network, and 1,355 voodoo dolls in the same map compute it. The winning digit's doll lights the display. Python
      checks all 248 values against NumPy. 
       30 of 30 scripted digits read right and exact. A READ takes 273 game tics, about 8 s.
       How it works  ·
       drawpad.mp4 , 16 s, 1.5 MB 
     
   
   # arrows walk, hold Ctrl to draw, Space: READ 
doomformer draw
 # headless: the marine walks a 7 
doomformer draw --digit 7  
 

 
   His brain is the level 
   
     
       
       brain_is_the_level_raw.mp4 
     
     
       The marine's brain is compiled into the level he fights in. The dots on the right are 1,345 voodoo dolls of
      him. A level script senses the nearest demon, the dolls pick an action, and the level turns him and fires. Python
      only advances the clock and reads. 50 of 50 decisions exact. 
       Time-lapse. The demons are frozen while he thinks.
       Details  ·
       brain_is_the_level_raw.mp4 , 53 s, 22.6 MB 
     
   
 

 
   Commands 
  pip install git+https://github.com/mottopanikeiku/doomformer    # Python 3.11+, Linux or macOS   
   The first run builds ACC, the ACS compiler, so git, cmake and a C compiler must be installed. 
   
   
       Command  What DOOM does  Time  Skill level   
     
         doomformer hello   a small MLP, 5 random inputs  2 s  I'm too young to die  
         doomformer draw --digit 7   the marine walks a 7, the level reads it  15 s    
         doomformer mnist   reads 4 test digits, or your own image  1.5 to 3 min  Hey, not too rough  
         doomformer demo   a transformer writes a level name  15 to 60 s  Hurt me plenty  
         doomformer demo --nightmare   the 2-layer model, 106 tile maps  3.5 to 7 min  Nightmare!  
         doomformer ask "what does iddqd do"   answers from 189 DOOM facts  about 11 min  Ultra-Violence  
     
   
   
   Times are from a 16-core arm64 Linux machine. DEMON CANYON, the name  --nightmare  writes, is a
  hand-picked sample, and the default  demo  seed is picked.  ask  answers 94.7 % of its training
  questions and 35.4 % of new wordings.  Every command  
 

 
   How it works 
   
      your network  PyTorch / NumPy  
      integers  quantised  
      a DOOM map  lanes, gates, lava lines, doors  
      ViZDoom runs it  voodoo dolls walk  
      read back  light levels and plane heights  
      EXACT  every value equals the NumPy integer reference  
   
   
     DOOM turns every extra player start into a voodoo doll: a copy of the player that rides conveyors and triggers
    every line it crosses. An activation of 5 is five dolls. A staircase lets a doll past each step only if the value
    clears it, which gives ReLU, rounding and clamping in one shape. 
     The engine has sharp edges. A second floor move on one sector in the same tic is lost. A teleport cancels lines
    crossed earlier in the same tic. Things far from a BSP node land in the wrong room. The full list is in
     HOW_IT_WORKS.md . 
   
   Computers in DOOM maps exist already.  counter.wad  (2006) counts with voodoo dolls,  conway.wad  runs Game of Life, and  Danny Spencer's calculator  adds numbers. Doomformer adds a compiler for neural networks, a list of engine behaviours that break exactness, and the tolerance-0 check. 
 

 
   Bigger experiments 
   Each run is exact against its reference. Scope and picked seeds are in
   DEMOS.md . 
   

     
       
         
         trilogy.mp4 
       
       
         DOOM dreams of DOOM 
         A 2-layer name model writes DEMON CANYON, a hand-picked sample. A Python generator builds the level, and a
        marine whose policy runs on 55 games plays it. Halfway through, 3 of his neurons close. 120 decisions, all exact. 
          trilogy.mp4 , 48 s, 11.5 MB 
       
     

     
       
         
         doom_beats_doom.mp4 
       
       
         DOOM plays DOOM 
         A 1-layer policy walks the generated level: doors, two kills, exit. Python supplies the compass and enemy
        positions. 102 decisions, all exact. Seed 118 of 120, picked. 
          doom_beats_doom.mp4 , 37 s, 10.4 MB 
       
     

     
       
         
         one_game.mp4 
       
       
         DOOM learns 
         A 38-weight perceptron inside one map. Its weights are ceiling heights, and 156 dolls raise and lower them
        from an aimbot's labels. Python bins the features and gives the labels. The film is an older run. 
          one_game.mp4 , 44 s, 19.3 MB 
       
     

     
       
         
         lobotomy.mp4 
       
       
         Lobotomy 
         One 7-pellet blast to his DOOM brain makes him a pacifist: 0 kills over 74 decisions, all exact. It is a
        pick from 3,000 random blasts. 
          lobotomy.mp4 , 29 s, 4.7 MB 
       
     

     
       
         
         full_brain.mp4 
       
       
         The big one 
         A 4-layer transformer writes UNHOLY STRONGHOLD over 10,166 tile runs and 208,598 voodoo dolls. The runs share
        a pool of games. 
          full_brain.mp4 , 28 s, 2.6 MB 
       
     

     
       
         
         fly_alive.mp4 
       
       
         A fruit-fly circuit 
         255 neurons derived from the FlyWire connectome drive the marine through four stations: eat, refuse, groom,
        take off. The dynamics are simplified and the input spikes synthetic. 169 of 169 steps exact. 
          FLY.md  ·
         fly_alive.mp4 , 71 s, 5.8 MB 
       
     

     
       
         
         onemap_shil_raw.mp4 
       
       
         A whole transformer in one map 
         Embedding, attention, MLP and logits with no Python between layers. Each dot is one of 3,548 voodoo dolls
        writing SHIL. A small model: 1 layer, d=8. 
         Time-lapse.  onemap_shil_raw.mp4 , 58 s, 6.5 MB 
       
     

     
       
         
         selfgen.mp4 
       
       
         Generation without Python 
         The winner's doll writes the next token and the level rewinds itself. Python only advances the clock and
        reads. It wrote DAN. ViZDoom draws at most 4,096 objects, so some dolls are not shown
        ( engine limit ). 
          selfgen.mp4 , 56 s, 6.9 MB 
       
     

     
       
         
         showreel.mp4 
       
       
         The showreel 
         All of it in one minute: voodoo dolls on lava, attention gates, the DOOM brain naming a level, the marine
        playing it, learning, lobotomy, a transformer in one map and his brain inside the level. 
          showreel.mp4 , 56 s, 25.1 MB 
       
     

   
   Run it yourself 
   From a clone, after  pip install -e . .  demos/README.md  has times
  and sample output. 
 
    python -m demos.brainlevel : his brain is the level 
    python -m demos.aimlearn : a perceptron learns to aim 
    python -m demos.flyloop : the fruit-fly circuit 
    python -m demos.lobotomy : lesions 
 
 

 
   Build your own 
   Compile a network into a map and let its outputs open doors, flash lights or shove the marine. 
  import numpy as np
import doomformer as df

 # 2 inputs -> [a AND b, a OR b] -> 2 outputs, all integers 
net = df.MLP(
    weights=[np.array([[1, 1], [1, 1]]), np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1]])],
    biases=[np.array([-1, 0]), np.array([0, 0])],
    thresholds=[np.array([1]), np.array([1])],
    signed_input=False,
)
with df.compile(net) as brain:
    for x in ([0, 0], [1, 0], [1, 1]):
         # computed by voodoo dolls; raises df.MismatchError on any difference from net.reference 
        print(x, "->", brain(np.array(x)).tolist())
    brain.record([np.array([0, 1]), np.array([1, 1])], "dolls.gif")    # film the dolls doing it   
   The guide is  BUILD_YOUR_OWN.md ,
  and there are twelve small runnable  examples . 
 

 
   Limits 
   
     DOOM is slow. A small MLP runs about 23,000 times slower than NumPy ( Speed ). 
     Only the runs are checked. EXACT means DOOM equals the integer network. It does not say the answer is right. 
     Attention is integer attention. No model has LayerNorm. 
     The marine's policies imitate a scripted aimbot. There is no reinforcement learning. 
     Showcased seeds, lesions and names are picked ( list ).

Quick start · Walk a digit · The museum · How it works · What is checked · Films · Docs 10,000 / 10,000 1,355 0 4 MNIST test digits exact voodoo dolls in one MNIST map mismatches in 20,000 fuzzed nets other DOOM engines run the museum exactly Quick start pip install git+https://github.com/mottopanikeiku/doomformer # Python 3.11+, Linux or macOS doomformer hello # 2 s: a small MLP, every value checked doomformer draw --digit 7 # 15 s: the marine walks a 7 and the level reads it doomformer doctor checks your setup. It builds ACC, the ACS compiler, if it is missing. That needs git, cmake and a C compiler. On Fedora: sudo dnf install git cmake gcc gcc-c++ make . Tip No install needed for the Colab notebook . Draw a digit in your browser and DOOM reads it. Walk a digit, DOOM reads it The marine holds FIRE and inks the floor. Then he presses READ. 1,355 voodoo dolls in the same map run an MNIST network. The winning digit's doll crosses a line. That line lights the digit on the display. ▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄ ▄████████████████ ████▀▀ ▀████▀ ▀▀▀ ▄███▀ ████ ███ ███ ███ ████ ███▀ ████ ▀███ DOOM reads: 7 (right) -- the winner's doll lit it on the 7-segment display EXACT: all 248 values DOOM computed [...] equal the NumPy integer reference (tolerance 0) READ pass: 273 game tics = 8 s of real-time DOOM at 35 tics/s, 3 s wall [...] Python reads back 248 values and checks every one. With --digit , Python presses the keys for you. Without it, you walk and draw yourself. Full output Note EXACT means DOOM got the same numbers as the integer network. It does not mean the digit is right. run right exact first 100 MNIST test digits 99 100 1,000 sampled test digits, one map each 966 1,000 all 10,000 test digits, tile maps 9,716 (97.16 %) 10,000 The float model scores 97.58 %. The network also trained on the strokes the scripted marine walks. Details · Film The museum: rewire one connection Tip Play it without Python. Download museum.wad ( sha256 ) and the free Freedoom IWAD. Then run gzdoom -iwad freedoom2.wad -file museum.wad . Step on seven floor pads to light a digit. Press READ. 136 voodoo dolls run a tiny network and light the answer. Press MUTATE and the level rewires one connection while it runs. The same 7 now reads as 1. You can watch it happen: one doll stops at its gate. $ doomformer museum verify 7 pads abc w_7a +1 DOOM reads 7 scores [4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 3, 2, 7, 3, 4] EXACT (148 values; 744 tics; [...]) 7 after MUTATE pads abc w_7a -1 DOOM reads 1 scores [4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 3, 2, 5, 3, 4] EXACT (148 values; 744 tics; [...]) 7 after RESTORE pads abc w_7a +1 DOOM reads 7 scores [4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 3, 2, 7, 3, 4] EXACT (148 values; 744 tics; [...]) A self-test version runs exactly in GZDoom, LZDoom, UZDoom and ZDoom 2.8.1. Details How it works Every part of a network becomes a part of the map: in a neural network in the DOOM map a value of 5 5 voodoo dolls a weight a line on the floor; each doll that crosses it adds the weight a sum a sector's light level or floor height an activation (ReLU) a staircase of gates the dolls must climb attention dolls squeezing under ceilings that another value lowered a lesion a closed door One layer, from dolls to dolls: flowchart LR A["input value
= a crowd of dolls"] --> B["weight lines
each crossing adds w"] B --> C["the sum
= a light level or height"] C --> D["staircase of gates
= the activation"] D --> E["next layer's dolls"] Loading A matrix multiply. Each doll is one unit of a value. Each lava line it crosses adds a weight. Attention. Dolls squeeze under ceiling gates. Counting who gets through is a multiply. The engine has sharp edges, and the compiler works around them: A floor mover ignores a second request while it is still moving. A teleport cancels lines a doll crossed earlier in the same tic. Things far from a BSP node can land in the wrong room, so every map fits in 32,000 units. doomformer facts checks these in about 10 s. Engine facts · Engine features it needs · Other ports Computers in DOOM maps are not new. counter.wad counts with voodoo dolls, conway.wad runs Game of Life, and Danny Spencer's calculator adds numbers. New here: a compiler for neural networks, and an exact check on every value. Related work What is checked Every run compares each value the map exposes with NumPy. That proves the inputs that ran, nothing more. So the repo also attacks its own check: attack result Tamper with one weight line the check fails on exactly the inputs that cross it Fuzz 20,000 random nets at the range limits 0 mismatches; CI fuzzes a fresh seed on every push Mutate one line of a map, 1,004 times 297 caught; no survivor is proven harmless Extract the weights back out of the map, without DOOM equal to the source net Guard every readout page with a poison value a page that never runs cannot pass old values The MNIST map exposes 248 values. It does not expose its 903 staircase counts and 1,351 gate comparisons. Those are checked only through the sums they feed. Fuzzing and tests found four bugs in the compiler. All are fixed. Verification Who computes what run Python voodoo dolls mnist , df.compile writes the inputs, waits, reads every sum, activation, comparison and the choice demo , ask (tile maps) writes tokens, copies values between maps, samples letters every sum and activation draw , --loop , the marine's brain, the fly only advances the clock and reads everything, including the choice machine loads the program, then advances the clock and reads program counter and registers museum , played in GZDoom nothing every sum, comparison and the choice ACS level scripts move gates, rewind the dolls, sense the world and copy results out. Two do more. df.Agent takes an argmax in ACS. --opt 3 copies each layer's values into the next layer with a script. Per demo The maps need ZDoom (UDMF and ACS). This repo runs ViZDoom 1.3.2 with Freedoom assets. Commands Command What DOOM does Time Skill level doomformer hello a small MLP, 5 random inputs 2 s I'm too young to die doomformer draw --digit 7 the marine walks a 7, the level reads it 15 s Hey, not too rough doomformer museum build a playable map that reads a digit 1 s Hey, not too rough doomformer mnist reads 4 test digits, or your own image 1.5 to 3 min Hurt me plenty doomformer demo a transformer writes a level name 15 to 60 s Hurt me plenty doomformer machine subleq all a tiny computer runs three programs about 5 min Ultra-Violence doomformer learn digits --classes 4 --steps 300 a blank brain learns digits inside the map about 5 min Ultra-Violence doomformer ask "what does iddqd do" answers from 189 DOOM facts about 11 min Ultra-Violence doomformer demo --nightmare the 2-layer model, 106 tile maps 3.5 to 7 min Nightmare! Times are from a 16-core arm64 Linux machine. Every command Some outputs are picked. DEMON CANYON, the name --nightmare writes, is one hand-picked sample. ask gets 94.7 % of its training questions right, and 35.4 % of new wordings. Bigger experiments His brain is the level. The level senses the nearest demon. 1,345 voodoo dolls of the marine run his brain and pick an action. The level turns him and fires. Python only steps the clock and reads. 50 of 50 decisions are exact. Film · Code Warning He is not playable. One decision takes 22 s of game time, and the demons are frozen while he thinks. With the demons awake ( --live ), he dies in 5.5 s without a kill. Live demons run it from a clone what you see python -m demos.brainlevel his brain is the level python -m demos.brainlevel --live the same brain against awake demons python -m demos.brainlevel --lesion-when near the level closes neuron doors when a demon gets close python -m demos.aimlearn a perceptron learns to aim inside one game python -m demos.flyloop a fruit-fly circuit drives the marine python -m demos.lobotomy lesions that turn him into a pacifist A transformer names a level. It writes DEMON CANYON. A Python generator builds the level. One hand-picked sample. A marine plays the level it named. Doors, two kills, exit. 102 decisions, all exact. Python gives the compass. Seed 118 of 120, picked. A perceptron learns inside one game. Its 38 weights are ceiling heights. Dolls raise and lower them. Python gives the labels. Lesions. A shotgun blast closes 7 neurons. The marine stops firing. Picked from 3,000 random blasts. A fruit-fly circuit. 255 neurons from the FlyWire connectome drive the marine. Simplified dynamics. A transformer in one map. No Python between layers. 3,548 dolls write SHIL. A small model. Generation without Python. The winner's doll writes the next letter. The level rewinds itself. One model, one prompt. A 4-layer transformer. It writes UNHOLY STRONGHOLD over 10,166 tile runs. Runs share a pool of games. All demos, numbers and picked seeds Build your own Compile a network into a map. Let its outputs open doors, flash lights or shove the marine. This runs as pasted: import numpy as np import doomformer as df # 2 inputs -> [a AND b, a OR b] -> 2 outputs, all integers net = df .
