# Lasm

**Lean 4 for the JavaScript and WebAssembly world.** Lasm compiles ordinary Lean 4
programs ahead of time to WebAssembly. One Lean code base can become a Node server,
a serverless or edge function, a WASI/Fastly module or a browser app. Because it is
Lean, you can prove properties of the code you deploy. The flagship example,
[Conduit](#flagship-example-conduit-with-117-proved-theorems), is the RealWorld app
with 117 proved theorems. Lasm ships on npm and brings
Lean, Lake and its build tools with it; you only need Node (or Bun or Deno).

```sh
npm create @lasm@latest my-app -- --template hono    # then: cd my-app && npm install && npm run dev
```

AI agents: this README is complete on its own. [`llms.txt`](llms.txt) is the short
index, and [docs/AI.md](docs/AI.md) lists the rules that save you from wrong turns.

If Lasm is useful to you, I'd appreciate your [sponsorship](https://github.com/sponsors/lastmjs) ([more below](#support-lasm)).

## Quick facts

| Fact | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Current version | `@lasm/cli` 0.3.5 ([release notes](docs/release/)); `npm view @lasm/cli version` |
| Install | `npm install -D @lasm/cli` (bin: `lasm`), or no install: `npx @lasm/cli …`; new project: `npm create @lasm@latest` |
| Lean | exactly **4.35.0** (`lean-toolchain`: `leanprover/lean4:v4.35.0`); Lasm installs it, and you need no elan to build |
| Develop on | Linux x64/arm64 (glibc 2.34+), macOS x64/arm64, Windows x64 |
| Compiler runs on | Node ≥ 24 (tested 24.0.0, 24.22.1, 26.12.1); Bun 1.4.4 and Deno 2.9.6 (tested, as the only runtime) |
| Output | `dist/` with `program.wasm` + a JS launcher (Node); or a platform package (`--target …`) |
| Node apps run on | Node ≥ 24, Linux x64/arm64 (glibc 2.28+ or musl) from any build machine, plus the build machine's own OS; ≥ 512 MB memory |
| JS/npm interop | `import Lasm.JS`; one `@[js "pkg" "export"]` line per function you call; no premade bindings ([guide](docs/JS_BINDINGS.md)) |
| Frameworks in Lean | `Lasm.Fetch` (HTTP, every server target), `Lasm.UI` (browser, Elm architecture, proved diff), `Lasm.RPC` (typed client/server API), `Lasm.Web` (DOM and web APIs), `Lasm.KV` |
| Not available at run time | elaboration, `#eval`-style evaluation, loading `.olean`, Lean's kernel ([exact list](#lean-support-and-restrictions)); all of these work at build time |
| License | MIT (Lasm); templates, examples and README code samples also MIT-0 |
| Repository / issues | https://github.com/Millillion/lasm · [report a bug](https://github.com/Millillion/lasm/issues/new?template=bug.yml) (include `npx lasm --version`) |

## Platforms

Every row is tested in CI with the platform's own local runtime, image or emulator.
By project policy CI never deploys to a real cloud account
([how each is tested](#supported-platforms)).

| Deploy to | `lasm build Main.lean --target …` | Output | Since |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Node server or program (any host, Docker/Kubernetes, Cloud Run, Fly.io, Railway, Render, Heroku, DigitalOcean) | `node` (default) | `dist/` → `node dist/main.mjs` | 0.1.0 |
| AWS Lambda (.zip, `nodejs24.x`) | `lambda` | `lambda.zip` | 0.1.0 |
| AWS Lambda (container image) | `lasm init … --deploy lambda` | `Dockerfile.lambda` | 0.1.0 |
| Lambda@Edge | `lambda-edge` | `lambda-edge.zip` | 0.1.0 |
| Vercel Functions | `vercel` | `.vercel/output` | 0.1.0 |
| Netlify Functions | `netlify` | `netlify/functions/lasm` | 0.1.0 |
| Azure Functions | `azure` | `azure-functions/` | 0.1.0 |
| Google Cloud Functions (gen2) | `gcf` | `gcf/` | 0.1.0 |
| Cloudflare Workers | `workers` | `workers/` | 0.2.0 |
| Vercel Edge | `vercel-edge` | `api/lasm.mjs`, `api/_lasm/` | 0.2.0 |
| Netlify Edge | `netlify-edge` | `netlify/edge-functions/lasm.mjs` | 0.2.0 |
| Deno Deploy | `deno-deploy` | `deno/main.mjs` | 0.2.0 |
| Supabase Edge Functions | `supabase-edge` | `supabase/functions/<name>/` | 0.2.0 |
| Bun (≥ 1.3.14) / Deno (2.x) | `bun` / `deno` | `bun/main.mjs` / `deno/main.mjs` | 0.2.0 |
| Fastly Compute | `fastly` | `bin/main.wasm`, `pkg/<name>.tar.gz` | 0.3.0 |
| WASI (wasmtime, wasmer, `node:wasi`) | `wasi` | `wasi/main.wasm` | 0.3.0 |
| wasi-http (`wasmtime serve`, Spin) | `wasi-http` | `wasi-http/main.wasm` | 0.3.0 |
| Browsers (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari) | `browser` (or the Vite plugin `@lasm/cli/vite`) | `dist/` static site | 0.3.0 |

Node builds have Lean's full runtime (threads, files, processes, sockets). The
edge, Bun/Deno, WASI and browser builds run Lean single-threaded, without sockets
or processes (and without files, except on WASI); the rest of Lean works.

## Start here

| I want to build… | Run | Then look at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A command-line program | `npm create @lasm@latest my-tool` | [examples/hello](examples/hello), [examples/wasi-cli](examples/wasi-cli) |
| A REST API on Node with an npm framework | `npm create @lasm@latest my-api -- --template hono` (or `express`, `fastify`) | [examples/js-crud](examples/js-crud) (Postgres + JWT, Express and Hono) |
| A server in pure Lean (no npm) | `npm create @lasm@latest my-api -- --template fetch` (any target) or `--template std-http` (Node, also native Lean) | [examples/fetch](examples/fetch); the `std-http` template |
| A serverless function (Lambda, Vercel, Netlify, Azure, GCF) | `npm create @lasm@latest my-fn -- --template hono --deploy lambda-zip` (or `vercel`, `netlify`, `azure`, `gcf`, `lambda-edge`) | [docs/deploy](docs/deploy/README.md) |
| An edge function (Workers, Vercel/Netlify Edge, Deno Deploy, Supabase) | `npm create @lasm@latest my-edge -- --template hono --deploy workers` (or `fetch`) | [examples/edge-pure](examples/edge-pure), [docs/EDGE.md](docs/EDGE.md) |
| A Fastly, WASI or Spin service | `npm create @lasm@latest my-svc -- --template fetch --deploy fastly` (or `wasi-http`, `spin`, `wasi`) | [examples/fetch](examples/fetch), [docs/WASI.md](docs/WASI.md) |
| A browser app | `npm create @lasm@latest my-web -- --template web` | [examples/ui](examples/ui) (counter, TodoMVC with proofs, feature demo, benchmark) |
| A complete real-world app (API, browser frontend, SQL, auth) with proofs, on Node, Workers or Bun | `cd examples/conduit && npm install && npm run build && npm start` | [examples/conduit](examples/conduit), the flagship (below) |
| A full-stack app with a verified API | `npm create @lasm@latest my-app -- --template fullstack` | [templates/fullstack](templates/fullstack) |
| To call npm packages or `fetch` from Lean | add `import Lasm.JS` and one `@[js]` line per function | [examples/js-fetch](examples/js-fetch), [JS bindings](#calling-javascript-and-npm-from-lean) |
| To run on Bun or Deno | `bun create @lasm my-app --template hono` / `deno run -A npm:@lasm/create my-app --template hono` | [docs/BUN_DENO.md](docs/BUN_DENO.md) |

Every example has a README with a one-command run; [examples/README.md](examples/README.md)
lists them all.

## Flagship example: Conduit, with 117 proved theorems

[examples/conduit](examples/conduit) is [Conduit](https://github.com/gothinkster/realworld),
the RealWorld app (a Medium clone), written entirely in Lean: the REST API, the
server-rendered browser app and the proofs.

- **117 theorems** about the code that actually runs, checked with no `sorry` and
  only Lean's standard axioms (`npm run proofs`; [PROOFS.md](examples/conduit/PROOFS.md)
  lists each one in plain English). They cover authorization (only authors change
  their articles and comments), follows and favorites, slugs that never collide,
  pagination that never skips or repeats, validation shared by client and server
  (the app never sends what the server would reject), JSON round trips and
  Markdown link safety. The endpoints are written against a `Store` of functions,
  and the proofs run that same code on a model of the tables.
- **What is trusted, not proved:** that each SQL statement does what its model
  says, the JSON text layer, concurrency between requests, and Lean, Lasm and the
  JavaScript runtime. Conformance to the whole RealWorld spec is tested, not
  proved.
- **API:** the official RealWorld API suite passes unmodified (13 of 13 files,
  154 requests) on Node (`node:sqlite`), Cloudflare Workers (D1) and Bun
  (`bun:sqlite`). Each target has one hand-written `@[js]` binding module.
- **Frontend:** `Lasm.UI` on RealWorld's official templates, with server-side
  rendering, hydration and Markdown parsed in Lean. The official Playwright
  end-to-end suite passes with no retries on Node with Chromium, Firefox and
  WebKit, and on Workers and Bun with Chromium.

All of this runs in CI ([conduit.yml](.github/workflows/conduit.yml), run 40615274657,
with `@lasm/cli` 0.3.4).

```sh
cd examples/conduit
npm install                                   # @lasm/cli, Hurl and Playwright (the official suites' runners)
npm run build && npm start                    # http://localhost:3000: the app and its API on Node
npm run proofs                                # check all 117 theorems
npm test                                      # the official API suite (also test:workers, test:bun)
npx playwright install chromium && npm run test:e2e   # the official end-to-end suite
npm run build:workers && npx wrangler dev     # Cloudflare Workers with local D1
npm run build:bun && npm run start:bun        # Bun with bun:sqlite
```

## 60-second start

A single file needs no project. Save this complete program as `Main.lean`:

```lean
def main : IO Unit := do
  IO.println s!"Hello from Lean! 2 + 3 = {2 + 3}"
```

```sh
npx @lasm/cli Main.lean          # builds and runs: Hello from Lean! 2 + 3 = 5
npx @lasm/cli build Main.lean    # writes dist/; run it with: node dist/main.mjs
```

The first build on a new machine fetches Lean and the build tools once (about
250–275 MB; 19 s for that first build on the Linux CI runner). Later dev builds of a
one-line change take about 1–2 s.

## Recipes

Each recipe is complete: create, develop, build, deploy. Lasm never installs or
starts a platform's own CLI (`wrangler`, `vercel`, `fastly`, …); you run those.
`npm run dev` is `lasm dev`: it rebuilds about 2 s after each save and restarts
the server, and keeps the last good build running when there is a type error.

**Node server (Hono; also `express`, `fastify`, `std-http`, `fetch`).**

```sh
npm create @lasm@latest my-api -- --template hono
cd my-api && npm install
npm run dev                                   # http://localhost:3000/hello/Ada
npm run build && npm start                    # dist/ needs only Node 24+
docker build -t my-api . && docker run -p 8080:8080 my-api   # the generated Dockerfile
```

**AWS Lambda / Vercel / Netlify / Azure / Google Cloud Functions.**

```sh
npm create @lasm@latest my-fn -- --template hono --deploy lambda-zip   # or vercel, netlify, azure, gcf, lambda-edge
cd my-fn && npm install
npm run build:lambda                          # dist/ and lambda.zip (handler lasm-lambda.handler)
# deploy lambda.zip with the AWS console, aws CLI or SAM; recipes: docs/deploy/lambda.md
```

**Cloudflare Workers (and Vercel Edge, Netlify Edge, Deno Deploy, Supabase).**

```sh
npm create @lasm@latest my-edge -- --template hono --deploy workers
cd my-edge && npm install
npm run build:workers                         # workers/ (wrangler.toml came from lasm init)
npx wrangler dev                              # local workerd; npx wrangler deploy to publish
```

**Fastly Compute, WASI, Spin.**

```sh
npm create @lasm@latest my-svc -- --template fetch --deploy fastly --deploy spin
cd my-svc && npm install
npm run build:fastly && fastly compute serve  # Viceroy on http://127.0.0.1:7676
npm run build:wasi-http && spin up            # or: wasmtime serve wasi-http/main.wasm
```

**Browser app.**

```sh
npm create @lasm@latest my-web -- --template web
cd my-web && npm install
npm run dev                                   # http://127.0.0.1:5173, live reload
npm run build                                 # dist/: a static site for any host or CDN
```

**Full stack (server + browser + verified API).**

```sh
npm create @lasm@latest my-app -- --template fullstack
cd my-app && npm install
npm run dev                                   # one URL: http://127.0.0.1:3000
npm run build && npm start                    # Node; also build:workers, build:bun, build:deno
```

**Editor.** Run `npx lasm editor` once per project; `lasm init`, `lasm dev` and
`lasm build` also do it. The Lean editor (VS Code's Lean 4 extension) then resolves
`import Lasm.*` ([details](docs/GETTING_STARTED.md#editor)).

## The whole stack in Lean, verified

The `fullstack` template is one Lean project with a server (`Lasm.Fetch`), a
browser app (`Lasm.UI`) and the API between them (`Lasm.RPC`). The rule a request
must satisfy is written and proved once, in `Shared.lean`, which both sides import
([templates/fullstack](templates/fullstack)):

```lean
-- Shared.lean
@[irreducible] def checkTitle (title : String) : Except String Unit :=
  let n := (clean title).length
  if n = 0 then .error "Write something first."
  else if n > maxTitle then .error s!"Keep it under {maxTitle} characters."
  else .ok ()

/-- Proved once, holds in the browser and on the server. -/
theorem checkTitle_ok {title : String} (h : checkTitle title = .ok ()) :
    0 < (clean title).length ∧ (clean title).length ≤ maxTitle := by
  unfold checkTitle at h
  by_cases h0 : (clean title).length = 0
  · simp [h0] at h
  · by_cases h1 : (clean title).length > maxTitle
    · simp [h0, h1] at h
    · omega

def addTodo : Endpoint NewTodo Todo := { name := "addTodo", validate := fun r => checkTitle r.title }
```

```lean
-- Server.lean: storing a todo demands the proof that its title passed the check,
-- and `addTodo.serve` hands the handler that proof (`ok`) after re-validating.
def Store.add (s : Store) (title : String) (_ : checkTitle title = .ok ()) : Store × Todo :=
  let t := { id := s.next, title := clean title, done := false }
  ({ todos := s.todos.push t, next := s.next + 1 }, t)

  addTodo.serve fun req ok => do
    let (s, t) := (← load kv).add req.title ok
    save kv s
    return .ok t
```

```lean
-- Client.lean: a theorem about the browser app: it never sends an invalid title.
theorem add_invalid (m : Model) (e : String) (h : checkTitle m.draft = .error e) :
    (update .add m).2.effects = [.msg (.added (.error (.invalid e)))] :=
  addTodo.call_invalid { title := m.draft } Msg.added "" e h
```

**Where proofs live and how they are checked.**

| Proof | Where | Checked by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Your theorems (like `checkTitle_ok`, `add_invalid`) | your `.lean` files | every `lasm build`/`lasm dev` (Lean elaborates them; a broken proof is a build error); pure modules also with `lake build` |
| `Lasm.RPC`: the handler only runs on requests that pass `validate` (`Endpoint.decodeRequest_valid`); the client never sends one that fails it (`Endpoint.call_invalid`) | [library/Lasm/RPC](library/Lasm/RPC) | compiled into Lasm's library on every build |
| `Lasm.UI`: the DOM diff is correct against a DOM model, keyed moves included (`diff_correct`, `mount_correct`, `session_correct`) | [library/Lasm/UI/Proofs](library/Lasm/UI/Proofs) (about 1,260 lines, no `sorry`, standard axioms only) | `node scripts/ui/lean-tests.mjs` in a checkout (CI: `ui.yml`) |
| Conduit: 117 theorems about authorization, follows, favorites, slugs, pagination, shared validation, JSON round trips and Markdown link safety | [examples/conduit/Proofs](examples/conduit/Proofs), listed in [PROOFS.md](examples/conduit/PROOFS.md) | `npm run proofs` in `examples/conduit` (no `sorry`, standard axioms only; CI `conduit.yml`) |
| TodoMVC: every reachable model is valid | [examples/ui/todomvc/Todo.lean](examples/ui/todomvc/Todo.lean) | `lasm build`; CI `ui.yml` |

Not proved, tested in CI instead: the JSON/HTTP transport between client and
server, the JavaScript that applies patches to the real DOM, the Lasm compiler and
runtime, and the browsers. Lean's own compiler is trusted, as in any Lean program
([UI.md](docs/UI.md#what-is-proved), [RPC.md](docs/RPC.md#what-is-proved)).

## Calling JavaScript and npm from Lean

Declare each JavaScript function you call with one line; the Lean type says how
values convert. A complete program (Node's global `fetch`):

```lean
import Lasm.JS
open Lasm.JS

/-- `await fetch(url, init)` (Node's global fetch) -/
@[js "globalThis" "fetch"] opaque fetch : String → Data → IO Value

def main : IO Unit := do
  let response ← fetch "https://example.com" (obj [])
  IO.println s!"{← response.get "status" Nat}: {(← response.callMethodAwait "text" #[] String).length} characters"
```

The rules for writing bindings:

- `@[js "module" "export"] opaque name : A → B → IO R` binds `module.export`. The
  module is an npm package (`"marked"`), a Node built-in (`"node:fs"`), or
  `"globalThis"` for globals. `"new Hono"` calls a constructor, and `""` is the
  module's own value.
- End the type in `IO R` for a value returned at once and in `Async R` for a
  promise. An `Async` binding is awaited without holding a Lean thread.
- Use `String`, `Nat`, `Int`, `Float`, `Bool`, `ByteArray`, `Array`, `List`, `Option`,
  tuples, `Data` (any JS data) or `Value` (a JS object reference: `get`, `callMethod`, `callMethodAwait`).
  Your own structures convert with `deriving ToJS, FromJS`.
- `Function.ofFn` / `Function.ofFnReply` turn Lean functions into JS callbacks.
  Framework handlers use them (see the `hono`, `express` and `fastify` templates).
- `npm install` the package next to the lakefile. `lasm build` checks every binding
  against the installed package (`Lasm.JS binding check failed: … export "x" is
  missing`) and copies production dependencies into `dist/node_modules`.
- Each call crosses from a Lean thread to Node's main thread (about 24 µs), so
  prefer one coarse call over many small ones.

Full guide, with Express, Hono, `pg`, `jose` and `fetch` examples and an agent
checklist: [docs/JS_BINDINGS.md](docs/JS_BINDINGS.md).

## Measured numbers

All numbers are from CI on a free GitHub runner (4-CPU AMD EPYC, Linux x64),
candidate 0.1.0-experimental.40494203854 (2026-10-27) unless another run is named.
Full tables, method and caveats: [BENCHMARKS.md](docs/BENCHMARKS.md).

| What | Number |
| --- | --- |
| Node: Hono + Lean handler, cold start to first HTTP response | 159 ms (plain Node `http`: 4.1× faster) |
| Node: Hono + Lean handler, throughput / p99 latency | 24,911 req/s / 4.2 ms (plain Node `http`: 103,134 req/s, so 0.24×) |
| Node: Express + Lean handler, throughput | 18,678 req/s |
| Node: Hono app `program.wasm` (brotli) / `dist/` | 166 KiB / 8.5 MiB plus 1.4 MiB `node_modules` |
| Node: memory, Hono app idle / under load | 148 MiB / 329 MiB RSS |
| Lean → JS call round trip (p50) | 24 µs |
| Cloudflare Workers: Hono app bundle | 1.40 MiB, 245 KiB gzip (limit 64 MiB; workers run 40128600109) |
| Browser: counter app total transfer / first frame (Chromium) | 152 KiB brotli / 30 ms (browser run 40288509500) |
| Browser: js-framework-benchmark vs hand-written JS | within 1.7× on every operation, most within 1.2× (browser run 40302274897) |
| WASI: `Lasm.Fetch` module / per request on Fastly's Viceroy | 0.90 MiB / 1.17 ms with a fresh instance per request (wasi run 40293231963) |
| Build: clean Hono build / dev rebuild after a one-line change | 4.7 s / 2.0 s |
| `npm install @lasm/cli`: download / installed; tool cache after the first build | 71 MiB / 403 MiB; 2.5 GB |

Lean on Node pays for WebAssembly and its threads. A cold start is CPU-bound, so it
grows on small serverless CPU shares, and every JavaScript call crosses threads.
Pure-Lean `Std.Http` on Node is slow (1,290 req/s), so use Hono, Express, Fastify
or `Lasm.Fetch` for production HTTP. Arithmetic on numbers with thousands of digits
is slower than native Lean (no GMP).

## Known limitations

- **Ahead of time only.** A deployed program cannot elaborate, evaluate or compile
  Lean, load module data or plugins, or use Lean's C++ compiler/kernel at run time
  ([exact list](#lean-support-and-restrictions)). Proofs, tactics, macros and
  `#eval` run while compiling, as usual.
- **Lean 4.35.0 exactly.** Other `lean-toolchain` versions are rejected with a
  message.
- **Node:** give an app at least 512 MB; it reserves about 22 GB of virtual address
  space. Prebuilt native libraries (`-l`, shared libraries) cannot be linked; a
  package's bundled C source is compiled for you.
- **Edge, Bun/Deno, browser, WASI:** single-threaded Lean; no sockets, processes or
  signals; no files except on WASI. In the browser, blocking waits stop the app
  unless it is built with `--suspend jspi` for a browser with JSPI; use `Async`.
- **No premade bindings** for npm packages; `Lasm.Web` covers the core web platform.
- **Editor:** `Lasm.*` imports resolve in the editor after `npx lasm editor` (above).
- **Platforms:** no Windows ARM64 and no Alpine/musl build machines (built apps run
  on Alpine). Hosted platforms are tested with their local tools, never with a real
  account.

# Reference

Everything below is the precise contract: every command and option, supported
machines and platforms, and exactly what a deployed Lean program cannot do.

## CLI reference

Install in a project with `npm install -D @lasm/cli` (the bin is `lasm`), or run
without installing: `npx @lasm/cli Main.lean`. `npm create @lasm` runs `lasm init`
of the same `@lasm/cli` version with the arguments unchanged. With the `Main.lean`
from the [quick start](#60-second-start):

```sh
npx lasm Main.lean                          # build (dev profile) and run: Hello from Lean! 2 + 3 = 5
npx lasm build Main.lean                    # write dist/ (release profile)
npx lasm --version                          # version, Lean, runtime and platform (for bug reports)
node dist/main.mjs                          # run the deployment: only Node is needed
npx lasm build Main.lean --target lambda    # dist/ and an AWS Lambda zip
```

| Command or option | Example | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Run (default) | `npx lasm Main.lean` | Build (dev profile) and run Lean `main`. `npm run dev` in a `plain` project runs this. |
| Explicit run | `npx lasm run Main.lean` | Same as the default command. |
| Run a release build | `npx lasm Main.lean --release` | Build and run exactly what `lasm build` deploys. |
| Program arguments | `npx lasm Main.lean -- hello "two words"` | Pass arguments to `main (args : List String)`. |

`--rebuild` and `--verbose` work with run and build. `--output` and `--target` are
build-only; arguments after `--` are run-only. The application's exit status is
preserved. `npx lasm --version` (`-v`) prints the version, Lean release, JavaScript
runtime and platform (include it in bug reports). There is no install, clean or
uninstall subcommand.

**Build profiles.** Both link the same program with the same libraries and are
deterministic. **release** (`lasm build`, `lasm Main.lean --release`): the full
Binaryen size optimization; byte-reproducible; the one to deploy. **dev**
(`lasm Main.lean`, `lasm dev`, `lasm build --dev`): leaves those passes out and
compiles your modules at `-O1`; it behaves the same, builds several seconds faster,
and its `program.wasm` is about 15–20 % larger. A dev rebuild starts from the
project's previous build, so its bytes can depend on that build. `build-info.json`
records `"profile"`. `lasm package` and `lasm build --dev --target <platform>`
refuse a dev build unless you pass `--allow-dev`.

**Environment variables** (all optional):

| Variable | Example | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LASM_TOOLCHAIN_CACHE` | `LASM_TOOLCHAIN_CACHE=/data/lasm-cache npx lasm Main.lean` | Move the managed tool cache ([default locations](docs/NODE_SUPPORT.md)). |
| `LASM_BUILD_JOBS` | `LASM_BUILD_JOBS=2 npx lasm build Main.lean` | Threads for Binaryen's optimizer (default: the CPUs, at most 8). The output is the same for any value. |
| `LASM_EDITOR` | `LASM_EDITOR=0 npx lasm build Main.lean` | `0`: `lasm init`, `lasm dev` and `lasm build` leave the editor setup alone ([editor setup](docs/GETTING_STARTED.md#editor)). |
| `LASM_THREAD_POOL` (built apps; 0.3.0) | `LASM_THREAD_POOL=0 node dist/main.mjs` | Lean thread Workers started before `main` (0–64, default 1). [Measurements](docs/BENCHMARKS.md#cold-start-on-a-fraction-of-a-cpu). |
| `LASM_ARTIFACT_SOURCE` | `LASM_ARTIFACT_SOURCE=npm npx lasm Main.lean` | `auto` (default): `@lasm/…` npm tool packages when present, else HTTPS; `npm`: never download directly; `https`: ignore the npm packages. |
| `LASM_DOWNLOAD_ATTEMPTS`, `LASM_DOWNLOAD_CONNECT_MS`, `LASM_DOWNLOAD_IDLE_MS`, `LASM_DOWNLOAD_TOTAL_MS` | `LASM_DOWNLOAD_TOTAL_MS=14400000 npx lasm Main.lean` | Download retries and timeouts ([defaults and ranges](docs/INSTALLATION_HARDENING.md#transfers)). |
| `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `NO_PROXY`, `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` (Node's own) | `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy:8080 npx lasm Main.lean` | Proxies and private CAs ([corporate networks](docs/INSTALLATION_HARDENING.md#corporate-networks)). |

Other `LASM_*` variables in the source are maintainer diagnostics, not a supported
interface.

**Installation.** `npm install @lasm/cli` brings Lean and the build tools as
exact-pinned `@lasm/…` npm packages for your platform through your own registry,
proxy and cache. The Lake/`Lean`-import data and, only for Lake projects with C
code, the C tier (`@lasm/lean-c-<platform>`) are fetched with your npm on first use.
The terminal shows progress; later builds reuse verified tools and unchanged
outputs. On a new machine, without the download, a first Hono build took 25.7 s
(Linux x64), 27.8 s (Linux arm64), 44.4 s (Windows), 58.7 s (Apple Silicon) and
141.9 s (Intel Mac) on the CI runners
([build time](docs/BENCHMARKS.md#build-time-where-it-goes-and-the-two-profiles-current-source), run 40131930601).
Cache locations and recovery: [NODE_SUPPORT.md](docs/NODE_SUPPORT.md),
[INSTALLATION_HARDENING.md](docs/INSTALLATION_HARDENING.md).
**Git** is needed only for Lake projects with Git or Reservoir dependencies; Lasm
uses the `git` on your `PATH` and says how to install it when it is missing.

**Existing Lake projects** build with `npx lasm build Main.lean` from the project
directory. Pin `leanprover/lean4:v4.35.0` in `lean-toolchain`; other versions are
rejected with `Unsupported Lean toolchain … Lasm supports Lean v4.35.0`. A
[per-package compatibility list](docs/COMPATIBILITY.md) covers Batteries, Cli,
LSpec, Plausible, Aesop, Qq, leansqlite, UnicodeBasic, MD4Lean, lean-zip,
lean4-parser, lean-redis and others; packages not on it are untested.

## Lean support and restrictions

**Builds enforce ahead-of-time execution.** Ordinary functions, recursion,
closures, inductive types, pattern matching, type classes, dependent types and
compiled IO are supported. Imports, macros, elaboration, tactics, deriving, proofs
and `#eval` run **during compilation** in managed native Lean. Initializers count
as runtime dependencies: a broad `import Lean` can retain the compiler; use
`meta import Lean` when only macros or tactics need it, and narrower imports for
runtime data libraries (`import Lean` with `Lean.Json`, and `deriving ToJson,
FromJson`, build and run). Each rejection is explained: Lasm prints the chain from
your code to the compiler code and, when a broad import is the cause, the narrower
modules your code uses. Deployed programs honor `LEAN_ABORT_ON_NONLINEAR=1` as
native Lean does. Per-platform results: [language coverage](docs/LANGUAGE_COVERAGE.md).

The deployed application cannot use:

| Unavailable at runtime | Examples and exact boundary |
| --- | --- |
| Load Lean module data or locate a compiler installation | `Lean.importModules`, `Lean.withImportModules`, module-data readers/writers, `Lean.findSysroot`, `Lean.initSearchPath`; deployed `.olean`/IR loading. |
| Evaluate or compile new Lean code | `Lean.Environment.evalConst`, interpreter evaluation, a Lean REPL, runtime elaboration/compilation, evaluation of declarations loaded by name. Calling an ordinary compiled function is allowed. |
| Use Lean's compiler/kernel runtime state | Runtime elaboration, kernel proof checking, compiler environments, language-server machinery needing Lean's C++ compiler/kernel. Pure Lean data operations are allowed if their reachable dependencies pass the check. `LeanExport.parseStream` builds `Lean.Expr` values through the kernel and is rejected. |
| Load executable plugins dynamically | Lean/Wasm plugin loading, `dlopen`/`dlsym` (C code calling `dlopen` gets an implementation that always fails), runtime Lean symbol lookup. |

The build checks **reachable runtime dependencies**, including imported libraries
and indirect calls; a reachable forbidden call is rejected even if your input would
not take that branch, and dead code removed by the linker does not count. The
launcher also rejects missing, stale or incompatible capability records before
loading the application (a consistency check, not a security sandbox). There is no
large compatibility fallback.

**Lake packages.** Modules imported only for compilation (tactics, elaborators,
for example Aesop, Qq or `import Lean` for macros) do not keep Lean's compiler in
the deployment. Lasm runs a module's initializers only when the program uses
something they define or register, or when they are the program's own code doing
IO or calling C (`--verbose` shows how many were skipped). C source that a package
bundles (`extern_lib`, `moreLinkObjs`, for example leansqlite's SQLite) is compiled
with Lean's own clang, fetched once as the C tier (39–52 MB); no system C compiler
is needed (macOS needs the Xcode Command Line Tools SDK for C library headers).
Prebuilt native libraries (shared libraries, `-l` options: libcurl, OpenSSL,
libpq, BLAS) cannot be linked; the build names the library and the package.

**Not release guarantees.** Console output, arguments, exit codes, local Lake
imports and selected language/filesystem fixtures have native-versus-Node tests,
and before 0.1.0 Lean's runtime-capable upstream suite and 19 ecosystem projects
ran on all five platforms with zero regressions against the previous accepted
candidate ([0.1.0 gate](docs/release/0.1.0-gate.md)). Complete `IO.FS`, concurrency,
subprocess/signal/terminal parity, every third-party library and the full upstream
suite are not guaranteed ([IO gaps](IO_LIMITATIONS.md)). **Big numbers** (`Nat`/`Int`
beyond 63 bits) use Lean's own arbitrary-precision code instead of GNU MP, so apps
contain no LGPL code; results equal native Lean's, but at 10,000 digits
multiplication is about 5× and `Nat.gcd` about 60× slower than with GMP in Wasm
([numbers](docs/BENCHMARKS.md#big-numbers-without-gmp)). **Lake dependencies** use
your system Git ([system Git](docs/MANAGED_GIT.md)).

## Releases and provenance

0.1.0 was the first npm release ([notes](docs/release/0.1.0-notes.md)); 0.2.0 adds
edge targets and Bun/Deno ([notes](docs/release/0.2.0-notes.md)); 0.3.0 adds the
browser, `Lasm.UI`, full-stack apps, WASI/Fastly and the editor support
([notes](docs/release/0.3.0-notes.md)); 0.3.1 puts the starter code under MIT-0 and
adds bug-report pointers ([notes](docs/release/0.3.1-notes.md)); 0.3.2 fixes
`Std.Internal.UV` sockets, timers and signals ([notes](docs/release/0.3.2-notes.md)); 0.3.3 was never
published, and its changes shipped in 0.3.4 ([notes](docs/release/0.3.4-notes.md)); 0.3.5 updates the README and the Conduit example ([notes](docs/release/0.3.5-notes.md)). Lasm's npm
packages (`@lasm/cli`, `@lasm/create` and the `@lasm/…` tool packages) are
published only by the [`release.yml`](.github/workflows/release.yml) workflow,
through npm trusted publishing with provenance: no npm tokens exist. A release is a
pull request that bumps the `package.json` version and is published only after the
`release-checks` status (five-platform candidate checks; edge, Bun/Deno, browser,
Lasm.UI, WASI/Fastly, fullstack, unit and dev-loop checks; and an npm rehearsal of
the exact packages) passed for the released
commit. Found a bug? `npx lasm --version` gives the version line the
[bug report form](https://github.com/Millillion/lasm/issues/new?template=bug.yml) asks for. `npm view @lasm/cli@<version>` shows the provenance, and `npm audit
signatures` in a project verifies it. Details: [RELEASING.md](docs/RELEASING.md).

  Lean 4 for the JavaScript and WebAssembly world.  Lasm compiles ordinary Lean 4
programs ahead of time to WebAssembly. One Lean code base can become a Node server,
a serverless or edge function, a WASI/Fastly module or a browser app. Because it is
Lean, you can prove properties of the code you deploy. The flagship example,
 Conduit , is the RealWorld app
with 117 proved theorems. Lasm ships on npm and brings
Lean, Lake and its build tools with it; you only need Node (or Bun or Deno). 
  npm create @lasm@latest my-app -- --template hono      #  then: cd my-app && npm install && npm run dev   
 AI agents: this README is complete on its own.   llms.txt   is the short
index, and  docs/AI.md  lists the rules that save you from wrong turns. 
 If Lasm is useful to you, I'd appreciate your  sponsorship  ( more below ).

 Node builds have Lean's full runtime (threads, files, processes, sockets). The
edge, Bun/Deno, WASI and browser builds run Lean single-threaded, without sockets
or processes (and without files, except on WASI); the rest of Lean works. 
  Start here

 Then look at

  npm create @lasm@latest my-tool

 Every example has a README with a one-command run;  examples/README.md 
lists them all. 
  Flagship example: Conduit, with 117 proved theorems     
  examples/conduit  is  Conduit ,
the RealWorld app (a Medium clone), written entirely in Lean: the REST API, the
server-rendered browser app and the proofs. 
 
  117 theorems  about the code that actually runs, checked with no  sorry  and
only Lean's standard axioms ( npm run proofs ;  PROOFS.md 
lists each one in plain English). They cover authorization (only authors change
their articles and comments), follows and favorites, slugs that never collide,
pagination that never skips or repeats, validation shared by client and server
(the app never sends what the server would reject), JSON round trips and
Markdown link safety. The endpoints are written against a  Store  of functions,
and the proofs run that same code on a model of the tables. 
  What is trusted, not proved:  that each SQL statement does what its model
says, the JSON text layer, concurrency between requests, and Lean, Lasm and the
JavaScript runtime. Conformance to the whole RealWorld spec is tested, not
proved. 
  API:  the official RealWorld API suite passes unmodified (13 of 13 files,
154 requests) on Node ( node:sqlite ), Cloudflare Workers (D1) and Bun
( bun:sqlite ). Each target has one hand-written  @[js]  binding module. 
  Frontend:   Lasm.UI  on RealWorld's official templates, with server-side
rendering, hydration and Markdown parsed in Lean. The official Playwright
end-to-end suite passes with no retries on Node with Chromium, Firefox and
WebKit, and on Workers and Bun with Chromium. 
 
 All of this runs in CI ( conduit.yml , run 40615274657,
with  @lasm/cli  0.3.4). 
   cd  examples/conduit
npm install                                     #  @lasm/cli, Hurl and Playwright (the official suites' runners) 
npm run build  &&  npm start                      #  http://localhost:3000: the app and its API on Node 
npm run proofs                                  #  check all 117 theorems 
npm  test                                         #  the official API suite (also test:workers, test:bun) 
npx playwright install chromium  &&  npm run test:e2e     #  the official end-to-end suite 
npm run build:workers  &&  npx wrangler dev       #  Cloudflare Workers with local D1 
npm run build:bun  &&  npm run start:bun          #  Bun with bun:sqlite   
  60-second start     
 A single file needs no project. Save this complete program as  Main.lean : 
   def   main  : IO Unit :=  do 
  IO.println s!  " Hello from Lean! 2 + 3 = {2 + 3} "    
  npx @lasm/cli Main.lean            #  builds and runs: Hello from Lean! 2 + 3 = 5 
npx @lasm/cli build Main.lean      #  writes dist/; run it with: node dist/main.mjs   
 The first build on a new machine fetches Lean and the build tools once (about
250–275 MB; 19 s for that first build on the Linux CI runner). Later dev builds of a
one-line change take about 1–2 s.

 Each recipe is complete: create, develop, build, deploy. Lasm never installs or
starts a platform's own CLI ( wrangler ,  vercel ,  fastly , …); you run those.

the server, and keeps the last good build running when there is a type error.

  Editor.  Run  npx lasm editor  once per project;  lasm init ,  lasm dev  and
 lasm build  also do it. The Lean editor (VS Code's Lean 4 extension) then resolves

  The whole stack in Lean, verified     
 The  fullstack  template is one Lean project with a server ( Lasm.Fetch ), a
browser app ( Lasm.UI ) and the API between them ( Lasm.RPC ). The rule a request
must satisfy is written and proved once, in  Shared.lean , which both sides import
( templates/fullstack ): 
    --  Shared.lean 
 @[irreducible]   def   checkTitle  (title : String) : Except String Unit :=
   let  n := (clean title).length
   if  n =  0   then  .error   " Write something first. "  
   else   if  n > maxTitle  then  .error s!  " Keep it under {maxTitle} characters. "  
   else  .ok ()

 /-- Proved once, holds in the browser and on the server. -/ 
 theorem   checkTitle_ok  {title : String} (h : checkTitle title = .ok ()) :
     0  < (clean title).length ∧ (clean title).length ≤ maxTitle :=  by 
  unfold checkTitle  at  h
  by_cases h0 : (clean title).length =  0 
  · simp [h0]  at  h
  · by_cases h1 : (clean title).length > maxTitle
    · simp [h0, h1]  at  h
    · omega

 def   addTodo  : Endpoint NewTodo Todo := { name :=   " addTodo "  , validate := fun r => checkTitle r.title }  
    --  Server.lean: storing a todo demands the proof that its title passed the check, 
  --  and `addTodo.serve` hands the handler that proof (`ok`) after re-validating. 
 def   Store.add  (s : Store) (title : String) (_ : checkTitle title = .ok ()) : Store × Todo :=
   let  t := { id := s.next, title := clean title, done := false }
  ({ todos := s.todos.push t, next := s.next +  1  }, t)

  addTodo.serve fun req ok =>  do 
     let  (s, t) := (← load kv).add req.title ok
    save kv s
    return .ok t  
    --  Client.lean: a theorem about the browser app: it never sends an invalid title. 
 theorem   add_invalid  (m : Model) (e : String) (h : checkTitle m.draft = .error e) :
    (update .add m). 2 .effects = [.msg (.added (.error (.invalid e)))] :=
  addTodo.call_invalid { title := m.draft } Msg.added   "  "   e h

  Calling JavaScript and npm from Lean     
 Declare each JavaScript function you call with one line; the Lean type says how
values convert. A complete program (Node's global  fetch ): 
   import  Lasm.JS
 open  Lasm.JS

 /-- `await fetch(url, init)` (Node's global fetch) -/ 
 @[js   " globalThis "     " fetch "  ]  opaque fetch : String → Data → IO Value

 def   main  : IO Unit :=  do 
   let  response ← fetch   " https://example.com "   (obj [])
  IO.println s!  " {← response.get  "  status  "  Nat}: {(← response.callMethodAwait  "  text  "  #[] String).length} characters "    
 The rules for writing bindings: 
 
  @[js "module" "export"] opaque name : A → B → IO R  binds  module.export . The
module is an npm package ( "marked" ), a Node built-in ( "node:fs" ), or
 "globalThis"  for globals.  "new Hono"  calls a constructor, and  ""  is the
module's own value. 
 End the type in  IO R  for a value returned at once and in  Async R  for a
promise. An  Async  binding is awaited without holding a Lean thread. 
 Use  String ,  Nat ,  Int ,  Float ,  Bool ,  ByteArray ,  Array ,  List ,  Option ,
tuples,  Data  (any JS data) or  Value  (a JS object reference:  get ,  callMethod ,  callMethodAwait ).
Your own structures convert with  deriving ToJS, FromJS . 
  Function.ofFn  /  Function.ofFnReply  turn Lean functions into JS callbacks.
Framework handlers use them (see the  hono ,  express  and  fastify  templates). 
  npm install  the package next to the lakefile.  lasm build  checks every binding
against the installed package ( Lasm.JS binding check failed: … export "x" is missing ) and copies production dependencies into  dist/node_modules . 
 Each call crosses from a Lean thread to Node's main thread (about 24 µs), so
prefer one coarse call over many small ones.

 Lean on Node pays for WebAssembly and its threads. A cold start is CPU-bound, so it
grows on small serverless CPU shares, and every JavaScript call crosses threads.
Pure-Lean  Std.Http  on Node is slow (1,290 req/s), so use Hono, Express, Fastify
or  Lasm.Fetch  for production HTTP. Arithmetic on numbers with thousands of digits
is slower than native Lean (no GMP). 
  Known limitations     
 
  Ahead of time only.  A deployed program cannot elaborate, evaluate or compile
Lean, load module data or plugins, or use Lean's C++ compiler/kernel at run time
( exact list ). Proofs, tactics, macros and
 #eval  run while compiling, as usual. 
  Lean 4.35.0 exactly.  Other  lean-toolchain  versions are rejected with a
message. 
  Node:  give an app at least 512 MB; it reserves about 22 GB of virtual address
space. Prebuilt native libraries ( -l , shared libraries) cannot be linked; a
package's bundled C source is compiled for you. 
  Edge, Bun/Deno, browser, WASI:  single-threaded Lean; no sockets, processes or
signals; no files except on WASI. In the browser, blocking waits stop the app
unless it is built with  --suspend jspi  for a browser with JSPI; use  Async . 
  No premade bindings  for npm packages;  Lasm.Web  covers the core web platform. 
  Editor:   Lasm.*  imports resolve in the editor after  npx lasm editor  (above). 
  Platforms:  no Windows ARM64 and no Alpine/musl build machines (built apps run
on Alpine). Hosted platforms are tested with their local tools, never with a real
account.

  Build profiles.  Both link the same program with the same libraries and are
deterministic.  release  ( lasm build ,  lasm Main.lean --release ): the full
Binaryen size optimization; byte-reproducible; the one to deploy.  dev 
( lasm Main.lean ,  lasm dev ,  lasm build --dev ): leaves those passes out and
compiles your modules at  -O1 ; it behaves the same, builds several seconds faster,
and its  program.wasm  is about 15–20 % larger. A dev rebuild starts from the
project's previous build, so its bytes can depend on that build.  build-info.json 
records  "profile" .  lasm package  and  lasm build --dev --target <platform> 
refuse a dev build unless you pass  --allow-dev .

  Lean support and restrictions     
  Builds enforce ahead-of-time execution.  Ordinary functions, recursion,
closures, inductive types, pattern matching, type classes, dependent types and
compiled IO are supported. Imports, macros, elaboration, tactics, deriving, proofs
and  #eval  run  during compilation  in managed native Lean. Initializers count
as runtime dependencies: a broad  import Lean  can retain the compiler; use
 meta import Lean  when only macros or tactics need it, and narrower imports for
runtime data libraries ( import Lean  with  Lean.Json , and  deriving ToJson, FromJson , build and run). Each rejection is explained: Lasm prints the chain from
your code to the compiler code and, when a broad import is the cause, the narrower
modules your code uses. Deployed programs honor  LEAN_ABORT_ON_NONLINEAR=1  as
native Lean does. Per-platform results:  language coverage .

 Runtime elaboration, kernel proof checking, compiler environments, language-server machinery needing Lean's C++ compiler/kernel. Pure Lean data operations are allowed if their reachable dependencies pass the check.  LeanExport.parseStream  builds  Lean.Expr  values through the kernel and is rejected.

 The build checks  reachable runtime dependencies , including imported libraries
and indirect calls; a reachable forbidden call is rejected even if your input would
not take that branch, and dead code removed by the linker does not count. The
launcher also rejects missing, stale or incompatible capability records before

      Title: How to Loop Your Transformer: Loop Scaling, Specialization, and Parallel Inference 
      Authors:  Chanakya Ekbote ,  Artidoro Pagnoni ,  Devendra Singh Sachan ,  Shruti Bhosale ,  Mike Lewis ,  Maryam Fazel-Zarandi ,  Shashank Rajput ,  Sujan Kumar Gonugondla               View a PDF of the paper titled How to Loop Your Transformer: Loop Scaling, Specialization, and Parallel Inference, by Chanakya Ekbote and 7 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Looping in transformer models reuses weights by repeatedly applying the same transformer, or parts of it, making the model deeper without increasing its parameter count. Whether looping is useful depends on which constraint dominates: model size, training compute, or autoregressive inference efficiency. We study these trade-offs jointly in dense decoder-only transformers trained from scratch, varying which parts of the model are looped, how many loops are applied, and how information is passed between loops. Our experiments span models with up to 1B parameters, trained on up to 155B tokens with up to $1.07\times10^{21}$ FLOPs and 32 loops. We find that looping the full transformer generally gives the strongest quality at a fixed parameter budget, whereas looping a middle block of layers gives a better return when training FLOPs are constrained. Adding loops is not uniformly beneficial: gains eventually saturate, reverse, or become unstable. This motivates asking whether forcing every loop to use the same weights limits the benefit of deeper looping. We address this by adding small loop-specific low-rank adapters that improve quality, with larger gains as more loops are added. Looped transformers also suffer a decoding slowdown proportional to the number of loops. Parallel Loop Transformers address this by passing hidden states between loops across adjacent token positions, allowing loop stages to run concurrently. However, in our experiments the original formulation does not consistently retain the quality gains of ordinary looping. We find that preserving the current-token embedding and separately normalizing it and the previous-token hidden state before combining them recovers strong performance across model scales and training budgets. Together, these results show that effective looping requires matching the design to the resource constraint and inference setting.

  Abstract

transformer, or parts of it, to token representations, effectively making the

depends on which constraint dominates: model size, training compute, or
autoregressive inference efficiency. We study these trade-offs jointly in dense
decoder-only transformers trained from scratch, varying which parts of the model
are looped, how many loops are applied, and how information is passed between
loops. Our experiments span models with up to  1B parameters , trained on
up to  155B tokens  using up to     1.07  ×   𝟏𝟎  𝟐𝟏    \mathbf{1.07\times 10^{21}}   
 training FLOPs , with up to    𝟑𝟐  \mathbf{32}     loops . We find that
looping the full transformer generally gives the strongest quality at a fixed
parameter budget, whereas looping a middle block of layers gives a better return
when training FLOPs are constrained. These trade-offs also depend on the number
of loops: adding loops is not uniformly beneficial, and gains eventually
saturate, reverse, or become unstable. This saturation motivates asking whether
forcing every loop to use exactly the same weights limits the benefit of deeper
looping. We address this by adding small loop-specific low-rank adapters that
improve quality, with larger gains as more loops are added. A separate practical
concern for looped transformers is the sequential dependency during
autoregressive generation, which causes a slowdown proportional to the number
of loops. Parallel Loop Transformers address this limitation by passing
information between loops across adjacent token positions via hidden states,
allowing loop stages to run concurrently during decoding. However, in our
experiments the original formulation does not consistently retain the quality
gains of ordinary looping. We find that preserving the current-token embedding
and separately normalizing it and the previous-token hidden state before
combining them recovers strong performance across model scales and training
budgets. Together, these results show that effective looping requires matching
the design to the resource constraint and inference setting.

 Looping in transformer models reuses weights by repeatedly applying the same transformer, or selected parts of it, to token representations, allowing the model to behave like a deeper network without storing a new set of parameters at every ‘depth’  ( Dehghani et al., 2018 ;  Saunshi et al., 2025 ;  Geiping et al., 2025 ) . This makes looping attractive when model size is constrained, but the additional depth is not free: every extra loop must still be executed. As a result, a design that uses parameters efficiently may not use training compute efficiently.
Prior work reflects this trade-off, showing that repeated shared computation can recover some of the benefits of additional depth, while adding independently parameterized layers can be preferable when training compute is constrained  ( Schwethelm et al., 2026 ;  Prairie et al., 2026 ) . The same weight reuse, however, raises another question as more loops are added. In ordinary looping, every loop applies the same weights, even though later loops operate on representations that have already been transformed several times. This suggests that exact weight sharing may
give diminishing returns
with deeper looping. Prior work has relaxed this constraint by giving each loop iteration a different low-rank adapter while keeping the main transformer weights shared  ( Bae et al., 2025 ) . 
 
 
 Looped transformers also suffer from a separate issue during autoregressive generation: each loop for a token still depends on the output of the previous loop, so the model must execute them one after another, increasing the sequential computation required to generate each token. Parallel Loop Transformers (PLTs) reorganize this dependency by passing hidden states from one loop to the next across adjacent token positions, allowing multiple loop stages to be evaluated in parallel during decoding  ( Wu et al., 2025 ) . This change alters the information available to each loop, and recent work reports that gains can decrease as more parallel loops are added  ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . This leaves open what information the shifted transition must preserve for parallel looping to remain effective at greater loop depth. Together, these studies show that looping is not a single design choice but a set of coupled trade-offs. Repeating more of the model can make better use of a fixed parameter budget but requires more training compute; reusing the same weights across more loops can make exact sharing increasingly restrictive; and changing the dependency between loops can parallelize sequential looping while also changing the information available to each loop. These trade-offs may also change with model scale and training budget. Despite prior work studying these choices in different settings, it remains unclear which conclusions generalize and how the choices interact. We therefore study them within a common training from-scratch setting across model scales and training budgets, and ask:

  2  Background and Methods 

 
  2.1  Different Ways to Loop a Transformer 

 
 We consider several ways to loop a transformer by varying which parts of the model are looped and the order in which the loops are applied. In  Full-Stack Looping , the output of the final transformer block is fed back to the first block, so the entire stack of transformer blocks is applied again at each loop. In  Per-Layer Looping , the output of each transformer block is fed back to the same block for all loops before moving to the next transformer block. We also consider looping only a contiguous set of transformer blocks in the middle of the model. In  Middle-Stack Looping , the output of the last block in this region is fed back to the first, so the middle blocks are looped as a group. In  Middle-Layer Looping , each transformer block in the middle region is looped before moving to the next transformer block. The transformer blocks outside this region are applied once. Finally, we vary which part of a transformer block is looped: the full block, attention only, the MLP only, or attention and the MLP independently. See   Fig. 2   and   Subsec. B.1   for details. 
 
 
 
  2.2  Loop-Specific Specialization 

 
 In standard transformer looping, every loop uses the same transformer weights. This keeps parameter storage low, but may limit what later loops can learn, since they operate on representations already transformed by earlier loops. Giving each loop a separate set of weights would remove this constraint, but would also give up much of the parameter savings from looping. We instead use Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)  ( Hu et al., 2021 )  to give each loop a small loop-specific adapter while keeping the main transformer weights shared, as defined in   Subsec. 2.2  . We refer to this as  loop-specific specialization . 
 
    
 
 
 We also evaluate alternative ways of parameterizing and combining these loop-specific low-rank adapters; see   Fig. 4   and   Subsec. B.2   for details. 
 
 
 
  2.3  Parallelizing Loops During Inference 

 
 In ordinary looping, each token is processed through each loop one after another: loop    ℓ  \ell    receives the representation of that same token produced by loop     ℓ  −  1   \ell-1   . As a result, loop    ℓ  \ell    cannot begin until loop     ℓ  −  1   \ell-1    has finished. Parallel Loop Transformers (PLTs)  ( Wu et al., 2025 )  change this dependency through  Cross-Loop Parallelism  (CLP). Instead of passing the hidden state between loops at the same token position, CLP passes the state from the previous loop at the preceding token position. As these previous-token states are already available during autoregressive decoding, all the loop computations for the current token can be evaluated simultaneously. To make this
dependency (CLP) precise, let     𝒆  n   \bm{e}_{n}    denote the embedding of token    n  n   , let     𝒃  n   (  ℓ  )    \bm{b}_{n}^{(\ell)}    and     𝒉  n   (  ℓ  )    \bm{h}_{n}^{(\ell)}    denote the input and output of loop    ℓ  \ell   , and let     ℱ  θ   \mathcal{F}_{\theta}    denote the transformer whose weights are shared across loops. 
 
    
 
 
 The original PLT combines CLP with two mechanisms that reduce KV-cache memory:  KV sharing  and  (G-SWA) .
 KV sharing  lets later loops reuse the full KV cache produced by the first
loop instead of storing a separate full cache for every loop. Each later loop
also keeps a small local sliding-window cache, and  gated sliding-window
attention  (G-SWA) combines the attention outputs from the shared and local
caches. In our experiments, we separate CLP, KV sharing, and G-SWA to study
their effects independently. See   Fig. 6   and
  Subsec. B.3   for details. 
 
 
 
 
  3  Experiments 

 
  3.1  Experimental Setup 

 
 We train models with 70M, 100M, 200M, 300M, 500M, and 1B parameters,
containing 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 16 stored transformer layers, respectively.
Training budgets range from 10 to 160 tokens per parameter (TPP). All models
use the same pretraining mixture of natural language, code, mathematical, and
scientific content, with the data sources, sampling distribution, preprocessing,
tokenizer, and training setup held fixed across architectures. We use a fixed subset of the DCLM Baseline 1.0 validation set
 ( Li et al., 2024 ) , containing approximately 41 million tokens, as our
primary measure of language-modeling quality and report bits per byte (BPB;
lower is better). To test whether the trends observed on DCLM hold across
datasets, we additionally evaluate on other language-modeling corpora and a
broader set of mathematical, code, reasoning, and question-answering
benchmarks. These results, together with the full model configurations,
training details, evaluation protocols, and task-level results, are provided
in the appendix (see   App. C  ).

required training tokens outweighs this additional cost: across model sizes
from 100M to 1B, two-loop models trained at TPP 80 reach a given BPB using
fewer training FLOPs than  Vanilla  models trained at TPP 160. This
advantage does not hold uniformly across numbers of loops: although     L  =  4   L=4   
can achieve lower absolute BPB, it provides a weaker improvement per training
FLOP (  Subsec. H.4  ). 
 
 
 
 
  4  Related Work 

 
 Prior work studies looping from several complementary angles. Scaling studies ask how much additional looping is worth under different parameter, data, and compute budgets, either through scaling laws or by comparing shared recurrence with added physical depth  ( Prairie et al., 2026 ;  Schwethelm et al., 2026 ) . Other work explores particular choices for where and how recurrence is introduced in the transformer  ( Cai et al., 2026 ;  Zeitoun et al., 2026 ) . As these studies use different looping designs and evaluate them under different resource constraints, it is difficult to separate the effect of the design from the effect of the budget. We instead vary where and how much to loop within a common dense model family and evaluate these choices under both parameter and training-compute constraints. Another line of work asks whether every loop should use exactly the same weights. Relaxed Recursive Transformers  ( Bae et al., 2025 )  give each loop a small set of additional parameters when converting a pretrained transformer into a looped model. We instead train the looped transformer and its loop-specific adapters together from scratch and test whether these adapters become more useful as the number of loops increases. Looping also raises a separate challenge during autoregressive inference. In ordinary looping, the model must finish one loop for a token before starting the next. Parallel Loop Transformers (PLTs) combat this by shifting information across adjacent token positions so that loop computations can be parallelized during decoding  ( Wu et al., 2025 ) . This change alters the information available to each loop, and recent work reports that gains can diminish as more parallel loops are added  ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . This leaves open what the shifted transition must preserve to retain quality as the number of loops increases. We find that preserving the current-token embedding and separately normalizing it and the state passed from the previous token substantially improves parallel looping at larger loop counts. Our work therefore connects three aspects of looping within a common setting: where and how much to loop, whether different loops should use exactly the same weights, and how loops can be parallelized during autoregressive inference. See   App. A   for a more detailed discussion. 
 
 
 
  5  Conclusion and Future Directions 

 
 We show that looping is a multidimensional design
problem that must jointly account for stored parameters, training FLOPs, data
efficiency, and inference efficiency. A promising future direction is to
find ways of combining PLT with speculative decoding to further reduce inference latency.
Another is to develop a theory of how normalization and current-token
embedding reinjection affect stability in both the cross-token recurrence of
PLT and the same-token recurrence of standard looping, and to identify which
regimes favor each approach.

  Appendix A  Related Work 

 
 Looped Transformers. 

 
 Looped Transformers increase effective depth by repeatedly applying shared computation  ( Dehghani et al., 2018 ) .   Saunshi et al. (2025)   show that shared looping can recover much of the benefit of unique depth on iterative reasoning problems.   Geiping et al. (2025)   instead study looping as a mechanism for scaling latent test-time computation, training a language model whose loop depth can vary at inference. More recently,   Zhu et al. (2026)   combine looped pretraining with learned depth allocation at substantially larger data scale. Relatedly, Staircase Attention  ( Ju et al., 2022 )  combines looping across sequence time and depth, with its Ladder variant repeatedly applying a shared Transformer core. Together, these works establish that repeated computation can provide useful capability and reasoning benefits. Compared with prior looping work, we provide a more systematic account of the trade-offs among parameter efficiency, training FLOPs, specialization, and the architectural requirements for efficient autoregressive inference. Our analysis shows that looping is not uniformly beneficial: the preferred design depends on which resource is constrained. 
 
 
 
 Scaling and efficiency of weight reuse. 

 
 Recent work studies looping from scaling, capacity, and efficiency perspectives.   Prairie et al. (2026)   develop a stable looped architecture by analyzing the looped residual stream as a dynamical system, and use it to derive scaling laws for loop depth and data under fixed parameter and compute budgets.   Schwethelm et al. (2026)   instead quantify the effective capacity of repeated shared computation relative to unique depth, finding that each additional loop provides only partial equivalence to an additional untied block. Other work modifies the looping architecture itself. Hyperloop combines a looped middle block with hyper-connections to improve parameter efficiency  ( Zeitoun et al., 2026 ) , while T 2 MLR introduces a temporal pathway through intermediate layers  ( Cai et al., 2026 ) . Mixture-of-Recursions uses token-level routing to allocate different loop depths across tokens  ( Bae et al., 2026 ) . Sparse looped models use expert routing to allow the same physical layers to realize different effective transformations across loop applications  ( Lee et al., 2026 ) . Unlike work that studies a single scaling relation or advocates a particular architectural modification, we hold the backbone dense and the training setup fixed while jointly varying loop placement, loop depth, loop-specific specialization, and state propagation during autoregressive decoding. We evaluate these choices under fixed parameter, training-data, and training-FLOP budgets. This design reveals trade-offs that are obscured when only one resource is considered. Our goal is therefore not to identify a universally optimal looping mechanism, but to characterize how the preferred design changes with the resource constraint. 
 
 
 
 Relaxing Exact Parameter Sharing. 

 
 Strict looping requires the same parameters to serve every depth application. Relaxed Recursive Transformers (RRTs) relax this constraint by converting a pretrained untied Transformer into a compact looped model and adding depth-specific low-rank adapters  ( Bae et al., 2025 ) . This procedure substantially improves over strict tying and can recover much of the performance lost when originally distinct layers are collapsed into a shared block. Related work introduces flexibility through different mechanisms. Hyperloop augments a looped middle block with loop-level hyper-connections, allowing the residual pathway to vary across loop applications with little additional parameter cost  ( Zeitoun et al., 2026 ) . Mixture-of-Recursions instead uses routers to assign individual tokens different loop depths, combining parameter sharing with adaptive computation  ( Bae et al., 2026 ) . Sparse looped models select different experts at different loop applications, so weight sharing need not imply that every loop realizes the same effective transformation  ( Lee et al., 2026 ) . Our setting isolates a different question. Rather than converting a pretrained untied model or introducing routing and expert-specific capacity, we train a dense looped model from initialization and add small loop-specific corrections to the shared block. We use these corrections primarily as a diagnostic: does the value of depth-specific capacity increase as the same shared transformation is applied more times? This controlled comparison distinguishes the general cost of exact sharing from the benefits of a particular architectural mechanism, while preserving a common backbone, training setup, and parameter-sharing structure. 
 
 
 
 Parallel Looping and State Propagation. 

 
 Conventional looping reduces the number of unique parameters, but places successive loop applications on the sequential path of autoregressive generation. Parallel Loop Transformers (PLTs) reorganize this dependency through Cross-Loop Parallelism (CLP): recurrent state is shifted across token positions, allowing loop stages to be pipelined during decoding. PLTs combine this schedule with shared KV caches and gated sliding-window attention to bound cache growth  ( Wu et al., 2025 ) . LoopCoder-v2 studies this design at larger scale and finds a strongly non-monotonic dependence on loop count: a second loop improves performance, whereas three or more loops regress as the benefit of further refinement is outweighed by the positional mismatch introduced by CLP  ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . Related work studies how looped dynamics can remain stable and input-dependent.   Labovich (2026)   analyze fixed-point stability in looped Transformers, showing that recall together with outer normalization can yield reachable, input-dependent, and trainable dynamics.   Kim et al. (2026)   develop source-centered state evolution, which preserves an input-conditioned anchor while allowing deviations from that anchor to drive recurrent computation. Our work addresses the interface created specifically by cross-token parallelization. Under CLP, a loop stage must combine a representation of the current token with a shifted state produced at a different token position and loop depth. We find that the main limitation of naïve PLT is this shifted re-injection transition, rather than cache sharing itself. Our controlled ablations isolate the contributions of the cross-token shift, attention and cache mechanisms, normalization, recurrent-state mixing, and access to the current-token representation. This identifies separate normalization of the current-token and shifted-state streams, together with preservation of the current-token path, as the central repair. Thus, rather than proposing normalization or input preservation as general primitives, we characterize their role in making the parallel looping interface effective.

 Why the form of looping matters. 

 
 Looping is often described simply as a way to obtain more computation from a
fixed set of parameters. This description is correct, but incomplete. In
practice, the usefulness of weight reuse depends on  which resource is
scarce . Parameters, training FLOPs, memory movement, communication, and
sequential inference time impose different constraints, and different looping
constructions trade among these resources in different ways. Consequently,
two architectures that reuse the same number of parameters can behave very
differently as computational systems. The choice of what to loop, where to
loop it, and in what order to execute the repeated computation is therefore
not merely an architectural detail; it determines what kind of resource
efficiency the model is attempting to obtain. 
 
 
 Consider first the distinction between full-stack and middle looping.
Full-Stack Looping repeatedly evaluates the entire Transformer, and therefore
uses the additional compute budget everywhere in the network. If parameter
memory is the primary constraint while additional FLOPs are comparatively
cheap, this is a natural strategy: every extra loop provides another complete
pass through attention, MLP computation, and the hierarchy of learned
representations. In such a regime, there is little reason to leave part of the
network idle simply to save computation. The situation changes when training
FLOPs themselves become the limiting resource. Repeating the complete network
may then spend substantial compute on layers for which additional evaluation
provides relatively little marginal benefit. Middle looping offers a different
trade-off: the beginning and end of the network are evaluated once, while the
additional compute is concentrated in a smaller recurrent core. Thus, even
when full-stack and middle looping are motivated by the same goal of parameter
reuse, they answer different resource-allocation questions. The former asks
how much quality can be extracted from a fixed parameter budget when more
compute is available, while the latter asks whether that additional compute
can be spent more selectively. 
 
 
 Computation order introduces a different systems consideration. Suppose the
same collection of layers is evaluated the same number of times. Stack looping
cycles through the entire collection before returning to the first layer,
whereas Per-Layer Looping repeatedly evaluates one layer before moving on to
the next. Their arithmetic FLOPs can therefore be identical, yet their
execution patterns are different. This distinction can matter in regimes where
the cost of moving parameters is comparable to, or larger than, the cost of
performing arithmetic with parameters that are already resident on the
accelerator. A per-layer schedule repeatedly uses the same weights in
consecutive operations, potentially allowing more computation to be performed
while those weights remain locally available. Stack looping instead revisits a
layer only after the intervening layers have been executed. We do not assume
that one design is universally faster; the answer depends on the hardware,
batch size, and whether execution is compute- or memory-bound, but the two
designs expose different opportunities for parameter reuse at the systems
level even when their nominal FLOP counts are matched. The distinction between attention and MLP looping is similarly motivated by
the fact that Transformer components need not have comparable costs. In a
standard dense Transformer, repeating attention spends additional computation
on token-to-token interaction, whereas repeating the MLP spends it on
position-wise feature transformation. In other model families, however, the
systems consequences can be much larger. Consider a mixture-of-experts (MoE)
Transformer in which the MLP is replaced by routed experts distributed across
different accelerators or nodes. Repeating the MLP may then require not only
additional matrix multiplications, but also repeated token routing,
all-to-all communication, and expert-weight access. Attention-only looping
would increase effective computational depth without repeatedly incurring
those expert-related costs. Conversely, for very long sequences, attention
itself can become an increasingly expensive part of the model because its
compute and memory traffic depend on sequence length, making additional MLP
computation comparatively attractive. These examples are not claims about our
dense experiments as we do not evaluate MoE models here, but they illustrate
why deciding whether to loop attention, the MLP, or the complete block can
become an important systems choice rather than a cosmetic architectural
ablation. Finally, reuse depth determines how aggressively the model makes this
parameter–compute trade. Increasing the number of loops allows the same
parameters to support progressively greater effective depth, which is the
central appeal of looping. At the same time, every additional application
must still be executed. Training FLOPs therefore increase with loop count, and
under conventional looping the loops are also executed sequentially, leading to slower autoregressive generation during inference.
A model can consequently become more parameter-efficient while becoming less
attractive from the standpoint of training compute or autoregressive latency.
This tension becomes particularly important at large loop factors: the
question is not simply whether more loops continue to improve loss, but
whether their marginal improvement justifies the additional computation and
sequential depth. 
 
 
 Taken together, these examples show why there is no single notion of the
“best” looping architecture independent of the resource regime. Full-stack
looping may be preferable when parameters are expensive and additional FLOPs
are available; middle looping may be preferable when compute must be allocated
more selectively; Per-Layer Looping changes the pattern with which shared
weights are reused by the hardware; and attention- versus MLP-level looping
can become important when the two components have different computational or
communication costs. The architectural choices introduced above therefore
correspond to different ways of allocating a fixed parameter budget across
computation, memory movement, communication, and sequential depth. 
 
 
 
 Our architectural ablations. 

 
 Motivated by these trade-offs, we systematically vary loop placement, computation order, sublayer choice, and reuse depth across model scales and training budgets. We compare these constructions both at matched data and as a function of executed FLOPs, since the two views answer different questions: the former measures how much quality can be extracted from a fixed parameter budget when additional computation is available, while the latter measures how effectively each construction uses a constrained compute budget. Individual points in this design space have precedents. Prior work repeats complete Transformer stacks  ( Saunshi et al., 2025 ) , while other approaches retain distinct outer layers and apply looping to a middle stack  ( Zeitoun et al., 2026 ;  Prairie et al., 2026 ) . We therefore do not treat any individual looping primitive as the contribution of this work. Rather, our goal is to compare these choices within a common dense, from-scratch setting and determine how their relative behavior changes with model scale, training budget, loop depth, and the resource under which they are compared. 
 
 
 
 Sequential inference. 

 
 The discussion above concerns  how much  repeated computation should be performed and  where  that computation should be allocated. It leaves open a separate issue that becomes especially important at inference time: in conventional looping, the additional effective depth is realized through a sequence of dependent computations. Since      𝑯   (  ℓ  )    =    ℱ  θ   ​   (   𝑯   (   ℓ  −  1   )    )     \bm{H}^{(\ell)}=\mathcal{F}_{\theta}\!\left(\bm{H}^{(\ell-1)}\right)   , loop    ℓ  \ell    cannot be evaluated before loop     ℓ  −  1   \ell-1    has completed. Increasing the loop factor therefore increases not only executed computation, but also the amount of sequential computation on the inference critical path. This creates a tension that is not captured by training FLOPs alone. A looping construction may be attractive because it achieves better quality for a fixed parameter budget, or even because it provides a favorable quality–FLOP trade-off, yet still be unattractive for autoregressive decoding if obtaining that gain requires proportionally more sequential model evaluations for every generated token. In other words, reducing the  amount  of repeated computation, for example by looping only a middle region, does not resolve the fact that the remaining loop iterations are still ordered sequentially. Parameter efficiency, compute efficiency, and inference latency are therefore distinct objectives. This observation motivates the next question we study: whether the benefits of repeated computation can be retained while relaxing the serial dependency imposed by conventional looping. 
 
 
 
 
  B.2  Low-Rank Adaptation and Relaxed Weight Sharing 

 
 A looped Transformer repeats the same layer, or group of layers,    L  L    times.
Normally, every loop uses the same attention and MLP weights. Sharing the
weights in this way keeps the model small, since adding loops does not require
storing new Transformer layers. However, the loops do not all receive the same
kind of input. The first loop processes the initial representation, while later
loops process representations that have already passed through the shared
layers one or more times. It may therefore be useful for different loops to
learn slightly different transformations. 
 
 
 One option would be to give every loop its own attention and MLP weights. This
would provide complete specialization, but it would also make the loops
equivalent to separately parameterized Transformer layers. The number of
stored parameters would then grow with the number of loops, removing much of
the motivation for weight reuse. We instead use Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)
 ( Hu et al., 2021 )  to place a small loop-specific correction around a larger
shared weight matrix. 
 
    
 
 
 For one adapted weight matrix, using the same weights in every loop requires
     d  in   ​   d  out    d_{\mathrm{in}}d_{\mathrm{out}}    parameters. Loop-specific LoRA requires
      d  in   ​   d  out    +   L  ​  r  ​   (    d  in   +   d  out    )     d_{\mathrm{in}}d_{\mathrm{out}}+Lr(d_{\mathrm{in}}+d_{\mathrm{out}})    parameters, while giving every loop
a different weight matrix requires
    L  ​   d  in   ​   d  out    Ld_{\mathrm{in}}d_{\mathrm{out}}    parameters. Loop-specific LoRA therefore
lies between these two choices: most parameters remain shared, but each loop
has a small amount of capacity with which to specialize. 
 
 
 Prior work explores a similar middle ground in Relaxed Recursive Transformers
(RRTs)  ( Bae et al., 2025 ) . RRT begins with a pretrained Transformer whose
layers have different weights and converts it into a smaller looped model by
replacing groups of those layers with repeated uses of shared weights. Because
this conversion removes differences among the original layers, RRT gives each
loop a low-rank adapter initialized from a truncated SVD of the difference
between the original weight and its shared replacement. The converted model is
then trained further. Our setting differs because we do not begin with a
larger pretrained model or attempt to preserve its layer-specific weights.
Instead, the Transformer is looped from the beginning, and the shared weights
and loop-specific adapters are trained jointly from initialization. We use this
setting to ask whether loop-specific specialization is useful during looped
pretraining itself and whether its value increases as the same weights are
reused across more loops.
